# Amulet Atlas — every record, flattened

## Agadez cross (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tuareg-cross/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tuareg-cross.json
id: tuareg-cross
native: ⵜⴰⵏⴰⵖⵉⵍⵜ (Tifinagh)
aliases: Croix d'Agadez · Agadès cross · Cross of Niger · tanaghilt · talhakim · zakkat · kaulé
said: tanaghilt (tanaɣilt), or tasagalt — 'cast in a mould'; the plate-shaped kind is talhakim
when: 1900 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NE
root: Tamashek tanaghilt / tasagalt, 'cast in a mould' — the name is a description of the method, not of a shape. Talhakim covers jewellery resembling a plate or a plate shield. Zakkat is the general Tamashek word for pendants; kaulé is widespread across the Sahel.
object: form=pendant materials=silver,copper worn=neck,head
against: travel — said by the father in Dieterlen and Ligers's account, handing it to a son at the age of nomadism [s:wp-agadez-cross]
against: poverty — said by users who describe it as a reserve of wealth [s:wp-agadez-cross]
against: bad-luck — said by users who attribute to it the function of a grigri, the source's word [s:wp-agadez-cross]
what: A cast pendant, usually silver, with a ring or loop at the top and a flared, spreading body below — sometimes a cross, more often a shape between a cross and a shield. Blacksmiths cast it by the lost-wax process and never hammer the metal. The plate-shaped kind, talhakim, is cut from soft stone or from platelets of copper, aluminium or another metal; the tanaghilt is made in stone or copper.
story: This is the best-known category of Saharan Berber jewellery, made especially by the Tuareg of Niger — and its use is narrower than its fame. Current use of tanaghilt and talhakim is restricted to a few Tuareg groups, the Kel Aïr and the Kel Geress, and to non-Berber peoples across Niger who have taken it up: Songhai, Zarma, Fulani, Hausa. Other Tuareg barely use them. Worn as ornaments, the pieces hang at the neck; a tanaghilt is also fixed to a woman's veil or to her forehead, and fixed upside down.

Ask the people wearing them what the shape means and the answers go vague. The source says so flatly: any question about their symbolism put to the users generally elicits only vague answers. Some name it a grigri; some call it a reserve of wealth.

The ethnologists Germaine Dieterlen and Ziedonis Ligers recorded one occasion that does give the object a sentence of its own. A father handed the jewel to his son at the age of virility, marriage and nomadism, and said: "My son, I give you the four directions of the world, because we do not know where you will go to die."

A Tuareg elder's narration gives another origin. A young nomad wanted to declare his love to a girl shut up at home and out of reach. The village blacksmith had an important place in Tuareg society and the right to enter the houses of all the families he traded with, so the young man had a jewel forged that combined the two syllables of the Tamashek word tara, love, written ⵜⵔ in Tifinagh, and sent the blacksmith in with it.

*Tradition holds —* the image may go back to ancient stylised images of the Carthaginian goddess Tanit. The source offers that as a possibility and this atlas leaves it there.
how: Cast by a blacksmith in silver by the lost-wax process — a wax model, a mould, the wax melted out, the metal poured in — and never hammered. The stone and platelet kinds are cut. Worn at the neck, or fixed to a woman's veil or forehead, upside down.
today: Made and worn, and also the standard thing a visitor to Niger brings home. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for the split between the two, and no source that says Tuareg smiths object to either.
kin: gris-gris — the word some wearers reach for when asked what this is — a Mande word travelling north across the Sahel with the object it names
kin: silver — the metal the smiths cast it in, and never hammer
kin: cross — the sign in the European name, which most of these pieces do not actually make
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition of the region it is worn in, though nothing in the sources read here puts writing inside this object
kin: marrakesh-souk — the northern market where Saharan silver of this kind reaches buyers
kin: hirz-pouch — the other silver charm in this batch, and the contrast: that one is a container for a text, this one is solid
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on what a visitor buys and what a wearer wears
sources: s:wp-agadez-cross s:wp-silver s:wp-gris-gris-talisman
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Agnus Dei (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/agnus-dei/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/agnus-dei.json
id: agnus-dei
native: Agnus Dei (Latin)
aliases: Agnus Dei wax · wax lamb · Agnus Dei disc · pascal wax medallion
said: AHN-yoos DAY-ee, 'Lamb of God'
when: 800 CE to now
countries: IT ES GB
root: Latin Agnus Dei, 'Lamb of God' — from John 1:29, where John the Baptist says of Jesus, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
object: form=medal worn=neck,chest
against: fire — said by Herbert Thurston, reporting the claims made for the object in the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1907 [s:web-cathen-agnus-dei]
against: drowning — said by the same 1907 account, which names storm and flood among the perils [s:web-cathen-agnus-dei]
against: fever — said by the same account, which names pestilence [s:web-cathen-agnus-dei]
against: childbirth — said by the same account, which names the dangers to which women are exposed in childbirth [s:web-cathen-agnus-dei]
what: A disc of wax, round or oval, with a lamb pressed into one face. The lamb carries a cross or a flag; the reverse usually takes a saint, or the name and arms of the reigning pope. The wax is made from what is left of the previous year's paschal candle. It hangs at the neck, or it is kept somewhere safe and looked at.
story: The oldest sacramental in the Roman Church is a lump of recycled candle.

Herbert Thurston, writing the Catholic Encyclopedia entry in 1907, puts the ninth-century practice like this: the archdeacon made the Agnus Deis early on Holy Saturday morning out of clean wax mixed with chrism, and handed them out to the people on the Saturday following. What changed later is who does the blessing. The great consecration of Agnus Deis takes place only in the first year of a pontificate and every seventh year after it — a rule Thurston says was still followed in 1907 — and it is the pope who performs it. That schedule is the whole economics of the object: a papal Agnus Dei is scarce by design.

The claims Thurston records are stated plainly and stated wide: protection "from all malign influences", and specifically "perils from storm and pestilence, from fire and flood, and also of the dangers to which women are exposed in childbirth". He also records the reported results rather than asserting them: "Fires are said to have been extinguished, and floods stayed." That is the exact grammar this atlas uses, arrived at independently and a century earlier.

The Agnus Dei is also where the Roman habit of blessing an object and attaching indulgences to it got started, or at least where the Catholic Encyclopedia says it got started. Writing on devotional medals, the same encyclopedia dates the sixteenth-century practice of giving a papal blessing to medals — and then enriching them with indulgences — to a usage "long previously in vogue in the case of Agnus Dei (discs of wax impressed with the figure of a lamb and blessed at stated seasons by the Pope, which could be worn suspended round the neck)". *Inference —* every struck medal later in this batch descends from this wax disc, procedurally if not physically.

The Church's line between a sacramental and an amulet runs straight through it. A sacramental, by the Catholic Church's own definition, is a sacred sign that works by the Church's prayer and "does not confer the grace of the Holy Spirit in the way that the sacraments do"; it disposes a person to receive grace rather than acting on its own. Set that beside a wax disc credited with stopping a flood and the tension is not hypothetical. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy names the boundary in general terms: popular piety "may never incorporate rites permeated by magic, superstition, animism, vendettas or sexual connotations", and elsewhere it warns against keeping blessed palms as amulets or for therapeutic or magical purposes. Both positions are the Church's. This atlas prints both and settles neither.
how: Cast from the remains of the previous year's paschal candle, mixed with chrism, impressed with the lamb, and blessed by the pope in the first year of his pontificate and every seventh year after. Distributed by the pontiff, often through envoys, and usually in a case or a cloth mount when worn. It is not renewed on a cycle and it is not burnt at retirement; it is kept.
today: This project has read nothing dated later than the 1907 encyclopedia entry on whether the seven-year consecration still happens, and it will not guess. Old Agnus Deis survive in Catholic households, in reliquary frames, and in museum and papal-artefact collections. That is what can be said: the object exists, its present manufacture is unverified here, and a reader who needs to know should ask a diocese.
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the category, and the object the Catholic Encyclopedia treats as its oldest member
kin: miraculous-medal — the struck descendant — the practice of blessing a medal and attaching an indulgence to it is traced back to this wax
kin: st-christopher-medal — the other neck-worn Roman sacramental, in metal and in quantity
kin: brown-scapular — the cloth sacramental worn on the same chest, with a promise attached instead of a papal blessing
kin: ladanka — the Orthodox pouch that does the same job — a blessed thing worn at the neck, with the same argument attached about what it is
kin: cross — the sign the lamb carries
kin: consecration — the act that makes it — a papal blessing on a seven-year cycle, which is the scarcest consecration schedule in this atlas
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read where the Church's word sacramental meets the reader's word amulet, on an object credited with stopping floods
sources: s:web-cathen-agnus-dei s:wp-agnus-dei s:wp-devotional-medal s:wp-sacramental s:web-vatican-directory-popular-piety
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## Akua'ba (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/akuaba-figure/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/akuaba-figure.json
id: akuaba-figure
aliases: akuaba · akwaba · akuba · Akan fertility doll
said: a-KWA-ba
when: 1800 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GH CI
object: form=figurine materials=wood
against: infertility — said by young Akan women, who the source says use them 'traditionally by young women seeking to conceive a child' [s:wp-akuaba]
against: bad-luck — said by enslaved Africans in the Americas, who used them as good-luck charms and as a link to home; and present-day users, for whom the form has become a broader sign of good luck [s:wp-akuaba]
what: A small wooden figure with a large flat disc for a head, a ringed neck and a short body, usually with arms out to the sides. The head is the whole signature: a smooth circle or oval, set on a cylinder, with the features low on the face.
story: Akua'ba come from western Ghana and nearby, and are particularly associated with the Fanti, part of the Akan group of peoples in Ghana and Ivory Coast. Young women seeking to conceive carry them, and carry them also so that the children they have will be good-looking.

When the figure is not in use it is not put away: it is ritually washed and cared for in the homestead, which is why writers describing the practice reach for the phrase sympathetic magic — the doll is treated the way the wanted child would be.

Other peoples in the region carve their own. The Kru and the Igbo have distinctive styles of fertility figure, used in similar ways.

The form crossed the Atlantic. Akua'ba were taken to the Americas by enslaved Africans, where they stood for a connection to home and were used as good-luck charms.

*Inference —* the collecting came early and it came in volume. Europeans visiting Africa in the 1800s were highly interested in Fante dolls, and that interest is why the figure is in so many European museums; what a museum case holds here, as with the Kongo material, is a record of nineteenth-century European taste as much as of Akan practice.
how: Carved in wood. Washed and cared for in the homestead when not being carried. The sources read here name no maker's restriction and no consecration rite, and this record does not supply one from a neighbouring tradition.
today: Both things at once, and the tradition's own account says so. Akua'ba are now more commonly seen as mass-produced works of art or souvenirs than as heirlooms in ritual use — and traditional use continues in some areas among the Fante and other Akan peoples. The shape has also become a general sign of good luck, detached from conception.
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the wider practice it sits inside, though its makers are Akan carvers rather than marabouts or diviners
kin: nkisi — the other African wooden figure in this atlas, and a useful contrast: this one is carried and washed, that one is charged and nailed
kin: taweret-amulet — the Nile's charm for the same wish, four thousand years earlier and made as a hippopotamus
kin: tree — the sign behind the material — a figure cut from a living thing and then washed and kept like one
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read it belongs to — a charm carried before the child exists
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on souvenir against heirloom, which the tradition's own account of akua'ba states plainly
sources: s:wp-akuaba s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum s:wp-cultural-appropriation
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ankh amulet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ankh-amulet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ankh-amulet.json
id: ankh-amulet
native: 𓋹 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: ankh · key of life · crux ansata · handled cross
said: ANK, a modern guess at the Egyptian ꜥnḫ
when: 2700 BCE – 2 BCE
countries: EG SD SY LB IL PS TR GR
root: Egyptian ꜥnḫ, three consonants that spell 'live', 'life', and also 'mirror', 'floral bouquet' and 'oath' — Egyptian oaths opened with a form of the word 'live'. The Coptic stage of the language gives ⲱⲛϩ, ōnh.
object: form=pendant materials=gold,silver,faience worn=neck,grave
against: illness — said by Egyptian amulet practice as summarised in the source, which says amulets cut as hieroglyphs 'were meant to impart to the wearer the qualities represented by the sign' — and this sign's quality is life [s:wp-ankh]
against: the-dead — said by Egyptians who placed them in tombs, the source says, 'to ensure the well-being of the deceased in the afterlife' [s:wp-ankh]
what: A T with a loop on top, the loop shaped like a droplet. As an amulet it is small and strung at the neck; the earliest ones are gold or electrum, the alloy of gold and silver, and later ones are mostly faience — quartz paste glazed blue or green in the kiln. Painted versions in tomb and temple art are blue or black. The Coptic variant, the crux ansata, swaps the droplet for a circle.
story: The ankh is everywhere in Egyptian art and rare as an amulet, and the gap is the interesting part. Amulets cut in the shape of a hieroglyph were meant to hand the wearer whatever the sign meant, and this sign meant life itself; yet ankh-shaped amulets first appear only late in the Old Kingdom, around 2700 to 2200 BCE, and stay uncommon right through to the late first millennium BCE. The composite amulet — ankh, was and djed run together, 'life, dominion and stability' — was more widespread than the ankh on its own.

On walls the sign is a thing gods hold. They carry it by the loop, they hold it up to the king's nose as the breath of life, and in scenes of purification the zigzag lines that usually mean water are replaced by chains of ankhs poured over the king's head. Before the end of the Middle Kingdom almost nobody but the pharaoh is shown receiving one. Because the same three consonants spelled 'mirror' and 'floral bouquet', mirrors, mirror cases and bouquets were made in the sign's shape.

It travelled. Syria and Canaan took it up in the Middle Bronze Age, about 1950 to 1500 BCE, and of all the Egyptian hieroglyphs they borrowed it was by far the most common. Anatolian hieroglyphs absorbed it for the word 'life'. Minoan artists on Crete combined it, or the related tyet, with the double axe. Meroitic Nubia used it heavily in temples, in funerary art and on pottery. A clay seal of King Hezekiah of Judah, about 700 BCE, found in Jerusalem in 2015, carries ankhs on either side of a winged sun.

Then Christianity kept it. When Christians were pulling down the Serapeum in Alexandria in 391 CE, according to Socrates of Constantinople, cross-like signs turned up cut into the stone blocks; the pagans present said the sign meant 'life to come' and the Christians said the sign was theirs. Egyptian Coptic Christians used the crux ansata in many media, especially on textiles. There is little evidence for it in the western half of the Roman Empire.
how: Cut from gold or electrum in the earliest examples, moulded in faience later — that ceramic is usually blue or green, and the colour is read as life and regeneration, which may be why it took over. Pierced and strung, or built into the composite ankh-was-djed amulet. On a wall it is painted blue or black.
today: Worn worldwide. The sign came back through the counterculture of the 1960s and its interest in ancient religions, and it is now a standard design for jewellery and tattoos. People of African descent in the United States and Europe wear it as a sign of African cultural identity; Kemetism, a group of movements built on the religion of ancient Egypt, uses it as its symbol; the goth subculture adopted it, tied to vampires, after an ankh pendant featured in the 1983 film The Hunger. In the twenty-first century it is the most widely recognised symbol of Egyptian, and more broadly of African, origin in the Western world. Unicode encodes it twice: U+2625 ☥ and U+132F9 𓋹.
kin: tyet-knot — the sign it may share an origin with — Schäfer and Fischer read both as knots of cloth, and early ankhs show the lower bar as two loose ends
kin: djed-pillar — the third of the run 'life, dominion and stability'; the composite amulet joining them was commoner than the ankh alone
kin: wedjat-eye — made in the same workshops and strung on the same cords, and far more often — the eye is what Egypt actually wore
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the sign's Christian afterlife in Egypt: the crux ansata is an ankh with a round loop, and the cross Copts carry is the same faith in a different mark
kin: cross — the sign it is most often mistaken for, and the sign it fed
kin: knot — the family most Egyptologists put its origin in
kin: faience — the material that made it cheap, and whose blue-green the source ties to life and regeneration
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that cut it and the one that mostly preferred other shapes
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this sign lands in — worn now by Kemetists, by goths and by people with no line to Egypt at all
sources: s:wp-ankh s:wp-tyet s:wp-djed s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-coptic-cross s:wp-british-museum s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Anting-anting (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/anting-anting/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/anting-anting.json
id: anting-anting
native: anting-anting (Latin)
aliases: agimat · anting · virtud · galing · gayuma · mutya · orasyon
said: AN-ting AN-ting
when: 1565 CE to now (still carried)
countries: PH
root: Tagalog anting-anting, from Javanese anting-anting, 'ear-hanging ornament'; the wider family includes Indonesian and Malay gantung, 'hanging'. Agimat is the other Filipino word for the same thing, with virtud (virtue) and galing (prowess) as general terms
object: form=medal materials=copper,brass,gold,paper,cloth,wood worn=neck,sewn-in,swallowed,pocket
against: weapons — said by Filipino fighters against Spain and the United States; Macario Sakay wore a vest of religious images and Latin phrases against bullets, and the subtypes kabal and tagaliwas are named for cuts and for turning a bullet aside [s:wp-agimat]
against: curse — said by the Philippine occult tradition, in which the most frequent kind of agimat removes hexes [s:wp-agimat]
against: spirits — said by the same tradition: the other frequent kind drives out evil spirits [s:wp-agimat]
against: attraction — said by owners of a gayuma, the love charm that makes its owner more attractive [s:wp-agimat]
against: bad-luck — said by Trinidad Pardo de Tavera, who defined it as an amulet of supernatural power that saves lives [s:wp-agimat]
what: Most often a flat pendant on a necklace — round, triangular or cross-shaped, in gold-coloured metal, its face crowded with figures and Latin words. But the class is wider than the pendant. An anting-anting can be a stone said to have come out of the sky, or a fulgurite fang left where lightning struck, pangil ng kidlat, or a mutya, a drop of liquid taken from the heart of a banana tree at midnight, which is swallowed rather than worn. It can be a garment with words written on it. It usually comes with a small book of incantations, orasyon, which has to be read on Good Friday or another set date for the thing to work at full strength.
story: The Philippine occult tradition matches an agimat to a department of life. The commonest kinds remove hexes and drive out spirits. A gayuma is the love charm, which makes its owner more attractive. Most of the amulets carry Latin inscriptions, and most of the dealers set up near a church — in the courtyard or in the market beside it — of which the Quiapo district in Manila is the example everyone names.

The written record starts with the colonisers. The earliest reports of anting-anting come from Spanish priests in the early colonial period, which in the Philippines begins with Miguel López de Legazpi's settlement of 1565. Trinidad Pardo de Tavera defined the thing in Spanish: amuleto que salva la vida, da poder sobre natural — an amulet of supernatural power that saves lives. As Christianity took hold, the anting-anting took on the new religion's forms, and later took in the esoteric symbols of Freemasonry as well. An Islamic version exists in the southern Muslim islands.

The charm has a political history, which is unusual in this atlas. Filipino fighters wore anting-anting against the Spanish and then against the Americans. Macario Sakay wore a vest carrying religious images and Latin phrases, to stop bullets. Ferdinand Marcos claimed that Gregorio Aglipay had given him an anting-anting — a sliver of wood inserted into his back before the Bataan campaign in 1942 — that could make him invisible. Whose claim that was, and what it was for, is left standing here as his.

The subtypes are named by what they do. Kabal, also kunat, makes the skin proof against cuts and sword slashes. Pamako nails an entity in place so it cannot move. Tagabulag turns the wearer invisible to an enemy, or blinds them. Tagaliwas turns a bullet aside.

Filipino cinema took all of it and went further: on screen the wearer gains strength, invisibility, healing, flight, telekinesis, the power to stop a bullet in the air. Ramon Revilla Sr., playing Nardong Putik, carried one that made him invulnerable. The 1939 film The Real Glory shows Moro characters saying theirs will stop bullets and knives. Screen and street are not the same object and this record keeps them apart.
how: Cast or cut, then charged by reading: the orasyon that comes with the amulet has to be recited on Good Friday, or on another appointed date, for the piece to reach full power. Other routes to getting one are described and are not gentle — taking the liquid drained from an exhumed body, or setting out food and drink for the spirits in a cemetery at midnight on Holy Wednesday or Holy Thursday. A mutya is swallowed. Bought at a stall by a church, most often.
today: Still sold from stalls around Quiapo Church in Manila and at markets beside other churches, as of the accounts this project has read. Quiapo is a major Catholic shrine, which is the point: the trade stands in the churchyard rather than away from it.
kin: quiapo-church — the Manila church whose courtyard and surrounding market are where these are bought
kin: jimat — the Malay and Indonesian class the word comes from — Javanese anting-anting, the ear-hung ornament
kin: keris-pusaka — the other charm of the islands carried into a fight, and still forged in the Muslim-inhabited south of the Philippines
kin: st-christopher-medal — the Catholic medal this most resembles on a tray, and does not behave like: an anting-anting takes its charge from an orasyon read on Good Friday
kin: talismanic-shirt — Sakay's vest belongs with these — a written garment worn against shot
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the nearest tradition in this atlas: church forms taken up and worked by people outside the clergy, in another Spanish colony
kin: divine-name — the sign on most of them — Latin words and holy names carried as the working part
kin: buying-in-a-market — how one is got: from a stall in a churchyard, with the book of incantations thrown in
kin: washing-off-ink — the nearest practice in this atlas to swallowing a mutya — a charm taken into the body rather than hung on it
sources: s:wp-agimat s:wp-quiapo-church s:web-wp-spanish-east-indies s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Azabache (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/azabache/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/azabache.json
id: azabache
native: azabache (Latin)
aliases: mano de azabache · higa · figa · black hand · jet fist
said: ah-sah-BAH-cheh, Spanish for jet
when: 1400 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ES PR CU DO US
root: Spanish azabache, from Arabic sabaj, the black stone — the amulet is named for its material, jet, and not for its shape
object: form=pendant materials=jet worn=neck,wrist,cradle,sewn-in
against: evil-eye — said by parents in Hispanic families, as surveyed by Edward Tabor [s:web-hektoen-azabache]
against: child-harm — said by Tabor's respondents, who name sudden infant death first [s:web-hektoen-azabache]
against: illness — said by Tabor's respondents [s:web-hektoen-azabache]
what: A piece of jet — fossil wood, black, warm to the touch, light in the hand — cut either as a small clenched fist with the thumb pushed between the first two fingers, or as a faceted black bead. Edward Tabor, writing in Hektoen International in 2023, measures the fist at about 8 mm long and the polyhedron at 3 to 4 mm across, each with a small red bead at the end of the chain. It is pinned to a baby's clothing or worn on a bracelet.
story: Jet has been cut for amulets since the Neolithic, and in Spain the trade had a centre: the deposits are in Asturias, but by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects and amulets was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino. The Asturian version handed to small children was, and is, a higa — the jet fist.

Tabor's account follows the object across the Atlantic. He traces the form to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among "the Moors of Barbary", into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492, and then into the Spanish Caribbean colonies. Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican families put one on an infant within days of birth, and Tabor found that the practice continues into adulthood.

What parents told Tabor it is for is specific: the evil eye, and with it diarrhoea, respiratory infections, deformities, and above all sudden infant death. He reports that 29% of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71% the polyhedron. He gives a price: US$3 to US$10 in a botánica, a folk-medicine shop, and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote in 2023.

*Inference —* the red bead is worth noting. Red thread and red beads run with black stone across the whole Mediterranean, and the pairing here is the same pairing Naples makes with coral. This project files that as a family resemblance and not as a descent.
how: Cut and polished from jet, which is soft enough — Mohs 2.5 to 4 — to work with hand tools but chips if the carver pushes detail. Strung with a red bead, then pinned to the baby's shirt or fastened as a bracelet. It is given, usually by a grandmother or godparent, not bought by the wearer. Nothing in the sources read here describes a blessing; the giving is the act.
today: Sold in botánicas and online across the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, Spain and the United States. Tabor's 2023 figures — US$3 to US$10 in a shop, US$9 to US$55 online — are the last dated prices this project has read. Much of what is sold now is moulded black resin rather than cut jet; jet takes a brown streak on unglazed porcelain and burns like coal, which is how a buyer tells.
kin: figa — the gesture this fist is a frozen copy of, and the reason it is also called a higa
kin: jet — the material the amulet is named after — azabache is simply the Spanish for it
kin: fist — the sign, filed in this atlas with the eye and the horn as things that catch a glance
kin: ojo-de-venado — the other charm put on a Latin American newborn against mal de ojo, in seed rather than stone
kin: cornicello — the Neapolitan answer: red coral instead of black jet, a horn instead of a fist
kin: red-string — the red bead on the end of the chain, which runs with black stone right across the Mediterranean

## Bagua mirror (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/bagua-mirror/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/bagua-mirror.json
id: bagua-mirror
native: 八卦鏡 (Han)
aliases: Pa Kua mirror · eight trigram mirror · feng shui mirror
said: bā guà jìng
when: undated (still carried)
countries: CN HK TW
root: Chinese 八卦 bāguà, 'eight trigrams', + 鏡 jìng, 'mirror'
object: form=mirror materials=glass,brass,copper,wood,plastic worn=door,wall,shop,roof
against: house — said by feng shui practice, in which sharp building corners and a road running at a house are sources of poison-arrows the mirror is hung to deflect [s:wp-bagua]
against: spirits — said by the account of the bronze mirrors this one descends from, used by Taoist masters in Mirror Techniques said to reveal or destroy evil spirits [s:wp-bagua]
against: bad-luck — said by householders who hang one to alter the feng shui conditions of a residence [s:wp-bagua]
what: An octagonal or circular plaque with the eight trigrams set around a mirror at its centre. The mirror is flat, convex or concave, and which one it is decides what the object claims to do. It is screwed or hung above a front door or a window, facing out. It resembles a luopan, the feng shui compass, but it is not an instrument — nothing is read off it.
story: The thing it answers is a direction, not a person. In feng shui, sharp corners of neighbouring buildings and an open road running at a house count as sources of poison-arrows — Sha Qi, 煞氣 — and a bagua mirror is hung to deal with the arrow rather than the archer. A flat mirror is held to reflect it, a convex one to disperse it, a concave one to converge or absorb it, and so to alter the feng shui of the residence.

Modern bagua mirrors are described as evolved from ancient bronze-cast versions used by Taoist masters to perform Mirror Techniques, 鏡術, said to reveal or destroy evil spirits, or even to overcome natural calamities. The household version is the cheap end of that: an inexpensive, often self-administered quick fix to a specific feng shui concern.

Which is exactly where the trouble is. Whatever the mirror sends back goes in the direction the mirror faces, so pointing one at a neighbour's home is generally considered offensive and is a feng shui taboo — and the do-it-yourself nature of the object makes it easy to misuse for a private vendetta. Conflicts caused by offensive installations are well known in dense Chinese communities such as Hong Kong, and feng shui mirror feuds have been parodied in popular culture. *Inference —* this is one of the few charms in this atlas whose recorded quarrels are between neighbours rather than between believers and sceptics; the argument is not whether it works but where it is aimed.
how: Bought ready-made and mounted by the householder, above a door or a window, facing the corner or the road that is the problem. No consecration is described in the source read, and no specialist is required — which is the difference between this and the bronze mirrors of the Taoist masters it is said to descend from.
today: Sold in hardware shops, feng shui shops and online across the Chinese-speaking world as of 2026, in plastic and wood as often as in metal. A mirror over a doorway is also read by neighbours, which is why some cities treat their appearance as news.
kin: mirror-sign — the sign family it belongs to: a surface that sends a thing back where it came from
kin: toli-mirror — the steppe cousin — a metal mirror worn on a shaman's body as armour, where this one is bolted to a building
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition behind the Taoist mirror techniques it is said to descend from
kin: charm-coin — the pocket-sized carrier of the same eight trigrams, cast in bronze
kin: fu-talisman — the written remedy at the same doorway, where this is the optical one
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice: a charm fixed to a building, aimed outward, guarding a threshold and not a body
kin: hex-sign — Pennsylvania's painted answer on the same part of a building, argued over in the same way
kin: nazar — the other thing hung facing out over a door, which answers a look rather than a corner
kin: ping-an-fu — the portable Taiwanese charm for the same household, renewed yearly while this stays up
sources: s:wp-bagua s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-fulu

## Bes amulet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/bes-amulet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/bes-amulet.json
id: bes-amulet
native: Ⲃⲏⲥ (Coptic)
aliases: Bes · Bisu · Beset (the feminine counterpart)
said: BESS; Arabic ويصا, Wīssa
when: 2055 BCE – 999 CE
countries: EG SD SY ES CY IR GR
root: Uncertain. 'Bes' means 'cat' in Nubian, which fits a god regularly drawn with feline features; the name may instead come from the hieroglyphs bs 'flame' or bz 'to be initiated, to introduce', the latter possibly pointing at masks used in his cult.
object: form=figurine materials=faience,terracotta,gold,skin worn=neck,door,cradle,skin,hearth
against: child-harm — said by Egyptian household practice, as summarised in the source: Bes watched after children, and his face was moulded onto faience baby bottles found at el-Lisht [s:wp-bes]
against: childbirth — said by Egyptian household practice — Bes aided women in labour by fighting off evil spirits, and was present with Taweret at births [s:wp-bes]
against: snakebite — said by the source, which lists killing snakes first among his tasks [s:wp-bes]
against: demons — said by Egyptian householders, who kept his image indoors; the source says he scared demons away from houses, so his statue was put up as a protector [s:wp-bes]
against: infertility — said by Egyptologists, reading the Ptolemaic Bes chambers at Saqqara as built for curing fertility problems or for general healing [s:wp-bes]
what: A squat bearded figure with a lion's face, a feathered crown, a protruding tongue and bandy legs, shown full-face when every other Egyptian god is shown in profile. He is ithyphallic, sometimes in a soldier's tunic, sometimes brandishing a knife. He comes as an amulet, as a mask, moulded onto faience baby bottles, cut into the legs of furniture and headrests, painted on storage jars, and inked into skin.
story: Bes faces you. That is the whole design argument: Egyptian gods are drawn in profile, and Bes is drawn head-on, dressed for a fight, so that anything approaching the house meets him looking straight at it.

He is a household god, not a temple one. What he is for is specific and domestic — killing snakes, driving off evil spirits, watching children, and standing with Taweret at a birth to fight off what comes for women in labour. Because he drove off harm he also came to stand for the good things: music, dance, sexual pleasure.

His origin is southern. People in Upper Egypt venerated him long before Lower Egypt did, his sub-Saharan features and his feathered crown point at Kush or the C-Group, and Donald Mackenzie in 1907 called him a Middle Kingdom import from Nubia whose cult only spread from the start of the New Kingdom. That story has since been complicated: thirteen Bes-like figurines were found at Tell el-Farkha in deposits from the predynastic Naqada period.

He travelled further than most. His image reaches Syria in the north and the Balearic Islands in the west, then the Roman and Achaemenid empires. From the end of the sixth century BCE Bes spreads across the Achaemenid empire while Egypt is part of it; he turns up at Susa and as far as central Asia, and over time gets redrawn in Persian clothes and a Persian headdress. Beset, the female form, was more popular on Minoan Crete; the male form took with the Phoenicians and the Cypriots.

He was also worn under the skin. A wall painting from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina, Nineteenth Dynasty, shows a dancing Bes tattooed on the thigh of a female musician playing her instrument; New Kingdom tattoos of Bes are recorded on the thighs of dancers, musicians and servant girls. A female mummy from Aksha in Nubia, fourth century BCE, carries a Bes on her thigh.

He lasted. In the Ptolemaic period chambers were built at Saqqara painted with Bes and Beset, which Egyptologists take to have been for curing fertility problems or for general healing. A Bes-vase of the second century BCE has been found to carry traces of Peganum harmala and of the blue water lily, Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea. The latest evidence the source names is a jug showing Bes from Tell Edfu, dated to the tenth century CE — Coptic Egypt, long after the temples closed.
how: Moulded in faience, carved, or painted on. Kept in the house rather than worn only on the body: a statue set up as a doorkeeper, a face on the jar, a face on the bed, a face on the baby's bottle. Tattooed on the thigh in the New Kingdom. Nothing in the sources read here restricts who may own one.
today: Not made as a household god. Bes turns up now as a museum object, as a character in fiction and games, and as a tattoo design. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anyone standing a Bes at a door for what the Egyptians stood him there for.
kin: taweret-amulet — the goddess he stands beside at a birth; the two are the working pair of Egyptian domestic protection
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that made him, and the part of it that stayed in the house instead of going into the tomb
kin: lion — the sign in his face; James Romano read his earliest form as a lion rearing on its hind legs
kin: phallic-sign — the other thing he is drawn with, and the same interception logic Rome put in the fascinum
kin: tattooing — the practice that put him on the thighs of New Kingdom dancers and musicians
kin: hanging-at-door — where his statue stood — the source says he was put up as a protector because he drove harm off
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read he belongs to: a god whose day job was watching somebody else's baby
kin: pazuzu-head — Mesopotamia's grimacing household figure, hung for the same reason and looking just as unpleasant on purpose
kin: faience — the material that put his face on a baby's feeding bottle
kin: gorgoneion — the Greek face-on-the-object, staring out the same way for the same reason
sources: s:wp-bes s:wp-taweret s:wp-tattoo s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-british-museum s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art

## Brigid's cross (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/brigids-cross/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/brigids-cross.json
id: brigids-cross
native: Cros Bhríde (Latin)
aliases: St Brigid's cross · Crosóg Bhríde · Bogha Bhríde · St Brigid's Bow · wheel cross
said: kross VREE-djeh
when: 1600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IE GB
root: Irish Cros Bhríde, 'Brigid's cross', for Brigid of Kildare; the variants Crosóg Bhríde, 'Brigid's little cross', and Bogha Bhríde, 'Brigid's bow'.
object: form=door-piece materials=straw,wood,thread worn=roof,wall,door,lintel
against: house — said by Irish households, who hang the cross in the rafters and over entryways to invoke the saint's blessing and protection for the year [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: livestock — said by the same custom, which puts crosses in the outhouses and stables as well as the dwelling [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: infertility — said by the practice of giving newly married couples womb crosses to hang above their door, Brigid being a patron of fertility [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: illness — said by one of the two stories attached to the cross, in which Brigid wove it to neutralise a poisoned drink handed to her by a woman of ill intent [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
what: A small cross woven from straw or rushes, defined by its material rather than its shape. The National Museum of Ireland sorts them into seven classes: diamond, single or multiple; the swastika type, with four arms or three; the wheel type; the interlaced type; plain Latin crosses made of straw or rush; bare wooden crosses in the Latin or Greek style bound with straw; and a miscellaneous class. The commonest is the diamond or lozenge: two sticks crossed to make a frame, with straw woven into a diamond at the centre, and sometimes further diamonds on each of the four arms.
story: The cross is woven on 1 February, the feast day of Brigid of Kildare and the date of Imbolc in pre-Christian Ireland, and hung from the rafters to bring the saint's blessing and protection for the rest of the year. The practice of making them is first attested in the seventeenth century.

Brigid herself left no historical record; she was born around 450 in Leinster, and almost everything about her comes from a hagiography written by the monk Cogitosus some two hundred years later. The story attached to the cross is a deathbed conversion: telling a pagan chieftain — in some versions her father — about the Crucifixion, Brigid gathered rushes from the floor and wove them into a cross, and the chieftain asked to be baptised. In another story she was handed a poisoned drink by a woman who meant her harm, and wove the cross to neutralise it.

The household version has a timetable. Families gathered rushes on 31 January. After the evening meal the head of the household supervised the rest of the family weaving, the finished crosses were left out overnight to receive Brigid's blessing, and on 1 February they went up in the main dwelling, the outhouses and the stables. Some households took the old ones down and replaced them each year; others let them accumulate between feasts. Discarded crosses were burned or buried, burial preferred, because of Brigid's associations with agriculture. The weaving was not confined to the feast: friends gave each other crosses to strengthen a bond, and newly married couples were given womb crosses to hang over the door, Brigid being a patron of fertility too. Outside Ireland, the crosses are hung in Glastonbury, on a local legend that Brigid visited the town in 488, and Irish families send them to relatives abroad or carry one when they leave.

The shape carries arguments. Some historians compare the central lozenge to the Mexican god's eye and to the Eurasian magic square. The swastika type, with its arms set at right angles off a central diamond, reads as a wheel in motion and may have originally stood for the sun; in parts of Ulster the same motion is made with three arms, which has been compared to the triskelion.

Its second life is national. After the Irish Free State gained independence in 1922 the cross became one of the motifs artists used to build a cultural identity separate from Britain's, alongside the shamrock and the harp. It went into the logo of the Irish Department of Health in the 1950s and, as of 2024, was still part of the logo of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland. It was chosen as the first station identification marker for Raidió Teilifís Éireann in 1962 — Alice Curtayne wrote that it was picked to evoke "the image of quiet, serene places in the springtime of our history, of rush-bordered rivers in a serene arcadian landscape" — survived nine redesigns, and was dropped in 1995 in favour of what the broadcaster called "a clean striking piece of modern design". Carol Coulter wrote in The Irish Times that Saint Brigid's cross had lost its place as a symbol of national identity, at least as far as the national broadcaster was concerned.
how: Gather rushes or straw on the eve of the feast, 31 January. Weave after the evening meal, the household together. Leave the crosses out overnight for the saint's blessing. Hang them on 1 February in the house, the outhouses and the stables. Take them down and replace them at the next feast, or leave them to accumulate. Retire by burning or, preferably, burying. The direction they were hung in is not recorded — but the centre is described as a lozenge rather than a square, which suggests the cross was displayed as a saltire rather than upright.
today: Still woven. The weaving declined through the twentieth century, partly because house renovations made the crosses hard to hang in the old way, and 1 February has since been declared a national holiday in Ireland. In 1942 the Irish Folklore Commission ran a questionnaire on the Feast of Saint Brigid and collected several hundred crosses; in 2022 twenty-one of them went on display at the National Museum of Ireland – Country Life in Castlebar.
kin: corn-dolly — the other straw weave of these islands: the same hands, the other end of the year, and the harvest knots of County Armagh use the same lozenge
kin: cross — the sign it is named for, made in the one material a cross is almost never made in
kin: swastika-sign — the National Museum of Ireland's own name for one of its seven classes, and a reason this object needs the long read
kin: knotting — the making: rushes gathered on the eve, woven by the household after the meal, left out overnight
kin: renewing-yearly — the rhythm — one a year on 1 February, or a rafter's worth accumulating over decades
kin: hanging-at-door — where it goes: the rafters, the entryway, the outhouse and the stable
kin: burning-retirement — one of the two disposals the custom allows; burial is the preferred one, for a saint associated with agriculture
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it sits inside, and the clearest case of a Christian saint's day carrying an older calendar date
kin: catholic-sacramentals — what it is not, formally: no priest blesses it, no indulgence attaches, and the blessing is asked of the saint overnight
kin: rowan-cross — the other cross of two crossed things bound at the centre, made for the same rafters against a differently named harm
kin: the-swastika-problem — the long read the museum's own class name requires
sources: s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-corn-dolly s:wp-cross s:wp-swastika

## Brown Scapular (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/brown-scapular/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/brown-scapular.json
id: brown-scapular
native: scapulare (Latin)
aliases: Scapular of Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Carmelite scapular · escapulario · devotional scapular
said: SKAP-yuh-ler, from Latin scapula, 'shoulder'
when: 1250 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB PT PL IT US
root: Latin scapula, 'shoulder' — the garment hangs from them
object: form=garment materials=cloth,thread,wood,paper worn=chest,neck,sewn-in
against: the-dead — said by Carmelite tradition, as reported by the National Catholic Register in 2001 — and denied, in the same breath, by the Carmelites themselves [s:web-ncregister-not-a-magic-charm]
what: Two small rectangles of brown wool, a few inches across, joined by two cloth bands. One rectangle sits on the chest, the bands run over the shoulders, the other rectangle hangs down the back. Some carry an image or a line of scripture; some are wood or laminated paper instead of cloth. It is worn under the clothes and it is meant not to show. The rule is that it must be in good repair with both bands intact, and a damaged one is replaced rather than mended.
story: Start with the full-sized version, because the small one is a quotation of it. The monastic scapular is a length of cloth hanging front and back from a monk's or nun's shoulders, and item 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict refers to it in the seventh century. It began as an apron. Over centuries it hardened into the mark of the religious life the way a stole marks a priest, and a long scapular still identifies its wearer as a member of an order.

The small one is how lay people got a share of that. Tertiaries — lay members affiliated to the mendicant orders — were not permitted the full habit, so they were given a shrunken version, and over time it shrank again to two rectangles on bands. In 1883, in Misericors Dei Filius, Leo XIII ruled that the miniature form earned the same indulgences as the medium-sized one. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists eighteen approved small scapulars with their dates: white for the Most Blessed Trinity in 1193, brown for Our Lady of Mount Carmel in 1250, black for the Seven Sorrows of Mary in 1255, and on down to white for St Dominic in 1903. The brown one is the best known of them, and by 1912 Joseph Hilgers could write in the Catholic Encyclopedia that "Like the rosary, [the Brown Scapular] has become the badge of the devout Catholic".

What carried it was a promise. Carmelite tradition holds that the Virgin appeared to Simon Stock at Cambridge in 1251 and — as the National Catholic Register puts the tradition — told him that "whoever wore the scapular would be saved from the fires of hell". A second promise, the Sabbatine privilege, held that the wearer would be released from purgatory on the first Saturday after death.

And here the object's own order is the one taking it apart. The Discalced Carmelite Friars' Catechesis on the Brown Scapular states that the Simon Stock vision "cannot be seen as historical events", that the earliest written account of it appears around the fourteenth century, roughly 150 years after the date it claims, with nothing contemporary behind it. On the Sabbatine privilege it is blunter: the 1322 vision attributed to John XXII rests on a papal bull "forged in Sicily", and in 1613 the Holy See declared the privilege unfounded. What the Order asks for instead is a list of obligations — Mass and Communion, reading and meditating on scripture, at least part of the Liturgy of the Hours — and it says why: "to wear the scapular without accepting the responsibilities attached to it would be to reduce this precious sacramental to the status of a charm or good-luck piece." Fr Robert Colaresi, of the Carmelite Spiritual Center, says the same thing shorter: "The scapular is not a magic charm of protection, an automatic guarantee of salvation or an excuse for not living a Christian life." Fr Patrick McMahon, the Carmelite provincial delegate quoted in the same 2001 report, gives the reason the Order bothered: "Many people were beginning to realize that if we clung to pious legend, instead of sound theology, there would be no future for any devotion to the scapular."

*Inference —* this atlas prints that argument at length because it is the clearest case it has of a tradition arguing with its own object in public, in writing, and losing. The scapular is still worn by the million on the strength of the promise the Order has spent decades qualifying. Both halves are the record. Neither is settled here.

The brown one keeps turning up at the hinge of things. In the reported 1917 apparitions at Fátima the Virgin appears "with a Rosary in one hand and a scapular in the other", and Sister Lúcia said she was told "The Rosary and the Scapular are inseparable". Scapular Magazine in the United States enrolled a million Americans to pray the rosary on the strength of the Fátima messages. John Paul II said he received his first Brown Scapular at ten and wore it into the papacy. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy lists it among approved practices and describes it as an external sign of a filial relationship with Mary — which is a careful sentence, and the carefulness is the point.
how: Invested, not bought. A scapular tied to a confraternity must be given by an ordained representative of that group; one tied to a devotion may be blessed by a priest and handed over. The benefits attach only while it is worn, they lapse while it is set aside, and they resume when it goes back on. If it wears out it is replaced, and the wearer is not reinvested — the Church's own reasoning being that the devotion of the wearer, not the object, is what carries the benefit. In 1911 Pius X sanctioned wearing a blessed medal in place of the brown and other scapulars.
today: Still worn under the shirt across the Catholic world in 2026, still stocked beside the Miraculous Medal and the St Christopher medal, and still sold in the metal-medal substitute Pius X allowed. The Carmelite catechesis is a click away and most wearers have not read it. No dated retail price was read for this record.
kin: miraculous-medal — the medal a 1911 ruling by Pius X allowed to be worn in place of this, and the one on the next shelf
kin: st-christopher-medal — the metal version of the same argument — a promise struck into an object that its own church spends its time qualifying
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the category it belongs to, and the word the Carmelites use when they say what it is not
kin: agnus-dei — the other Roman sacramental worn on the body, and the older one
kin: senninbari — the other cloth worn against the body with a promise sewn into it, and the other one whose makers were a thousand women
kin: wearing-hidden — the practice this object is built for — it goes under the shirt and is meant not to show
kin: cloth — the material, and the reason it wears out and gets replaced instead of inherited
kin: counting-beads — the rosary it is paired with — "The Rosary and the Scapular are inseparable", Sister Lúcia said she was told at Fátima
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read this is the sharpest case in: the Carmelites use the word charm to say what the scapular must not become
kin: sewing-in — the older habit of stitching protection into clothing, which the scapular formalised and shrank
sources: s:wp-scapular s:web-carmelite-scapular-catechesis s:web-ncregister-not-a-magic-charm s:wp-sacramental s:wp-devotional-medal s:web-vatican-directory-popular-piety

## Bujeok (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/bujeok/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/bujeok.json
id: bujeok
native: 부적 (Hangul)
aliases: pujŏk · 符籍 · Korean paper talisman
said: POO-jŏk
when: 1100 CE to now (still carried)
countries: KR
root: Korean 부적, from Sino-Korean 符籍 — fu, a tally or talismanic mark, plus a register; the same fu that stands at the head of the Chinese fulu
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,ink,cloth worn=pocket,wall
against: bad-luck — said by the mudang who make them, described as providing the bearer with good fortune [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: attraction — said by clients who take one home from a gut and put it on the wall — the rite itself is often sponsored to increase prosperity, or to mark a new venture such as the opening of a mall or an office building [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: spirits — said by Korean vernacular religion, in which mudang are the specialists called to deal with jabkwi, the wandering dead whose touch causes affliction [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
what: A paper talisman drawn by a mudang, the ritual specialist of Korean vernacular religion. The figures on it are built out of Hanja, the Korean forms of Chinese logograms, worked into shapes that are not ordinary writing. It goes one of two ways: folded into a small brocade bag and carried on the person, or pasted onto an interior wall of the client's house.
story: Bujeok descend from fulu, the Daoist talismanic script of China — the same stock that produced Japan's ofuda. Fulu are described by their own scholars as deliberately hard to read: Yang Zhaohua notes that the earliest Taoist talismans were simple and legible and that later ones became cryptic to signal their divinity, and Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls their unreadability a linguistic archaism designed so that only qualified clergy can produce them. A bujeok inherits that logic in Hanja.

Who draws one matters more than what is on it. Mudang — the majority of them women — are the specialists of Musok, and they hand these out to the people who attended a gut, the large rite that is their central work, at the end of it. Korean vernacular religion also runs ritual specialists who divine and make amulets without performing gut at all.

The practice has been under pressure for six hundred years and is still here. Under the Joseon dynasty Confucian elites taxed and prosecuted the mudang: they were one of eight outcast groups expelled from the capital, the Gyeonggukdaejeon prescribed a hundred public lashes for anyone who supported them, a mudang was beheaded in 1398, and the Jeju governor Yi Hyŏngsang purged the island's simbang in 1702, destroying 129 shrines. The ritual taxes ran until the Kabo reforms of 1895. In 1896 police arrested mudang, pulled down shrines and burnt their equipment. Suppression continued in the mid-twentieth century through Syngman Rhee's New Life Movement and Park Chung Hee's Saemaul Undong, with a surge of police action against mudang in the 1970s.

Then it turned. From the late 1970s the mudang were re-read as carriers of Korean cultural identity, several were tied to the minjung pro-democracy movement, and from the 1980s the South Korean government designated certain mudang Human Cultural Treasures. By 2009 ten regional gut styles were on the national intangible heritage register, and one of them — the Yŏngdŭng gut of Ch'ilmŏri Shrine on Jeju — went onto UNESCO's Representative List that year. Disapproval has not gone away: the anthropologist Chongho Kim's account and the survey this record draws on both record that mudang are still widely regarded in South Korea as charlatans, Christians especially.
how: Drawn by a mudang, in figures built from Hanja. Distributed to those present at the end of a gut, or made on commission. Then either sealed into a small brocade bag and kept on the body, or pasted up on the inside wall of a house. This project has read no published account of the drawing itself — what is used, in what order, with what said over it — and prints none.
today: South Korea holds over 200,000 mudang as of the survey this record draws on, and practitioners work abroad as well. Mudang have advertised on the internet since the 1990s and have been steadily visible on South Korean television since the 2010s, which has improved their standing. Paper talismans are sold in tourist and antique districts too, Insadong among them.
kin: korean-bujeok-craft — the tradition that makes it, and the six centuries of state pressure it survived
kin: fu-talisman — the Chinese Daoist ancestor — the same illegible-on-purpose script, one border north
kin: ofuda — the Japanese sibling out of the same fulu stock, printed with a shrine seal where this is drawn by hand
kin: omamori — Japan's pouch charm, which this matches move for move: a paper inside a small brocade bag, carried and not opened
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the craft the script comes from, where the unreadability is the point
kin: dolhareubang — the other Korean guard in this atlas — that one stone and fixed at a gate, this one paper and pasted on an inside wall
kin: insadong — the Seoul district where paper talismans reach a buyer through the antique and craft trade rather than through a rite
kin: inscribing — the act that makes it: Hanja pushed out of legibility into a figure
kin: hanging-at-door — the half of its use that never leaves the house, pasted to an interior wall after a gut
kin: unesco-ich — the body that listed the Jeju Yŏngdŭng gut in 2009, one of the rites these talismans are handed out at the end of

## Bulla (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/bulla/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/bulla.json
id: bulla
native: bulla (Latin)
aliases: bulla aurea · Roman boy's locket
said: BUL-la, plural bullae
when: 300 BCE – 399 CE
countries: IT
object: form=box materials=gold,lead,leather,cloth worn=neck,chest
against: child-harm — said by Roman practice: the bulla was given nine days after birth and worn through boyhood [s:wp-bulla-amulet]
against: bad-luck — said by the cited account, which describes the phallus inside as a symbol that brought good luck in antiquity [s:wp-bulla-amulet]
against: evil-eye — said by Pliny, on the phallic charm the bulla usually contained [s:wp-fascinus]
what: A locket on a neckchain: a round hollow pouch with something shut inside it, usually a phallus. What it was made of tracked the family's money — gold or gold foil at the top, lead, leather or cloth further down. It was given to a freeborn Roman boy nine days after he was born and he wore it until he stopped being a boy.
story: The bulla has an end date built into it. Before a young man put on the toga virilis, the toga of manhood, he handed his boyhood bulla to the household's Lares, the family's own gods, and it stayed with them. The girls' version, the lunula, came off on the eve of a wedding, together with her childhood toys.

Who could wear one was not open. The bulla marks a freeborn Roman boy and a Roman citizen in the making; the object and the status are the same statement. Some modern readers take a single line in Macrobius about an amulet worn by a general in his triumph as evidence that the childhood bulla was also standard triumphal regalia. The cited account reports that reading without endorsing it, and so does this record.

*Tradition holds —* the amulet inside was usually a phallus, a shape the cited account calls a bringer of good luck in antiquity. The container is the interesting part. The protection is real enough to be worth wearing and private enough to be shut in a case: nobody is meant to see what is working.

Ireland has bullae too, and they are not these. A small number of Late Bronze Age objects, roughly 1150 to 750 BCE, are called bullae because they look like the Roman ones — base metal or clay under a folded-over sheet of gold foil, incised with geometry, hung round the neck by a cord through a hole below the flat top. Whether they were ornament, amulet or something else is unclear, and that is why Ireland does not appear in this record's country list.
kin: lunula — the girls' counterpart, worn until the eve of the wedding instead of until the toga virilis
kin: fascinum — what was usually inside it — this record is the box, that one is the charm
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition, and its clearest case of an amulet that marks legal status as much as it guards
kin: wearing-hidden — the practice this object is built around: the working part is shut in a case and never seen
kin: gold — the material at the top of the range; lead, leather and cloth did the same job for families who could not buy gold
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read; a Roman boy got his on day nine and gave it up at manhood
kin: azabache — the same idea in Spanish and Latin American hands — a charm put on an infant at once, against the same look

## Car saint (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/car-saint/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/car-saint.json
id: car-saint
aliases: dashboard saint · St Christopher medal · visor medal · dashboard statue
said: in French, Saint Christophe; in Spanish, San Cristóbal
when: 1900 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR ES
object: form=medal materials=silver,brass,plastic,paper worn=vehicle,neck,wrist,pocket,wallet
against: traffic — said by the Spanish medals themselves [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: travel — said by the French medals [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: drowning — said by the Roman Catholic Church's patronage list, which names mariners, boatmen, floods and storms [s:wp-saint-christopher]
what: A stamped metal medal clipped to a sun visor or glued to a dashboard, or a miniature statue standing on it, showing a giant wading a river with a child on his shoulder. The same image is worn as a pendant, fixed to a bracelet or carried in a pocket. Medals are aluminium, tin, brass or silver, usually 15 to 30 mm across; dashboard statues are painted resin.
story: The image is legible before the text is. The Golden Legend, the thirteenth-century compendium of saints' lives, tells how Christopher, after his conversion, spent his life carrying travellers across a river; one day a boy asked to be carried, grew heavier with every step as the water rose, and on the far bank revealed himself as Christ. From that story various Christian denominations made him the patron saint of travellers, and small images of him are worn at the neck, on a bracelet, carried in a pocket or placed in a vehicle. Miniature statues are frequently displayed in automobiles. He is named patron of motorists and drivers alongside mariners, ferrymen, archers, bookbinders and gardeners.

The medals say out loud what they are for. The widespread French phrase is "Regarde St Christophe et va-t-en rassuré" — look at Saint Christopher and go on reassured. The Spanish medals and holy cards carry a harder promise: "Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás" — if you trust in Saint Christopher, you will not die in an accident. This atlas prints those two sentences as what the object says of itself, names who says it, and stops there.

The Church's own position moved under the object. Christopher's commemoration was of relatively late date, around 1550; by 1954 it had been extended to all Masses; in 1970 it was dropped from the general calendar of the Roman rite and restricted to particular calendars. *Inference —* the medal did not go with it. A devotional object with a working use outlived the liturgical decision that demoted it, which is the ordinary pattern for this whole class and not a Catholic peculiarity.

He is not alone on the dashboard. Japan's shrines sell a kōtsū-anzen omamori specifically for traffic safety, and it hangs from the same mirror in Nagoya that the medal is clipped under in Marseille.
how: Bought at a church shop, a shrine stall, a service station or online, and fixed where the driver can see it: clipped to the visor, adhered to the dash, hung from the mirror, slipped behind a licence plate. A medal may be blessed by a priest as a sacramental; nothing requires it to be. It stays with the car more often than with the driver, and is passed on with the vehicle.
today: Still sold and still fixed in cars across Catholic Europe and the Americas in 2026, and still stocked alongside the Miraculous Medal and the scapular in the same shops. No dated price was read for this record.
kin: st-christopher-medal — the same saint worn at the neck rather than fixed to a car — this record is what happens when the medal gets a dashboard
kin: omamori — the Japanese object doing the same job from the same mirror: kōtsū-anzen, sold for traffic safety
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the Church's category a blessed medal falls into, and the framework the object outlived a calendar decision inside
kin: miraculous-medal — the other stamped medal on the same shop counter, for a different promise
kin: ojo-de-venado — what hangs from the other side of the same Mexican rear-view mirror

## Caul (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/caul/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/caul.json
id: caul
aliases: silly hood · veil · born in a shirt · né coiffé · nato con la camicia · w czepku urodzony
said: KAWL
when: 1000 CE – 1999 CE
countries: GB NL FR IT PL RU RO JM
object: form=folded-paper materials=skin,paper worn=pocket,boat
against: drowning — said by sailors, who bought them from the women who had them, and for whom this was the caul's main claim [s:wp-caul]
against: bad-luck — said by Polish, Italian, French and Russian speakers, whose everyday idioms for a lucky person all mean born in a caul [s:wp-caul]
against: witchcraft — said by some early modern European traditions, which linked caul birth to defending fertility and the harvest against witches and sorcerers such as the benandanti [s:wp-caul]
against: spirits — said by Jamaican folklore, in which duppies cannot harm a person born with a caul [s:wp-caul]
what: A piece of birth membrane that comes away with a newborn and clings to the head and face — usually the thin translucent inner lining, the amnion. The midwife lifts it off, presses it onto a sheet of paper, and it dries there. That sheet is the amulet. Birth with a caul occurs in fewer than one in 80,000 births, a figure that includes en-caul births, in which the whole infant is delivered inside the intact sac.
story: In medieval Europe a caul on a newborn was read as good luck and as an omen that the child was destined for greatness, and gathering the caul onto paper was an important part of the birth: the midwife rubbed a sheet across the baby's head and face and presented the result to the mother, to be kept as an heirloom. Some early modern European traditions connected caul birth to the power to defend fertility and the harvest against witches and sorcerers — the benandanti of Friuli are the named example.

The caul's main career was at sea. Folklore held that possessing a baby's caul brought its bearer luck and protected them from death by drowning, and cauls were therefore prized by sailors. Medieval women sold them to sailors for large sums; a caul counted as a valuable talisman. Charles Dickens opened David Copperfield in 1850 with the narrator's own: "I was born with a caul, which was advertised for sale, in the newspapers, at the low price of fifteen guineas." Copperfield then follows the thing through a decade of resale and raffle. Fifteen guineas is a price in a novel, printed in 1850, and this record quotes it as that and not as a market rate.

The idioms carried the belief further than the objects did. Polish w czepku urodzony, 'born in a bonnet'; Italian nato con la camicia, 'born with a shirt'; French né coiffé, 'born with a hat on'; Russian родился в рубашке, 'born in a shirt' — all of them mean someone who is very lucky, and the Russian phrase is still applied to people who walk away from disasters, as if the caul persisted as armour.

Not every tradition reads it as good. In Romanian folklore babies born with a caul are said to become strigoi on death. In England the same birth was also read as the mark of someone destined to hang, on the proverb that he who is born to be hanged will never drown. In Jamaican folklore duppies are powerless against a person born with a caul. The 16th-century Dutch physician Levinus Lemnius, who wrote The Secret Miracles of Nature, was unconvinced by the claims made for preserved cauls; the 19th-century comic writer Thomas Hood ended his poem "The Sea-Spell" with a drowning sailor's charm failing him.
how: Not made and not chosen. The midwife, physician or parent removes the membrane at birth and presses it onto paper; a thicker chorionic caul has to be cut across the nostrils so the child can breathe and then eased off, and taken too fast it leaves scars. The dried sheet is kept in the family, given to the child, sold, or inherited. There is no rite over it.
today: Not a living trade. Cauls are still removed at birth, as a medical routine, and research in the 2020s has found that delivering severely premature infants with the caul intact can improve their chances, which is a use of the membrane with nothing folkloric in it. *Inference —* what remains of the amulet is the language: the Russian, Polish, Italian and French idioms for a lucky person are still in everyday use by speakers who have never seen one.
kin: st-christopher-medal — the other charm a European traveller carried against drowning, and the one you could buy rather than be born with
kin: hei-matau — the charm carried for safe passage over water at the other end of the world
kin: inheriting — the practice that kept these — a caul is handed down, or sold, never made
kin: skin — what it is, and the reason so few survive
kin: paper — what it is pressed onto and what a museum actually holds
kin: buying-in-a-market — the trade this object had: advertised in newspapers, raffled, sold to sailors for large sums
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and its one charm nobody can choose to acquire
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read it complicates: this charm comes off a child and is then carried by adults
kin: amulet-word — the word the sources reach for here, alongside talisman, for an object that is a body part and an omen at once
sources: s:wp-caul s:wp-amulet s:wp-luck
