## Challenge coin (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/challenge-coin/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/challenge-coin.json
id: challenge-coin
aliases: military coin · unit coin · commander's coin · memorial coin · airman's coin
said: CHAL-enj coin
when: 1950 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US CA GB CH AU NZ
root: English challenge, from the demand — the 'coin check' — that every member present produce theirs
object: form=coin materials=copper,brass,silver worn=pocket,wallet
against: fire — said by United States fire departments, whose coins carry the firefighter's prayer text engraved on the reverse [s:wp-challenge-coin]
what: A struck metal disc the size of a large coin, bearing a unit's insignia or an organization's emblem, carried in a pocket. Modern ones come in other shapes and sizes and take pop-culture figures as readily as regimental crests. Defacing one — drilling it for a keyring, say — is widely held to stop it counting, which is the only design rule the tradition enforces.
story: This one is here for an unusual reason: its claim is not protection. A challenge coin proves you belong. Somebody calls a coin check; everyone present produces theirs; whoever cannot buys the round. That is the whole mechanism, and it is a membership test with a drinking forfeit attached, not a charm against anything.

The origin is contested, and this atlas reports the contest and picks no winner. The cited account is explicit that "the historicity of these stories is unclear", and there are at least five:

Roman soldiers who did well in battle were given a bonus coin alongside their day's wages — specially minted, by some accounts, with the marks of their legion — and some kept them instead of spending them. Renaissance portrait medals commemorated an event for a patron and were exchanged among friends. French Huguenots, after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, carried a méreau communion token and produced it at the door of a secret service to prove they were not a state spy — which is the first instance of a coin answering an actual challenge. An American volunteer flying squadron in the First World War had a wealthy lieutenant strike bronze medallions; a pilot wearing his in a leather pouch was shot down, stripped of his identification by a German patrol, escaped, and was taken for a saboteur by the French until the squadron insignia on the medallion identified him. And a Vietnam-era bar run by infantrymen made outsiders buy a round if they could not prove combat service, the proof escalating from enemy bullets to grenades and unexploded ordnance until somebody sensibly substituted a unit-marked disc.

Against all five stands one dated object. The oldest surviving challenge coin belongs to the 17th Infantry Regiment and was minted by the then Colonel William "Buffalo Bill" Quinn between 1950 and 1958, to mark the end of a tour. *Inference —* that is the only hard floor in the whole story, and everything earlier is a claim about ancestry rather than a coin somebody can hand you.

From US units the practice went sideways into everything. The FBI's Crisis Response unit issued the Bureau's first in the late 1980s. Air Force training instructors give an airman's coin at the end of basic training. The United States Congress makes them for members to give constituents. Presidents have issued them since the late 1990s: Bill Clinton kept racks of the ones service members gave him on the credenza behind his Oval Office desk, and they are in his official portrait; Barack Obama left them on the graves of dead soldiers. In Canada the practice arrived as "an Americanism" and was pushed by General Rick Hillier as the army worked more closely with US forces; the Royal Military College issues one to every officer cadet at the end of First-Year Orientation. In Switzerland officers order and pay for their own. In the United Kingdom, after commanders tightened restrictions on drinking, the traditional coin check has largely become a collection instead.

Non-military bodies took it up wholesale: NASCAR, the NFL, Eagle Scouts, the World Series of Poker, police and fire departments, labor unions, the Utah Symphony and Opera in 2007, motorcycle clubs, television crews. *Inference —* an object that authenticates membership is useful to any group with a boundary, and the drinking forfeit travelled with it more reliably than the military content did.

Where a protective claim does attach, it is on the fire-department coins. The obverse takes the classic image of a firefighter; the reverse is engraved with the prayer text. Set that beside what Samuel Stouffer and his colleagues found among American soldiers in the Second World War, reported in the study George Gmelch cites: facing great danger and uncertainty, soldiers developed magical practices, particularly protective amulets and good-luck charms — crosses, Bibles, rabbits' feet, medals — and guarded articles of clothing they associated with past escapes. *Inference —* that is the neighbouring practice, not this one, and this record keeps them apart. The challenge coin's own documented job is the coin check.
how: Commissioned by a unit, a commander or an organization, struck by a commercial minter, and presented — for an achievement, a visit, a graduation, a donation, a death. Carried at all times is the rule the challenge enforces. Not blessed, not charged, not retired. A defaced coin, including one modified to make it easier to carry, generally stops qualifying for a challenge.
today: Issued by most units in the United States military and by a wide range of civilian bodies as of the cited account. Presidential coins have been a running controversy: the White House Communications Agency released one in May 2018 showing Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un ahead of the Singapore talks scheduled for June; Trump's own coin dropped the presidential seal, the motto E pluribus unum and the thirteen arrows, and carried a campaign slogan on both faces; Joe Biden's shows Delaware and the 261st Theater Tactical Signal Brigade, his late son Beau's unit. No dated retail price was read for this record.
kin: charm-coin — the Chinese coin-shaped charm that was never currency either, and the other object in this atlas that borrows a coin's authority without being one
kin: coin-square — the sign a coin carries, and the reason a disc reads as worth something before anybody looks at the device
kin: senninbari — the other soldiers' object here — that one was made by a thousand strangers' hands, this one is issued by a commander
kin: game-day-charm — the coin that gets carried for luck rather than for identification, and Gmelch's list of fetishes starts with coins
kin: st-christopher-medal — the struck disc carried in the same pocket by the same soldier, for a different reason entirely
kin: inheriting — what happens to a coin issued for a death, a fallen officer or a grave
kin: mascot-word — the word for a thing that stands for a group, which is what this coin is before it is anything else
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read this complicates: an object carried at all times, struck for a group, that claims to protect nobody
sources: s:wp-challenge-coin s:web-gmelch-baseball-magic s:wp-devotional-medal

## Chinese charm coin (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/charm-coin/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/charm-coin.json
id: charm-coin
native: 厭勝錢 (Han)
aliases: yansheng coin · yasheng coin · huaqian · flower coin · patterned coin · play coin · Chinese numismatic charm
said: yàn shèng qián
when: 206 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN TW VN KR JP
root: Chinese 厭勝錢 yànshèng qián; the formal older pronunciation was yāshèng qián, 押勝錢 / 压胜钱
object: form=coin materials=brass,copper,iron,lead,silver,gold,jade,paper worn=pocket,waist,door,wall,grave
against: bad-luck — said by the good luck charms class, which the source says was traditionally used to scare away evil and protect families [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: travel — said by the safe journey charms class [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: animal-attack — said by the five poisons charms, worn on the fifth day of the fifth month against snakes, scorpions, centipedes, toads and spiders [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: spirits — said by Taoist charms, the Lei Ting curse charms, which ask Leigong to kill evil spirits and bogies [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: exams — said by good luck charms wishing the carrier good results in the imperial examination system [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: the-dead — said by burial coins, placed in graves from the Shang onward — first cowrie shells, later replica currency, in the belief the money would serve in the afterlife [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: war — said by peace charms, privately cast with the wish for peace and used daily through China's turbulent history [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
what: A cast bronze disc with a hole through it, shaped like a Chinese cash coin and never spendable as one. Where a government coin carries two or four characters, a charm coin usually carries more, and often a picture as well: a dragon, a zodiac animal, a scene, an eight-trigram diagram, a line of Taoist talismanic script. Most are cast, not struck — machine striking only reaches China in the 19th century. They have also been made in iron, lead, tin, silver, gold, porcelain, jade and paper.
story: They start as coins going strange. Yansheng coins first appear in the Western Han as a variant of the Ban Liang and Wu Zhu cash then in circulation, used to speak to the dead, to pray for a favourable outcome, to terrify ghosts, or as lucky money. From the start of the Han to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, 206 BCE to 589 CE, most of them look like the circulating coinage; the difference is on the reverse — tortoises, snakes, double-edged swords, sun, moon, stars, famous people, the twelve zodiac animals. They were mostly privately funded and cast by wealthy families for their own ceremonies, though governments and religious orders cast some, and they circulated alongside real money because a copper-alloy disc was worth its metal.

The typologies are published and large. In Cast Chinese Amulets, 2020, the British numismatist David Hartill documented over 5,000 different types. Catalogues sort them by shape, by size, by meaning, by an emperor's name, or by any other shared feature; some deliberately refuse those categories, on the grounds that a novice cannot tell whether a given amulet is a lucky, religious, family or coin type. The standing classes run by function — good luck, safe journey, peace, burial, marriage and sex education, house, palace; by shape and design — gourd, vault protector, open-work, 24-character, spade, lock, nine-fold seal script, fish, peach, little shoe, pendant, palindrome, Ming cloisonné, money tree; and by theme — astronomy, zodiac, Eight Treasures, the Book of Changes and Bagua, five poisons, Confucian, Taoist, Buddhist temple coins, horse coins, even xiangqi pieces.

Some classes are exact enough to identify by measurement. "Laid to Rest" burial charms are bronze, 2.4 to 2.45 cm across and 1.3 to 1.4 mm thick, with the obverse inscription rù tǔ wéi ān, 'to be laid to rest', and a blank reverse; they turn up mostly in late Qing graves. They are often left out of reference books on Chinese coins and charms, because they were placed in the mouths of the dead and are considered unlucky and disturbing, and most collectors do not want them.

The five poisons charms are dated to a day: the fifth day of the fifth month, the most inauspicious in the calendar, when summer opened with dangerous animals, infectious disease and, in the account, evil spirits. The five poisons are snakes, scorpions, centipedes, toads and spiders, sometimes with lizards, the three-legged toad or the tiger, and the reasoning given is that poison can only be thwarted with poison. One example carries the legend 五日午时, 'noon of the 5th day', and the charms were worn on that day.

Peace charms have an archaeology. A find of the 1980s established that the tài píng bǎi qián was first cast by the Kingdom of Shu after the collapse of the Han, worth a hundred cash and cut in a calligraphic style closer to a charm than to the coinage of its day. Under the Qing, charms reading tiān xià tài píng — peace under heaven — became a common sight.
how: Cast in moulds, privately and in temples, then carried, hung, sewn on or buried. Open-work charms of the Tang and Song were used as clothing accessories, as ornament, and to decorate horses; fish charms meant to be worn at the waist come in under the Khitan Liao. House charms were set into buildings during construction, and into temples; Bagua charms decorate ridgepoles alongside red paper and cloth banners. Palace cash, which David Hartill notes were only produced at the establishment of a new reign era title, were wrapped in a rectangular cloth and given at New Year to imperial guards and eunuchs, who hung them below lamps, and were replaced with new reign titles each time an emperor died.
today: Collected, catalogued and reproduced. Use was revitalised in the Republic of China era, and the charms remain the best-catalogued class of amulet in this atlas — Hartill's 5,000-odd types are a finding aid a reader can actually use, which is a thing almost no other tradition here has. Feng shui coins on red cord are sold worldwide as of 2026; whether a modern cast disc is the same object as a Qing one is the same argument the dzi market has.
kin: coin-square — the sign it is: a round disc with a square hole, the shape money had for two thousand years and the shape a charm borrowed
kin: fu-talisman — the writing cast into the Taoist ones — fulu open and close their inscriptions
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition behind the Taoist and Buddhist classes of them
kin: bagua-mirror — the other object that puts the eight trigrams to work, on a wall rather than in a pocket
kin: challenge-coin — the modern descendant of a coin that is not money: carried, shown, and valued for who issued it
kin: grave-deposit — the practice behind the burial classes, and the reason the "Laid to Rest" charms are documented at all
kin: ping-an-fu — the paper peace charm that carries the same two characters, ping'an, at a fraction of the weight
kin: jade — one of the costlier materials the same charms were cut from
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read this class is the best evidence for: reign titles, inscriptions and 5,000 catalogued types make these the datable end of the whole atlas
kin: cowrie-strand — what the burial money started as, before replica coins replaced shells to deter grave robbers
sources: s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-numismatic-charm s:wp-fulu s:wp-bagua s:wp-cowrie

## Cimaruta (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/cimaruta/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/cimaruta.json
id: cimaruta
native: cimaruta (Latin)
aliases: sprig of rue · cima di ruta
said: chee-mah-ROO-tah; plural cimarute
when: 1899 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IT US
root: Neapolitan cimaruta, from Italian cima di ruta, 'sprig of rue' — cima 'top, tip' plus ruta, the flowering medicinal herb the whole charm is shaped as.
object: form=pendant materials=silver worn=neck,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by Italian wearers, who name the harm mal'occhio [s:wp-cimaruta]
against: child-harm — said by the same practice, in which the charm is hung above an infant's bed rather than worn [s:wp-cimaruta]
what: A silver sprig of rue with charms on the ends of its branches. From a central stalk the branches radiate and each one blossoms into a different object: a rose, a hand holding a wand or a sword, a flaming heart, a fish, a crescent moon, a snake, an owl, a plumed medieval helmet, a vervain blossom, a dolphin, a cock, an eagle. One cimaruta might carry a key, a dagger, a blossom and a moon and no more. Most are double-sided and fairly large — some almost four inches across.
story: The cimaruta is worn round the neck or hung above an infant's bed, and what it is hung against is named in Italian: mal'occhio, the evil eye. Which charms go on the branches varies by region of origin, and the form is particularly associated with southern Italy.

The piece has been studied as a structure rather than as a symbol. R. T. Günther published "The Cimaruta: Its Structure and Development" in Folk-lore in 1905, working on how the branches and their charms are put together and how that arrangement changed.

There is a live argument about whose object it is. Some practitioners of the neopagan religion of witchcraft called Stregoneria or Stregheria treat the cimaruta as a survival of an older Italian magic tradition, of the kind Charles Leland described in his 1899 Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches, which claimed a pagan witch-cult still active in Italy. Raven Grimassi, in The Cimaruta: And Other Magical Charms from Old Italy (2012), argues the cimaruta was originally a witches' charm, a sign of membership in what he calls the Society of Diana, later taken over by Italian folk magic, with Christian symbols added to the original pagan ones. Wikipedia's own account of the same material describes the cimaruta as alleged to be in borrowed use among self-identified Italian-American witches, which is a different claim about the same objects. This atlas reports both and settles neither; what is not in dispute is that the charm is worn in southern Italy and by descendants of Italian emigrants, against the eye, and that some of its branches carry Christian imagery.
how: Cast, commonly in silver, as a single piece: stalk, branches, and the charms that terminate them. Some modern versions are cast in bronze or pewter. Worn on a cord or chain at the neck, or hung over the bed of a child too young to wear one.
today: Still cast and sold, in Italy and in the Italian-American market, in silver and in cheaper alloys, and sold alongside books that make the Stregheria claim for it. *Inference —* the object's present-day buyers are not the same population as its nineteenth-century wearers, and the argument recorded above is mostly an argument between the two.
kin: cornicello — the other Italian answer to the same eye, and the one that says it with a single shape instead of a dozen
kin: eye — the harm this charm is aimed at, stated in its own language as mal'occhio
kin: hand — one of the charms on its branches — a hand holding a wand or a sword — and a sign that stands alone elsewhere in this atlas
kin: serpent — the snake on one branch; the cimaruta is the rare amulet that stacks signs rather than choosing one
kin: crescent — the moon on another branch, doing in miniature what a lunula does on its own cord
kin: key — another of the terminal charms, and one that carries its own meanings across Europe
kin: silver — the metal it is nearly always cast in, and the metal Naples associates with the moon
kin: herb — what it is a portrait of: rue, a medicinal plant, reproduced in metal so it never wilts
kin: lunula — the older Italian charm hung on a child, and the one this atlas dates properly
kin: san-gregorio-armeno — the Naples street where charms of this kind are still cast and sold
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian who travelled Italy and Spain collecting charms against the eye and published on them in 1895
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the Stregheria argument belongs in: who a folk object belongs to once a revival claims it
sources: s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-cornicello s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-frederick-thomas-elworthy s:wp-via-san-gregorio-armeno

## Cippus of Horus (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/cippus-of-horus/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/cippus-of-horus.json
id: cippus-of-horus
aliases: magical stela · healing stela · Horus on the Crocodiles · Horus stela · Horus cippus
said: SIP-us, plural cippi, from the Latin for a small pillar or marker
when: 1069 BCE – 30 BCE
countries: EG
root: Latin cippus, a small pillar or boundary stone — an archaeologist's borrowing, not an Egyptian word for the object.
object: form=plaque materials=earth worn=wall,neck
against: snakebite — said by the spells cut on the stela itself, as summarised by the Metropolitan Museum's Wikipedia entry: 'thirteen magic spells to protect against venomous bites and wounds and to cure the illnesses caused by them' [s:wp-metternich-stela]
against: animal-attack — said by the carving — Horus holds a lion by the tail and an antelope by the horns while standing on two crocodiles [s:wp-metternich-stela]
against: illness — said by the instructions on the cippi, which the source says were used to heal afflictions caused by snake or scorpion venom [s:wp-horus-on-the-crocodiles]
what: A slab of stone carved with the child Horus standing on two crocodiles, gripping snakes and scorpions in his fists, and often an antelope by the horns and a lion by the tail. Rows of hieroglyphs cover the rest of it. Sizes run from house-sized stelae down to amulets small enough to carry: the Metternich Stela is one block of greywacke about 35.8 inches tall and 13.25 wide, and the Metropolitan Museum also holds a miniature.
story: This is an amulet you drink. The instruction is on the object: water is poured over the carved spells and the carved figures, collected at the base, and given to the person who has been bitten or stung, to swallow or to wash the wound with. The words come off the stone into the water. Priests recited alongside.

The Metternich Stela is the fullest of them. It dates to about 380–342 BCE, the Thirtieth Dynasty, under Nectanebo II, and it carries thirteen spells against venomous bites and wounds and against the illnesses they cause — including the story of Isis and the Seven Scorpions, which is among the most complete versions found on any monument. The logic is precedent: Horus as a child was stung in the marshes at Khemmis and was cured, and the spell puts the patient in the child's place.

It disappeared for two thousand years and turned up in a wall excavated in a Franciscan monastery. Muhammad Ali Pasha gave it to Prince Metternich in 1828; it sat at Kynžvart Castle in Bohemia until 1950, when the Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired it.

The class runs from the Third Intermediate Period to the end of Ptolemaic rule in Egypt. Not all of them are museum monuments — some are amulet-sized, and the same image of Horus on the crocodiles is carried. The Egyptian Museum in Cairo holds the healing statue of Djedhor, the Louvre a Priest of Bastet statue, and the Brooklyn Museum another cippus; Keith Seele, Robert Ritner and Jane Draycott have written on them.

*Inference —* an amulet that is used up by being washed is a different kind of object from one that is worn, and it puts this stone closer to an Ethiopian scroll read aloud, or to a Qur'anic bowl rinsed and drunk, than to the faience beetle in the next tray.
how: Carved in stone with the Horus figure on the front and the spells around it. Water is poured over it, caught, and drunk or applied to the body by the person suffering the poisoning, with rites recited by priests. The large ones stay where they stand; the small ones are carried.
today: Not in use. Cippi are museum objects — the Metropolitan Museum shows them at The Met Fifth Avenue, and the Brooklyn Museum, the Louvre and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo hold others. As of 2026 this project has read no account of water being poured over one for a patient.
kin: washing-off-ink — the practice this object is built for — the spell leaves the stone in the water and is swallowed
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — a later charm on the same principle, further up the Nile: words that have to be got off the page and into the patient
kin: incantation-bowl — Mesopotamia's written-spell vessel — the same trick of putting the words on the container
kin: wedjat-eye — the eye of the same god, worn small; this is the god himself as a child, carved large and rinsed
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that cut it, at the end of its long life and at its most textual
kin: serpent — the sign in his fists, and the harm the stone is aimed at
kin: inscribing — the step that does the work — without the cut spells the water is water
kin: met-egyptian-galleries — where the Metternich Stela stands, two thousand years after somebody walled it up
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read it lands in: a pasha's gift to a prince, a castle in Bohemia, and a New York accession in 1950
sources: s:wp-horus-on-the-crocodiles s:wp-metternich-stela s:wp-taweret s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Concealed shoe (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/concealed-shoe/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/concealed-shoe.json
id: concealed-shoe
aliases: hidden shoe · chimney shoe · immured shoe · spiritual midden shoe
when: 1308 CE – 1991 CE
countries: GB DE US CA AU
object: form=garment materials=leather,wood worn=hearth,foundation,wall,roof,door
against: witchcraft — said by the explanation favoured by most scholars, in which a witch drawn by the human scent of a shoe enters it and cannot reverse out [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
against: demons — said by Brian Hoggard, on what the hiding places suggest: charms against evil influences such as demons, ghosts and witches [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
against: spirits — said by M. Chris Manning, who reads the deposits against the northern European household spirit — the brownie, the hob, the domovoi [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
against: infertility — said by the fertility reading, which Ralph Merrifield connects to the Lancashire custom of smickling — a woman hoping to conceive trying on the shoes of a woman who has just given birth [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
against: house — said by early modern building custom, which put written charms, dried cats, horse skulls, witch bottles and shoes into the structure of a house [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
what: An ordinary worn shoe, walled into a building where nobody will see it: up a chimney, under a floor, above a ceiling, in the roof, beside a door or window frame, occasionally in the foundations. Almost all of them have been worn — 98 per cent — and many have been repaired. Most finds are single shoes rather than pairs, and about half of them belonged to children. Archaeologists call a cache of this kind a spiritual midden.
story: Northampton Museum keeps the count. Its Concealed Shoe Index held more than 1,100 reports by 1998 and 1,900 by 2012, mostly from Britain but some from as far as Canada, with almost half dating from the nineteenth century. June Swann's analysis of the index, published in 1996, gives the hiding places by share: chimney, fireplace or hearth 26.2 per cent; under the floor or above the ceiling 22.9 per cent; almost as many again in the roof. The rest come from around doors and windows, under stairs and among foundations. Of the thousands reported, thirteen in Swann's analysis were in foundations, and she raised — carefully — a possible connection with the Carthaginian practice of putting infants into the foundations of buildings, with the shoe standing in for the person.

The earliest reported example was found behind the choir stalls in Winchester Cathedral, which were installed in 1308. The buildings are otherwise unremarkable: country cottages, town houses, manor houses, hospitals, workhouses, factories, public houses, two Oxford colleges — St John's and Queen's — a Benedictine monastery in Germany and a Baptist church in Cheshire. In the United States the deposits cluster in New England and the north-east, the regions first colonised from East Anglia.

What they were for is argued, and the arguers are named. The independent researcher Brian Hoggard observes that the places the shoes turn up — chimneys, floors, ceilings, doors, windows, roofs — suggest that at least some were hidden as charms protecting the occupants against evil influences such as demons, ghosts and witches. The explanation most scholars favour runs on scent: a witch is drawn by the human smell of a shoe, enters it, and is trapped, being unable to reverse. The archaeologist Ralph Merrifield suggested the belief may descend from John Schorne, an unofficial fourteenth-century English saint said to have trapped the Devil in a boot — a legend Merrifield thought might itself sit on an older folk belief the Church was trying to convert into an approved rite.

A second reading is about birth rather than defence. Shoes and fertility are linked in English custom, from the old woman who lived in a shoe to the shoe thrown after a bride and the shoes tied to a departing couple's car; Merrifield recorded that in Lancashire a woman who wished to conceive might try on the shoes of a woman who had just given birth, a custom called smickling. A third belongs to the archaeologist and architectural historian M. Chris Manning, who proposes that immuring shoes and garments may be connected to the belief in a household spirit found across northern Europe from Ireland to western Russia — the brownie and the hob of England and Scotland, who could be driven off by a gift of clothing, and the Russian domovoi, who could be drawn to a house with an old boot or bast shoe put under the stove or hung in the yard.

The custom faded through the twentieth century without quite stopping. Only fifty post-1900 instances have been recorded. In 1964 the shoe manufacturer Norvic put a pair of their women's high-leg boots into the foundations of a new factory; in 1991, at Knebworth House, an estate worker's shoe replaced an old court shoe that had been found behind some panelling.
how: Take a shoe somebody has actually worn — not a new one — and build it into the fabric of the house at a threshold: the chimney is the commonest choice, then the void under a floor or above a ceiling, then the roof. It is not charged, not inscribed, not renewed, and not meant to come out. The Knebworth case is the one recorded instance in this record of a replacement: the old shoe found, a new one put back.
today: Not a living custom in Britain, on this record's sources: it died out during the twentieth century, and the fifty recorded instances after 1900 are the exceptions that say so. The shoes themselves keep arriving, one demolition at a time, and Northampton Museum keeps adding them to the index. Apart from their folklore, they are the largest surviving body of evidence for what ordinary people actually put on their feet.
kin: witch-bottle — the other object out of the same chimney, and the one with a written recipe where this one has none
kin: the-charm-in-the-wall — the long read this record is the backbone of: 1,900 indexed finds and nobody's word for why
kin: foundation-deposit — the practice thirteen of Swann's shoes belong to, and the one that raised the question of a substitute body
kin: burying — the act itself — the charm's whole method is putting it somewhere it will not be found
kin: wearing-hidden — the same instinct at the scale of a person; here the building wears the charm under its own floor
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the count that supports the long read: about half the indexed shoes belonged to children
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and its most thoroughly counted object
kin: hagstone — the charm hung where visitors could see it, against the one built in where nobody could
kin: rowan-cross — the same household's charm on the outside of the door, renewed yearly, while this one stayed in the chimney for six centuries
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read about how any of these objects get a date; the shoes get theirs from the building's carpentry
sources: s:wp-concealed-shoes s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-apotropaic-magic
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Coptic cross tattoo (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/coptic-cross-tattoo/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/coptic-cross-tattoo.json
id: coptic-cross-tattoo
native: ⲥⲧⲁⲩⲣⲟⲥ (Coptic)
aliases: Coptic wrist cross · the cross on the wrist
said: in Egyptian Arabic the mark is simply the salib, the cross
when: 640 CE to now (still carried)
countries: EG
object: form=tattoo materials=ink,skin worn=wrist,skin
against: curse — said by Copts, who wear it as a sign of faith — the Coptic cross article says many have it tattooed on the inside of the right arm at the wrist for that reason [s:wp-coptic-cross]
against: child-harm — said by Coptic parents, as reported by Farah Rafik quoting Jean-Philippe Belleau [s:web-egyptian-streets-coptic-cross-tattoo]
what: A small cross tattooed on the inside of the right wrist. The usual design is the Coptic cross: two bold lines of equal length crossing at right angles, each arm ending in three points — twelve points in all. Often blue. In a Cairo studio it takes under ten minutes.
story: Many Copts have the cross tattooed as a sign of faith on the inside of their right arm at the wrist. That is the whole of what the Coptic cross article says about it, and every other thing on this page had to be sourced elsewhere, which is itself worth noticing about a practice this widespread.

The Egyptian Streets writer Farah Rafik, in February 2022, traces the tattooing tradition among Egyptians to the Coptic period, and says it intensified after the Muslim conquest of Egypt around 640 CE, when Christians faced conversion or the religious tax, and some were marked with crosses on the wrist so the authorities could tell who had kept their faith. What began as a mark applied from outside became a mark applied by parents. Rafik quotes the researcher Jean-Philippe Belleau: "The fear of conversion among members of the Christian minority of Egypt has led many Coptic parents to tattoo their children with a small blue cross." The reason parents gave was blunt — a child whose parents were killed would still be recognised, and raised, among Christians. In some churches the wrist has also served as the check at the door.

The people who put it on are named and working. Girgis Gabriel Girgis has run a studio in Muqattam, the quarter above Cairo, for over thirty years, and does five to seven tattoos a day, mostly Coptic crosses. Another tattooist, Magdy Girgis, calls the practice "a sign of resistance, perseverance and solidarity".

*Inference —* this is the only amulet in this batch whose bearer cannot take it off, sell it, lose it or leave it to anybody, and the tradition's own account of why it is permanent is exactly that.

The sign has Egyptian company. The ankh survived Christianisation in Egypt as the crux ansata, an ankh with a circular loop, and Coptic Christians used that form in many media, especially in textiles. Bertran de la Farge dates the trefoil Coptic cross to the fourth century and reads it as a predecessor of the Occitan cross.
how: Applied by a tattooist, usually on the inside of the right wrist, commonly in childhood within Coptic families and also on adults. The design is small and fast. The sources read here name no rite, no fasting and no blessing attached to it; what they describe is a studio, a queue and a needle.
today: Living, and worked at daily. As of 2026 Girgis Gabriel Girgis's Muqattam studio is the one the reporting names, and the mark functions as a permanent visible sign of Christian identity. Whether a reader outside the community should wear the same design is an argument with named people in it, and this atlas reports it rather than settling it: the tattooists quoted describe the mark as resistance and solidarity, which is a claim about who is inside.
kin: cross — the sign, in its Coptic form: four equal arms, three points on each, twelve points for the Apostles
kin: ankh-amulet — the sign this one replaced and absorbed — the crux ansata is an ankh kept by Egyptian Christians
kin: tattooing — the practice, and the reason this charm cannot be taken off, sold or inherited
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the other African Christian protective object in this atlas, made by a cleric rather than a tattooist and read aloud rather than shown
kin: sak-yant — the other living tattooed charm here — Thailand's, applied by a monk or an ajarn with rules attached; this one comes with none the sources name
kin: skin — the material, which is also the wearer
kin: st-christopher-medal — the Christian charm you can take off, which is the whole difference
kin: khan-el-khalili — the Cairo market a visitor is likelier to meet Coptic crosses in, sold as silver rather than worn under the skin
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this mark belongs to — the tattooists call it resistance and solidarity, which is a statement about who may wear it
sources: s:wp-coptic-cross s:web-egyptian-streets-coptic-cross-tattoo s:wp-copts s:wp-tattoo s:wp-ankh s:wp-cross

## Corn dolly (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/corn-dolly/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/corn-dolly.json
id: corn-dolly
aliases: corn mother · Corn-maiden · Kirn Dolly · Kirn Baby · Kern Baby · the Neck · Cailleach · Carlin · Caseg Fedi · vetula
said: KORN DOL-ee
when: 600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE DE AT PL FR BE SE
root: English corn in its British sense of grain in general — in American English this would be a grain dolly — plus dolly, a small figure. The Latin vetula, 'little old woman', is the name used for the same object among the Germanic pagans of seventh-century Flanders.
object: form=figurine materials=straw,palm-leaf,thread,cloth worn=field,wall,roof
against: house — said by the custom at Bruck in Styria as recorded by James Frazer, in which the Corn-mother was laid down in the barn to keep off the mice [s:wp-corn-dolly]
what: A hollow shape plaited from the last sheaf of a harvest: a figure, a knot, a lantern, a crown, a fan, a horseshoe. British ones are wheat, oats, rye or barley; Irish ones are rush; in southern France they are palm leaves. In Scandinavia and the German-speaking countries the straw is tied with yarn or raffia rather than plaited. Some are whole sheaves dressed as a woman and carried home on the last waggon.
story: The explanation usually given for it is a scholars' explanation, and it is worth saying so first. Writers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries theorised that before Christianisation the spirit of the corn was held to live among the crop, and that the harvest made it homeless; the last sheaf, plaited into a shape, gave it somewhere to spend the winter until it was ploughed into the first furrow of the new season. James Frazer gave four chapters of The Golden Bough to the Corn-Mother and the Corn-Maiden in northern Europe, drawing on the enormous body of European folklore that Wilhelm Mannhardt had collected.

What Frazer's informants actually described is more concrete. Near Danzig, whoever cut the last ears made them into a doll called the Corn-mother or the Old Woman and it came home on the last waggon. In parts of Holstein the last sheaf was dressed in women's clothes, called the Corn-mother, carried home and then thoroughly drenched with water — a rain-charm, Frazer says. In the district of Bruck in Styria the Corn-mother was made by the oldest married woman in the village, a woman of fifty to fifty-five; the finest ears were plucked out and twisted into a wreath, which the prettiest girl in the village carried on her head to the squire, while the Corn-mother herself was laid down in the barn to keep off the mice. In East Prussia the reapers called out to the woman binding the last sheaf that she was getting the Old Grandmother. In Scotland, when the last corn was cut after Hallowmas, the figure made from it was sometimes the Carlin, the old woman.

The oldest dated mention is a prohibition. In seventh-century Flanders, Saint Eligius told his congregation not to make vetulas — little figures of the Old Woman — nor little deer nor iotticos, nor set tables at night, nor exchange New Year gifts.

Mechanised harvesting effectively ended the craft at the beginning of the twentieth century. It came back in Britain in the 1950s and 1960s as a craft revival: farm workers made new things, including replicas of farm implements, windmills and large figures, new shapes and new techniques appeared, and several books came out in the 1960s and 1970s. The source is blunt about what that revival did: the simple origins of the craft had been lost, and new folklore stories were added to the original ideas. Anyone reading a modern account of what a particular corn dolly means is reading something from that period unless it is sourced to Mannhardt or earlier.

The old long-stemmed, hollow-stemmed wheats the work needs were replaced by short pithy varieties bred for the combine. A number of English and Scottish farmers still grow the old sorts — Maris Wigeon, Squarehead Master, Elite Le Peuple — mainly because thatchers want them.
how: Cut from the last sheaf standing, at the end of harvest, by a person the local custom names — the one who cuts the last ears, the woman who binds the last sheaf, the oldest married woman in the village. Plaited hollow, or tied with yarn, or dressed as a figure. Carried home on the last waggon, set at the centre of the harvest supper, hung in the house or laid in the barn, and kept over winter. Then it goes back into the ground: ploughed into the first furrow of the new season.
today: Made as a craft rather than as a harvest rite, and the Heritage Crafts Association lists corn dolly making as endangered. The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, the Museum of English Rural Life in Reading and the Ryedale Folk Museum in Yorkshire hold collections of them from around the world.
kin: brigids-cross — the other straw weave of these islands, and the one made on a fixed feast day rather than at the end of a harvest — the National Museum of Ireland files harvest crosses with it
kin: knotting — the making itself: the countryman's favour is three straws plaited and tied into a loose knot shaped like a heart
kin: renewing-yearly — the rhythm it runs on — one made each harvest, last year's gone into the furrow
kin: burying — how it is retired: ploughed into the first furrow of the new season, which is the only disposal the tradition names
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and its clearest case of an object made from the thing it is meant to protect
kin: horseshoe — a shape it is plaited into — the Suffolk Horseshoe is a corn dolly, not a piece of iron
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — where a tray of them can be seen, alongside the rowan loops and the holed stones
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the 1950s revival belongs in: new folklore attached to an old craft, and the source saying so outright
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read about evidence, which this object tests — straw rots, so almost everything known about it comes from what people said, not from what survived
sources: s:wp-corn-dolly s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Cornicello (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/cornicello/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/cornicello.json
id: cornicello
native: cornicello (Latin)
aliases: cornetto · corno · corno portafortuna · curniciello · Italian horn
said: kor-nee-CHEL-lo; in Neapolitan curniciello
when: 1500 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IT US
root: Italian corno 'horn' with the diminutive -icello: 'little horn'. The fuller name corno portafortuna is 'horn that brings luck'.
object: form=horn materials=gold,silver,plastic,bone,terracotta,coral worn=neck,vehicle,wall
against: evil-eye — said by Italian wearers, who name it malocchio [s:wp-cornicello]
against: infertility — said by the tradition's own account, in which the horn answers harm aimed at nursing mothers, bearing fruit trees, milking animals and the sperm of men [s:wp-cornicello]
against: bad-luck — said by the name itself: corno portafortuna, the horn that brings luck [s:wp-cornicello]
against: livestock — said by the older custom the car charm descends from — hanging horns on draft horses [s:wp-cornicello]
against: traffic — said by present-day Italian drivers, who hang one from the rear-view mirror [s:wp-cornicello]
what: A single twisted horn, a few centimetres long, tapering to a point and pierced at the wide end for a chain. Gold, silver, plastic, bone, terracotta or red coral. The red ones look like a chili pepper, which is an accident of history: chilis only reached Europe after the Columbian exchange, and the horn shape is much older than the resemblance.
story: The cornicello is worn against the evil eye — malocchio — and against bad luck in general, and historically to promote fertility and virility. The harm it answers is described precisely by the people who wear it: the eye is held to strike nursing mothers and their babies, fruit-bearing trees, milking animals and the sperm of men. Those are the forces of generation, and a horn is an answer in kind.

The shape is said to be modelled on an eland horn, for fertility, virility and strength. Its materials carry their own connections in the tradition's own telling: coral is sacred to Venus, goddess of love, fertility, sex and prosperity; silver to Luna, goddess of the moon; the phallic shape and the red colour point to Priapus, a male fertility god; the horn itself is tied to Pan, and the broken goat's horn Zeus filled with fruit and flowers became the cornucopia.

It is a regional object, not a national one. Cornicelli are most often worn by men in southern Italy, above all in Campania, then Lazio, Apulia and Basilicata, and to a lesser extent Sicily and Calabria — and by the descendants of Italian emigrants elsewhere. Dried chili peppers are hung in some southern Italian homes against the same harm, which is how the resemblance became a second charm.

The horn also has a hand. The mano cornuta, the horned hand, is an Italian gesture — and an amulet imitating the gesture — made with the hand levelled or pointing down, usually with a swivelling or oscillating motion, against the same eye.
how: Cast or carved: gold and silver for the good ones, red coral for the old ones, plastic for the cheap ones, bone and terracotta in between. Pierced at the broad end and hung on a neck chain. It is also hung from the rear-view mirrors of cars — a move the source ties to the older custom of hanging them on draft horses — and in houses. Nothing is recorded about charging it or retiring it.
today: Made and sold in enormous numbers, in gold at jewellers and in plastic at every tourist stall in Naples, and worn worldwide by people of Italian descent and by people with no connection to Campania at all. *Inference —* the horn has crossed from a charm against a named harm to a badge of origin, and the two uses are worn on the same chain by the same people without anyone being asked to choose.
kin: horn — the sign itself, and the reason this atlas files a phallic charm, a gesture and a goat's horn in one family
kin: eye — the harm it answers; southern Italy substitutes a horn where the eastern Mediterranean draws an eye
kin: coral — the old material, red, sacred to Venus in the tradition's own account, and the one a Naples workshop still cuts
kin: fascinum — the Roman ancestor in the same peninsula: a different body part, the same interception
kin: cimaruta — the other Italian charm against malocchio, which puts a dozen signs on one branch where this one puts one
kin: fist — the gesture-amulet family the mano cornuta belongs to — a hand frozen mid-sign against the same eye
kin: phallic-sign — what the shape and the red colour point to in the tradition's own telling, through Priapus
kin: san-gregorio-armeno — the Naples street where these are cast, carved and sold by the tray
kin: car-saint — where it hangs now: from the rear-view mirror, beside or instead of a saint
kin: nazar — the object it competes with across the Mediterranean, answering the same harm with the opposite strategy
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian who collected charms of this kind in Italy and published The Evil Eye in 1895
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that runs the horn and the eye together and asks which one came first
sources: s:wp-cornicello s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-fascinus s:wp-coral s:wp-frederick-thomas-elworthy s:wp-via-san-gregorio-armeno

## Cowrie strand (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/cowrie-strand/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/cowrie-strand.json
id: cowrie-strand
aliases: cowry shells · buzios · miigis shells · whiteshells · bulikula · nzimbu
said: COW-ree, from Hindi कौडि kaudi
when: 3000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: NG BJ SL KE EG IL IN NP FJ BR CA GH
root: Hindi कौडि kaudi, from Sanskrit कपर्द kaparda. The Italian word for the shell, porcellana, is where English gets 'porcelain', from the resemblance.
object: form=bead materials=cowrie,shell,thread worn=neck,waist,hair,grave,pocket
against: infertility — said by users in certain parts of Africa, where the source says cowries were prized charms 'associated with fecundity, sexual pleasure, and good luck' [s:wp-cowrie]
against: bad-luck — said by the same users, in the same sentence [s:wp-cowrie]
against: poverty — said by worshippers of Lakshmi, who use cowries in her worship and treat them at Tihar as a sign of the goddess and of wealth [s:wp-cowrie]
against: the-dead — said by West Bengali funerary practice, where a cowrie is the token fare for the departed soul's ferry across the Vaitarani; and predynastic Egyptian and Neolithic Levantine burials, where cowries were arranged around the skull in female graves [s:wp-cowrie]
against: childbirth — said by Mende and Kikuyu users, for whom the source says the shells stand for womanhood, fertility and birth [s:wp-cowrie]
RESTRICTED: This record does not describe Midewiwin ceremony. The Ojibwe use of miigis shells is named here and stops there: what the shells do in that ceremony is not printed, and no neighbouring practice is used to fill the gap.
what: Small sea-snail shells, egg-shaped, glossy, with a long toothed slit down the flat underside. Strung on cord, sewn onto cloth, hung at the neck, or thrown in handfuls. Most run about the size of a thumbnail; the family runs from 5 mm to 19 cm across its species. The money cowrie, Monetaria moneta, is the one that travelled.
story: This is the only amulet in the atlas that was also, for centuries and across three continents, money. Cowries were used as currency by Africans for centuries, and the money cowrie was almost impossible to counterfeit until the late nineteenth century. The Classical Chinese character for money, 貝, began as a stylised drawing of a Maldivian cowrie shell, and characters for money, property and wealth still carry it as a radical.

The volume matters for what follows. After the 1500s European traders, chiefly through the slave trade, moved huge numbers of Maldivian cowries into Africa; between 1500 and 1875 at least 30 billion were imported to the Bight of Benin, making up 44% of the total value of trade there. Around 1850 the German explorer Heinrich Barth found them still in use at Kano, Kuka, Gando and Timbuktu, and reported that in Muniyoma, an old division of Bornu, the king's revenue was reckoned at 30,000,000 shells, with every adult male owing 1,000 a year for himself, 1,000 for each pack-ox and 2,000 for each enslaved person he held. In parts of British West Africa cowries were accepted for tax until the early twentieth century, and their use as currency persisted in unregulated settings into the 1960s. Ghana's national currency, introduced in 1965, is the cedi, named after the shell.

What the shell does when it is not money is spread just as far. Yoruba diviners in West Africa cast cowries, as do the annual customs of Dahomey in Benin. In Brazil, as a result of the Atlantic slave trade, the shells — búzios — are cast to consult the Orixás and to hear their replies. The Kaniyar Panicker astrologers of Kerala used them among their devices. In West Bengal a cowrie is the token fare for the departed soul's ferry across the Vaitarani, and cowries are used at cremations and in the worship of Lakshmi. In Nepal sixteen are thrown in a gambling game at Tihar, and in the same festival the shells are worshipped as a sign of Lakshmi and of wealth.

As a charm it is tied to the body and to birth. In certain parts of Africa cowries were prized charms, said to be associated with fecundity, sexual pleasure and good luck. In Mende and in Kikuyu culture the shells stand for womanhood, fertility, birth and wealth. One modern ethnographic author reads the underside as a vulva or an eye — the source attributes that reading rather than asserting it, and so does this atlas.

And it goes in graves. In predynastic Egypt and the Neolithic southern Levant, cowries were placed in the graves of young girls, and modified Levantine cowries were found ritually arranged around the skull in female burials. In the Bronze Age they became more common as funerary goods, again with women and children. Egypt made an imitation of it: the cowroid, a seal amulet in the shape of a cowrie, with copies in stone or faience appearing in the early second millennium BCE.

The Ojibwe use miigis shells in Midewiwin ceremonies, and how shells from a warm-sea species reached that far inland and that far north is an open question. Oral stories and birch-bark scrolls say the shells were found in the ground, or washed up on the shores of lakes and rivers.

On the Fiji Islands, a golden cowrie — bulikula, Cypraea aurantium — was drilled at both ends and worn on a string at the neck by chieftains as a badge of rank.
how: Drilled at the ends or ground open on the back, then strung, sewn or hung. In divination they are not worn at all but thrown: a set number goes down and the reading is made from which ones land aperture-up. That same throw is a dice mechanism in Pachisi and Ashta Chamma.
today: Still worn, still cast, still sold by the sack in West African and Indian markets. The cedi is still named after it. As of 2026 this project has read no source that dates the end of any of these uses.
kin: cowrie — the material this object is — and the only material in the atlas that was legal tender for tax in living memory
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition that casts them for divination, in Ifá and in the customs of Dahomey
kin: eye — the sign one modern ethnographic author reads in the shell's slit underside — an attribution the source makes and this atlas repeats as an attribution
kin: charm-coin — the other object here that is money and charm at once, cast in bronze rather than grown in the sea
kin: scarab — the Egyptian seal-amulet whose cowrie-shaped cousin, the cowroid, copies this shell in stone and faience from the early second millennium BCE
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that put them around the skulls of girls in predynastic Egypt and the Neolithic Levant
kin: counting-beads — the practice of handling a set number, which here becomes a throw and a reading
kin: akodessewa-market — a West African market where shells and charm materials are traded by the sack
kin: hei-matau — another shell-and-sea charm worn at the neck, on the far side of the Pacific
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this shell complicates: 30 billion of them reached the Bight of Benin as trade goods in the era of Atlantic slavery
sources: s:wp-cowrie s:wp-shell-money s:wp-ojibwe s:wp-west-african-vod-n s:wp-amulet

## Crystal pendant (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/crystal-pendant/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/crystal-pendant.json
id: crystal-pendant
aliases: healing crystal · crystal point pendant · rose quartz pendant · amethyst pendant · tumbled stone pendant
said: KRIS-tl PEN-dnt
when: undated (still carried)
countries: US GB MG
root: Greek κρύσταλλος krýstallos, 'ice' — the ancient Greek reading of clear quartz was water frozen so hard it stayed solid
object: form=pendant materials=agate,turquoise,amber,silver worn=neck,chest,pocket
against: illness — said by adherents of crystal healing, as summarised by the cited account, which attaches its own contradiction in the same sentence [s:wp-crystal-healing]
against: bad-luck — said by practitioners, in the cited account's summary of what they hold the stones do [s:wp-crystal-healing]
what: A cut or tumbled stone hung at the neck, usually in a wire cage or a silver bezel: a six-sided quartz point, a rose quartz lozenge, a lump of amethyst, a polished bead of agate or turquoise. It is worn, held, placed on the body, or meditated with. The same stones are sold loose by the kilo, and the pendant is the wearable end of a trade that also fills bowls in shop windows.
story: Two arguments run through this object, and they are not the same argument. This record reports the first and stays out of it, and reports the second at length because there are names and dates in it.

The first argument is whether the stones do anything. The cited account calls crystal healing "a pseudoscientific, alternative medicine practice" and says adherents "claim that these have healing powers, but there is no scientific basis for this claim". Practitioners, in the same account's words, hold that they can "boost low energy, prevent bad energy, release blocked energy, and transform a body's aura"; that physical properties — shape, colour, markings — decide what a stone can treat, with published lists of the correspondences; and, at the same time, "that crystals have no intrinsic qualities but that, instead, their quality changes according to both" the participants, which the account itself flags as a paradox. Stuart McLean calls the practice "the middle-class New Age healing activity par excellence". Against all that, Christopher French of the anomalistic psychology research unit at the University of London and colleagues from Goldsmiths College ran eighty volunteers meditating with either a quartz crystal or an indistinguishable placebo stone, reported typical crystal effects either way, and concluded at the British Psychological Society Centenary Annual Conference in 2001: "There is no evidence that crystal healing works over and above a placebo effect." Every sentence in this paragraph belongs to somebody named. This atlas does not add one.

The second argument has coordinates. Worldwide retail sales of crystals were estimated at more than US$1 billion a year in 2019. India, China, Brazil and Madagascar are the main producers. In Madagascar most crystals come out of unsafe, non-industrial mines — "homemade", in the cited account's word — dug with shovels by parents and children working together in pits and tunnels. Miners are paid between 17 and 23 US cents per kilogram for rose quartz, which is roughly 8 to 11 cents a pound; a miner's income may be 0.1 per cent of the final retail price. The reporting behind those figures is Tess McClure's, published in The Guardian on 17 September 2019 under the title "Dark crystals: the brutal reality behind a booming wellness craze"; this project could not fetch the original and read it instead through Aaron Gilbreath's Longreads piece of 25 September 2019, which gives the rose quartz village as Anjoma Ramartina, puts the going rate at 800 ariary — about 23 US cents — per kilo, enough to buy a cup of rice at the village market, and quotes one mine worker, Rakotondrasolo: "I was afraid, and was afraid for my children because of this soil. It can collapse on them."

On why the pay is that low, the cited account gives both industry answers and endorses neither: "Some people in the industry say that the low pay for miners is because customers in developed countries want low retail prices; others say that it is due to shops in developed countries wanting to be more profitable." Those are the two sides, in the trade's own mouths, and this atlas prints them and stops.

One further hazard is documented and belongs to whoever handles the stone rather than to whoever mined it: some crystals sold in the trade, shungite among them, frequently contain heavy metals and carry a toxicity risk for people handling them over long periods or ingesting anything that has been in contact with them.

*Inference —* the useful thing about this object for the rest of the atlas is that its supply chain is documented and a Bronze Age bead's is not. What a reader can see here — a wage, a village, a named miner, a retail figure, a 0.1 per cent — is the thing every other record in this collection would want and cannot have.
how: Mined, tumbled or faceted, wire-wrapped or set, and sold in mineral shops, gift shops, wellness retailers and online. Practitioners select stones by colour or by the qualities they attribute to them and place them on parts of the body; the pendant version keeps one stone at the sternum permanently. There is no consecration and no restriction on who may make or wear one. Nothing is said in the sources read here about retiring one.
today: Sold everywhere in 2026, in every price band, alongside reiki, flower essences and homeopathy in the same shops. The sourcing argument has been in print since 2019 and this project has read nothing showing it changed the supply chain. The worry stone record points here for exactly this reason: it is the same stones, the same trade, the same question.
kin: worry-stone — the same stones and the same trade, cut for the thumb instead of the throat — that record sends its sourcing question here
kin: turquoise — one of the stones cut for it, and one with a much older amulet history of its own
kin: amber — another, and the one whose protective claims predate the crystal trade by millennia
kin: jade — the stone this trade's logic was already applied to in China and Mesoamerica, long before anybody said aura
kin: navaratna-ring — the older system that also assigns stones to conditions, with nine of them and a planetary scheme behind it
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the other mass-produced charm in this atlas whose hand-made and factory versions are argued over
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read where a supply chain and a spiritual claim end up in the same paragraph
kin: buying-in-a-market — the act that makes it yours, and the point at which the 0.1 per cent gets decided
kin: the-fake-market — the long read about what a charm costs and who gets the money

## Curse tablet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/curse-tablet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/curse-tablet.json
id: curse-tablet
native: κατάδεσμος (Greek)
aliases: defixio · katadesmos · binding tablet · judicial prayer
said: ka-TA-des-mos; Latin tabella defixionis, defixio
when: 500 BCE – 399 CE
countries: GR IT GB
root: from the Greek and Latin words for 'pierce' and 'bind' — katadesmos from katadeō, to bind down; defixio from defigere, to fix or nail down
object: form=plaque materials=lead,iron worn=grave,wall,foundation
against: lawsuit — said by the writers of the Athenian tablets, who ask that an opposing litigant botch his performance in court, forget his words and become dizzy [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: theft — said by the 130 tablets from the sacred spring at Bath, all but one of which concern the restitution of stolen goods [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: loneliness — said by the writers of erotic binding spells — the agogai that bind a target to oneself and the diakopai that drive a rival away by making them repulsive [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: the-dead — said by the writers of the tablets that are not curses at all: some were laid at the graves of people who died young or violently, to help lay their souls to rest [s:wp-curse-tablet]
what: A very thin sheet of lead with tiny letters scratched into it, then rolled, folded, or pierced through with a nail. It goes into the ground: buried in a grave or tomb, thrown down a well or a pool, shut in an underground sanctuary, nailed to a temple wall. Some are found with small bound figurines, hands and feet tied, sometimes pierced too. Some have hair or a scrap of clothing folded into them.
story: This is the amulet turned around, and the atlas keeps it here on purpose. Everything else in this batch is written to keep a harm off a person. A defixio is written to put one on. Same lead, same scratched letters, same divine names, same burial in a grave — and the target is a named human being.

About 1,600 of them have been found, most in Greek, 220 from Attica alone. The first set came from Selinus in Sicily: twenty-two tablets, mostly early fifth century BCE, aimed at somebody the writer was suing. The Athenian tablets are full of lawsuits — may he botch his performance in court, forget his words, become dizzy. Others are erotic binding spells, or aimed at thieves, business rivals and sporting rivals.

In 1979 and 1980, 130 tablets came out of the sacred spring at Aquae Sulis, now Bath. All but one concern the restitution of stolen goods. More than eighty similar tablets were found at a temple of Mercury at West Hill, Uley, which makes south-western Britain one of the great centres of Latin defixiones. Some scholars refuse to call these curses at all and prefer 'judicial prayers', because what they mostly do is list a crime in detail and hand the punishment to a god.

The writing is doing work beyond its sense. Voces mysticae — words in no known language — recur; Stanley J. Tambiah proposed in 1968 that they represent "the language that demons can understand". Clement of Alexandria, around 200 CE, held that human language was not fit for addressing gods at all. Tablets survive with blank spaces where a name should go, prepared in advance and finished when a customer paid.

*Inference —* the blank space is the tell. An object sold ready-made with a gap for the buyer's enemy is a product, and the professional who wrote it had the same relationship to his customers as the man selling gems with Abrasax on them two streets away.
kin: magical-gem — the same names and the same nonsense-words, cut in stone to protect a wearer instead of scratched in lead to harm a stranger — this record is that one inverted
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition, seen from the side it does not advertise
kin: christopher-faraone — the scholar who split these spells into passion-inducing and affection-encouraging, and found men and women using different halves
kin: lead — the metal that made them: soft enough to scratch, cheap enough to throw away, stable enough to survive a well
kin: palindrome-word — the neighbouring habit — palindromes and boustrophedon used on these tablets to give the writing its own mystique
kin: witch-bottle — the European object that answers one of these: a counter-charm buried against a named person's harm
kin: burying — the practice the whole genre depends on; the tablet works by going into the ground
kin: incantation-bowl — the later eastern object that buries writing under a house for the opposite purpose
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read about the words; this record is why the atlas needs more than one of them
sources: s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-abraxas s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-magic-supernatural

## Daruma (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/daruma/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/daruma.json
id: daruma
native: 達磨 (Japanese)
aliases: daruma doll · だるま · okiagari-koboshi kin · hime daruma · onna daruma · Goshiki Daruma
said: DA-ru-ma
when: 1764 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese 達磨, the transcription of Dharma in Bodhidharma — the fifth- or sixth-century monk credited with carrying Chan, later Zen, to China
object: form=figurine materials=paper,ink,wood,terracotta worn=shop,wall,hearth
against: bad-luck — said by Josef Kyburz, on the New Year charms the Daruma-dera's founder drew [s:wp-daruma-doll]
against: illness — said by Edo households during measles and smallpox outbreaks, who set daruma figures on a small altar for the God of Smallpox [s:wp-daruma-doll]
against: attraction — said by buyers at the Takasaki market, where gold ones are sold for luck in money matters [s:wp-daruma-doll]
against: exams — said by the goal-setting use, of which the best-documented public instance is a political party inking one at election time [s:wp-daruma-doll]
what: A hollow papier-mâché figure, round, weighted at the base so it rights itself when knocked over, usually red, with a bearded scowling face and two oversized white eyes left blank. Sold with no pupils. The owner inks one in when they set a goal and the other when they reach it. Other colours exist: a set of five — blue, yellow, red, white, black — is sold as Goshiki Daruma, and gold ones are sold for money.
story: The doll has a home town. Shorinzan Daruma Temple in Takasaki, Gunma, north of Tokyo, is where its present sense as a luck charm starts. Josef Kyburz records that the founder of that Daruma-dera drew New Year charms of Bodhidharma, which parishioners kept to "bring happiness and prosperity and ward off accidents and misfortune". The charms expired after a year, so the demand came round again every twelve months, and the ninth priest, Togaku, solved the problem near the start of the Meiwa period (1764–72) by cutting wooden block moulds and handing them to the parishioners to make their own papier-mâché charms. Kyburz notes it is not known when the Bodhidharma charm and the tumbler toy merged; by the mid-nineteenth century the two were treated as the same thing. Takasaki's families were mostly silk farmers, a crop that turns on luck, and the doll became the region's mascot.

The red has a second history. *Tradition holds —* red is the colour of a high-ranking priest's robe, and the art historian James T. Ulak has traced depictions of Bodhidharma in red robes before any doll existed. In the late Edo period red was tied to smallpox: during measles and smallpox outbreaks in Edo and nearby cities, households strung red paper strips on ropes around the house, dressed the sick child in red, and set up a small altar with daruma figures on it for the God of Smallpox. The red was to please the deity; the self-righting body was to tell the patient to get up as fast as they went down.

The eye-painting reached national television through politics. Time reported in 1967 that in the Tokyo headquarters of the Liberal Democratic Party, Premier Eisaku Satō inked the right eye of his daruma and said: "The eyes, are as big as my own." Party headquarters at election time are still photographed with a large one.

A feminine line runs alongside. Hime daruma and onna daruma — Princess and Lady Daruma — began in the Edo merchant culture that made fun of what its betters held sacred, including a version of Bodhidharma drawn as a prostitute, on the grounds that prostitutes showed the same okiagari resilience. The satire faded; the dolls stayed, wholesome.
how: Bought blank-eyed, often at a New Year market. The owner picks one goal, inks the left eye with a brush, and keeps the figure in view; the right eye is filled in when the goal is met. Traditionally only the head of the household did the painting. Matsukawa daruma are sold with both eyes already painted, because their job is to watch over the house rather than to track a goal. At the end of the year every daruma goes back to the temple it came from for the daruma kuyō, a burning held just after New Year's Day — the best known at Nishi-Arai Daishi in Tokyo and Dairyū-ji in Gifu — where tens of thousands are burnt together after the monks' procession, sutras and horns. Then you buy next year's.
today: Takasaki still holds its Daruma Doll Festival, the daruma-ichi, at the Shorinzan. The city's own website says over 400,000 people come from across the Kanto Plain to buy new dolls for the year, and that Takasaki makes 80% of Japan's daruma. The festival also carries a 24-hour reading of sutras by the Shorinzan monks for world peace. The shape is common property now: snowmen in Japanese are yukidaruma, the children's game Darumasan ga Koronda is the local Red Light Green Light, and Pokémon put out Darumaka and Darmanitan in 2010.
kin: maneki-neko — the other figure sold off the same tray, and the opposite deal: this one has a year and a fire waiting at the end of it
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition it sits at the centre of, with its own annual market at Takasaki
kin: omamori — the pocket charm from the same economy, working on the same twelve-month clock
kin: renewing-yearly — the rule that gave the doll its shape: the founder's charms expired in a year, so the parishioners came back
kin: burning-retirement — the ending: daruma kuyō, tens of thousands burnt together after New Year
kin: teru-teru-bozu — the other Japanese figure made to be discharged — one is burnt at the temple, the other floated down a river
kin: ekeko — another figure a household buys and asks a year's worth of gain from
kin: exam-charm — the genre the blank eye feeds: a goal, a deadline, and a physical thing that watches you
kin: mascot-word — what Takasaki turned it into, and the route from a temple charm to a civic emblem
sources: s:wp-daruma-doll s:web-ja-wikipedia-engimono s:wp-list-of-lucky-symbols

## Djed pillar (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/djed-pillar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/djed-pillar.json
id: djed-pillar
native: 𓊽 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: djed · djt · backbone of Osiris · pillar of stability
said: JED, anglicised; Ancient Egyptian ḏd, Coptic ϫⲱⲧ jōt, 'pillar'
when: 1550 BCE – 1069 BCE
countries: EG
root: Egyptian ḏd 'pillar', surviving into Coptic as ϫⲱⲧ jōt. The sign writes the word for stability.
object: form=pendant materials=gold,faience worn=neck,chest,grave
against: the-dead — said by the Book of the Dead, as summarised in the source: a spell spoken over a gold djed hung at the mummy's neck promises the mummy will regain use of its spine and be able to sit up [s:wp-djed]
what: A column with four flat bars stacked across its top, like a capital with too many collars. As an amulet it is small and hung at the neck; the Book of the Dead specifies a gold one for a mummy. It is also painted onto coffins, and carved life-size in wood for a ceremony that raises it upright.
story: The djed is a spine that had to be set up again. In the Osiris myth, Set tricks Osiris into a coffin cut to fit him exactly and throws it in the Nile; it drifts to Byblos, a tree grows around it, the king of the land has the tree cut and stood in his palace as a pillar. Isis, searching, gets herself into the royal household, asks for that pillar, takes the coffin out of it, and then anoints the wood with myrrh and wraps it in linen. That is the pillar of djed.

So the ceremony is a resurrection staged as carpentry. At the Sed festival, the pharaoh with priests pulling on ropes hauls a wooden djed column upright at Memphis. It was read as Osiris's win over Set. The timing is agricultural: the month of Koiak, the fourth month of the Season of the Inundation, when the fields are being sown, inside the Osiris festival that ran from the thirteenth to the thirtieth of that month. A relief in Amenhotep III's Luxor temple shows the raising at his third Sed festival, in his thirty-seventh regnal year: the pillar stands in a shrine with a human body under a djed head, wedjat eyes, crook and flail, the feather crown and the sun disc; the king presents a loaded offering table; below, food-bearers weave between heavy-stepping dancers, singers give a short hymn to Ptah, and men box and do a stick dance. Sigrid Hodel-Hoenes, who describes the scene, reads the young women rattling Hathor sistra as the king's daughters, from the line of hieroglyphs above their heads: 'Children of the king praising (or charming) the noble djed pillar.'

The amulet is the private end of the same idea. It goes near the spine of a mummified body to make the resurrection happen, and the Book of the Dead gives a spell to be spoken over a gold djed hung at the mummy's neck: it promises the mummy will get the use of its spine back and be able to sit up.

*Tradition holds —* the sign starts somewhere agricultural, in a pillar of reeds or sheaves with grain piled round it, and only later attaches to Ptah and then to Osiris. Ptah was called 'the noble djed' and carried a sceptre that fused the djed with the ankh. By the New Kingdom the sign belongs to Osiris.
how: Cut or moulded small and hung at the neck, laid near the spine inside the wrappings, or painted on the coffin. The Book of the Dead's spell is spoken over a gold one. At festival scale it is a wooden column raised by ropes, with the king pulling and priests supporting it.
today: Not made and not raised; the ceremony ended with the religion. The sign survives as a museum label and as a design in jewellery sold to Egypt's visitors. As of 2026 this project has read no source describing anybody carrying a djed for what the Book of the Dead promised it would do.
kin: ankh-amulet — the sign it is run together with — 'life, dominion and stability' — and the composite of the three was worn more than either alone
kin: tyet-knot — the sign it is regularly paired with in writing; Egyptologists read the two together as the duality of life
kin: heart-scarab — the other amulet the wrappings required at the chest, aimed at a different organ and a different threat
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that placed it, by the rules of a funeral
kin: grave-deposit — the practice this amulet exists inside
kin: gold — the material the Book of the Dead's spell specifies for it
kin: the-charm-in-the-wall — the long read on charms built into structures — and the raised djed is the largest one Egypt built
sources: s:wp-djed s:wp-ankh s:wp-tyet s:wp-taweret s:wp-ancient-egyptian-funerary-practices s:wp-british-museum s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology
