## Dol hareubang (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/dolhareubang/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/dolhareubang.json
id: dolhareubang
native: 돌하르방 (Hangul)
aliases: tol harubang · harubang · useongmok 우석목 · ongjungseok 옹중석 · beoksumeori · stone grandfather
said: tol ha-ru-BANG
when: 1416 CE to now (still carried)
countries: KR
root: Jeju language dol 돌 'stone' + hareubang 하르방 'grandfather' — stone grandfather
object: form=statue worn=door
against: spirits — said by the record of the 1754 order at Jeju-mok, made after famines in the reigns of Sukjong and Yeongjo, when vengeful spirits were held to be roaming and tormenting the living [s:wp-dol-hareubang]
against: infertility — said by the folk belief recorded on Jeju: a woman with fertility trouble could take part of a statue's nose, grind it and consume the powder; others hold that touching the nose is enough [s:wp-dol-hareubang]
against: house — said by the statues' position — at gates and at the entrances of fortresses, at the boundaries of settlements, projecting power and security [s:wp-dol-hareubang]
what: A standing figure cut from Jeju's volcanic rock, wearing a round hat, with large eyes, a closed mouth, and one shoulder set higher than the other. Some have big ears; the hands sit in front, on the belly, or round the back. No two are alike. Many carry grooves cut into them for wooden logs — the jeongnang bars, whose position told a passer-by whether the entrance behind was open or shut. They stood at gates, and at the entrances of fortresses, which is to say at the edges of settlements, usually in pairs facing one another.
story: Nobody knows when the first ones were cut, and the record before 1914 on their number and location is thin. Three theories are in play: that a sea-faring people brought them to Jeju; that they developed out of jangseung or beoksu, the wooden guardian posts set up around mainland Korea; and a third the source leaves unnamed. What is on paper is this. Around 1416 six statues, in three pairs, reportedly stood on the island. By 1754 there were reportedly 48, of which 24 were at Jeju-mok — the town that is now Jeju City — four pairs each at the fortress's west, south and east gates. There is a record that ongjungseok statues were built at Jeju-mok in 1754, and some scholars take that as the earliest appearance of the figures in their present form. The reason given for the 1754 order is specific: after several famines in the reigns of Sukjong and Yeongjo, vengeful spirits were held to be roaming and tormenting the living, and the head of Jeju-mok ordered the statues built.

They were treated badly in the twentieth century. During the Japanese colonial period of 1910 to 1945 they were disregarded and moved around, and that continued through the rapid urban development after liberation. Because they were shifted, they wore, and it became hard to say where any of them came from. Research began in the 1960s; two were moved to the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul in 1968.

There are 47 or 48 pre-modern ones left. Twenty-one are in Jeju City, twelve in Seongeup-ri in Seogwipo, twelve across Inseong-ri, Anseong-ri and Boseong-ri, and two in Seoul. Everything else a visitor sees is recent.

The noses are worn down. One folk belief held that a woman with fertility trouble could secretly take a piece of a statue's nose, grind it to powder and swallow it; many statues have worn noses as a result. Others hold that touching the nose is enough.
how: Cut from volcanic basalt, set in pairs at a gate facing each other, sometimes on a stone platform called giseok — the statues at Jeju-seong and Jeongeuihyeon-seong tend to stand on one, those at Daejeonghyeon-seong do not. Grooves take the jeongnang logs. Some people reportedly paid their respects to the statues in passing. No consecration rite is described in this project's source, and none is invented here.
today: The figure is Jeju's emblem, and the souvenir trade is dated: the first replica was made in 1963 by the sculptor Song Jong-Won, a 25 cm copy of the statue at the south gate of Jeju-mok. Souvenir goods now run from miniatures to full-size recreations. Full-size ones have gone out as diplomatic gifts — to Mikhail Gorbachev at the 1991 Soviet–South Korean summit on Jeju, to Laizhou in China in 2002, and to the city hall of Santa Rosa, California, in 2003. Whether the thing on the shelf and the thing at the gate are the same object is the question this atlas puts and does not answer.
kin: bujeok — the other Korean guard in this atlas — paper, portable, and drawn by a mudang, where this is basalt and does not move
kin: korean-bujeok-craft — the Korean tradition of guarding a threshold that this stands at the monumental end of
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice at its heaviest: a doorway guard weighing more than the door
kin: phallic-sign — the sign read into the round hat, which is what ties the statue to the fertility use of its nose
kin: ongon — the steppe figure a spirit is seated in — the nearest thing in this atlas to a guardian carved to be inhabited
kin: hei-tiki — another carved ancestor-figure that became a national emblem and then a souvenir, and carries the same argument with it
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this belongs in: 47 or 48 originals, an island's worth of replicas, and three of them given away as state gifts
kin: insadong — Seoul's antique and craft district, where the replica trade meets the buyer far from Jeju

## Dreamcatcher (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/dreamcatcher/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/dreamcatcher.json
id: dreamcatcher
native: ᐊᓴᐱᑫᔒᓐᐦ (Canadian Aboriginal syllabics)
aliases: asabikeshiinh · asubakacin · bwaajige ngwaagan · spider web charm · dream snare
said: asabikeshiinh, the inanimate form of the Ojibwe word for spider
when: 1929 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US CA
root: Ojibwe asabikeshiinh, 'little net maker', the word for spider; White Earth Nation asubakacin, 'net-like'; Curve Lake First Nation bwaajige ngwaagan, 'dream snare'
object: form=knot materials=wood,thread,plastic worn=cradle,wall,vehicle
against: child-harm — said by Frances Densmore's Ojibwe informants, 1929 [s:wp-dreamcatcher]
RESTRICTED: Named Native writers say making and selling dreamcatchers belongs to Native makers. This record describes the object, its published history and the objection, and prints no instructions for making one.
what: A willow hoop with a net woven across it in sinew or plant cordage, tied off at a centre point, sometimes with feathers or beads added. Hung over a cradleboard or a bed. The mass-market version substitutes a steel or plastic ring, synthetic cord, dyed craft feathers and glass or plastic beads, and comes in sizes from earring to wall hanging.
story: It is Anishinaabe, and its oldest published account is a record of a charm for infants, not for dreams. The ethnographer Frances Densmore wrote down an Ojibwe account in 1929 of Asibikaashi, Spider Woman, who looks after the children and the people on the land; when the Ojibwe Nation spread to the corners of North America she could no longer reach every child, so mothers and grandmothers wove webs for them on willow hoops. Densmore's own words are plain about the purpose: the webs hung on the hoop of a cradle board "caught any harm that might be in the air as a spider's web catches and holds whatever comes in contact with it". In the old days the netting was nettle fibre, and two webs usually went on the hoop. Basil Johnston, an elder from Neyaashiinigmiing, gives Spider as a trickster catching Snake in his web in Ojibway Heritage, 1976.

Then it travelled. Derivative forms were taken up in the Pan-Indian movement of the 1960s and 1970s as a symbol of unity across different Native American cultures, and as a general mark of identification with Native or First Nations identity. Native Languages of the Americas, which is run by a Native-language non-profit, puts the spread carefully: "Ojibway dreamcatchers started to get popular in other Native American tribes, even those in disparate places like the Cherokee, Lakota, and Navajo. So dreamcatchers aren't traditional in most Indian cultures, per se, but they're sort of neo-traditional."

The name reached mainstream non-Native media in the 1970s; by the 1980s it was a widely marketed craft item, and by the early 1990s Wikipedia's account calls it "one of the most popular and marketable" of them. Forms appeared that bear little resemblance to traditional styles and use materials that were never traditionally used, made and sold by New Age groups and individuals.

That is the argument, and it has named people on both sides of it. Nudrat Karim, writing for The Indigenous Foundation, states the objection: "The appropriation of dreamcatchers exemplifies the dismissiveness of Native American culture and the borrowing of their spirituality to accommodate settlers," and draws the line by maker, not by object — "when non-Native people make and sell dreamcatchers it is in fact cultural appropriation however, when Indigenous people choose to make and sell dreamcatchers as they always have, it is not." Native Languages of the Americas is blunter about the trade: "Most of what you see when you search for 'Native American dreamcatchers' are cheap objects mass-produced in an Asian sweatshop somewhere or glued together by non-native teenagers with eBay accounts," and points readers to the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 and to buying from Native artists. Against that sit the pan-Indian communities for whom the hoop became a shared sign in the first place, and Ojibwe makers who sell them. This atlas prints both and settles neither.

The object is also still doing work in its own communities. A mounted and framed dreamcatcher is used as a shared symbol of hope and healing by the Little Thunderbirds Drum and Dance Troupe from the Red Lake Indian Reservation in Minnesota, who have taken it to students at other schools where shootings have happened, and passed it on.
how: This record does not give instructions. Named Native writers say the making is not open, and the atlas prints the restriction rather than the method. What is published and reported here is the material: a hoop of willow, and a net of sinew or of cordage made from plants, historically nettle fibre; two webs to a cradle hoop, per Densmore.
today: Made and sold by Ojibwe and other Native artists; made and sold in enormous volume by everybody else, worldwide, as of 2026, in craft shops, service stations and airports. The Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 governs what may be marketed as Native American-made in the United States.
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this record is the test case for — who may make a thing, and what changes when somebody else does
kin: hei-matau — the Pacific parallel: an Indigenous form mass-produced abroad, and objected to by name on the same grounds
kin: tupilaq — the Arctic parallel — an object that acquired a second life as a thing carved for visitors
kin: hei-tiki — another taonga sold in plastic beside the original, and another argument this atlas reports rather than settles
kin: the-fake-market — the long read about what a label is worth, which the Indian Arts and Crafts Act is one answer to
kin: nagpra — the other United States statute in this atlas about Native material and who holds it
kin: thread — the material that does the catching — nettle fibre, then sinew, then nylon
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this belongs in — the earliest published account is a charm for an infant on a cradleboard
kin: knot — the sign: a net, which holds what touches it
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read explaining why this record carries a restriction and no method
sources: s:wp-dreamcatcher s:web-indigenous-foundation-dreamcatchers s:web-native-languages-dreamcatchers s:wp-ojibwe s:wp-cultural-appropriation

## Dzi bead (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/dzi-bead/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/dzi-bead.json
id: dzi-bead
native: གཟི། (Tibetan)
aliases: gzi · zi bead · 天珠 · tian zhu · heaven's bead
said: zee
when: 700 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN NP BT IN TW
root: Tibetan gzi, 'shine, brightness, clearness, splendor'
object: form=bead materials=agate,carnelian worn=neck,wrist
against: evil-eye — said by the account of the beads' origin given in the source, which says the makers put eyes on them as a fight-fire-with-fire answer to the harmful look [s:wp-dzi-bead]
against: illness — said by Tibetan medicine, in which a portion of a bead is ground off and used, leaving dig marks [s:wp-dzi-bead]
against: spirits — said by Tibetan owners, for whom the beads attract local protectors, dharmapalas, deities, beneficial ghosts, ancestors or bodhisattvas [s:wp-dzi-bead]
what: A tube of agate, brown to black, carrying pale ivory-white patterns that were etched into the stone rather than cut: circles, ovals, squares, waves, zigzags, stripes, lines, diamonds, dots. The surface is usually smooth and waxy from long wear. The circular marks are called eyes, and the number and arrangement of them is the first thing a buyer counts. Strung on a Tibetan necklace, a dzi is normally flanked with coral, sometimes with amber and turquoise.
story: Nobody has settled where dzi come from, and this record does not pick a story. The account in the source read here says the stones first appear between 2000 and 1000 BCE in ancient India, and repeats a claim that a few hundred thousand were supposedly brought back by Tibetan soldiers from Persia during a raid. In the same passage the geographic origin is called uncertain, and the manufacturing method is called mysterious: treatments may have included darkening with plant sugars and heat, bleaching and white-line etching with natron, and masking areas with grease, clay or wax. What can be dated is narrower and firmer. Dzi-type agate beads were made in the Indus Valley in the Harappan period and at agate-rich sites in India such as Khambhat since Neolithic times, and the earliest archaeologically controlled find of an agate bead with dzi-style decoration — straight and curved lines and a circular eye — comes from a Saka-culture excavation at Uigarak in Kazakhstan, dated to the seventh to fifth century BCE, and was read as an import from India, evidence of long-distance trade with Saka or Scythian nomads.

Drilling is the one part of the making that is described in detail: the hole was made before the bead was decorated, because drilling caused most of the breakage, and a drilled bead could be strung and dipped for colouring. The earliest holes are conical, bored from both ends with solid flint tips; Neolithic beads were also drilled with hollow reed bits driven with abrasive, and copper ones in the Chalcolithic, which leave a parallel-walled hole. All of it was bow-drill work, and the time it took depended on the abrasive, from ground quartz to corundum.

*Tradition holds —* shepherds and farmers sometimes find dzi lying in soil or grassland, and some Tibetans have held on that evidence that the beads form naturally and are not made at all. In Tibetan culture the beads are said to attract local protectors, dharmapalas, deities, beneficial ghosts, ancestors or bodhisattvas, and are always treated with respect. They are handed down, which is how a single bead can pass through hundreds of wearers over centuries.

Beads also get eaten. Some carry small dig marks where a portion was scraped or ground away for use in Tibetan medicine; others show grinding and polishing from service as a burnishing tool for applying gold leaf to thangka paintings and gilded bronzes.
how: The bead is not made by its wearer and, for the old ones, not made by anyone alive. A new dzi is a different matter: the tradition holds it can be brought to the same standing by having a lama or guru bless it, by carrying it on pilgrimage to stupas and shrines, and by reciting mantras and taking religious vows with it. A stone thought to carry bad energy is submerged in salt water for several hours and then fanned with incense; sun-basking and herbal smudging are also named as purification, and spirit aroma offering and recitation of the Cintamani dharani as charging. New beads are held to carry one advantage the old ones cannot: none of the bad karma of a previous owner.
today: A market with a forgery problem at every price. Ancient beads can reach hundreds of thousands of US dollars, more for beads with more eyes and for the tiny red bloodspots that iron inclusions leave; new dzi run from about ten to two thousand US dollars by quality and lustre. The source read in September 2026 does not date those figures, so read them as undated. Modern-era dzi-style beads were made at Idar-Oberstein in Germany at least as early as the 19th century by agate cutters who had worked there since Roman times and who brought agate colouring to a science. Imitation dzi are made of glass, resin, lampwork, wood, bone, plastic, metal and non-traditional etched stones; some resin ones are filled with lead for weight; older mock dzi have collectible value of their own. At the bottom, mass-produced machine-carved beads sell for under two US dollars, often by the strand, with etching that does not penetrate the core — mostly to mainland Chinese buyers as feng shui charms. Tibetans also buy new beads, as an affordable and obtainable alternative, and whether a new bead is the same object as an old one is argued inside the tradition, not only outside it.
kin: eye — the sign counted on its surface — an eye here is a circle, and the number of them sets the price
kin: gau-box — what hangs on the same cord: the box holds the written amulet, the bead hangs beside it
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that receives it, blesses new ones, and hands old ones down
kin: coral — what a dzi is flanked with on a Tibetan necklace — and, like the bead, something that reached Tibet from somewhere else
kin: turquoise — the third stone on the same string, and the one Tibet could supply itself
kin: carnelian — the stone of the chung dzi, the ordinary etched beads counted as a lesser kind of the same thing
kin: nazar — the other eye-bead with a market in the millions — glass instead of agate, and priced by the tray instead of by the eye
kin: the-fake-market — the long read this bead belongs in: imitations run from 19th-century German cutting to two-dollar machine beads, and the tells are the whole trade
kin: barkhor-lhasa — the Lhasa circuit where beads change hands
kin: kathmandu-thamel — the other Himalayan street they are sold on, mostly to visitors
kin: rudraksha — the South Asian bead graded the same way — by counting the marks on it — and costing a fraction as much
sources: s:wp-dzi-bead s:wp-turquoise s:wp-coral s:wp-carnelian s:wp-tibetan-buddhism

## Ekeko (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ekeko/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ekeko.json
id: ekeko
native: Iqiqu (Latin)
aliases: Iqiqu · Ekhako · Eqaqo · Ekhekho
said: eh-KEH-ko
when: 1781 CE to now (still carried)
countries: BO PE
root: Aymara Ekhako or Eqaqo, popularised as Ekhekho — the name of the god of fortune and prosperity in Qullasuyu; contemporary Aymara spelling Iqiqu
object: form=figurine materials=terracotta,paper,coin worn=hearth,neck,pocket,shop
against: poverty — said by the figure's owners [s:wp-ekeko]
against: attraction — said by Alasitas buyers, who give a miniature so the recipient gets the real thing within the year [s:wp-alasitas]
against: house — said by Aymara households; the cited source says the Ekhako was invoked when a disgrace disturbed the home [s:wp-ekeko]
what: A short, moustached man in Andean dress, above all a poncho, loaded to the shoulders with everything a household could want: bags and baskets of grain, food, pots, tools, banknotes. Most are cast plaster now; the colonial ones were clay. Modern figures have a hole in the mouth sized for a lit cigarette. Small versions go on key rings and necklaces.
story: The Ekeko is the Tiwanakan god of abundance and prosperity in the folklore of the Altiplano, and in Bolivia he is the figure the Alasitas fair is built around. That fair opens on 24 January in La Paz and runs for a month; in Peru the main festival is 3 May, in Puno, on the Machallata hill. Elsewhere the Ekeko's festival falls in October under the name Calvario.

Four named scholars argue about what he was before the colony. Ernesto Cavour, in his book Alasitas, points to anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures in stone, mud and gold found in the Bolivian departments of La Paz, Oruro and Potosí, made from basalt out of the pre-Columbian mines on the shores of Lake Poopó and andesite from the Copacabana peninsula. Carlos Ponce Sanginés works on humped, phallic figures he places in the Inca period and reads as the colonial Ekeko's predecessors. Antonio Paredes Candia takes them for the remains of summer-solstice festivals. Arthur Posnansky observed that around 22 December the Tiwanaku population offered miniatures of what they wanted to their gods.

The story Bolivians tell puts him in 1781, during the siege of La Paz. As Antonio Díaz Villamil narrates it, Paulita Tintaya, an Indigenous girl working for Doña Josefa Ursula de Rojas Foronda, had been given a small Ekeko by Isidoro Choquehuanca before she left the hacienda where they grew up. Isidoro, serving in the Indigenous army besieging the city, left food by the statue outside the house each week without saying so. Paulita and her employer survived the siege on it. *Tradition holds —* La Paz tells that story as the origin of the Ekeko's power to provide.

What the figure is offered is specific. Banknotes are clipped to him. Grain is given for good harvests. Statuettes with the mouth opening are given a lit cigarette — in the most recent form of the practice, once a year, to secure a full year of prosperity.
how: Cast in plaster, painted, then loaded. The Ekeko goes in a place of honour in the house and is added to rather than replaced: more miniatures, more banknotes, a cigarette on the day. Miniatures bought at Alasitas can be blessed by the men and, less often, women working the fair as shamans, and at midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses the gifts at the main cathedral in La Paz. Small Ekekos ride on key rings and necklaces and are not offered anything.
today: Sold across western Bolivia and southern Peru, and central to a fair that fills streets and parks across central La Paz every January. In March 2011 Elizabeth Salguero, Bolivia's Minister of Cultures, nominated Alasitas along with two other Bolivian festivals to UNESCO for recognition as intangible cultural heritage. In 2016 the Feast of Alasita and the miniatures of the Altiplano of Puno were declared Cultural Heritage of the Nation of Peru.
kin: andean-illa-practice — the tradition this figure is the public face of — a miniature is a claim on the full-size thing
kin: illa — the older Andean miniature, kept by herders for their animals rather than by households for their money
kin: mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz — the La Paz market where he is sold year-round, not only in January
kin: maneki-neko — the other figure in this atlas that sits at a till and is expected to pull custom in
kin: feeding-the-charm — the practice this record turns on: banknotes clipped on, grain offered, a cigarette lit once a year
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — what happens to the miniatures at midday on 24 January, at the cathedral in La Paz
kin: buying-in-a-market — how one is got — and at Alasitas, buying is the rite
kin: unesco-ich — the body Bolivia nominated Alasitas to in March 2011
sources: s:wp-ekeko s:wp-alasitas

## Ethiopian talismanic scroll (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ethiopian-magic-scroll/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ethiopian-magic-scroll.json
id: ethiopian-magic-scroll
native: ክታብ (Ge'ez)
aliases: healing scroll · protective scroll · kitab · ketab
said: kitab, ketab
when: 1500 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ET
object: form=scroll materials=parchment,ink,cloth,leather worn=neck,wall,pocket
against: evil-eye — said by the scrolls themselves — the spells, prayers and formulas they carry offer protection or cure against the Evil Eye [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: spirits — said by the same texts, against malevolent spirits [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: illness — said by the source, which gives the range as 'bed bugs, to home intruders, to smallpox', and says the scroll treats the spiritual cause while homeopathic medicines address the physical symptoms [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: childbirth — said by the historical manuscript record, which the source says shows the majority made for women's reproductive health conditions [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: theft — said by the source's own list, which names home intruders [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
RESTRICTED: The prayers, the mystical names of God and the invocations written on a scroll are the dabtara's craft and are not reproduced here. This record prints what the scroll is, what it is for, and how it is made — not its text, and no formula.
what: A long strip of parchment — goat or sheep hide, soaked, dried, stretched, scraped and washed until it takes ink — painted with prayers in Ge'ez and with talismanic drawings, then rolled. A personal one is cut to the height of the person it is for. Larger ones hang on a wall. The colours are black, white, red, blue, green and yellow. Crosses and eight-pointed stars recur; so does the gätsä säb'e, a face inside an eight-pointed star; so do eyes, painted in geometric pairs and rimmed in red.
story: The scroll is the size of its owner. That is the first fact anybody who handles one notices, and it is the fact that explains the rest: this is not a text about a person, it is a stand-in for one.

It is made by a dabtara — an unordained cleric of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church who has gone past memorising the Psalms into poetry, liturgy and writing. In Ethiopia the power to write includes the power to write prayers and spells, so the word carries a second sense as well. The making involves the sacrifice of an animal, usually a goat or a sheep, standing for the person the scroll is for; the patron is rubbed by and bathed in the contents of the animal, and the hide becomes the parchment.

The writing is Ge'ez, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church's liturgical language. Because few speak it now, a scroll does not work by being owned: a third party literate in Ge'ez has to read it aloud to the afflicted person. *Inference —* that makes the scroll one of the few amulets in this atlas that needs another human being present to function at all.

What it is against runs from the small to the fatal. The range the source gives is bed bugs, home intruders, smallpox. It treats the spiritual cause; homeopathic medicines are used alongside it for the physical symptoms. Historical manuscripts show the majority were made for conditions of women's reproductive health.

The oldest surviving examples are sixteenth-century, though the practice is held to go back to the tenth. The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds several, including an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century scroll of parchment, pigments and cotton.
how: An animal is sacrificed for the person the scroll is for. The hide is soaked for several days, dried, stretched, then scraped, washed and dried again into parchment. The dabtara writes the prayers and the mystical names and paints the talismanic figures in the six standard colours. A personal scroll is cut to the owner's height, though it may be made longer. It is rolled, often kept in a leather case, and carried; a larger one hangs. To work, it is read aloud in Ge'ez by somebody who can read Ge'ez.
today: Still made and still commissioned, and still being collected. The Museum of Witchcraft and Magic in Boscastle publishes one, and the Metropolitan Museum publishes several. As of 2026 the split between scrolls made for a patron and scrolls made for the trade in old Ethiopian manuscripts is not something this project has read a figure for.
kin: ethiopian-scroll-craft — the tradition that makes it — the dabtara's writing, and the church it sits beside without being ordained into
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the other African Christian mark in this atlas, worn by neighbours up the same river and carried on skin rather than on hide
kin: cippus-of-horus — the older Nile answer to the same problem — words that must be got off a surface and into a patient
kin: parchment — the material, and the animal that stood in for the patron before it became one
kin: eye — the sign painted on it in geometric pairs, rimmed in red, against the harm that arrives by looking
kin: cross — the other sign it carries, and the church whose language it is written in
kin: divine-name — what is written on it: prayers, saints, the Trinity, and the mystical names
kin: talismanic-shirt — another garment-shaped text amulet, cut to a body and covered in writing
kin: merkato-addis — the market in Addis Ababa where scrolls and church goods are traded
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read behind the restriction on this page — the scroll's text is not printed here
sources: s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls s:wp-amulet s:wp-talisman s:wp-wellcome-collection
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Evil eye bracelet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/evil-eye-bracelet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/evil-eye-bracelet.json
id: evil-eye-bracelet
native: nazar boncuğu (Latin)
aliases: nazar bracelet · eye bead bracelet · mati bracelet · 🧿
said: nah-ZAR bon-joo-OO
when: 1600 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: TR GR
object: form=bracelet materials=glass,thread,plastic,silver worn=wrist,neck,phone,vehicle,door,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by wearers across Turkey, Greece, the Balkans, West and South Asia and the diaspora [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
against: envy — said by the usual explanation given by carriers of the eye across its whole range [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: bad-luck — said by wearers, per the Turkish account the cited source gives [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
what: One or more blue-and-white eye beads on an elastic cord, a chain or a red string, sized for a wrist. The bead itself is handmade glass with concentric circles or teardrop shapes in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes with a yellow or gold edge. The cheapest versions replace the glass with printed enamel, resin or a stamped metal disc. The sign has been a Unicode character since 2018: U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET.
story: The bead is old and the bracelet is not, and it is worth keeping the two apart. Written documentation and surviving glass eye beads run back to the sixteenth century BCE, and the form spread with glassmaking from Mesopotamia to Egypt, Carthage to Greece, Phoenicia to Persia, and through the Roman empire. The bead on a stretchy cord at a checkout counter is a recent packaging of that, and this project cannot date it.

What the bead is made of is itself part of the claim. The cited account says it is made from a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water and salt — "ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil" — and that "according to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity". One further explanation is given for why the colour is blue: in the Middle East and the Mediterranean blue eyes are relatively rare, so light-eyed people were held able to curse with a look.

Somebody still makes the glass ones by hand. The Kültürel Araştırmalar Vakfı records the traditional production continuing at Nazarköy, in Kemalpaşa near İzmir, where the beads are made by a few simple hand tools, mostly in blue and white glass; Görece, in Menderes, is the other village named for the craft. Set against that is the mass-produced bracelet, the volume of which is the reason most of the world's eye beads are now within anybody's reach. Whether the two are the same object is a live argument. This project did not reach a source it could cite giving the bead-makers' own account of competition from imported beads, and so does not report their side in their words here — a gap, and named as one.

The bead's own instruction for failure is the detail worth keeping. If one breaks, the account goes, a very strong nazar hit the wearer and the bead stored it all up and broke in order to protect them. *Inference —* a charm with a published failure mode that is also a success story is a charm that cannot be disproved by breaking, which is one reason the object survives packaging changes that would kill a less well-designed one.
how: Glass is melted in a furnace, drawn and layered — dark blue ground, white, light blue, black centre — one bead at a time, then strung. Mass-market versions are moulded or printed and strung by machine. There is no consecration and no specialist: a bracelet is bought, or given, and worn until it breaks, at which point it is replaced rather than repaired.
today: Sold everywhere, in every price band, in 2026: airport shops in Istanbul and Athens, market stalls from Tbilisi to Mumbai, fast-fashion chains worldwide, and as an emoji on every phone. This project has no dated price to print and no production figure.
kin: nazar — the bead itself, which this record is the wrist-sized retail packaging of
kin: eye — the sign, and the reason a factory bead and a hand-blown one make the same claim
kin: glass — the material that made the sign cheap enough to sell by the tray, three thousand years ago and again now
kin: red-string — the other thing tied to a wrist against the same harm, with no image on it at all
kin: hamsa — the hand that usually carries this eye in its palm, sold from the same stands
kin: charm-coin — another mass-produced charm this atlas describes in the same terms as a hand-cut one
kin: the-charm-goes-digital — the long read this belongs in: the sign is now a Unicode character as well as a bead
kin: grand-bazaar — one place a reader can stand and see the whole price range on one street
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that follows this sign across four continents
kin: ojo-de-venado — Mexico's answer to the same harm, and it breaks for the same stated reason

## Exam charm (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/exam-charm/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/exam-charm.json
id: exam-charm
native: 合格祈願 (Han)
aliases: gōkaku kigan · gakugyō-jōju omamori · kitto katsu Kit Kat · yeot · chapssaltteok · exam omamori
said: gōkaku kigan, 'prayer for passing'; in Korean, the gift is yeot (엿) or chapssaltteok (찹쌀떡)
when: 1979 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP KR
root: Japanese 合格祈願 gōkaku kigan, from 合格 gōkaku 'passing an examination' and 祈願 kigan 'prayer, petition'
object: form=packet materials=cloth,paper,wood,thread worn=pocket,phone,wall
against: exams — said by Dazaifu Tenmangū, in its own words on its own English page [s:web-dazaifu-tenmangu-amulets]
against: exams — said by Japanese shrines and temples generally, whose standard omamori list includes gakugyō-jōju, education and passing examinations [s:wp-omamori]
against: exams — said by Japanese students, one in three of whom buys a Kit Kat before entrance examinations, on the figure Japan House at the University of Illinois publishes [s:web-japanhouse-kitkat]
against: exams — said by Korean families and friends, who give a student sticky yeot and chapssaltteok before the Suneung [s:wp-yeot]
what: Four different objects doing one job. A brocade pouch a few centimetres long, the shrine's name woven into it, a paper or wooden prayer sealed inside and not to be opened. A wooden plaque about 15 by 9 centimetres, written on and hung at the shrine. A two-finger chocolate bar in a printed wrapper. A stick of boiled-down grain taffy. The first two come from a shrine; the last two come from a supermarket, and a student carries any of them into the same room.
story: Japan's examination charm has a god, and he was a real man. Sugawara no Michizane was a Heian-period scholar and poet who was exiled to Kyushu and died there; he is enshrined as Tenjin, god of scholarship and learning — and of natural disasters, which is a detail worth keeping. Dazaifu Tenmangū, the shrine built where he was exiled, states it plainly on its own English page: "As Tenjin is the deity of learning, amulets for academic success are one of the most popular items to take home from Dazaifu Tenmangu." Many of the amulets carry the plum flower, which the shrine says Michizane loved and which is its symbol. The shrine's own framing of the exchange is careful and worth quoting as printed: "At Shinto shrines you can receive an omamori, or amulet, to bring good luck, for a small donation." Received, for a donation. Not bought.

The omamori for this is gakugyō-jōju, education and passing examinations, one of a standard list that also runs to traffic safety, safe childbirth, a good marriage, business prosperity and family peace. The rule is the same as for every omamori: do not open it, and return the old one to the shrine it came from — traditionally to be burnt rather than binned, out of respect to the deity that carried you through the year.

The second Japanese object is the Kit Kat, and the wordplay has to be got right. キットカット, Kitto Katto, is what the brand is called in Japanese. Kitto means surely. Katsu means to win. The Kyushu phrase is きっと勝つとぉ, kitto katsutoo, 'you shall surely win', and that is the thing the brand name sounds like. Peter Davis, writing for Japan House at the University of Illinois, gives the figure: "In fact, one in three students in Japan will buy a Kit-Kat in anticipation of entrance examinations." The English Wikipedia article is more guarded and says the marketing "is believed to have benefited from the coincidental false cognate", and that market research shows the brand strongly correlated with good-luck charms among students ahead of exams. *Inference —* the two accounts differ on how much of this Nestlé made and how much of it Nestlé found, and this project does not have the internal documents to settle that. What is dated is the marketing: the 'Lucky Charm' campaign won the Asian Brand Marketing Effectiveness Award in 2005, and in 2009 Nestlé and Japan Post ran a campaign letting people write on the bars and post them from 20,000 post offices — which won the Media Grand Prix at Cannes Lions in 2010.

Korea works the same joke on a different verb. Families and friends give a student 엿, yeot — a taffy boiled down from steamed rice, glutinous rice, sorghum, corn or sweet potato — and 찹쌀떡, chapssaltteok, glutinous rice cake, before the Suneung university entrance examination. Both are sticky. The Korean verb for sticking to something is also the verb for passing an exam, so the gift says what it means without saying it. The English Wikipedia entry on yeot confirms students receive it before examinations and otherwise concentrates on the same word's career as an obscenity, which is the other thing a Korean reader knows about it.

The shrine end of the trade has been argued about in public, with a date attached. In 1979 two shrines dedicated to education sold ema — the wooden prayer plaques — for examination success; after public outcry, the funds were turned into a scholarship in 1980. *Inference —* that is the cleanest instance this atlas has of a charm trade answering a complaint by converting the takings into the thing the charm was asking for.
how: An omamori is received at the shrine office for a donation, carried on the person or tied to a bag, not opened, and returned to the same shrine at the New Year to be burnt. An ema is bought at the shrine, written on, and hung on the rack until it is ritually burnt at a ceremony — the burning treated as freeing the wish. A Kit Kat is bought at a convenience store, sometimes posted, and eaten. Yeot and chapssaltteok are given by family and friends and eaten. Nothing consecrates the last two, and nobody claims anything does.
today: Running every winter. Japanese entrance-examination season and the Korean Suneung both fall in the cold months, and the shelves change accordingly. As of 2026 the shrine goods, the exam-season chocolate packaging and the taffy all coexist, with the shrine goods carrying a deity's name and the other two carrying a pun. No dated price was read for any of them, and neither Dazaifu Tenmangū's page nor the sources on the Korean gifts print one.
kin: omamori — the object itself — this record is the one variety of it that has grown a supermarket aisle of its own
kin: ofuda — the shrine's paper talisman, sold from the same counter and kept at home rather than carried
kin: omikuji — the other thing bought at the same window on the same visit, and the one that answers back
kin: daruma — the other Japanese object bought against a goal — one eye filled in when the vow is made, the other when it comes off
kin: bujeok — the Korean written talisman, made by a specialist where the exam gift is made by a confectioner
kin: phone-charm — where a student's omamori actually hangs — the cited account says they are often spotted on cellphone straps
kin: game-day-charm — the same object with a scoreboard instead of an answer sheet, and the same argument about what carrying it does
kin: burning-retirement — what happens to the omamori and the ema afterwards — returned and burnt, not binned
kin: fushimi-inari — one shrine where the charm counter is a shop floor and the scale of the trade is visible from the queue
kin: insadong — the Seoul quarter where the Korean end of this shelf is sold
kin: the-charm-goes-digital — the long read this belongs in: the charm that is also a chocolate bar, a postcard and a marketing award

## Fascinum (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/fascinum/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/fascinum.json
id: fascinum
native: fascinum (Latin)
aliases: fascinus · winged phallus · phallic pendant · fist-and-phallus amulet
said: FAS-ki-num; also fascinus
when: 300 BCE – 399 CE
countries: IT GB LY
root: Latin fascinum, and the verb fascinare, 'to use the power of the fascinus' — to work magic, hence to enchant or bewitch; English fascinate comes from it
object: form=pendant materials=copper,bone,silver,gold worn=neck,finger,wall,door,vehicle
against: evil-eye — said by Pliny the Elder [s:wp-fascinus]
against: envy — said by Roman practice: the Vestals hung the effigy under a triumphing general's chariot against invidia [s:wp-fascinus]
against: child-harm — said by Varro, who records the custom of hanging a phallic charm on a baby's neck; rings survive sized only for children [s:wp-fascinus]
against: house — said by the rite of Father Liber reported by Augustine from Varro, in which the image went round the fields to repel fascinatio from them [s:wp-fascinus]
against: war — said by Roman soldiers, among whom the fist-and-phallus type was prevalent; the largest known collection is from Camulodunum [s:wp-fascinus]
what: A phallus, worn. Usually cast in bronze, often winged, pierced or looped for a cord; also cut as finger rings, carved in relief on walls, made into lamps and into wind chimes called tintinnabula. The soldiers' type adds a clenched fist at the base of the shaft, pointing away from the glans, and on several examples the fist is making the manus fica, the fig sign. Some combine vulvar imagery with the rest.
story: Pliny called the fascinus a medicus invidiae — a doctor, a remedy, for invidia. Invidia is envy, and it is built from a word for looking upon. That is the whole theory of the object in two Latin words.

Rome put it everywhere. The Vestal Virgins tended the cult of the fascinus populi Romani, a sacred phallus counted among the tokens of the state's safety alongside the Palladium; when a general celebrated a triumph, the Vestals hung an effigy of it under his chariot to protect him from invidia. Augustine, reading Varro, reports the phallus carried on a little trolley through the countryside crossroads at the festival of Father Liber and then into the city, to secure the growth of seeds and "repel enchantment (fascinatio) from the fields".

On the body it was mostly for children, and mainly boys. Varro records hanging a phallic charm on a baby's neck, and phallus-bearing rings survive that are too small for anyone but a child to wear. There are very few Roman images of a person actually wearing one. A 2017 experimental archaeology project found that some pendant types were designed to stay pointing outwards, in the wearer's direction of travel, facing whatever was coming.

The imagery is not shy about the mechanism. Reliefs from Leptis Magna in present-day Libya and several instances on Hadrian's Wall show the phallus ejaculating towards a disembodied eye; a first-century BCE terracotta figurine shows "two little phallus-men sawing an eyeball in half". The largest known collection of fist-and-phallus amulets comes from Camulodunum, the Roman colony under modern Colchester.

*Tradition holds —* the protective force is usually explained by the virile and regenerative power of an erect phallus. The cited account puts a second explanation beside it and does not choose: in most cases what diverts the evil eye is the emotion the obscenity produces — shame, or laughter.
kin: phallic-sign — the sign this object is, in its plainest form
kin: fist — the second sign bolted onto it in the soldiers' type — a clenched hand making the fig
kin: eye — the thing it is aimed at, and on the Leptis Magna and Hadrian's Wall reliefs, literally
kin: bulla — the locket a Roman boy wore, with one of these usually inside it
kin: lunula — the girls' equivalent — a crescent instead of a phallus, and the same nine-days-to-adulthood logic
kin: cornicello — southern Italy's living descendant: the same interception, reshaped as a horn in red coral
kin: gorgoneion — the Greek answer to the same problem — terror where Rome used laughter
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and the one place in it where the state itself kept a charm
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian who assembled the European evidence for the eye and its substitutes, and put this object in the same drawer as the horn and the hand
sources: s:wp-fascinus s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-fig-sign s:wp-cornicello
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Figa (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/figa/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/figa.json
id: figa
native: figa (Latin)
aliases: higa · cigua · fig hand · mano fica · manus fica · fig sign amulet
said: FEE-gah
when: 100 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: PT BR ES IT GR
root: Latin ficus, 'fig' — Italian far le fiche, 'to make the fig'; Spanish higa, Galician and Portuguese figa, Asturleonese cigua
object: form=pendant materials=jet,coral,silver,gold,bone worn=neck,wrist,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by the ancient Greeks, who wore amulets of the gesture at the neck, and present-day wearers in Portugal, Brazil, Galicia and Asturias [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: spirits — said by the Roman pater familias, who made the sign during the Lemuria [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: child-harm — said by Asturian families, who give jet ones to small children [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: bad-luck — said by wearers in Portugal, Brazil and parts of Spain, where the sign means good luck [s:wp-fig-sign]
what: A closed fist with the thumb pushed up between the index and middle fingers, carved small and drilled for a cord. In Asturias it is cut from jet; elsewhere from coral, silver, gold, bone or moulded resin. Worn at the neck or wrist, or pinned on a small child.
story: The gesture came first and it was rude. In ancient Rome the manus fica was made by the pater familias during the Lemuria, the festival of the restless dead, to drive the dead spirits off. The ancient Greeks wore amulets of the same gesture around the neck against the evil eye and used it in their artwork: what they took to be an overtly sexual gesture was expected to distract an evil spirit from doing harm. Early Christians called it the manus obscena.

In Italy it stayed rude. Fica in mano, far le fiche, comparable to the finger; Dante puts it in Inferno, Canto XXV; medieval painters give it to the tormentors in a Man of Sorrows. The gesture there has long since fallen out of use.

What survived, and where, is the point. In Portugal, Brazil, and parts of Spain — Galicia and Asturias especially — the fig is a gesture of good luck and a ward against the evil eye, and an amulet of a hand making it is worn for exactly that. In Asturias the amulets are jet, and it is usual to give one to a young child. The same hand shape, in Britain, Ireland, France, Germany, Argentina, Uruguay and the United States, carries no charge at all and is the joke where an adult steals a child's nose.

*Inference —* one hand shape, running simultaneously as an obscenity in Turkey, a refusal in Poland, a sexual invitation in Denmark and a child's amulet in Asturias, is the clearest case this atlas has of a sign whose meaning is entirely local while its form is continent-wide. The eye travels with its reading attached. The fist does not.
how: Carved from jet, coral, precious metal or bone, pierced at the wrist end, strung on a cord — red, where the tradition uses red. Given to a child rather than bought by one. No consecration is described in the source read here.
today: Sold in Portugal, Brazil, Galicia and Asturias as jewellery and as a child's charm, and made in every grade from cut jet to moulded resin. Whether the resin one does the same job as the jet one is an argument with people on both sides of it, and this atlas reports it without joining.
kin: fist — the sign itself, and this is its commonest carved form
kin: azabache — the Caribbean and Spanish jet version of this exact hand, under a name taken from the stone
kin: hand — the wider family — the open palm answers the same look with the opposite gesture
kin: fascinum — the Roman substitute for the same job, the phallus instead of the fist
kin: cornicello — southern Italy's surviving answer, after the fig fell out of use there
kin: jet — the Asturian material, and the one that carries the child's version
kin: eye — the sign this substitutes for — something startling enough to take a look
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that asks why the eye travels with its meaning and this hand does not
sources: s:wp-fig-sign s:wp-jet-gemstone s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-apotropaic-magic
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Four-leaf clover (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/four-leaf-clover/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/four-leaf-clover.json
id: four-leaf-clover
aliases: quadrifoglio · lucky clover · four-leaved shamrock
when: 1600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IE GB US
root: English four-leaf clover; Italian quadrifoglio, 'four-leaf'.
object: materials=herb,plastic,paper worn=pocket,wallet
against: bad-luck — said by an eleven-year-old girl, writing to St. Nicholas Magazine in 1877 [s:wp-four-leaf-clover]
against: loneliness — said by an 1869 description, of young girls who sought the plant by day as a token of perfect happiness [s:wp-four-leaf-clover]
against: spirits — said by the folk tradition that a four-leaf clover grants the power to see fairies [s:wp-four-leaf-clover]
what: A clover leaf with four leaflets instead of three, usually white clover, Trifolium repens. It is a mutation, not a species. Found ones are pressed flat in a book or sealed in plastic; grown ones are sold the same way. Collectors in Ireland prize the five-leaflet version, which they call a rose clover.
story: The arithmetic is the whole appeal, and it has been measured. A 2017 survey of about 5.7 million clovers across six European countries put the frequency at roughly one four-leaf clover in every 5,076 — around 5,000 to one, which is almost twice as common as the 10,000-to-one figure people usually quote. The same survey gives 24,390 to one for five leaflets and 312,500 to one for six.

The luck attached to it goes back to at least the seventeenth century. A description from 1869 splits the practice by who is doing it: the clovers were "gathered at night-time during the full moon by sorceresses, who mixed it with vervain and other ingredients, while young girls in search of a token of perfect happiness made quest of the plant by day." Eight years later an eleven-year-old girl put the folk version in a letter to St. Nicholas Magazine: "Did the fairies ever whisper in your ear, that a 4-leaf clover brought good luck to the finder?" Some traditions assign a meaning to each leaflet — Christians have used them for hope, faith, love and luck — and others say the clover grants the power to see fairies.

The charm's condition is that you find it, and industry has been steadily dissolving that condition. There are reports of farms in the United States producing as many as 10,000 a day, sealed in plastic and sold as lucky charms, by introducing a genetically engineered ingredient that encourages the aberration. Cultivars that reliably throw extra leaflets have existed for a long time — Trifolium repens "Purpurascens Quadrifolium", "Quadrifolium", and a cultivar actually called "Good Luck". A 2009 study exposed white clover flowers to gamma radiation during pollination and produced a cultivar yielding up to 60 per cent four-leaf clovers. Phosphate fertiliser and the plant hormone auxin both raise the rate.

Finding them is also a sport. Guinness World Records lists the clover with the most leaflets ever found at 63, discovered by Yoshiharu Watanabe of Nasushiobara, Tochigi prefecture, Japan, on 2 August 2023, beating a 56-leaf clover found by Shigeo Obara of Hanamaki, Iwate prefecture, on 10 May 2009. Both men bred for it. An expert finder interviewed by the New York Times described the technique as scanning a patch for ruptures in the pattern: three leaflets make a triangle, four make a square.
how: Found, in spring, before the first mowing. Picked, pressed flat between the pages of a book or laminated, and carried in a wallet or a pocket. Nothing is said or done over it. There is no retirement rite; it fades.
today: Carried as a personal charm, farmed by the thousand and sold sealed in plastic, and used as a corporate emblem by organisations that have nothing to do with either. Alfa Romeo has used the quadrifoglio on its racing and performance cars since the driver Ugo Sivocci painted a green clover on a white ground for the 1923 Targa Florio. SpaceX has embroidered a four-leaf clover on every mission patch since the first successful Falcon 1 launch in 2008, which the company describes as being for luck. *Inference —* a charm whose whole claim rests on being rare is the charm most exposed to being manufactured, and the farm and the meadow versions are sold in the same packet.
kin: rabbits-foot — the other charm that must be taken under conditions nobody observes any more, and the other one a factory now supplies
kin: horseshoe — the other object whose oldest rule is that it must be found and not bought
kin: herb — what it actually is: a plant, carried dead and flattened, and the only charm in this atlas measured by a botanical survey
kin: luck-word — the word that has entirely replaced protection here — nothing in this record names a harm it turns away
kin: mascot-word — where it ends up: an emblem on a racing car and a rocket patch rather than an object in a pocket
kin: exam-charm — what a student carries now, and often this, flattened in a wallet
kin: game-day-charm — the sporting end of the same habit, from Ugo Sivocci's 1923 Targa Florio clover onward
kin: the-fake-market — the long read this belongs in: 10,000 a day, grown to order, sold as the thing you were supposed to find
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it came out of, and its least protective object
sources: s:wp-four-leaf-clover s:wp-luck s:wp-list-of-lucky-symbols s:wp-mascot

## Fu talisman (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/fu-talisman/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/fu-talisman.json
id: fu-talisman
native: 符籙 (Han)
aliases: fulu · fu · 符箓 · talismanic script · Taoist talisman
said: foo-LOO
when: 317 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN TW
root: Chinese 符 fú — instructions for deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions or charms used to treat ailments — with 籙 lù, a registry of the memberships of priests that also lists the skills they are trained in
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,ink,cloth,coin worn=pocket,door,wall,vehicle
against: illness — said by Chinese medical writing, where the practice is called zhuyou and was used alongside drugs, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage [s:wp-fulu]
against: spirits — said by Taoist coin talismans, most of which ask Lei Gong to protect their carriers from evil spirits and misfortune [s:wp-fulu]
against: demons — said by the exorcism use named in the word itself: fu are instructions for deities and spirits and symbols for exorcism [s:wp-fulu]
against: bad-luck — said by the same coin talismans, which name misfortune alongside evil spirits [s:wp-fulu]
RESTRICTED: How the characters of talismanic script are written is passed from a Taoist priest to their disciples in secret, and differs from sect to sect. This atlas describes what the writing looks like and what scholars say about its illegibility, and does not reproduce a talisman or a method for drawing one.
what: A sheet — usually paper, sometimes cloth, sometimes a coin's face — written over in a script nobody is meant to read. The strokes are irregular and resemble Chinese characters, often stretching an existing word out of shape and mixing in marks that are not characters at all. Taoist priests are the main interpreters of this writing, and the characters differ from sect to sect.
story: The illegibility is the design, and it has a history. Yang Zhaohua notes that a number of the earliest known Taoist talismans were simple and legible, and that later examples became deliberately cryptic in order to signal their divinity. James Robson and Gil Raz have argued that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority and efficacy, and is one of talismanic script's defining features. By the Eastern Jin dynasty, 317 to 420, it was already held unnecessary for a user to be able to decipher the writing: Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi that as long as the inscription was correct, use did not depend on the user reading it. Ge Zhaoguang, of Fudan University, calls the unreadability a kind of linguistic archaism, built to be incomprehensible — "a veil of unfathomable otherwordliness" that lets only a small number of qualified clergy produce them properly.

The writing has been medicine for as long as it has been anything. Known in medical writings as zhuyou, the use of talismans ran alongside drugs, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage; the Way of the Taiping was healing patients with it at least as far back as the Eastern Han. Zhuyou held official support from the Sui to the late Ming, and declined when acupuncture was recognised by the imperial court as a medical discipline in the sixth century. It is rejected by traditional Chinese medicine and still widely used by folk healers, and in the twentieth century, as Western psychology arrived, it began to be read as a Chinese counterpart of hypnosis.

The script also travelled. Fulu are not confined to Taoism: they were taken into several forms of Chinese Buddhism, and they lie behind the ofuda used in Japanese Buddhism and Shinto and the bujeok of Korean shamanism. On coins, fulu usually open and close the inscription of a Taoist coin charm, and most of those charms ask Lei Gong, the god of thunder, to protect the carrier from evil spirits and misfortune. Many coin talismans in the script have not been deciphered; in one specimen talismanic script was written side by side with Chinese characters that may be its gloss.

The Daozang records the fulu sect's history in the second chapter of each of its three grottoes, where fulu are said to originate in the condensation of clouds in the sky.
how: Written by a priest of the fulu pai, an informal grouping of priests from different schools of Taoism. The way of writing the characters is passed down in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples and treated as a special craft for communicating with local deities and spirits; style, incantations and the mudras used in making them differ from sect to sect, and even the invocations for a single deity vary. This atlas prints that and no script.
today: Still written. Zhuyou continues to be widely used among Chinese folk healers, and paper talismans are issued at temples across the Chinese-speaking world — the Taiwanese peace charm is the everyday form. Whether a talisman works has never been the question a priest is asked; the question is who wrote it.
kin: ping-an-fu — the everyday form: this script folded into yellow paper, sleeved in red and issued at a Taiwanese temple
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition of the priesthood that writes it and holds the script
kin: ofuda — the Japanese descendant — the same idea of a written slip from a shrine, reached through this script
kin: bujeok — the Korean descendant, taken up by Korean shamanism
kin: charm-coin — where the script goes when it is cast in bronze: fulu open and close the inscription of a Taoist coin charm
kin: fu-word — the word, and the two different fu it keeps getting confused between — the tally and the fortune
kin: divine-name — the sign family it belongs to: writing that acts because of whose name it is, not because of what it says
kin: inscribing — the practice itself, taught privately and differing by sect
kin: bagua-mirror — the other Taoist fixture at a doorway, working by reflection where this works by writing
kin: the-drawn-signs — the long read on signs made to be looked at rather than read
sources: s:wp-fulu s:wp-fu-character s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-ofuda s:web-taiwanese-gods-fulu
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Game-day charm (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/game-day-charm/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/game-day-charm.json
id: game-day-charm
aliases: lucky shoes · rally cap · lucky number · rally chew · rally shoe · lucky jersey
said: in the anthropological literature, a fetish; in a clubhouse, a lucky one
when: 1887 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US CA
root: English mascot, from French mascotte, 'lucky charm', itself from Provençal masco, 'sorceress' — a gamblers' slang word before it was anything else
object: materials=cloth,coin,leather worn=head,pocket,wallet
against: bad-luck — said by George Gmelch, reporting what professional baseball players say about the objects they carry [s:web-gmelch-baseball-magic]
against: attraction — said by Mark LaRosa, a Montreal Expos farmhand, on the round rock he picked up at Elmira [s:web-gmelch-baseball-magic]
against: bad-luck — said by baseball fans, on the rally cap — worn inside out and backwards to turn a game around, and no good unless the team's logo shows [s:wp-rally-cap]
what: Whatever was in the room the last time it went well. A pair of borrowed baseball shoes. A round rock picked up off a field. A uniform number. A cap turned inside out and worn backwards. A crucifix touched before every at-bat. A stick of gum, a yellow sandal, a particular arrangement of footwear in a locker. The object is ordinary and the selection rule is the only thing that is not: it gets chosen by what it was present for.
story: The best-documented charm in this atlas is a pair of shoes a man borrowed because he forgot his own.

George Gmelch, an anthropologist at Union College who played professional baseball before he wrote about it, defines the class flatly: "Fetishes or charms are material objects believed to embody 'supernatural' power that can aid or protect the owner. Good luck charms are standard equipment for some ballplayers." His list runs from coins, chains and crucifixes to a favourite hat. And the origin rule is the interesting part: "The fetishized object may be a new possession or something a player found that happens to coincide with the start of a streak and which he holds responsible for his good fortune." Alan Foster, playing in the Pacific Coast League, left his baseball shoes behind on a road trip and borrowed a teammate's. He pitched a no-hitter that night, attributed it to the shoes, bought them off the teammate afterwards, and they became a fetish.

Mark LaRosa, a farmhand in the Montreal Expos system, gave Gmelch a different account of the same kind of object: "I found it on the field in Elmira after I had gotten bombed. It's unusual, perfectly round, and it caught my attention. I keep it to remind me of how important it is to concentrate. When I am going well I look at the rock and remember to keep my focus, the rock reminds me of what can happen when I lose my concentration." *Inference —* that is a charm whose owner says out loud it is a memory aid and not a power, and it sits in the same pocket as the shoes. Both accounts are the wearers' own and this atlas prints both without deciding which kind of object it is.

Numbers work the same way. Ricky Henderson paid outfielder Turner Ward US$25,000 in 1993 for the right to wear number 24 when he joined the Blue Jays. Vida Blue switched from 35 to 14 — his high-school quarterback number — at the Oakland A's, and switched back when it produced nothing. Jack Clark went from 25 to 00 to break a slump, got four hits in a doubleheader that day, hurt his back, and was hit in the cheekbone by a batting-practice ball three days later. Larry Walker of the Colorado Rockies wore 33, took three practice swings, showered from the third nozzle, set his alarm three minutes past the hour and married on 3 November at 3:33 p.m. Gmelch notes there is no consensus on number 13: some refuse it, some do not care, a few ask for it.

On the fan's side of the rail the same logic produces the rally cap — a baseball cap worn inside out and backwards, or otherwise wrongly, to turn a game around; the team's logo has to show for it to work. The documented instances start early: on 23 August 1887 a Giants mascot turned his cap inside out during a close game against Pittsburgh and outfielder George Gore followed. Detroit Tigers fans recalled players doing it in the 1940s without the comeback meaning attached. The Texas Rangers used it in 1977 and 1978. Mets fans at Shea Stadium were wearing caps inside out in 1985, and the practice reached national attention during the 1986 World Series when Mets players wore rally caps in the dugout in Game 6. The genre has since branched: rally chew, rally gum during Detroit's 2006 run, and a yellow Birkenstock worn on a fan's head before the Mariners' 10–9 comeback on 8 October 2022.

Gmelch's own explanation is borrowed twice over and he says so. From Bronisław Malinowski: Trobriand islanders used no magic for lagoon fishing, where skill was enough, and a great deal of it for the open sea, where it was dangerous and the catch varied — and Gmelch maps that onto baseball, where magic clusters around pitching and hitting rather than fielding. From B. F. Skinner: a pigeon rewarded on a fixed timer starts repeating whatever it happened to be doing, and one of Skinner's birds hopped side to side ten thousand times without a pellet before giving up. Gmelch's closing sentence gives his own verdict, and it is his and not this atlas's: the rituals "do not make a pitch travel faster or a batted ball find the gaps between the fielders, nor do the Trobriand rituals calm the seas or bring fish. What both do, however, is give their practitioners a sense of control, with that added confidence, at no cost."

*Inference —* the phrase worth keeping from him is "standard equipment". A charm nobody in the trade regards as remarkable is the hardest kind for an atlas to find, because nobody writes it down. Gmelch wrote it down because he had been in the clubhouse.
how: Not made and not bought. Retained. An object acquires the status by having been present at a win, and keeps it by being carried, worn or arranged the same way every time. Clothing gets the same treatment: Jim Davenport found he had missed a buttonhole the day he hit two home runs and left the same button undone for the rest of his career; Brian Hunter switched between high-top and low-top shoes by which pair had failed to get a hit; Bo Kennedy told the clubhouse boys never to move his shoes, wanting the Ponys in front and the turfs to the right, each pair touching. The object is dropped when the streak ends, which is the one respect in which Gmelch says ballplayers beat pigeons.
today: Live in every clubhouse and half the stands. The published record this atlas relies on runs to Gmelch's 2000 revision and the rally-cap instances up to 2022; no survey newer than that was read for this record, and no dated price, because almost nothing here is bought.
kin: mascot-word — the word for this whole family, and a gamblers' slang term before it was a costume
kin: rabbits-foot — the charm on Stouffer's list of what American soldiers carried in the Second World War, which Gmelch cites as the same behaviour under worse stakes
kin: challenge-coin — the coin in the same pocket that claims nothing — Gmelch's list of fetishes opens with coins, and this is the one that does not qualify
kin: exam-charm — the same object with an answer sheet instead of a scoreboard, and a shrine counter behind it instead of a locker
kin: worry-stone — the other found stone in this atlas whose owner says its job is to tell him something rather than to keep something away
kin: hagstone — the other charm here that is picked up rather than made
kin: luck-word — the word the whole practice runs on, and the one nobody in a clubhouse defines
kin: alan-dundes — the folklorist who took this kind of everyday American material as a serious object of study
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this cuts against — here the charms are carried by adults at work, and the work is televised
sources: s:web-gmelch-baseball-magic s:wp-rally-cap s:wp-mascot s:wp-luck
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Gau (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/gau-box/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/gau-box.json
id: gau-box
native: ག་འུ། (Tibetan)
aliases: ga'u · ghau · gao · amulet box · portable shrine
said: GAH-oo
when: 2000 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN NP IN BT MN
object: form=box materials=silver,gold,copper,brass,cloth,paper worn=neck,chest,upper-arm,wall
against: travel — said by Himalayan Art Resources, which gives the purpose as general protection and protection when travelling [s:web-har-amulet-box]
against: illness — said by the practice of carrying consecrated medicine and relic pills inside the box [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
against: bad-luck — said by the general protective purpose both sources give, without naming a harm [s:web-har-amulet-box]
RESTRICTED: What goes inside a gau is selected, prepared and consecrated by a lama for a particular wearer, and the box is kept closed — the published example shows one item through its window and conceals the rest. This atlas prints what a named lama's published catalogue entry shows and stops. It does not reconstruct a filling or a consecration, because those belong to tantric practice, and Tibetan Buddhism holds that without having gone through initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras.
what: A metal box worn shut. Himalayan Art Resources calls the type a portable shrine, generally made from metal worked in repoussé — hammered from the back so the design stands out at the front. Small ones are round or oblong and hang at the neck on a cord; medium ones come in three parts, a metal container, a cloth outer cover and the contents, and usually carry a window with an image behind it; the largest are shrine-shaped, too big to carry, and stand on a household or temple altar. Men's boxes run from about an inch to over fourteen inches tall. What is inside is the point, and it is not on show.
story: James Gentry, writing for Project Himalayan Art at the Rubin Museum in 2023, catalogues one box closely enough to see into it. It was made in Kathmandu in the first decade of the twenty-first century, measures 9 × 8 × 4 cm, and is a golden nimbus-shaped box built to imitate a Buddhist reliquary, with the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel above its window and offerings below. Behind the window sits an amulet diagram wrapped in five-coloured cords with three dark brown pills; also inside are two reddish brown pills composed of relics said to be from the eighth-century Indian tantric master Padmasambhava, and two small golden pills of unknown composition. The box shows the diagram through the window and keeps the rest concealed behind it.

The contents were handselected by Chokling Rinpoche, who prepared them and consecrated the box, and the box was a personal gift from the Tsike Chokling, Fourth Karma Mingyur Dewe Dorje (1953–2020), to two of his students. That chain — a named lama fills it, a named lama gives it, a named student wears it — is what the object is. A gau bought empty is a case.

More broadly the boxes hold miniature statues, photographs of lamas, votive plaques, amulets, Sanskrit mantras written on small pieces of paper, relic pills, and materials taken from sacred sites; Himalayan Art Resources adds small texts, blessing cords and consecrated medicine, and notes they are typically carried on pilgrimage or on long business trips, with larger ones serving as makeshift shrines while travelling.
how: Assembled and consecrated by a lama, then closed. Smaller boxes hang from a cord or strap at the neck; larger ones are worn over the chest or under the arm on a leather strap or a cloth band. This atlas does not print how a gau is filled or what is said over it: the filling is a lama's work, done for a particular wearer, and the rite belongs to a body of practice Tibetan Buddhism restricts to those who have received empowerment.
today: Made and worn across the Tibetan-Buddhist world as of 2026 — Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal, Ladakh, Sikkim, Mongolia — and made for sale in Kathmandu, where Gentry's example was made. Empty gaus are also a standard item in the Himalayan visitor trade, sold as jewellery, and whether an empty one is the same object is a question the tradition answers by asking who filled it.
kin: sungkhor — the thing most often found inside — the folded, thread-wrapped protection diagram that the window of a gau usually shows
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that fills it, and that decides who is entitled to
kin: dzi-bead — what hangs on the same necklace, and the other Himalayan object whose value depends on a history nobody can read off its surface
kin: tabiz — the same idea two mountain ranges west: a written text sealed in metal that the wearer is not meant to open
kin: hirz-pouch — the leather-cased cousin from North Africa, carried the same way at the neck
kin: barkhor-lhasa — the circuit boxes are worn on, and bought beside

kin: wearing-hidden — the practice the object exists for: the contents are covered, and stay covered
kin: consecration — the step no buyer can perform for themselves — a lama's, and the reason a bought case is not yet a gau
