## Gorgoneion (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/gorgoneion/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/gorgoneion.json
id: gorgoneion
native: γοργόνειον (Greek)
aliases: Gorgon head · Medusa head · Medusa mask
said: gor-GO-nay-on, plural gorgoneia
when: 660 BCE – 399 CE
countries: GR IT TR
object: form=plaque materials=terracotta,copper,gold,silver,glass worn=neck,door,wall,roof
against: evil-eye — said by the consensus of classical scholars, who read the gorgoneion as an apotropaion — a device to ward away unwanted things [s:wp-gorgons]
against: weapons — said by Homer, on Athena's aegis, which the head makes proof against Apollo's spear and Zeus's thunderbolt [s:wp-gorgons]
against: house — said by Greek builders, who set the face on pediments, antefixes and acroteria [s:wp-gorgons]
against: witchcraft — said by Greek practice generally, as summarised in the account of apotropaic magic: the Gorgon was the most widely used image among the Greeks for averting evil [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
what: A face, not a body: wild eyes, tusks, tongue out, snakes for hair. It is moulded, cut or struck onto whatever needs guarding — a shield boss, a temple pediment, a terracotta roof antefix, a coin, the bottom of a drinking cup, a pendant. The archaic ones are hideous on purpose. From the fifth century BCE the face begins to be carved beautiful instead, and the Medusa Rondanini, a Roman copy of a Greek original, is the earliest such gorgoneion named in the literature.
story: Homer had already fixed what the thing was for. On Agamemnon's shield in the Iliad sits "the Gorgon, grim of aspect, glaring terribly, and about her were Terror and Rout"; on Athena's aegis the same head makes the aegis proof against Apollo's spear and Zeus's thunderbolt alike. Hector at his most frightening has "the eyes of the Gorgon". Odysseus, standing in the underworld and determined to stay, bolts at the thought of meeting "the head of the Gorgon, that awful monster".

Over six hundred Gorgon representations are catalogued in the Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae, and of all the depictions of Greek demons, the gorgoneion is by far the most frequent. The consensus among classicists is that its function was apotropaic — a device for turning unwanted things away — and that it began as a mask worn by a dancer. Jane Ellen Harrison put that view in the form everyone still quotes: the gorgoneion is "a ritual mask misunderstood".

Her argument runs backwards through the myth. What came first, she wrote, was "a grinning mask with glaring eyes and protruding beast-like tusks and pendent tongue", known in ritual. Then: "How did this Gorgoneion come to be? A hero had slain a beast called the Gorgon, and this was its head." The object comes first; the monster is invented to explain it; the hero is supplied to kill the monster. Two seventh-century BCE groups of terracotta Gorgon-like masks support her — wearable helmet masks from Tiryns, and votive masks, not wearable, from the Sanctuary of Orthia at Sparta.

*Inference —* the gorgoneion is the clearest case in the atlas of a charm that works by being looked at. Everything the sources say it does, it does to a viewer: terror, rout, flight. That is the same mechanism a Neapolitan coral horn or a blue glass bead is described as using, with the volume turned up.
kin: eye — the sign underneath this one; the gorgoneion's whole force sits in the glare, and Homer describes the eyes before anything else
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition whose loudest object this is
kin: fascinum — the Roman alternative for the same interception — a phallus instead of a face, and laughter instead of terror
kin: pazuzu-head — Mesopotamia's version of the argument: a frightening head, mounted facing the way in
kin: holy-rider-pendant — the medieval lead amulets whose main image resembles a gorgoneion and is read as a womb symbol — the face outliving the myth
kin: nazar — the same mechanism reduced to a bead, and the version still sold in Athens and Istanbul
kin: lion — the beasts flanking the full Gorgon on the oldest standing Greek temple
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the temple antefix is the monumental form of — put the guard where the thing gets in
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read; this is the family's most-copied member in the classical world
sources: s:wp-gorgons s:wp-medusa s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-evil-eye

## Gris-gris (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/gris-gris/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/gris-gris.json
id: gris-gris
aliases: grigri · gregory · gerregery · saffi
said: GREE-gree
when: 1700 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ML SN GH HT US
root: From the Mande languages spoken by the Mandinka and Bambara peoples of West Africa, where it is taken to mean 'magic'.
object: form=bag materials=cloth,paper,ink,herb worn=neck,pocket,skin
against: bad-luck — said by the source's summary of what wearers hold: the gris-gris protects the wearer from evil or brings luck [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: infertility — said by women in Senegal, in a 1982 survey that found gris-gris among the top three contraception methods known — the source's phrase is 'a purported method of birth control' [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: illness — said by Mande Muslims, among whom the source says Islamic scholars' powers are held to be 'employed to prevent misfortune, cure illness, heal wounds, and forecast the future' [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: curse — said by nineteenth-century Louisiana, where the word meant both the amulet and the act of bewitching, and where gris-gris were used against enslavers [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: war — said by the source's account of contemporary wear in West Africa: 'from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives' [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
RESTRICTED: This record does not print a formula. The marabout's craft is a course of study in the siri division of Karamokobara, and the contents of a given charm are the specialist's; what is printed here is what the pouch is, who makes it and what carriers say it is for.
what: A small cloth pouch, worn on the body, usually at the neck. Inside: verses of the Qur'an written on pieces of paper, herbs, and a set number of small objects. In West Africa the writing is the point — some charms were the written sheets themselves, carried by scholars without any bag at all.
story: Two lines run out of this object and they need keeping apart, because the sources that cover one do not cover the other.

The first line is West African and Muslim. The gris-gris originates in the Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa. Travellers through the Volta Basin, in what is now Ghana, reported Mande speakers such as the Dyula distributing Islamic charms they called gris-gris, and the practice spread to other Muslim peoples, among them the Dagomba, who wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts with magic formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets. Among Mande Muslims the craft has a name and a course of study: Karamokobara, which divides into seli, prayer, and siri, path. Those who take seli become scholars of Qur'anic law, karamokos; those who take siri become scholars of the written talismans, marabouts. Some cross over. The tools of the siri side are spoken prayers, numerical squares called katemi, and written inscriptions from the Qur'an.

The second line is American, and the word changes on the way. Atlantic slavery carried the gris-gris to the Americas with enslaved Muslims, and it was kept up by practitioners of the traditions Wikipedia names "Louisiana Voodoo" and Haitian Vodou. In Haiti it held its original sense: an amulet with good intentions. In the United States it went the other way. It came to be thought of as something brought down on a victim; enslaved people used gris-gris against their owners, and gris-gris were found in burials. New Orleans court cases of 1773 convicted enslaved people of using gris-gris to kill those who held them, and those are among the earliest legal mentions of the tradition in Louisiana. Enslaved conjure women made gris-gris to start rebellions, and the bags were held to have guided people to freedom on the Underground Railroad and shielded them on the way. In October 1849 authorities arrested an enslaved man for carrying a human finger wrapped in flannel that he believed brought good luck; people in New Orleans sought human remains from tombs for this work, and gravesites were disturbed for it. In Cajun communities the term means black magic and ill fortune. Against that, Gris-Gris doctors have worked in the Louisiana Creole community for centuries and are looked on favourably by the Black community at large. Both of those are reported here and neither is settled here.

It is also, in West Africa now, an everyday object with a measured place in public health data. A 1982 survey found gris-gris among the top three methods of contraception known to women in Senegal — the three named were abstinence, roots and herbs, and charms. Over 60% of women reported knowing such traditional methods; the pill, the best known modern method, was known to a little over 40%. Gris-gris are worn across the whole of society, the source says, "from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives, and can feature anything from monkey to snake to mouse".
how: Written, then bagged. A marabout or another literate specialist writes Qur'anic verses, or a numerical square, on paper; the paper goes into a small cloth sack with herbs and a set number of small objects; the sack is worn, usually at the neck. In the American line the contents shift with what the conjurer has and what the job is, and the bag is kept on the body.
today: Living on both sides of the Atlantic, and not the same object on each. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for how many are made by marabouts and how many are sold over a counter.
kin: gris-gris-word — the word itself, and the argument about what it means on which side of the Atlantic
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition the West African line belongs to, alongside the Fon bǒ that Francophone Beninese also call by this name
kin: islamic-talismanic — the other tradition it belongs to — the writing inside it is Qur'anic, and the maker is a marabout
kin: taweez — the same object in South Asia: a written verse folded into a case and worn
kin: hirz-pouch — the Arabian version — the same Qur'anic verses, but in a silver case rather than a cloth sack
kin: nkisi — the Central African container it is repeatedly compared with, and the one the American mojo bag descends from instead
kin: mojo-word — the American word for the neighbouring bag, from Kikongo mooyo — a different ancestry in the same city
kin: vodou-not-voodoo — the spelling argument this object sits inside, because the word for the tradition changed with the Atlantic crossing too
kin: paper — the material that carries the verse, and the part that does the work
kin: sewing-in — the practice of closing a charm into cloth so nobody can read it
kin: akodessewa-market — the Lomé market where West African charm materials are traded in the open

## Hagstone (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hagstone/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hagstone.json
id: hagstone
native: Glain Neidr (Latin)
aliases: adder stone · witch stone · fairy stone · serpent's egg · snake's egg · milpreve · adderstane · Gloine nan Druidh · Hühnergötter
said: HAG-stone; the Welsh name is said glyne NAY-dir
when: 1 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB DE RU
root: English hag 'witch' + stone; the parallel English name adder stone comes from the claim that snakes made it. Welsh Glain Neidr is 'snake's gem', Cornish milpreve, Scots adderstane, and northern Scottish Gaelic Gloine nan Druidh 'Druids' glass'. In Germany the same stones are Hühnergötter, 'chicken gods'.
object: form=pendant materials=flint,thread worn=neck,wall,door
against: lawsuit — said by the Druids of the Gallic provinces, as reported by Pliny the Elder [s:wp-adder-stone]
against: demons — said by Reginald Scot, printing the cure for the night-mare in The Discoverie of Witchcraft, 1584 [s:wp-adder-stone]
against: livestock — said by Thomas Blundeville, 1565, citing an older English writer, on hanging a naturally holed flint above a horse [s:wp-adder-stone]
against: bad-luck — said by a woman in Essex, to researchers in 1984 [s:wp-adder-stone]
against: house — said by Russian folklore, in which the stones housed the Kurinyi Bog and were placed in farmyards against the Kikimora [s:wp-adder-stone]
what: A stone with a hole worn right through it by water, usually flint, usually glassy. Nobody makes one: a hagstone is found, on a beach or in a field, and a stone holed by human hand does not count. Most are hung on a loop of string or red ribbon and put where the hole can be looked through.
story: The oldest account is Roman and second-hand. In Natural History book XXIX, Pliny the Elder reports what the Druids of the Gallic provinces told about the anguinum: snakes twist together in summer, the slime and foam they secrete hardens into an egg, and their hissing throws it into the air, where a man must catch it in a cloak before it touches the ground and then flee on horseback until a river is between him and the snakes. They said it could be tested by setting it in gold and seeing whether it floats upstream. Pliny says he has seen one — round, about the size of a moderate apple, its shell cartilaginous, covered in cup-like marks. He also says what it was carried for, and how that ended: "The possession of it is marvellously vaunted as ensuring success in law-suits, and a favourable reception with princes", and a Roman of equestrian rank from the territory of the Vocontii was put to death by Tiberius for having one in his bosom during a trial.

The English record is about sleep. English folklore collectors record the same use of a holed stone hung over a person or a horse against nightmares, attested from at least the fifteenth century. Reginald Scot printed the cure in The Discoverie of Witchcraft in 1584: hang over the bed "a stone, which stone hath naturallie such a hole in it, as wherein a string may be put through it, and so be hanged over the diseased or bewitched partie; be it man, woman, or horsse." Thomas Blundeville had already written it into a 1565 book on horsemanship, citing an older English writer, with a verse to be written on paper and hung up with the stone.

The practice did not stop. Edward Lovett, collecting folklore in Surrey and Sussex, reported in 1928 that the favourite objects for warding off nightmares were horseshoes and natural perforated stones, common on the beach at Brighton, and that the stones were usually on a loop of red ribbon or string, "or are occasionally simply hooked on to one of the knobs of the bedstead." A woman in Essex told researchers in 1984: "I still keep stones with holes in them on my window-sill for luck. I used to pick them up as a child from the beach in South Shields, and all my family still pick them up--because we think they're lucky."

The same stone does other work elsewhere. In Welsh folklore the Glain Neidr are made by a congress of snakes in spring, most auspiciously on May Eve. In Russian folklore the holed stones housed spirits called Kurinyi Bog, the chicken gods, who guarded hens and were set in farmyards against the Kikimora.
how: Found, not made. Picked off a beach or out of a ploughed field, strung on string or red ribbon, and hung: over a bed, over a horse, on a door, on a windowsill. Several sources say the stone works best used together with a spoken or written charm about Saint George. Nothing is done to charge it and nothing is recorded about retiring it; a hagstone is kept.
today: Still picked up and kept, and sold online and in shops that sell crystals and folk charms. The Hastings legend attached to it is live enough to name: the town is said to be under Crowley's Curse, which compels anyone who has lived there to return, and which can only be broken by taking a stone with a hole through it from Hastings beach.
kin: rowan-cross — the other thing a British household hung on the same nail, and the one that had to be cut and bound rather than found
kin: horseshoe — the object Edward Lovett found beside it on Sussex bedsteads in 1928, doing the same job against the same night
kin: witch-bottle — the answer when the harm was already inside the house — this stone hangs, that bottle is buried
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition this belongs to, and one of its few objects that costs nothing and is made by nobody
kin: serpent — the sign in the name: Glain Neidr, snake's egg, from the Druids' account of how it is made
kin: edward-lovett — the collector who recorded these on Brighton beach and on Surrey bedsteads, and who published the red-ribbon detail in 1928
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — where English charms of this class sit in a public case, alongside the rowan loops
kin: worry-stone — the present-day pocket stone, found the same way and carried for a different reason
kin: eye — the family this atlas files a hole-you-look-through beside — though no source in this record says the hagstone is an eye, and this record does not say it either
kin: iron — the metal English folklore trusts against the same harms; the hagstone is the stone answer to the same question
sources: s:wp-adder-stone s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-edward-lovett s:wp-iron-in-folklore
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Hamsa (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hamsa/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hamsa.json
id: hamsa
native: خمسة (Arabic)
aliases: khamsa · khmisa · Hand of Fatima · Hand of Miriam · Hand of Mary · hamesh · afus
said: KHAM-sa, Arabic for 'five'
when: 800 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: MA DZ TN EG IL ES TR IR IQ IN PK
root: Arabic khamsa, 'five' — the five fingers; Maghrebi variants khmisa and khmisa; Hebrew hamesh, also 'five'; Berber afus, 'hand'
object: form=pendant materials=silver,jet,gold worn=neck,door,wall,vehicle,shop,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across North Africa and the Middle East, who say khamsa fi ainek — 'five [fingers] in your eye' [s:wp-hamsa]
against: envy — said by the same users; the evil eye is glossed in the cited article as a malicious stare held to cause illness, death or general misfortune [s:wp-hamsa]
against: child-harm — said by households that paint or hang it on the doorway of a room holding an expectant mother or a new baby [s:wp-hamsa]
against: infertility — said by the hand-amulet tradition the cited article traces it to — the Hand of Venus and the Hand of Mary, used to protect women from the eye, boost fertility and lactation and promote healthy pregnancies [s:wp-hamsa]
against: illness — said by the Mesopotamian precedent von Kemnitz names: amulets of the hand of Ishtar, used to keep evil or disease from entering a building [s:wp-hamsa]
what: An open palm, usually made symmetrical so it has a thumb on both sides, in silver more often than anything else, historically also carved in jet. An eye is often set in the palm. Fingers spread turns evil away; fingers together brings luck; pointing up wards off, pointing down blesses. The most stylised versions stop looking like a hand at all and become five circles around a sixth. It is also painted in red on house walls, sometimes with the blood of a sacrificed animal, and hung on the doorway of a room where a woman is expecting or a baby has just arrived.
story: The open hand is old in the Near East and the line back from the modern object is argued rather than established. Amulets of the hand of Ishtar were used in Mesopotamia and Babylon to keep evil or disease out of a building. An Iron Age tomb at Khirbet el-Qom in Judah carries an engraved hand beside an inscription, generally read as protective in a funerary setting, though the exact meaning is debated. Another line runs to the Mano Pantea, known to ancient Egyptians as the Two Fingers, where the two fingers are Isis and Osiris and the thumb is Horus, used to call a parent's protection over a child.

Eva-Maria von Kemnitz traces the medieval route in one sentence: "the Berbers brought the khamsa to al-Andalūs. Later, the expelled Muslim and Jewish population took it back to North Africa, introducing different motifs and techniques." In al-Andalus its use as an amulet is well documented from the thirteenth century on. Among the Moriscos of Granada, khamsa pendants were described as large engraved medals with a hand inscribed with letters — likely Qur'anic verses. A reform council banned them as Islamic symbols in 1526 and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the prohibition in 1554. Christians wore them anyway, and a Nasrid-period gold pendant survives inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

The disagreement is live and it is not between insiders and outsiders. Von Kemnitz, citing Bruno Barbatti, calls the hamsa the most important apotropaic sign in the Islamic world. Salafi authorities reject it: one fatwa states that hanging the khamsa is impermissible, and another lists hands of Fatima among prohibited amulets. In Shia Islam the five fingers are read as the panjtan — Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, Husayn — with invocations written on the fingers, and the open palm became an emblem in Muharram processions and on ʿalams. In Judaism the hand doubles as the letter shin, first letter of Shaddai; Shalom Sabar suggests Jews exiled from Spain in 1492 carried it as protection into the countries they reached, while noting the assumption is hard to prove.

What people say while using it is the plainest evidence of what they take it for. Khamsa fi ainek — 'five [fingers] in your eye' — said while raising the right palm, fingers slightly apart, to blind the aggressor. Khamsa wa-khamis, 'five and Thursday'. Or the whole formula with the spitting sound: "Khamsa, Khamsa, Khamsa, tfu, tfu, tfu."
today: The hamsa is one of Algeria's national symbols and appears in its emblem. In Egypt it is the most popular amulet against the evil eye, ahead of the eye itself and the hirz; women in baladi quarters make khamaysa, five objects — peppers, hands, circles, stars — hung from hooks on a child's hair or black apron. Its use fell away in some places during periods of modernisation and came back as a secular good-luck charm: necklaces, keychains, postcards, lottery cards, advertisements, tilework, wall decorations. It was added to Unicode as U+1FAAC in 2021.
kin: hand — the sign this object is, and the reason it works in traditions that share nothing else
kin: open-palm — the gesture it freezes — right hand up, fingers slightly apart, aimed at the looker
kin: eye — the sign usually set in the palm; two charms stacked on one piece of silver
kin: nazar — the bead it is most often sold beside, and most often combined with
kin: islamic-talismanic — one of the traditions that carries it, and the one whose Salafi authorities rule against it by name
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the other tradition that carries it, where the hand doubles as the letter shin for Shaddai
kin: silver — the metal it is usually made of, named in the tradition for purity
kin: jet — the black stone it was historically carved from, and the same stone Spain cuts a fist out of
kin: figa — the Iberian and Brazilian hand-charm this one sits next to in a Spanish tray
kin: khan-el-khalili — the Cairo market where it outsells every other charm against the eye
kin: hamsa-word — the word itself, which is just the number five
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read; the hand and the eye travel together across this whole map
sources: s:wp-hamsa s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-silver s:wp-jet-gemstone
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Heart scarab (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/heart-scarab/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/heart-scarab.json
id: heart-scarab
aliases: heart scarab amulet · Chapter 30B scarab
said: the Egyptian word for the heart is ib; the object is named for where it lies
when: 1690 BCE – 664 BCE
countries: EG
object: form=pendant materials=gold worn=chest,neck,grave
against: the-dead — said by Chapter 30B of the Book of the Dead, as summarised by Egyptologists [s:wp-heart-scarab]
against: lawsuit — said by Egyptian funerary texts — the Weighing of the Heart is a trial, and the spell is written to stop a witness [s:wp-heart-scarab]
what: An oval beetle, larger and heavier than the scarabs of the living, cut from a dark green or black stone — green jasper, serpentine, basalt — and usually not drilled for suspension. New Kingdom examples run four to five centimetres long. The base carries Chapter 30B of the Book of the Dead, cut into the stone or onto a gold plate fixed to it. It is hung at the mummy's neck on gold wire, the stone held in a gold frame, and laid over the heart.
story: The spell on the base is an instruction to an organ. At the Weighing of the Heart the dead person's heart goes on one pan of the scales and a single feather from Ma'at's headdress on the other. A heart lighter than the feather lets its owner start the journey to Aaru; a heart heavy with wrongdoing tips off the pan into the jaws of Ammit, and the soul is left restless in the Duat. Chapter 30B commands the heart not to give evidence against its owner. The scarab is there to hold it to that, or to speak in its place.

That is why the heart, alone among the organs, stayed in the body. Egyptians held it to be the seat of the mind, so the embalmers took out the other viscera and preserved them separately and left the heart where it was — with the stone beetle on top of it.

The first known depictions are Sixteenth or Seventeenth Dynasty, about 1690 BCE, though the amulet was in use as early as the Eleventh Dynasty. Until the Eighteenth Dynasty it stayed close to Theban royalty; then it turns up in other people's burials. In the Twenty-first Dynasty it is an important piece of protection among the priesthood of Amun. After that it thins out of human burials and attaches to particular gods instead.

The object shrank. New Kingdom heart scarabs are large, four to five centimetres. By the Third Intermediate Period a smaller variant appears, two to four centimetres — and because it is small it is left uninscribed. These small ones are not laid over the wrappings but put inside the chest cavity, next to the real heart. *Inference —* a spell-bearing amulet that stops bearing its spell is a change worth naming: the shape is doing the work the words used to do.

The Book of the Dead specifies a stone it calls nmhf, nemehef. Nobody has identified it.
how: Cut from dark stone, inscribed on the base with Chapter 30B, set in a gold frame and hung at the neck on gold wire, or — in the smaller late form — put into the chest cavity beside the heart during mummification. Some were worked into pectorals, the rectangular chest ornaments laid on a mummy's breast.
today: Not made and not used; the practice ended with the religion that needed it. Heart scarabs sit in museum cases, and the Israel Museum and the British Museum both publish examples. As of 2026 what a reader is most likely to meet is a photograph of one, captioned with a spell about a heart being asked to keep quiet.
kin: scarab — the parent shape — the same beetle, worn by the living and used to stamp their letters
kin: wedjat-eye — its partner in the wrappings: one speaks for the dead at the weighing, the other guards the cut the embalmer made
kin: scarab-sign — the sign it carries, read as the sun rolled up at daybreak and so as rebirth
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that placed it, by the rules of a funeral rather than by a wearer's choice
kin: grave-deposit — the practice this object exists inside; it was never meant to be seen again
kin: inscribing — the step that makes it work as a heart scarab rather than as a large beetle — and the step the late small ones drop
kin: wallis-budge — the translator through whom most English readers first met Chapter 30B
kin: tyet-knot — another amulet the wrappings required, placed on the upper torso rather than the heart
sources: s:wp-heart-scarab s:wp-scarab-artifact s:wp-ancient-egyptian-funerary-practices s:wp-e-a-wallis-budge s:wp-british-museum
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Hei matau (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hei-matau/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hei-matau.json
id: hei-matau
native: hei matau (Latin)
aliases: fish hook pendant · matau
said: hei MAH-tow
when: undated (still carried)
countries: NZ
root: Māori hei, 'to wear around the neck', + matau, 'fish hook'
object: form=pendant materials=bone,jade,shell,wood worn=neck,boat
against: drowning — said by the tradition as summarised by the cited source: the hei matau represents safe passage over water [s:wp-hei-matau]
against: travel — said by the same — safe travel across water is the first thing the cited source names [s:wp-hei-matau]
against: infertility — said by the same, which names fertility among what the hook represents [s:wp-hei-matau]
against: poverty — said by the same, which names prosperity [s:wp-hei-matau]
what: A heavily stylised fish hook, carved in bone or pounamu — the Māori term for the hard green stones, chiefly nephrite jade, found only in the South Island — and worn at the neck on a cord. Most modern pieces are not working hooks. Older matau were, and came in several forms, some plain and utilitarian, some highly ornate, some composite, and some whose function is no longer known.
story: The shape carries a story about the country it is worn in. Māui caught the North Island out of the sea using a woven line and a hook made from his grandmother's jawbone; the Māori name for the North Island, Te Ika a Māui, the fish of Māui, holds the account, and the shape of Hawke's Bay is where the hook caught in the fish's side.

For Māori the hei matau is taonga, a cultural treasure. Wikipedia's summary of what it stands for is not a list of wishes: it represents the land, and prosperity, fertility and safe passage over water; it marks the importance of fishing to Māori and their relationship to Tangaroa, god of the sea. Matau were worn as pendants for safekeeping and were often treasured family heirlooms.

Material is where the modern record gets complicated. Traditionally matau were carved from bone, ivory, shell, wood or pounamu. Today most are cattle bone. Some Māori carvers still work whale bone, valued for its beauty, its cultural and historical weight and its scarcity; under current law against whaling they must use ancient stock, pre-existing supplies, or bone from whales that strand. New Zealand tradition and law give Māori first claim on part of the skeleton of any whale that strands and cannot be refloated, which is a very limited supply.

And then there is the other production line. Manufacturers in China mass-produce items resembling hei matau for the New Zealand visitor market, usually in a paste of bone and resin, and, in the words of the cited account, "have attracted criticism for their appropriation of Māori designs". That criticism is reported here with its subject named and is not adjudicated.
how: Carved from bone, whale bone, shell, wood or pounamu, worked down and polished, drilled and strung. Pounamu work is slow: the stone is smoothed by abrasion and bored with sticks and water. A hei matau is worn, given and inherited, not retired.
today: Carved by Māori artists and by collectives established by iwi that export their work, and worn by Māori and by other New Zealanders who take the hook as a New Zealand sign. Viggo Mortensen wore one after filming The Lord of the Rings, which the cited account names as part of a wider international interest in Māori art. The Chinese-made bone-and-resin versions sell on the same tourist market.
kin: maori-taonga — the tradition this belongs to, which is why this record does not call it a lucky charm
kin: hei-tiki — the other pendant from the same stone and the same cord, for ancestors rather than for water
kin: fish — the sign behind the shape, and behind the name of the North Island
kin: jade — the material class pounamu falls into; Māori classify the stone by colour instead
kin: bone-ivory — what most of them are carved from now — cattle bone, and whale bone under strict limits
kin: te-papa — the museum that holds them and publishes about them in Māori terms
kin: dreamcatcher — the North American parallel — a form mass-produced abroad and objected to by name on the same grounds
kin: st-christopher-medal — the other object in this atlas most often worn against danger on a crossing
kin: the-fake-market — the long read about copies, which this record is one of the clearest cases in
sources: s:wp-hei-matau s:wp-pounamu s:wp-hei-tiki s:web-tepapa-taonga-maori s:wp-cultural-appropriation

## Hei-tiki (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hei-tiki/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hei-tiki.json
id: hei-tiki
native: hei tiki (Latin)
aliases: tiki · pounamu pendant
said: hei TEE-kee; hei means to wear around the neck
when: undated (still carried)
countries: NZ
root: Māori hei, 'to wear around the neck', + tiki, which originally refers to the first mortal
object: form=pendant materials=jade,bone,plastic worn=neck,grave
against: infertility — said by Māori families, per Robley's account: a hei-tiki was often given to a woman by her husband's family if she was having trouble conceiving [s:wp-hei-tiki]
against: war — said by the crew of HMS New Zealand, who attributed the ship's lack of casualties to the hei-tiki their captain wore [s:wp-hei-tiki]
what: A pendant of a human figure, head tilted, hands on thigh and chest or both on the thighs, carved from pounamu and suspended on a plaited cord fastened with a loop and toggle. Pounamu is the Māori term for several hard, tough stones found only in the South Island — nephrite jade in the varieties Māori classify by colour as kahurangi, īnanga and kawakawa, and the translucent bowenite called tangiwai. A hei-tiki is a taonga: a treasure with whakapapa, an ancestral line of its own.
story: Hei-tiki are, in Te Papa's summary of Māori adornment, the most famous and most highly prized of Māori personal ornaments. Two readings of the figure are given by Horatio Gordon Robley in A History of the Maori Tiki: that they are memorials to ancestors, or that they represent Hineteiwaiwa, the goddess of childbirth. Both have practices attached. A hei-tiki was often buried when its kaitiaki, its guardian, died, and retrieved later to be brought out at tangihanga, the mourning. And because of the connection with Hineteiwaiwa, hei-tiki were often given to a woman by her husband's family if she was having trouble conceiving.

The mana of one is not in the carving. Dougal Austin's 2014 thesis, supervised by Peter Adds and based on Te Papa's hei-tiki collection with early-contact pieces in overseas collections, finds that the mana of hei-tiki comes from the "agency of prolonged ancestral use", and that the form was "highly developed ... from the outset to conform to adze-shaped pieces of pounamu". Pounamu taonga gain mana as they pass between generations; the stone is held to take on the mana of past owners, and heirloom pieces are named after former owners. That is why the most prized taonga are the ones with known histories running back many generations, and why they were given to seal agreements.

The collections are large and their history is not neutral. Te Papa holds over 200 hei-tiki and the British Museum about 50; some were exchanged or gifted to European travellers and sailors at the earliest point of contact, and, in Wikipedia's words, "the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes".

One story sits oddly beside the rest and is reported here as somebody else's reading, not this atlas's. The captain of HMS New Zealand, a battlecruiser funded by the New Zealand government in 1911, wore a hei-tiki and a piupiu into three First World War battles; the crew attributed the ship's lack of casualties to it and called her a lucky ship. That is a Pākehā crew's account of a taonga, and it is what a taonga becomes when it is read by people outside the whakapapa it belongs to.

In 1997 the Crown returned ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu to Ngāi Tahu, the South Island iwi, under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement.
how: The stone was first cut roughly as a small adze — pounamu is hard and valuable enough that a carver removes as little as possible, which is why the head tilts. It is then smoothed by abrasive rubbing, shaped and bored with sticks and water, and polished over a long time. Finished, it is hung on a plaited cord with a loop and toggle. It is not retired; it is inherited, and its history is the point of it.
today: Carved by Māori artists, including collectives set up by iwi that export jewellery and carvings, and worn by Māori and by other New Zealanders as a mark of identity. Retailers also sell visitor versions in jade, other stone, plastic and other materials; the Wikipedia account of pounamu notes that much of the carved "greenstone" in souvenir shops is jade sourced overseas. As of 2026 the two trades run side by side, and this atlas reports the difference without ranking the buyers.
kin: maori-taonga — the tradition this belongs to, and the one that decides that this is a treasure with whakapapa and not an ornament
kin: hei-matau — the other pendant worn at the same neck, carved from the same stone, for water rather than for ancestors
kin: jade — the material class pounamu falls into for a mineralogist, and does not fall into for Māori, who classify it by colour
kin: te-papa — the museum holding over 200 of them and publishing about them in Māori terms
kin: te-papa-taonga — the room a reader can stand in and see them
kin: british-museum — the overseas collection holding about fifty, and part of the reason repatriation is a live question
kin: inheriting — the practice that makes one: mana accumulates by passing between generations, not by carving
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this record is central to
kin: dreamcatcher — the North American parallel — an Indigenous form now also made by everybody else, and objected to by name
kin: grave-deposit — the practice recorded here: buried with a kaitiaki, and lifted again for the tangihanga
sources: s:wp-hei-tiki s:wp-pounamu s:web-tepapa-taonga-maori s:wp-te-papa s:wp-british-museum
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Hex sign (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hex-sign/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hex-sign.json
id: hex-sign
native: Hexefoos (Latin)
aliases: barn star · Blume · Sterne · witch foot · painted prayer
said: HEKS sine
when: 1800 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US
root: English hex sign, from Pennsylvania German hex (German Hexe, Dutch heks), 'witch'. The compound is not old: the term was not used until the twentieth century, after Wallace Nutting's Pennsylvania Beautiful appeared in 1924.
object: form=plaque materials=wood,paper worn=wall,door,shop
against: livestock — said by modern hex sign artists, who stress the symbolic meanings — a horse head used to protect animals from disease [s:wp-hex-sign]
against: fire — said by the same modern artists, for whom the horse head also protects the building from lightning [s:wp-hex-sign]
against: house — said by the talismanic school of interpretation, and Lee R. Gandee, who called the signs painted prayers in 1971 [s:wp-hex-sign]
what: A painted disc on the side of a barn: usually a star inside a circular border, in bright colour on white. The later commercial ones are separate discs, screen-printed and mounted, carrying stars, compass roses, hearts, tulips, a tree of life, or the stylised bird called a distelfink. They are found on Pennsylvania Dutch barns in central and southeastern Pennsylvania, densest in Berks, Lancaster and Lehigh counties. The Amish do not use them.
story: Two schools of thought exist about what these are, and this atlas's job here is to give both. One ascribes a talismanic nature to the signs. The other holds that they are purely decorative. Both schools accept that "there are sometimes superstitions associated with certain hex sign themes", and neither ascribes strong magical power to them.

The decorative side has a name and a date: Alfred L. Shoemaker, whose 32-page Hex, No! came out from the Pennsylvania Dutch Folklore Center in Lancaster in 1953 and whose title is its argument. *Inference —* this record has read that book's catalogue record and not its pages, and takes the phrase usually quoted from it, "chust for nice", from accounts of it rather than from the text. The scholarship the argument has run through since is Thomas E. Graves's 1984 doctoral dissertation at the University of Pennsylvania, The Pennsylvania German Hex Sign: A Study in Folk Process, and Hex Signs: Pennsylvania Dutch Barn Symbols and Their Meaning, by Don Yoder and Graves, published by Stackpole in 2000.

The chronology matters to the argument, because it is short. Barn painting of this kind is a late development in Pennsylvania Dutch folk art. Before the 1830s the cost of paint meant most barns went unpainted; the stars-in-circles began to appear in the early nineteenth century and became widespread decades later, when commercial ready-mixed paint became easy to buy. Barn decorating peaked in the early twentieth century, when there were many artists who specialised in it, drawing on a large repertoire and combining elements. The geometric patterns of quilts show up in the designs; the hearts and tulips are the ones found on fraktur, the elaborately lettered birth, baptism and marriage certificates of the same community.

The mountable sign is a documented commercial invention. Jacob Zook of Paradise, Pennsylvania, claimed to have originated it in 1942, based on traditional designs, to be sold in souvenir shops along the Lincoln Highway; Edward Buchak of Gilbertsville designed and screen-printed many of the Zook signs. William Schuster, Milton Hill, Johnny Ott and Johnny and Eric Claypoole also worked in that revival. It is the modern artists who tend to stress meanings: a horse head to protect animals from disease and the building from lightning, a dove for peace and contentment. The Pennsylvania Bureau of Radiation Protection built the international radiation symbol into a yellow-and-red hex sign design for its official logo.

Two more readings have names attached. Lee R. Gandee, in Strange Experience: The Autobiography of a Hexenmeister (1971), called hex signs "painted prayers". Others read the designs as decorative markers of ethnic identity, possibly arising in reaction to nineteenth-century government attempts to suppress the Pennsylvania German language. In recent years the signs have been taken up as talismans for folk magic by people who are not Pennsylvania Dutch, and neopagans have taken up making them, working other pre-Christian signs into the designs on the argument that the hex designs are of pre-Christian Germanic origin and related to Alpine German work — a circled rosette is called the Sun of the Alps in the Po Valley. Anabaptist sects in the region, the Amish and the Mennonites, take a negative view of hex signs, and the signs are rarely if ever seen on their farms.
how: Painted directly onto barn siding, in a circular border, by a specialist barn painter working from a repertoire of designs. The commercial version since 1942 is screen-printed on a separate disc and mounted on a barn or hung indoors. Nothing in this record's sources describes a blessing, a consecration, or a retirement.
today: Still painted, still sold, and still argued over. *Inference —* the argument is unusually hard to settle because the commercial sign arrived in 1942 with an explicit set of meanings attached for the buyer, which means most published lists of what a hex sign means postdate the tourist trade rather than the barns.
kin: tree — one of the designs by name — the tree of life is a standard theme on the commercial signs
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice it is the biggest version of: a sign fixed to a building, facing outward, in public
kin: bagua-mirror — the other painted geometric disc in this atlas fixed to the outside of a building, and a useful comparison because nobody argues about what that one is for
kin: concealed-shoe — the opposite instinct in the same kind of building: one charm walled up where nobody can see it, one painted six feet across on the gable
kin: horseshoe — the other thing on an American barn, and the one whose protective claim nobody disputes
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition the emigrants brought, and the one this object may or may not still belong to — that is the argument
kin: the-fake-market — the long read the 1942 souvenir sign belongs in: a traditional design, a new object, and a meaning printed on the box
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read for the rest of it: neopagans making them, the Amish refusing them, and a state radiation office using one as a logo
kin: apotropaic-word — the word the talismanic school uses and the decorative school will not
sources: s:wp-hex-sign s:book-shoemaker-hex-no s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-folk-religion

## Hirz (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/hirz-pouch/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/hirz-pouch.json
id: hirz-pouch
native: حرز (Arabic)
aliases: herz · Qur'an case · amulet box · Qur'an necklace
said: HIRZ
when: 1900 CE to now (still carried)
countries: OM YE
root: Arabic حرز ḥirz, from a root meaning to guard or fortify — the word means fortification, and implies a search for protection.
object: form=box materials=silver,paper,ink worn=neck,hair,head
against: bad-luck — said by the catalogue entry, which says wearers use these pieces for spiritual protection through their sacred textual contents [s:web-mwnf-hirz-oman]
against: demons — said by the hadith reported in the source on the Throne Verse: reciting it wards off devils, shayatin, and fiends, afarit [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: evil-eye — said by Islamic talismanic practice as summarised in the source, which lists protection against the evil eye, misfortune, jinn and demons first among what such talismans are used for [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: infertility — said by the same summary, which names increasing fertility among the purposes [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
what: A small case on a chain, rectangular or cylindrical, holding verses of the Qur'an written on paper inside. Usually silver. The case may hang from a plain silver chain or sit at the centre of an elaborate necklace strung with beads, coins and other pendants; smaller versions are worn as hair ornaments or built into a headdress. The example the National Museum in Muscat publishes is silver with geometric and silver-leaf work, 30.6 cm long and weighing 152.9 g, and is dated to the fourteenth century AH — the early twentieth century CE — under the Al Bu Said dynasty.
story: The case is the amulet's body and the verse is its content, and Islamic talismanic practice is clear about which of those is doing the work. Talismans in this tradition usually carry Qur'anic verses, pious phrases or invocations, and one description quoted in the literature calls the result "a supercharged prayer". Virtually all Muslim scholars permit a talisman that invokes God or one of His intercessors; addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. That is the line this object sits on the safe side of, and it is why the hirz differs from European charms, which often address minor deities or demons rather than God.

The verse most often named for protection is Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, al-Baqara 2:255, the 255th verse of the Qur'an's second chapter, widely memorised and widely displayed. A hadith says reciting it wards off devils, shayatin, and fiends, afarit. Al-Suyuti narrates that a man and a jinn met and wrestled, and the jinn, as a reward for being beaten, taught the man a verse which, recited, keeps no devil able to enter his house with him — the Throne Verse.

*Inference —* the case, then, is a solution to a practical problem: paper in a hot, dusty, sweaty place does not last, and a verse that must stay legible has to be shut into metal. The jewellery around it is a second solution, to a different problem: what is worn every day has to be worth wearing.

The form is widespread on the Arabian Peninsula. Old Yemeni silver amulets called hirz were made to keep Qur'anic verses inside, and this sort of pendant is found across Oman, Yemen and the peninsula.
how: A case is cast or worked in silver and given a hinge or a sliding end. Verses are written on paper and folded into it. It is hung at the neck, or worked into a larger necklace, or scaled down for the hair or a headdress.
today: Made and worn, and also collected. The National Museum in Muscat publishes one through the Discover Islamic Art database of Museum With No Frontiers, and the form is sold new by silver dealers across the Gulf. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for the split between pieces made for wearers and pieces made for buyers.
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition that fills it, and the rule it obeys: invoke God, never jinn
kin: quran-pendant — the same verses worn as a solid inscribed piece rather than as paper in a box
kin: taweez — the same object under its South Asian name
kin: gris-gris — the West African cousin — the same Qur'anic writing, carried in cloth instead of silver, by way of Mande scholars
kin: mezuzah — the other Abrahamic case with a written text sealed inside it, fixed to a doorpost rather than hung at a neck
kin: silver — the metal it is nearly always made in
kin: folding — the practice that gets a verse into a case that size
kin: divine-name — what is written inside — God's names, the names of angels or of prophets, or a verse
kin: tuareg-cross — the other silver charm in this batch, and the contrast: that one holds nothing
kin: grand-bazaar — a market where the same case is sold under the Turkish name muska
sources: s:web-mwnf-hirz-oman s:wp-throne-verse s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-talisman s:wp-silver

## Holy rider pendant (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/holy-rider-pendant/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/holy-rider-pendant.json
id: holy-rider-pendant
aliases: rider saint amulet · Sisinnios amulet · Solomon amulet · hystera amulet · Abyzou amulet
when: 501 CE – 1299 CE
countries: TR GR EG
object: form=pendant materials=copper,lead worn=neck
against: childbirth — said by the amulets themselves, which name the demon blamed for miscarriage and order her away [s:wp-abyzou]
against: child-harm — said by the Testament of Solomon, in which the demon says she walks the world looking for women about to give birth and strangles newborns [s:wp-abyzou]
against: demons — said by the amulet's own labels: Solomon, Arlaph or Saint Sisinnios doing the driving off [s:wp-abyzou]
against: evil-eye — said by the Bawit wall painting, which sets the piercing of the evil eye in the same composition as the trampled demon [s:wp-abyzou]
against: illness — said by the Testament of Solomon, where the demon also claims deafness, eye trouble, obstructions of the throat, madness and bodily pain [s:wp-abyzou]
what: A small disc or pendant, bronze on the early Byzantine examples and lead on the medieval ones. One face carries the scene: a standing figure whipping a bound kneeling woman, or — on the later type — a horseman trampling her under the hooves. The other face often carries a whirling face-like device read as a womb, the hystera, sometimes ringed by an ouroboros, a snake biting its own tail. Everybody in the scene is labelled.
story: The woman on the pendant is Abyzou, the demon blamed for miscarriage and infant mortality, and said to be driven by envy because she is infertile herself. She is Alabasandria in Coptic Egypt and Gylou in Byzantine Greek, and in the texts she has more names than anyone can count. In the Testament of Solomon she tells the king she never sleeps, that she walks the world looking for women about to give birth, and that she will strangle a newborn if she gets the chance.

The amulets take the healing-charm grammar of the late antique Mediterranean — address the affliction by name and order it out — and apply it to her. One bronze amulet labels the standing figure Arlaph and reads "The Seal of Solomon [is] with the bearer; I am Noskam." The reverse, written inside the ouroboros, reads: "Flee, flee, Abyzou, [from] Sisinios and Sisinnia; the voracious dog dwells here."

Who does the driving off varies: Solomon, or Arlaph — called Afarof in the Testament of Solomon and identified with the archangel Raphael — or, on Christian examples, Saint Sisinnios. On one medieval piece the rider is Sisinnios, the demon is named twice over as Abizou and Anabardalea, and an angel called Araph stands by with one wing raised.

The same scene exists in paint. At the monastery of St Apollo in Bawit, in Egypt, a wall painting shows the childbirth demon named Alabasandria trampled under a horse; the rider wears a belted tunic and trousers in the Parthian style, and the inscription, faded by the time it was read, was read as Sisinnios. Round the central image are a centaur, the piercing of the evil eye, and the demon's winged, reptile-tailed daughter, named in her own inscription.

*Inference —* the amulets are usually described as protecting women in childbirth and their infants, and Jeffrey Spier's survey notes that some of the names of the people seeking protection on surviving examples are men's. Whatever these pendants were understood to be doing, they were not only for mothers.
kin: lamashtu-plaque — the same demon's job description two thousand years earlier and one region east — A. A. Barb traced this family of she-demons back to the Mesopotamian primeval sea
kin: gorgoneion — the face on the reverse; the medieval lead amulets carry a device that resembles one and is read as a womb symbol
kin: magical-gem — the practice this grew out of — named powers, named demons, cut small and worn
kin: incantation-bowl — the eastern contemporary, naming Lilith where these name Abyzou, and buried instead of worn
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition whose grammar these keep — name the affliction, order it to flee
kin: serpent — the ouroboros the reverse inscription is written inside
kin: divine-name — the working part of the object: Solomon's seal, Arlaph, Sisinnios, and the demon's own name used against her
kin: st-christopher-medal — what this becomes in Latin Christendom — a saint on a small metal disc, worn against a named danger
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read; the largest class of amulet in the world is the one aimed at whatever takes babies

## Horseshoe (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/horseshoe/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/horseshoe.json
id: horseshoe
aliases: lucky horseshoe · door horseshoe · cold iron shoe
when: 910 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE IT DE DK SE NO LT EE TR US
object: form=door-piece materials=iron,steel,terracotta,glass worn=door,lintel,wall,shop
against: spirits — said by the account of why iron was chosen: horseshoes were originally made of iron, a material held to ward off evil spirits [s:wp-horseshoe]
against: demons — said by the legend of Saint Dunstan, who is said to have extracted a promise that the Devil would never enter a household with a horseshoe nailed to the door [s:wp-horseshoe]
against: house — said by European householders, who put worn shoes above doorways to guard houses, barns and stables [s:wp-horseshoe]
against: bad-luck — said by carriers in England, Denmark, Lithuania and Estonia, among whom the shape, fabrication, placement and manner of sourcing all matter [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
against: evil-eye — said by Turkish practice, in which metal or blue glass horseshoes are combined with the all-seeing eye [s:wp-horseshoe]
against: demons — said by an alternative explanation recorded in Irish and British folklore: fairies are repelled by iron, and a horseshoe was the readiest source of it [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
what: A U of iron, drilled with nail holes, that spent its first life nailed to a hoof. As a charm it is the used one: worn thin at the toe, still carrying nail stubs, fixed over a doorway. Traditionally it is held up by seven nails. Model shoes in card and plastic are given at weddings, and paper ones go into confetti.
story: The object arrives late and the charm arrives after it. Historians differ on the origin of the nailed shoe, partly because worn iron was valuable and got reforged; there is no hard evidence that the Druids invented it. Four bronze horseshoes with apparent nail holes were found in an Etruscan tomb in 1897, dated around 400 BCE, and a horseshoe complete with nails came out of the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai, dated to the fifth century CE. Written references are later: the earliest clear record of iron horseshoes is a mention of "crescent figured irons and their nails" in 910, with occasional mentions by 973. Around 1000 CE cast bronze shoes with nail holes were common in Europe; the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries brought widespread iron manufacture, and during the Crusades iron was valuable enough that horseshoes were accepted in lieu of coin to pay taxes.

Why this piece of scrap and not another: they were made of iron, a material held to turn away evil spirits, and they were held on with seven nails, seven being the luckiest number. Worn shoes were put above or beside doorways to guard houses, barns and stables, a custom whose remnants can still be seen across Italy, Germany, Britain and Scandinavia. In the Middle East the same shape is made as blue-glazed terracotta plaques; in Turkey metal or blue glass horseshoes are combined with the all-seeing eye.

Then there is the argument about which way up. In much of Europe, the Middle East and Latin America the shoe is hung facing downward, so that blessing pours onto whoever passes beneath. In parts of Ireland and Britain it is hung upward, so the luck is caught and cannot run out. Both went to the United States with their emigrants: English and Irish descent hangs it up, French, German, Italian, Spanish and Balkan descent hangs it down. Other conditions get attached in some traditions and not others — that the shoe must have been used and not new, that it must have been found and not bought, that any luck belongs to the owner of the shoe rather than to whoever hung it.

The Christian version names a blacksmith. Saint Dunstan, who worked as a smith before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 959, is said to have been asked by the Devil to shoe his horse, and to have nailed the shoe to the Devil's own foot instead, removing it only on a promise that the Devil would never enter a household with a horseshoe nailed to the door.

One English town has been collecting them since the fifteenth century. Every noble visiting Oakham, the county town of Rutland, presents a horseshoe to the Lord of the Manor, and it is nailed to the wall of Oakham Castle; the oldest of that accumulation date from the 1400s. The county flag is a golden horseshoe on a field of acorns.
how: Found, not bought, in the strictest versions. Nailed up over a door, a barn or a stable, points up or points down according to which tradition you inherited, ideally with seven nails. Nothing is done to charge it. It is not retired: it stays on the door until the door goes.
today: Still nailed over doors across northern Europe and North America, still sold new in gift shops as a wedding token, and still hung as a decorative wall piece with no claim attached. Edward Lovett found them on Sussex bedsteads in 1928, beside holed stones, against nightmares. *Inference —* a new shoe bought for luck breaks two of the tradition's own rules at once, and the people who sell them and the people who quote the rules are rarely the same people.
kin: iron — the reason it was picked up in the first place: cold iron, the metal European folklore says contains and repels
kin: crescent — the shape it shares with an older sign, and the shape the earliest written record names it by — crescent figured irons
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice in its plainest form, and the one this atlas has the longest argument about direction in
kin: nazar — what it is combined with in Turkey — the shoe and the all-seeing eye on one object
kin: hagstone — what Edward Lovett found hanging beside it on Sussex bedsteads in 1928, against the same nightmares
kin: cornicello — the southern European answer at the same doorway, and now on the same rear-view mirror
kin: four-leaf-clover — the other charm that must be found rather than bought, and the other one a factory now supplies anyway
kin: rabbits-foot — the two objects Theodore Roosevelt was given: a gold-mounted rabbit's foot from John L. Sullivan, and a penholder Bob Fitzsimmons made out of a horseshoe
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and its most-copied object
kin: luck-word — the word that has replaced protection in most present-day talk about it
kin: edward-lovett — the collector who recorded it in London and Sussex homes in the 1920s rather than in the past tense
sources: s:wp-horseshoe s:wp-iron-in-folklore s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-edward-lovett s:wp-luck

## Illa (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/illa/

id: illa

countries: PE BO
object: form=figurine worn=field,hearth
against: livestock — said by Inca religious leaders and, per the cited account, present-day Andean highland communities [s:web-dma-llama-iconography]
against: house — said by the same, for fields as well as herds — the cited source names agricultural alongside pastoral fertility [s:web-dma-llama-iconography]
what: A small carved animal, usually a llama or alpaca, cut from hard stone — the Dallas Museum of Art's Inca example is green and black — with a cylindrical hole sunk into the back between the shoulders. It sits in the hand. The hole is the working part: it is a container, not a decoration.
story: Dana Olesch, writing for the Dallas Museum of Art in 2017 about a camelid-form vessel made between 1400 and 1540, describes what the hole was for: "Inca religious leaders likely inserted a mixture of llama fat, blood, and other ceremonial objects into the hole located at the top of this vessel during various fertility rituals." The point was agricultural and pastoral fertility. Several Inca-related groups ended the rite by placing the illa in a pasture.

That is the whole logic of the object, and it is not the logic of a pendant. An illa is not worn where somebody can see it; it is fed and then put into the ground the herd walks over. The charm is a deposit.

*Inference —* an object that is buried is an object that is found, which is why museums hold so many of them and why nearly every one has left the corral it belonged to. This atlas notes that as a fact about collections rather than about the Andes.

Olesch writes that highland communities in the Andes still use illa in fertility rituals for their camelid herds. The word travels with variants — conopa, canopa in colonial Spanish sources, inqaychu and enqa in Quechua-speaking herding communities — and the objects under those names are not all the same object.
how: Carved from hard stone with hand tools, the cavity drilled. Charged by filling: llama fat, blood, and other offerings placed in the hole. Then set in a pasture or field, or kept in the house and brought out for the rite. The illa is not retired; it is refilled.
today: Still in use in Andean highland herding communities as of the account cited here, and held in numbers by museums in Europe and North America. This project has read no dated field report of a present-day rite and does not describe one.

kin: foundation-deposit — the same move made under a building instead of under a field
kin: nkisi — the other object in this atlas whose power is what was packed into a cavity in it

kin: british-museum — one of the collections holding Inca conopas

## Incantation bowl (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/incantation-bowl/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/incantation-bowl.json
id: incantation-bowl
aliases: magic bowl · demon bowl · devil-trap bowl · Aramaic incantation bowl
when: 501 CE – 800 CE
countries: IQ IR SY
object: form=bowl materials=terracotta,ink,copper worn=foundation,door,grave,hearth
against: demons — said by the bowls themselves, which name Lilith and Bagdana [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: evil-eye — said by the Jewish bowls from Nippur, which list it among the evil influences they are set against [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: house — said by the users, who buried them under thresholds, in courtyards and in the corners of houses [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: illness — said by the medieval Islamic talismanic bowls, used for healing by drinking the water left in them overnight [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
what: A plain earthenware bowl with writing inside it. The text is inked in a spiral that starts at the rim and winds inward to the centre, most often in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, sometimes Mandaic, Syriac, Arabic or Persian. Then the bowl is turned upside down and buried — under a threshold, in a courtyard, in the corner of a house where somebody has just died, in a cemetery. Around one in ten carries no real language at all.
story: John Charles Arnold sets out the mechanism the way its users described it: "When placed upside down under each corner of a house, demons would follow the inscribed charms that spiraled from the outer rim inward, only to be caught in the center."

The bowls belong to Sasanian Mesopotamia, sixth to eighth century, in a population that was Christian, Manichaean, Mandaean, Jewish, Zoroastrian or still Babylonian in religion, and largely Aramaic-speaking whatever else it was. They were commissioned across those lines. Nearly eighty Jewish bowls survive from Babylon under Sasanian rule, most from the Jewish settlement at Nippur, where almost every excavated house had them buried in it. They name what they are against: the evil eye, Lilith, Bagdana. Their inscriptions quote scripture and rabbinic texts alike, which scholars read as evidence that the rabbinic material was held to carry the same power as the biblical.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly. The bowls often call themselves amulets, and the Talmud, which was being written in the same place and period, discusses the use of amulets to drive away demons — so the text on these bowls is the only written material documenting Jewish language and religion recovered from that time and place. And the corpus is a scandal: about 2,000 bowls are registered as archaeological finds, while the trade digs them up freely, so there may be tens of thousands in private hands.

There is an Islamic branch. In the medieval period, talismanic bowls did the same work in metal rather than clay, covered in Arabic — Qur'anic verses, a hadith, sometimes numerology or astrology — and used for healing by drinking water left standing in them overnight.
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition these bowls are the earliest bulk evidence for — written amulets in divine and angelic names, centuries before anyone called it that
kin: mesopotamian-apotropaic — the older practice in the same ground: name the demon, bind it, put the object where it enters
kin: lamashtu-plaque — the same argument in bronze a millennium earlier, with the demon pictured instead of written
kin: kamea — the descendant that keeps the writing and drops the bowl
kin: joseph-naveh — with Shaul Shaked, the editor whose 1985 Amulets and Magic Bowls put these texts in front of readers who are not Aramaists
kin: shaul-shaked — the other half of that edition, and the reason a bowl text can be quoted at all here
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition that carried the bowl on in metal, inscribed with Qur'an and hadith and drunk from
kin: foundation-deposit — the practice that puts protection under the floor rather than on the body
kin: holy-rider-pendant — the same demon-naming logic in the Byzantine west, worn instead of buried
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this corpus forces: 2,000 bowls excavated, tens of thousands dug and sold
sources: s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-amulet s:wp-islam-and-magic
