## Inuit amulet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/inuit-amulet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/inuit-amulet.json
id: inuit-amulet
aliases: Netsilik amulet · Iglulik amulet · arnguaq
said: the Inuit terms vary by group and are not collapsed into one here
when: 1900 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CA GL US
object: materials=bone,tooth,skin,hair worn=neck,sewn-in,pocket
against: illness — said by the published ethnography of Inuit religion, which holds that illness can be caused by offending the spirits [s:wp-inuit-religion]
against: spirits — said by the same record: amulets are worn among the means of avoiding offence and retribution [s:wp-inuit-religion]
against: child-harm — said by the Netsilik, in the recorded instance of a boy carrying eighty [s:wp-inuit-religion]
RESTRICTED: This record prints only what published ethnography and Inuit institutions have themselves made public. It does not set out which amulet answers which spirit, and does not reconstruct any rite from scattered sources.
what: Small worked or unworked pieces of animal and bird — bone, claw, tooth, skin, feather — sewn to clothing or carried, one amulet to one spirit. There is no single form. The class is defined by the relation, not the shape: published ethnography states that the effect of an Inuit amulet is attributed to the spirit that corresponds to it.
story: Two numbers in the ethnographic record say more about this practice than any description of an object does.

The first is 80. Wikipedia's summary of the published ethnography of Inuit religion records that the Netsilik used a great many amulets — even dogs could have them — and gives one recorded instance of a young boy who had eighty, so many that he could hardly play. The second is 17: one man carried seventeen names taken from his ancestors, and the names were themselves intended to protect him. Beside that sits the Iglulik, who used few.

Amulets sit inside a system with other parts. Inuit religion holds that human illness can be caused by offending the spirits, and that fear of retribution produces caution; to avoid giving offence, people have observed rules and taboos, offered prayers and songs, worn amulets, and consulted the angakkuit, the ritual specialists who mediate between people and spirits. An amulet might be made by an angakkuq, but lay people made them too.

*Inference —* an eighty-amulet child and a seventeen-name man describe a practice where protection is cumulative rather than singular, which is a different logic from the one-charm-one-neck traditions that fill most of this atlas. This project states that as its own reading of the published record and not as anybody's account of their own practice.

This record prints what published ethnography and Inuit and Greenlandic institutions have made public, and no more. It does not reconstruct which animal answers which spirit, and it does not fill the gaps from a neighbouring tradition.
how: Selected and attached: sewn to a parka, hung at the neck, set into a hood. An amulet corresponds to a spirit, and the rest of the making is not printed here. Names function alongside objects — a name taken from an ancestor is described in the ethnography as protective in itself.
today: Inuit amulet practice is documented by twentieth-century ethnographers working in the Canadian Arctic and Greenland; Inuit religious practice continues alongside Christianity across the Arctic. This project has read no dated present-day account it can cite, so no claim is made here about what any community carries in 2026.
kin: tupilaq — the object this one is most often confused with, and its opposite: an amulet is carried for its owner, a tupilaq was sent at somebody else
kin: tooth-and-claw — the sign family most of these belong to — the animal, kept as a part of itself
kin: ongon — the Siberian parallel, across the same Arctic, with its own specialists and its own rules
kin: sewing-in — how one is carried: stitched into a parka rather than hung where it can be seen
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read explaining why this record stops where it stops
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this belongs in — the best-known figure in this record is a child carrying eighty
kin: bone-ivory — the material the Arctic works, and the one most of these are made from
sources: s:wp-inuit-religion s:wp-tupilaq s:wp-shamanism-in-siberia
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Jimat (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/jimat/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/jimat.json
id: jimat
native: جيمت (Jawi)
aliases: azimat · tamimah · tangkal · rajah · uang gobog · pis bolong
said: JI-mat
when: 1200 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ID MY
root: Malay and Indonesian azimat, borrowed from Arabic عزيمة ʿazīmah, 'determination, firmness of resolve'; shortened in Indonesian to jimat. The Malay synonym is tangkal (Jawi تڠكل); the Arabic-derived tamimah is also used
object: form=coin materials=copper,brass,paper,ink,cloth worn=neck,vehicle,wall,pocket
against: illness — said by Indonesian Wikipedia's definition: a jimat is hung to protect its owner and to ward off illness — menangkal penyakit [s:web-id-wikipedia-jimat]
against: bad-luck — said by the same definition: tolak bala, to repel misfortune [s:web-id-wikipedia-jimat]
against: attraction — said by Balinese use of pis bolong in Hindu rites, as tokens of faith and as bringers of good fortune; and the Malay definition of azimat as an object giving tuah, luck [s:web-wp-indonesian-numismatic-charm]
against: weapons — said by the Pis Anoman type, which a collector's account says gives its holder more strength and energy, like the wind [s:web-wp-indonesian-numismatic-charm]
what: A class rather than a shape. Jimat covers any object or piece of writing hung on a body, a vehicle or a building to keep its owner from harm. Inside the class, three things are described in detail by the sources this record uses: a rajah, a charm written out in inscribed characters; a baju rajah, a garment carrying that writing; and the cast coin-charms of Java and Bali, flat discs of copper and brass with a square hole, made like Chinese cash coins but never spent.
story: The coin-charms are the part of this class with dates on it. Indonesian collectors call them uang gobog, gobog wayang or koin gobog; in Bali they are pis bolong; Dutch sources called them Indonesische tempelmunten, Indonesian temple coins. The first gobog amulets in Java appeared during the Majapahit Empire. Gobog wayang in copper and brass were produced in the eighteenth century, and evidence for making them at scale runs only from the beginning of the twentieth.

They left the island early. Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles took 106 gobog wayang cash coins with him from Java to Britain, and they are in the British Museum. Joe Cribb built the standard catalogue on them: Magic coins of Java, Bali, and the Malay Peninsula, 13th century to 20th century — A Catalogue based on the Raffles Collection of Coin-shaped charms from Java in the British Museum, published in 1999. That subtitle is also the clearest published statement of the span.

What the pieces are held to do is stated type by type. A Yogyakarta numismatist describes the function of gobog amulets as "a complement to the requirements or ritual offerings in Java". In Bali they remain in use in Hindu rites, as tokens of faith and as bringers of good fortune, and individual types carry individual claims — the Pis Anoman is said to give its holder strength and energy like the wind.

The class carries an argument inside it. Indonesian Wikipedia's article on jimat states the Islamic position flatly: "Penggunaan jimat di dalam ajaran Islam adalah perbuatan terlarang. Hal ini dikarenakan perbuatan tersebut merupakan bentuk meminta perlindungan dan penyembuhan kepada selain Allah" — using a jimat is forbidden in Islamic teaching, because it amounts to seeking protection and healing from other than God — and adds that the practice belongs to pre-Islamic society and should not be followed. The same article illustrates the baju rajah as a thing people wear. Both statements sit on the same page. That is where the word stands in Indonesian and Malay now, and this atlas reports it without settling it.
how: Cast, for the coins: metal of a composition close to Chinese cash, in moulds, with wayang figures on the face. Written, for the rajah: characters inscribed on paper or onto cloth, as in the baju rajah. Then hung — on the body, on a vehicle, on a building — or set out with ritual offerings, which is the use a Yogyakarta numismatist names for the gobog in Java. This project has read no published account of the making rite for either, and prints none.
today: Still in use in Bali in Hindu rites as of the accounts this project has read, and still argued over in Indonesian-language religious writing, where the class is described as forbidden by Islamic teaching and illustrated at the same time. The Raffles pieces remain in London.
kin: keris-pusaka — the heirloom blade of the same islands, which is a jimat with a name, a smith and a lineage attached
kin: anting-anting — the Philippine cousin: the Javanese anting-anting, an ear-hung ornament, is where the Tagalog word comes from
kin: charm-coin — the Chinese coin-shaped charm the gobog is modelled on — same square hole, different pantheon on the face
kin: taweez — the written Islamic charm this word's Arabic root belongs to, and the practice the Islamic objection to jimat is aimed at too
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition the word azimat comes out of, and the one whose scholars argue against the object
kin: takrut — the mainland Southeast Asian written charm doing the same work one sea north
kin: british-museum — where the Raffles coins ended up, and where the standard catalogue of them was written
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the Indonesian definition leads with: hung on a body, a vehicle or a building
kin: inscribing — what makes a rajah a rajah — the characters, not the paper
sources: s:web-id-wikipedia-jimat s:web-ms-wikipedia-azimat s:web-wp-indonesian-numismatic-charm s:wp-kris s:wp-agimat s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Kamea (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/kamea/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/kamea.json
id: kamea
native: קמיע (Hebrew)
aliases: kame'a · Jewish written amulet · segullah object
said: ka-MEY-a, plural kame'ot
when: 201 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL ES DE PL GB
object: form=folded-paper materials=parchment,paper,silver,copper,ink worn=neck,pocket,wall,door,cradle
against: demons — said by the Hekhalot literature and the later baal shem tradition, in which angels are bound by names and formulae [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
against: illness — said by the Talmud, which mentions charms for healing, and the rabbis who sanctioned a wide range of magical cures — it was ruled that any practice actually producing a cure was not to be counted among the forbidden ones [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
against: witchcraft — said by the practitioners recorded in the cited article, including the baal shem said to have exorcised a dybbuk [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
against: evil-eye — said by the older Jewish written-amulet practice the incantation bowls document, which names the evil eye directly [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
RESTRICTED: Practical Kabbalah is restricted inside its own tradition. It was held to be permitted only to an elite who could keep its spiritual source separate from the realms of evil, and only under conditions of holiness and purity; most Kabbalists have taught that its use is forbidden outright. Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets and taught that, in generations without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer, its pursuit by a person with an impure body is very detrimental. This atlas therefore prints no formula, no arrangement of divine or angelic names, and no construction for any kame'a. What is above is history and prohibition; the working content is not published here and is mostly not published anywhere.
what: A written amulet: a small sheet of parchment, paper or thin metal, inscribed in Hebrew with divine and angelic names, sometimes laid out as a grid of letters or numbers, then folded or rolled and carried, hung at a bed, or fixed in a house. What is written on it is the object; the case, where there is one, is a case.
story: The practice has a name in its own tradition — Kabbalah Ma'asit, practical Kabbalah — and that tradition mostly forbids it.

Gershom Scholem's point about it is the historical one: a large part of the content of practical Kabbalah predates speculative Kabbalah and does not depend on it. What ended up under the label was an agglomeration of all the magical practices that developed in Judaism from the Talmudic period through the Middle Ages, and the doctrine of the Sefirot hardly ever played a decisive role in them. Amulet-making using the esoteric names of angels dates from Talmudic times.

The split between contemplative and practical Kabbalah was complete by the beginning of the 14th century, and most of the writing of the practical branch was never published. Abraham Abulafia condemned it. One tradition of it flourished in Spain in the second half of the 15th century, before the Alhambra Decree, around a text called Sepher ha-Mashiv; Moshe Idel describes its practitioners as interested in demonology and in coercive incantations to summon demons, angels and even God, in order to hasten the Messianic Age. Joseph Della Reina's failure at that was held up by later Kabbalists as a warning.

Then Isaac Luria, in 16th-century Safed, forbade his students to write amulets at all, and because Luria is the central teacher of modern Kabbalah and the foundation for later Hasidism, that prohibition carries authority rather than opinion. His reasoning was about purity: without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer to purify with, the pursuit of practical Kabbalah by a person with an impure body is very detrimental.

It kept going anyway, at the border. The Baal Shem healers worked with methods between practical and meditative Kabbalah, amulets among them — Elijah Ba'al Shem of Chelm (1550–1583), the Baal Shem of London (1708–1782). Yisrael Baal Shem Tov (1698–1760) began as one, used amulets, and by the end of his life wrote only his own name on them, Yisrael ben Sara or Yisrael ben Eliezer, and no names of God at all. In the 1750s Jacob Emden accused Jonathan Eybeschütz of being a secret Sabbatean, chiefly on his reading of some amulets Eybeschütz had written. Rabbi Hirsch Fraenkel was imprisoned in Germany in 1713 for owning a library said to contain oaths and amulets for overcoming demons, seeing the future and speaking to the dead.

*Inference —* a practice whose own authorities forbid it and whose writings were mostly never published is a practice an atlas can describe and should not demonstrate. This record names who restricts it and stops there; see the restricted note below.

One word of warning about the name. In Western ceremonial magic, 'kamea' also means the planetary number squares that Cornelius Agrippa expounded in De Occulta Philosophia in 1531, used as grids on which to trace the sigils of spirits by converting a name to numbers. That is a different object with a borrowed Hebrew word, and the atlas keeps them apart.
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition this object is the whole material output of
kin: incantation-bowl — the same writing, seven centuries earlier, buried under a floor in Nippur instead of folded into a pocket
kin: mezuzah — the object Maimonides used to draw the line — write angel names inside one and you have turned a commandment into this
kin: tefillin — the commandment the Talmud specifically differentiates from amulets, and which a kame'a is not
kin: magic-square — the grid the Western occult tradition borrowed this word for, after Agrippa's planetary squares of 1531
kin: divine-name — the sign this object is made of, and the one it does not print here
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest surviving Hebrew written charm, six centuries before the Talmudic practice this record starts from
kin: taweez — the Islamic parallel, argued over inside its own tradition on almost identical terms
kin: red-string — the one piece of this world that went fully public, and the one its own scholars are most dismissive of
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read about the restricted block; this record is one of its examples
sources: s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-kabbalah s:wp-magic-square s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-mezuzah
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Keris pusaka (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/keris-pusaka/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/keris-pusaka.json
id: keris-pusaka
native: ꦏꦼꦫꦶꦱ꧀ (Javanese)
aliases: kris · keris · dhuwung · wangkingan · tosan aji · karih · sele
said: KREES pu-SA-ka
when: 1200 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ID MY BN PH
root: Old Javanese kris, 'dagger'; keris ꦏꦼꦫꦶꦱ꧀ in the Javanese ngoko register, dhuwung in krama, wangkingan in krama inggil. Pusaka is a sanctified heirloom
object: form=nail materials=iron,gold,silver,brass,wood,bone worn=waist,wall
against: bad-luck — said by Javanese owners, who test a blade by cutting a leaf or by sleeping with it under the pillow and reading the dream — a bad dream and the blade is discarded [s:wp-kris]
against: poverty — said by holders of the Beras Wutah type, which was held to grant its possessor an easy life without famine and was assigned mainly to officers paid in foodstuffs [s:wp-kris]
against: fire — said by Javanese accounts of what a kris could prevent — fires, death and agricultural failure among them [s:wp-kris]
against: attraction — said by the same accounts, on the other side of the ledger: some kris were held to bring fortune, such as bountiful harvests [s:wp-kris]
against: weapons — said by the Barong dance of Bali, in which dancers in trance turn their own blades on their chests and are held to be made invulnerable to sharp objects [s:wp-kris]
what: An asymmetrical dagger in three parts: blade (bilah), hilt (hulu) and sheath (warangka). The blade is forged from alternating laminations of iron and nickelous iron, and the contrast between them stands out on the finished surface as pamor, a pattern. Many blades are wavy — the waves are luk — and many are straight. Each part is worked: carved wood, ivory, brass, iron, silver or gold, set with stones. A blade is described by its dhapur, the form, of which there are around 60 variants; by its pamor, of which there are around 250; and by its tangguh, which is its age and origin. Worn in the belt at the back.
story: The kris is a weapon that is also a member of the family. Javanese calls a heirloom blade tosan aji, sacred heirloom weapon, and counts it a pusaka. Blades are handed down through generations and worn at weddings and other ceremonies. A kris given by a Javanese king to a noble or a subject carried the king's confidence with it and was a great honour; the property the blade confers is piyandel, which means to add self-confidence. A Javanese groom wears one with a chain of jasmine wound round it, and the flowers say he should not be quick to anger.

The smith is the point. Making a kris was the work of an empu — 'possessor' — the honorary title in Java for an ironsmith with the skill to forge one, as against a pandai besi who makes tools and peasants' weapons. A kris empu was held to need knowledge, technical skill and spiritual prowess together, because the blade has a physical and a spiritual presence. The metal is layered from different iron ores and meteorite nickel, folded dozens or hundreds of times on a high-quality blade. Some take a short time; some take years. Empu are described as craftsmen who also know literature, history and the occult.

The blade is treated as alive and, more to the point, as not necessarily friendly. Kris are held to be vessels for spirits, good or bad. A blade can be tested: cuts on a leaf, read against the blade's width, say whether it is a good one; or the owner sleeps with it under the pillow and reads the dream — a bad dream and the blade has to go, a good one and it stays. A blade bad for one person is not bad for another, and the fit between weapon and owner is what matters. Types carry their own claims: Beras Wutah was held to grant its possessor a life without famine, and was given mainly to officials paid in foodstuffs. Pointing a kris at someone means they will die soon, so silat practitioners touch the blade tips to the ground before a demonstration.

The legends have names and centuries. The Pararaton tells of Mpu Gandring, the smith killed by his impatient customer Ken Arok in the last days of Kediri in the thirteenth century, who cursed the unfinished blade to kill seven men, Ken Arok among them. The Sejarah Melayu of Tun Sri Lanang tells of Taming Sari, made by a Javanese empu, won in a duel by the Melakan admiral Hang Tuah in the fifteenth century, and so well made that whoever held it could not be beaten. Setan Kober, 'devil of the grave', forged with thirteen luk by Empu Bayu Aji and disturbed at its charging by a crying djinn from the graveyard, made its wielders overly ambitious and impatient and finally killed Arya Penangsang in the sixteenth century.

Colonial law disarmed it. Firearms came into the archipelago in the sixteenth century; the forging of edged weapons fell away as sultans and rajas were subjugated, and in some regions carrying cutting and stabbing weapons was banned. The turning point in Java was 1830, when Prince Diponegoro, defeated at the end of the five-year Java War, handed his kris to the Dutch. The early twentieth century brought a ban on carrying edged weapons in the Dutch East Indies. The ceremonial and protective use continued anyway, in the kraton and istana of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Muslim-inhabited southern Philippines.

It is a live object still, with the danger that implies. In the Balinese Barong dance the segment called the keris dance has male dancers in trance stabbing themselves in the chest with their own blades and coming away unhurt. In February 2021 a 16-year-old kris dancer was stabbed to death in the heart by his own kris during a Rangda dance in Denpasar.
how: Forged by an empu from layers of different iron ores and meteorite nickel, folded and folded again, the pamor raised by the contrast between the laminations. The smiths carried out old rites that were held to put power into the blade; this project's sources do not print them, and nor does this record. A kris needs a yearly cleaning, called jamasan in Javanese, which is part of what is owed to it — the repeated cleanings leave old blades worn and thin. Repairs used whatever was to hand locally, so a blade from Java can end up with a hilt from Bali and a sheath from Madura. Warriors made offerings to their kris at a shrine.
today: In 2005 UNESCO put the Indonesian kris on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Making it had nearly stopped by the 1990s, under economic pressure and changing values; concerned specialists pushed a revival and craftsmanship picked up. Smiths still work in Madura, Surakarta, Yogyakarta, Makassar and Palembang, but their numbers are falling sharply and successors are hard to find. The craft survives in villages such as Banyu Sumurup in Imogiri, Bantul, near Yogyakarta, where a blade is made either as a sacred amulet ordered by an enthusiast who wants its spiritual power, or as a souvenir for a visitor — the same workshop, two customers, and the argument about whether those are the same object sits inside the trade rather than outside it.
kin: jimat — the Malay and Indonesian class of protective objects this belongs to, and outranks: a kris is a jimat with a smith's name on it
kin: iron — the material argument in full — laminations of iron and nickelous iron, folded to raise the pamor, and the reason a blade is read like a face
kin: inheriting — what makes it a pusaka: handed down through generations, worn at weddings, given by a king to mark his confidence
kin: feeding-the-charm — jamasan, the yearly cleaning the blade is owed, which wears old blades thin
kin: unesco-ich — the body that inscribed the Indonesian kris in 2005
kin: anting-anting — the Philippine charm carried in the same fights; kris forging continued in the Spanish East Indies while Java's was being banned
kin: hei-tiki — the other heirloom in this atlas treated as a person rather than a possession, and handed down the same way
kin: phra-khrueang — the Thai parallel in how worth is set: maker, lineage and age decide the price, not the metal
kin: mjolnir-pendant — the other weapon worn as a charm in this atlas, though that one is a hammer in miniature and this one is a working blade
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the Banyu Sumurup workshop belongs in: one bench, one blade for an enthusiast's shrine and one for a visitor's shelf
kin: serpent — the sign read into the wavy blade, whose luk are counted and named
sources: s:wp-kris s:web-wp-indonesian-numismatic-charm s:wp-iron s:wp-agimat
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ketef-hinnom-scrolls/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ketef-hinnom-scrolls.json
id: ketef-hinnom-scrolls
native: כתף הינום (Hebrew)
aliases: Ketef Hinnom amulets · the silver scrolls · KH1 and KH2
said: KEH-tef hi-NOM, 'shoulder of Hinnom'
when: 625 BCE – 575 BCE
countries: IL
object: form=scroll materials=silver worn=grave
against: bad-luck — said by the excavation report, which describes the scrolls as apparently once used as amulets; the text on them is a blessing rather than a named harm [s:wp-ketef-hinnom]
against: the-dead — said by the findspot: an Iron Age Judahite burial chamber [s:wp-ketef-hinnom]
what: Two sheets of silver, tiny, rolled tight, each scratched with a passage of the Priestly Blessing from the Book of Numbers. They were found rolled and had to be opened; the method for doing it without losing them took three years to develop. They hold what may be the oldest surviving text of the Hebrew Bible.
story: Ketef Hinnom is the shoulder of rock where the Valley of Rephaim meets the Valley of Hinnom, on the old road from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, beside St Andrew's Church. Gabriel Barkay reported the first season there in 1975: a salvage excavation on the hill between the church road and the road down into the valley, prompted by a block of stone 2.80 m long lying on the surface, which turned out to be a threshold still in place in a monumental complex. Underneath were rock-cut burial chambers in natural caverns, Iron Age Judahite, of the seventh and sixth centuries BCE.

In 1979 the two silver scrolls came out of one of those chambers. The excavation report describes them as apparently once used as amulets. They are dated to the First Temple period, late seventh to early sixth century BCE, before the Babylonian Exile. They are now in the Israel Museum.

*Inference —* two things about this object are unusual for the atlas at once. It is a written charm that survives from before the tradition it belongs to had a canon to quote from, and it is a charm whose text is not a spell but a blessing. Whether the people who rolled them up would have called them amulets is a question the excavation cannot answer, and the cited report does not claim more than 'apparently'.
how: Silver, hammered thin, inscribed, rolled, and worn or carried. How they were suspended is not published in what this project read; what is documented is where they ended up, which is a burial chamber.
kin: tefillin — the commandment that puts the same kind of verses in a box on the body — and the object this one keeps getting read backwards through
kin: mezuzah — the other Jewish text-in-a-container, fixed to a doorpost instead of worn
kin: kamea — the written Jewish amulet as a class, of which this is the oldest dated survivor
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition of writing a holy text to carry, a thousand years before it had that name
kin: silver — the metal that let a text this small survive two and a half thousand years in a tomb
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that is the reason this object exists to be read
kin: taweez — the same object in another scripture — a verse, rolled small, worn
kin: quran-pendant — scripture in a case at the throat; this is that idea's oldest dated instance in the atlas
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read about what it means to date an amulet; this one is dated by a tomb, a threshold stone and three years of unrolling
sources: s:wp-ketef-hinnom s:wp-tefillin s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ladanka (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ladanka/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ladanka.json
id: ladanka
native: ладанка (Cyrillic)
aliases: ладонка · ковчежец · incense pouch · Orthodox reliquary pendant
said: LA-dan-ka
when: undated (still carried)
countries: RU
root: Russian ладан, 'incense, frankincense', plus a diminutive — the little thing you keep incense in
object: form=packet materials=cloth,thread,silver,gold,paper worn=neck,chest
against: bad-luck — said by wearers, in the practice the Russian encyclopedic entry describes and the Orthodox reference portal warns against [s:wp-ru-ladanka]
what: A small pouch or a small hinged case hung at the neck on the same cord or chain as a baptismal cross. Cloth for the old kind, stamped or cast metal for the kind sold now, often with an icon on the lid. Inside goes incense, or a fragment of a relic, or a written prayer — commonly the Lord's Prayer, Psalm 90 or the Jesus Prayer. It is worn next to the skin and it is not opened for show.
story: The Orthodox reference portal Azbyka very defines it in one line: a ковчежец со священными реликвиями в виде иконы, носимый на шее — a small reliquary with sacred relics, in the form of an icon, worn at the neck. The Russian encyclopedic entry adds the older layer: a fabric pouch, worn on the body, holding ладан, incense, and sometimes a bone from a saint's remains. Ivan Shmelev, in Bogomolye, gives it in a child's voice: "У бабушки ладанка из Иерусалима с косточкой... от мощей..." — grandmother has a ladanka from Jerusalem with a little bone in it, from the relics.

The positional rule is the first thing every Orthodox source states, and it is the whole argument in miniature. Её принято носить вместе с ним, но не вместо него: it is worn together with the cross, never instead of it. The cross is the baptismal object and cannot be displaced by this one.

The second thing every Orthodox source states is what a ladanka is not. Azbyka very is categorical: никаких оберегов и амулетов православный христианин носить на себе не должен — an Orthodox Christian should wear no protective charms and no amulets at all. The same entry says that wearing a ladanka with a prayer inside carries no sacred meaning without knowledge of the prayer and a personal appeal to God, and that treating an object with Christian symbolism as an amulet does the soul no good. The Russian encyclopedic account, describing what people do rather than what the Church teaches, records the object as functioning as both талисман and амулет, and notes that the pouches have carried protective signs.

*Inference —* set those two paragraphs side by side and this is the Orthodox twin of the Catholic argument on this shelf. In Rome the Church built a legal category — the sacramental — that lets a blessed object be devotional without being magical, and then spent centuries policing the edge of it. Here there is no such category to stand on; the instruction is simply not to. The object is still sold, still filled, still worn under the shirt, and the instruction is still printed.

The trade has moved with the money. Monastery and church shops sell ladanki in sterling silver and gold with enamelled icons on the lid; one Moscow Orthodox shop's catalogue page, read on 17 September 2026, listed twenty-five of them priced between 5,377 and 50,037 roubles. The cloth pouch with incense in it costs a fraction of that and is the older thing.
how: Bought at a church or monastery shop, or given. Filled with incense, a relic fragment, or a written prayer, and hung on the cross cord at the neck. The Orthodox sources this record cites do not describe a consecration rite for the pouch itself and this project has not gone looking for one; what they describe instead is where the relic or the incense came from, which is what carries the weight. Nothing is said about retiring one.
today: Sold in Russian church and monastery shops in 2026 in every price band, from a fabric pouch to a gold locket. The Orthodox reference portal that explains what it is spends most of the entry explaining what it must not be taken for, which is a fair description of the object's position now.
kin: agnus-dei — the Roman object closest to it — a blessed thing worn at the neck, with the same question attached about what it is
kin: st-christopher-medal — what a Catholic neck carries where this hangs beside an Orthodox cross
kin: hirz-pouch — the Islamic sewn pouch doing the same work — a written prayer, carried on the body, not to be opened
kin: gau-box — the Tibetan version — a metal case at the neck with a consecrated thing inside, and a hinged lid
kin: mezuzah — the other container this atlas holds whose contents are a named text and whose rules are about placement
kin: cross — the sign it is worn with and never instead of
kin: wearing-hidden — the practice — under the shirt, on the cross cord, not opened
kin: tama-votive — the other Orthodox object in this atlas, and the one that goes on the icon rather than on the body
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read where a church's own word for an object collides with the reader's
sources: s:web-azbyka-ladanka s:wp-ru-ladanka s:web-vazhe-ladanki
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## Lamashtu plaque (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/lamashtu-plaque/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/lamashtu-plaque.json
id: lamashtu-plaque
native: 𒀭𒈕𒈨 (cuneiform)
aliases: Lamashtu amulet · Lamastu plaque · Dimme amulet
said: la-MASH-tu, Akkadian dLa-maš-tu; Sumerian Dimme
when: 1000 BCE – 301 BCE
countries: IQ SY
object: form=plaque materials=copper,terracotta worn=neck,wall,door,grave
against: child-harm — said by the Mesopotamian incantations, which name her victims as unborn and newly born babies [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: childbirth — said by Mesopotamian ritual practice; pregnant women were the second class of victim after the babies [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: illness — said by the Mesopotamian texts, where she also functions as a bringer of disease to adolescents, adults and the old [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: demons — said by the ritual imagery, which sets Pazuzu against her on the same object [s:wp-pazuzu]
what: A small plaque, pierced or looped so it can hang, carrying the figure of the demon it is aimed at. Lamashtu is cut on it as a composite: a lion's or dog's head, donkey's teeth, bare breasts, bird-of-prey talons, a serpent gripped in each hand. She stands on a donkey in a boat; a dog and a piglet suckle at her. Her seven names, and an incantation telling her to keep away, run across the object in cuneiform. Bronze is the material of the big Neo-Assyrian examples; smaller ones are fired clay and cut stone.
story: Lamashtu is the daughter of the sky god Anu, and she acts on nobody's instructions but her own — the reason Assyriologists argue she is a goddess rather than a demon, and the reason her name is written with the cuneiform sign that marks deity. Her victims are the unborn and the newly born. She touches a pregnant woman's stomach seven times to kill the baby, or takes it from the wet nurse. Adolescents, adults and the old are on her list too, as a bringer of disease.

The incantations open by addressing her directly. One amulet, catalogued as AO 8184, runs through her names — 'Dimme', 'Daughter of Anu', 'Who was named by the gods', 'Victoria, heroine among ladies' — and then delivers the whole point of the object: "you must not approach (this) person." The names matter because knowing them is the hold.

The largest surviving pieces are scenes rather than signs. The Neo-Assyrian plaque in the Louvre known as the Plaque des Enfers sets divine symbols above a sickroom: a patient on a bed, ritual specialists at work, and in the bottom register Lamashtu on her donkey in the boat with the serpents in her fists, while Pazuzu drives her off down the river.

*Inference —* the object is not a picture of the demon so much as a place to put her. Iconographic studies distinguish an earlier threatening figure with raised hands, a middle type holding a comb and spindle, and the elaborate serpent-holding compositions of the first millennium BCE; what stays constant across all three is that she is shown named, held, and on her way out.
kin: pazuzu-head — the counter-figure cut on the same plaques, shown chasing her down the river; a household could own both and they were not opposites in the tray
kin: mesopotamian-apotropaic — the tradition this object is the centre of — a named demon, a named opponent, an incantation, and a thing to hang
kin: incantation-bowl — the same soil a thousand years later, with the demon caught in a spiral of ink under the floor instead of nailed to a wall
kin: holy-rider-pendant — the childbirth demon again, now called Abyzou and trampled by a rider on Byzantine bronze
kin: taweret-amulet — Egypt's answer to the same danger, and a guardian rather than a demon held off
kin: bes-amulet — the Egyptian household protector scholars compare to Pazuzu, and so to this plaque's other half
kin: serpent — the sign in both her fists on the first-millennium compositions
kin: hanging-at-door — where these went — beds, doorways, and the places a household counted as open
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this object opens: the oldest named amulet-demon in the atlas hunts newborns
sources: s:wp-lamashtu s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-mesopotamian-mythology s:wp-apotropaic-magic
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Lung ta prayer flag (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/lungta-flag/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/lungta-flag.json
id: lungta-flag
native: རླུང་རྟ། (Tibetan)
aliases: lungta · rlung-rta · wind horse flag · prayer flag · darchog
said: LOONG-ta, 'wind horse'
when: 1040 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN NP IN BT
root: Tibetan rlung-rta, 'wind horse' — rlung wind, rta horse
object: form=cord materials=cloth,ink worn=roof,wall
against: bad-luck — said by the reading of the wind horse itself, which stands for speed and for the transformation of bad fortune to good fortune [s:wp-prayer-flag]
what: A square or oblong of coloured cloth, printed from a woodblock, sewn along its top edge to a long string with others. Flags come in sets of five and always in the same order of colours: blue for sky and space, white for air and wind, red for fire, green for water, yellow for earth — the five elements, whose balance Tibetan medicine reads as health. Strings are hung on a diagonal, high to low, between two fixed points: a rock and a pole, a roof and a tree, the top of a temple, a stupa, a mountain pass. The vertical kind, darchog, is a single large rectangle fixed along its side to a pole and planted in ground, cairns and rooftops.
story: The centre of the printed field is a horse carrying three flaming jewels on its back. The horse stands for speed and for the turning of bad fortune into good; the three jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. Around the horse run versions of some four hundred traditional mantras, each addressed to a particular deity, including mantras of Padmasambhava, Avalokiteśvara — Chenrezig, patron of the Tibetan people — and Manjusri. The four corners carry the Four Dignities: the dragon, the garuda, the tiger and the snow lion. Prayers for a long life of good fortune are often added for whoever puts the flags up, and wishes are written on them.

The flags are held to have come out of Bon, where shamanistic Bonpo used plain flags in primary colours. Sutras first written on cloth banners travelled as prayer flags; legend ascribes the origin to the Buddha, whose prayers were written on the battle flags the devas carried against the asuras. That knowledge reached Tibet by 800 CE, and the flags themselves no later than 1040 CE, where they were modified further; the Indian monk Atisha (980–1054) brought the Indian practice of printing on cloth flags to Tibet and Nepal.

What the flags do is stated in the negative as often as the positive. They do not carry prayers to gods — the source calls that a common misconception. As wind passes over the cloth the air is held to be purified and sanctified by the mantras, and the blessings are carried to all beings. The printed images fade with exposure, and the fading is not decay in this reading: the prayers become a permanent part of the universe as the images go, and new flags are mounted beside the old ones, which is read as a welcome to life's changes.

During the Cultural Revolution prayer flags were discouraged but not eliminated, and many traditional designs may have been lost.
how: Printed from woodblocks onto the five colours, strung, and raised. Timing matters: some hold that flags hung on inauspicious astrological dates may bring negative results for as long as they fly, and the best time to put new ones up is the morning of a sunny, windy day. Because the symbols and mantras are treated as sacred, flags are not to be put on the ground or used on clothing. In Tibet old flags are replaced with new ones every year at the Tibetan New Year, and old flags should be burned.
today: Strung across passes, roofs, bridges and monastery courtyards throughout the Tibetan world as of 2026, and sold worldwide as decoration, often in the right five colours and the wrong order, and often hung where nothing is renewed and nothing is burned. Different styles can now be seen across the Tibetan region.
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that prints it, and that says what the wind does with it
kin: sungkhor — the same printed mantras folded onto a body instead of left open to the wind
kin: gau-box — the household's other printed protection, kept shut in metal while this one is left out to fade
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice that keeps it going — replaced each Tibetan New Year, the old string left flying beside the new
kin: burning-retirement — how it ends: old flags are burned, never binned and never put on the ground
kin: ofuda — Japan's paper parallel, taken from a shrine each year and burned at the next
kin: ink — the woodblock printing that makes a mantra repeatable by the hundred
kin: barkhor-lhasa — one of the circuits they are strung over and sold beside
sources: s:wp-prayer-flag s:wp-tibetan-buddhism
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Lunula (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/lunula/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/lunula.json
id: lunula
native: lunula (Latin)
aliases: crescent pendant · Roman girl's crescent
said: LOO-nu-la, plural lunulae, 'little moon'
when: 300 BCE – 399 CE
countries: IT
object: form=pendant materials=gold worn=neck
against: evil-eye — said by the cited account of Roman amulet practice, which names the evil eye as the thing Romans guarded against above all [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: demons — said by Roman practice, as summarised in the cited article: against evil forces, demons and sorcery [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: witchcraft — said by the same account, which names sorcery alongside demons [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: child-harm — said by Roman families; Plautus has a lunula given to a girl as a birthday present and a bulla given to a girl on the day of her birth [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
what: A crescent moon on a chain, usually gold, worn by girls in ancient Rome. Isidore of Seville defines it exactly: "Lunulae are female ornaments in the likeness of the moon, little hanging gold bullae." It came off on the eve of her marriage, with her childhood toys and the rest of her child's clothes, and she put on women's dress.
story: Two lines of Plautus are most of what a reader can hold onto. In Epidicus, the speaker asks the girl Telestis: "Don't you remember my bringing you a gold lunula on your birthday, and a little gold ring for your finger?" In Rudens, Palaestra says her father gave her a golden bulla on the day she was born. Girls got a crescent, boys got a locket, and the plays treat both as the ordinary furniture of a childhood.

The cited account is direct about what Romans wore amulets for: against evil forces, demons and sorcery, and especially against the evil eye. It also draws a map line worth keeping. Lunulae were common right across the Mediterranean; the bulla, the boys' version, was mostly an Italian object. This record lists Italy alone in its countries because Italy is where the source names the practice; the wider Mediterranean spread is stated in the source without countries attached to it.

*Inference —* an amulet with a removal ceremony is doing two jobs. It guards a child, and it counts. Take it off and something has ended — a wedding in this case, a toga in the boys'. The atlas has a small class of these, and the Bulgarian martenitsa, which comes off when the wearer sees a stork, belongs to it.
kin: bulla — the boys' counterpart, and the object Isidore defines this one against
kin: crescent — the sign it is, and the one it shares with a thousand years of later Islamic and Balkan silver
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to
kin: gold — the metal Isidore specifies and Plautus's characters can afford
kin: martenitsa — the other amulet in this atlas that is defined by when it comes off
kin: fascinum — the Roman charm aimed at the same look, with none of this one's discretion
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read; both Roman childhood amulets end at the moment the child stops being one
sources: s:wp-lunula-amulet s:wp-bulla-amulet s:wp-crescent s:wp-evil-eye

## Magical gem (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/magical-gem/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/magical-gem.json
id: magical-gem
aliases: Graeco-Egyptian magical gem · Abraxas stone · gnostic gem · magical intaglio
when: 100 BCE – 399 CE
countries: EG GR IT
object: form=pendant materials=agate,carnelian,lapis,glass worn=neck,finger,grave
against: illness — said by the Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database [s:web-cbd-magical-gems]
against: poverty — said by the same description, which names prosperity as one of the three things an owner wanted [s:web-cbd-magical-gems]
against: loneliness — said by the same description, which names love as the third [s:web-cbd-magical-gems]
against: witchcraft — said by the cited account of the stones, which reads many of them as amulets and instruments of magic, written in the same formulae as the papyri [s:wp-abraxas]
against: attraction — said by the Roman gem tradition generally: stones were paired with gods so the wearer took on the associated powers, rather than out of piety [s:wp-amulet]
what: A cut stone between one and three centimetres across, engraved on both faces and often round the edge as well. One face carries a figure — most famously the cock-headed, serpent-legged anguipede named Abrasax, holding a shield and a whip. The other carries names and lines of letters, many of them in no known language. It was set in a ring or pierced and hung. The Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database, which catalogues them, describes gems "designed to bring their owners health, prosperity and love".
story: The name Abrasax, or Abraxas, appears on nearly all the legends on these gems, sometimes filling the whole face on its own. It turns up in the same breath as other names across the Greek magical papyri and on Greek metal curse tablets: "I conjure you by Iaō Sabaōth Adōnai Abrasax, and by the great god, Iaeō." E. A. Wallis Budge described the composite figure as a Pantheus, an All-God, "with the head of a cock (Phœbus) or of a lion (Ra or Mithras), the body of a man, and his legs are serpents which terminate in scorpions".

The stones were classed and re-classed for three centuries by collectors who wanted to know whose they were. Antiquarians sorted them into Abraxas proper, taken as Basilidian and Gnostic; Abraxastes, older forms adapted; and Abraxoïdes, unconnected to Basilides altogether. The cited account is blunt about where that got them: no attempt to identify the figures on existing gems with the personages of Gnostic mythology has succeeded, and Abrasax is the only term in the legends that is not already known from other religions.

What can be said is that the gems and the magic papyri reflect the same ideas, and that the papyri contain directions for making and using gems with similar figures and formulas — which is why, as the cited account puts it, it can scarcely be doubted that many of these stones are amulets and instruments of magic.

*Inference —* this is the atlas's clearest case of a corpus without a findspot. The Campbell Bonner database lists contributing institutions across fifteen countries and a string of galleries and auction houses; the whole corpus is estimated at around 5,600 pieces. The countries on this record are where the gems were made and used according to the cited accounts, not where they were dug up, because for most of them nobody recorded that.
kin: curse-tablet — the same voces magicae, the same divine names, scratched on lead and aimed at a person instead of hung on one
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition, at its most literate and most expensive
kin: campbell-bonner — the scholar the standing database of these stones is named for
kin: divine-name — the sign most of these stones actually carry, once the figure is set aside
kin: palindrome-word — the other class of written charm that works by the shape of the letters rather than their sense
kin: carnelian — one of the stones cut for this, and the one the later Islamic tradition singles out as the Prophet's
kin: holy-rider-pendant — what this practice turns into once it is Christian: named demons, named angels, and a rider
kin: incantation-bowl — the eastern cousin — the same late-antique habit of writing names to bind a power, in ink on clay rather than cut in stone
kin: abracadabra — the word that came out of this world and outlived every deity named on these stones
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read; most of these gems reached museums through the trade, and their findspots went with the diggers
sources: s:web-cbd-magical-gems s:web-cbd-about s:wp-abraxas s:wp-amulet s:wp-curse-tablet

## Maneki-neko (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/maneki-neko/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/maneki-neko.json
id: maneki-neko
native: 招き猫 (Japanese)
aliases: beckoning cat · lucky cat · calling cat · marushime-neko · zhāocáimāo 招財貓
said: ma-NE-ki NE-ko
when: 1852 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP CN
root: Japanese maneki 招き 'beckoning' + neko 猫 'cat' — the beckoning cat
object: form=figurine materials=terracotta,plastic,wood,iron,copper worn=shop,door
against: attraction — said by shopkeepers, in the paw rule: left paw raised to bring in customers, right paw raised to bring in money [s:wp-maneki-neko]
against: bad-luck — said by the colour scheme as it developed alongside feng shui — black is the one kept to turn evil away [s:wp-maneki-neko]
against: illness — said by the colour scheme: red is the health cat [s:wp-maneki-neko]
against: poverty — said by the colour scheme: yellow or gold is for wealth [s:wp-maneki-neko]
against: loneliness — said by the colour scheme: pink is for romance [s:wp-maneki-neko]
what: A seated cat, one forepaw raised palm-down in a beckoning fold, usually holding an oval koban coin in the other. The classic figure is a calico Japanese Bobtail. Ceramic or plastic now; antique ones are carved wood, stone, cast metal or handmade porcelain. It sits near the entrance of a shop, a restaurant, a pachinko parlour, a laundromat, a bar, a hotel, and in houses. Some have a mechanical paw that swings, driven by a battery or a solar cell through a coil and a magnet.
story: The dated record starts in 1852. The Bukō nenpyō, a chronology of Edo, carries an entry for that year; Utagawa Hiroshige's print Joruri-machi Hanka no zu, also 1852, shows the marushime-neko — a variant of the beckoning cat — being sold at Sensō-ji in Asakusa. A Meiji newspaper picked it up in 1876, kimono-clad ones were handed out at an Osaka shrine around then, and by a 1902 advertisement the thing was established.

Behind that lies clay. Potting clay was found at Imado in Asakusa during the Tenshō era of the Azuchi-Momoyama period, local people started making Imado ware, potters from Mikawa Province moved in and developed it, and in the Genroku era (1688–1704) Imado dolls appear — which is the lineage most accounts give the beckoning cat.

*Tradition holds —* four different origin stories, each with a temple attached. Ii Naotaka's hawking party shelters at Gōtoku-ji in the Kan'ei era after a cat beckons them in at the gate, a thunderstorm breaks, and the Ii clan makes the temple its own. Ōta Dōkan, lost and outnumbered at Ekodahara, is beckoned into Jishōin and wins. A poor old woman near Imado Shrine dreams of the cat she had to give up, makes an Imado-ware figure of it, sells it at Asakusa Shrine and prospers. The courtesan Usugumo of Miuraya in Yoshiwara loses her cat to a rumour and a sword; the severed head kills the snake in the privy that would have killed her, and a customer gives her a wooden cat in its place. Each temple claims the birthplace.

It is routinely taken for Chinese. It is made and sold in China too, as zhāocáimāo, and in Chinatowns abroad it is often labelled a Chinese lucky cat or a golden cat. That is a fact about where the object circulates, not an error to be corrected off the page.
how: Bought, not consecrated: this is a shop-counter object with no shrine rite behind it, though shrines and temples sell them. Which paw is up carries a reading, and the reading varies with time and place — a raised left paw for more customers, a raised right for more money; hence also the saying that the left is for a business and the right is for a house. Colour was added later, in combination with feng shui: the original white is for good fortune generally, black to turn away evil, red for health, yellow or gold for wealth, pink for romance. It is not retired, renewed or burnt. It sits by the till until it breaks.
today: Mass-produced worldwide as of 2026, in ceramic, plastic, keychains, piggy banks, air fresheners and pots. Hikone City's mascot Hikonyan is drawn from the Gōtoku-ji story and the Ii clan; the cat has been worked into Pokémon's Meowth and into the card game Balatro; a Trinidad and Tobago party ran one in an election advertisement in 2015, waving goodbye to the incumbent prime minister.
kin: japanese-engimono — the class it belongs to — a shop-luck object sold at shrine markets beside the daruma and the rake
kin: daruma — the other figure on the same shelf, and the opposite contract: the daruma is bought blank and burnt in a year, this one just sits there
kin: senso-ji — where Hiroshige drew it being sold in 1852 — the earliest picture of the thing in trade
kin: charm-coin — the coin in its paw: a koban, which makes this a coin charm with a cat wrapped round it
kin: ekeko — the Andean household figure loaded with goods and asked for more of them — the same job, a hemisphere away
kin: mascot-word — what it became: a corporate and civic mascot, Hikonyan included, which is where the charm and the brand meet
kin: ofuda — what sits behind the same till in Japan, consecrated where this is not
kin: omamori — the portable charm from the same shrine counter; this one never leaves the shop
sources: s:wp-maneki-neko s:wp-sens-ji s:web-ja-wikipedia-engimono s:wp-list-of-lucky-symbols
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Martenitsa (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/martenitsa/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/martenitsa.json
id: martenitsa
native: мартеница (Cyrillic)
aliases: martinka · mărțișor · mártis · verore · Pizho and Penda
said: MAR-te-nit-sa; Macedonian martinka, Romanian mărțișor, Greek mártis, Albanian verore
when: 801 CE to now (still carried)
countries: BG MK RO MD GR AL
object: form=cord materials=thread worn=wrist,neck,chest
against: illness — said by Bulgarian and Macedonian tradition, in which the red and white threads carry the wish for good health [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: spirits — said by the ancient practice the ethnographers connect it to, in which red or otherwise coloured threads protected children and young people from evil spirits [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: witchcraft — said by the same account, which names witchcraft alongside evil spirits [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: bad-luck — said by UNESCO's description of the element: a red and white thread, untied when the first blossom tree, swallow or stork is seen, held to protect against harsh and unpredictable seasonal change [s:web-unesco-march-1]
what: Twisted white and red yarn, most often made into two small wool dolls: Pizho, the male one, mostly white; Penda, the female one, mostly red and wearing a skirt. It is pinned to clothing or tied at the wrist or neck from Baba Marta Day, the first of March. Modern ones take other shapes and add coloured beads.
story: Two rules govern the object, and both are about other people and about time. It is always given, never bought for oneself — to family, friends, anyone you feel close to. And it comes off on a sign, not a date: the wearer takes it off on first seeing a stork, a swallow returning from migration, or a tree in blossom. Failing all three, the end of March.

Baba Marta means Grandma March, and Bulgarian and Macedonian folklore makes her a bad-tempered old woman whose mood turns fast. Wearing her colours is described as asking her for mercy, so that winter passes and spring comes; the first stork or swallow says she is in a good humour and about to retire.

Taking it off has its own local rules. Some tie the martenitsa to the branch of a fruit tree, giving the tree the health and luck the wearer has had while wearing it. Others put it under a stone and look the next day: a larva or a worm means a healthy, successful year; an ant means the same but with hard work for it; a spider means trouble.

On where it comes from, the cited account offers several accounts and settles none. The custom is tied to the pre-Christian history of the Balkans and to agricultural cults of nature; the twisted white-and-red woollen threads specifically are said to suggest Thracian, possibly Hellenic or Roman origins. Some ethnographers trace it to the Eleusinian Mysteries, with the ancient equivalent of the Greek mártis being the kroke; the custom is mentioned in Photios' Lexicon, which records that the priests wrapped a red thread round the right hand and foot. At that time red and other coloured threads were used to protect children and young people from evil spirits and witchcraft. An early twentieth-century Bulgarian story puts the first martenitsa at the seventh-century Battle of Ongal: after the Bulgar victory, Khan Asparuh sent doves with white threads to carry the news, and the threads turned bloody in flight.

*Inference —* the ethnographers' colour readings are worth quoting rather than choosing between. White for the purity of melting snow, red for the setting sun growing stronger as spring comes; white for purity, red for life and passion; the two together for the cycle of life and death, for good and evil, for sorrow and happiness, for the male and female beginnings and the balance between them. A charm that means that many things at once is a charm doing social work, and the rule that it must be given rather than bought says so out loud.
kin: red-thread — the sign, and the reason this record and a Jerusalem wrist bracelet are filed together
kin: red-string — the other red thread on a wrist in this atlas — that one has no text behind it, this one has a UNESCO file
kin: thread — the material; wool, twisted, and nothing else
kin: knotting — the practice — twisting and tying is the whole making
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice this object defines: one month, then it goes on a fruit tree or under a stone
kin: lunula — the other amulet here that is defined by the moment it comes off
kin: corn-dolly — the European neighbour: a figure made of a plant, worn or kept for a season, then given back to the field
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it sits in, at its most calendar-bound
kin: unesco-ich — the body that inscribed it in 2017, on a file four countries submitted together
sources: s:wp-martenitsa s:web-unesco-march-1 s:wp-red-string-kabbalah s:wp-apotropaic-magic

## Mezuzah (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/mezuzah/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/mezuzah.json
id: mezuzah
native: מְזוּזָה (Hebrew)
aliases: mezuza · klaf
said: me-zu-ZAH, plural mezuzot; the word means 'doorpost'
when: 300 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL US
root: Biblical Hebrew mezuzah, 'doorpost' — the upright that carries the lintel; it takes on the meaning 'inscribed parchment' only in post-Biblical Hebrew, from the Deuteronomy commandment to write the words on the doorposts
object: form=door-piece materials=parchment,ink,silver,wood,terracotta worn=door,lintel
against: demons — said by early rabbinic sources named in the cited article — Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:12, Babylonian Talmud Bava Metziya 102a, Babylonian Talmud Pesahim 113b — which witness a belief in an anti-demonic function [s:wp-mezuzah]
against: house — said by about three-quarters of adults in Israel, according to sociological research summarised in the cited article [s:wp-mezuzah]
against: war — said by the Chabad campaign of the 1970s for systematic checking of mezuzot, begun after a series of attacks at Ma'alot, on the assumption that adhering to the mitzvot would guarantee personal safety [s:wp-mezuzah]
what: A strip of parchment, handwritten by a trained scribe in indelible black ink with a quill, carrying Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. It is rolled, put in a case, and fixed to the right-hand doorpost, in the upper third at about shoulder height, within about eight centimetres of the opening. The case can be anything — silver, wood, stone, ceramic, pewter, polymer clay — and the case is not the point; a photocopy on paper inside a beautiful case is not a valid mezuzah.
story: Jewish law does not class a mezuzah as an amulet, and the atlas has to say so before it says anything else. It is a mitzvah, a commandment, one of the 613, and its stated purpose in the verses that command it is educational: to keep God's words in front of a person, taught to their children, spoken of at home and on the road.

The objection is on the record and it is old. Maimonides, in the Mishneh Torah, allows writing Shaddai on the outside of a mezuzah and then draws the line hard: "Those, however, who write the names of angels, other sacred names, verses, or forms, on the inside [of a mezuzah] are among those who do not have a portion in the world to come." And the reason: "Not only do these fools nullify the mitzvah, but furthermore, they make from a great mitzvah ... a talisman for their own benefit." A commandment converted into a charm stops being a commandment.

So why is it in an atlas of amulets? Because people have in fact used it that way, in writing, for a very long time, and that argument is itself documented. The cited account states that in later generations the mezuzah began to be interpreted as an apotropaic device protecting the house from evil, and names early rabbinic sources that explicitly witness a belief in an anti-demonic function: Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:12, Babylonian Talmud Bava Metziya 102a, Babylonian Talmud Pesahim 113b. It also notes that some Jewish sources construe the mezuzah as a guard against divine anger and that others vehemently reject that reading. In the 1970s, after a series of attacks at Ma'alot, Chabad began a campaign to have mezuzot systematically checked, on the assumption that keeping the mitzvot would guarantee personal safety. And sociological research summarised in the cited article reports that about three-quarters of adults in Israel hold that the mezuzah guards their houses.

That is the record this atlas prints: a tradition that calls it a commandment, a legal authority who wrote down exactly why calling it a talisman degrades it, and a large documented practice of treating it as protection anyway. The atlas does not settle it.

Karaite Jews read the Deuteronomy verse as metaphor and traditionally use no mezuzah, putting up instead a small plaque shaped like the two Tablets of the Law with the Ten Commandments — though in Israel many Karaites also fix a mezuzah so as not to make other Jews uncomfortable. Samaritans read the commandment as displaying any selected text from the Samaritan Torah, on marble, wood, parchment or good paper, above the door or on a prominent wall inside; stone plaques of the Ten Commandments from the Byzantine and early Muslim periods survive, and are in the Israel Museum. For Samaritans, the more of them in a house, the better.
how: Written on klaf, parchment, by a sofer stam — a scribe trained both in the relevant laws and in Ktav Stam calligraphy — in indelible black ink, with a quill made from a feather or, rarely now, a reed. On the back it is customary to write Shaddai, a name of God which also reads as an acronym for Shomer Daltot Yisrael, Guardian of Israel's doors; many cases carry the letter shin for the same reason. Ashkenazi custom adds a second line that is a one-letter Caesar shift of three words of the Shema, written on the back opposite the words it shifts; Sephardi custom, following the Shulchan Aruch and the Rambam, leaves it out. It is held against the spot, a blessing is said, and it is fixed. Where the doorway is wide enough, many Ashkenazim tilt it — a compromise proposed by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher between Rashi, who held it should be vertical, and his grandson Rabbeinu Tam, who held it horizontal. Most Sephardi, Mizrahi and other non-Ashkenazi Jews fix it vertically. Many observant Jews have a scribe check the parchments for tears or faded letters at least twice every seven years. Torn or damaged wording invalidates it.
today: Contested in American housing law, repeatedly, since 2001. A condominium association at Shoreline Towers in Chicago banned objects outside unit doors and management removed tenants' hallway mezuzot; complaints went to the Chicago Commission on Human Relations, the Illinois Attorney General and the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. Alderman Burton Natarus drafted a city ordinance making it illegal to prohibit a religious sign, symbol or relic on a door, doorpost or entrance; it passed that December with a maximum $500 fine, the first such legislation in North America. A federal judge found in 2006 that the rule did not violate the Federal Fair Housing Act, the district court upheld that in 2008, the Seventh Circuit reversed in 2009, and the disputes settled confidentially in 2011. Illinois amended its Condominium Property Act in 2006, effective 1 January 2007; Florida followed in 2008 after a Fort Lauderdale case; Texas passed HB1278 in June 2011 after a Houston couple lost in federal court in 2008. A national bill introduced by Congressman Jerrold Nadler in 2008 never became law.
kin: tefillin — its partner commandment and its partner problem — the other object Jewish law refuses to call an amulet, carrying some of the same verses on the body instead of on the door
kin: kamea — the line Maimonides was drawing: write angel names inside a mezuzah and you have made one of these out of a mitzvah
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest surviving Hebrew text-object in the atlas, and the thing every argument about this one eventually reaches for
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition whose whole practice Maimonides is refusing, in one paragraph, on this object
kin: parchment — the material the law specifies, and the reason a printed copy in a silver case is not one
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice, in the atlas's most legally defined form — right post, upper third, eight centimetres from the opening
kin: divine-name — Shaddai on the back, read as an acronym for the Guardian of Israel's doors
kin: ofuda — the Japanese paper the household fixes where the house opens, from a tradition that has no objection to calling it protective
kin: quran-pendant — scripture in a case, put where a person passes it daily — the same object in another book
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read; this record is the atlas's sharpest case of a tradition rejecting the word the site is organised by
sources: s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-tefillin s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-amulet s:wp-apotropaic-magic

## Milagro (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/milagro/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/milagro.json
id: milagro
native: milagro (Latin)
aliases: ex-voto · dije · promesa · milagrito
said: mee-LAH-gro, Spanish for 'miracle'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: MX US ES
root: Spanish milagro, 'miracle' — the word for the answered prayer, used for the token that asks for it or thanks for it
object: form=pendant materials=silver,gold,lead,wood,bone worn=wall,neck,pocket
against: illness — said by petitioners, who choose the shape to match the ailment [s:wp-milagro-votive]
against: travel — said by petitioners; the source notes a leg may stand for a journey rather than a limb [s:wp-milagro-votive]
against: bad-luck — said by people who carry rather than pin them [s:wp-milagro-votive]
what: A small flat metal shape of the thing you are praying about — a leg, an eye, a heart, a lung, a kneeling man, a cow, a house, a car. Most are stamped tin or silver a few centimetres long, pierced or pinned so they can be fastened to a saint's robe, a shrine rail or a retablo; some are modelled in the round. Gold, silver, tin, lead, wood, bone and wax all turn up, depending on what the local trade works in.
story: Milagros are religious folk charms used for healing and as votive offerings in Mexico, the southern United States, other parts of Latin America, and parts of the Iberian Peninsula. They are pinned to altars, shrines and sacred objects, and bought in churches and cathedrals or from vendors outside them.

The custom is traced to the ancient Iberians of the Spanish coast and travelled with the Spanish into Central and South America. It has thinned since, but it holds in rural Spain — Andalusia, Catalonia and Majorca — alongside its American forms.

A milagro is offered to a saint's image either as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered. The shape does the pointing. But the code is local, not universal: a leg can mean a leg that hurts or a journey to be made; a heart can mean a heart condition, a romance, or something else again. *Inference —* that ambiguity is the interesting part. The object is precise enough to aim a prayer and loose enough that only the petitioner and the saint need know what it is about, which is a useful property for a token left in public on a church wall.

Milagros also get carried rather than pinned, for protection and luck, and the same stampings end up as earrings and necklace charms. They correspond almost exactly to the tamata of the Eastern Orthodox churches — the same body parts, in the same thin metal, on the same kind of icon.
how: Stamped, cast or cut, then pinned, wired, glued or nailed to the image. A vendor's tray outside a shrine is sorted by body part. Nothing is consecrated before it is offered; the offering is the act. Old milagros accumulate on a much-visited image until the metal is a second garment, and are periodically taken down and stored or sold by the church.
today: Still sold at church doors and in markets across Mexico, the southwestern United States and rural Spain as of the most recent accounts this project has read. They also sell as craft jewellery to buyers with no shrine in mind, which is the same argument this atlas reports about every charm that reached a gift shop, and does not settle.
kin: tama-votive — the Greek Orthodox object this one corresponds to almost exactly — same body parts, same thin metal, same icon
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the tradition this belongs to, and the one that decides which saint gets which limb
kin: ex-voto-wall — what a church wall looks like after a few hundred of these have been pinned to it
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the Church's own category of blessed objects, which a milagro sits beside without being one
kin: st-christopher-medal — the other metal token bought at the same counter, worn instead of pinned
kin: mercado-de-sonora — one Mexico City market where these share an aisle with herbs, candles and the deer's-eye seed
kin: silver — the metal that makes an expensive milagro, and the reason old ones were worth taking down
kin: azabache — the other Hispanic charm pinned to a body rather than a saint — that one goes on the baby
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the act the object exists for
sources: s:wp-milagro-votive s:wp-ex-voto s:wp-votive-offering s:wp-mercado-de-sonora
