## Miraculous Medal (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/miraculous-medal/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/miraculous-medal.json
id: miraculous-medal
native: Médaille miraculeuse (Latin)
aliases: Medal of the Immaculate Conception · Medal of Our Lady of Graces · médaille de la rue du Bac
said: may-DIE mee-rah-kew-LERZ
when: 1832 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR IT CN
root: French médaille miraculeuse, 'miraculous medal' — a nickname the public gave it, not the name it was struck under
object: form=medal materials=silver,gold,brass,copper worn=neck,chest,pocket
against: attraction — said by the account Catherine Labouré gave of what the Virgin told her [s:wp-miraculous-medal]
against: illness — said by the Daughters of Charity and the people who reported cures during the cholera pandemic of the 1830s [s:wp-miraculous-medal]
what: An oval stamped medal, worn at the neck on a chain. The front shows a woman standing on a globe, crushing a serpent's head, rays coming from rings on her hands, inside an oval of words that reads "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee", with 1830 struck below. The back has a bar and a cross over a large letter M, twelve stars around the rim, and two hearts beneath — one crowned with thorns, one pierced by a sword. Aluminium at the cheap end, silver and gold at the other.
story: This one has a date, a witness and a goldsmith, which almost nothing else in this atlas does.

Catherine Labouré, a novice with the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac in Paris, said that on 18 July 1830 a child's voice woke her and led her to the convent chapel, where the Virgin Mary told her: "God wishes to charge you with a mission [...] You will be contradicted, but do not fear, you will have grace." On 27 November the same year, she said, Mary returned during her evening meditations, standing on a globe inside an oval frame, wearing rings that shed light — the rays, Mary told her, were "the graces I shed upon those who ask for them", and the gems that stayed dark "are the graces for which souls forget to ask". The frame turned, and the reverse design appeared. Then the instruction, which is the whole point of the object: have a medal struck after this model, and "all who wear them will receive great graces".

Her priest watched her ordinary daily behaviour for two years before taking it to Archbishop Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen of Paris. Approval came; the goldsmith Adrien Vachette made the die; the first 1,500 medals were minted on 30 June 1832. Then the arithmetic gets strange. The Daughters of Charity distributed them during a deadly cholera pandemic, cures were reported, and the public renamed the object. Over 500,000 had been distributed by 1834. By 1835, more than a million worldwide. By 1839, over ten million. By Labouré's death in 1876, more than a billion had been produced. *Inference —* a devotional object that reached a billion within a single lifetime is an industrial fact as much as a religious one, and the cholera years are where the curve bends.

On the Church's side the object sits inside a category. The Miraculous Medal is a sacramental — by the Catholic Church's definition a sacred sign that works "through the intercession of the Church", which prepares a person to receive grace and disposes them to cooperate with it, and which does not act by itself the way a sacrament does. The Enchiridion Indulgentiarum of 2004 grants a partial indulgence to the faithful who use a crucifix, a crown, a scapular or a medal blessed by a priest. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy lists Marian medals among approved practices while holding that popular piety "may never incorporate rites permeated by magic, superstition, animism, vendettas or sexual connotations". *Inference —* the medal's own promise, struck into it, is that wearing it brings graces; the doctrine is that the wearing disposes rather than delivers. Both sentences are on the record, they are not the same sentence, and this atlas does not decide between them.

One wearer's account is famous enough to be in the liturgy. In 1842 Marie-Alphonse Ratisbonne, a Jewish man, took a bet to wear the medal on a trip to Rome, entered the basilica of Sant'Andrea delle Fratte, and reported a vision of the Virgin exactly as the medal depicts her. He converted, became a Jesuit, and the event has its own canonical inquiry behind it and a place in the Feast of the Miraculous Medal. Maximilian Kolbe, founding the Militia of the Immaculate in 1917 under this Virgin's patronage, handed the medals out and called them his "ammunition".
how: Struck from the 1832 die design by religious-goods manufacturers worldwide. Bought or given; the giving is the commoner route, and the Daughters of Charity have handed them out free since the first batch. A priest may bless one, which is what attaches the indulgence; nothing requires it. Worn at the neck under clothing more often than over it. Never retired — a lost one is simply replaced.
today: Still struck to the 1830 design, still sold and given at the rue du Bac chapel, where Catherine Labouré's body lies, and in religious-goods shops everywhere the Catholic Church is. In 2026 it shares a counter with the St Christopher medal and the Brown Scapular. No dated retail price was read for this record.
kin: st-christopher-medal — the other stamped medal on the same counter — that one promises a safe road, this one promises graces
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the category the Church files it under, and the doctrine that says a medal disposes rather than delivers
kin: brown-scapular — the cloth sacramental it is usually sold beside, and the one a 1911 ruling allowed a blessed medal to replace
kin: agnus-dei — the sacramental that came first — wax before struck silver, and a papal blessing instead of a parish one
kin: ladanka — what hangs beside an Orthodox cross where this hangs beside a Catholic one
kin: milagro — the other small metal offering of the Catholic world — that one is pinned to the saint, this one is worn by the petitioner
kin: cross — the sign over the M on its reverse
kin: serpent — the creature under the woman's heel on its face, and the oldest thing on the medal
kin: silver — the metal of the costly version, and the one that makes an old medal worth keeping
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read where a promise struck into an object meets a doctrine that qualifies it
sources: s:wp-miraculous-medal s:wp-sacramental s:wp-devotional-medal s:web-vatican-directory-popular-piety
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Mjölnir pendant (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/mjolnir-pendant/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/mjolnir-pendant.json
id: mjolnir-pendant
native: Mjǫllnir (Latin)
aliases: Thor's hammer pendant · hammer amulet · Torshammare · Thorshammer
said: MYOL-neer
when: 700 CE – 1100 CE
countries: DK SE NO IS FI GB DE EE LV LT RU
root: Old Norse Mjǫllnir, from Proto-Norse *melluniaR. Historical linguists disagree on where it goes next: one derivation links it to Old Church Slavonic mlŭnuji and Russian molnija 'lightning', giving 'lightning-maker'; a second to Old Norse mjǫll 'new snow', giving 'shining lightning weapon'; a third to Old Norse mala 'to grind', giving 'the grinder'.
object: form=pendant materials=iron,silver,amber,copper worn=neck,grave
against: demons — said by the carver of the Kvinneby amulet, 11th-century Öland, in Mindy MacLeod and Bernard Mees's translation [s:wp-mj-lnir]
against: curse — said by the same inscription, which asks that the lightning hold all evil away from its owner Bofi [s:wp-mj-lnir]
what: A small hammer worn head-down at the throat: short haft, wide splayed head, a suspension loop or ring where the handle should end. Most are plain iron or silver; about a hundred of the thousand or so known carry ornament. Wear one and the weapon hangs upside down, which is how you tell it from a cross at arm's length.
story: Around a thousand hammer pendants have come out of the ground in what are now the Nordic countries, England, northern Germany, the Baltic states and Russia. As of 2004, a tenth of the finds came from graves, nearly all cremations, and those burials are often identified as women's. The rest turn up in hoards and in the dirt of trading towns.

The pendants appear to have grown out of an older north Germanic habit of wearing pendants, and scholars have connected them to the club-of-Hercules amulet worn by other ancient Germanic peoples. Their surge in popularity during the Viking Age, and some of the shapes that surge produced, may have been an answer to Christian cross pendants, which were appearing in the same region as Christianisation advanced. Two signs, two workshops, one neck.

What the hammer was for is said out loud on one object. The Kvinneby amulet, an 11th-century copper plate from Öland in Sweden, was likely worn at the neck and carries a Younger futhark inscription that runologists Mindy MacLeod and Bernard Mees translate: "May Thor protect him with his hammer which came from out of the sea. Flee from evil!" The poems agree on the hammer's second job. In Þrymskviða, Mjölnir is fetched to hallow a bride; in Gylfaginning, Thor consecrates Baldr's burning ship with it. A hammer that kills is also a hammer that blesses.

In 1999 the German archaeologist Jörn Staecker proposed a typology of the finds by decoration and material — amber, iron, silver. In 2019 the American scholar Katherine Suzanne Beard extended it by hammer shape and suspension type and launched Eitri, an online database of hammer finds with their composition and discovery context.

The second span starts much later. The hammer is worn again today by adherents of Heathenry, and scholars Jenny Blain and Robert J. Wallis wrote in 2006 that Thor's hammer is the most common of heathen sacred artefacts. In the United States the National Cemetery Administration issues the Hammer of Thor as emblem #55 for veterans' headstones. The symbol has also been taken up in white nationalist and neo-Nazi circles: the Anti-Defamation League's symbol database records that white supremacists sometimes build swastikas and other hate symbols into the decoration, while noting that its traditional origins are non-racist. Beard's position is that "most people who wear hammer pendants today do so for cultural, religious, or decorative reasons and maintain absolutely no ties to any racist groups or beliefs". The dating block below covers the excavated Viking-Age span only; the revival is a separate, living span that this record describes in prose rather than folding into the same bar.
how: Cast or cut in iron or silver, occasionally amber, pierced or looped at the haft end, and strung. In Viking-Age cremation graves around Mälaren, in Åland and in Russia, archaeologists also find Thor's hammer-rings: iron rings hung with several amulets, many but not all of them hammers, recovered from cinerary urns and found in graves of both sexes but more often women's. Their exact function is unknown, and this atlas leaves it unknown.
today: Made and sold worldwide as of 2026, in silver, steel and pewter, by museum shops, by Heathen craftworkers and by mass-market jewellers. Whether a cast reproduction is the same object as an excavated one is the argument this atlas reports rather than settles; so is who gets to wear the sign, and the ADL entry and Beard's sentence above are the two ends of it.
kin: iron — the commonest metal these pendants are cut from, and the metal the rest of northern Europe reaches for against the same kind of harm
kin: silver — the other common metal, and the one the ornamented hundred are nearly all made in
kin: amber — the third material in Jörn Staecker's 1999 typology of the finds
kin: cross — the sign arriving from the other direction — hammer pendants multiply as cross pendants spread through Scandinavia, and scholars read the one as an answer to the other
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the wider northern European habit of wearing metal against harm that this pendant is the oldest dated member of in Scandinavia
kin: swastika-sign — the other Germanic Iron Age sign this atlas carries, and the one whose modern politics run closest to the hammer's
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that put a tenth of these pendants where archaeologists found them, mostly in cremations, mostly in women's graves
kin: horseshoe — the other iron object northern Europe hangs against harm, and the one that outlived it by a thousand years
kin: st-christopher-medal — what a Christian traveller in the same waters wore instead, once the north had changed religion
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this pendant forces: a sign claimed at once by Heathen practitioners, by a national cemetery service and by white supremacists
kin: the-swastika-problem — the companion argument, about a sign from the same region with the same modern wound
sources: s:wp-mj-lnir s:wp-swastika-germanic-iron-age s:wp-iron-in-folklore s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

against: demons — said by Sri Suta Goswami, narrating the Garuda Purana, chapter 68, verse 17 [s:wp-navaratna]

against: illness — said by the same passage, which names diseases [s:wp-navaratna]
against: bad-luck — said by the Agni Purana, chapter 246, which calls a flawless gem an escort of good luck and forbids a flawed one [s:wp-navaratna]
what: Nine stones set together in gold or silver, one for each of the nine bodies of Hindu astrology, with a ruby at the centre for the Sun. The traditional arrangement runs clockwise from the top: diamond, natural pearl, red coral, hessonite, blue sapphire, cat's eye, yellow sapphire, emerald. Nothing but a ruby or a red spinel goes in the middle, because the Sun sits at the centre of the system the ring is a model of. It is made as a ring, a pendant, a necklace and a star worn on the chest.
story: The nine are fixed and the list is old enough to be quoted rather than explained. A Sanskrit sloka attributed to the Brihat Jataka, and repeated in the Mani-mala and the Jataka Parijata, assigns ruby to Surya, pearl to Chandra, red coral to Mangala, emerald to Budha, yellow sapphire to Brihaspati, diamond to Shukra, blue sapphire to Shani, hessonite to Rahu, the ascending lunar node, and cat's eye to Ketu, the descending one. The late Thai astrologer Horacharn Thep Sarikabutr gives the same nine in his Parichad-Jataka, chapter 2, verse 21: "Top quality and flawless ruby is the gem for the Sun, natural pearl for the Moon, red coral for Mars, emerald for Mercury, yellow sapphire for Jupiter, diamond for Venus, blue sapphire for Saturn, hessonite for Rahu (ascending lunar node), and cat's eye for Ketu (descending lunar node)."

The sloka's two words that matter most are sujatyam-amalam — high-born and flawless. The Garuda Purana, chapter 68, verse 17, has Sri Suta Goswami say that "Pure, flawless gems have auspicious powers which can protect one from demons, snakes, poisons, diseases, sinful reactions, and other dangers, while flawed stones have the opposite effect." The Agni Purana, chapter 246, agrees in the negative: a gem that is cracked, fissured, dull, rough or sandy "should not be used at all".

*Inference —* that is an unusual clause for an amulet. Most charms in this atlas work whatever they look like; this one is cancelled by a flaw, and a flaw is a thing only a dealer can price. The prescription and the trade are the same sentence.

In Thailand the nine gems are a state emblem. The king awards the Noppharat Ratchawaraphon, the Ancient Auspicious Order of the Nine Gems, in a single class: a Pendant of the Nine Gems on a yellow sash trimmed red, blue and green, worn over the right shoulder to the left hip by men and on a silk ribbon at the front left shoulder by women; a Star of the Nine Gems on the left chest; and a Gold Ring of the Nine Gems, for men, on the right ring finger.
how: Prescribed before it is made. In Hindu astrology the placement of the navagrahas in a person's sidereal horoscope is read first, and either a single gem or a combination of compatible stones is advised — to draw on a beneficial planet or to counter a harmful one — which is why the tradition says to consult an astrologer before wearing one. Paramahansa Yogananda, writing in Autobiography of a Yogi, adds a weight and a placement: "the proper jewels, metals, or plant preparations are valueless unless the required weight is secured, and unless these remedial agents are worn next to the skin", and puts the floor at faultless jewels of not less than two carats.
today: Made and sold across southern and southeastern Asia as of 2026, in gold for the wealthy and in small stones for everyone else, and worn regardless of religious difference — the arrangement is treated as auspicious in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia. The claimed astrological or piezoelectric benefit of wearing or donating gems has not been scientifically quantified, and this atlas does not adjudicate it either way.
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition it belongs to — an object worn on the body because a text and a horoscope together say which object
kin: rudraksha — the other South Asian thing worn at the body's surface, and the cheap one: a seed anybody may string, against nine graded stones an astrologer prescribes
kin: coral — the red stone in the ring, standing for Mars, and the one material here this atlas files on its own
kin: gold — the usual setting, and — in Yogananda's account — part of the prescription rather than the frame
kin: yantra-plate — the drawn version of the same astrology: nine bodies laid out as a diagram on metal instead of nine stones set in it
kin: magical-gem — the Mediterranean parallel — a cut stone prescribed by a specialist and worn against a named harm
kin: crystal-pendant — what the logic becomes in a 21st-century wellness shop, with the horoscope and the flawlessness rule dropped
kin: thai-wicha — the Thai side of it: in Thailand the nine gems are a royal honour as well as a charm
sources: s:wp-navaratna s:wp-coral s:wp-amulet

## Nazar (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/nazar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/nazar.json
id: nazar
native: نَظَر (Arabic)
aliases: nazar boncuğu · göz boncuğu · eye bead · máti · cheshm nazar · nazar qurbani
said: na-ZAR, Arabic for 'sight', 'surveillance', 'attention'
when: 1600 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: TR GR IR AF IN PK BD AL AZ IL
root: Arabic naẓar, 'sight' or 'looking' — the same word for the look that does the harm and for the bead that answers it; Turkish nazar boncuğu adds boncuk, Turkic for 'bead'
object: form=bead materials=glass,iron,copper,salt worn=neck,wrist,door,vehicle,shop,cradle,phone
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across Turkey, Greece, Iran, Afghanistan and South Asia [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
against: envy — said by the same users; the Hindi-Urdu slogan chashm-e-baddoor asks that the eye keep away [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
against: bad-luck — said by the mythology of the bead itself: if one breaks, it took the whole hit and broke to protect the wearer [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
what: A handmade glass bead: concentric circles, or a teardrop, in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes rimmed in yellow or gold. The Turkish boncuk is blue glass with a blue, white and black dot set on a white or yellow centre. It hangs at a neck, on a wrist, over a door, from a mirror, above a till, on a cradle.
story: The bead is older than any of the countries that sell it. Glass eye beads are documented and extant from as early as the 16th century BCE, and the design spread with glassmaking itself — Mesopotamia to Egypt, Carthage to Greece, Phoenicia to Persia, and right through the Roman imperial period.

The explanations people give for the colour are specific. "According to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity." And the materials are part of the claim, not just the manufacture: "The bead is made of a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil." A second explanation in the cited account runs the other way round — in the Middle East and the Mediterranean, blue eyes are relatively rare, so people with light eyes were held able to curse with a look, and the Assyrians already had turquoise and blue-eye amulets.

The bead also has a rule for its own death. If one breaks, a very strong nazar has hit the wearer, and the bead stored it all up and broke in order to protect them. That is the only retirement instruction in this batch that the object gives itself.
today: Mass-produced and sold everywhere: the Grand Bazaar in Istanbul, Monastiraki in Athens, airport shops, phone cases. A Turkish budget airline, Fly Air, carried the nazar boncuğu on the tail fins of its aircraft. The bead was added to Unicode as U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET in 2018, which makes it one of the very few amulets in this atlas that a reader can send in a message. Whether a factory bead is the same object as a lampworked one is argued by sellers and buyers alike; this atlas reports the argument and describes both the same way.
kin: eye — the sign, in the form most of the world now buys it in
kin: wedjat-eye — the same argument four thousand years earlier, drawn in faience instead of blown in glass
kin: hamsa — the hand this bead is usually set into, and sold beside
kin: glass — the material that turned a sign into something a market could sell by the tray
kin: grand-bazaar — the market that sells more of these than anywhere else
kin: monastiraki — the Athens equivalent, where the same bead is called máti
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — what it becomes on a modern wrist, and the version the argument about factories is actually about
kin: nazar-word — the word — sight, the look, and the bead, all one noun
kin: gorgoneion — the Greek ancestor in the same soil: a frightening face doing by terror what the bead does by looking back
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read this bead is the cover of
kin: the-charm-goes-digital — the long read about charms on screens; this one has its own Unicode code point
sources: s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-hamsa s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-grand-bazaar-istanbul

## Nimbu mirchi (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/nimbu-mirchi/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/nimbu-mirchi.json
id: nimbu-mirchi
native: नींबू मिर्ची (Devanagari)
aliases: lemon and chillies · lime and seven chillies · nazar battu
said: NEEM-boo MIR-chee
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IN PK
root: Hindi nīmbū 'lime, lemon' + mirchī 'chilli' — the object is named by its two ingredients and nothing else
object: form=door-piece materials=herb,thread worn=door,shop,vehicle
against: evil-eye — said by wearers and householders in North India and Pakistan, for whom this is one of the nazar battu class [s:wp-nazar-battu]
against: envy — said by the North Indian and Pakistani account of nazar: excessive admiration, even from well-meaning people, draws it [s:wp-nazar-battu]
against: bad-luck — said by Hindu households in northern India, in the Alakshmi reading of the string [s:wp-alakshmi]
what: A lime and seven green chillies threaded on a string and hung at a doorstep, over a shop counter or from the back of a vehicle. Nothing is worn and nothing is written. The thing rots in the sun, browns, and is replaced.
story: Two explanations of the same string circulate, and they disagree about who the string is for.

In Hindu households, especially in northern India, hanging a lime and seven green chillies at the doorstep is a ritual to either ward off or acknowledge Alakshmi, the goddess of misfortune and grief, whose name means not-Lakshmi. One version holds that the sourness of the lime and the pungency of the chillies together make a smell even Alakshmi cannot tolerate. The other holds that Alakshmi is pleased by sour and spicy offerings, and will take her share standing at the door — which makes the string a payment at the threshold rather than a barrier across it. Alakshmi is not named in Vedic, Upanishadic or early Puranic literature; she is named in the Linga Purana, the Padma Purana and the Śrī Sūkta.

The string also belongs to a wider North Indian and Pakistani class, the nazar battu, whose logic is spoilage. A nazar battu is often a deliberate blemish introduced to prevent perfection: a black mark on the face or neck of a loved one, a flaw built into an otherwise faultless house, a stitching or colouring error put into an expensive carpet or sari. Mothers lightly spit to the side of their children to imply disparagement, and children are marked with a black spot on the cheek, because excessive admiration — even from well-meaning people, even a mother's own love — is held to draw nazar.

*Inference —* a lime and chillies at a shop door belong to that logic rather than to the eye-against-the-eye logic of the Mediterranean. The object is not looking back. It is either an imperfection hung where the perfect thing is, or a plate left out for the guest nobody wants inside.
how: Bought made up, at the price of a lime. Threaded so the chillies hang below the fruit, tied at a lintel, a counter, a bumper or a dashboard. It is a household act, not a specialist's: no source read here names a priest, a mantra or a consecration for it.
today: Ordinary street furniture in North Indian and Pakistani towns as of 2026, on shopfronts, new cars and trucks. The phrase nazar battu has also gone idiomatic: commentators in North India and Pakistan use it for a person or thing that is unwanted but has to be tolerated, as some of the press did of Pervez Musharraf during Pakistan's transition to democracy at the 2008 general election.
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice this object is: a charm that guards a threshold instead of a person
kin: eye — the harm it answers, though not the method — this string does not look back, it spoils the look
kin: nazar — the glass bead sold for the same harm two thousand kilometres west, and the one this atlas usually shows first
kin: tabiz — the written answer to nazar in the same streets, worn on the body while this hangs at the door
kin: horseshoe — Europe's door-hung answer, nailed above the same opening for a different reason
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition this sits at the household end of, far from any consecrated plate
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that asks whether a lime in Delhi and a bead in Istanbul are answering the same thing
sources: s:wp-nazar-battu s:wp-alakshmi s:wp-evil-eye

## Nkisi (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/nkisi/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/nkisi.json
id: nkisi
native: nkisi (Latin)
aliases: nkishi · minkisi · nkisi nkondi · nkondi · kozo
said: n-KEE-see; plural minkisi, and also mikisi, zinkisi, nkisi
when: 1600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CD CG AO
root: From the Proto-Njila root *-kitį, an ancient subdivision of the Bantu language family, meaning a spiritual entity or the material object it inhabits.
object: form=figurine materials=wood,iron,earth,herb,glass,cloth
against: witchcraft — said by Kongo practice as summarised in the source: banganga defend the living against harmful workings and against the sicknesses that result from them [s:wp-nkisi]
against: theft — said by the nkondi's own name, from -konda, 'to hunt' — and the German Loango expedition's Mabiala mu ndemba, described as a thief-finder [s:wp-nkondi]
against: illness — said by Kongo practice — many minkisi are used for healing, and a nkondi can cause or cure a sickness tied to it [s:wp-nkisi]
against: curse — said by oath-takers, who declare themselves open to a nkondi's sickness should they break the oath [s:wp-nkondi]
against: lawsuit — said by villages, which used publicly held nkondi to affirm oaths, seal treaties and locate and punish wrongdoers [s:wp-nkondi]
against: poverty — said by the source, which lists success in hunting or in trade among the purposes minkisi serve [s:wp-nkisi]
RESTRICTED: This record prints no recipe and no invocation. The composition of the bilongo and the words that awaken an nkisi belong to the nganga who assembles it; the nganga does that work isolated, in a hidden camp away from the village, and learns the object's proper use and its songs before bringing it back. What is printed here is the class of substances, the reasoning behind choosing them, and what Kongo testimony says the nails are for.
what: A container with a spirit in it. The container can be a ceramic vessel, a gourd, an animal horn, a shell, a cloth bundle — anything that will hold spiritually charged substances — and it can also be a carved wooden figure, human or animal, with a cavity cut in the belly, the head, or a pouch at the neck. The cavity is closed with a mirror or a disc of reflective glass fixed in resin, and the eyes are often mirrors too. On the aggressive class, nkondi, the surface bristles with nails and blades hammered in. The word names the spirit and the object at once.
story: The first thing to get right is the word for the person, not the object. A nganga — plural banganga — is a healer, diviner and mediator who defends the living against harmful workings and supplies remedies against sicknesses caused either by them or by the demands of the bakisi, the spirits who are emissaries from the land of the dead. Banganga harness those powers by making minkisi. Nothing here happens without one.

The substances that go inside are bilongo, singular nlongo, a word usually translated 'medicine'. Wyatt MacGaffey's objection to that translation is the useful one: bilongo are not applied to the sick or swallowed, so 'therapeutic substances' is closer. They are chosen by metaphor. Bird claws go in to catch a wrongdoer. Minerals come from places associated with the dead — earth from graves, earth from riverbeds. White clay matters because white carries dead skin, moral rightness and spiritual positivity against the black of negativity, and red ochre where the powers of the dead are being mediated. Some minkisi have been described as portable graves, and many contain earth or relics from the grave of a powerful person as a prime ingredient.

The nails are not decoration. Nkondi comes from -konda, 'to hunt'; a nkondi hunts. The phrase used for hammering a nail in is koma nloka, to attach or hammer in a curse, from two ancient Bantu roots — one whose field includes hammering, one that covers witchcraft and cursing. According to Kongo testimony of the early twentieth century, people drive the nails in as a petition: for help, for healing, or as a witness to a contract or a pledge. Each nail stands for a vow, a signed treaty, an effort to abolish an evil. The purpose is to wake the nkisi, and sometimes to enrage it, for the task in hand. An oath-taker may declare himself open to the sickness a particular nkondi causes should he break the oath, and a person who falls ill with that sickness consults the nganga who mediates with that spirit to find out how to be cured. Kindoki, from the same root, covers any action that enlists spirits to harm others: used privately and selfishly it is condemned as witchcraft, used publicly by a village, a tribe or political leaders, or defensively by innocent people, it is not.

The nailed figures are narrower in time and place than the museum trays suggest. Minkisi nkondi have probably been made since at least the sixteenth century, but the nailed ones were probably made mainly in the northern part of the Kongo cultural zone in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Nailed minkisi are not described by missionaries or anyone else writing in the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. MacGaffey, reading the late seventeenth-century Capuchin missionary Luca da Caltanisetta, notes that banganga then sometimes banged minkisi together, and suggests nails — which he argues were first being made around that time — eventually replaced the metaphor. Other scholars think Portuguese missionaries' images of Christ nailed to the cross and of Saint Sebastian influenced the practice; MacGaffey argues against that, on the grounds that nailing is tied up with too many other Kongo concepts to be a misreading of a missionary's picture. The earliest firmly dated nailed nkondi is one Commodore A. P. Eardley Wilmot acquired in 1864 while suppressing Solongo piracy at the mouth of the Congo River; another, named Mabiala mu ndemba and described as a thief-finder, is illustrated in the notes of the German Loango expedition of 1873–76.

How they got to Europe is part of the object. European collectors wanted the nailed ones as soon as the German Loango expedition published them. Robert Visser, a German trader and diplomat, collected a great many for German museums, especially Berlin and Stuttgart. In the nkondi entry's own words, "Many were purchased, others confiscated or removed by colonial authorities, and often found their way to museums, but many also remain in private hands." In the art world they arrived as a stimulus: the source says Bantu themes "previously considered primitive or gruesome were now viewed as aesthetically interesting" — a sentence about European taste, not about the objects. MacGaffey's counter is that the banganga's intentions were practical, the characteristics of the object dictated by the work it had to do, and the nails never decorative.

The argument about where they should be now is live and has names on it. The 2018 Report on the Restitution of African Cultural Heritage by Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy set out the case for return and moved the debate onto moral rather than only legal ground. In Belgium the Royal Museum for Central Africa holds more than 180,000 cultural and natural history objects, mainly from the former Belgian Congo, and has run its first major renovation in more than a century as a decolonisation programme. The Pitt Rivers Museum has built its own programme on four tenets — provenance, transparency, repatriation and redress — and in 2020 joined Savoy and other art historians at Technische Universität Berlin in a research project called Restitution of Knowledge. The British Museum has consistently refused to return objects, citing the British Museum Act 1963.

*Inference —* the European label for these objects entered this atlas as a term, not as a description. This record files the word under fetish-word for that reason, and writes about it there.
how: The nganga gathers the bilongo and assembles them, most often into a carved figure with a cavity cut for them, and then either becomes possessed by the spirit or leaves the finished object in a graveyard or another place spirits frequent. Once it is charged it can be handed to the client. Nkondi are often composed at the edge of the village, on the reasoning that a village, like a body, must have its entrances guarded; the nganga works isolated in a hidden camp and returns covered in paint and behaving strangely, to show he has come back from the land of the living's far side. Personal minkisi are kept in a private house. Community ones are put where the village can see them, though often inside their own enclosure by day.
today: Contested, and split across three places: Kongo communities, European and American museum stores, and private hands. Artists have taken the form up — Renee Stout, whose exhibition Astonishment and Power at the Smithsonian paired her own versions with commentary by MacGaffey; Tania Bruguera, who in 1998–99 performed Destierro in a suit made to resemble a nailed nkondi and then went looking for people who had broken promises; Kara Walker, Dread Scott, Karen Seneferu, Wesley Clark, Stephanie Dinkins, Michael MacGarry, Andrew Lamprecht, Justin Par. The Republic of the Congo painter Trigo Piula made a New Fetish series and said of it: "is a way of engaging with my community and a way of denouncing things that I believe are impacting us, like television for example". As of 2026 this project has read no count of how many minkisi sit in European collections.
kin: bakongo-nkisi-craft — the tradition that makes it, and the banganga without whom there is no nkisi at all
kin: fetish-word — the European label applied to this object from outside, and the word's own history — which is about Portuguese traders on the West African coast, not about Kongo practice
kin: mojo-word — the Kikongo word mooyo, the cavity of an nkisi where the charged substances sit, carried to the American South as the name of a bag
kin: gris-gris — the other African bag that reached Louisiana, by a different route — Mande Muslim writing rather than Kongo bilongo
kin: tooth-and-claw — the sign inside it — bird claws go into the bilongo to catch a wrongdoer, chosen by metaphor rather than by pharmacy
kin: mirror-sign — the reflective disc over the belly cavity and in the eyes, which is how the nkisi is said to see into the spirit world
kin: iron — the material of the nails, and the reason the nailed figures are datable at all
kin: feeding-the-charm — the practice of keeping a charged object working, which here means waking and enraging it for a task
kin: consecration — the step that turns an assembled container into an nkisi, done away from the village
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this object is the centre of: purchased, confiscated or removed by colonial authorities, and argued over by name since 2018
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — one of the museums holding examples, and one running a repatriation and redress programme over them
kin: quai-branly — the Paris museum at the centre of the French restitution debate, holding 70,000 of France's 90,000 sub-Saharan objects
sources: s:wp-nkisi s:wp-nkondi s:wp-fetishism s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-repatriation-cultural-property s:wp-mus-e-du-quai-branly-jacques-chirac s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum s:wp-british-museum

## Ofuda (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ofuda/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ofuda.json
id: ofuda
native: 御札 (Japanese)
aliases: gofu 護符 · shinsatsu 神札 · kamifuda · kifuda · Jingū Taima
said: o-FU-da
when: 710 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese fuda 札 'slip of paper, card, plate', with the honorific prefix o-/go-; the Buddhist and Daoist-derived synonym is gofu 護符, 'guarding tally'
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,wood,cloth worn=wall,door,lintel,hearth
against: house — said by the shrines, which issue ofuda specifically for safety within the home and for the hearth [s:wp-ofuda]
against: bad-luck — said by the shrines, in the class issued against calamity or misfortune [s:wp-ofuda]
against: loneliness — said by the shrines, which issue ofuda for finding love among the purpose-specific kinds [s:wp-ofuda]
against: spirits — said by temple practice: the Tsuno Daishi gofu, the monk Ryōgen drawn as a yaksha, goes on the doorway [s:wp-ofuda]
what: A flat talisman issued by a shrine or a temple: a sheet of paper, a thin rectangular plaque in a paper sleeve, or a wooden tablet, carrying the name of the shrine or of the deity enshrined there and stamped with the shrine's seal. Paper ones are kamifuda, wooden ones kifuda. It is not carried on a person. It stands on a household altar, or goes on a wall above eye level, or is fixed at a gate, a doorway, a kitchen or a ceiling.
story: Two lines run into the ofuda. One is Daoist: the lingfu, the talismanic script of China, which reached Japan through Onmyōdō. The other is print — the woodblock sheets of Buddhist text and image that temples were turning out from the Nara and Heian periods on. In the medieval period the three Kumano shrines in Wakayama stamped their paper talismans with stylised crows and called them Kumano Goōfu, Ox King Talismans; oaths and contracts were written on the blank side, so the sheet held the agreement and the sanction at once.

The standard modern form comes from Ise. Wandering preachers attached to the Ise shrines, the oshi, handed out purification wands called Oharai Taima as a sign that prayers had been said on a devotee's behalf. The wand came folded into paper shaped like a sword blade — kenharai — or boxed. Distribution started in the Muromachi period and peaked in the Edo: a document of 1777 records that eighty-nine to ninety per cent of households in the country held an Ise talisman. That is close to universal coverage, three centuries before mass media.

Then the state took it over. An imperial decree of 1871 abolished the oshi and moved production of the talisman, renamed Jingū Taima, to the shrine's own offices. In 1900 a new Department of Priests, the Kanbesho, took over; in 1927 the National Association of Shinto Priests; after the Second World War, the Association of Shinto Shrines, which still distributes Jingū Taima to affiliated shrines across Japan. *Inference —* an object whose issuing body is renamed four times in seventy-five years is an object the state has an opinion about.
how: Received at a shrine or temple counter, in exchange for hatsuhoryō, a first-fruit offering rather than a price. Shinsatsu are set on a kamidana, a household Shinto altar, or on a stand; failing that, upright in a clean space above eye level, facing east, south or south-east. The Association of Shinto Shrines recommends three per household: the Jingū Taima from Ise, the ofuda of the tutelary kami of where you live, and the ofuda of a shrine you are personally attached to. In a three-door altar the Ise one goes in the middle. Other ofuda go elsewhere in the house — hearth deities in the kitchen, a talisman of the Buddhist figure Ucchuṣma in the toilet, the horned Tsuno Daishi, the Tendai monk Ryōgen drawn as a yaksha, on a doorway. They are replaced annually, ideally before the year turns, and the old ones are burnt at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire in mid-January. Most shrines will take back another shrine's ofuda; many will not take a Buddhist one.
today: Issued year-round by shrines and temples with permanent staff, and distributed nationally through the Association of Shinto Shrines as of 2026. Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association and roughly 20,000 unaffiliated, which is the network the Ise talisman travels down.
kin: omamori — its own portable child — same origin, same counter, but sewn into a pouch and carried instead of stood on an altar
kin: fu-talisman — the Chinese ancestor: the Daoist talismanic sheet that reached Japan through Onmyōdō and set the form
kin: bujeok — the Korean cousin out of the same Daoist stock, drawn from Hanja rather than printed with a shrine seal
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that sells it, alongside the daruma, the rake and the beckoning cat
kin: hanging-at-door — where half of them end up — gate, doorway, kitchen, ceiling, one per job
kin: renewing-yearly — the twelve-month clock that governs it, and the reason Japan burns so much paper each January
kin: burning-retirement — the ending: Sagichō or Dondoyaki, the Little New Year fire on 14 or 15 January
kin: mezuzah — the other household text fixed at a doorway and inspected on a cycle, four thousand miles west
kin: fushimi-inari — one of the shrines that issues its own alongside the Ise talisman
kin: divine-name — the sign it carries: the name of the kami or the Buddhist figure is the talisman's working part
sources: s:wp-ofuda s:wp-omamori s:wp-fulu s:wp-amulet s:web-wp-shinto

## Ojo de venado (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ojo-de-venado/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ojo-de-venado.json
id: ojo-de-venado
native: ojo de venado (Latin)
aliases: deer's eye · ojo de buey · ojo de toro · ojo de caballo · semilla de mucuna
said: OH-ho deh veh-NAH-do, 'deer's eye'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: MX
root: Spanish ojo de venado, 'deer's eye' — a name for the look of the seed, not for its plant
object: form=bead materials=seed,thread worn=neck,wrist,vehicle,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by sellers in the Mercado de Sonora, Mexico City [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
against: child-harm — said by parents, who put one on a newborn [s:web-mexicodesconocido-ojo-de-venado]
against: travel — said by drivers, who hang one from the rear-view mirror [s:web-mexicodesconocido-ojo-de-venado]
what: A hard round seed of a Mucuna vine, dark and glossy with a broad black band across it, which is why it reads as an eye at arm's length. Sellers dress it: a red cord or ribbon, often a tuft of coloured wool, sometimes a tiny image or a bead glued to the face. It is sold loose on a string, as a bracelet, or on a cord long enough to hang from a rear-view mirror.
story: Wikipedia's account of the Mercado de Sonora in Mexico City puts it in one line among the market's magical stock: crosses of ocote wood for good luck, chains of garlic to ward off evil, and a seed called "deer's eye" to protect against the "evil eye".

México Desconocido traces the seed's career as a good-luck amulet to Xichú, a municipality in the northeast of Guanajuato, and notes that Mucuna also grew in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, so other regions may have reached the same use independently. Newborns get one against mal de ojo; adults take one up for a hard stretch; drivers hang one where they can see it.

The object has a public opponent. The priest Eduardo Hayen Cuarón condemned it as "un amuleto y por tanto una práctica esotérica, maligna y 'obra de Satanás'" — an amulet, and therefore an esoteric practice, malign, and the work of Satan. *Inference —* a charm that draws a priest's condemnation by name is a charm being carried by people who also go to Mass, which is where most of this atlas's Latin American material sits. Both statements are reported here; neither is settled here.

The seed reached national pop culture too: the band Caifanes put it on their 1988 debut album.
how: Gathered from the vine, dried, drilled or bound, and finished with red thread. No consecration is published in the sources this project read. Wearers say a seed that cracks or splits has taken a hit meant for the person carrying it — the same account Turkish sellers give of a broken nazar bead — and it is replaced rather than repaired.
today: Sold across central and southern Mexico in markets, at church doors and online as of 2026, and hung in cars as often as worn. No dated price was read for this record, so none is printed.
kin: eye — the sign this seed already is without anybody cutting it — a dark band on a pale ground, read as a pupil
kin: nazar — the same logic in glass, and the same story about a charm that breaks because it took the look
kin: azabache — the other charm Hispanic families put on an infant against mal de ojo, in jet rather than seed
kin: mercado-de-sonora — the Mexico City market where it is sold beside garlic chains and ocote crosses
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the tradition it is carried inside, and the one a priest was condemning when he condemned it
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this seed belongs in — it goes on the newborn first
kin: car-saint — what hangs on the other side of the same rear-view mirror
kin: buying-in-a-market — how one is got: an aisle, a tray, a red cord tied on the spot

## Omamori (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/omamori/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/omamori.json
id: omamori
native: 御守 (Japanese)
aliases: o-mamori · お守り · Japanese shrine charm
said: o-MA-mo-ri
when: 1603 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese mamori 守り 'protection', with the honorific prefix o- (sonkeigo) — 'the honoured protection'
object: form=packet materials=cloth,paper,wood worn=pocket,phone,vehicle,neck
against: traffic — said by the shrines, in the category kōtsū-anzen — road safety for drivers and travellers of every kind [s:wp-omamori]
against: exams — said by the shrines, in the category gakugyō-jōju — for students and scholars, passing examinations [s:wp-omamori]
against: attraction — said by the shrines, in the categories shōbai-hanjō for prosperity in business and en-musubi for finding a partner [s:wp-omamori]
against: childbirth — said by the shrines, in the category anzan — a healthy pregnancy and an easy delivery [s:wp-omamori]
against: house — said by the shrines, in the category kanai-anzen — the well-being of a household [s:wp-omamori]
against: bad-luck — said by the shrines, in the category yaku-yoke — avoidance of evil, and the year just gone [s:wp-omamori]
what: A small brocade pouch, a few centimetres tall, drawn shut at the top with a cord and printed with the name of the shrine or temple that issued it. Inside is a slip of paper or a chip of wood carrying a prayer or an invocation. The pouch stays shut: nobody who carries one opens it. Most hang from a bag, a school satchel, a phone strap or a car mirror rather than round the neck.
story: Omamori are issued by Shinto shrines and by Buddhist temples alike, dedicated to particular kami or to Buddhist figures, and sold to anyone regardless of what they believe. The shrine consecrates the contents by rite; a Shinto one is described as holding busshin, spiritual offshoots of the deity, a Buddhist one kesshin, manifestations.

The folklorist Yanagita Kunio dated the thing a reader now recognises to the Tokugawa period at the earliest. Writing in 1969 he put it this way: "Japanese have probably always believed in amulets of one kind or another, but the modern printed charms now given out by shrines and temples first became popular in the Tokugawa period or later, and the practice of a person wearing miniature charms is also new. The latter custom is particularly common in cities." Two claims sit in that sentence — the printed charm is early modern, the pocket-sized charm is later still, and urban.

The demand outgrew the shrines. Where a popular shrine or temple cannot keep up, it orders omamori from a factory, and priests have objected to the quality and to what they call the "authenticity" of the factory product. Both halves of that get reported here: the factory pouch and the hand-finished one come off the same counter, and the argument over whether they are the same object is an argument inside the tradition.

*Inference —* a charm designed to be replaced every twelve months is a charm with a business model, and the New Year crowds are the year's trade. Fushimi Inari-taisha alone drew 2.69 million worshippers over three days at the New Year in 2006, a police figure and the largest in western Japan. No source this project has read publishes what any shrine takes in omamori money, so no figure is given here.
how: Received, not bought — the verb the tradition uses is sazukaru, to be granted, and the money handed over is hatsuhoryō, a first-fruit offering. If a visitor cannot find one for their need, they may ask a priest to have one made; if enough people ask for the same one, the shrine starts stocking it. The pouch is then carried, tied to a bag or a strap, and not opened; opening it loses what is in it. It is customarily swapped for a new one once a year. The old one goes back to the shrine or temple it came from, usually on or just after New Year, and is burnt rather than thrown out, at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire held at the Little New Year on 14 or 15 January. Most Shinto shrines will accept another shrine's omamori; many will not accept a Buddhist one, and the reverse holds too.
today: Still issued by nearly every shrine and temple in Japan as of 2026, in a spread of categories a buyer picks from: kōtsū-anzen for the road, gakugyō-jōju for exams, shōbai-hanjō for trade, en-musubi for finding a partner, anzan for a safe delivery, kanai-anzen for the household, yaku-yoke against a bad year. Alongside them, shops sell omamori-shaped goods with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, issued by no shrine and consecrated by nobody — a separate product that borrows the shape.
kin: ofuda — the parent: omamori shares its origin with the ofuda and is the smaller, portable version of it, the one that leaves the house
kin: omikuji — the other paper a visitor leaves the same counter with — but a drawn fortune, not a charm, and tied to a rack rather than carried
kin: japanese-engimono — the class of shrine-and-temple goods this belongs to, sold on the same trays as the daruma and the beckoning cat
kin: renewing-yearly — the rule that shapes the whole object — twelve months, then a new one
kin: burning-retirement — how it ends: returned to the shrine and burnt at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire in mid-January
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the rite that makes the pouch more than brocade, performed before it reaches the counter
kin: fushimi-inari — the shrine whose New Year crowds are the clearest published measure of what this trade moves — 2.69 million over three days in 2006
kin: senso-ji — a Buddhist counter issuing the same class of charm, in Tokyo's oldest temple
kin: bujeok — Korea's paper charm carried in a small brocade bag — the same solution to the same problem, one sea away
kin: exam-charm — the genre omamori feeds: gakugyō-jōju is an exam charm printed and priced as one
kin: phone-charm — where most of them now hang, which is the modern answer to 'worn at the neck'
kin: senninbari — the charm Japanese women made by hand for soldiers when a shrine pouch was not enough
sources: s:wp-omamori s:wp-ofuda s:wp-fushimi-inari-taisha s:wp-sens-ji s:wp-amulet s:web-ja-wikipedia-engimono
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Omikuji (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/omikuji/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/omikuji.json
id: omikuji
native: 御神籤 (Japanese)
aliases: o-mikuji · おみくじ · sacred lot
said: o-mi-KU-ji
when: 1409 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese kuji 籤 'lot, drawn slip', with honorific mi- and o-; literally 'the sacred lot'
object: form=card materials=paper,ink worn=pocket,wall
against: bad-luck — said by the practice as recorded: a bad fortune is folded onto a pine so the bad luck waits by the tree rather than attaching itself to the bearer [s:wp-o-mikuji]
what: A narrow strip of printed paper drawn at random from a box at a shrine or temple, for a small offering. It carries a graded verdict at the top — great blessing down to misfortune — then a run of short readings for particular departments of a life: auspicious directions, a wish, a person being waited for, a lost article, travel, business, study, market speculation, disputes, love, moving house, childbirth, illness, a marriage proposal. It is not a charm anybody wears. It is filed in this atlas because of what happens next: a bad slip is folded and tied to a pine branch or to a rack of wire in the grounds, and left behind. The disposal is the charm-act.
story: The dating here is unusually firm for a paper object. A wooden container of oracular lots dated 1409 survives at Tendai-ji in Iwate Prefecture, which puts the method in Japan before the Muromachi period. The system it belongs to was modelled on the Chinese kau chim — a tube of bamboo sticks read against a numbered sequence of printed oracles — and the hundred five-character quatrains used in Japanese Buddhist temples descend from a Southern Song set, the Tiānzhú língqiān.

Those hundred verses are attributed to Ryōgen (912–985), the Tendai monk known posthumously as Ganzan Daishi, and the sequence is called the Ganzan Daishi Hyakusen after him. *Tradition holds —* Avalokiteśvara revealed the verses to him. The attribution itself has a date and an author: Tenkai (1536–1643) is credited with attaching Ryōgen's name to the set, and a story from one of Tenkai's disciples has Ryōgen appear to Tenkai in a dream to reveal that the hundred quatrains, lost for centuries, still existed. Copies duly turned up at Togakushi Shrine in Shinano. The sequence spread through the Edo period into temples of every school, Tendai or not, and publishers put out books explaining what the oracles meant.

The pine is a pun. Matsu 松, pine, is a homophone of matsu 待つ, to wait: tie the bad fortune to the tree and the bad luck waits there instead of following you home. A good fortune can be tied up too, to make it work harder, or kept.

Omikuji still do public work beyond personal fortune. Provincial festivals use the same drawing to pick the tōnin, the person responsible for a coming year's religious duties: names go on slips, and the choice is settled by a ritual strike of a gohei wand.
how: Make a small offering, shake or draw from the box, take the slip you get. Read the grade first. The standard Ganzan Daishi sequence runs great blessing (dai-kichi), blessing (kichi), small blessing (shō-kichi), half-blessing (han-kichi), future blessing (sue-kichi), future small blessing (sue-shō-kichi), misfortune (kyō); other sequences add middle blessing, great misfortune, or a grade that says the outcome is still undetermined and depends on what you do. A bad slip is folded and knotted onto a pine or onto the wire racks set up for it. A good one is either tied up as well or pocketed.
today: Available at shrines and temples across Japan as of 2026; since 2024 vending machines dispense them in some places. The paper fortune in a Western fortune cookie may descend from this: the claim is made by Seiichi Kito of Fugetsu-Do, and rests on evidence that American fortune cookies derive from nineteenth-century Kyoto crackers called tsujiura senbei.
kin: omamori — the other paper from the same counter, and the opposite transaction: an omamori is chosen by category and carried shut, an omikuji is drawn blind and mostly left behind
kin: ofuda — the household tablet from the same issuing body; omikuji never goes on the altar
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that runs the counter this is drawn at
kin: senso-ji — a temple where the drawing goes on beside the charm stalls in Tokyo's oldest temple grounds
kin: fushimi-inari — one of the shrines the racks of folded slips stand in, thickest at New Year
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the visit this is part of — offering, draw, read, tie
kin: hanging-at-door — the nearest practice in this atlas to knotting a fortune onto a pine: a paper fixed in place to do its work where it hangs
kin: luck-word — the word this object grades, in seven or nine steps from great blessing to great misfortune
sources: s:wp-o-mikuji s:wp-omamori s:wp-ofuda s:wp-sens-ji s:wp-fushimi-inari-taisha
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ongon (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ongon/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ongon.json
id: ongon
native: онгон (Cyrillic)
aliases: ongod · yazguur ongod · geriin ongod · lineage talisman · household talisman
said: ON-gon; plural ongod
when: 1700 CE to now (still carried)
countries: MN RU
object: form=figurine materials=wood,iron,cloth worn=wall,field,hearth
against: spirits — said by Mongolian shamanic practice, in which the made ongon plays a central part in the ritual that invokes the protection of the spirit [s:wp-ongon]
against: the-dead — said by the practice of consecrating an idol to a dead shaman within three years of the death [s:wp-ongon]
against: house — said by Darkhad households, many of which own lineage talismans (yazguur ongod) or household talismans (geriin ongod) that both contain and attract spirits [s:wp-ongon]
RESTRICTED: This record names the people each practice is recorded among — Darkhad, Tuvan, the yellow shamans Otgony Purev describes — and does not generalise any of it to Mongolians or Siberians at large. It prints no procedure for making or consecrating an ongon, because the sources read describe objects and not methods, and filling that gap from a neighbouring people's practice would be a guess.
what: Two things under one word. An ongon is a spirit in the shamanic belief of Mongolia — after death, shamans become shamanic souls, ongod — and it is also the made object that stands for that spirit in the physical world, put together by a shaman and central to the ritual that calls on the spirit's protection. Idols can be consecrated to a dead shaman within three years of the death, and are kept in the house, as a home ongon, or out in the open in a shelter, as a field ongon.
story: The objects are described one at a time in the ethnography, and this record keeps them that way. For the Tuvan shamaness Yamaan, an ancestor spirit is represented in the handle of a drum: a carved figure with a pink head and chest, a black crown, and red eyes and forehead, with a wire for arms and, on a second wire, suspended holbogo standing for the spirit's earring.

Some ongod are not made at all but inhabited. Agaaryn Khairhan, a mountain in Khövsgöl Province, carries the name of one of the most powerful shamanesses of the Darkhad clan — Agaaryn Khairhan, also called Bagdan Udgan — who lived on that mountain in the eighteenth century.

Among the Darkhad in present-day Northern Mongolia, clusters of ongod stand in transitional places: the mouths of rivers, the border between taiga and steppe. That border is also a religious one, with the taiga and the mountains the traditional ground of shamanism and the steppe the ground of Buddhism. Many Darkhad households own lineage talismans, yazguur ongod, or household talismans, geriin ongod, which both contain and attract spirits.

The ongon matters most in black shamanism: the main job of the khar talynkh, the black shaman, is to bring people into contact with the ongon, whose spirit they call up while drumming in a trance. Otgony Purev records that in late-nineteenth-century Mongolia yellow shamans revered ongod as well, and that every three years they gathered at Dayan Deerh monastery in Khövsgöl Province to renew these ancestral spirits. Dayan Deerh is itself one of the well-known ongod.
how: Made by a shaman, not by a household member, and consecrated to a particular dead shaman. The renewal Purev records for yellow shamans ran on a three-year cycle at a named monastery. This atlas does not print how an ongon is made or what is said over it: the sources read describe particular objects among particular peoples — a Tuvan shamaness's drum handle, Darkhad household talismans — and do not publish a procedure, and neither a Darkhad practice nor a Tuvan one stands in for the other.
today: Recorded in the Darkhad Valley of Northern Mongolia in the ethnography of the 2010s, with household and lineage talismans in ordinary houses and clusters of ongod at the edges between taiga and steppe. Morten Axel Pedersen's Not Quite Shamans, 2011, and Ágnes Birtalan's 2011 study of Dayan Deerh are the recent published accounts this record leans on; Dmitry Zelenin's Культ онгонов в Сибири, 1936, is the old one.
kin: toli-mirror — the other object on the same shaman's body — the mirror worn as armour, where this one holds an ancestor
kin: nkisi — the Kongo parallel: an object a specialist assembles so that a spirit will live in it and work through it
kin: tupilaq — the Arctic made figure with a spirit put into it, and the other place this atlas has to name a people rather than a region
kin: inuit-amulet — the neighbouring northern practice, recorded people by people in the same way
kin: tibetan-protection — what stands on the other side of the line the ongod cluster along — the steppe is Buddhist ground where the taiga is shamanic
kin: consecration — the step that makes an idol an ongon, done within three years of a shaman's death
kin: inheriting — how a yazguur ongon moves — down a lineage, with the house
kin: gau-box — the Buddhist container that shares Mongolia with it, filled by a lama rather than by a shaman
sources: s:wp-ongon s:wp-shamanism-in-siberia s:wp-toli-shamanism
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Palad khik (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/palad-khik/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/palad-khik.json
id: palad-khik
native: ปลัดขิก (Thai)
aliases: palakhik · palat khik · honorable surrogate penis
said: pā-làt kʰìk
when: undated (still carried)
countries: TH
root: Thai ปลัดขิก; the phrase is rendered in English as 'honorable surrogate penis' — palad, a deputy or stand-in, and khik
object: form=figurine materials=wood,copper,bone,tooth worn=waist,pocket,shop
against: weapons — said by Thai men who wear one, for protection from dangerous objects — the source names bullets and knives [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: attraction — said by Thai men, who wear several at once in hope of attracting women and of luck in gambling; and shopkeepers, who display one at the register for trade [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: theft — said by women in Thailand who carry one in a purse; the source names mugging and rape [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: infertility — said by the animist reading of the form as a fertility sign, through the linga of Shiva [s:wp-palad-khik]
what: A carved phallus, from a couple of inches to several feet long, in wood, metal, bone, horn or ivory, usually with sacred inscriptions cut into it. The small ones are worn by men and boys on a cord round the waist, under the clothes, hanging to one side of the wearer's own. Wearing several at once is ordinary. The large ones are not worn at all: they stand in shops, restaurants and other premises, often by the till. Cast metal ones do not always carry the inscriptions; some carry animal figures instead.
story: The form came from India, tied to Shiva, who is represented by the linga; the Cham carried it into Southeast Asia and it stayed. Where the linga is set with a yoni, the pair stands for creation and destruction together, and the Chinese yang is named as the comparable idea. As a phallic representation of Shiva, the palad khik is also an animist fertility sign. In Thailand a penis amulet hanging in a convenience store or a restaurant, or sold by an older woman on the street, is unremarkable.

Who wears one and why is documented, and it is not what the outside write-ups usually make of it. Men wear them for three named reasons: to attract women, for luck in gambling, and for protection from dangerous objects — bullets and knives are the two the source names. Women in Thailand carry one in a purse against rape and mugging. Shopkeepers set one by the cash register to protect the business and to bring in sales.

The rule that tells you what kind of object this is has nothing to do with sex. A palad khik can be taken into places counted as lowly or unclean — a bar, a gambling house, a brothel. An amulet carrying the Buddha cannot. It is the charm you can take where the Buddha may not go, and that, not the shape, is its place in the Thai kit.
how: Carved by monks who specialise in the form. Cutting the sacred inscriptions is treated as a rite in itself and can take days. The piece is then empowered by the repetition of incantations Thais call Kata Bucha, from the Sanskrit ghata puja; which kata depends on the maker's lineage and school. Worn on a waist cord under the clothing, off-centre; carried in a bag; or stood by a till. It is not renewed on a cycle and not retired.
today: Still carved, still sold, still hanging by tills in Thailand as of the accounts this project has read — and routinely written up abroad as a curiosity, which is a fact about the writers rather than about the charm. This atlas describes it the way the trade does: an object with a stated function, a named maker, a lineage of incantation, and a waist cord.
kin: phra-khrueang — the amulet it is the complement of: a Buddha tablet cannot be taken into a bar or a casino, and this can
kin: takrut — the other non-Buddha charm on the same waist cord, and the same rule about what may hang below the belt
kin: phallic-sign — the sign it is — the linga of Shiva, carried at the hip
kin: fascinum — Rome's version of the same intervention: a phallus hung on a child to take the look meant for him
kin: cornicello — Naples' answer to the same problem in a different shape — a horn cut in coral rather than a linga cut in wood
kin: thai-wicha — the craft it belongs to, whose incantations run by lineage rather than by book
kin: tha-phrachan — the Bangkok market that sells it, from behind the counter as often as from the tray
kin: wearing-hidden — how it is worn: under the clothes, on a cord, off-centre
kin: dolhareubang — the other charm in this atlas whose fertility claim rests on a shape read as phallic — Jeju's stone grandfather and its worn nose
sources: s:wp-palad-khik s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-takrut
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Patuá (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/patua/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/patua.json
id: patua
native: patuá (Latin)
aliases: pátua · bolsa de mandinga
said: pah-too-AH
when: undated (still carried)
countries: BR
object: form=packet materials=cloth,wood,cowrie,thread worn=neck,pocket,vehicle
against: bad-luck — said by the Duke catalogue, describing the object's purpose [s:web-duke-sacred-arts-patua]
what: A small sewn packet, worn at the neck or carried, closed over whatever was put inside it. The example catalogued by Duke University's Sacred Arts of the Black Atlantic project is 43 by 35 by 11 mm: cloth and blue vinyl, wood pieces, white thread, and a cowrie shell. It is not meant to be opened.
story: Duke's catalogue entry is blunt about what the object is for: "This amulet, called a pátua, used the power of the Brazilian goddess Iemanjá to protect the owner."

The construction is a set of claims stitched into cloth. Iemanjá's name is embroidered in white thread on blue vinyl — her colour — in twenty-one stitches, a number the catalogue says is sacred to her. Wood pieces reference Catholic relics. A Star of David sits on the back. A cowrie is set in, the shell that is both an instrument of divination and, in Candomblé, a body the gods are present in. The entry reads the combination as sacred colour, sacred number, and references that follow the trade routes between West Africa and Brazil.

*Inference —* the Catholic relic and the Star of David on an Iemanjá packet are the record of a religion that spent centuries being illegal and learned to be legible in more than one language at once. This atlas states that as its own reading and not as the catalogue's.

What this record cannot do is tell a reader how a patuá is filled, closed or charged. That happens inside a terreiro, a Candomblé house, under people entitled to do it; this project has read no published account of the procedure that it can cite, and does not fill the gap from a neighbouring tradition. The entry stops here.
how: Sewn shut. The Duke example is closed with a counted number of stitches carrying the name of the orixá it belongs to. Beyond that, the making is not described here — see the note above. A patuá is worn under clothing at the neck, or carried in a bag, wallet or car.
today: Patuás are made and sold in Brazil, in terreiros and in shops selling to Umbanda and Candomblé practitioners, and are a regular subject of Brazilian religious-goods retail online as of 2026. This project has no dated price and no maker's name for the current trade.
kin: gris-gris — the West African-descended sewn packet this is kin to across the Atlantic, in New Orleans rather than Bahia
kin: hirz-pouch — the same object in Islamic West Africa — a written charm sewn shut and worn
kin: cowrie — the shell set into it, which is a divination instrument before it is an ornament
kin: sewing-in — the practice that makes it — the closing is the charging
kin: west-african-charm-craft — where the form comes from, before the Atlantic crossing
kin: cowrie-strand — the other object built from the same shell, strung instead of sewn in
