## Pazuzu head (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/pazuzu-head/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/pazuzu-head.json
id: pazuzu-head
native: 𒀭𒅆𒊒𒍪𒍪 (cuneiform)
aliases: Pazuzu amulet · Pazuzu pendant
said: pa-ZU-zu, Akkadian pà.zu.zu
when: 800 BCE – 63 BCE
countries: IQ SY
object: form=pendant materials=terracotta,copper,iron,gold,glass,bone worn=neck,wall,door,grave
against: childbirth — said by ritual texts from Uruk, which prescribe a bronze Pazuzu necklace against miscarriage caused by Lamashtu [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: child-harm — said by the householders who set his image in dwellings to protect infants, and the pregnant women who wore his head [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: illness — said by an Assyrian ritual text, which prescribes a Pazuzu head to banish sickness [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: demons — said by Pazuzu himself, in a text narrated in his voice [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: fever — said by Mesopotamian religion, which pairs him with plague and with winds that carry pestilence [s:wp-pazuzu]
what: A head, cast or carved, with a hole or a loop through the top for a cord. The face is the point: gazelle horns, human ears, a dog's muzzle, bulging eyes, wrinkled cheeks. Terracotta is the common material; bronze, iron, gold, glass and bone examples survive too. Some heads were fixed to cylinder seals or worn as brooches; larger stone versions hung on a wall. The full figure, where it appears, has a scaled canine body, two pairs of wings, a scorpion's tail, bird talons, right hand up and left hand down.
story: Pazuzu is a demon employed as a doorman. He is the south-western wind, he carries plague, and the texts that address him call him "Agony of Mankind" and tell him to stay out of the house — and the same culture hung his face over the bed. In the bilingual Compendia he introduces himself: "I am Pazuzu, son of Ḫanbu, king of the evil lilû-demons. I was enraged (in violent motion) against the strong mountains and ascended them."

What he is for is Lamashtu. She snatches babies; he forces her back to the underworld. Ritual texts from Uruk direct that a woman be given a bronze Pazuzu necklace so that Lamashtu cannot make her miscarry; a Late Babylonian incantation against Lamashtu tells the reader to make a Pazuzu necklace and hang it round the afflicted person's neck; an Assyrian ritual text prescribes a Pazuzu head to banish sickness. Franz Wiggermann dates the figure's sudden appearance to the Early Iron Age, with the first images in the eighth century BCE from the tombs at Nimrud, the first texts in the seventh, the bulk of the finds in the seventh and sixth, and the latest under the Seleucids.

One of the large wall amulets was found where it fell. At Dur-Katlimmu, a Neo-Assyrian town, it lay on the floor of the main reception room, facing the entryway it had been hung to watch.

*Inference —* the heads are uniform and there are a great many of them. Eckart Frahm's study finds the appearance barely changes across his history. An object that looks the same everywhere and turns up everywhere was made in quantity by people who were not improvising, which is what the cited scholarship means when it calls the representations mass-produced.
kin: lamashtu-plaque — the demon he is bought for; the necklace in the Uruk texts exists because she is in the room
kin: mesopotamian-apotropaic — the tradition that made a household guard out of a wind that brings plague
kin: bes-amulet — the Egyptian counterpart scholars keep comparing him to — both lion-parted, winged, long-phallused, and both standing over mothers and infants; five Pazuzu heads turned up near a Bes amulet in a 7th-century fort at Nimrud
kin: gorgoneion — the same device in Greek: a face too frightening to walk past, mounted where the danger comes in
kin: horn — the gazelle horns that identify the face at a glance
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the Dur-Katlimmu find caught in the act — hung on the wall facing the entryway
kin: terracotta — the material most of the surviving heads are made of, and the reason there are so many
kin: grave-deposit — why some of these are still here: they were buried with the people who wore them
kin: incantation-bowl — the later Mesopotamian object doing the same job with writing instead of a face
sources: s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-lamashtu s:wp-mesopotamian-mythology s:wp-bes
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Phone charm (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/phone-charm/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/phone-charm.json
id: phone-charm
native: 携帯ストラップ (Han)
aliases: keitai strap · phone strap · phone dangler · phone lanyard · phone chain
said: keitai sutorappu, 'mobile strap'
when: 1995 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP US GB IE KR
root: Japanese 携帯 keitai, 'portable', used on its own for a mobile phone, plus English strap borrowed as ストラップ sutorappu
object: form=pendant materials=plastic,cloth,thread,wood worn=phone,pocket
against: traffic — said by Japanese shrines and temples, whose kōtsū-anzen omamori is sold for traffic safety and is one of the things hung on a phone strap [s:wp-omamori]
against: bad-luck — said by Japanese shrines and temples, in the cited account's summary of what an omamori is sold to do [s:wp-omamori]
against: attraction — said by the same shrine range, which includes en-musubi for finding a partner and shōbai-hanjō for prosperity in business [s:wp-omamori]
what: A small figure, bead, tassel or brocade pouch on a thin cord, knotted with a lark's head through a hole in a phone or a case. Where a handset has no hole, it goes on a silicone plug pushed into a jack port, a lobster clasp, a circle cotter or a lanyard. The cord is the object; what hangs on the end of it is negotiable.
story: This started as a safety feature and turned into a charm rack, and the sequence is documented.

The Japanese account gives the mechanism first: handsets carried a ストラップホール, a strap hole, and a thin loop was passed through it. One explanation it records for why straps spread in Japan is the Product Liability Law of 1995: carriers told users to put a hand through the strap so the phone would not be dropped. 落下防止 — fall prevention. That is a claim about gravity, and it is the only claim in this record that nobody argues with.

Then the hole filled up. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, hanging ten or more straps at once was a fashion among young people in Japan, to the point where the straps could outweigh the phone. The English account says phone charms "first originated in Japan and later in the United States", and spread from there to the United Kingdom and Ireland. When the iPhone 3GS arrived in 2008 without an attachment slot, a Korean company answered with hanging charms fixed by screws. The British designer Anya Hindmarch put charms into a collection called Pimp Your Phones in 2018.

What gets hung there is the reason this object is in an amulet atlas rather than an accessories one. Omamori — the brocade pouches Japanese shrines and temples issue, with a prayer or an invocation sealed inside and a rule against opening them — are, in the cited account's words, "often spotted on bags, hung on cellphone straps, in cars, etc." The shrine's range is specific about what each is for: kōtsū-anzen for traffic safety, gakugyō-jōju for passing examinations, en-musubi for finding a partner, anzan for a safe delivery, shōbai-hanjō for business. Dazaifu Tenmangū sells a keychain amulet for safe travel and a bracelet amulet, which is the same shift in fastening. *Inference —* a charm designed to be tied to something found a phone waiting with a hole already drilled in it, and the reason there was a hole had nothing to do with the charm.

The argument attached to this object is the usual one and the shrines are on record in it. The cited account notes that when demand outruns what a shrine can make, popular shrines and temples turn to factories, and that "priests have been known to complain about the quality and authenticity of the products made by factories". It also records the other end: generic omamori sold in ordinary Japanese shops with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, issued by no shrine and typically not spiritual in nature. That is two named positions, and this atlas reports both and settles neither.

*Inference —* the strap is also the clearest case in this atlas of a charm losing its mounting. The flip phone had a hole; the slab phone mostly does not, and the workarounds — the jack plug, the screw, the case with a loop moulded in — are all later inventions answering the same problem. What happens to a carried charm when the thing it was tied to changes shape is a question this collection will keep meeting.
how: Bought at a phone shop, a shrine office, a souvenir counter, a convenience store, or given away with a drink or as promotional merchandise. Attached with a cow-hitch or lark's-head knot through the strap hole, or by whatever adapter the handset forces. An omamori on a strap follows the omamori rules: not opened, replaced about once a year, returned to the shrine it came from to be burnt. A character strap follows no rules at all.
today: Still sold in 2026, and still standard on Japanese shrine counters, where the strap format is one of several the same prayer is sold in. No dated price was read for this record, and neither the Japanese nor the English account this project read publishes a market figure.
kin: omamori — the thing most often on the end of the cord in Japan, carrying its own rules about not being opened
kin: exam-charm — the variety a student hangs there in January, and the one with a chocolate bar attached to it
kin: maneki-neko — one of the figures the strap trade shrank to thumb size, and the shop-counter original it came from
kin: daruma — another, and the other Japanese object that is bought small as a souvenir and large as a vow
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the other charm in this atlas whose cited worn-list already includes a phone
kin: worry-stone — the other thing in a modern pocket that gets touched all day without being looked at
kin: car-saint — what hangs from the mirror where this hangs from the handset, doing the same job from the next surface over
kin: knotting — the practice that attaches it — a lark's head through a drilled hole, which is the oldest technique in this record
kin: the-charm-goes-digital — the long read this is the hinge of: the charm did not go into the phone, it was tied to the outside of it
kin: senso-ji — one temple where the strap format sits on the counter beside every other format of the same prayer
sources: s:wp-ja-strap s:wp-mobile-phone-charm s:wp-omamori s:web-dazaifu-tenmangu-amulets

## Phra khrueang (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/phra-khrueang/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/phra-khrueang.json
id: phra-khrueang
native: พระเครื่อง (Thai)
aliases: Thai Buddha amulet · phrakhrueang · votive tablet · Phra Somdej · Benja Phakhi
said: prá krêuang
when: 1866 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TH
root: Thai พระ phra, the honorific for a Buddha image or a monk, + เครื่อง khrueang, a thing worn or carried — the Buddha one wears
object: form=plaque materials=earth,terracotta,copper,wood,bone,hair worn=neck,chest
against: weapons — said by Ayutthaya-period warriors, who carried tablets into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or herbal charms; invulnerability is named among the amulet's functions [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: witchcraft — said by the functions Thai collectors list for the Phra Somdej: protection from black magic and the blocking of disasters [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: attraction — said by the Khun Phaen type, whose main function is named as enhancing relationships, marriage and career — after the folklore hero who used a love formula [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: illness — said by the Phra Kring, the rattling Medicine Buddha statuette, which Thai accounts describe as sounding the name of Bhaisajyaguru as the wearer walks [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: bad-luck — said by the Jatukham Rammathep's buyers in 2006 and 2007, who held that it kept its owner from danger and made its owner rich [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
what: A small pressed image of the Buddha, a revered monk, a bodhisattva or a deva — a tablet a couple of centimetres across, in plaster, metal, wood or bone, often with ash, a monk's hair or temple relics in the mix. Most are cased in clear plastic or a gold frame and worn on a chain at the neck. The Jatukham Rammathep type is round and about 5 cm across. A collector reads one with a loupe: the clay's texture, the mould's flaws, the temple it was pressed at, the monk who chanted over it.
story: The line runs from votive tablets, which are older than the idea of an amulet. Buddhism reached what is now Thailand in the Dvaravati period and brought India's votive-tablet practice with it; Dvaravati tablets were made to perpetuate the religion, tied to doctrines like the Five Disappearances. Under Srivijaya and Mahayana influence, tablets were pressed to dedicate merit to the dead and to accumulate it towards becoming a bodhisattva. By the Ayutthaya period they were being made for protection, and warriors carried them into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or a herbal charm. In the early Rattanakosin period the protective amulet took off, the class acquired the name phra khrueang, and temples used them to raise money — a monk would give an amulet as a gift in return for a donation. That transaction is the hinge of everything that follows.

The famous ones have dates, diggings and names. Phra Somdej Wat Rakhang was made around 1866 to 1871 by Somdej Toh of Wat Rakhang Khositaram, one of Thailand's most respected monks, and is called the king of amulets. Somdej Toh had found Phra Sum Kor amulets at Wat Phraboromthat Nakhonchum in 1849, while visiting relatives in Kamphaeng Phet, along with tablets explaining how they were made, and used those instructions for his own. Phra Rod came out of a partly collapsed stupa at Wat Mahawan in Lamphun in the early reign of King Chulalongkorn. Phra Nang Phaya turned up when workers dug at Wat Nang Phaya in Phitsanulok to prepare a stage for Chulalongkorn's visit. Phra Phong Suphan came out of a formal dig the Suphanburi governor ordered in 1913, after thieves had gone under the temple's great stupa and taken amulets, some of them gold. Those five — Somdej, Rod, Nang Phaya, Phong Suphan, Sum Kor — are the Benja Phakhi, valued at over 10 million baht; the source names no year for that figure, so it is given without one.

The market can move like a market. In 1987 a policeman, Khun Phantharak Rajjadej, created the Jatukham Rammathep amulet for the establishment of Nakhon Si Thammarat's city pillar; locals hold the two Srivijaya princes it names to be the city's guardians. It caught on in the early 2000s, and hard from his funeral on 5 July 2006 into mid-2007. As many as 150 series were planned for 2007, and the market for that one type reached twenty billion baht that year. In late 2007 the bubble burst, and the amulets were left lying about cheap.

A royal series is the cleanest record of how provenance is priced. King Bhumibol made the Phra Somdet Jitlada himself and awarded them from 1965 to 1970 to selected soldiers, police, officials and citizens: no more than 3,000, each with a certificate carrying the recipient's name, the date and the amulet's number. As of 2013 one was worth at least two million baht. The certificate is the price.
how: Pressed from a mould: temple dirt, pollen, plaster, crushed flowers, ash, a monk's hair, sometimes a fragment of a revered monk's robe. Monks chant and bless the batch, a process that runs from a week to several years. Amulets are also placed under stupas as they are built, which is why so many come to light when a temple structure collapses. What a piece is worth rests on appearance, scarcity, maker, age and reputed power — and on whether a specialist will certify it, because forgeries are common and buyers pay for an expert eye. There are rules for wearing: above the waist, at the neck or chest, never below; not in a bedroom where sex is expected; a prayer before and after putting one on; taken off to bathe. The takrut, which carries no monk and no Buddha image, is exempt and may go in a trouser pocket.
today: Traded daily at Tha Phrachan beside Thammasat University in Bangkok and at markets across the country, as of the most recent published accounts this project has read. Whether that trade is devotion or dealing is argued among Thai commentators rather than between Thais and outsiders, and this atlas reports the argument without joining it.
kin: tha-phrachan — the market this object built: trays, glass cases, loupes and certificates, in the lanes beside Thammasat University
kin: takrut — the amulet it shares a chain with and is ranked against — no Buddha image on a takrut, so it may go where this may not, including a trouser pocket
kin: palad-khik — the other Thai charm on the same tray, and the one that may be carried into a bar or a casino where this may not
kin: sak-yant — the same protection cut into skin instead of pressed into clay, by masters rather than moulds
kin: thai-wicha — the body of craft and lineage this belongs to, and the reason a monk's name sets a price
kin: consecration — what turns a pressed tablet into a phra khrueang — chanting that runs from a week to several years
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice in its most monetised form, with a 20-billion-baht year on the record
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on forgery and appraisal, which starts with this object because the loupes are pointed at it
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read this is a hard case for: temple, mould and monk are the date, and a certificate is the evidence
kin: keris-pusaka — the Indonesian parallel — an object whose worth sits in its maker, its lineage and its age rather than in its material
kin: grave-deposit — why so many surface at once: tablets were sealed into stupas at construction and come out when the stupa falls
sources: s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-takrut s:wp-palad-khik s:wp-yantra-tattooing
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ping'an fu (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/ping-an-fu/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/ping-an-fu.json
id: ping-an-fu
native: 平安符 (Han)
aliases: ping an fu · peace talisman · safety charm
said: PING-ahn foo, 'peace talisman'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: TW
root: Chinese 平安 píng'ān 'peace, safety' + 符 fú 'talisman, tally'
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,ink,cloth worn=pocket,wallet,vehicle,neck
against: travel — said by the Taiwanese Gods account, which describes the charm as carried on the person for safe passage [s:web-taiwanese-gods-fulu]
against: bad-luck — said by its own name — ping'an, peace and safety — and the yearly renewal that goes with it [s:web-taiwanese-gods-fulu]
against: spirits — said by Taoist talismanic practice generally, where most coin talismans ask Lei Gong to protect their carriers from evil spirits and misfortune [s:wp-fulu]
what: A sheet of yellow paper inscribed with sacred symbols, folded into a bagua shape or a rectangle and slipped into a red cloth sleeve. In Taiwan it is the commonest amulet there is: the little red pouch tucked in a wallet, the folded yellow-paper bagua hanging from a scooter key.
story: The charm is obtained rather than bought outright, and the asking is specific. A worshipper offers incense, states their name, birthday and address and what they are asking for, and seeks the deity's permission with divination blocks. If it is granted, the talisman is raised above the main incense burner and circled clockwise three times — in the Taiwanese Gods account, to let it drink in the incense energy and switch on its power.

*Inference —* that sequence is worth reading closely. A name, a birth date and an address are the same details a registry takes; the charm is issued to a person, not to a pocket, and the censer is where it is stamped.

The writing on it belongs to the Taoist talismanic tradition, where the script is deliberately hard to read. Scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz have argued that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority, and Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi, in the Eastern Jin period, that successful use did not depend on the user being able to decipher the script.
how: Requested at a temple, activated over the censer, carried on the person, then retired on a calendar. A peace talisman is usually replaced once a year: before Lunar New Year the old one goes to the temple's furnace to be burned, and a fresh one is requested for the coming year.
today: Handed out at temples across Taiwan and kept in nearly every household there, as of the account read in September 2026 — in wallets, on scooter keys, in car glove boxes and in bags. Whether the charm on a scooter key is a devotional object or a habit is not a question this atlas settles; the temple's own procedure treats it as the former, and the wallet treats it as the latter.
kin: fu-talisman — the class it belongs to — this is the ordinary, household end of Taoist talismanic writing
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition that writes it and the priesthood that keeps the script
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the step that issues it: incense, a name, a birth date, divination blocks, three clockwise circles over the censer
kin: renewing-yearly — its clock — one year, then the furnace
kin: burning-retirement — how it ends, at the temple, before Lunar New Year
kin: omamori — Japan's sealed brocade pouch, taken from a shrine and returned to be burned a year later: the same cycle, the same year
kin: ofuda — the Japanese paper talisman descended from the same Taoist writing
kin: bujeok — the Korean paper charm from the same root, and the third of the three
kin: bagua-mirror — the fixed version at the same door: this one rides in a pocket, that one is screwed above the lintel
kin: paper — the material that lets a temple issue thousands and burn them all a year later
sources: s:web-taiwanese-gods-fulu s:wp-fulu s:wp-fu-character s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm

## Qur'an pendant (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/quran-pendant/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/quran-pendant.json
id: quran-pendant
native: آية الكرسي (Arabic)
aliases: miniature Qur'an · Ayat al-Kursi pendant · Qur'an case · hirz
said: Āyat al-Kursī, the Throne Verse — the text most often inside one
when: 901 CE to now (still carried)
countries: EG TR IR PK IN
object: form=box materials=silver,gold,carnelian,paper,ink,lead worn=neck,vehicle,wall,pocket
against: demons — said by hadith, in which reciting the Throne Verse wards off devils (šayāṭīn) and fiends (ʿafārīt); the verse is also used in exorcism against jinn [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: evil-eye — said by the tradition summarised in the cited article, which reads the verse's association with protection as extending to the evil eye [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: travel — said by Muslims who recite it before setting out on a journey and before going to sleep [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: house — said by al-Suyuti's narration, in which a jinn teaches a man the verse that keeps any devil from entering his house with him [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: illness — said by the wider Islamic amulet tradition, which the cited account says was meant to promote health, longevity, fertility and potency [s:wp-amulet]
what: A metal case at the throat with scripture inside it. Sometimes a whole miniature Qur'an, protected by an illuminated metal cover; sometimes a single verse on paper or engraved on the metal itself. The verse is most often Āyat al-Kursī, the Throne Verse, Qur'an 2:255 — the 255th verse of the second chapter, and the one the tradition names the greatest in the book. Others hang the same verse framed on a wall or from a mirror in a car.
story: The verse opens: "Allah: there is no god but Him, the Ever-Living, the Ever-Watchful. Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him." It is built concentrically, in the symmetry most common in the Qur'an, where each segment answers its pair across a centre.

What the tradition says it does is on the record in hadith and in commentary, and this atlas reports it without weighing it. Reciting the verse is said in hadith to ward off devils, šayāṭīn, and fiends, ʿafārīt; recited after every obligatory prayer it is held to admit the reciter to Paradise with nothing in the way but death. Al-Suyuti narrates a man of humanity meeting a man of the jinn, and the jinn, beaten in a wrestling match, teaching him the verse that keeps any devil from entering his house with him — this one. The Throne Verse is used in exorcism, against jinn and devils. Because it is associated with protection, the tradition also reads it as a shield against the evil eye. It is recited before a journey and before sleep, morning and evening as a daily adhkār.

The material tradition round it is documented. Miniature Qur'ans kept in illuminated metal cases are one form; block-printed text amulets sealed into lead cases with lugs, so they could be sewn on or hung, are another. Preferred materials are precious and semi-precious, and the reasons given for them are explicit: carnelian, ʿaqīq, is favoured because it was counted the stone of Muhammad, who was said to have worn a carnelian seal set in silver on the little finger of his right hand; jade and jasper are held to assure victory in battle, guard against lightning and treat diseases of the internal organs. A combination of jade and carnelian is read for fertility and embryogenesis — the reddish, light-carrying carnelian standing for blood, which echoes the clot of congealed blood God created the human from, Qur'an 96:2.

*Inference —* the cited accounts are careful to separate early Islamic amulets from what came before them: these appeal to God in the first instance, where Byzantine, Roman and early Iranian magic addressed demonic forces or the spirits of the dead. That is a claim about direction of address, not about efficacy, and it is the line the tradition's own scholars keep returning to when they argue about whether to wear one at all.
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition, and the argument about whether this object should exist
kin: taweez — the same scripture folded into a packet rather than sealed in a case
kin: talismanic-shirt — the same verses at the scale of a garment
kin: hirz-pouch — the silver box of Qur'anic verses the Egyptian tradition names alongside the eye and the hamsa
kin: mezuzah — scripture in a case, fixed where a person passes it — the same object in another book, with the opposite ruling about what to call it
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest dated instance of this idea anywhere in the atlas: a blessing, rolled small, carried
kin: carnelian — the stone the tradition singles out as the Prophet's, worn set in silver
kin: divine-name — the sign underneath: the names and attributes of God doing the work
kin: car-saint — where this one most often ends up now — hung from a mirror rather than worn
kin: khan-el-khalili — the Cairo market where the cases are sold
sources: s:wp-throne-verse s:wp-amulet s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-carnelian
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

against: bad-luck — said by carriers across Europe, Africa, Australia and the Americas, as summarised by the source [s:wp-rabbit-s-foot]
against: curse — said by the folk song There'll Be a Hot Time in the Old Town Tonight [s:wp-rabbit-s-foot]
against: bad-luck — said by Newbell Niles Puckett, recording an African American cook in the Mississippi Delta who wore a mojo bag containing a rabbit's foot among other ingredients for good luck [s:wp-mojo-bag]
what: A rabbit's hind foot, dried, carried in a pocket. Grander ones are capped in metal and hung from a chain; Theodore Roosevelt wrote in his autobiography that the boxer John L. Sullivan gave him a gold-mounted one. The strictest version is specific about which foot: the left hind one.
story: This charm is usually filed under European luck, beside the clover and the horseshoe, and its American history says otherwise. The conditions attached to it in North America are conditions about a graveyard. The foot must be the left hind foot of a rabbit shot or otherwise taken in a cemetery. Some accounts require a full moon, others a new moon; some a Friday, a rainy Friday, or Friday the thirteenth; some a silver bullet; some that the foot be cut off while the rabbit is still alive. Folklorists read the use of graveyard dust as a symbolic appropriation of the parts of a corpse as a relic, and as sympathetic magic.

The folklorist Newbell Niles Puckett recorded the reasoning about whose grave: "the more wicked the person who is dead, the more effective the charm associated with his remains." Puckett noted that during Grover Cleveland's 1884 election campaign the candidate was said to have been sent the foot of a rabbit killed on the grave of the outlaw Jesse James. Puckett also documented an African American cook in the Mississippi Delta whose mojo bag held "a lizard's tail, rabbit's foot, a fish eye, snake skins, a beetle, and a dime with a hole in it", worn for good luck — the rabbit's foot as one ingredient in a Hoodoo working rather than as a standalone token.

The folk song record says the same thing plainly. "There'll Be a Hot Time in the Old Town Tonight", once popular in minstrel shows, runs: "And you've got a rabbit's foot To keep away de hoo-doo". The foot turns up in blues lyrics as well. A 1905 anecdote has Booker T. Washington and Baron Ladislaus Hengelmuller, the Austrian ambassador, confusing their overcoats at the White House while both waiting to speak to Roosevelt; the ambassador realised the coat was not his when he reached for his gloves and found instead "the left hind foot of a graveyard rabbit, killed in the dark of the moon."

Other accounts pull in other directions. Benjamin Radford has suggested the charm may be connected to the Hand of Glory, a European charm made from the hand of a hanged man and pickled. The belief in a lucky rabbit's foot is reported from Europe, Africa, Australia and both American continents, with the same pattern everywhere: the rabbit must have been killed in a particular place, or by a particular method, or by a person with a particular attribute — in one version, by a cross-eyed man. A related British and American ritual is to say "rabbit rabbit rabbit" on waking on the first day of a month, for luck through the rest of it.
how: Taken from the animal under the conditions the tradition names — place, day, moon, method — then dried and carried in a pocket, or mounted in metal and hung. The strictures are described by the source as now mostly observed in the breach. Nothing is said over it and nothing retires it.
today: Sold dyed in bright colours on keychains, and carried by people who have never heard of a graveyard rabbit. *Inference —* what the mass-market version keeps is the object and what it drops is every condition that made it one, which is the same story this atlas tells about the horseshoe bought new. The Hoodoo lineage is the part most often left out, and it is the part the nineteenth- and early twentieth-century record documents best.
kin: gris-gris — the African American charm tradition this object's American history runs through, and the frame the graveyard conditions make sense in
kin: mojo-word — the word for the bag Puckett found it inside, worn by a cook in the Mississippi Delta
kin: tooth-and-claw — the sign family it belongs to: a piece of an animal, carried for what the animal was
kin: bone-ivory — what is left after drying, and the reason these survive in collections at all
kin: four-leaf-clover — the charm it is usually sold beside, and the other one whose original condition the market has quietly dropped
kin: horseshoe — the two objects Theodore Roosevelt was given — this from John L. Sullivan, and a penholder Bob Fitzsimmons made out of a shoe
kin: luck-word — the single word that now covers everything this charm was once specific about
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read it belongs in: a Black folk-magic object sold as generic American luck, with the lineage left off the packet
kin: game-day-charm — where a great many of them ended up, in a pocket on the day of a match
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it gets shelved under, which this record's sources do not support for its American form
sources: s:wp-rabbit-s-foot s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-luck s:wp-list-of-lucky-symbols

## Red string (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/red-string/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/red-string.json
id: red-string
native: חוט השני (Hebrew)
aliases: scarlet thread · Kabbalah bracelet · khutt hashani
said: khut ha-sha-NI, 'the scarlet thread'
when: 1489 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL US
object: form=cord materials=thread worn=wrist,finger
against: evil-eye — said by the Jewish folk custom as described in the cited article: worn to ward off misfortune brought about by the evil eye, ayin hara [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: bad-luck — said by the same custom, and the wider use of red strings for luck in Hindu and Chinese practice the article names alongside it [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
what: A thin scarlet or crimson thread, usually wool, tied round the wrist as a bracelet or band. That is the whole object.
story: The honest version of this record starts with an absence. There is no written requirement anywhere — not in the Torah, not in Halacha, not in the Kabbalistic texts — to tie a red string round a wrist. Sources mention red strings as a good omen, and it is not evident whether they were widely worn.

What there is instead is a scatter of references. Genesis 38 has a scarlet thread tied about a wrist, at the birth of Tamar's twins. Rabbi Shmuel ben Hafni Gaon noted that placing a red string on the hand may be a good omen, and some sources imply it could go round a finger. Aggadas Bereishis holds that Joseph's coat was the same as his brothers' and that Jacob marked it with a red string on the cuffs.

There is exactly one public exhortation to wear one, and it is dated. In the 1490s, when Jews were not permitted to wear tefillin, Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended that they wear a red string on their hands instead, to remember the commandment. A substitute object, recorded because the real one had been banned.

The modern trade is documented too. In Israel it is common to see elderly women selling scarlet thread to pilgrims and tourists, especially in the Old City of Jerusalem. Outside Israel the string became popular in the late 1990s with celebrities, most of them not Jewish — Madonna and her children, Leonardo DiCaprio, Michael Jackson, Ariana Grande, Tucker Carlson, Jared Kushner — and that wave is usually linked to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. Editors of a 2007 study of trend analysis recorded a surge in sales attributed to Madonna. Michael Laitman's public position is in the article's own critical links: practical Kabbalah has no use for red strings.

*Inference —* every other record in this batch can say what its object is made of and who makes it. This one cannot, because the object is a piece of wool and the thing being sold is the association. That is worth stating rather than dressing up, and it is also the reason the red string is the most-argued-about Jewish charm in the atlas.

The red string is not only Jewish. The cited article notes that Hinduism and Chinese culture wear a red string or bracelet for luck, love and to keep evil off.
kin: red-thread — the sign, and the one that runs from the Mediterranean to Mongolia without needing a text
kin: tefillin — the commandment this stood in for in the 1490s, when Rabbi Abraham Saba told Jews barred from wearing tefillin to wear a red string to remember it
kin: martenitsa — the Balkan red thread on a wrist, with a fixed season and a documented history where this one has an absence
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition it is marketed under, and whose own teachers say it has no use for red strings
kin: thread — the whole material inventory of this object
kin: knotting — the practice — the tying is what there is to do
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the shelf it now shares: a wrist, a colour, and a claim sold to people outside the tradition
kin: hamsa — the other Jewish charm against the eye, and the one with a long documented object history
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read; a custom with no textual basis, sold worldwide under the name of a restricted tradition
sources: s:wp-red-string-kabbalah s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-martenitsa

## Rowan cross (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/rowan-cross/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/rowan-cross.json
id: rowan-cross
native: caorann (Latin)
aliases: rowan and red thread · rowan loop · witch-wood cross · quickbeam cross
said: ROH-an; the Gaelic name for the tree is said KUR-an
when: 1846 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE IM
root: English rowan, recorded from 1804 and detached from an earlier rowan-tree, rountree, attested in northern English and Scots from the 1540s; probably from a North Germanic source related to Old Norse reynir, ultimately from Germanic *raud-inan 'to redden', for the berries.
object: form=knot materials=wood,thread worn=pocket,sewn-in,door,field
against: witchcraft — said by Victorian folklorists reporting British practice — Edwin Lees for the Wyre Forest in 1856, James Frazer for Scotland in 1890, Charles Godfrey Leland for England in 1891 [s:wp-rowan]
against: livestock — said by Scottish practice, as recorded of rowan boughs taken into byres in May and trees planted in pastures [s:wp-sorbus-aucuparia]
against: spirits — said by Thomas Keightley, on mortals who put a rowan branch over their doors to watch the fairy rades safely [s:wp-rowan]
against: house — said by English building practice, in which rowan was chosen for the post or mantel over a fireplace to discourage witchcraft [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
what: Two rowan twigs laid across each other and bound at the crossing with red thread or wool, a few inches across. A variant is a loop rather than a cross: a single withy bent round and tied. Both are cut green, and both are meant to be renewed.
story: The rowan's reputation is older than the charm's paperwork. British folklorists of the Victorian era reported the belief in the tree's power to turn away witches: Edwin Lees wrote it up for the Wyre Forest in 1856, James Frazer reported it from Scotland in 1890 — where the tree was often planted by a gate or a front door — and Charles Godfrey Leland reported English traditions of the same in 1891, citing the Denham Tracts, collected between 1846 and 1859. Frazer singled out the flying rowan, a rowan seeded by bird droppings into the fork of an oak or a maple and growing as an epiphyte, as especially potent against witches and as a counter-charm against sorcery.

What the twigs were for is agricultural before it is anything else. In Scottish folklore boughs of rowan were taken into cattle byres in May to protect the livestock, rowan trees were planted in pastures for the same reason, and twigs were used to drive cattle out to grass for the first time in spring to secure their health and fertility. In English folklore the wood was worked into the shafts of farm implements to keep animals and produce out of reach of witches' spells, and rowan was chosen for the post or mantel over a fireplace. Thomas Keightley recorded that mortals could safely watch the fairy rades — the mounted processions the fairies were said to hold at the onset of summer — by putting a rowan branch over their doors.

The objects survive because a clergyman posted them to Oxford. On 28 February 1893 the Rev. Canon John Christopher Atkinson, of Danby Parsonage, Grosmont, in the North Riding of Yorkshire, gave the Pitt Rivers Museum three rowan loops, accessioned as 1893.18.1–3, the smallest 70 mm across; Atkinson had published on the practice in 1891. The museum's account records that from Scotland to Cornwall crosses of the same wood were bound with red thread and carried in pockets or sewn into the linings of coats, and that in Strathspey a loop of rowan was made at May Day and flocks of sheep and lambs were driven through it morning and evening.

*Tradition holds —* the charm goes with a couplet, usually given in Scots as "Rowan tree and red thread, gar the witches tyne their speed" — gar is to compel, tyne is to lose. This record has not read that rhyme in any of the sources it cites, and prints it here as a thing people say rather than as a documented text.
how: Cut green, from a living tree, at a named time — the Pitt Rivers account gives St Helen's Day for collecting, and May Day and Lammas for the rites the loops belong to. Two twigs are crossed and lashed at the join with red thread or wool; a loop is bent from one withy and tied. The finished charm goes over a door or a byre lintel, into a pocket, or into a coat lining. *Tradition holds —* it is cut fresh each year, the old one discarded, which is why so few reach museums.
today: Made and sold by British craftworkers and by shops trading in folk charms, and made at home by people who have read about it. *Inference —* the continuous farming practice the Victorian folklorists recorded is not what is happening now; what is happening now is a revival working from those same published accounts, and this record separates the two rather than running them together.
kin: red-thread — the second half of the charm and the half that does the binding — wood alone is not the object
kin: tree — the sign behind it: this is the one British charm whose power is attributed to a named species and not to a shape
kin: hagstone — what hung on the next nail, found rather than cut, and not renewed each year
kin: horseshoe — the iron answer to the same door, and the one that stayed up all year
kin: brigids-cross — the other woven cross of these islands, made on one named day, hung in the rafters, and replaced at the next feast
kin: knotting — the practice that makes it — the red thread at the crossing is the whole operation
kin: sewing-in — how it was carried where it could not be seen, stitched into a coat lining from Scotland to Cornwall
kin: hanging-at-door — where it mostly went: over a door, over a byre lintel, above a hearth
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and its clearest case of a plant used as a metal would be
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — the case these loops have sat in since 1893, and the reason we can say how big they are
kin: witch-bottle — the same fear answered indoors and out of sight, with urine and pins instead of wood and thread
sources: s:wp-rowan s:wp-sorbus-aucuparia s:web-prm-rowan-loop s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum

## Rudraksha (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/rudraksha/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/rudraksha.json
id: rudraksha
native: रुद्राक्ष (Devanagari)
aliases: rudraksha · rudrākṣa · blueberry bead
said: rud-RAAK-sha
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IN NP ID
root: Sanskrit rudra (Shiva) + akṣa (eye) — 'eye of Rudra'
object: form=bead materials=seed worn=neck,wrist
against: bad-luck — said by Shaiva wearers, as summarised in the source [s:wp-rudraksha]
against: poverty — said by Kalagni Rudra, in the Upanishadic dialogue with Sage Bhusunda [s:wp-rudraksha]
what: A hard brown seed-stone, ridged from top to bottom, drilled and strung at the throat. The stone is the pit of the fruit of Elaeocarpus ganitrus, a fast-growing evergreen of the Himalayan foothills; ripe, the fruit wears a blue husk, which is why sellers call the bead a blueberry bead. The ridges are read as faces — mukha, Sanskrit for face — and the count of faces on one bead is the first thing a buyer looks for. Nepalese beads run 20 to 35 mm, Indonesian ones 5 to 25 mm.
story: The bead belongs to Shiva, and the texts say why. Several late-medieval Upanishads give a scene: the sage Bhusunda asks Kalagni Rudra where rudraksha begin, and the god answers that he closed his eyes to destroy the Tripurasura, drops fell from the closed eyes to the earth, and those tears became the stones. In the same passage the promise attached to the bead is not protection but merit — the god says that uttering the name alone earns the benefit of giving ten cows in charity, and seeing and touching it doubles that.

The Tamil Tirumurai reads the bead as a mark you can see across a street: those who walk the paths of charya and kriya wear twin rings in the earlobes and a twin rudraksha garland at the neck, and the text calls that a sign of piety.

The counts are specific and published. A bead may carry between one and twenty-one faces; instances of twenty-six or twenty-seven have been reported and are rare. One face, ekamukha, is the rarest of all. A rudraksha with eleven faces is worn by renunciants, a two-faced bead by the married, and a five-faced bead stands for Hanuman. Naturally joined beads have their own names — savar for a conjoined pair, Gauri Shankar where the two are of a size, Garbha Gauri where one is smaller, Ganesha where a bead carries a trunk-like protrusion, Trijuti for three grown together.

*Inference —* every one of those distinctions is a price. A tradition that sorts a seed into twenty-one grades, then again by how many grew together, has built the apparatus a market needs, and the rarest grades are the ones a buyer cannot check by eye.
how: Strung as a mala — a garland — usually of 108 beads plus one, which the wearers call the meru, bindu or guru bead and use to mark where a cycle of recitation begins and ends. Shorter strings run 27+1 and 54+1. Silk or black or red cotton thread is the common stringing; jewellers less often use copper, silver or gold wire, and a bead strung too tightly can split. The Devi Bhagavata Purana describes how a garland is prepared. The recitation the beads count is most often Om Namah Shivaya.
today: Grown and sold as a crop. Cultivation centres on the Himalayan foothills in Nepal and India — Kathmandu and the Arun Valley in Nepal, Kulu and Rameshwaram in India — with groves in Uttarakhand, and a 184-acre grove, the Ch. Devi Lal Rudraksha Vatika in Yamunanagar district, Haryana, is planted to the tree along with some 400 endangered ayurvedic herbs. Nepal, India and Indonesia are the three sources named for the jewellery trade as of 2026, and the bead is priced alongside semi-precious stones.
kin: counting-beads — the practice the string exists for — 108 beads plus a guru bead is a counter before it is an ornament
kin: seed — the material: a fruit stone, hard enough to drill and outlast the wearer
kin: tree — the sign behind the object — this bead is the one amulet in the atlas that is simply a tree's fruit, named for a god's eye
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition that files it: an object worn on the body because a text says what wearing it does
kin: navaratna-ring — the other South Asian body-worn prescription, and the opposite kind — nine bought stones set by an astrologer's reading, against one grown seed anyone may wear
kin: dzi-bead — the Himalayan bead worn at the same throat, graded the same way by counting marks on its surface, and priced far higher
kin: kathmandu-thamel — one of the streets the Nepalese beads reach a buyer on
kin: crystal-pendant — what the bead becomes in a wellness shop outside the tradition — a stone sold by its properties, with no mantra to count
sources: s:wp-rudraksha s:wp-amulet s:web-wisdomlib-kavaca

## Sak yant (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/sak-yant/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/sak-yant.json
id: sak-yant
native: สักยันต์ (Thai)
aliases: yantra tattooing · សាក់យ័ន្ត (Khmer) · ສັກຢັນ (Lao) · yant tattoo
said: sàk yan
when: 800 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TH KH LA MM
root: Khmer សាក់ sak 'to tattoo', from the Proto-Mon-Khmer root *cɔkʔ 'to prick', + Sanskrit yantra, from yam 'to hold, sustain' and tra 'instrument' — a sacred instrument, pricked into skin
object: form=tattoo materials=ink,skin worn=skin
against: weapons — said by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and others in trades they count as dangerous, who take the protective class of yant [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: bad-luck — said by the protective class of yant, described as warding off evil and hardship [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: attraction — said by bearers who take yant for power, fortune, charisma — and, on cloth and metal, to increase wealth and attract lovers [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: illness — said by those who hang yant-marked cloth or metal in a house, a place of worship or a vehicle against danger and illness [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
RESTRICTED: A yant's design and the words said over it belong to the master's lineage, and the tattoo is described as holding only while the bearer keeps the rules and taboos taken on with it. This atlas prints what the sources publish and does not print a design's incantation or reconstruct the rules a particular master sets.
what: A tattoo. Geometric yantra, animals and deities, set about with phrases in Pali, Khmer or Northern Thai, pricked into the skin with a long needle — traditionally a metal rod sharpened to a point, the khem sak. The scripts are local: Khmer script in Cambodia, the Khmer-derived Khom script in central Thailand, Shan, Northern Thai or Tai Lu in the north, Lao Tham in Laos. The same designs go onto cloth and onto metal and are then hung in a house, a place of worship or a vehicle, so the tattoo is one surface among several.
story: The practice comes out of the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, built on indigenous mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing that runs back as far as 2,500 BCE, with the yantra designs themselves drawn from India. Tattoos held to give protection are recorded across mainland Southeast Asia and as far south as Indonesia and the Philippines; Chinese records show tattooing common in the first millennium CE among peoples as far north as the Yangzi. The yantra designs began as meditation diagrams and were taken into the body during the Khmer Empire, then spread through Cambodia, Thailand and Laos under rules meant to keep them working.

The rules are the bearer's half of the bargain. A yant confers what it confers only while the person carrying it observes certain taboos — abstaining from a named food is the example the source gives. Break them and the tattoo stops.

Three kinds of effect are named. One works on the bearer, making them more eloquent. One protects, turning away evil and hardship, and is the one taken by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and people in trades they consider dangerous. One works on everybody else, invoking fear.

The tattooists are monks, Brahmin priests, ruesi and lay wicha practitioners. Wat Bang Phra in Nakhon Chaisi district, Nakhon Pathom, about 50 km west of Bangkok, is the temple most associated with the practice; its Wai Khru is held on the grounds once a year in March, honouring a former abbot, and the tattoos of those who come are renewed. The abbot in question is Phra Udom Prachanart, known as Luang Phor Pern, who ordained at Wat Bang Phra at 25 and died in 2002 at 79.

Then there is the argument about foreigners, which has named people on both sides. Angelina Jolie was tattooed by Ajahn Noo Ganpai in Old Khmer script, and took a Bengal tiger yant in 2004 to mark acquiring Cambodian citizenship; the source credits that with making sak yant popular among women abroad. In 2011 Thailand's Culture Ministry moved against the trade in sacred images on foreign skin. Culture Minister Niphit Intharasombat said his ministry had complaints from residents that parlours were inking Buddha images on non-Buddhist visitors, called on parlours nationwide to stop, asked provincial governors to inspect studios, and pushed for a law: "Foreigners see these tattoos as a fashion. They do not think of respecting religion, or they may not be aware" that it can be offensive. Ladda Thangsupachai, director of the ministry's Cultural Surveillance Center, noted that tattooing religious images was "not yet illegal under Thai law". The Thai journalist Saksith Saiyasombut, writing at Siam Voices on 31 May 2011, put the case the other way: he read the move as the ministry once again defining Thai-ness on everyone's behalf, questioned what he called a monopoly claim over Buddhism, and pointed out that the Vatican does not police tattoos of Jesus. This atlas reports both and joins neither.
how: Hand-poked with a khem sak, a metal rod sharpened to a point, by a monk, a Brahmin priest, a ruesi or a lay master. The design carries the master's lineage, and the words said over it belong to that lineage. The bearer accepts rules and taboos as part of receiving it, and the tattoo's power is described as holding only while they are kept. At Wat Bang Phra's Wai Khru in March, bearers return to pay respects and have their yant renewed.
today: Practised in Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and parts of Burma as of 2026, and sold to visitors in Bangkok and Chiang Mai. The 2011 ministry move did not become law in anything this project has read; Ladda Thangsupachai's sentence — that the practice was not yet illegal — is the last legal statement in this record's sources.
kin: takrut — the same yant in the same scripts, rolled into metal foil instead of pricked into skin
kin: phra-khrueang — the pressed Buddha tablet that does the same work and can be taken off; this one cannot
kin: thai-wicha — the craft that holds the designs, the lineages and the rules for the bearer
kin: tattooing — the practice itself — hand-poked with a sharpened rod, under a master's hand
kin: yantra-plate — the same geometry on a flat sheet, which is where the designs started before they went into skin
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the other tattooed charm in this atlas, marked on the body and not removable either
kin: yant-flash — the sheet of designs a master works from, and the thing a visitor now picks off
kin: skin — the material this one is made of, which is what makes the argument about who may receive it sharp
kin: the-drawn-signs — the gallery of drawn geometries this one belongs in, before any of them reach a body
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the 2011 ministry move belongs in, with both sides named
sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-yantra s:wp-tattoo s:web-wp-wat-bang-phra s:web-ap-buddha-tattoo-ban s:web-saiyasombut-religious-tattoos s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet

## Scarab (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/scarab/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/scarab.json
id: scarab
native: 𓆣 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: scarab seal · scarabaeus · dung-beetle amulet · royal-name scarab
said: SKARR-ab, from Latin scarabaeus, a beetle
when: 2000 BCE – 30 BCE
countries: EG IL PS SY LB TN IT ES TR
root: Latin scarabaeus 'beetle' — the museum's word, not Egypt's. The beetle the shape copies is usually identified as Scarabaeus sacer, and the god it stands for is Khepri.
object: form=pendant materials=faience,carnelian,gold,glass,agate worn=neck,finger,chest,grave
against: the-dead — said by Egyptian funerary practice, as summarised by Egyptologists [s:wp-scarab-artifact]
against: bad-luck — said by the later use of the hieroglyphs Men Kheper Re, which the source says 'seem to have become regarded as a protective charm in themselves' [s:wp-scarab-artifact]
what: A beetle, carved or moulded, with a flat underside cut as a seal. The back shows the head, the wing case and the legs; the base carries hieroglyphs — a king's name, an official's title, a short prayer, a hunting scene. Most are drilled end to end so they can be strung on a thread or swung in a ring. Common length runs 6 mm to 40 mm, and most fall between 10 mm and 20 mm. Carved from steatite, a soft stone that hardens when fired, or moulded in faience, a quartz paste glazed blue or green in the kiln; the costly ones are green jasper, amethyst or carnelian.
story: The scarab is the one Egyptian amulet that is also a signature. From the end of the First Intermediate Period, about 2055 BCE, it becomes extremely common, and it pushes aside the cylinder seal and the button seal with its geometric designs. In the Middle Kingdom, officials have their names and titles cut on the base and press them into clay: the same object that guards its wearer also signs his letters.

By the early Middle Kingdom, about 2000 BCE, the beetle shape is enormously popular, and it stays popular through the rest of the pharaonic period. Neighbours take it up. From the middle Bronze Age, other peoples of the Mediterranean and the Near East import Egyptian scarabs and cut their own in Egyptian or in local styles, most of all in the Levant. Canaanite engravers add cross-hatching, native animals and the palm branch. Phoenician engravers pick the shape up in the Achaemenid period, from the later sixth century BCE into the mid-fourth, and Tharros on Sardinia becomes a production centre; Greek and Phoenician merchants carry them to the Etruscans in the fifth century BCE, and the Etruscan scarab runs at Vulci and Tarquinia from the last decades of the sixth century BCE.

Dating one is harder than it looks. A scarab bearing a pharaoh's name is usually of his reign — but not always. Scarabs carrying Old Kingdom names like Khufu, Khafre and Unas were most probably made much later, in the Twenty-fifth or Twenty-sixth Dynasty, when the old kings were being imitated. The throne name of Thutmose III, Men Kheper Re, turns up in vast numbers, many of them centuries after him: the hieroglyphs themselves came to be treated as protective, and the carver may not have understood what he was reproducing. *Inference —* an amulet whose whole point is a name is the amulet most likely to be copied, which is why the scarab is both the best dating tool Egyptology has and one of its worst traps.

One scarab fixes a shipwreck. A golden scarab inscribed with the name of Queen Nefertiti was lifted from the Uluburun wreck off Turkey, among the luxury cargo, and its inscription gives a frame for when the ship went down.
how: Carved from steatite and fired hard, or moulded in faience and glazed blue or green. The base is cut with the inscription, the back drilled lengthways, and the thing strung on thread, hung from a necklace or mounted on a swivel ring. Ring mounts change over time: threads tied to the finger in the Old Kingdom, bezels in the Middle Kingdom, cast scarabs on gold wire in the New Kingdom. Most glazes have worn off, so a steatite scarab that reads white or brown in a museum tray was green or blue when it was made.

Three classes go with the dead rather than the living: heart scarabs, pectoral scarabs sewn onto the chest with a separate pair of outstretched wings from the Twenty-fifth Dynasty on, and naturalistic scarabs, 2 to 3 cm long, carved in the round with a suspension loop running crossways.
today: The shape outlived the practice. Scarabs are made now as jewellery and sold in Cairo, Luxor and the airport shops, and cut stone and faience versions turn up in every dealer's tray. Forgery is old: the Twenty-fifth Dynasty was already making scarabs with fourth-dynasty names on them, so a 'later copy' is a category inside the ancient material, not only a modern problem. As of 2026 no source read for this record puts a figure on how much of the market is modern.
kin: heart-scarab — the funerary member of this family — same beetle, but sized to the chest, inscribed with a spell and told to keep quiet at the weighing
kin: scarab-sign — the sign this object is a body for: the beetle that rolls the sun up at daybreak
kin: wedjat-eye — the other amulet Egypt made by the thousand; the eye went over the embalmer's incision, the scarab over the heart
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that cut it, and the one that turned an amulet into an office seal
kin: faience — the moulded material that made it cheap by the tray
kin: carnelian — the hardstone version, cut not moulded, and costlier
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that is why so many survive at all
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator whose sequence work made a scarab something you could date a layer with
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on how a charm gets a date — and this object is its hardest case, because a king's name on it need not be his century
kin: met-egyptian-galleries — a room where a tray of them can be read against each other

## Senninbari (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/senninbari/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/senninbari.json
id: senninbari
native: 千人針 (Japanese)
aliases: thousand-person stitches · one thousand stitch belt · senninbari haramaki · tasuki
said: sen-nin-BA-ri
when: 1894 CE – 1945 CE
countries: JP
root: Japanese sen 千 'thousand' + nin 人 'person' + hari/bari 針 'needle, stitch' — a thousand people's stitches
object: form=garment materials=cloth,thread,hair,coin worn=waist,head,chest,sewn-in,pocket
against: weapons — said by the general belief recorded of the belts — courage, good luck and immunity from injury, bullets especially [s:wp-senninbari]
against: war — said by the women who stitched it, in the slogan they worked into the cloth: bu-un chō-kyū, eternal good luck in war [s:wp-senninbari]
against: illness — said by wearers of the senninbari haramaki, the waist form, which was held to maintain good health as well as luck [s:wp-senninbari]
what: A strip of cloth, usually white, about 15 centimetres wide and 90 to 120 centimetres or more long, carrying a thousand stitches or knots — commonly red, because white and red together were held to be auspicious. Each stitch was put in by a different woman. The ends might have strings, snaps or buttons to fasten it round the waist; ends without them were tucked in. Longer ones, tasuki, were worn crossed over the chest, shoulders and back. Others were never worn at all, but folded into a helmet liner, a pocket or a pack.
story: The practice starts with the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95. The earliest senninbari were handkerchief-sized squares of cloth with a thousand knots or stitches worked into them to strengthen the material — and the implication carried was that the strength passed to the man who carried it.

The making was done in public, and by the women of one household first. A soldier's mother, sister or wife stood outside the local temple, or at the train station, or by a department store, and asked women passing to put in one stitch. At the height of the Second World War the demand outran that arrangement and women's organisations gathered to produce senninbari in bulk; the belts went into imonbukuro, comfort bags, and were shipped overseas.

The rules inside the thousand had exceptions. A woman born in the year of the Tiger could sew twelve stitches, or as many stitches as she had years. Some belts were lined with a woman's hair, or with several women's — a custom recorded as originating in folk belief on Okinawa. Coins were sewn in as well.

What the stitching said is on the cloth. The commonest slogan worked into a senninbari was bu-un chō-kyū 武運長久, eternal good luck in war. Tigers were stitched or painted on, because a tiger was known to travel a long way from home and come back.

What the men made of it varied, and the source is careful about this. The women who stitched them and the men who wore them held the belts to confer courage, luck, and immunity from injury, bullets above all. Some Japanese soldiers rejected the protection outright and held instead that the belt would let them do the most damage to the enemy before giving up their own lives. Others wore it as neither — a keepsake of the women who had made it. Three positions, in one army, about one object.
how: White cotton cut to a strip; a thousand French knots or stitches worked in red thread, set in rows, or laid out to make a flag, a slogan or a tiger. Yellow, red and green cloth were used too, with yellow, gold, red or white thread. Variants were made as hachimaki headbands, vests and caps; the rarest were good-luck flags. The belt made for the waist, the senninbari haramaki, was held to keep the wearer in health as well as in luck. Fastened at the waist under the uniform, or folded into the kit. No priest, no shrine, no consecration: the charging is the thousand hands.
today: Not a living practice in this project's sources, which carry it no further than the Second World War. Surviving belts are in private hands, in militaria collections and in museums; Michael A. Bortner's Imperial Japanese Good Luck Flags and One-Thousand Stitch Belts (Schiffer, 2008) is the collectors' reference, and Kazuhiro Watanabe's study at the Graduate University for Advanced Studies treats the bullet-protection belief as folklore of the war years. Whether a belt made by a thousand women for a conscript should now be traded as militaria is an argument this atlas reports and does not settle.
kin: omamori — the shrine's version of the same errand, bought over a counter; this one was assembled from a thousand strangers on a street
kin: thread — the whole material argument: a thousand stitches were said to strengthen the cloth, and the strength to pass to the man in it
kin: hair — what some belts were lined with — one woman's, or several — a custom recorded as coming from Okinawa
kin: knotting — the act that makes it: one knot, one woman, a thousand times
kin: sewing-in — the other half of the act, and how the belt was fastened or folded into a pack and a helmet liner
kin: talismanic-shirt — the Islamic garment written over against blades and shot — the same idea worn, in ink rather than thread
kin: challenge-coin — the other soldier's token in this atlas: issued by a unit rather than made by civilians, and kept rather than worn
kin: japanese-engimono — the Japanese luck-object tradition this stands outside — no shrine issued it and no priest charged it
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this belongs in: a belt made by a thousand named-nobody women, now bought and sold as militaria
sources: s:wp-senninbari s:wp-omamori

## St Christopher medal (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/st-christopher-medal/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/st-christopher-medal.json
id: st-christopher-medal
native: Ἅγιος Χριστόφορος (Greek)
aliases: Saint Christopher medal · travellers' medal · San Cristóbal medal · Christophorus medal
said: in French, médaille de Saint Christophe; in Spanish, medalla de San Cristóbal
when: 452 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR ES IT HR GR US
root: Greek Χριστόφορος, from Χριστός 'Christ' and φέρειν 'to bear' — Christ-bearer
object: form=medal materials=silver,brass,gold,copper worn=neck,chest,wrist,pocket,wallet,vehicle
against: traffic — said by the Spanish medals and holy cards themselves [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: travel — said by the French medals themselves [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: drowning — said by the Roman Catholic patronage list, which names mariners, boatmen, ferrymen, floods and storms [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: fever — said by the Roman Catholic Church, which counts Christopher among the Fourteen Holy Helpers and names lightning and pestilence in his patronage [s:wp-saint-christopher]
what: A stamped metal disc, 15 to 30 mm across, showing a bearded giant wading a river with a staff in one hand and a child on his shoulder. Aluminium, tin, brass, silver and gold all get struck. It hangs at the neck on a chain, clips to a bracelet, rides in a pocket, or goes in a car. Most carry a sentence around the rim; the French and the Spanish sentences are not the same sentence.
story: Read the medal and you have the story. In the thirteenth-century Golden Legend, Christopher — a giant of twelve cubits, by that account — goes looking for the greatest master in the world, ends up serving Christ, and is set to carrying travellers across a dangerous river. A child asks to be carried. The water rises, the child grows heavier with every step, and on the far bank he says: "You had on your shoulders not only the whole world but Him who made it." From that, various Christian denominations made him patron of travellers, and the Roman Catholic Church counts him among the Fourteen Holy Helpers. The patronage list ran wide before cars existed: mariners, ferrymen, archers, bachelors, bookbinders, fruit dealers, fullers, gardeners, surfers, toothache, floods, storms, lightning, pestilence, a holy death.

What the medals promise depends on the language they are struck in. The French rim reads "Regarde St Christophe et va-t-en rassuré" — look at Saint Christopher and go on reassured. The Spanish medals and holy cards go further: "Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás" — if you trust in Saint Christopher, you will not die in an accident. This atlas prints both sentences as what the object says of itself, names the languages they are struck in, and stops.

Then there is the thing everybody thinks they know. In 1969 the Roman Catholic Church revised the General Roman Calendar; Christopher's celebration was left, in the revision's own phrasing, to particular calendars, because his feast had entered the Roman calendar relatively late and because the written Acts of him are, in the same document's words, "merely legendary" while the ancient veneration of the martyr is not in doubt. The English-language telling of that decision, from 1969 onward, was that the Church had abolished him — decanonised, demoted, declared never to have existed, patron saint of nothing. Catholic Answers answers it flatly: "St. Christopher was never 'de-canonized,' nor did the Church declare him a myth." Patrick Mott, writing in Orange County Catholic in 2015, calls it "not so much a demotion as a reassignment" and adds that "He has never ceased to be recognized as a saint by the Church." The Roman Martyrology still remembers him on 25 July; the Eastern Orthodox Church keeps him on 9 May and calls him Great Martyr. *Inference —* the medal outsold the correction by a wide margin, and the correction has now been in print for more than fifty years.

The official line runs through the object too, not around it. A medal blessed by a priest is a sacramental, which the Catholic Church defines as a sacred sign that works by the Church's prayer rather than by itself, and which "does not confer the grace of the Holy Spirit in the way that the sacraments do". An unblessed medal is a piece of jewellery. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy sets the boundary the other way round, holding that popular piety "may never incorporate rites permeated by magic, superstition, animism, vendettas or sexual connotations". *Inference —* the Church draws that line in writing precisely because the line gets crossed, and the Spanish rim sentence is a good example of a claim the object makes that the doctrine does not.
how: Struck by religious-goods manufacturers, sold at church shops, shrine stalls, jewellers, service stations and online. A priest may bless it, at which point the Church calls it a sacramental; nothing requires that, and nothing stops an unblessed one being worn. It is given more often than bought for oneself — to a traveller, a new driver, a child leaving home — and it is commonly passed on.
today: Still struck, still sold, still worn across Catholic Europe and the Americas in 2026, and still stocked beside the Miraculous Medal and the Brown Scapular in the same shops. Most buyers meet the 1969 story in one of its garbled forms first. No dated retail price was read for this record.
kin: car-saint — the same medal once the traveller got an engine — clipped to a visor instead of worn at the throat
kin: miraculous-medal — the other stamped medal on the same shop counter, and the one whose origin story has a date, a witness and a goldsmith
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the category the Church puts a blessed medal in, and the doctrine the Spanish rim sentence outruns
kin: brown-scapular — the cloth version of the same argument — a devotional object with a promise attached that its own order spends its time qualifying
kin: agnus-dei — the older Roman sacramental worn at the neck, in wax rather than struck metal
kin: ladanka — what an Orthodox neck carries instead, and the Orthodox version of the same line between devotion and charm
kin: holy-rider-pendant — the late-antique ancestor of a saint on a disc worn against danger
kin: omamori — the Japanese object sold for the same road, with kōtsū-anzen written on it instead of a Latin rim
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the act that turns this medal from jewellery into what the Church calls a sacramental — optional, and often skipped
kin: cross — the sign stamped on the reverse of most of them
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read this record is the hardest case for: the Church calls it a sacramental, the rim calls it insurance
sources: s:wp-saint-christopher s:wp-devotional-medal s:wp-sacramental s:web-catholic-answers-st-christopher s:web-occatholic-saint-who-aint s:wp-general-roman-calendar-1969 s:web-vatican-directory-popular-piety

## Sungkhor (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/sungkhor/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/sungkhor.json
id: sungkhor
native: སྲུང་འཁོར། (Tibetan)
aliases: srung 'khor · sungwa · srung ba · protection wheel · protective amulet
said: SUNG-kor
when: 2000 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN NP IN BT
object: form=packet materials=paper,ink,thread worn=neck,chest,pocket
against: travel — said by James Gentry, summarising Tibetan use [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
against: weapons — said by the same sentence, which names injury during battle [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
against: illness — said by the same sentence; the Wellcome Collection's Tibetan cosmological amulet is catalogued as a protection against diseases [s:web-wellcome-tibetan-amulet]
against: spirits — said by the same sentence, which names harmful spirits [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
RESTRICTED: The design drawn inside a sungkhor and the rite that consecrates it are a lama's work and are not published for outsiders. This atlas prints what a named scholar's published description of a catalogued example shows — that the amulet is a geometric diagram with mantra formulas and images, consecrated, folded and wrapped in five-coloured cords — and prints no diagram, no mantra and no consecration formula.
what: A diagram on paper, folded down to a small packet and bound in coloured thread. James Gentry's description for Project Himalayan Art is exact: protective amulets — sungwa, sungkhor — "are geometric diagrams drawn on paper with a combination of mantra formulas and images, and consecrated through contemplative ritual proceedings, before being folded up, wrapped in cords of five colors with sacred substances, and distributed for use." Folded, the drawing is gone; what a wearer sees is a thread lattice in five colours over a square or a lozenge.
story: The sungkhor is what the window of an amulet box usually shows. In the gau Gentry catalogues — made in Kathmandu in the first decade of the 2000s, its contents handselected and consecrated by Chokling Rinpoche — the item behind the window is an amulet diagram wrapped in five-coloured cords, with three dark brown pills, while the other contents sit concealed behind it. Gentry adds that amulets of this kind can be included among the contents of amulet boxes or worn separately.

What they are carried against is listed plainly: Tibetans have used them to protect against misfortune during travel, injury during battle, illness, harmful spirits, and any other potential calamity.

*Inference —* the folding is the design, not the packaging. A diagram meant to be read would not be bound shut in thread; a diagram meant to be carried and not read would be. That is as far as this record goes, because the drawing inside and the rite said over it belong to a body of practice that is not published for outsiders.
how: Drawn, consecrated, folded, wrapped, given. This atlas does not print the drawing, the mantras written into it, or the consecration, and does not assemble a version of them from scattered sources. What is published is that the consecration is a contemplative ritual proceeding and that a named lama performed it for the catalogued example; Tibetan Buddhism holds that without having gone through initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras, and the making of these amulets sits inside that body of practice.
today: Worn at the neck, kept in a wallet or a pocket, and carried inside a gau across the Tibetan Buddhist world as of 2026, with the diaspora market since 1959 putting them in shops from Kathmandu to Europe and North America. A wrapped amulet sold over a counter carries no record of who consecrated it, which is the same problem the dzi market has, in paper and thread instead of stone.

kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that draws it, consecrates it and gives it out
kin: folding — the step that turns a readable diagram into a carried object
kin: knotting — the five-coloured cords that bind it shut, which are part of the amulet and not its wrapping
kin: yantra-plate — the South Asian relative it descends from in form — a deity diagram with mantras written in, except that this one is closed up instead of hung open
kin: takrut — Southeast Asia's version of the same move: an inscribed sheet rolled tight and bound, worn without being read
kin: lungta-flag — the printed sibling that is left open to the wind rather than folded onto a body
