## Ta'wiz (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/taweez/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/taweez.json
id: taweez
native: تعویذ (Arabic)
aliases: taweez · tawiz · taʿwīdh · hafiz · himala
said: ta-WEEZ; Arabic taʿwīdh, Urdu and Hindi ta'wiz, Hindi तावीज़
when: 901 CE to now (still carried)
countries: PK IN BD EG TR AF AL IR MA
root: Arabic taʿwīdh, 'amulet' or 'charm', from the verb ʿawwadha, 'to fortify someone with an amulet or incantation'; Urdu and Hindi take the word from the Arabic
object: form=packet materials=paper,ink,lead,silver,leather,cloth worn=neck,upper-arm,sewn-in,pocket,wall
against: evil-eye — said by the cited account of Islamic amulets, which names warding off the evil eye as one of their main functions [s:wp-amulet]
against: demons — said by the same account, which names the jinn; Islamic talismans invoke God, angels or prophets, and addressing jinn or demons is prohibited [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: war — said by Ottoman soldiers, who carried scrolls with Qur'anic quotations in combat, among them 'victory is from God and conquest is near' (Qur. 61:13) [s:wp-amulet]
against: child-harm — said by households in Central and West Asia, who attached triangular packets containing a sacred verse to the clothing of babies and young children [s:wp-amulet]
against: illness — said by the cited account, which says these objects were meant to promote health, longevity, fertility and potency as well as to ward off misfortune [s:wp-amulet]
what: Writing, folded up and worn. A ta'wiz can be a paper packet in a black pouch, a scroll in a tubular pendant case, letters carved into metal, or a framed dua on a wall. The text is Qur'anic verses, names of God, names of prophets and companions, hadith, religious narratives, or duas. In Central and West Asia the packet is often triangular and pinned to a baby's clothes.
story: The trade in these has a documented shape. Texts packaged in ta'wiz were most often pre-made for the public; a literate wearer could change the verse at his own discretion. Scrolls with Qur'anic quotations, prophetic references and sacred symbols were common in war in the Ottoman Empire, carrying verses such as 'victory is from God and conquest is near', Qur'an 61:13, worn in combat.

One of the oldest surviving examples is a printed object, not a written one. Diminutive amulets made in the medieval Mediterranean Islamic world were executed with a block print or die, called tarsh, and folded down small enough for a tiny box or tubular case. The Aga Khan Museum in Toronto holds an Egyptian block-printed amulet of the tenth or eleventh century, ink on paper, 7.2 by 5.5 centimetres; the last line of its text is Qur'an 20:46, "So God will safeguard you from them. He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing". Such text amulets were housed in lead cases stamped with surat al-Ikhlas, with lugs so the packet could be sewn to clothing or hung from the body. The cases were kept sealed, so the printed contents were invisible to an owner who could not afford a handwritten one.

Whether a Muslim should wear one at all is disagreed about, by name, and this atlas reports both sides without joining either. Some hadith condemn the wearing of talismans, and some Muslims, notably Salafis, hold that amulets and talismans are forbidden and that using them is shirk — associating a partner with God. Other hadith support their use, and some denominations count it permissible magic, usually on conditions: that the wearer holds the talisman to help only through God's will. The formulation reported for Sunni practice is that a ta'wiz may be worn as long as it consciously strengthens the wearer's bond with Allah, and not out of a belief that the ta'wiz itself cures or protects. Set against that, virtually all Muslim scholars are described as permitting talismans that invoke God or an intercessor — Muhammad, Ali, the saints — while addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab treated sorcery as one of the few sins carrying a divinely sanctioned death penalty; Muhammad Nasiruddin al-Albani held that those convinced sorcery has effect of its own accord, rather than by God's decision and will, will not enter paradise; the Wahhabi preacher Bilal Philips has tried to draw the line by way of a hadith in which a sura with supernatural properties was recited but not written down and used as a charm.

The numbers are surveyed. A Pew Research Center survey of Muslims worldwide in 2011–2012 found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers ranging from about a quarter to a half of Muslims in the Middle East and North Africa, Turkey, South Asia and Southeast Asia — less widespread than belief in jinn. Ta'wiz use is reported at 41 per cent of Muslims in Pakistan and 39 per cent in Albania.

*Tradition holds —* a ta'wiz worn by Hindus often carries the sacred Om symbol instead, which is the plainest evidence in the atlas that the container and the writing can come apart.

kin: quran-pendant — the same scripture in a metal case rather than a folded packet
kin: talismanic-shirt — the same writing scaled up until it is a garment
kin: hirz-pouch — the North African and Nile version of the same container
kin: tabiz — the South Asian object under the same word, carried by Muslims and by Hindus with an Om on it instead
kin: taweez-word — the word, from a verb meaning to fortify somebody with an amulet
kin: kamea — the Jewish parallel, argued over inside its own tradition on almost the same terms
kin: paper — the material, and the reason the cheap ones were printed and sealed unread
kin: folding — the practice that makes a page into a thing you can wear
kin: magic-square — the other thing written inside these — the wafq, whose 3×3 form the tradition tied to the four archangels
kin: khan-el-khalili — one of the markets that sells them by the tray

## Tabiz (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tabiz/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tabiz.json
id: tabiz
native: تعویز (Arabic)
aliases: taweez · ta'wiz · taʿwīdh · तावीज़
said: ta-WEEZ
when: 900 CE to now (still carried)
countries: PK IN AF
root: Arabic taʿwīdh 'amulet, charm', from the verb ʿawwadha, 'to fortify someone with an amulet or incantation'; into Urdu and Hindi as ta'wiz
object: form=packet materials=paper,ink,silver,lead,thread worn=neck,upper-arm,sewn-in,wall
against: evil-eye — said by wearers in North India and Pakistan, where threads with a taveez attached are among the objects used against nazar [s:wp-nazar-battu]
against: demons — said by Muslim users, as summarised in scholarship on Islamic talismanic practice [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: child-harm — said by parents in Central and West Asia, who fasten triangular packets holding a sacred verse to the clothes of babies and small children [s:wp-amulet]
against: illness — said by Islamic amulet practice generally, which the same account says was meant to promote health, longevity, fertility and potency [s:wp-amulet]
what: A written prayer, folded small and shut inside something. In South Asia the container is usually a flat or tubular metal case on a black cord at the neck or tied to the upper arm; the paper inside carries Qur'anic verse, a hadith, one of the ninety-nine names of God, or the names of prophets and their companions. A tabiz may also be a pendant with the text carved straight into metal, or a framed du'a on a wall. Cases are meant to stay shut, so most wearers have never seen the page they carry.
story: The writing is the object. In Muslim practice the texts chosen for amulets are prayers, passages from the Qur'an, hadith, religious narratives and religious names; the word Allah is especially common, and many hold that touching or seeing it turns evil away. Names of prophets and of religious figures are used to connect the wearer to the person named — Solomon, Ali ibn Abi Talib and his sons Hasan and Husain, and the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus are among the favoured.

The oldest dated thing of this kind read for this record is not South Asian. In the medieval Mediterranean Islamic world, prayers were printed from a block or die — tarsh — onto paper, then folded down small enough for a tubular case. The Aga Khan Museum in Toronto holds an Egyptian block-printed amulet of the tenth or eleventh century, ink on paper at 7.2 by 5.5 cm, whose last line is Qur'an 20:46: 'So God will safeguard you from them. He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing.' Such text amulets were housed in lead cases stamped with surat al-Ikhlas, with lugs so the package could be sewn to clothing or hung from the body. The cases were most likely kept sealed, which means the contents were invisible to an owner who could not afford a hand-written one.

In South Asia the tabiz crosses the line the word implies. Amulets in North India and Pakistan include threads with a taveez attached — a small cylinder holding a prayer verse — worn against nazar, the harmful look. A tabiz worn by Hindus often bears the Om sign instead.

Whether a Muslim should wear one at all is argued in the tradition, not about it. Some hadith condemn wearing talismans, and some Muslims, notably Salafis, hold that amulets and talismans are forbidden. On the other side, virtually all Muslim scholars permit a talisman that invokes God or an intercessor — Muhammad, Ali, the saints — while addressing jinn or demons is prohibited; and Sunni Muslims are permitted to wear ta'wiz so long as it strengthens the wearer's bond with Allah and does not come from a belief that the ta'wiz itself cures or protects.
how: Written by hand, or pre-made. Texts packaged in tawiz are most often pre-made for the public, though a literate wearer can change the verse at will. The paper is folded, sometimes to a triangle, and closed in metal; in Central and West Asia triangular packets holding a sacred verse are fastened to the clothes of babies and small children. The same triangle is woven into kilims, where, as the carpet scholar Jon Thompson puts it, the amulet in a rug is not a theme: "the device in the rug has a materiality, it generates a field of force able to interact with other unseen forces and is not merely an intellectual abstraction."
today: Worn and sold across Pakistan, India and Afghanistan as of 2026. In Afghanistan fortunetellers work from small shops or outside mosques and shrines and sell amulets against evil spirits alongside marriage advice, and their clients are mostly women and the elderly; the same trade is widespread in Iran and Pakistan.
kin: taweez — the same object under its Arabic name, written up from the Arabic-speaking side of the practice
kin: taweez-word — the word itself, and the verb it comes from — to fortify someone with an amulet
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition that sets what may be written on it and who may be addressed by it
kin: quran-pendant — the same text worn without a fold — the verse legible on the surface rather than sealed in a case
kin: nimbu-mirchi — what hangs in the doorway of the same street against the same look, made of a lemon rather than a verse
kin: nazar — the glass answer to the harm this paper answers in words
kin: sewing-in — the practice the lugs on a lead case were for — the amulet stitched to clothing rather than hung
kin: gau-box — the Himalayan neighbour: another sealed metal container whose contents the wearer is not expected to open
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition next door that borrowed the object and changed the writing to Om
kin: paper — the material that made a prayer portable, and printable from a block long before Europe printed
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-nazar-battu s:wp-throne-verse s:wp-talisman
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Takrut (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/takrut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/takrut.json
id: takrut
native: ตะกรุด (Thai)
aliases: tangkai · rolled yant scroll
said: tà-krùt
when: 1200 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TH
root: Thai ตะกรุด; the word is the same in singular and plural, and takes no -s
object: form=scroll materials=silver,gold,copper,lead,palm-leaf,ink,thread worn=waist,neck,chest,pocket
against: weapons — said by Thai wearers, in the category Kong Grapan — invincibility; the source says takrut are blessed mainly for safe keeping [s:wp-takrut]
against: war — said by Thai practice in a period of constant warfare, when takrut were blessed for people going to war [s:wp-takrut]
against: travel — said by Thai wearers, blessed for safety in daily work and on business trips [s:wp-takrut]
against: attraction — said by Thai wearers, in the categories Maha Sanaeh (attraction), Metta Mahaniyom (popularity and business success) and Maha Pokasap (drawing riches) [s:wp-takrut]
against: poverty — said by Thai wearers, in the category Maha Lap — the drawing of wealth [s:wp-takrut]
RESTRICTED: Which yant goes on a takrut, and the incantation said over it, belong to the maker's school and lineage. This atlas prints what the sources publish about the object and does not print a consecration formula.
what: A tube. A thin sheet of metal or a strip of palm leaf is inscribed with yant — sacred geometry and Pali phrases — then rolled tight into an elongated scroll and bound with cord, or sealed in a case. Nothing on the outside shows what is inside. It is tied to the body on a cord at the waist, hung at the chest on a chain, or worn like any other piece of jewellery. Some are small enough to hold between the teeth.
story: The takrut is the amulet Thai literature reaches for first. It is the form mentioned more often than any other in Khun Chang Khun Phaen, the Thai epic, and the source this record follows puts it in Thai culture before Buddhism arrived, with the monk-made takrut becoming the earliest form of Buddhist amulet around 1200 to 1300 CE. That last claim carries no citation in the source, so it is dated here with a flag rather than a full stop.

What goes on the sheet is yant — yantra — incantations and geometric designs carrying Pali gatha and Buddhist invocations. The script is usually Khom Pali, the variant of Khmer script used in Thailand; in the north, Lan Na Tai Tham. The same writing appears on cloth, on metal plates and in skin, so a takrut is one surface among several for a single body of design.

The demand was practical. In older Thailand, with constant warfare and poor security, takrut were blessed mainly for safe keeping — invulnerability — and issued to people going to work, to travel on business, or to war.

The positions carry meanings. A takrut is worn about a part of the body to protect that part, or to grant it power. The one held between the teeth is for speech: the power is called sariga, after the golden-tongued celestial magpie of Vedic and Thai Buddhist legend, and it makes the carrier a stronger speaker.
how: Inscribe the yant on metal foil — or on palm leaf — roll it into a tube, bind it with cord, case it. Which yant, and what is said over it, belongs to the maker's lineage. Thai amulet rules place the takrut outside the Buddha-image restrictions: because it carries no monk and no Buddha image, it may be put in a trouser pocket, where an amulet bearing the Buddha may not go below the waist at all. Worn at the waist or at the chest, the purpose is the same either way — protection of the person carrying it.
today: Still made, still sold, still worn, and sold from the same trays as the pressed Buddha tablets at Tha Phrachan in Bangkok, as of the accounts this project has read. Online dealers list them by monk, by temple and by year in the same way collectors grade a phra khrueang.
kin: phra-khrueang — the pressed tablet it hangs beside, and the rule that separates them: no Buddha image here, so this one may go in a pocket
kin: sak-yant — the same yant, same script, same lineages — put into skin instead of rolled into foil
kin: yantra-plate — the South Asian version of the design on metal, flat rather than rolled
kin: taweez — the Islamic rolled written charm in a case — the same solution reached along a different road
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the other great rolled text in this atlas: written protection kept in a tube and carried on the body
kin: thai-wicha — the craft that makes it, in which the yant and the incantation are a lineage's property
kin: inscribing — the act that charges it: the writing, not the metal, is the amulet
kin: wearing-hidden — how it works — a sealed tube whose contents nobody sees, tied under the clothes
kin: tha-phrachan — the Bangkok market that sells it from the same tray as the clay tablets
kin: yant-flash — the sheet of designs the yant on this tube is drawn from
sources: s:wp-takrut s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-yantra s:wp-palad-khik

## Talismanic shirt (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/talismanic-shirt/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/talismanic-shirt.json
id: talismanic-shirt
native: پیراهن طلسمات (Arabic)
aliases: talisman shirt · tılsımlı gömlek · pirâhan telesmat · talismanic tunic
said: pirâhan telesmat (Persian); tılsımlı gömlek (Turkish)
when: 1375 CE – 1899 CE
countries: TR IR IN RU
object: form=garment materials=cloth,ink worn=chest
against: weapons — said by Hürrem Sultan, who gave Suleiman the Magnificent a talismanic shirt and told him its inscriptions would protect him from bullets [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: war — said by the cited account, which finds that although the shirts could be worn against many evils, most seem intended as a shield in battle [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: illness — said by Surah Yusuf, in which the prophet Joseph's shirt cures his father's blindness [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: bad-luck — said by the inscribed names themselves, which the tradition holds capable of offering protection and guidance to the carrier [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
what: A shirt covered in writing. Verses from the Qur'an, the names of God, the names of prophets, or numbers, laid across the cloth in blocks and grids and roundels, sometimes with astrological images or magic squares among them. Four types are distinguished by style and by which symbols they use: Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and West African.
story: The shirt has a scriptural warrant, and it is a specific one. In Surah Yusuf, Joseph's shirt protects him and works miracles; he sends it to cure his father's blindness. "Go with this my shirt, and cast it over the face of my father: he will come to see" — Qur'an 12:93. A shirt that heals by being put on a body is the model, and the shirts follow it.

Most of them, though, are for battle. The Ottoman ruler Suleiman the Magnificent was given one by his wife Hürrem Sultan, who told him its inscriptions would protect him from bullets. His shirt is in the Topkapı Palace Museum, along with one made for Sultan Cem in 1480, while Cem was still a şehzade — unusual in that the beginning and the end of its manufacture are both inscribed on it, which makes it one of the few objects in this atlas that dates itself.

The earliest surviving shirts were made in or near the fifteenth century; one in the Turkish and Islamic Arts Museum in Istanbul is dated to the end of the fourteenth or the beginning of the fifteenth. The cited account adds that the tradition might be much older, and does not say how much. Two of the Khalili Collection's four shirts, from seventeenth-century Turkey and sixteenth- or seventeenth-century Mughal India, are covered with the holy sites of Mecca and Medina alongside prayers and Qur'anic extracts; the Turkish one is unusual for depicting the sites realistically rather than schematically. The latest named example belonged to Jembulat Boletoqo, Chemguy Grand Prince of Circassia from 1827 to 1836, and is displayed at the National Museum of the Republic of Adygea.

*Inference —* every other written charm in this batch is small enough to hide. This one is a garment, which means it is either worn under armour where nobody sees it or worn where everybody does. The atlas has read no account of which, and says so.
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition, in its most expensive and most royal form
kin: taweez — the same writing folded into a packet instead of spread across a body
kin: quran-pendant — the same verses in a case at the throat
kin: magic-square — the wafq that appears among the inscriptions, and the reason numbers sit beside scripture on these shirts
kin: senninbari — Japan's thousand-stitch belt: another textile a soldier wore into battle, made by somebody else's hands for him
kin: tefillin — scripture bound to the body under a law that refuses to call it an amulet — the contrast this record is sharpest against
kin: cloth — the material, and the one that turns a text into a thing you can put on
kin: divine-name — the sign doing the work: the names of God, of prophets, and of the angels
kin: sak-yant — the Southeast Asian answer to the same problem — script worn against blades, cut into skin instead of onto cotton
sources: s:wp-talismanic-shirt s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-amulet s:wp-magic-square

## Tama (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tama-votive/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tama-votive.json
id: tama-votive
native: τάμα (Greek)
aliases: tamata · τάματα · Greek votive plaque · Orthodox votive
said: TAH-ma, plural tamata
when: undated (still carried)
countries: GR IT
root: Greek τάμα, plural τάματα — the vow itself, used for the metal thing that carries it
object: form=plaque materials=silver,gold,copper worn=wall
against: illness — said by petitioners, who choose the shape to match the affliction [s:wp-tama-votive]
against: loneliness — said by petitioners again, for the heart that means love rather than a heart condition — the cited source gives the two readings of the same shape side by side [s:wp-tama-votive]
what: A small metal plaque, base metal or precious, with an image embossed on it: a heart, an eye, a hand, a leg, a whole kneeling figure, a house, a baby, a ship. A ribbon runs through it. It gets hung on a pole or a hook beside the icon of a saint, and it is left there.
story: Go and stand in front of a much-visited Greek icon and you will not see the icon. You will see silver.

A tama is offered either as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered — the cited account puts both uses on the same object and does not separate them, and the offering is usually made with a prayer and sometimes with a votive candle lit beside it. The shape aims it. A heart may mean a heart condition or it may mean love. Eyes mean an eye affliction. Hands or legs mean maladies of the limbs.

The Spanish-speaking world's milagro is the same object and the atlas says so on that record. Here is what a reader standing on this page gets that the milagro page cannot give: the tama has a named origin story with a hand in it. John of Damascus, serving as vizier to the caliph al-Walid I, was falsely accused of treachery and had his hand cut off. Praying before an icon of the Theotokos, he found the hand restored. In thanks he had a silver replica of it made and fixed it to the icon. That icon, called Trojeručica — the Three-handed — is preserved at Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos, and it is the reason the story is not just a story: the object it describes is still on the wall.

*Inference —* the difference between the two traditions is where the metal goes, not what it means. A milagro hangs on a robe or a retablo in a Catholic church and also, sometimes, gets carried in a pocket for luck. A tama goes onto the icon, and the icon is not a picture of a saint in Orthodox practice but the place the saint is met. The plaque is therefore pinned to a person, in the tradition's own terms, rather than to a painting of one.

Tamata are not the only thing left. Orthodox Christians also offer candles, prosphora — the bread baked for the liturgy — wine, oil and incense, and many leave something of their own worth instead: jewellery, a pectoral cross, a military decoration. *Inference —* a medal a man was given for war, hung on an icon because a prayer was answered, is the most compressed object in this whole atlas.

They are bought in shops selling Greek Orthodox religious goods, and the practice runs beyond Greece: the cited account records tamata in Italy too, particularly in the south, where they stand next to the Catholic ex-voto trade rather than instead of it.
how: Stamped or cast, pierced, threaded with a ribbon, and hung on a pole or a hook by the icon — the hanging done by the petitioner, with a prayer, sometimes with a candle. Nothing consecrates the plaque before it is offered; the offering is the act. They accumulate. What a church does with a wall of them after some years is not described by the sources read here, and this record does not guess.
today: Still sold in Greek Orthodox religious-goods shops and still hung on icons in Greece and in southern Italy, and wherever the Greek diaspora has built a church. No dated price was read for this record.
kin: milagro — the same object in Spanish — the cited accounts on both sides call them equivalents, and this is the one that goes on an icon rather than on a robe
kin: ex-voto-wall — what a much-visited icon looks like after some hundreds of these have been hung on it
kin: ladanka — the other Orthodox object in this atlas — that one is worn on the body, this one is given away
kin: votive-wall — the wall this ends up on, and the form the offering takes when there are enough of them
kin: silver — the metal of the costly version, and the reason a wall of these is worth something
kin: eye — one of the shapes stamped on them, here meaning an eye that hurts rather than an eye that looks
kin: hand — the shape with the oldest story attached to it — John of Damascus had a silver one made for the hand he said was restored
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the act the object exists for, done by the petitioner and not by a priest
kin: monastiraki — one Athens market where the religious-goods shops selling these are within a few streets
sources: s:wp-tama-votive s:wp-votive-offering s:wp-ex-voto s:wp-milagro-votive

## Taweret amulet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/taweret-amulet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/taweret-amulet.json
id: taweret-amulet
aliases: Taurt · Ta-weret · Tawaret · Thoeris · hippopotamus goddess amulet
said: ta-WER-et, from Ancient Egyptian tꜣ-wrt, 'she who is great'; Greek Θουέρις, Thouéris
when: 3000 BCE – 390 CE
countries: EG SD GR LB SY
root: Egyptian tꜣ-wrt, 'she who is great' or simply 'great one' — a pacificatory address, the form of words used to calm a dangerous deity rather than to describe a kind one.
object: form=pendant materials=faience,bone,terracotta,gold worn=neck,cradle,grave,hearth
against: childbirth — said by Egyptian household practice — the source calls her the protective goddess of childbirth and fertility, with the epithet 'Lady of the Birth House' [s:wp-taweret]
against: child-harm — said by Egyptian mothers; the source says her amulets protected mothers and children from harm and that her powers were invoked particularly to protect children and their mothers [s:wp-taweret]
against: infertility — said by Egyptian household practice, which grouped her with the fertility goddesses [s:wp-taweret]
against: the-dead — said by Egyptologists, reading the hippopotami placed in tombs as the goddess facilitating rebirth after death as she aided earthly births [s:wp-taweret]
what: A hippopotamus standing upright on two legs, with a lion's limbs and paws, a Nile crocodile down her back and tail, human breasts and a pregnant belly. She usually holds the sa sign, the hieroglyph that means 'protection'. She comes as a pendant, as a face on furniture, chairs, stools and headrests, on children's feeding cups, and as a vessel whose spout is a nipple.
story: Egypt made two decisions about hippopotami and kept both. The male was chaos, hunted down by kings to show divine power. The female was the opposite, because she guards her young with everything she has — so the protective goddesses of the household are female hippopotami, and amulets in their likeness are among the oldest in the country. They start before 3000 BCE, in the Predynastic period, and the making and wearing of them runs the whole length of Egyptian history into the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, to about 390 CE.

Her amulet peaks in popularity at the very end. In the Ptolemaic and Roman centuries, when the temples were changing hands and the old state religion was thinning out, household amulets of Taweret and her fellow hippopotamus goddesses sold better than ever.

She worked at both ends of a life. In the Middle Kingdom her image is carved onto a class of curved implement made from hippopotamus ivory that Egyptologists call a wand or a knife; tomb paintings show these in the hands of nurses, and wear on the tips indicates they were used to draw protective patterns in the sand. Taweret is on almost all known wands. The other figures on them are the gods who escort the sun through the underworld at night. At the same time hippopotami decorated with marsh flora were being put in tombs, which Egyptologists read as the same goddess helping a dead person be reborn the way she helped a living one be delivered.

She survived Akhenaten. Objects bearing Taweret were found at Amarna, from a reign, about 1352–1336 BCE, when the worship of the traditional gods was proscribed in favour of the sun disc. *Inference —* what people keep when the state tells them to stop is a good measure of what an object is for, and a birth charm is not easy to give up.

She travelled by trade. Middle Kingdom contact with the Levant carried her into the religions there in the same maternal role. From the Levantine coast she reached Crete, where Minoan artists redrew her in their own style as the figure Aegean archaeologists call the Minoan Genius, and from Crete the image reached the mainland and appears in palace art at Mycenae. Nubia took her into its pantheon in the late Middle Kingdom, and she features in royal rituals at Kerma.

Do not confuse her with Ammit. Ammit is also a composite hippopotamus and she is there to eat the unjust at the weighing; Taweret and her kin nourish and help.
how: Moulded or carved as a pendant, cut into furniture, moulded onto feeding cups, and poured from: New Kingdom vessels in her shape are taken to have purified the liquid poured out of them, since one of her epithets is 'She of the Pure Water', and some have their openings through the nipples. The hippopotamus-ivory wands were drawn with, in sand, by the nurse.
today: Not made as a birth charm. She is a museum object, a name in Egyptology, and a character in a television series. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anybody in Egypt using a Taweret at a birth.
kin: bes-amulet — the god who works the same birth with her; the sources put the two of them in the room together
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that made her, and the oldest amulet shape in it
kin: lamashtu-plaque — Mesopotamia's answer to the same fear — but there the danger to mother and baby is the figure on the plaque, and here she is the guard
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read she heads: the largest class of amulet in the world is the one hung on somebody who cannot ask for it
kin: bone-ivory — the material of the Middle Kingdom wands her face is cut into
kin: faience — the material that made her cheap enough to hang over a cradle
kin: grave-deposit — the other end of her work — hippopotami with marsh flora put in tombs for a second birth
kin: met-egyptian-galleries — a room where her amulets and the wands sit within sight of each other
kin: tabiz — a later charm for the same fear, made of a written verse in a case rather than a goddess in faience
sources: s:wp-taweret s:wp-bes s:wp-lamashtu s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-british-museum s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Tefillin (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tefillin/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tefillin.json
id: tefillin
native: תְּפִלִּין (Hebrew)
aliases: phylacteries · shel yad · shel rosh
said: tfi-LIN; singular tefillah
when: 1 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL US
root: Mishnaic Hebrew plural of tefillah; Jastrow connects it to Syriac tefiltha, 'attachments' or 'hangings'. In the Hebrew Bible the objects are totafot, 'headband' or 'frontlet', from a reduplicated root ṭ-p-ṭ-p meaning 'to encircle'
object: form=box materials=leather,parchment,ink worn=head,upper-arm,finger
against: demons — said by Numbers Rabbah 12:3, which has tefillin defeating a thousand demons emerging on the left side, and the rabbis Yohanan and Nahman, who used their sets against the demons of privies [s:wp-tefillin]
against: illness — said by the early rabbinic tradition, in which tefillin are credited with life-lengthening qualities [s:wp-tefillin]
against: war — said by the story of Elisha the Winged, scrupulous in this mitzvah and saved from Roman persecution [s:wp-tefillin]
what: Two small black leather boxes with long black straps. The arm box goes on the upper non-dominant arm and its strap winds down the forearm, round the hand and round the middle finger; the head box sits between the eyes at the hairline. Each box is made from a single piece of hide, cubical, on a wider base, with a passage at the back for the strap. On both sides of the head box the letter shin is moulded — with four branches on the wearer's left instead of three. The head strap's knot forms a dalet, the arm strap's a yud; with the shin those three letters spell Shaddai. Inside are parchment scrolls with four Torah passages: Exodus 13:1–10, Exodus 13:11–16, Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and Deuteronomy 11:13–21. Three thousand one hundred and eighty-eight letters, and a scribe can take as long as fifteen hours to write a set.
story: Like the mezuzah, tefillin are a commandment and not an amulet, and the tradition guards that distinction itself. The cited account puts it exactly: tefillin are sometimes mentioned together with amulets in the Talmud because of certain similarities of form, but they are never identified as such — they are specifically differentiated from them. Maimonides counts the arm box and the head box as two separate positive commandments. His account of what they do is about the wearer's mind: as long as they are on the head and the arm of a man, "he is modest and God-fearing and will not be attracted by hilarity or idle talk". The Sefer ha-Chinuch, in the 14th century, adds that they help subjugate worldly desire. Joseph Caro, in the 16th, explains the positions: next to the heart and above the brain, to show both organs willing to serve.

The argument that they are also apotropaic is made, and made by named people. Yehudah B. Cohn argues that tefillin should be read as an invented tradition, aimed at countering the popularity of Greek amulets with a Jewish one. Joshua Trachtenberg took every ornament worn on the body, whatever its declared function, to have begun as an amulet. And the early rabbinic sources are explicit enough on their own: Numbers Rabbah 12:3 has tefillin defeating "a thousand demons" coming up on the left side; rabbis Yohanan and Nahman use their sets to repel the demons of privies; Elisha the Winged, scrupulous in this mitzvah, is saved from Roman persecution. Tefillin are also credited with lengthening life, and are listed in one breath with objects that are amuletic in nature.

So the atlas includes them and states the objection rather than dissolving it. The object is dated: Jews were wearing physical tefillin by at least the first century CE, which is shown by the finds at Qumran and by the reference in Matthew 23. Karaite Judaism reads the commandment as metaphor and does not.

Who wears them is governed. The obligation rests on Jewish males from thirteen; women are exempt, as they are from most time-bound positive commandments, and since Rema in the 16th century the prevalent practice among religious Jews has strongly discouraged women from wearing them. Claims that Rashi's daughters and the wife of Chaim ibn Attar wore tefillin have no historical evidence behind them. In Orthodox practice it remains a male obligation; Conservative women often wrap; SAR High School in Riverdale allowed girls to wrap at morning prayer from 2013, probably the first Modern Orthodox high school in the United States to do so; a Jerusalem District Court judge ruled in 2013 that Women of the Wall wearing tefillin at the Western Wall did not violate 'local custom'; in 2018 students at Hebrew College in Boston made a series of videos teaching female and transgender Jews to wrap.
how: Cubical boxes from a single piece of hide, in three grades — peshutim, made with several pieces of parchment forming the inner walls of the head box; dakkot, stretched from one thin piece; and the more durable gassot. Painted black by custom now, though the archaeological finds do not show that this was always so. Straps must be black on the outside and any colour but red inside. The four passages go on one strip in the arm box, which has a single compartment, and on four separate scrolls in the head box, which has four — because the verses name the hand device in the singular and the head device in the plural. Written by a scribe in Ashuri script in one of three lettering styles: Beis Yosef for Ashkenazim, Arizal for Hasidim, Velish for Sefardim. The letters must be written in order; a mistake found later cannot be corrected, because the replacement would be out of sequence, and the set is invalid. Talmudic commentators disagreed on the order of the scrolls: Rashi held to the order the passages appear in the Torah, Rabbeinu Tam switched the last two. Most follow Rashi; some also lay Rabbeinu Tam briefly, a custom of the Ari taken up by Hasidim, many Sephardic communities and some Ashkenazim. The Vilna Gaon, who wore Rashi's, rejected the stringency, pointing out that there are 64 possible arrangements and one cannot put on 64 sets. Worn during Shacharit on weekdays and removed after morning services; Jewish men once wore them all day.
today: Worn daily wherever weekday morning prayer is kept, as of 2026. The live question inside the tradition is gender, and it is being answered differently by different communities — see the story above, which names the rulings and the dates.
kin: mezuzah — the partner commandment, carrying two of the same four passages, fixed to the door instead of bound to the body — and the object Maimonides used to say what happens when a mitzvah is treated as a talisman
kin: phylactery-word — the Greek word for 'safeguard' that English fastened onto these, and that the tradition's own usage never uses
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest surviving Hebrew verses written small and carried — six centuries before the earliest tefillin finds
kin: red-string — in the 1490s, when Jews were barred from wearing tefillin, Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended a red string on the hand to remember this commandment — the one documented moment where one substitutes for the other
kin: kamea — the written Jewish amulet these are constantly mistaken for and formally separated from
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition the apotropaic reading of tefillin belongs to, named here and not joined
kin: parchment — what the passages are written on, and where a single out-of-order letter invalidates the set
kin: talismanic-shirt — scripture worn on the body in another book's tradition, with none of this one's objection to the word
kin: inscribing — the practice at its most exacting: 3,188 letters, in order, no corrections
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read; this record is here under protest from the tradition it belongs to, and says so
sources: s:wp-tefillin s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-phylactery s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-red-string-kabbalah
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Teru teru bōzu (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/teru-teru-bozu/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/teru-teru-bozu.json
id: teru-teru-bozu
native: 照る照る坊主 (Japanese)
aliases: teru teru bozu · てるてる坊主 · fine-weather priest · shine-shine monk
said: TE-ru TE-ru BOH-zu
when: 1603 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese teru 照る 'to shine', doubled, + bōzu 坊主 'Buddhist monk' — 'shine, shine, monk'
object: form=figurine materials=paper,cloth,thread,ink worn=door,wall,roof
against: bad-luck — said by children making one the day before an outing, in the chant recorded from the Edo period: 'Fine-weather priest, please let the weather be good tomorrow' [s:wp-teru-teru-b-zu]
what: A small handmade doll of tissue paper or cloth, white, a ball of stuffing for a head with the cloth falling loose below it and a string tied round the neck. It hangs outside a door or a window, made the day before a day the maker wants dry. Children make them; most Japanese meet one in kindergarten or daycare.
story: The practice came from China and changed sex on the way. In the Chinese version, Saoqing Niang 掃晴娘, the figure is a young girl with a broom, set on the end of a broom to sweep the sky clear; the story attached has a girl ascending to the heavens in a heavy rainfall to sweep the clouds off and save her city, and paper cut-outs of her hung outdoors afterwards in her memory. Japan took the practice up in the Heian period, inside an older weather-watching culture, hiyorimi, that runs with certainty from the Heian period through the Edo.

The Japanese doll seems to come out of the resemblance between origami dolls and the names recorded in mid-Edo literature. The reference this project can name is Kiyū Shōran, written in 1830 by Nobuyo Kitamura, a scholar of Japanese classical literature: "If the weather becomes fine, I write my pupils on the paper, offer sake to the gods, and pour it into the river." Painting in the eyes after the sun comes out, and the libation, and the river — the whole disposal is in that one sentence.

It became popular in the Edo period among city dwellers, whose children made them the day before and chanted, "Fine-weather priest, please let the weather be good tomorrow." A warabe uta released in 1921 fixed the modern version, and children sing it while making the doll. The song is not soft: it promises the doll plenty of sake if the wish comes off, and decapitation if it does not.
how: Tissue paper or a scrap of white cloth, gathered over a ball of stuffing, tied at the neck with string, hung from an eave, a window frame or a door on the eve of the day in question. The face is often left blank and drawn on afterwards, when the weather has behaved. If the day comes up fine, a libation of sake is poured over the doll and it is floated away in a river. Hanging one upside down is the reverse request, for rain — a use this project has not read in a cited source and so does not assert here.
today: Still made by Japanese children in 2026, taught through the 1921 nursery rhyme. Ikeda in Nagano Prefecture has built its town mascot on the shape.
kin: daruma — the other Japanese figure bought or made against a deadline and then discharged — that one burnt, this one floated away
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition it sits at the edge of: made at home, by a child, with nobody's seal on it
kin: omamori — the counterpart from the shrine counter — consecrated, bought, and for the year rather than for tomorrow
kin: corn-dolly — the other figure twisted out of cheap material for the weather and the harvest, and then destroyed on purpose
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this belongs in: a charm children make with their own hands, for their own day out
kin: hanging-at-door — where it works from — an eave, a window frame, outside, where the weather can see it
kin: ofuda — the printed sheet a Japanese household hangs indoors for the year; this one hangs outdoors for a night
sources: s:wp-teru-teru-b-zu s:wp-ema-shinto s:web-ja-wikipedia-engimono
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Toli (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/toli-mirror/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/toli-mirror.json
id: toli-mirror
native: толь (Cyrillic)
aliases: toli mirror · neker-toli · shaman's mirror
said: TOL-ee
when: 1940 CE to now (still carried)
countries: MN RU CN
object: form=mirror materials=brass,copper worn=neck,chest
against: spirits — said by the account of the mirrors as ritual armour, which has them ward off harmful or attacking spirits and collect and trap hostile ones [s:wp-toli-shamanism]
RESTRICTED: This record names the people each detail is recorded among — Daur, Hure Banner shamans, Buryats, Tsaatan — and does not generalise across them or to Siberia at large. It prints no making, charging or transmission of a toli, because the sources read describe the object and its use and publish no procedure.
what: A metal disc, brass, copper or bronze, ornamented on one face and polished on the other, worn on a shaman's body. Small ones are sewn onto the deel or the apron in quantity, laid like overlapping scales; large ones hang at the neck and over the chest. Worn together they are armour, and they are described that way.
story: The counts are recorded people by people, and this record keeps them apart. Among the Daur, small toli were set on the costume like overlapping scales, with eight large mirrors and one medium one to protect the heart — the neker-toli, which might be plated in nickel. In Hure Banner, shamans wore nine mirrors, and nine is a number of particular weight in Mongolian religion and mythology. The practice is also recorded among the Buryats in the Republic of Buryatia and among the Tsaatan in Mongolia.

Walther Heissig, documenting shamans in Hure Banner in the 1940s, recorded that the toli held the white horses of the shamans and served as a vehicle for the shaman.

What the mirrors are said to do beyond armour: purify and empower water or vodka; collect and trap hostile spirits; give helper spirits somewhere to live. In Mongolia they are described as vessels for the shaman's spiritual power, the wind horse, and as collecting and storing the power of blessings. A toli also says what its wearer is — the mirrors signify the shaman's authority and role, and how many of them there are is read as a measure of standing.

*Inference —* a polished disc worn at the chest does two jobs at once that this atlas usually finds split between two objects: it faces outward like a door charm and it is worn like a pendant. The Chinese bagua mirror does the first from a wall. This one walks.
how: Worn on the costume and at the neck, in numbers. The sources read describe what the mirrors are and what they are for, and do not publish how one is made, charged or passed on; this record stops where they stop and does not borrow a procedure from a neighbouring people.
today: Still worn by practising shamans in Mongolia, Buryatia and among the Daur, as the published ethnography describes them; the atlas has not read a survey dated to 2026 and does not claim numbers. Bronze mirrors of this kind also circulate as collectibles, which is a different object with the same shape.
kin: mirror-sign — the sign it is — a polished surface that sends a thing back, worn instead of hung
kin: ongon — the other object in the same shaman's kit: the ongon holds an ancestor, the toli holds power and turns spirits away
kin: bagua-mirror — the Chinese neighbour doing the same optical job from a doorway, on a building rather than on a body
kin: lungta-flag — the other thing in this region called wind horse — there a printed flag left to the wind, here the power a mirror is said to hold
kin: tibetan-protection — the Buddhist practice that shares the same territory, and sometimes the same households
kin: wearing-hidden — the opposite rule: a toli is worn to be seen and to catch the light, where most of this atlas's charms are worn out of sight
kin: gorgoneion — the far-off parallel — a disc worn on the chest as armour, meant for whatever is looking
sources: s:wp-toli-shamanism s:wp-ongon s:wp-shamanism-in-siberia
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Tupilaq (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tupilaq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tupilaq.json
id: tupilaq
native: ᑐᐱᓚᒃ (Canadian Aboriginal syllabics)
aliases: tupilak · tupilait
said: TOO-pee-lak; plural tupilait
when: undated (still carried)
countries: GL CA
object: form=figurine materials=bone,tooth,wood,skin worn=pocket,shop
RESTRICTED: The making of a tupilaq was done in secret, at night, alone. Published ethnography describes the procedure; this atlas prints the fact of the secrecy and not the procedure, and does not reconstruct it from scattered sources.
what: Two different things share this name, and a reader should hold them apart. The first is what the word originally named in Greenland: an avenging creature assembled by an angakkuq from animal parts — bone, skin, hair, sinew — and, in the accounts, from parts taken from the bodies of children, brought to life by chants and sent into the sea after a named enemy. None survive; they were made in secret, in isolated places, out of materials that rot. The second is the carved figure: a small grotesque cut from sperm whale tooth, and today from narwhal and walrus tusk, wood and caribou antler, a few centimetres high, made to be looked at and bought.
story: The second object exists because of the first. Early European visitors to Greenland were fascinated by the accounts they heard and wanted to see what a tupilaq looked like, so Inuit began carving representations of them out of sperm whale teeth. That carving is now an important part of Greenlandic Inuit art and is prized by collectors. It is a picture of a thing, made for an audience that had asked. That is not the same as the thing.

The first object came with a risk attached. Sending a tupilaq at somebody with greater power than the maker could turn it back on its maker — and the escape from that was public confession of the deed. The published ethnography places this inside a wider Greenlandic logic in which concealment carries magical consequences and confession neutralises them: a concealed miscarriage or infanticide could produce a monster called an anngiaq, a concealed breach of taboo could bring harm on the whole community, and angakkuit resolved a taboo breach by getting the breacher to confess in public. A young hunter's first kill was neutralised the same way, by making every adult share in it.

The word also does not mean the same thing across the Arctic. At Igloolik a tupilaq was an invisible ghost, the restless soul of a dead person whose death taboo had been breached, visible only to the angakkuq, and it drove the game away until the angakkuq scared it off with a knife. Among the Kivallirmiut it was an invisible chimera with a human head and parts of different animals, dangerous to the settlement, which the angakkuq fought and devoured with helping spirits. Among the Copper Inuit, the Inuinnait, tupilak came to mean something close to the Christian devil. Only in Greenland is it primarily a physical, human-made object.

*Inference —* the tupilaq is the clearest case in this atlas of a word that a museum label flattens. A tray of carved tupilait in a gift shop in Nuuk and a sentence in Knud Rasmussen's notebooks are not describing the same category, and the difference is not one of quality.
how: The carved figure is cut from tusk, tooth, antler or wood with hand tools and polished; it is signed and sold. How the older object was made is not printed here. See the note below.
today: Carved tupilait are made in many shapes and sizes in Greenland from narwhal and walrus tusk, wood and caribou antler, form an important part of Greenlandic Inuit art, and are highly prized as collectibles. This project has read no dated price and names no living carver.
kin: inuit-amulet — the thing this is not: an amulet stays with its owner, a tupilaq was sent at somebody else
kin: curse-tablet — the Mediterranean parallel — an object made to reach a named person and do them harm
kin: nkisi — the other figure in this atlas made to go after somebody, with its own specialists and its own rules
kin: the-fake-market — the long read about what a label promises — this record's two objects share a name and nothing else
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read explaining the restriction on this record
kin: bone-ivory — what the carved figures are cut from: sperm whale tooth, then narwhal and walrus tusk, then antler
kin: dreamcatcher — the North American parallel — an object that acquired a second life made for outsiders, and an argument about whether that is the same object
sources: s:wp-tupilaq s:wp-inuit-religion
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Tyet (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/tyet-knot/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/tyet-knot.json
id: tyet-knot
native: 𓎬 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: knot of Isis · girdle of Isis · blood of Isis · tit · Gardiner V39
said: TEE-et, from Ancient Egyptian tjt
when: 1550 BCE – 30 BCE
countries: EG
root: Egyptian tjt. The sign is usually translated 'welfare' or 'life', which is close to what the ankh means.
object: form=pendant materials=carnelian,glass,faience worn=neck,chest,grave
against: the-dead — said by Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead [s:wp-tyet]
against: theft — said by Chapter 156, which says the amulet "will drive away whoever would commit a crime against him" [s:wp-tyet]
against: illness — said by Egyptologists, who tie the sign to Isis and to the healing powers that are an important part of her character [s:wp-tyet]
what: A looped knot with two arms hanging down and a tail below — an ankh whose crossbar has drooped. Cut small and laid in the wrappings, usually on the upper torso. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for one of red jasper at the mummy's neck, and the surviving ones are red jasper, carnelian or red glass, or else green faience, whose colour Egyptologists read as the renewal of life.
story: The sign is older than the goddess it belongs to. An early tyet comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, dug by Zaki Saad in the 1940s; it predates the first written references to Isis, so at that point it was probably not hers. Later it attaches to her, and to the healing that is a central part of her character.

As an amulet it starts in the early New Kingdom, about 1550 BCE, with the earliest examples in the reign of Amenhotep III. From then to the end of dynastic Egypt, few people were buried without one placed inside the mummy wrappings. That is an unusually strong statement to be able to make about any amulet anywhere: not that it was common, but that its absence was rare.

Chapter 156 gives the words. The red jasper tyet is laid at the neck and the spell says the power of Isis will be the protection of the mummy's body, and that the amulet will drive away whoever would commit a crime against him.

A second knot gets confused with this one. From the Late Period, Egyptian women wore a large knot in a mantle, and because it turns up on Hellenistic and Roman statues of Isis it picked up the name 'Isis knot' — but Robert Bianchi's 1980 paper is titled 'Not the Isis-Knot', and apart from the name the two have nothing to do with each other. Elsewhere the comparison runs the other way: the Minoan sacral knot at Knossos, a knot with a loop projecting from it, is close enough in shape that Egyptologists set the two side by side.
how: Cut from red jasper, carnelian or red glass, or moulded in faience, and placed inside the wrappings on the upper torso — Chapter 156 puts it at the neck. Egyptian funerary texts carry spells to be recited over amulets, and this one has its own.
today: Not made and not placed. The sign is in Unicode's hieroglyphic block and in every Egyptology textbook, and it sells as jewellery in Cairo and online alongside the ankh and the wedjat. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anyone using one the way Chapter 156 describes.
kin: ankh-amulet — the sign it may share an origin with — early ankhs draw the lower bar as two loose ends of a knot, which is what this is
kin: djed-pillar — the sign it is written beside; paired, Egyptologists read the two as the duality of life
kin: knot — the family it belongs to — a tied thing worn because it is tied
kin: heart-scarab — the other amulet the wrappings required, one organ lower and with a spell cut on it rather than spoken over it
kin: carnelian — the red stone that stands in for the red jasper Chapter 156 asks for
kin: knotting — the practice the sign is a picture of, frozen in stone
kin: grave-deposit — the practice this amulet exists inside, and the reason so many survive
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that placed it — and the one case where the tradition's own text says where on the body it goes
sources: s:wp-tyet s:wp-ankh s:wp-djed s:wp-carnelian s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-british-museum s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Wedjat eye (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/wedjat-eye/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/wedjat-eye.json
id: wedjat-eye
native: 𓂀 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: Eye of Horus · udjat · udjat eye · Horus eye amulet
said: WED-jat, from wḏꜣt, 'the sound one'
when: 2686 BCE – 641 CE
countries: EG SD SY LB IL PS
root: Egyptian wḏꜣt, feminine of wḏꜣ 'whole, sound, uninjured' — the eye after it was healed, not before
object: form=pendant materials=faience,carnelian,lapis,gold,glass worn=neck,chest,grave
against: illness — said by Egyptian religious texts, as summarised by Egyptologists [s:wp-eye-of-horus]
against: the-dead — said by Egyptian funerary practice [s:wp-eye-of-horus]
against: evil-eye — said by later Mediterranean use of the same shape [s:wp-evil-eye]
what: A stylised human eye with a falcon's cheek-mark curling below it, cut or moulded small enough to string at the throat. Most surviving examples are faience — quartz paste, glazed blue-green in the kiln — and run a few centimetres across. Egypt made more of these than of any other amulet shape, for the living to wear and for the dead to be wrapped in.
story: The eye comes out of a fight. Set tears out Horus's eye; Thoth, or another god, puts it back; Horus gives the restored eye to his dead father Osiris, and the offering keeps Osiris going in the afterlife. That is why the sign stands for an offering as much as for an eye, and why it turns up on temple walls beside the meat and bread.

As an amulet it runs from the Old Kingdom to the Roman period — roughly 2686 BCE to the seventh century CE, which is close to three thousand years of continuous use, and the longest run of any object in this atlas. Coffins of the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom carry a pair of eyes painted on the side, positioned so the mummy inside could look out through them. Boats carried them on the bows. *Tradition holds —* the eye also travelled: Syria, Canaan and especially Nubia took the sign up from Egypt, and Nubian versions are common enough that a museum tray of them is rarely all Egyptian.

*Inference —* the arithmetic on the shelf is worth stating plainly. An object that was cheap to mould, buried by the thousand, and made of a material that does not rot is an object that survives; the reed, cloth and dough charms that stood beside it did not. What a museum drawer holds is a record of what lasts, not a census of what Egypt wore.
how: Moulded in faience or cut from carnelian, lapis, gold or glass, pierced at the top or through the back, and strung. Size was the variable, not the design — the same eye scaled from a bead to a pectoral. In mummification the eye went into the wrappings, and one class of it covered the embalmer's incision.
today: Nobody makes a wedjat as a wedjat any more in Egypt's ancient sense; the practice ended with the religion. It is made by the million as jewellery, sold in Cairo, Luxor and every airport shop that sells to Egypt's visitors, and worn worldwide by people with no connection to Osiris. As of 2026 the sign is also standard tattoo flash. Whether the mass-market version is the same object is an argument this atlas reports and does not settle.
kin: eye — the sign this amulet carries, and the oldest dated member of the family that runs from here to a glass bead in Istanbul
kin: scarab — the other amulet Egypt made by the thousand; the scarab went under the wrappings at the heart, the eye over the incision
kin: heart-scarab — its partner in the wrappings — one guards the body's opening, the other speaks for the dead at the weighing
kin: faience — the material that made it cheap enough to bury by the thousand, and durable enough to still be here
kin: carnelian — the red stone version, cut rather than moulded, and costlier
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that produced it, on a scale no other ancient practice matches
kin: ankh-amulet — made in the same workshops and strung on the same cords, for life rather than for soundness
kin: nazar — the eye answering the eye, four thousand years later and in glass rather than faience
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that is the reason this amulet survives at all
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator who sorted Egypt's amulets into the classes museums still use
sources: s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-amulet s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-british-museum s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Witch bottle (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/witch-bottle/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/witch-bottle.json
id: witch-bottle
aliases: bottled spell · Bellarmine bottle · Greybeard jug · Bartmann jug
when: 1500 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB BE US
object: form=bottle materials=terracotta,glass,iron,hair,herb worn=foundation,hearth,wall,door
against: witchcraft — said by folk magic, as summarised of the whole class: countermagical devices meant to draw in and trap harmful intentions directed at their owners [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: spirits — said by the same account, which names evil spirits alongside magical attacks [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: illness — said by the travelling old man in Joseph Glanvill's 1681 Suffolk account, prescribing the bottle for a wife who had been long in a languishing condition [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: curse — said by the same source, which describes the bottle as breaking a spell already laid — and, in Glanvill's telling, killing the man who laid it [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: house — said by early modern building custom, which hid bottles alongside written charms, dried cats and horse skulls in the fabric of a house [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
what: A stoppered vessel filled with the afflicted person's urine and with sharp iron — pins, needles, nails — then hidden. The earliest documented ones are salt-glazed stoneware Bartmann jugs, also called Bellarmines or Greybeards, brown or grey, embossed with a bearded face; later ones are ordinary glass bottles and small vials. It is not worn and not seen: it goes under the hearth, inside a wall, or into the farthest corner of the property, and it is supposed to stay there.
story: The earliest surviving description is a story about a bird. In 1681 Joseph Glanvill printed it in Saducismus Triumphatus: a Suffolk man tells a travelling old man that his wife has been long in a languishing condition and is haunted by a thing in the shape of a bird that flurrs near her face. The old man tells him to take his wife's urine, cork it in a bottle with pins, needles and nails, and set it to the fire. The cork blows out with a report like a pistol and the wife is no better. The old man comes back and changes the instruction: bottle it the same way and bury it in the earth. She recovers. Then a woman arrives from a town some miles off crying that they have killed her husband, who told her on his deathbed that he was a wizard and had bewitched the man's wife.

That is the logic the whole class runs on. A witch bottle is countermagic: it draws in harm aimed at its owner and holds it. Folk magic contends that the bottle protects against evil spirits and magical attacks and counteracts spells cast by witches. It stays active as long as it stays hidden and unbroken, which is why people took so much trouble over the hiding — bottles buried under fireplaces have turned up only after the rest of the building was pulled down.

The bottles keep being found. In 2016 a glass bottle dug out of the threshold of a Cornish house appeared on Antiques Roadshow, filmed at Trelissick; the glass specialist Andy McConnell tasted a little of the contents and guessed port or wine, noting a rusty flavour and the nails. A 2019 episode gave the laboratory answer: Loughborough University found it contained "urine, a tiny bit of alcohol, and one human hair", along with brass pins dating from the late 1840s, and an ostracod. In 2020 a sixteenth-century jug used against witchcraft was found during the renovation of the De Zwarte Ruiter pub in Turnhout, Belgium — reported as the first witch bottle found in Europe outside England.

In the United States fewer than a dozen possible witch bottles have been identified. The archaeologist Marshall Becker was the first to identify one in an archaeological context: the Essington witch bottle, recovered during excavations on Great Tinicum Island in Delaware County, Pennsylvania. A mid-nineteenth to early twentieth-century slave or tenant site in Dorchester County, Maryland, yielded a buried bottle whose cork stopper bristled with straight pins. In 2016 a bottle filled with nails came out of the hearth of a Civil War site in Virginia.
how: A white witch or folk healer prepared it. The historical fill is the victim's urine, hair or nail clippings, or red thread from sprite traps; later bottles take rosemary, needles and pins, and red wine. Other recorded fills include sand, stones, knotted threads, feathers, shells, herbs, flowers, salt, vinegar, oil, coins and ashes; sea water or earth stand in for urine. Then it is corked and buried — at the farthest corner of the property, beneath the hearth, or somewhere inconspicuous indoors. Carriers describe the mechanism: evil is drawn in, impaled on the pins and needles, drowned by the wine, and sent away by the rosemary. One variant is destructive rather than protective: throw the bottle into a fire, and when it explodes the spell is broken.
today: Still made. Modern practitioners bottle and bury them, and the historical ones surface at a steady rate during building work in England and, now, Belgium. *Inference —* the finds are a function of demolition as much as of belief: a charm designed never to be found is only counted when a wall comes down.
kin: concealed-shoe — the same custom's commonest object by a wide margin — shoe and bottle go into the same chimney, and archaeologists call the deposit a spiritual midden
kin: the-charm-in-the-wall — the long read about objects built into houses, which begins with this bottle and the shoe beside it
kin: burying — the practice that completes it: Glanvill's first attempt, at the fire, fails; the bottle only works buried
kin: foundation-deposit — the older, wider habit this belongs to — something put into a building to hold it
kin: iron — what does the work inside: pins, needles and nails, the same metal English folklore hangs over the door
kin: glass — the later body of the object, once stoneware jugs went out of use
kin: incantation-bowl — the same idea fifteen centuries earlier and three thousand miles east — a vessel buried in a house to catch what is coming for the household
kin: curse-tablet — the other buried written object of European magic, and the one aimed outward rather than defensively
kin: hagstone — what hung visibly over the bed while this was hidden under the hearth
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition it belongs to, and the object of that tradition with the best-documented recipe
kin: hex-sign — the other charm in this atlas whose scholarship is an argument between archaeologists and decorators

## Worry stone (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/worry-stone/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/worry-stone.json
id: worry-stone
aliases: palm stone · thumb stone · fidget stone · soothing stone · sensory stone
when: undated (still carried)
countries: GR IE US
object: form=bead materials=agate,jade,turquoise,amber worn=pocket,wallet
against: illness — said by writers on cognitive behavioral therapy, as summarised by the cited source [s:wp-worry-stone]
what: A smooth polished gemstone, usually an oval with a thumb-sized dish worn into one face, about 3 centimetres across. It is held between index finger and thumb, and the thumb is moved back and forth across the dish. That motion is the whole of the object's use.
story: There is no single origin claimed for it, and the sources do not pretend otherwise. Variations are traced to ancient Greece, to Tibet, to Ireland and to several Native American peoples; the Greek ones were stones the sea had smoothed, and the concept begins, as the cited account puts it, with the simple act of picking up a smooth stone and fiddling with it. A worry stone is one of the few objects in this atlas that anybody can find on a beach.

What it claims is unusually narrow, and the cited source hedges it in the same breath: the motion "is thought to reduce stress, but there is no conclusive scientific evidence to support this". This atlas does not test that and does not settle it.

Where it is documented most precisely is in a clinic. Writers on cognitive behavioral therapy treat the worry stone as one of a set of folk practices that work as psychologically healthy self-soothing exercises, taught early in treatment to displace familiar but destructive coping habits — nail-biting, scratching, lip-biting — and to ready a patient to face anxiety or trauma safely. The cited account singles out short-term treatment of refugees, where complexity and unfamiliarity are the constraints and a stone is simple and intuitive enough to be useful. Later, once a patient has learned a fuller relaxation script, the stone becomes a reminder of it: the impulse to reach for it is itself the signal that the person is anxious.

*Inference —* that last function is the interesting one for this atlas, because it is the only charm here whose stated job is to tell its carrier something rather than to keep something away. The stone reports.
how: Tumbled and polished, or picked up already smooth. Sold in a box with a card, or handed over in a session, or found. There is no consecration, no maker's restriction and no retirement rite. A lost one is replaced.
today: Sold worldwide in mineral shops, gift shops, pharmacies and therapy-supply catalogues, and given out in clinical settings. The stones are the same stones the crystal trade sells, which means the same sourcing questions attach to them; that argument is set out on the crystal pendant record and is not repeated here.
kin: crystal-pendant — the same stones, sold through the same trade, with the same sourcing argument attached
kin: counting-beads — the practice this is a single-bead version of — repetition in the hand, without the count
kin: hagstone — the other charm in this atlas that is picked up rather than made
kin: phone-charm — the other thing in a modern pocket that gets touched all day without being looked at
kin: rudraksha — the seed handled the same way, in a tradition that gives the handling a count and a text
kin: turquoise — one of the stones it is commonly cut from
sources: s:wp-worry-stone s:wp-crystal-healing
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Yantra plate (amulet)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/amulet/yantra-plate/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/amulet/yantra-plate.json
id: yantra-plate
native: यन्त्र (Devanagari)
aliases: yantra · yantrá · Sri Yantra · Sri Chakra
said: YAN-tra
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IN NP LK TH
root: Sanskrit yantrá, from the root yam 'to sustain, support' with the instrument suffix -tra: literally a machine or contraption
object: form=plaque materials=copper,paper,ink worn=wall,neck,shop,door
against: spirits — said by the source's summary of occult yantras, which lists exorcism among their uses [s:wp-yantra]
against: illness — said by the same summary, which lists preventative medicine [s:wp-yantra]
against: bad-luck — said by users of occult yantras, for whom they serve as good luck charms and to ward off evil [s:wp-yantra]
against: poverty — said by buyers of the Sivali yantra, used mainly in Southeast Asian Buddhism for the attraction of wealth and good luck [s:wp-yantra]
what: A geometric diagram, drawn on paper, painted, or engraved into a sheet of metal, and usually smaller and less coloured than a mandala. Shapes radiate from a centre point, the bindu: triangles, hexagrams, circles, lotus petals numbering anything from two to a thousand, and an outer square standing for the four directions, often with a doorway cut in each side. Sanskrit mantras are written into the design. A downward triangle is read as Shakti and an upward one as Shiva; white, red and black stand for the three gunas — sattva, rajas and tamas. Plates are hung on a wall, set under a lamp or a vessel, or carried.
story: Yantras belong mainly to the Tantric traditions of the Indian religions, and are used for worship in temples and at home, as an aid to meditation, and — the reason they are in this atlas — as charms. Gudrun Bühnemann sorts them into three by use: yantras laid under a ritual implement such as a lamp or a vessel; yantras used in regular worship, the Sri Yantra among them, energised with mantras and often carrying written mantras in the design; and yantras made for a specific desire-driven rite, which are often drawn on birch bark or paper and can carry flowers, rice paste or ashes.

How old the form is depends on who is asked, and the source read here does not settle it. Representations of the yantra in India have been claimed to go back 11,000 to 10,000 BCE. G. R. Sharma, who excavated it, considered the Baghor stone the earliest example — a triangular stone with triangular engravings on one side, found daubed in ochre at what was read as a worship site in the Son River Valley, in an Upper Paleolithic context dated to 25,000–20,000 BCE. Kenoyer, also on the excavation, associated it with Shakti, and the triangle resembles the Kali Yantra and the Muladhara Chakra. Against that, the word's occult sense is medieval. *Inference —* a triangle scratched on a Paleolithic stone and a Tantric diagram consecrated with a seed syllable are separated by a gap this record cannot bridge with the sources it has, so it reports both claims and dates neither.

The Sri Chakra, which represents the goddess Tripura Sundari and includes Shiva as well, is the best-known form. The largest ever drawn covered 67,400 square feet on the ground at Cranbury, New Jersey, under the guidance of Guru Karunamaya.
how: Drawn, then woken. Yantras are traditionally consecrated and energised by a priest, using the mantras tied to that deity and that diagram; practitioners hold that a yantra not energised with a mantra is lifeless. Colour is not decoration — each colour denotes an idea or an inner state, and texts disagree about which colours belong to which yantra. As a talisman a yantra is treated as standing in for a deity who can be called on at will. In Sri Lankan Buddhism, practitioners are required to keep the yantra of the deity with them once the deity has shown acceptance of their prayer.
today: Engraved copper plates and printed paper sheets sell across India and Nepal, in temple shops and online, and the Sivali yantra, used mainly in Southeast Asian Buddhism, is bought for wealth and good luck. Designers now depart from the patterns in the older texts, and designers in the West copy elements from Nepali and Tantric imitations rather than from the texts — which is an argument about what a yantra is, running inside the tradition and outside it at once.
kin: sak-yant — the same geometry put under the skin instead of onto metal — that is the whole difference, and it changes everything: a plate can be sold, hung, given away or thrown out, a tattoo cannot, and the tattooed version carries rules of conduct the plate does not
kin: yantra-word — the word, from a Sanskrit term for a machine, and the road it took to mean a drawn sign
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition that consecrates it and decides who may
kin: consecration — the step that makes it work at all, in the practitioners' own account: unenergised, they say, the diagram is lifeless
kin: inscribing — the making itself — the mantra written into the geometry rather than beside it
kin: magic-square — the other family of drawn signs that runs on arrangement rather than image
kin: kamea — the Jewish parallel: a written square worn or hung, made by a specialist who names what it is for
kin: sungkhor — the Himalayan neighbour — a printed deity diagram folded and wrapped in thread rather than hung flat
kin: yant-flash — the sheets of designs a tattooist works from, which are these diagrams drawn for skin
kin: paper — the cheapest support it takes, and the one that lets a temple sell it by the sheet
sources: s:wp-yantra s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-magic-square
