## Bakongo nkisi craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/bakongo-nkisi-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/bakongo-nkisi-craft.json
id: bakongo-nkisi-craft
native: kinganga (Latin)
aliases: Kongo minkisi · nganga practice · nkisi nkondi making
said: the maker is an nganga, plural banganga; the object is an nkisi, plural minkisi
when: 1600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CD CG AO
object: form=figurine materials=wood,iron,earth,herb,glass,cloth,bone
against: witchcraft — said by Kongo practice, in which banganga defend the living against harmful workings and supply remedies against the sicknesses that follow [s:wp-nkisi]
against: illness — said by the same practice — many minkisi are used for healing [s:wp-nkisi]
against: theft — said by the nkondi class, whose name comes from -konda, 'to hunt', and whose commonest use the source gives as locating and punishing wrongdoers [s:wp-nkondi]
against: lawsuit — said by villages, which used publicly held nkondi to affirm oaths and seal treaties [s:wp-nkondi]
against: poverty — said by the source, which names success in hunting and in trade among the purposes minkisi serve [s:wp-nkisi]
against: curse — said by oath-takers, who declare themselves open to a nkondi's sickness should they break the oath [s:wp-nkondi]
RESTRICTED: This record prints no bilongo recipe and no invocation. Both belong to the nganga, and the tradition's own arrangement puts them out of sight: the nganga assembles and charges the object isolated in a hidden camp, away from the village, and learns its proper use and its songs before bringing it back. What is printed here is the class of substances, the reasoning that selects them, and what Kongo testimony says the nails and the mirrors are for.
what: The practice, among the Bakongo of the Congo Basin and the Songye of Kasai, of assembling containers that a spirit inhabits. The maker is an nganga: a healer, diviner and mediator. The container is an nkisi: a pot, a gourd, a horn, a shell, a bundle, a carved figure — or a grave, since the dead are what the practice draws on. The substances inside are bilongo. Everything else follows from those four words.
story: Close communication with ancestors, and confidence in what they can do, is what minkisi are for. Among the peoples of the Congo Basin, exceptional human powers are held to come from some kind of communication with the dead, and banganga are the people who do that communicating — working as healers, diviners and mediators, defending the living against harmful workings and supplying remedies against sicknesses caused either by those workings or by the demands of the bakisi, the spirits who are emissaries from the land of the dead.

The substances are chosen by metaphor, not by pharmacy. Wyatt MacGaffey's correction is the one this record follows: bilongo is usually translated 'medicine', but they are not applied to the sick or swallowed, so 'therapeutic substances' is closer. Bird claws to catch a wrongdoer. Fruit, charcoal, mushrooms. Minerals from places associated with the dead — grave earth, riverbed earth. White clay, because white carries dead skin, moral rightness and spiritual positivity against the black of negativity; red ochre where the powers of the dead are being mediated. Many minkisi contain earth or relics from the grave of a powerful person as a prime ingredient, which is why the objects have been described as portable graves.

The practice sorts itself. Minkisi and the afflictions that go with them are classed 'of the above' and 'of the below'. The above are the sky, rain and thunderstorms, counted masculine, tied to violence and violent forces, used to maintain order, serve justice and seal treaties; their motifs are birds of prey, lightning, weapons, fire, and they affect the upper body, so head, neck and chest pains are attributed to them. The below are the earth and the waters on land. Some figures are animals — most often dogs, kozo, sometimes carved with two heads, because a dog lives in two worlds at once, the village of the living and the forest of the dead. Na monanga minkisi are made carefully, with tranquil expressions, and are associated with a powerful person of great reasoning who brings happiness and fortune; npezo figures are made to look menacing and their power is held to be weakened by laughter. Personal minkisi are anonymous and kept in a private house; community ones are placed to be seen, often overlooking the village, though kept in their own enclosure by day.

The word is old in writing and older in use. Its earliest attestations are in Kikongo dialects in the early seventeenth century, transliterated into Dutch as mokissie; Dutch visitors to Loango used it in 1668 for both the object and the spirit in it; when Kongo converted in the sixteenth century, the Kikongo Catechism of 1624 used ukisi to translate 'holy'.

The practice crossed the Atlantic. Aspects of Kongo spirituality reached the Americas with the slave trade, and Hoodoo and Palo carry them; the art historian Robert Farris Thompson has been the influential identifier of Kongo elements in African-descended populations of the Americas. The Kikongo word mooyo, the cavity in an nkisi where charged items sit, is where the American word mojo comes from. Archaeologists working at the African Burial Ground in Lower Manhattan found Kongo-related material — minkisi and nkisi bundles — buried with African remains.

The objects left. Collectors wanted the nailed figures as soon as the German Loango expedition published them in the 1870s; Robert Visser, a German trader and diplomat, supplied Berlin and Stuttgart. Many were purchased, others confiscated or removed by colonial authorities, and often found their way to museums, while many also remain in private hands. Where they should be now is an argument with names attached: the 2018 Report on the Restitution of African Cultural Heritage by Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy, which moved the debate onto moral rather than only legal ground; the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Belgium, holding more than 180,000 objects mainly from the former Belgian Congo and rebuilt around decolonisation; the Pitt Rivers Museum's four tenets of provenance, transparency, repatriation and redress, and its 2020 Restitution of Knowledge project with Savoy and colleagues at Technische Universität Berlin; and the British Museum, which has consistently refused to return objects, citing the British Museum Act 1963.

*Inference —* the European word for these objects came out of Portuguese traders on the West African coast in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and was applied to Central African things from outside. This atlas treats it as a term with a history, filed under fetish-word, and does not use it to describe what an nganga makes.
how: The nganga gathers the bilongo and assembles them, most often into a carved figure with a cavity cut for them at the belly, the head, or in pouches at the neck, closed with a resin-fixed mirror. He then either becomes possessed by the spirit or leaves the object in a graveyard or another place spirits frequent. Nkondi are often composed at the edge of the village, on the reasoning that a village, like a body, must have its entrances guarded; the nganga works isolated in a hidden camp and comes back covered in paint and behaving strangely. Before use he recites invocations to wake the nkondi. Banganga paint themselves for performances — white circles around the eyes to see past the physical world, white stripes on participants — dress unlike anyone else, wear ornate jewellery and work knots into their clothing, knots being tied to closing up or sealing spiritual forces.
today: Contested, and split three ways: Kongo communities, museum stores in Europe and North America, and private hands. Artists have taken the form up — Renee Stout, Tania Bruguera, Kara Walker, Dread Scott, Karen Seneferu, Wesley Clark, Stephanie Dinkins, Michael MacGarry, Andrew Lamprecht, Justin Par. The Republic of the Congo painter Trigo Piula made a New Fetish series against what he called the rebuffing of traditional objects, and described the work as "a way of engaging with my community and a way of denouncing things that I believe are impacting us, like television for example". As of 2026 this project has read no count of how many minkisi are held outside Central Africa, and no source dating an end to the practice inside it.
kin: nkisi — the object this tradition makes, and the word that names the spirit and the container at once
kin: fetish-word — the European label applied to these objects from outside, with its own sixteenth-century coastal history
kin: mojo-word — the Kikongo mooyo — the cavity where the charged substances sit — carried to the American South as the name of a bag
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the practice a thousand miles up the coast that this one is regularly merged with in English, and shouldn't be
kin: consecration — the step that makes an assembled container into an nkisi, done in isolation away from the village
kin: feeding-the-charm — the practice of keeping a charged object working — here, waking it and sometimes enraging it for a task
kin: knotting — the practice worked into the nganga's own clothing, knots being tied to closing up and sealing spiritual forces
kin: mirror-sign — the reflective disc over the cavity and in the eyes, held to be how the nkisi sees into the spirit world
kin: iron — the nails, and the reason the nailed figures can be dated at all
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this tradition sits at the centre of: purchased, confiscated or removed, and argued over by name since 2018
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — a holder running a provenance, transparency, repatriation and redress programme over material like this
kin: quai-branly — the Paris holder at the centre of the French restitution debate after the Sarr and Savoy report
sources: s:wp-nkisi s:wp-nkondi s:wp-fetishism s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-repatriation-cultural-property s:wp-mus-e-du-quai-branly-jacques-chirac s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum s:wp-british-museum

## Bujeok craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/korean-bujeok-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/korean-bujeok-craft.json
id: korean-bujeok-craft
native: 부적 (Hangul)
aliases: pujŏk · Korean talismans · Musok amulet practice
said: bu-jeok; also romanised pujŏk
when: 1101 CE to now (still carried)
countries: KR
root: Korean bujeok, from Sino-Korean 符籍 — the same fu character as Chinese fulu, 'talisman', plus a register or record
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,ink worn=wall,door,pocket
against: bad-luck — said by the cited account of Musok: pujŏk are talismans which provide the bearer with good fortune [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: spirits — said by the gut itself, at whose close wandering spirits that may have gathered are expelled and talismans may be distributed to attendees [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: house — said by clients, who affix the talismans to the internal walls of their homes [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: exams — said by Korean families before the national university entrance exam, who give sticky rice cakes and toffee on the wordplay that the sitter will stick to the school [s:web-koreaherald-test-taker-gifts]
RESTRICTED: The forms a bujeok takes are a specialist's craft learned by apprenticeship, in a tradition that has no manual, no central authority and no doctrine, and that transmits orally. This record names the practitioners, the script's ancestry and where the object ends up, and prints no bujeok form, no accompanying invocation and no reconstruction of one. The Chinese parent craft states the reason plainly — the illegibility exists so that only qualified clergy can produce them — and Korean practice inherits it.
what: Talismans drawn by a mudang, the ritual specialists at the centre of Musok, Korean vernacular religion. A bujeok is usually built on Hanja — Korean versions of Chinese logograms — worked in the same deliberately unreadable manner as its Chinese ancestor, and handed to the people who attended a rite rather than sold across a counter. Clients take them home and fix them to the internal walls of the house.
story: Two facts about who makes them frame everything else. First, the makers are ritual specialists and the majority of them are women: approximately a fifth of mudang are male, with more male simbang on Jeju than on the mainland. Second, they hand the talismans out at the end of a gut — the large ritual that is the core of the practice — at the point where wandering spirits are expelled and the food is distributed. A bujeok is the take-home part of a rite, not a transaction on its own. Korean vernacular religion also runs ritual specialists who divine and make amulets without performing gut at all.

The script is inherited and the inheritance is documented. Fulu, the Taoist talismanic script, was carried into Korean practice as it was into Japanese; the scholarship on the Chinese side says the illegibility is deliberate, designed so that only qualified clergy can produce them. A bujeok takes that logic into Hanja.

What distinguishes this tradition from its neighbours is six centuries of state pressure, which it survived. Under the Joseon dynasty Confucian elites deemed the mudang's rites improper and suppressed them with taxation and legal restriction. From the late 19th century modernisers, many of them Christian, characterised Musok as misin — a Korean word the sources gloss as "superstition" — and backed its suppression. Under the Japanese occupation, nationalist folklorists began promoting Musok as Korea's ancient religion and a form of its national culture, an idea mudang themselves later took up strongly. Persecution continued in the mid-20th century, in North Korea and through the New Community Movement in the South.

Then it turned. From the late 1970s South Korean appraisal of the mudang improved, particularly as practitioners were associated with the minjung pro-democracy movement and came to be treated as a source of Korean cultural identity. There are now over 200,000 mudang in South Korea, with practitioners abroad as well.

The reversal is not complete and this record says so. Disapproval of mudang, often regarded as charlatans, remains widespread in South Korea, especially among Christians. Chongho Kim's 1990s fieldwork found most mudang he met were poor and with little formal education, and mudang have conventionally belonged to the lowest social class. Clients are mostly women — in Kim's fieldwork, in their late fifties and early sixties; in Laurel Kendall's, small entrepreneurs around Seoul; by the early 21st century, in Sarfati's account, many young people, as part of a spiritual search or for counselling. Clients do not generally regard themselves as exclusively committed to Musok and may consider themselves Buddhist or Christian.

*Inference —* that client profile is the most interesting thing about this tradition for an atlas of charms. A bujeok is not the property of a believer; it is something a Buddhist small-business owner in Seoul comes away from a rite holding. The tradition has no doctrine, no hierarchy and no central authority, and is transmitted orally, so what holds it together is the specialists and their training rather than a text.
how: Drawn by a mudang, generally on paper, in Hanja-based forms. Distributed at the close of a gut to the people who attended, sometimes alongside food charged with auspiciousness by its use in the rite. Clients affix them to the internal walls of the home. Training is by apprenticeship rather than by manual: an initiate who has accepted the call finds an established mudang willing to teach, becomes that person's chagŭn mudang, and the teacher is their sineomeoni, spirit mother, the apprentice a sinttal or sinadul. Each mudang keeps a personal pantheon, the chusin, which may differ from the pantheon of the mudang who trained them.
today: Live, with over 200,000 mudang in South Korea and a state that now protects what it once prosecuted: regional gut styles are on the national intangible heritage register, and the Yŏngdŭng gut of Ch'ilmŏri Shrine on Jeju went onto UNESCO's Representative List in 2009. Insadong in Seoul, which holds 40 per cent of the country's antique shops and art galleries, is where a visitor is likeliest to encounter the printed retail version. Korea also has a separate and much larger charm economy that runs on food rather than paper: sticky-rice cakes and toffee given to students before the national university entrance exam, on the wordplay that the sitter will stick to the school.
kin: bujeok — the object itself — handed out at the end of a rite and pinned to an inside wall, not bought at a gate
kin: chinese-fu-craft — where the script comes from, and where the reason for its unreadability is stated out loud
kin: japanese-engimono — the other descendant of the same Taoist stock, which went the opposite way: administered, seal-stamped, sold at a counter and replaced on a calendar
kin: dolhareubang — the monumental end of Korean threshold-guarding — stone at a gate rather than paper on a wall
kin: insadong — the Seoul quarter where the printed retail version concentrates
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice, done indoors: the talisman goes on the inside wall of the house it is for
kin: exam-charm — Korea's other charm economy, which runs on rice cake and toffee rather than on paper, and which far more people handle
kin: paper — the material, and the only one this tradition needs
sources: s:wp-korean-shamanism s:wp-fulu s:wp-insa-dong s:wp-dol-hareubang s:web-koreaherald-test-taker-gifts s:wp-chapssal-tteok s:wp-yeot s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## Catholic sacramentals (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/catholic-sacramentals/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/catholic-sacramentals.json
id: catholic-sacramentals
native: sacramentalia (Latin)
aliases: sacramental · devotional article · blessed object
said: sa-kra-men-TAH-lee-ah
when: 820 CE to now (still carried)
countries: VA IT FR GB PT US
root: Latin sacramentalia, the plural of sacramentale, from sacramentum — the word used for the seven sacraments, which these objects and rites deliberately resemble without being.
against: traffic — said by the description of ichthys emblems applied to vehicles: to signify that the owner is a Christian and to offer protection while driving [s:wp-sacramental]
against: demons — said by the Catechism itself, which lists exorcisms as one of the three kinds of sacramental [s:wp-sacramental]
against: curse — said by the Catechism of the Catholic Church, in the negative: paragraph 2117 condemns magic and sorcery and adds that wearing charms is also reprehensible [s:web-ccc-first-commandment]
what: The class of blessed objects and rites the Catholic Church puts around the sacraments: holy water, blessed candles given out at Candlemas, blessed palms, blessed ashes, blessed salt, a crucifix, a cross necklace, a headcovering, holy cards, a scapular, a medal. The Catechism sorts sacramentals into three kinds — blessings, consecrations and dedications, and exorcisms. They are also recognised, in their own forms, by the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, the Church of the East, the Lutheran churches, the Old Catholic Church, the Anglican churches and Independent Catholic churches.
story: This is the one tradition in this atlas that has published a boundary against being in it, and the boundary is the record.

The Church's own definition: sacramentals are "sacred signs which bear a resemblance to the sacraments: they signify effects, particularly of a spiritual nature, which are obtained through the Church's intercession." The machinery is deliberately different from the sacraments'. Sacramentals do not confer the grace of the Holy Spirit the way the sacraments do; by the Church's prayer they prepare a person to receive grace and dispose them to cooperate with it. Unlike the seven sacraments, which the Church holds were instituted by Christ, sacramentals were instituted by the Church, which can change their form and number; and they do not act ex opere operato, by the working of the work, but ex opere operantis, by the working of the one who does it. The Catechism puts the distinction in an example: the water of baptism causes the forgiveness of sins within the sacramental celebration, while holy water, which recalls baptism, has no effect in itself and depends on the faith of the person who crosses themselves with it at the church door.

That is the line. On the other side of it, in the same Catechism, comes the condemnation. Paragraph 2111 defines its terms — "Superstition is the deviation of religious feeling and of the practices this feeling imposes" — and says that attributing a magical importance to otherwise lawful practices, or crediting the efficacy of prayers to their external performance apart from the interior dispositions they require, falls under it. Paragraph 2117 is blunter: after condemning magic and sorcery as gravely contrary to the virtue of religion, it adds four words — "Wearing charms is also reprehensible."

And on the third side there is what people do. The Miraculous Medal was distributed by the Daughters of Charity during a cholera pandemic and passed a billion copies within fifty years. Saint Christopher medals are sold with the promise printed on them in French and Spanish. The Agnus Dei, a papal wax disc, was carried against storm, pestilence, fire, flood and the dangers of childbirth. The Brown Scapular carries a promise of salvation to those who wear it piously. The 2004 Enchiridion Indulgentiarum grants a partial indulgence to the faithful who use a crucifix or cross, a crown, a scapular, or a medal blessed by a priest — so the Church attaches a benefit to wearing the object, by its own procedure, in the same book of rules that says wearing charms is reprehensible.

The distinction the Church draws is between an object that disposes a wearer toward grace and an object worked to compel a result. This atlas prints that distinction, prints the condemnation, prints the promise, and prints what a driver with a medal on the dashboard says the medal is for. It does not rule on which of them is describing the same object.
kin: agnus-dei — the oldest dated object in this tradition and the one whose claims read least like a sacramental and most like the thing the Catechism forbids
kin: st-christopher-medal — the sacramental that travels, with its promise stamped on it in French and Spanish
kin: miraculous-medal — the one with a documented origin, a named visionary, a goldsmith, a mint date and a billion copies
kin: brown-scapular — the one that is worn as clothing, and the one whose promise is the largest
kin: consecration — the act that makes an object a sacramental at all: the Church's blessing, by a priest or by a qualified lay person where the ordinary permits
kin: counting-beads — the rosary, which the Church files as a popular devotion rather than as a sacramental, and the beads, which it files as a devotional article
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — where most of these objects are acquired and what is done to them there
kin: ex-voto-wall — the other half of the Catholic economy of objects: these are given to the wearer, those are given back to the shrine
kin: tama-votive — the Orthodox counterpart, which does the giving-back in stamped metal
kin: ladanka — the Orthodox object worn at the neck beside the cross, blessed the same way and argued over in the same terms
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — what happens to these objects where the Church's line is drawn in one place and the household draws it in another
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the neighbouring tradition, which this one has spent a thousand years defining itself against and borrowing from
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read about words, and the place where the Church's distinction between a sacramental and a charm gets set beside everyone else's
kin: car-saint — where the argument lives now: a medal on a dashboard, and two accounts of what it is doing there

## Egyptian amulet craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/egyptian-amulet-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/egyptian-amulet-craft.json
id: egyptian-amulet-craft
native: 𓋹𓊽𓎬 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: ancient Egyptian amulets · pharaonic amulet practice
when: 3000 BCE – 641 CE
countries: EG SD
object: form=pendant materials=faience,carnelian,lapis,gold,glass,terracotta,bone worn=neck,chest,wrist,finger,grave,cradle,door
against: the-dead — said by Egyptian funerary texts, which set out which amulet goes where on a body and what is said over it [s:wp-ancient-egyptian-funerary-practices]
against: child-harm — said by Egyptian households, which kept Bes and Taweret for mothers and infants [s:wp-taweret]
against: snakebite — said by the cippi, whose spells are against venomous bites and stings [s:wp-horus-on-the-crocodiles]
against: illness — said by Egyptian religious texts, as summarised by Egyptologists — the wedjat stands for well-being and healing before it stands for anything else [s:wp-eye-of-horus]
what: The practice of making, wearing and burying small protective objects in ancient Egypt: shapes cut from stone or moulded in faience — quartz paste glazed blue or green in a kiln — pierced and strung, worn in life and packed into the wrappings at death. It ran for roughly three thousand years, produced amulets by the million, and is the single largest body of amulet evidence anywhere on earth.
story: Egypt's amulets come in two economies and the same workshops served both.

The living wore them strung at the neck. The dead were wrapped in them, by rule. What went where was not a matter of taste: the funerary texts say which amulet goes on which part of the body, which stone it should be cut from, and what is to be recited over it. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead asks for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck. Chapter 30B goes on a heart scarab laid over the heart. A gold djed at the neck comes with a spell that promises the mummy the use of its spine back. That is an unusual thing for an amulet tradition to have: a manual.

The material made the scale possible. Faience is cheap, mouldable and does not rot, so a single mould turns out eyes and beetles and ankhs by the tray, and three thousand years later they are all still there. *Inference —* that is also the tradition's largest distortion. The reed, cloth, dough and wax charms that stood beside the faience ones are gone; what survives is what survives, and a museum drawer is a record of durability, not a census of what Egypt wore.

The shapes are hieroglyphs. An amulet cut in the form of a sign was meant to hand its wearer the quality the sign wrote: life for the ankh, stability for the djed, soundness for the wedjat, protection for the sa that Taweret holds. Composites run several signs together — ankh and was and djed, 'life, dominion and stability' — and were worn more often than the ankh on its own.

Not all of it was writing. Bes and Taweret are household gods with faces and bodies, moulded onto baby bottles, chairs, headrests and jars, and worn on the thigh as tattoos. The cippi are slabs you rinse and drink from. The scarab was an office seal as well as a charm.

The practice ended with the religion that needed it. Nothing in Egypt is now made to do what Chapter 156 describes. The shapes went on: the ankh survived into Coptic Christianity as the crux ansata, the wedjat into a worldwide jewellery trade, and Bes and Taweret into museum cases and fiction.
how: Moulded in faience or cut from stone — carnelian, lapis, green jasper, steatite fired hard — then pierced and strung, or set in gold. For the dead, placed by the embalmers at the position the funerary text specifies, with the spell recited over it. For the living, worn at the neck or the wrist, or set on a swivel ring.
today: Archaeological. The tradition is studied rather than practised, and the objects are concentrated in a handful of museums: the British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum's Egyptian galleries, the Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology in London, the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Flinders Petrie's excavation and sorting of amulets into classes is still the framework museums label by. The modern trade in Egyptian-shaped jewellery, sold in Cairo, Luxor and the airports and worn worldwide, is a separate thing and is described on the object records rather than here.
kin: wedjat-eye — the shape this tradition made more of than any other, for the living and for the dead
kin: scarab — its other mass product, and the one that doubled as an office seal
kin: heart-scarab — the piece it made to argue on a dead person's behalf at a trial
kin: ankh-amulet — the sign everybody knows and the amulet it rarely actually cut
kin: tyet-knot — the one whose placement its own text specifies, down to the stone
kin: djed-pillar — the spine it hung at a mummy's neck, and raised as a column at the Sed festival
kin: bes-amulet — the household half of the tradition — a god who guarded a door and a cradle rather than a tomb
kin: taweret-amulet — its oldest shape, and the one whose sales peaked at the very end
kin: cippus-of-horus — its most textual object: a spell you wash off a stone and drink
kin: faience — the material that made the whole scale of it possible
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator whose classes museums still label by
kin: wallis-budge — the British Museum keeper through whose translations most English readers met the spells
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-ancient-egyptian-funerary-practices s:wp-ancient-egyptian-religion s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-taweret s:wp-horus-on-the-crocodiles s:wp-flinders-petrie s:wp-e-a-wallis-budge s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology s:wp-british-museum s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art

## Engimono (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/japanese-engimono/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/japanese-engimono.json
id: japanese-engimono
native: 縁起物 (Han)
aliases: Japanese luck goods · shrine and temple charms · engi-mono
said: en-gi-mo-no
when: 1336 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
root: Japanese engi (縁起), an omen or an auspicious origin, plus mono (物), a thing — 'a thing of good omen'
object: form=packet materials=paper,wood,cloth,terracotta,ink,plastic worn=neck,pocket,phone,wall,vehicle,shop,door,burnt
against: traffic — said by Japanese shrines and temples, which issue kōtsū-anzen omamori for drivers and travellers of all sorts [s:wp-omamori]
against: exams — said by the same counters, which issue gakugyō-jōju for students and scholars — education and passing examinations [s:wp-omamori]
against: bad-luck — said by the tradition's own categories: yaku-yoke, avoidance of evil, and kaiun, opening luck [s:wp-omamori]
against: childbirth — said by shrines issuing anzan omamori for a healthy pregnancy and an easy delivery [s:wp-omamori]
against: house — said by shrines issuing kanai-anzen for the safety, peace and prosperity of a household, and ofuda placed on gates, doorways, kitchens and ceilings [s:wp-ofuda]
against: poverty — said by the shop-luck end of it — shōbai-hanjō omamori for success in business, the kumade rake sold at tori-no-ichi for raking in fortune, and the beckoning cat set near the entrance of shops, restaurants, pachinko parlours and bars [s:wp-maneki-neko]
against: loneliness — said by shrines issuing en-musubi omamori, for acquiring a mate and for marriage, sold to singles and to couples [s:wp-omamori]
what: Objects bought at a shrine, a temple or a fair to bring a named good thing: a brocade pouch for traffic safety, a paper or wooden tablet for the household altar, a red papier-mâché doll with blank eyes, a ceramic cat with a raised paw, a bamboo rake for raking in fortune, a folded paper fortune tied to a rack. Japanese Wikipedia's list runs across harvest, trade, household safety, health, long life, marital harmony and the turning-away of misfortune. Most are sold on an approach road, in a temple precinct or in the town outside the gate, and most are replaced once a year.
story: The tradition is distinctive for being administered. Ofuda — the tablet for the household altar — descend from the Taoist lingfu by way of Onmyodo, and from woodblock-printed Buddhist texts and images made by temples since the Nara and Heian periods. In the medieval period the three Kumano shrines in Wakayama stamped their paper talismans with stylised crows and called them Kumano Goofu; those sheets were used for oath-taking and contract-drafting, with the terms written on the blank side.

The national distribution system is dated at every step. The shinsatsu most shrines now issue are modelled on the Ise talisman, the Jingu Taima, which began as purification wands handed out across the country by the oshi, the wandering preachers attached to Ise, as a sign that prayers had been performed on a household's behalf. Distribution of these began in the Muromachi period and peaked in the Edo: a document of 1777 indicates that eighty-nine to ninety per cent of all households in the country owned an Ise talisman. In 1871 an imperial decree abolished the oshi and moved production to the shrine's administrative offices; in 1900 a new Department of Priests took it over; in 1927 it passed to the National Association of Shinto Priests, and after the Second World War to the Association of Shinto Shrines, which distributes Jingu Taima to affiliated shrines to this day. Very few charm traditions anywhere can be traced through four changes of administrative owner.

The market is the other half. Sensō-ji granted the shops that became the Nakamise permission to trade on its main approach in 1685, in exchange for their charging local residents for sweeping the grounds — a temple licensing a shopping street and taking maintenance labour as rent. The daruma has its own annual fair: Takasaki's daruma-ichi at Shorinzan draws, on the city's own figure, over 400,000 people from across the Kanto Plain to buy the year's dolls, and Takasaki produces 80 per cent of Japan's daruma. The doll itself came out of a production problem. The charms the Daruma-dera's founder drew were good for one year, so parishioners needed new ones annually; the ninth priest, Togaku, solved the demand by cutting wooden block moulds around the beginning of the Meiwa period (1764–72) and letting the peasants make their own papier-mâché charms. Most of those households were silk farmers, a crop the account describes as needing a great deal of luck.

The beckoning cat is dated from the other end, by pictures. The earliest figurine record is the marushime-neko, an Imado ware variant of the late Edo period; the Bukō nenpyō chronicle of Edo has an entry dated 1852, and Utagawa Hiroshige's ukiyo-e Joruri-machi Hanka no zu, painted the same year, shows marushime-neko being sold at Sensō-ji. A newspaper mentioned them in 1876; a 1902 advertisement shows they were popular by then. Four temples and shrines claim to be the birthplace.

The argument inside the tradition is about manufacture, and the complainants are priests. Where a popular shrine cannot keep up with demand for a charm, it turns to factories, and priests have complained about the quality of what comes back. Separately, shops sell generic omamori carrying licensed characters — Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy, Kewpie — that no shrine issued and no priest charged. *Inference —* the tradition has an unusually clean test for the argument, because its objects carry a shrine's name and seal. What a factory charm lacks is not craftsmanship but the stamp, and both sides of the argument know it.
how: Made or printed, then consecrated, then issued rather than sold. Omamori enclose paper or wood carrying a prayer inside a brocade bag; the practice describes them as made sacred through ritual and as holding busshin, spiritual offshoots, in a Shinto frame, or kesshin, manifestations, in a Buddhist one. They are not opened: shrines and their buyers alike hold that opening one loses the protection. Payment is treated as a donation: the objects are not bought but received, sazukaru or ukeru. Replacement is annual, customarily at or just after New Year, and the old one goes back to the shrine or temple that issued it to be burnt, as a mark of respect to the deity that helped through the year. If a visitor cannot find a charm for their need they can ask a priest to have one made, and if enough people ask for the same thing the shrine may start stocking it.
today: Live, and expanding into categories older shrines did not have. Kanda Myojin in Tokyo issues charms for IT equipment and electronics; Sega released free digital omamori in 2022 for success at school and work; omamori hang from phone straps, bags and car mirrors, and have been made as bumper decals, bicycle reflectors and card-shaped objects. The annual cycle holds: Japanese Wikipedia's own entry is organised as a month-by-month calendar of fairs — tori-no-ichi for the kumade rake, daruma-ichi for the dolls, hagoita-ichi for the decorated paddles. As of 2026 an engimono is still, in the tradition's own framing, something you receive at a counter, keep for a year, and bring back.
kin: omamori — the tradition's signature object: a brocade bag nobody opens, replaced every year and burnt at the shrine that issued it
kin: ofuda — the tablet the whole administered system runs on, from the Ise oshi to the Association of Shinto Shrines
kin: daruma — the object with its own annual market, its own city, and a documented production reason for existing
kin: maneki-neko — the shop-luck end of the tradition, dated from 1852 by a chronicle entry and a Hiroshige print of it being sold at Sensō-ji
kin: omikuji — the counter where the transaction is a draw rather than a purchase, and the paper is tied up rather than taken home
kin: teru-teru-bozu — the edge case: made at home, by a child, from tissue, with no shrine's name on it and nothing to return
kin: senninbari — the Japanese luck object this tradition did not issue — a thousand stitches from a thousand women, with no priest and no counter anywhere in it
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice this tradition runs at national scale, and the reason its output is an annual figure rather than a stock
kin: burning-retirement — the other end of that year — an old charm goes back to its own shrine to be burnt, not thrown away
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the step that separates an issued charm from a souvenir, and the one priests invoke when they complain about factory stock
kin: chinese-fu-craft — where the paper tablet comes from: the Taoist lingfu, carried into Japan through Onmyodo
kin: fushimi-inari — the counter at the scale of 32,000 branch shrines
kin: senso-ji — the approach road the tradition is sold on, licensed by the temple in 1685 in exchange for sweeping the grounds

## Ethiopian scroll craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/ethiopian-scroll-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/ethiopian-scroll-craft.json
id: ethiopian-scroll-craft
native: ደብተራ (Ge'ez)
aliases: dabtara craft · Ethiopian healing scrolls · kitab making
said: the maker is a dabtara, däbtära
when: 1500 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ET
object: form=scroll materials=parchment,ink,cloth,leather worn=neck,wall,pocket
against: evil-eye — said by the scrolls' own texts, which the source says offer protection or cure against the Evil Eye [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: spirits — said by the same texts, against malevolent spirits [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: illness — said by the source, whose published range is 'bed bugs, to home intruders, to smallpox' [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
against: childbirth — said by the historical manuscript record, in which most scrolls were made for women's reproductive health conditions [s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls]
RESTRICTED: No text from a scroll is printed here, and no formula. The prayers, the mystical names and the incantations are the dabtara's craft, and the tradition's own arrangement keeps them behind a reader: the scroll has to be read aloud in Ge'ez by someone trained to read it. This record prints the craft, not its contents.
what: The making of painted parchment scrolls by dabtaras — unordained clerics of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church — for named people, cut to their height, written in Ge'ez, and read aloud to them by someone who can read it. The craft sits beside the church without being inside its orders.
story: The dabtara is the whole tradition in one job description. He is a liturgical specialist who has gone past memorising the Psalms into courses in poetry, liturgy and writing. In Ethiopia the power to write includes the power to write prayers and spells, so the same word carries a second sense.

The scroll is made for one person and stands in for them. An animal, usually a goat or a sheep, is sacrificed as a substitute for the patron; the patron is rubbed by and bathed in its contents; the hide is soaked for days, dried, stretched, then scraped, washed and dried into parchment. The dabtara writes on it and paints it, and it is cut to the same height as the person it is for, though it may be made longer. A larger one hangs on a wall instead.

The writing is Ge'ez, the church's liturgical language, and the texts combine Christian prayers invoking saints and the Trinity with mystical names of God and with incantations. Because few speak Ge'ez, the scroll does not work by being owned: a third party literate in Ge'ez must read it to the afflicted person for its properties to take effect. *Inference —* that requirement is rare in this atlas. Most charms are worn and forgotten; this one needs a second human being in the room every time it is used.

The painted signs are their own vocabulary: crosses, eight-pointed stars, the gätsä säb'e — a face inside an eight-pointed star — and eyes, in geometric pairs, rimmed in red. The palette is fixed at six colours: black, white, red, blue, green, yellow.

What the scrolls are for runs from the trivial to the lethal — the range published is bed bugs, home intruders, smallpox — and they treat the spiritual cause while homeopathic medicines are used for the physical symptoms. In the historical manuscript record, most were made for conditions of women's reproductive health.

The earliest surviving scrolls are sixteenth-century. The practice is held to go back to the tenth, which is five hundred years this project cannot put an object behind.
how: Sacrifice, then parchment, then writing, then reading. The animal stands in for the patron; the hide becomes the surface; the dabtara writes the prayers and paints the figures; the finished scroll is rolled, kept, and read aloud in Ge'ez when it is needed.
today: Living. Scrolls are still made and still commissioned, and they are also collected: the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds several, and the Museum of Witchcraft and Magic in Boscastle publishes an example in Ge'ez on vellum. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for how many dabtaras work, or for what a scroll costs.
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the object this craft makes, cut to the height of the person it is for
kin: parchment — the material, and the animal that stood in for the patron before it became one
kin: inscribing — the practice at the centre of it — in this tradition, writing is the power
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the neighbouring African Christian mark, made by a tattooist rather than a cleric
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition it most resembles in method — scripture written out, folded and carried — across a religious line
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the other scriptural tradition here that writes divine names for protection, and argues about where the line is
kin: merkato-addis — the Addis Ababa market where church goods and scrolls change hands
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read behind the restriction on this page
sources: s:wp-ethiopian-talismanic-scrolls s:wp-amulet s:wp-talisman s:wp-wellcome-collection

## European folk apotropaic craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/european-folk-apotropaic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/european-folk-apotropaic.json
id: european-folk-apotropaic
aliases: European protective folk practice · household charms of Europe · cold-iron and threshold craft
said: ap-oh-TROH-pay-ik, from Greek apotrepo, 'to turn away'
when: 1308 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE IT ES DE BG DK LT EE RU
root: The label is Greek — apotrepo, 'to turn away' — and it is a scholar's word, not a carrier's. English speakers inside the practice said ward, charm, luck.
object: form=door-piece materials=iron,wood,thread,glass,herb,amber,leather,cloth,silver worn=door,lintel,hearth,wall,roof,neck,pocket,cradle,foundation
against: witchcraft — said by English and Irish households, per the cited survey — grotesque faces cut on churches and castles to frighten off witches, rowan chosen for a chimney post or mantel to discourage it, an iron knife buried under a threshold to keep witches out [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
against: spirits — said by the cold-iron rule, recorded across Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia: iron repels, contains or harms ghosts, fairies and witches [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
against: fire — said by Irish households at Imbolc — a Brigid's cross hung in the rafters to bring the saint's blessing and protection for the rest of the year [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: bad-luck — said by Irish households at Samhain, who fixed a 'parshell' of sticks and straw over the doorway against bad luck, illness and witchcraft [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across the Mediterranean, the Balkans and Eastern Europe; Frederick Elworthy assembled the European half of it into one subject in 1895 [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: child-harm — said by European households, for whom an amber necklace is a traditional remedy for colic or teething pain — the American Academy of Pediatrics and the FDA have warned strongly against them as a choking and strangulation hazard [s:wp-amber]
against: livestock — said by Irish families, who mounted the crosses in outhouses and stables as well as in the dwelling [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
what: Protective objects made and kept by European households outside the church's list: iron over a door, a bottle in a hearth, a shoe in a wall, rowan bound with red thread, a cross of rushes in the rafters, a bead against a look. No priesthood, no manual, no initiation. The maker is whoever needs the thing — a farmer, a mother, a blacksmith, a child gathering rushes on 31 January — and most of it is made at home from what the house already holds.
story: Start at the threshold, because the tradition does. Doorways and windows were held to be where harm gets in, and the answer went on them: grotesque faces cut over oven and kiln doors, gargoyles and sheela na gigs and hunky punks on churches and castles, a horseshoe nailed above a door, an iron knife buried under the entrance, a lantern cut from a turnip or a swede at Samhain. Everything else in this record is a variation on a guarded opening.

Iron carries most of the load. Cold iron is recorded across Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia as repelling, containing or harming ghosts, fairies and witches — hence the horseshoe on the door, hence the iron fence round a graveyard, said to hold the dead in rather than keep anything out. The horseshoe is where the tradition's internal disagreements become visible. Points up so the luck does not fall out; points down so it pours onto whoever stands beneath; in some tellings either is fine so long as the shoe was used, was found rather than bought, and can be touched. Where luck attaches to the owner and not the hanger, a stolen or borrowed shoe carries it back to the owner. One reputed origin is the story of St Dunstan, a blacksmith who became Archbishop of Canterbury in 959, nailing a shoe to the Devil's hoof and removing it only on a promise never to enter a house with one over the door.

The calendar does the rest. On 31 January Irish families gathered rushes; that night the head of the household supervised the weaving of Brigid's crosses; on 1 February they went up in the dwelling, the outhouses and the stables, and a year later they were taken down and burnt or buried, burial preferred because of Brigid's link to agriculture. The practice is first attested in the 17th century and was in decline by the 20th, partly because house renovations left nowhere to hang them. That is an unusually complete account of a folk object: a start date, a decline, and a building-trade reason for it.

*Inference —* the thing that makes this a tradition rather than a pile of customs is the absence of a gate. Every other tradition in this atlas restricts something — a script, a lineage, an initiation, a clan. This one's objects are made by the person who needs them, from rushes, rowan, a worn shoe, a bottle from the kitchen, a stone with a hole in it. That is why its evidence is so lopsided: what survives is what got walled in or thrown down a well, and what was said over it was almost never written.

It was assembled as a subject late, and by three men buying. Frederick Elworthy published The Evil Eye in 1895 and Horns of Honour in 1900, buying in Spain and Italy as he wrote. Siegfried Seligmann, a German ophthalmologist, put out the two volumes of Der böse Blick und Verwandtes in 1910 and gathered more than 1,500 amulets doing it. Edward Lovett, a bank cashier in the City of London, collected what Londoners were carrying in their pockets — a mole's foot, a dried frog, a blue bead, a caul — and published Magic in Modern London in 1925. *Inference —* the shape of every museum case of European charms follows the shape of those three men's buying, and so, to a degree this atlas cannot measure, does the shape of this record.
how: Made at home, from the house's own materials, usually at a fixed point in the year or at a moment of threat. Rushes woven on the eve of a feast; rowan cut and bound with red thread; a bottle filled and put under the hearth when the house was built or when somebody suspected a neighbour; a worn shoe pushed into a chimney breast during building work; a horseshoe found in a lane and nailed up. Renewal is annual where the object is vegetable and never where it is iron. Retirement is by fire or by burial, and the choice between them is itself traditional — Irish practice preferred burying a year-old Brigid's cross to burning it.
today: Alive and mostly unremarked. Horseshoes still go over doors, four-leaf clovers are still looked for, amber necklaces are still sold for teething in Europe and warned against by the American Academy of Pediatrics and the FDA, and Bulgarian martenitsi still go up on 1 March. The objects have largely left the farm for the souvenir shelf, and workshops like those on Via San Gregorio Armeno in Naples supply both at once. Whether a cornicello bought in a Naples lane by a visitor is the same object as one worn by the seller is a live argument with named people on both sides, and this atlas reports it on the object records rather than settling it here.
kin: iron — the tradition's one near-universal rule: cold iron turns the thing away, and a horseshoe is the cheapest piece of it a house could get
kin: horseshoe — its most-copied object, and the one whose own carriers argue about which way up it goes
kin: witch-bottle — its best-documented recipe, and the only one it writes down
kin: concealed-shoe — its most thoroughly counted object — a worn shoe walled into a chimney or a roof, by the thousand, and never explained in writing by anyone who did it
kin: brigids-cross — the calendar half of it: rushes gathered on 31 January, woven that night, hung on 1 February, taken down and burnt or buried a year later
kin: hagstone — the object that shows what the tradition costs — a stone with a hole, found not bought, made by nobody
kin: rowan-cross — its clearest case of a plant used the way iron is used, bound with red thread and kept at a door
kin: caul — its one charm nobody can choose to acquire, and the one with a documented resale market
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the neighbouring tradition, which this one has spent a thousand years borrowing from and being disowned by; a Brigid's cross sits on the line
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the ancient layer underneath, which supplied the word and some of the shapes and none of the households
kin: frederick-elworthy — the man who made this a single subject in English, in 1895, by buying the objects while he wrote about them
kin: edward-lovett — the collector who proved it was still alive, by taking a mole's foot and a blue bead off London streets in the 1900s rather than reading about the countryside
sources: s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-iron-in-folklore s:wp-horseshoe s:wp-concealed-shoes s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-rowan s:wp-corn-dolly s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-cornicello s:wp-hex-sign s:wp-amber s:wp-four-leaf-clover s:wp-martenitsa s:web-unesco-march-1 s:wp-via-san-gregorio-armeno s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-frederick-thomas-elworthy s:wp-edward-lovett s:web-siegfried-seligmann-dewiki s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum s:web-prm-amulets-guide s:wp-wellcome-collection s:wp-british-folklore

## Fulu — Taoist talismanic craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/chinese-fu-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/chinese-fu-craft.json
id: chinese-fu-craft
native: 符籙 (Han)
aliases: fulu · talismanic script · Taoist talismans · fu
said: fú-lù
when: 25 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN TW MY VN
root: Chinese fu (符), instructions for deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions or charms; lu (籙), a register of priestly membership listing the skills a priest is trained in
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,ink,cloth,copper,brass,coin,wood worn=door,wall,pocket,shop,burnt,swallowed
against: illness — said by Taoist zhuyou practice, used in China alongside medicine, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage, and with official support from the Sui to the late Ming [s:wp-fulu]
against: spirits — said by the coin talismans, most of which request Lei Gong to protect their carriers from evil spirits and misfortune [s:wp-fulu]
against: demons — said by the fu itself, defined in the tradition as instructions for deities and spirits and symbols for exorcism [s:wp-fulu]
against: bad-luck — said by Chinese households at New Year, who paste the character fu (福) upside down on a door so that it reads as good luck arriving [s:wp-fu-character]
against: house — said by users of the bagua mirror, installed to turn away negative energy and guard the entryways of a residence [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
RESTRICTED: This craft restricts its own script and the atlas prints no example. The method of writing fulu is passed in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples; forms, incantations and mudras differ from sect to sect; and, in the words of the scholarship, the illegibility exists so that only a small number of qualified clergy can produce them. So this record describes what fulu look like and what they are for, names the priesthood that writes them, and does not reproduce a character, an incantation or a mudra — nor reconstruct one from a museum photograph.
what: Writing that is not meant to be read. Fulu are Taoist talismanic characters — strokes that resemble Chinese characters, often an existing word elongated, with non-character symbols worked in, sometimes two characters stacked into one — painted or written on paper, cloth or metal by a Taoist priest. The same craft supplies the charm coins, the mirror that hangs over a doorway, and the New Year slips pasted on a door.
story: The unreadability is the point, and its own scholars say so. Yang Zhaohua notes that a number of the earliest Taoist talismans were simple and legible, and that later examples became deliberately cryptic in order to signal their divinity. James Robson and Gil Raz hold that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority and is one of talismanic script's defining features. Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls it a linguistic archaism, a veil of unfathomable otherworldliness designed so that only a small number of qualified clergy can produce them.

That had already settled by the Eastern Jin (317–420). Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi that successful use of a talisman did not depend on whether the user could decipher the script, so long as the inscription itself was right. By then illegibility was a sign of divine authority rather than a defect.

Style varies by sect, and so does everything else: the characters differ from sect to sect, each sect has its own incantations and its own mudras for making them, and even the invocations used for a single deity vary between sects. The method of writing is passed in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples and treated as a craft for communicating with local deities and spirits. The fulu pai — the informal grouping of priests across schools who work this way — take their name from it.

The medical strand has an institutional history. Talismanic technique has been used in China alongside medicine, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage, at least as far back as the Eastern Han, when the Way of the Taiping used it to heal. In medical writing it is called zhuyou, and it held official support between the Sui and the late Ming, declining after rival acupuncture practices were recognised by the imperial court as a medical discipline in the sixth century. Traditional Chinese medicine rejects zhuyou; Chinese folk healers still use it widely; and with the arrival of Western psychology in the 20th century it began to be read as a Chinese counterpart to hypnosis.

The craft also travelled, and two other traditions in this atlas are downstream of it. Fulu were incorporated into Chinese Buddhism; they inspired Japan's ofuda, by way of Onmyodo; and Korea's bujeok comes out of the same stock. Coin talismans carry fulu at the beginning and the end of the inscription, and many of them have not been deciphered — one specimen has talismanic script written beside Chinese characters suspected to be its gloss.

The household end of it is a different character and a different logic. Fu (福), good fortune, is mounted on doorways at Chinese New Year, printed on a square of red paper or stitched in fabric, and hung upside down: in nearly all varieties of Chinese the words for 'upside-down' and 'to arrive' are homophones, so an inverted fu reads as 'good luck arrives'. The practice dates to at least the Song dynasty and the account describes it as universal among Chinese people regardless of income.
how: Structure only, because the making is transmitted in secret. A priest of a particular sect writes the characters, using that sect's forms, incantations and mudras, on paper, cloth or metal. The result is displayed, carried, burnt, or — in the medical use — dissolved or otherwise administered. A lu, a register, records which priests hold which skills, so the entitlement to write one is a matter of record inside the tradition rather than of talent. Coin charms carry the script cast into metal instead of brushed, with fulu opening and closing the inscription.
today: Live in Taiwan, mainland China and the Chinese diaspora, in temples and in folk healing. Popular accounts of fulu are published for general readers, including by Taiwanese temple-culture sites, while the sect-specific forms stay inside the sects. The New Year fu on a red square is everywhere Chinese New Year is kept. Museum and numismatic collections hold large runs of charm coins whose inscriptions remain unread, which is the tradition's own design working on its own evidence.
kin: fu-talisman — the object itself: the priest's written slip, and the reason this record prints no script
kin: ping-an-fu — the peace-and-safety slip, issued over a censer with a name and a birth date rather than written for a private client
kin: charm-coin — the same script cast in metal — fulu opening and closing an inscription that in many cases nobody has yet read
kin: bagua-mirror — the door-piece whose techniques the tradition is credited with, and the one household object here that works by reflection rather than by writing
kin: fu-word — the two characters this record has to keep apart — 符 the talisman and 福 the fortune pasted upside down at New Year
kin: coin-square — the sign the charm coins carry: a round coin with a square hole, cast, inscribed and read within this tradition
kin: mirror-sign — the other technique it holds — deflection, which needs no script at all
kin: japanese-engimono — downstream: the ofuda is this craft's paper slip, carried into Japan through Onmyodo and then put on an administered national footing
kin: korean-bujeok-craft — the other descendant, where the unreadable script arrived in Hanja and the specialists who draw it are mostly women
kin: paper — the material the craft is built on, and the one it burns to deliver a message
kin: inscribing — the practice at its most restricted — the strokes are the secret, not the intention behind them
kin: hanging-at-door — where most of this output ends up: a slip, a mirror or a red square on a doorway
sources: s:wp-fulu s:wp-fu-character s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-numismatic-charm s:wp-bagua s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:web-taiwanese-gods-fulu s:wp-ofuda s:wp-korean-shamanism
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## Greek and Roman protective magic (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/greco-roman-apotropaic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/greco-roman-apotropaic.json
id: greco-roman-apotropaic
native: ἀποτρόπαιος (Greek)
aliases: apotropaic magic · Graeco-Roman amulet practice
said: apotrópaios, 'turning away'; the Greeks also said probaskania, periammata, periapta, phylaktiria, alexikaka
when: 700 BCE – 499 CE
countries: GR IT TR GB LY
root: Ancient Greek ἀποτρέπω, apotrépō, 'to turn away' — the whole theory of the practice in one verb
against: evil-eye — said by Greeks and Romans alike; the cited account names the Gorgon as the most widely used image among the Greeks for averting evil [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
against: envy — said by Pliny, on the fascinus as a medicus invidiae, and Roman hosts who set out laughter-provoking images against invidia [s:wp-fascinus]
against: child-harm — said by Greek parents, who hung amulets on infants and committed them to child-nurturing deities; and Roman parents, who gave a boy a bulla on his ninth day and a girl a lunula [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
against: house — said by Greek builders, who carved bearded satyr-like faces over the doors of ovens and kilns to protect the work from fire and mishap [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
against: illness — said by the wearers of carved gems, which the cited account describes as worn to take on the associated powers of a god rather than out of piety [s:wp-amulet]
what: A practice organised around one idea: harm arrives through a look, so the answer is to catch the look. The Greek word for it is apotrépō, to turn away. The objects are the ones that do the catching — a Gorgon face, a phallus, a bead, a crescent, a locket on a child — and the argument in the sources is about what makes a glance stop, not about what a charm contains.
story: The Greeks committed the child to kourotrophic deities and hung amulets on it. They put charms in houses and wore them against the evil eye, and hung them on their animals too. Peisistratus hung the figure of a kind of grasshopper before the Acropolis of Athens. They spat into the folds of their clothes. They dressed boys as girls to avert the eye, and told the story of Achilles dressed as a girl at the court of Lycomedes as a case of it. Exaggerated eyes were painted on the drinking cups called kylikes from the sixth century BCE to the end of the classical period, perhaps to stop anything entering the mouth while drinking; fishing boats in parts of the Mediterranean still have eyes on the bows.

Rome added laughter to terror. In Roman art, envy was thought to bring bad luck to the person envied, so hosts set out images meant to make guests laugh: outsized phalluses, deformities, hunchbacks, pygmies. Pliny called the phallus a medicus invidiae, a remedy for envy. The mechanism the sources describe is not power but interruption — in most cases what turns the eye is the shame or the laughter the obscenity produces.

The literate end of the practice is the gemstones and the lead. Carved gems, many thousands of them, pair a stone with a god so the wearer takes on the associated powers; one gold amulet box from the Thetford treasure in Norfolk was found to contain sulphur, for its evil-repelling qualities. And the same hands that cut gems scratched curse tablets, which run the machinery backwards and aim it at a named person.

*Inference —* the substitutions are the argument. Illyrians used the phallus, the hand, the leg and animal teeth against the same harm the eye was used against; Romans used a winged phallus; southern Italy still cuts a horn. Nothing about a horn resembles an eye. What they share is that each of them takes a glance.
kin: gorgoneion — its loudest object, and the one whose function classicists agree on
kin: fascinum — its most Roman object, and the one Pliny explains in two words
kin: bulla — what a Roman boy wore, from day nine to the toga virilis
kin: lunula — what a Roman girl wore, until the eve of her wedding
kin: magical-gem — the literate and expensive end of it, cut in stone and written in names nobody can read
kin: curse-tablet — the same craft aimed the other way, at a named person, and buried
kin: eye — the sign the whole practice is organised around, whether it is drawn or substituted for
kin: phallic-sign — the substitute Rome preferred, doing the same interception by a different route
kin: cornicello — its living descendant in southern Italy — the same look-catching, in red coral
kin: holy-rider-pendant — what the practice turns into once the Mediterranean is Christian: the same grammar, new names
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian who assembled the European evidence for the eye and its substitutes in 1895, and whose groupings museums still use
kin: christopher-faraone — the scholar of Greek binding spells and love magic, and the reason the curse tablets can be read as a system
sources: s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-fascinus s:wp-gorgons s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-amulet s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-bulla-amulet s:wp-lunula-amulet
