## Illa practice (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/andean-illa-practice/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/andean-illa-practice.json
id: andean-illa-practice
native: illa ()
aliases: conopa · canopa · inqaychu · enqa · Andean miniature practice
said: EE-ya, Quechua
when: 1400 CE to now (still carried)
countries: BO PE
root: Quechua illa, a term for the small carved stone figures used in herding and household rites; colonial Spanish sources call them conopa or canopa, and Quechua-speaking herding communities also say inqaychu and enqa
object: form=figurine materials=earth,wood,paper,terracotta,gold worn=field,wall,shop,pocket
against: infertility — said by Inca religious practice as described by the Dallas Museum of Art — the cavity filled with llama fat, blood and other ceremonial objects during fertility rituals, aimed at pastoral and agricultural fertility [s:web-dma-llama-iconography]
against: livestock — said by highland Andean communities, who the same account says still use illa in fertility rituals for their camelid herds [s:web-dma-llama-iconography]
against: poverty — said by Ekeko's worshippers, who clip banknotes to the figure and hold that he brings monetary wealth, generally on an offering first [s:wp-ekeko]
against: bad-luck — said by the Tiwanaku population as recorded by Arthur Posnansky, who offered miniatures of what they wished to have around 22 December to ask their deities for good luck [s:wp-alasitas]
against: house — said by Bolivian households, who bury a sullu — a dried llama foetus — under the foundations as an offering to Pachamama, bought at the same counters [s:wp-the-witches-market]
RESTRICTED: Two limits are stated rather than assumed. The illa rite is described in the source as something Inca religious leaders performed, and this record prints what the museum published about the mixture and the placement and does not reconstruct the wording or the sequence of the rite from other Andean material. And the Alasitas blessing is performed by people acting as shaman whose practice the sources describe but do not set out; this record names the step and leaves it there.
what: A practice of making the small thing stand for the large one. Its oldest form is the illa: a carved stone llama or alpaca, palm-sized, with a cylindrical hole sunk into the back between the shoulders — a container, fed with a mixture and then set in a pasture. Its most visible modern form is the Alasitas fair, where people buy miniature houses, cars, banknotes, tools and diplomas to give to somebody else, on the understanding that the full-size version follows within the year.
story: The Dallas Museum of Art's Inca camelid vessel, made between 1400 and 1540, is the object this record is named from. Dana Olesch, writing for the museum in 2017, describes what the hole was for: Inca religious leaders likely inserted a mixture of llama fat, blood and other ceremonial objects into it during fertility rituals. The aim was pastoral and agricultural fertility, and several Inca-related groups ended the rite by placing the illa in a pasture. Olesch records that highland communities in the Andes still use illa in fertility rituals for their camelid herds.

The second half of the practice is a fair with a date on it. Alasitas runs for a month from 24 January in La Paz, honouring Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance, and takes its name from the Aymara for 'buy from me'. Its pre-Columbian ancestor, according to the account, is an Aymara event called Guyatt, at which people prayed for good crops and exchanged basic goods; Arthur Posnansky observed that in the Tiwanaku culture, around 22 December, the population worshipped their deities for good luck by offering miniatures of what they wished to have. The colonial move is dated precisely: during the 1781 siege of La Paz, Sebastián Segurola re-established the celebration and shifted it from October to 24 January, as a gesture of gratitude to Our Lady of Peace. Transactions were made with stone coins; the cult of Ekeko was slowly reintroduced, appearing first modelled in clay, and cast in plaster now.

The figure himself carries the logic on his body: Ekeko is a moustached man in Andean dress, loaded with bags and baskets of grain and food, household objects and currency notes, and modern statues have a circular opening in the mouth so that a lit cigarette can be put in as an offering. Banknotes are clipped to him. Grain is offered for good harvests. He is placed in a good spot in the house.

The calendar is shared with the Church and both sides turn up. At midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses the gifts at the main cathedral in La Paz; before or after that, men and, less often, women acting as shaman bless the miniatures at the fair. In March 2011 Bolivia's Minister of Cultures, Elizabeth Salguero, nominated Alasitas to UNESCO alongside two other Bolivian festivals. In 2016 the Feast of Alasita and the miniatures of the Puno Altiplano were declared Cultural Heritage of the Nation of Peru.

*Inference —* the practice is the atlas's clearest case of buying being the rite rather than the preliminary to it. In most traditions here, purchase is how you acquire an object that a separate act then charges. At Alasitas the transaction is the ritual gesture: you buy the small thing, you give it away, and the claim is lodged. The illa says the same in the other direction — the object is fed and buried rather than worn, so the charm is a deposit and never an ornament.
how: For the illa: a figure is carved from hard stone with a cavity in the back, a mixture is put in, and it is set in the pasture the herd walks over. For Alasitas: a miniature is bought from a stall, blessed — by a person acting as shaman at the fair, by the Church at the cathedral at midday on 24 January, or by both — and given to somebody else. For Ekeko: the figure is placed in a good spot at home and fed. Banknotes go on him; grain is offered for harvests; a lit cigarette goes in the mouth of the versions built to take one, in the most recent form of the practice once a year.
today: Live, urban, and on two heritage registers. Alasitas fills streets and parks across central La Paz with smaller fairs in the neighbourhoods; other Bolivian fiestas fold alasitas into their own observances, including the feasts of the Virgin of Copacabana and the Virgin of Urkupiña; in Peru the main Ekeko festival is held on 3 May at Puno, on the Machallata hill, and elsewhere the Ekeko fair falls in October under the name Calvario. The Mercado de las Brujas on Calle Linares in La Paz supplies the year-round trade, with roughly 60 per cent of its sales falling in October, when Pachamama offerings cluster.
kin: illa — the object this tradition takes its name from — fed through a hole in the back and set in a pasture, which is the opposite of worn
kin: ekeko — its public face: a figure loaded with everything you could want, fed banknotes, grain and a lit cigarette
kin: feeding-the-charm — the practice at the centre of it — the cavity in the illa's back and the opening in Ekeko's mouth are the same idea in two materials
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice that here becomes the rite itself: at Alasitas the purchase and the gift are the claim, not the preparation for one
kin: burying — where the oldest form of this ends — an object placed in the ground the herd walks over, and a sullu under a house's foundations
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the tradition it shares a counter and a calendar with; the Church blesses the Alasitas miniatures at the cathedral at midday on 24 January
kin: mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz — the market that supplies it year-round, with roughly 60 per cent of the year's trade falling in October
kin: mercado-de-las-brujas-lima — the Peruvian counter selling the same herbs, offerings and cleansings, in a garment wholesaling district
kin: unesco-ich — the body Bolivia's Minister of Cultures nominated Alasitas to in March 2011; Peru declared the feast and its miniatures national heritage in 2016
sources: s:web-dma-llama-iconography s:wp-ekeko s:wp-alasitas s:wp-the-witches-market s:web-ulima-paseo-fe-magia s:web-unesco-ich-lists
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## Islamic talismanic craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/islamic-talismanic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/islamic-talismanic.json
id: islamic-talismanic
native: طِلَسْم (Arabic)
aliases: tilasm · ilm al-huruf · Islamic talismans · Qur'anic amulets
said: tilasm, plural talasim; the object is also called hafiz, 'protector', and himala, 'pendant'
when: 901 CE to now (still carried)
countries: SA EG TR IR IQ SY MA OM PK IN BD AF ID MY SN ML AL
root: Arabic ṭilasm, from ancient Greek telesma, 'completion, religious rite, payment', from teleō, 'I complete, perform a rite'; French talisman carried it into English
object: form=packet materials=paper,ink,parchment,silver,lead,leather,cloth,carnelian,brass worn=neck,upper-arm,sewn-in,pocket,wall,waist
against: evil-eye — said by the tradition as summarised in the cited account: talismans deflect disease, danger and the evil eye and attract divine protection [s:wp-talisman]
against: demons — said by the tradition's own rule — protection against jinn and demons is a stated function, and the text addresses God about them rather than addressing them [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: witchcraft — said by hadith literature, which reports Sura al-Falaq revealed to Muhammad as a prayer to God to ward off black magic [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: illness — said by Islamic healing practice; hadith permit magic for healing so long as it contains no act of shirk, and medieval talismanic bowls carry inscriptions naming what each was for — colic, childbirth, a nosebleed, a scorpion sting, the bite of a mad dog [s:wp-talisman]
against: war — said by Ottoman soldiers, who carried Qur'anic scrolls into combat, and the makers of talismanic shirts, many of which were made to be worn under armour [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: travel — said by the tradition's use of Ayat al-Kursi, recited before a journey, before sleep and after every obligatory prayer [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: infertility — said by the cited account of talismanic use, which names fertility alongside protection and the preservation of attractiveness [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
RESTRICTED: This tradition restricts material, and the atlas prints the restriction instead of the detail. Two lines are involved. The first is the tradition's own doctrinal one: a talisman may invoke God, angels, prophets or saints, and addressing jinn or demons is prohibited — so a formula that does the prohibited thing is not published here, and neither is a formula that does the permitted thing, because the ones in circulation are the property of the practitioners who write them. The second is the letter-and-number science, ʿilm al-ḥurūf and jafr, which this record names and does not demonstrate. No square is filled in, no name-combination is worked, no consecration wording is given. That is a deliberate blank; the reason is above it.
what: Writing, worn. The tradition makes protective objects out of text — Qur'anic verses, the ninety-nine names of God, names of angels and prophets, pious phrases, invocations — set on paper, parchment, metal, cloth or a bowl, and carried, folded, sewn in, hung or drunk off. The vehicle varies by region: a folded packet in a pouch on a Cairo child's shoulder, a rolled sheet in a silver tube on an Omani necklace, a whole inscribed shirt under a Mughal or Ottoman coat, a magic square engraved on a ring. One rule holds across all of it and the tradition states it out loud: the text calls on God, or on an intercessor the tradition recognises. It does not address jinn.
story: The scale is not marginal. Belief and practice in magic in Islam has been described by scholars of the subject as widespread and pervasive, and as a vital element of everyday life and practice, historically and now. Sixty-six Qur'anic verses are reported to bear on the subject, and the Qur'an describes magic in a negative light — but does not forbid it or prescribe a punishment for it. Three suras carry protective use in the tradition's own account: al-Falaq (113), used as a prayer to God against black magic and, per hadith literature, revealed to Muhammad to protect him against Jann, the ancestor of the jinn; al-Fatiha (1) and an-Nas (114), held to generate barakah, blessing. Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse at al-Baqara 2:255, is the verse the tradition names as the verse of protection, and it is the one written on amulets more than any other.

The craft has a history with dates in it. Until the ninth century, talismans often reflect pre-Islamic artistry. From the 12th century, for reasons the scholarship does not settle, pre-Islamic designs drop out in favour of the pentagram, the Seal of Solomon and zodiacal signs — and above all the wafq, the magic square. The earliest are 3×3 squares of the numerals 1 to 9 summing to 15 in every line, a square the tradition associated with the four archangels; 6×6 squares are attested by the late tenth century but do not enter the magical vocabulary until the thirteenth. Thabit ibn Qurra, the tenth-century Abbasid mathematician, was treated as the authority: 'The noblest part of astronomy is the science of talismans.' Talismanic shirts survive only from the 15th century, though the tradition is held to predate them.

The argument about whether any of this is permitted is internal, old, live, and conducted by name. This atlas reports it and joins neither side. Tobias Nünlist's summary is that Muslim writers generally distinguished licit from illicit practice rather than condemning the field. Virtually all Muslim scholars are described as permitting a talisman that invokes God or an intercessor — Muhammad, Ali, the saints — while addressing jinn or demons is prohibited as shirk, associating a partner with God. Hadith allow magic for healing so long as it contains no act of shirk. Ahmad ibn Hanbal (780–855) refrained from condemning those who used it to heal. Ibn al-Nadim (932–995) conceded white magic and condemned black, tracing the licit back to Solomon and the illicit to Iblis. Ibn Khaldun separated karamat, miracles, as gifts of God from sihr worked by a person's own psychic power.

On the other side stand scholars who denied the whole thing had any reality. The Hanafi jurist Abu Bakr al-Jassas argued that if magic worked its practitioners would be rich and powerful rather than poor men working a market crowd. The Mu'tazilite rationalists held it to be image-making without reality. Al-Jahiz offered psychological explanations for encounters with jinn. And the modern hard line is named too: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab treated sorcery as one of the few sins carrying a divinely sanctioned death penalty; Muhammad Nasiruddin al-Albani held that those convinced sorcery has effect of its own accord, rather than by God's decision, will not enter paradise; Salafi authorities hold that amulets are forbidden outright and that wearing one is shirk.

Remke Kruk's fieldwork is where the two sides meet on a stall. She found the handbooks and the pamphlets attacking them sold side by side in North African markets, and recorded how fine the line has become: contacting jinn in an exorcism to threaten them is acceptable, asking their help in a healing is shirk; dissolving Qur'anic text written on paper in water is forbidden, while writing in a bowl with ink the poured water washes off is recommended by the conservative cleric Wahid 'Abd al-Salam Bali. Kruk's own stated worry is that the rise of stricter forms of Islam has produced an attack on healing practices that used to be well integrated into Islamic life. Set against that, a Pew Research Center survey of Muslims worldwide in 2011–2012 found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers running from roughly a quarter to a half of Muslims across the Middle East and North Africa, Turkey, South Asia and Southeast Asia.

The argument has a body count in some jurisdictions and this record states that without editorial. Saudi Arabia formalised an Anti-Witchcraft Unit in 2009; in Makkah region alone that year at least 118 people were charged with practising magic or with using the book of God in a derogatory manner, and by 2011 the unit had nine bureaus and had processed at least 586 cases. Human rights workers allege the accused are often foreign domestic workers practising folk medicine from home.
how: Structure only, which is as far as this atlas goes. A text is chosen — a verse, a name, a square, a combination of letters. It is written by a person the client trusts to write it, in Arabic script, on paper, parchment, metal, cloth or the inside of a bowl. Where it is a packet it is folded small, sealed into a case of lead, silver or leather, and hung, pinned to a child's clothes or sewn into a garment. Where it is a bowl or a shirt it is used rather than worn hidden. Cheap ones were made at scale early: block-printed paper amulets, tarsh, are attested in the medieval Mediterranean Islamic world, sealed into cases so the contents stayed unread. The letter-and-number work that generates some of the texts is ʿilm al-ḥurūf, the science of letters, and the branch called jafr; this record names the technique and prints none of it.
today: Live everywhere the tradition is, and arguing with itself in print. Handbooks are on market stalls in Marrakesh and Khan el-Khalili with the pamphlets against them alongside; Salafi authorities rule against the objects by name; Pew's 2011–2012 survey found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers running from a quarter to a half of Muslims across the regions it covered, and its 2012 figures put belief in the evil eye in the majority in 20 of the 39 countries surveyed. Museum holdings run from a 10th- or 11th-century block-printed Egyptian sheet to Ottoman and Safavid talismanic shirts. Nothing in this record should be read as this atlas taking a view on whether a Muslim should wear one; both sides are named above, and the naming is the whole of the project's contribution.
kin: taweez — the everyday object of this tradition — folded text in a pouch — and the one the argument is usually had about
kin: hirz-pouch — the same writing in a North African and Nile container, and the clearest statement of the rule: invoke God, never jinn
kin: quran-pendant — scripture in a metal case worn at the throat, and an object some of this tradition's own authorities say should not exist
kin: talismanic-shirt — the tradition at its most expensive: the whole text scaled up to a garment, worn under armour, surviving from the 15th century
kin: magic-square — the wafq — the mathematics this tradition turned into an amulet from the 12th century, and tied to the four archangels
kin: divine-name — the sign at the centre of it: one of the ninety-nine names, or an angel's, written out and carried
kin: hamsa — one of its objects, and the one whose Salafi critics rule against it by name
kin: incantation-bowl — the late antique ancestor of the medieval Islamic talismanic bowl — the same idea of a vessel you inscribe and drink from, three centuries earlier and in Aramaic
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the neighbouring tradition, working the same region, the same materials and the same divine-name technique, and having almost the same internal argument about whether any of it is allowed
kin: ethiopian-scroll-craft — its closest method-cousin across a religious line: scripture written out, rolled, and carried against the body
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition the gris-gris belongs to as much as to this one — the writing inside is Qur'anic and the maker is a marabout
kin: washing-off-ink — the practice at the sharpest point of the modern argument: dissolving written Qur'an in water is ruled out, writing in a bowl the water washes off is recommended
sources: s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-talisman s:wp-amulet s:wp-throne-verse s:wp-magic-square s:wp-talismanic-shirt s:wp-seal-of-solomon s:wp-hamsa s:wp-incantation-bowl s:web-mwnf-hirz-oman s:web-ms-wikipedia-azimat s:web-id-wikipedia-jimat s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-evil-eye

## Kavacha — the Hindu armour tradition (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/hindu-kavacha/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/hindu-kavacha.json
id: hindu-kavacha
native: कवच (Devanagari)
aliases: kavaca · kavacham · kavach · armour hymn · Hindu protective amulet craft
said: KA-va-cha
when: 400 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IN NP LK
root: Sanskrit kavaca, 'armour, coat of mail'
against: bad-luck — said by the Devi Kavacham itself, which is said to protect the reader in all parts of the body, in all places and in all difficulties [s:wp-devi-mahatmya]
against: evil-eye — said by households in North India and Pakistan, at the folk end of the same tradition, where nazar is the harm and a lime and seven chillies the answer [s:wp-nazar-battu]
against: illness — said by users of occult yantras, for whom they serve as preventative medicine [s:wp-yantra]
against: demons — said by Sri Suta Goswami in the Garuda Purana, on flawless gems [s:wp-navaratna]
what: A family of practice in which protection is armour, said or worn. A kavacha is first a hymn that covers the body part by part, naming a deity for each; it is also the written text carried on the person, and by extension the whole class of South Asian objects worn or hung because a text, a horoscope or a household rule says to. Its objects are a seed bead, nine graded stones, a diagram engraved on copper, a cylinder of folded paper on a thread, and a lime with seven chillies at a doorstep.
story: The armour is a recitation before it is a thing. The Devi Kavacham runs to 61 slokas and sits in the Markandeya Purana; it is one of the subsidiary texts recited before the Devi Mahatmya, and what it claims is exactly the shape of armour — that the Kavacham protects the reader in all parts of the body, in all places and in all difficulties. The Devi Mahatmya is generally dated 400 to 600 CE, around 550 by Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty, and before the seventh century on the evidence of the Dadhimati Mata inscription of 608 CE.

The word then walks out of the text and onto the body. In Tantric practice kavaca is one of the six limbs into which a deity's mantra is divided, alongside the heart, the head and the topknot — the armour syllable. In the Pancharatra, the Jñānāmṛtasārasaṃhita speaks of amulets, kavaca, worn as a necklace and holding mantras. Monier-Williams records the object plainly: bark, birch-leaf or any substance inscribed with mystical words and carried about. The Jain Jñānārṇava, of the eleventh century, keeps the metaphor without the object: like the hero well-clad in armour, who is not pierced by arrows.

*Inference —* that is why this atlas files a seed, a ring, a plate and a lime under one head. They do not share a material, a maker or a price. They share a grammar: something is put between a person and what is coming, and a named authority — a text, an astrologer, a priest, a mother — says which something.

The authorities differ by object, and so does who may act. A yantra is consecrated and energised by a priest with the mantras of its deity, and practitioners hold that an unenergised one is lifeless. A navaratna is prescribed from a sidereal horoscope, and the tradition says to consult an astrologer before wearing one. A rudraksha needs nobody: it is strung and worn, and the texts promise merit rather than permission. The lime and chillies at a shop door need nobody either, and are hung by whoever opens the shop.

The tradition also borrows. A tawiz worn by Hindus often carries the Om sign instead of a Qur'anic verse — the Islamic container with the writing changed.
how: Recited, prescribed, consecrated, or simply hung. At the formal end, a priest energises the object with the mantra of a deity and the object stands in for that deity; at the astrological end, a specialist reads a chart and names a stone and its weight; at the household end, nobody is consulted at all.
today: Live at every level as of 2026: temple shops selling engraved copper plates and printed yantras, jewellers cutting navaratna to an astrologer's list, seed malas grown as a crop in Nepal and India, and limes and chillies at shop doors from Delhi to Karachi.
kin: rudraksha — the tradition's cheapest object and its most worn: a seed anybody may string, with no specialist between wearer and bead
kin: navaratna-ring — its most expensive: nine graded stones set to an astrologer's reading of one person's chart
kin: yantra-plate — its drawn form, and the one that needs a priest to be anything at all
kin: nimbu-mirchi — its household end — no text, no specialist, a lime at a doorstep
kin: tabiz — the Muslim neighbour it shares streets and shapes with, and which Hindu wearers borrow with the writing changed to Om
kin: sak-yant — what the drawn diagram became in mainland Southeast Asia — Indian yantras taken into a tattooing practice with its own rules
kin: counting-beads — the practice that turns a string into an instrument: 108 and one
kin: consecration — the step that separates this tradition's formal objects from its household ones
kin: tibetan-protection — the northern neighbour that took the same diagrams and mantras and put them inside sealed boxes
kin: kathmandu-thamel — the Himalayan street where the tradition's beads and plates reach buyers from outside it
sources: s:web-wisdomlib-kavaca s:wp-devi-mahatmya s:wp-yantra s:wp-navaratna s:wp-rudraksha s:wp-nazar-battu s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Latin American folk Catholic charm practice (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/latin-american-folk-catholic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/latin-american-folk-catholic.json
id: latin-american-folk-catholic
aliases: religiosidad popular · folk Catholicism of the Americas · Latin American popular devotion
said: religiosidad popular — the term Spanish-speaking clergy and scholars use for it
when: 1521 CE to now (still carried)
countries: MX PR CU DO PE BO GT ES US PH
object: form=medal materials=silver,gold,lead,jet,seed,wood,glass,thread,paper worn=neck,wrist,vehicle,wall,pocket,cradle,shop
against: evil-eye — said by Mexican and Caribbean households: a Mucuna seed called deer's eye against mal de ojo, and a jet fist tied on a newborn within days of birth [s:web-mexicodesconocido-ojo-de-venado]
against: child-harm — said by Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican parents, who told Edward Tabor the azabache is against the evil eye and with it diarrhoea, respiratory infections, deformities and above all sudden infant death [s:web-hektoen-azabache]
against: illness — said by petitioners at shrines, who pin a milagro shaped like the afflicted part to a saint's image as a reminder of the need or in thanks for an answer [s:wp-milagro-votive]
against: traffic — said by the medals themselves, which print the claim: 'Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás' — if you trust in Saint Christopher, you will not die in an accident [s:wp-saint-christopher]
against: witchcraft — said by customers at the Mercado de Sonora, whose back aisles sell goods for magic and the occult alongside medicinal herbs, the two not kept separate [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
against: bad-luck — said by the same market's stock, which includes crosses of ocote wood for good luck and chains of garlic to turn evil away [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
what: Catholic forms in lay hands, worked past the point the clergy sanctions. A tin leg pinned to a saint's robe; a jet fist tied on a newborn in the first week; a seed called deer's eye on a red cord; a Saint Christopher on the dashboard; a candle, a cleansing and a saint's image bought in the same market aisle as medicinal herbs. Nothing in the list is outside Catholicism's own vocabulary. What makes it a separate tradition is who decides where the line falls — and here the household decides, not the parish.
story: The objects arrived with the ships and most of them are older than the crossing. Milagros — small metal or wax body parts offered at a shrine — are traced to the ancient Iberians of the Spanish coast, travelled with the Spanish into Central and South America, and still hold in rural Andalusia, Catalonia and Majorca alongside their American forms. Jet amulets have been cut since the Neolithic; by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino, and the Asturian fist for a baby went from there into the Spanish Caribbean. Edward Tabor traces that fist further back, to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among the Moors of Barbary, into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492 and on to the colonies.

The local material entered the same kit. In Mexico the ojo de venado is a Mucuna seed; México Desconocido traces its career as an amulet to Xichú in northeastern Guanajuato and notes the plant also grew in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, so other regions may have arrived at the use independently. Newborns get one against mal de ojo; adults take one up for a hard stretch; drivers hang one where they can see it.

The argument in this tradition is unusually well documented because the clergy write it down. The Catechism of the Catholic Church condemns attributing a magical importance to otherwise lawful practices and crediting an object's efficacy to its material form. The priest Eduardo Hayen Cuarón condemned the ojo de venado by name, as an amulet and therefore an esoteric practice, malign and the work of Satan. Set against that, a Saint Christopher medal sold in Spanish-speaking markets carries a printed promise — 'Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás', if you trust in Saint Christopher you will not die in an accident — which is exactly the proposition the Catechism warns against, printed on a devotional article and sold in a shop. Both facts are on the record. This atlas prints them side by side and settles nothing.

The markets are where the tradition is legible as a system. At the Mercado de Sonora in Mexico City, established with other public markets by the city government on 23 September 1957 to regulate retail trade, medicinal herbs and magical and occult goods occupy aisles at the back of a single metal-framed nave. The two categories are not separate, and the account says so. Candles, saints' images, cleansings and herbs are bought in the same visit, from the same stallholders, by customers across the income range. In Lima and La Paz the equivalent counters sell the same combination with Andean material alongside.

*Inference —* the tradition's defining move is a doubling rather than a substitution. A saint does not replace a charm and a charm does not replace a saint; the same object is both, and which one it is depends on who is asked. That is why this record sits beside catholic-sacramentals rather than inside it: the sacramental tradition is defined by the Church drawing a line, and this one by households drawing it somewhere else.
how: Bought rather than made, in a church, a cathedral, a churchyard stall, a botánica or a market aisle, and then put to work in a named place: pinned to a saint's image or a shrine wall, tied to an infant's wrist within days of birth, hung from a rear-view mirror, set on a home altar, carried in a pocket. Some are blessed by a priest and some are not, and the tradition does not treat that as the deciding fact. Milagros can be offered as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered, and the shape does the pointing — though the code is local, not universal, so a leg can mean a leg or a journey.
today: Live across Mexico, the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, the Andes, parts of the United States, and the Philippines by the same galleon route. Prices have been published for one object: Tabor gives US$3 to US$10 for an azabache in a botánica and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote, in 2023, and reports that 29 per cent of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71 per cent the polyhedron. Quiapo Church in Manila draws millions on 9 January and thousands every Friday, with the stalls outside selling the amulets alongside. The Mercado de Sonora still trades, in a building the city put up in 1957 and has maintained badly since.
kin: milagro — the tradition's public object — left at the shrine rather than carried home, and the one that decides which saint gets which limb
kin: azabache — its earliest arrival: a jet fist out of Asturias by way of Santiago de Compostela, tied on a Caribbean newborn in the first week
kin: ojo-de-venado — the local material entering the same kit — a Mexican seed on a red cord, and the object a priest condemned by name
kin: car-saint — the dashboard end of it, where a devotional medal prints a promise the Catechism warns against
kin: figa — the fist as a sign, carried across the same Iberian route into Brazil and the Caribbean
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition this one is defined against: there the Church draws the line, here the household draws it somewhere else
kin: anting-anting — the same move in another Spanish colony — church forms taken up and worked by people outside the clergy, across the Pacific by the galleon route
kin: andean-illa-practice — the tradition it shares a counter with in La Paz and Lima, and the one whose January blessing the Church joins in on
kin: ex-voto-wall — the format this tradition keeps alive on tin — a painted account of the danger survived, hung where the next petitioner will read it
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the act most of these objects exist for, and the one the markets are laid out around
kin: buying-in-a-market — how one is got: an aisle, a tray, a red cord tied on the spot
kin: mercado-de-sonora — the tradition's clearest single address — a building the city put up in 1957 to regulate exactly this trade

## Mesopotamian household protection (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/mesopotamian-apotropaic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/mesopotamian-apotropaic.json
id: mesopotamian-apotropaic
aliases: Mesopotamian apotropaic magic · Babylonian white magic · Assyrian household magic
said: the apotropaic craft of Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia and Assyria
when: 2000 BCE – 63 BCE
countries: IQ SY IR TR
against: child-harm — said by the incantations, which name the unborn and newly born as the demon's first victims [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: childbirth — said by ritual texts from Uruk, prescribing a bronze amulet against miscarriage [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: demons — said by the ritual specialists, who set one demon against another [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: fever — said by Mesopotamian religion, in which Pazuzu is the south-western wind and is paired with plague [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: house — said by the household use the cited account describes: fearsome deities invoked in the home, not in state-run temples [s:wp-apotropaic-magic]
what: A craft with four moving parts: a demon with a name, a counter-power with a name, an incantation that addresses the demon directly, and a physical object — a plaque, a cast head, a figurine — placed where the danger comes in. Apotropaic ritual of this kind was practised throughout the ancient Near East, in houses rather than in state temples.
story: The method is verbal before it is material. The incantations open by naming the demon and then work through her epithets — 'Dimme, daughter of Anu', 'Who was named by the gods' — because the names are the hold. The object carries the words. An amulet with Lamashtu's image on it is not a portrait; it is her, held and instructed.

The counter-power does not have to be good. Pazuzu is a wind that brings plague and a text addresses him as 'Agony of Mankind', and his head hangs over the bed anyway, because he is the one thing that sends Lamashtu back underground. That is the tradition's most distinctive move: it hires demons.

Placement is documented rather than guessed. Amulets bearing Lamashtu's image could be worn, attached to the body or to clothing, or set near beds, doorways and other vulnerable spaces. A large Pazuzu wall amulet was found on the floor of the main reception room of a house at Dur-Katlimmu, where it had hung facing the entryway. Ritual texts from Uruk prescribe a bronze Pazuzu necklace for a woman at risk of miscarriage.

The objects were made at scale. The uniformity of the Pazuzu heads and their number across sites is read as mass production, which makes this the earliest industrialised amulet trade in the atlas.

*Inference —* the tradition does not end where the language does. Six hundred years after the last Pazuzu heads, the same ground is producing incantation bowls: a named demon, an incantation addressed to it directly, an object buried at the threshold. The scripts are Aramaic and Mandaic and the demons have new names, and the method is the one described above.
kin: lamashtu-plaque — the object at the centre of it — the demon, named and held, on a thing you can hang
kin: pazuzu-head — the counter-power, cast by the thousand and worn at the neck
kin: incantation-bowl — what this tradition becomes after the cuneiform stops: the same method in Aramaic ink, buried under the floor
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the neighbouring workshop tradition, which made more objects and named fewer demons
kin: bes-amulet — Egypt's household guardian, compared to Pazuzu by scholars on iconography and on function alike
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the Mediterranean tradition that inherits the threshold logic and drops the demon's name
kin: hamsa — the hand of Ishtar, used in Mesopotamia and Babylon against evil or disease entering a building, is one of the antecedents claimed for it
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice this tradition is built on: put the guard where the thing gets in
kin: foundation-deposit — the other placement — under the floor rather than on the wall
kin: british-museum — one of the collections where these objects can be seen
sources: s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-lamashtu s:wp-mesopotamian-mythology s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-incantation-bowl

## Practical Kabbalah (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/jewish-practical-kabbalah/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/jewish-practical-kabbalah.json
id: jewish-practical-kabbalah
native: קַבָּלָה מַעֲשִׂית (Hebrew)
aliases: Kabbalah Ma'asit · Jewish amulet craft · kameot
said: Kabbalah Ma'asit
when: 200 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL PS DE PL UA ES IT MA IQ IR GB US
root: Hebrew qabbalah, 'that which is received', plus ma'asit, 'practical, of deeds' — the branch defined by doing rather than by contemplating
object: form=plaque materials=parchment,silver,ink,paper,thread worn=neck,door,wall,pocket,wrist
against: demons — said by the practice as recorded in the German case of 1713 — Rabbi Hirsch Fraenkel was imprisoned for a library said to contain oaths and amulets for overcoming demons, seeing the future and speaking to the dead [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
against: illness — said by the Talmud, which mentions charms used for healing, and the rabbis who sanctioned a wide range of magical cures; segullot, folk remedies, have been widely used in Jewish communities since [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
against: evil-eye — said by Jewish folk custom, which is where the red string sits: a thin scarlet thread worn at the wrist against harm brought by the evil eye, ayin hara [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: spirits — said by the Hekhalot literature, in which the angels guarding each heavenly level are bound by formulae and seals — the technique the Talmud and Midrash call using the Divine Name [s:wp-practical-kabbalah]
RESTRICTED: This tradition restricts its own material and the atlas stops where it stops. Practical Kabbalah was held to be permitted only to an elite, and only under conditions the tradition calls holy and pure; most Kabbalists have taught that its use is forbidden; Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets at all. So this record prints no divine-name formula, no angelic name-combination, no seal and no square — not the wording, not a worked example, not a reconstruction from scattered sources. Maimonides' objection, written about the mezuzah and quoted on that record, is the tradition's own statement of what is at stake: writing names, verses or forms inside a sacred object turns a commandment into a talisman for the owner's benefit.
what: The branch of Jewish mysticism that makes things: amulets and incantations built from divine and angelic names, written on parchment or cut into silver, and carried, hung or worn. Its material output is small and its literature is mostly unpublished, because the tradition's own authorities spent six centuries telling it not to exist. This record prints that argument. It prints no name-formula, no seal and no square, because the tradition itself restricts them.
story: Begin with what it is not. Halakha forbids divination and soothsaying, and the Talmud lists condemned divining practices at a frequency that historians read as evidence of how common they were. What became practical Kabbalah is, in Gershom Scholem's account, not an outgrowth of the speculative Kabbalah at all: historically a large part of its content predates the speculative branch and does not depend on it, being an agglomeration of the magical practices that developed in Judaism from Talmudic times through the Middle Ages, in which the doctrine of the Sefirot hardly ever played a decisive role. Amulet-making using the esoteric names of angels dates from Talmudic times.

The split is dated. By the beginning of the 14th century the mystical and the magical had been separated into Kabbalah Iyyunit and Kabbalah Ma'asit, and the great majority of Kabbalistic writing thereafter belongs to the contemplative branch; most of the practical branch's writings stayed unpublished. Abraham Abulafia condemned it outright. A practical tradition flourished in Spain in the second half of the 15th century around a text called Sepher ha-Mashiv, whose practitioners Moshe Idel describes as interested in demonology and in coercive incantations to summon demons, angels and even God, in order to hasten the Messianic Age; Joseph Della Reina's failure at that, with his students, was held up by later Kabbalists as a warning.

Then the prohibition that matters most. In 16th-century Safed, Isaac Luria opposed Kabbalah Ma'asit and forbade his students to write amulets, developing instead a form of exorcism that moved the techniques from the practical side to the speculative. His reasoning was purity: without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer to purify with, pursuit of the practical realm by a person with an impure body is very detrimental. Because Luria is the central teacher of modern Kabbalah and the foundation of later Hasidism, that is not an opinion in a dispute — it is the position with authority behind it. The medieval Rabbi Yaakov ben Moshe Levi Moelin had already put a different objection: the person using a formula may lack the grounding, and the rite would then do nothing.

It continued anyway, at the border, and the people who continued it are named. The Baal Shem healers worked between the practical and the meditative, amulets included: Elijah Ba'al Shem of Chelm (1550–1583), the Baal Shem of London (1708–1782). Yisrael Baal Shem Tov (1698–1760) began as one, used amulets, and by the end of his life wrote only his own name on them — Yisrael ben Sara, Yisrael ben Eliezer — and no names of God. The Vilna Gaon recorded that he had attempted a golem in his youth and stopped when he perceived an impurity in it. In the 1750s Jacob Emden accused Jonathan Eybeschütz of being a secret Sabbatean, chiefly on his reading of amulets Eybeschütz had written; an amulet was the evidence in a dispute that split European Jewry. Rabbi Hirsch Fraenkel was sentenced to prison in Germany in 1713 for owning a library said to hold oaths and amulets for overcoming demons, seeing the future and speaking to the dead.

And there is a permission inside the prohibition, which is why the tradition never quite closed. The Talmud mentions charms used for healing, and a wide range of magical cures were sanctioned by rabbis; the ruling that any practice actually producing a cure was not to be dismissed opened the door that segullot — folk remedies — have walked through in Jewish communities across time and geography ever since.

*Inference —* two things follow for an atlas. First, this is the only tradition here whose own central teacher forbade its objects and whose objects went on being made; that is worth stating flatly rather than resolving. Second, a tradition whose writings mostly stayed unpublished cannot be described from its writings, so this record describes its argument, its people and its dates, and leaves the contents of the amulets where its authorities left them.
how: Structure only. A name — divine, angelic, or a combination worked from letters — is written by a person the client trusts, on parchment prepared to the standards Jewish law sets for sacred writing, or cut into silver, and then enclosed and worn or hung. Who may write one is exactly the contested question above: the elite, under conditions the tradition calls holy and pure, in one account; nobody, in Luria's. Hasidism displaced the whole apparatus with a different mechanism — the tzaddik altering the divine will through deveikut, cleaving to God — which Dov Ber of Mezeritch was at pains to distinguish from a magical process, though some Hasidic leaders kept using traditional amulets at the border.
today: Two distinct presents, and they should not be run together. One is the continuing use of segullot and of written amulets in Jewish communities, unbroken and largely private. The other is the retail red string, popularly attached to Kabbalah and sold to pilgrims and tourists in the Old City of Jerusalem and, from the late 1990s, to celebrities outside Israel — a wave usually linked to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. The Torah, Halacha and the Kabbalistic texts contain no requirement to tie one, and Michael Laitman's published position is that practical Kabbalah has no use for red strings. Both facts belong in the same paragraph; neither is this atlas's verdict.
kin: kamea — the whole material output of this tradition — the written amulet itself, and the object Emden read Eybeschütz's Sabbateanism out of
kin: divine-name — the technique this tradition is built on and then restricts: divine and angelic names used for amulets and incantations
kin: incantation-bowl — the late antique ancestor, and the only part of this practice that survives in bulk — Aramaic bowls written centuries before anyone used the name Kabbalah
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest object in the family: silver strips carrying the Priestly Blessing, written to be worn a thousand years before the tradition had a name
kin: mezuzah — the object Maimonides used to state the boundary — a commandment stops being one when it is turned into a talisman for the owner's benefit
kin: red-string — the charm sold under this tradition's name that its own teachers say it has no use for, and for which no text anywhere sets a requirement
kin: parchment — the material this tradition legislates and accepts no substitute for
kin: silver — the other page: metal thin enough to write on and durable enough that the oldest example survives
kin: islamic-talismanic — the neighbouring tradition in the same region, working the same divine-name technique on the same materials and having almost the same internal argument about whether it is allowed
kin: ethiopian-scroll-craft — the other scriptural tradition here that writes holy names to be carried, and argues about where the line falls
kin: joseph-naveh — one of the two editors who made the Aramaic evidence for the ancestor practice readable
kin: shaul-shaked — the other, and the scholar who traced how the same formulas cross between this tradition and its neighbours

## Taonga Māori (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/maori-taonga/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/maori-taonga.json
id: maori-taonga
native: taonga ()
aliases: taonga · Māori treasures · taonga tūturu
said: TAH-ong-a
when: 1750 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NZ
root: Māori taonga, a treasure; taonga tūturu, in New Zealand law, an object relating to Māori culture, history or society, made or modified in New Zealand by Māori, brought into New Zealand by Māori or used by Māori, and more than 50 years old
object: form=pendant materials=jade,bone,shell,wood,thread worn=neck,ear,chest
against: drowning — said by the hei matau, which the cited account says represents the land, prosperity, fertility and safe passage over water, and marks the relationship to Tangaroa, god of the sea [s:wp-hei-matau]
against: infertility — said by the practice recorded around the hei-tiki: because of the connection with Hineteiwaiwa, goddess of childbirth, hei-tiki were often given to a woman by her husband's family if she was having trouble conceiving [s:wp-hei-tiki]
RESTRICTED: This atlas follows the tradition's own published protocols here rather than summarising or completing them. That means three specific blanks. It prints no karakia and no rite. It prints no particular taonga's whakapapa or ancestral line — those belong to the descendants and to the iwi, not to an encyclopedia. And it does not attribute protective functions to taonga that the tradition's own publications do not attribute to them; where a source states what an object stands for, this atlas quotes the source and stops. Te Papa's stated position is that communities have a role in the care and understanding of taonga and that its aspirations include the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga; that is the framework, and the atlas works inside it.
what: Treasures with whakapapa. A hei-tiki, a hei matau, an adze reworked into a pendant, a cloak, a carving: Te Papa's own description of taonga Māori covers ancestral carvings, personal ornaments, garments and weaponry, alongside archaeological material and contemporary Māori visual culture. The atlas files these here rather than under charms because the tradition's own account of what they do is about descent and relationship, not about luck. This record uses the tradition's words.
story: Start with what mana is and where it comes from, because that is the whole difference. Pounamu taonga increase in mana as they pass from one generation to another; the stone is held to absorb the mana of its past owners, and some heirloom pieces are named after a former owner in memory of their position and authority. The most prized taonga are those with known histories running back many generations, and those are the ones given as gifts to seal important agreements. Peace between groups was cemented by exchanging carved heirlooms — a tautau pounamu, a door of greenstone — as in the saying Me tautau pounamu, kia kore ai e pakaru, ake, ake: let us conclude a peace that may never be broken, for ever and ever.

Dougal Austin's 2014 thesis, supervised by Peter Adds and based on Te Papa's hei-tiki collection with early-contact examples in overseas collections, locates the mana of a hei-tiki in the 'agency of prolonged ancestral use'. That is an argument about time and handling, not about design. A hei-tiki was often buried when its kaitiaki — its guardian — died, and brought out again at tangihanga.

The objects are also functional history. Adze blades of pounamu were wanted for carving wood and stayed in use after metal tools arrived; when they were no longer useful as tools they were often reworked into hei tiki and other taonga. Pounamu crafting and trade mattered to the economy of Ngāi Tahu, the South Island iwi, and production increased after their arrival in the South Island in the middle of the 18th century. There were a dozen major pounamu trails and many minor routes, walked in summer by parties of six to twelve.

How the collections were formed is part of the record and the sources state it plainly. Te Papa holds over 200 hei-tiki and the British Museum about 50; some were exchanged or gifted to Europeans at the earliest point of contact, and, in the cited account's own words, 'the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes'.

Two frameworks now sit over that. Te Papa works on a stated principle: 'Mana Taonga is a recognition of the power of taonga to communicate deep truths about our people.' The museum describes itself as recognising the role of communities in the care and understanding of collections and taonga, and names among its aspirations 'the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga' and 'the reclamation of Māori knowledge, language, and customs'. It also runs a repatriation programme, Karanga Aotearoa. And New Zealand law protects the objects by category: under the Protected Objects Act 1975, ngā taonga tūturu are one of nine classes of protected New Zealand object, unauthorised export of a protected object without permission from the chief executive of the Ministry for Culture and Heritage is an offence carrying fines of up to $100,000 for an individual and $200,000 for a body corporate, and the chief executive must consult two or more expert examiners on an application. Ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu was returned by the Crown to Ngāi Tahu in 1997 under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement.

The modern trade runs alongside all of that and is argued about by name. Most hei matau are now carved from cattle bone; carvers who work whale bone must use ancient standings, pre-existing supplies, or bone from whales that strand, since Māori have first claim under New Zealand tradition and law on part of the skeleton of a stranded whale that cannot be refloated — a very limited supply. Manufacturers in China mass-produce items resembling hei matau for the New Zealand visitor market, usually in a paste of bone and resin, and have, in the cited account's words, 'attracted criticism for their appropriation of Māori designs'. Retailers also sell tourist versions of hei-tiki in jade, other stone, plastic and other materials, and much of the 'greenstone' in souvenir shops is jade sourced overseas rather than pounamu, which occurs only in New Zealand.

*Inference —* an atlas of protective objects has to say where it has put this record and why. Taonga are here because the rest of the world meets them in the same museum cases and the same shop windows as charms, and because a reader who has just seen a hei matau on a cord deserves the tradition's own account of what it is. Calling one a lucky charm would be a category error the sources do not make, and this record does not make it either.
how: Carved, worn, handed on. Traditional method on a hei-tiki: the stone is first cut in the form of a small adze, smoothed by abrasive rubbing, shaped with sticks and water, the holes bored, then polished at length, and the finished pendant suspended on a plaited cord secured by a loop and toggle. The tilt of the head on one variety comes from the properties of the stone — its hardness and value make it important to remove as little as possible. Large pounamu boulders were and still are set at the entrances to significant sites as mauri stones, and visitors are invited to rub them gently with a dry or wet hand to connect with the mana of the place.
today: Live, and worn across New Zealand society. Bone and pounamu carvings relate to Māori cultural identity for many Māori, and are popular with young New Zealanders of all backgrounds for whom they relate to a more general New Zealand identity; several Māori tribal collectives create and export jewellery and other work. Pounamu appeared at London Fashion Week in 2013 in Kiri Nathan's collection. Te Papa charges international visitors an entrance fee and admits New Zealanders free.
kin: hei-tiki — the taonga this record is mostly written from — a treasure whose mana comes, in Austin's phrase, from prolonged ancestral use
kin: hei-matau — the other one the world meets, and the one whose overseas copies the tradition has publicly objected to
kin: jade — the material that is not a material here: pounamu is an inheritance, occurs only in New Zealand, and has belonged to Ngāi Tahu since 1997
kin: inheriting — the practice the word itself contains — a taonga gains mana as it passes from one generation to the next
kin: te-papa — the museum that states its terms out loud, holds over 200 hei-tiki, and runs the Karanga Aotearoa repatriation programme
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the rule this record is an application of: a tradition with published protocols of its own gets followed, not summarised
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this tradition is the sharpest case in — a resin copy made offshore, a statute with a $100,000 fine, and a collection whose sources are on the record
kin: unesco-ich — the international framework where the community-recognition clause, rather than a list, is the part that does the work here
sources: s:web-tepapa-taonga-maori s:wp-pounamu s:wp-hei-tiki s:wp-hei-matau s:wp-te-papa s:web-tepapa-karanga-aotearoa s:web-tepapa-visit s:web-lawofart-protected-objects s:wp-british-museum s:wp-cultural-appropriation s:wp-repatriation-cultural-property

## Thai wicha (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/thai-wicha/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/thai-wicha.json
id: thai-wicha
native: วิชา (Thai)
aliases: Thai amulet craft · saiyasat · Thai protective craft
said: wí-chaa — knowledge, a taught craft; from Sanskrit vidyā
when: 801 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TH KH LA MM
root: Thai wicha, 'knowledge, subject, learned craft', from Sanskrit vidyā through Pali vijjā — the same root as the yantra word the practice inscribes
object: form=plaque materials=terracotta,copper,brass,gold,silver,wood,bone,palm-leaf,hair worn=neck,chest,waist,skin,vehicle,shop,wall
against: weapons — said by the craft's own category kong grapan, invulnerability, and the takrut blessed for safe keeping; sak yant protection is taken by soldiers, police and taxi drivers [s:wp-takrut]
against: witchcraft — said by the cited account of phra khrueang, which names protection from black magic alongside danger and disaster [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: attraction — said by the craft's categories maha sanaeh, attraction, and metta mahaniyom, popularity and business success; the Khun Phaen amulet is named for a folklore figure who used a love formula [s:wp-takrut]
against: poverty — said by the same categories — maha pokasap, the drawing of riches — and shopkeepers who set a palad khik by the till to bring in sales [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: theft — said by Thai women, who the source says carry a palad khik in a purse against rape and mugging [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: illness — said by the Phra Kring, made in the image of Bhaisajyaguru the medicine Buddha, of whom the tradition says that whoever hears his name in passing or sees his image will be healed [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: war — said by Ayutthaya-period warriors, who carried votive tablets into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or a herbal charm [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
RESTRICTED: A yant's design and the words said over it belong to the master's lineage that holds them, and the incantations differ from school to school. This atlas prints what the tradition publishes — what the classes of effect are, who applies them, that rules come with them — and does not print an incantation, a consecration wording, or the specific taboos a particular master sets on a particular bearer. It does not reconstruct them from scattered sources either. The blank is deliberate.
what: The taught craft behind Thailand's protective objects: the designs, the scripts, the incantations and the rules that go with them. Its outputs are a pressed clay or metal tablet of the Buddha or a revered monk, a rolled metal or palm-leaf scroll in a case, a small carved phallus on a waist cord, and a tattoo. What ties them together is not the shape but the transmission — a yant and the words said over it belong to a master's lineage, and an amulet's price is set by which temple pressed it and which monk chanted over it.
story: The tablets come first and they are older than the idea of a charm. Buddhism reached what is now Thailand in the Dvaravati period carrying India's votive-tablet practice, and Dvaravati tablets were made to perpetuate the religion. Under Srivijaya and Mahayana influence, tablets were pressed to dedicate merit to the dead and toward becoming a bodhisattva. By Ayutthaya they were being made for protection, and warriors carried them into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or a herbal charm. In the early Rattanakosin period the protective amulet took off, the class acquired the name phra khrueang, and temples began using them to raise funds — a monk would give one as a gift in return for a donation. The term 'amulet' in this sense first appears under King Rama IV.

Takrut are older than Thai Buddhism in the sources' own account. They are the form the Khun Chang Khun Phaen epic mentions most, and after Buddhism took root monks were making them in 1200–1300 CE. The tattoo comes from the other direction: sak yant originates in the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, built on mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing that the sources run back as far as 2,500 BCE, with the geometry drawn from Indian yantras. Cambodia writes them in Khmer script, central Thailand in Khom, northern Thailand in Shan, Northern Thai or Tai Lu, Laos in Lao Tham.

The craft states its own rules and they run on the bearer, not the object. A yant confers what it confers only while the person carrying it observes the taboos taken on with it — abstaining from a named food is the example the source gives. Break them and it stops. Three classes of effect are named: one that works on the bearer, making them more eloquent; one that protects, taken by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and people in trades they count as dangerous; one that works on everyone else, invoking fear.

And there is a live economy with dated figures. In 1987 a policeman, Khun Phantharak Rajjadej, created the Jatukham Rammathep amulet for the founding of Nakhon Si Thammarat's city pillar; it names two Srivijaya princes the city holds to be its guardians, is round, and runs about 5 cm across. It caught on in the early 2000s, hard, from the time of its creator's funeral on 5 July 2006 into mid-2007. As many as 150 series were planned for production in 2007, and the market for that one amulet reached twenty billion baht that year. In late 2007 the bubble burst: the popularity faded fast, leaving plenty of stock that could be had at low prices. The source gives no figure for what the collapse cost anybody, so none is given here.

The other prices are collectors' prices and carry what their source carries. The Benja Phakhi — Phra Somdej, Phra Rod, Phra Nang Phaya, Phra Phong Suphan, Phra Sum Kor — are valued at over 10 million baht, with no year attached in the source, so none is printed. A Phra Somdet Jitlada, one of no more than 3,000 made by King Bhumibol and awarded between 1965 and 1970 with a numbered certificate naming its recipient, was worth at least two million baht as of 2013.

*Inference —* the argument about whether this is devotion or trade is Thai, conducted in Thai, and older than any foreign observer's version of it. The atlas reports both halves: temples have funded themselves this way since the early Rattanakosin period and say so plainly, and a market that can move twenty billion baht in twelve months behaves like a market. Neither half is a debunking of the other.
how: Amulets are pressed from plaster, metal, wood or bone, often with ash, a monk's hair or temple relics mixed in, then chanted over and blessed in a process that can take from a week to several years, and usually cased before wear. Takrut are inscribed with yant in Khom, Lan Na Tai Tham or another script, rolled into a tube, cased, and tied to the body — at the neck, at chest level, at the waist, or over a body part the wearer wants covered. Value afterwards turns on appearance, scarcity, maker, age and reputation, which is why buyers arrive at a market with a loupe and why specialist authenticators are part of the trade. A sak yant is applied by needle by a monk, a Brahmin priest, a ruesi or a lay wicha practitioner, and the rules travel home with the bearer.
today: Live and internationally visible, with the frictions that brings. Angelina Jolie was tattooed by Ajahn Noo Ganpai in Old Khmer script and took a Bengal tiger yant in 2004 on acquiring Cambodian citizenship, which the source credits with the practice's popularity among women abroad. In 2011 Thailand's Culture Ministry moved against parlours inking Buddha images on non-Buddhist visitors. Wat Bang Phra in Nakhon Pathom holds its Wai Khru on the grounds once a year in March, when the tattoos of those who come are renewed. In 2021 a Thai project put monk-blessed amulets on a blockchain as NFTs. Tha Phrachan market in Bangkok still trades the tablets, and forgery is common enough that expert authentication is a standing part of the transaction.
kin: phra-khrueang — the tradition's central object, and the one whose price is a monk's name and a temple's date
kin: takrut — its oldest strand — rolled metal or palm-leaf, made here before Buddhism arrived and by monks from 1200–1300 CE
kin: sak-yant — the same craft with the object removed: the yant goes into skin, and the rules stay on the person
kin: palad-khik — the piece of the kit that can go where the Buddha may not — a bar, a gambling house, a brothel
kin: yant-flash — the drawn sheets the practitioners work from, and the rules that come attached to them
kin: consecration — the step this tradition prices by: a week to several years of chanting, and the consecrating monk's name as provenance
kin: tattooing — the practice that holds the lineages, the refusals and the annual renewal at Wat Bang Phra
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice at its most monetised anywhere in this atlas — loupe, certificate, forgery, and a twenty-billion-baht year on the record
kin: tha-phrachan — the market this tradition's economy runs through, beside Thammasat University in Bangkok
kin: hindu-kavacha — where the geometry comes from: the Indian yantra, arriving through the Khmer Empire and staying under a Thai name
kin: yantra-word — the word at the other end of that journey, shortened to yant
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on authentication, which is a standing cost of doing business in this tradition rather than an occasional scandal

## Tibetan protection craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/tibetan-protection/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/tibetan-protection.json
id: tibetan-protection
native: སྲུང་བ། (Tibetan)
aliases: srung ba · Tibetan Buddhist amulet practice · Himalayan protective amulets
said: sung-wa, 'protection'
when: 755 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN BT NP IN MN RU
against: travel — said by James Gentry, summarising what Tibetans have used protective amulets against [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
against: weapons — said by the same sentence, on injury during battle [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
against: illness — said by the same sentence; and the Wellcome Collection's Tibetan cosmological amulet, catalogued as a protection against diseases [s:web-wellcome-tibetan-amulet]
against: demons — said by the account of a lama's ordinary work for lay people, which includes rites for avoiding harm from demonic forces and enemies [s:wp-tibetan-buddhism]
against: the-dead — said by Gentry on relic pills, held to protect against rebirth as an animal, an anguished spirit or a hell being [s:web-rubin-gau-gentry]
RESTRICTED: The designs inside Tibetan protective amulets, the mantras written on them, and the rites that consecrate them belong to tantric practice, which Tibetan Buddhism restricts to those who have received an empowerment from a qualified lama. This atlas prints published descriptions of what these objects are and what they are carried against, and does not reproduce a design, a mantra sequence or a consecration, and does not reconstruct one from scattered sources.
what: The protective end of Tibetan Buddhism: printed and drawn amulets consecrated by lamas, folded and bound in five-coloured cord, carried in worked-metal boxes at the neck or over the chest, hung on strings across passes and roofs, strung as agate beads, and painted as cosmological charts. Objects are made by specialists, given rather than sold, and mostly worn shut.
story: The frame is old and dated. Tibetan Buddhism preserves Indian Buddhist tantric practice of the post-Gupta early medieval period, 500 to 1200 CE, along with native Tibetan developments; the Buddhist Tantras date from around the seventh century onward. In the eighth century King Trisong Detsen, who reigned 755 to 797, made Buddhism the state religion and invited Indian scholars to his court — Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche, and Śāntarakṣita, 725 to 788, counted as the founders of the Nyingma, the oldest school. The Bengali monk Atisha, 982 to 1054, arrived in 1042. Before all of it the predominant tradition was Bon, which prayer flags are held to come out of.

Protection is part of a lama's ordinary work, not a sideline. There has been a close association in Tibet between the religious and the secular — chos srid zung 'brel — and lamas have tended to the lay population by helping with protection and prosperity: rites for purifying karma, for avoiding harm from demonic forces and enemies, for a successful harvest, with divination and exorcism among the methods. Even the word is read that way: Tibetan Buddhists take the etymology of mantra as mind protector, and Tsongkhapa says a mantra "protects the mind from ordinary appearances and conceptions".

What the objects claim is specific. James Gentry, writing for the Rubin Museum's Project Himalayan Art, says Tibetans have used protective amulets against misfortune during travel, injury during battle, illness, harmful spirits, and any other potential calamity — and that relic pills of the kind kept in an amulet box need not be consumed to have effect, and are held to protect not only against mundane dangers but against rebirth as an animal, an anguished spirit or a hell being.

The twentieth century broke the institutions that make these things. In 1959 the fourteenth Dalai Lama and a great number of clergy and lay people left for India and neighbouring countries; the Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976, targeted religion, most of the several thousand temples and monasteries in Tibet were destroyed, monks and lamas were imprisoned and forced to disrobe, and much of the textual heritage went with them. Prayer flags were discouraged but not eliminated, and many traditional designs may have been lost. *Inference —* the trade in Himalayan amulets that a visitor meets in Kathmandu today sits on the far side of that break, which is one reason provenance questions in this material are so hard.
how: Made and consecrated by lamas; given to named people. This atlas prints what published scholarship describes — that an amulet is a geometric diagram with mantras and images, consecrated through contemplative ritual proceedings, folded, wrapped in five-coloured cords with sacred substances, and distributed — and prints no diagram, no mantra sequence and no consecration. The reason is the tradition's own: these practices sit inside Vajrayana, the Secret Mantra, where a practitioner must receive an empowerment from a qualified lama, and without initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras.
today: Practised across Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal, Ladakh, Sikkim, Mongolia and the Buryat, Tuvan and Kalmyk regions of Russia, and in the diaspora since 1959. Amulet boxes, wrapped amulets, prayer flags and dzi beads are also made for sale to buyers outside the tradition, and an object bought that way carries no record of who consecrated it — the market's standing problem, in metal, paper and stone alike.
kin: gau-box — the container this tradition is best known by, and the one that keeps its contents out of sight
kin: sungkhor — what a lama actually makes: the drawn, consecrated, folded amulet the box exists to hold
kin: lungta-flag — its public form — the same mantras printed and left to the wind instead of sealed to a body
kin: dzi-bead — the object it received rather than made, and values as inherited
kin: hindu-kavacha — the southern tradition its diagrams and mantras come out of
kin: ongon — the shamanic practice on the other side of the taiga-steppe line in Mongolia, which the Buddhist side has lived beside for centuries
kin: consecration — the step it reserves to the initiated, and the reason an empty box is not an amulet
kin: wearing-hidden — its default: the amulet is folded, boxed, and not opened
