## West African charm craft (tradition)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/tradition/west-african-charm-craft/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/tradition/west-african-charm-craft.json
id: west-african-charm-craft
native: bǒ (Latin)
aliases: bo · gris-gris making · juju · marabout charms · Karamokobara
said: the Fon word for a charm is bǒ; Francophone Beninese say gris gris; the Hausa-derived English word is juju
when: 1600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: BJ TG GH NG SN ML NE CM
object: form=bag materials=cloth,paper,ink,herb,bone,cowrie,wood,leather worn=neck,pocket,upper-arm,door
against: bad-luck — said by the source on gris-gris: wearers hold that it protects from evil or brings luck [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: illness — said by the source on juju, which says it is most commonly used for treating both physical and spiritual ailments [s:wp-juju]
against: curse — said by the same source, which names counteracting and neutralising curses among its uses [s:wp-juju]
against: travel — said by buyers of bǒ, who the source says buy them to aid in attracting love, wealth, or protection while travelling [s:wp-west-african-vod-n]
against: attraction — said by the same buyers, for love [s:wp-west-african-vod-n]
against: lawsuit — said by the source on juju: it is sometimes used to enforce a contract or ensure compliance, and the practitioner requires payment for the service [s:wp-juju]
against: infertility — said by women in Senegal in a 1982 survey, who named charms among the three traditional contraceptive methods known to them [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
RESTRICTED: No recipe and no incantation is printed here. Bǒ recipes are kept as a closely guarded secret by the families and individuals who hold them, on the stated reasoning that whoever learns the exact ingredients gains power over the maker; bǒgbé, the language the charms are activated in, is not reproduced. The marabout's written formulae are a course of study and are not printed either.
what: Not one practice but a shelf of them, made by different specialists for different clients across Benin, Togo, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, Niger and Cameroon: written Qur'anic charms sewn into cloth sacks; assembled charms of plant and animal matter activated by words; carved figures; cast shells read for answers. Four different vocabularies cover them, and this record keeps them apart rather than merging them.
story: Start with the words, because they belong to different peoples and get used interchangeably in English.

Bǒ is Fon, and translates as charm. Bǒ are amulets made from zoological and botanical material, activated with secret incantations in a language called bǒgbé, 'bǒ's language'. Families and individuals keep their recipes closely guarded, on a widespread belief that anyone who learns the exact ingredients gains power over the maker. Many Francophone Beninese call them gris gris. They are sold: tourists buy them for love, for wealth, or for protection while travelling, and a diviner — a bokónó — charges a rate that varies with who the client is, less for family, more for a tourist or a middle-class Beninese client.

Gris-gris is Mande, and the line behind it is Muslim and scholarly. Mande speakers such as the Dyula distributed Islamic charms under that name; the Dagomba wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts with formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets. The craft has a curriculum: Karamokobara, divided into seli, prayer, and siri, path. Seli produces karamokos, scholars of Qur'anic law; siri produces marabouts, scholars of the written charms. The tools of the siri side are spoken prayers, numerical squares called katemi, and written Qur'anic inscriptions. Islam shows up inside non-Islamic practice too — Vodún charms occasionally use Islamic script.

Juju is from Hausa, where it means evil spirit; some derive it instead from the French joujou, a plaything. In its general English use it covers magical properties to do with luck of either kind, and it has been applied to West African traditional religions broadly. A juju man is a man vetted by local tradition and versed in traditional spiritual medicines; the practice is most often used for treating physical and spiritual ailments, and is also used to enforce a contract or ensure compliance, with the practitioner paid for the service. The same word gets attached to serious crime: the source records that crimes have been committed using the practice, human trafficking being the most extreme and prominent example, and that nineteenth-century traders and travellers in the Niger Delta and Benin published accounts of a list of practices they said they had witnessed. *Inference —* those nineteenth-century accounts were written by men with commercial and colonial interests in the region, and this atlas reports that they exist and who wrote them rather than treating them as a neutral inventory.

Cowries run through all of it as a fourth strand. They are cast in divination among the Yoruba, in Ifá, and in the annual customs of Dahomey in Benin, and in Brazil the same shells are thrown to consult the Orixás — a direct line out of this coast.

And there is a market with an address. The Akodessawa Fetish Market, Marché des Féticheurs, in the Akodessawa district of Lomé, Togo, sells the materials used in vodún practice: monkey heads, skulls, dead birds, crocodiles, skins and other products of dead animals. It is described as the largest such market in the world. *Tradition holds —* what is sold there is raw material for a specialist, not a finished charm for a buyer.
how: By specialist and by rule, and the rules are not the same from one strand to the next. A marabout writes; a bokónó divines and then supplies; a bǒ-maker assembles plant and animal matter and speaks over it in bǒgbé; a diviner casts cowries and reads what falls. Payment is normal and openly discussed in the sources: fees scale with the client.
today: Living, commercial and mixed with other religions rather than sealed off from them. Many people in West Africa draw on traditional religion, Christianity and Islam at once to deal with a problem, and a Vodún practitioner may read Jesus as a vodún. Since the 1990s there have been growing efforts to bring foreign visitors to West Africa to be initiated into Vodún, which puts the tourist inside the practice rather than outside it — an argument this atlas reports and does not settle. As of 2026 no figure has been read here for what any of this is worth.
kin: gris-gris — the object this tradition is best known abroad by, and the one that crossed the Atlantic under its own name
kin: akuaba-figure — the Akan carving in the same region, made for a wish rather than against a harm
kin: cowrie-strand — the shells this tradition casts to get answers, and wears for fertility and luck
kin: tuareg-cross — the Saharan silver worn at the northern edge of the same trade routes, and called a grigri by some of its wearers
kin: juju-word — the Hausa-derived word English took, and what it covers and does not
kin: gris-gris-word — the Mande word, and its change of meaning between Dakar, Port-au-Prince and New Orleans
kin: fetish-word — the European label stuck on this whole region's objects from the sixteenth century on, and the market in Lomé that now carries it as a name
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition the gris-gris strand belongs to as much as to this one — the writing is Qur'anic and the maker is a marabout
kin: bakongo-nkisi-craft — the Central African practice it is regularly confused with, and shouldn't be: different peoples, different specialists, different objects
kin: akodessewa-market — the Lomé market that sells this tradition's raw materials in the open
kin: inscribing — the practice at the centre of the Muslim strand: the verse is the charm and the sack is the carrier
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice the sources describe without embarrassment — fees are set, and they scale with the client
sources: s:wp-west-african-vod-n s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-juju s:wp-akuaba s:wp-cowrie s:wp-akodessawa-fetish-market s:wp-fetishism s:wp-islam-and-magic

## The beetle (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/scarab-sign/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/scarab-sign.json
id: scarab-sign
native: 𓆣 (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: scarab motif · dung beetle · kheper sign · Khepri
when: 2055 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG SD IL PS LB SY JO GR TR IT
object: form=seal materials=faience,carnelian,agate,gold,glass worn=neck,finger,chest,grave
against: the-dead — said by Egyptian funerary practice, in which the scarab stands for rebirth and regeneration [s:wp-scarab-artifact]
against: illness — said by the sign's association with Khepri and the daily renewal of the sun, as summarised by Egyptologists [s:wp-scarab-artifact]
what: A dung beetle seen from above — head, wing case and legs indicated, the underside left flat so it can be engraved. Usually identified as Scarabaeus sacer. Standard ones run between 6 mm and 40 mm long, most between 10 mm and 20 mm, drilled end to end for a thread or a swivel ring. It is the only sign in this atlas that doubles as a signature: the flat base takes a name, a title or a motto and prints it in clay.
story: The reading Egyptians gave the beetle is stated in the sources: Khepri rolls the sun across the sky at daybreak the way the beetle rolls a ball of dung, so the sign stands for the sun's journey, for rebirth and for regeneration. The beetle-shaped amulet became enormously popular by the early Middle Kingdom, around 2000 BCE, and stayed popular for the rest of the pharaonic period and beyond. By the end of the First Intermediate Period, about 2055 BCE, scarabs had become extremely common and largely replaced cylinder seals and circular button seals with simple geometric designs.

The sign travelled as an object, not as an idea. From the middle Bronze Age other peoples of the Mediterranean and the Middle East imported scarabs from Egypt and made their own, in Egyptian or in local styles, especially in the Levant. A scarab inscribed with Nefertiti's name was among the luxury goods on the Uluburun wreck off Turkey. *Inference —* a portable seal that also functions as a charm is unusually easy to export, and the Levantine copies are evidence of trade in the thing rather than of the Egyptian theology travelling with it.

What is cut on the base changed over time. Pharaohs' names in the Middle Kingdom, then officials' names and titles used as administrative seals, then short prayers or mottoes in the New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period, which are hard to translate. Some carry hunting scenes. Commemorative scarabs were made for political purposes, notably the large ones of Amenhotep III.

Materials are the other half of the story. Most were carved from steatite — a soft stone that hardens when fired — or moulded in Egyptian faience, then glazed blue or green and fired. Hardstone examples are green jasper, amethyst and carnelian. Most were originally green or blue; weathering has left most steatite ones looking white or brown, so a museum tray reads paler than the original trade did.
today: Scarabs are made by the thousand as souvenirs in Egypt, and the shape is standard jewellery and tattoo flash worldwide. The ancient ones are also the most forged class of Egyptian antiquity this atlas covers, which is a matter for the long read on authentication rather than for this page.
kin: scarab — the amulet and seal itself, which is the sign's body
kin: heart-scarab — the large one laid at the heart, inscribed to keep the heart from speaking against its owner
kin: eye — the other sign Egypt made by the thousand; the eye went over the incision, the beetle at the heart
kin: faience — the glazed quartz paste that made it cheap enough to bury in quantity
kin: carnelian — the red hardstone version, cut rather than moulded
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that produced it at industrial scale
kin: inscribing — the practice that makes the base matter more than the back
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator whose typology of scarabs is still how museums sort them
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on authentication, which has a chapter's worth of scarabs in it
sources: s:wp-scarab-artifact s:wp-heart-scarab s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-flinders-petrie s:wp-british-museum

## The bell (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/bell/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/bell.json
id: bell
native: tintinnabulum ()
aliases: wind chime · brass bells · chime
said: tintinnabulum, the Roman wind chime of bells
when: 100 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IT KR
object: form=bell materials=copper worn=door,lintel,shop
against: spirits — said by Roman householders, in whose practice the sounds of bells were held to keep away evil spirits [s:web-wp-tintinnabulum]
against: evil-eye — said by Roman wearers of the fascinum, whose winged phallus turns up as jewellery, lamps and wind chimes alike [s:wp-fascinus]
against: spirits — said by Korean mudang, whose brass bells are meant to attract the attention of the spirits rather than repel them [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
what: A small bell, hung or carried, that sounds when the air or the body it is attached to moves. The sign is audible rather than visible, which makes it the only entry in this atlas that a person could use with their eyes shut.
story: Rome hung its bells at the door and put a phallus on them. A tintinnabulum is a wind chime or assemblage of bells, often taking the form of a bronze ithyphallic figure or of a fascinum, the magico-religious phallus. They were hung near thresholds at a shop or house, under the peristyles, by the bedroom or the venereum, where the wind would set them tinkling, and some were rigged to a cord and bell pull to work as doorbells. The cited account gives the Roman reason for the noise: the sounds of bells kept away evil spirits. Examples have been found at Pompeii and Herculaneum, and a number of them are in the Secret Museum collection at the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli. The phallic charm and the bell are the same object: phallic charms, often winged, appear in Roman culture as jewellery, relief carvings, lamps and wind chimes.

Korea rings its bells to bring spirits in. During a gut, the mudang carries a fan and brass bells; the scholar Sarfati commented that these bells were "a central symbol" of Musok, and their purpose is to attract the attention of the spirits. The rite's music regularly involves cymbals, hourglass-shaped changgu drums and a gong, and the mudang dances by swirling in circles, which the same account reports as facilitating the possession trance.

*Inference —* those two uses are opposite, and that is the interesting fact about this sign. A Roman bell rings on its own, unsupervised, at a threshold, to push something out. A Korean bell is shaken by a named specialist, inside a rite, to pull something in. The noise is the same; the direction is reversed, and it is the practitioner's presence or absence that decides which way it runs. No source read here connects the two customs, and this atlas does not.
notes: This record is short because the sources read here document the bell in two places only. It is filed under the sound family, added to the vocabulary for it: a bell is a hollow vessel, but what it is carried for is the noise.
kin: fascinum — the same object seen from the other side: the winged phallus that the Roman bell hangs from
kin: phallic-sign — the sign the Roman bell is usually cut in, which is why these chimes ended up in a museum's locked room
kin: bujeok — the Korean written charm made in the same tradition as the bells, by the same practitioners
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the Roman half of this record belongs to entirely
kin: copper — the metal both halves are cast in, bronze at Pompeii and brass in Seoul
kin: san-gregorio-armeno — the Naples street a few minutes from the museum that holds these chimes, still selling small cast figures
sources: s:web-wp-tintinnabulum s:wp-fascinus s:wp-korean-shamanism

## The crescent (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/crescent/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/crescent.json
id: crescent
native: lunula (Latin)
aliases: lunula · increscent · decrescent · star and crescent · sickle moon
said: LOO-noo-la, 'little moon'
when: 2300 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IT IQ SY TR GR TN DZ IR YE RU
object: form=pendant materials=gold,silver worn=neck
against: evil-eye — said by Roman practice, in which amulets were worn especially against the evil eye [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: demons — said by the same account: against evil forces, demons and sorcery [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: witchcraft — said by Roman practice, as recorded of amulets worn as talismans [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: child-harm — said by the wearers were girls; Isidore of Seville defines the lunula as a female ornament [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
what: A moon with its middle cut out, two horns and a curved back, hung point-up at the neck. Roman ones are gold. Isidore of Seville defines them as female ornaments in the likeness of the moon, little hanging gold bullae. The shape is a lune in geometry and a crescent in heraldry only when the horns point up.
story: Rome gave the crescent to girls. A lunula was worn as an apotropaic amulet — a charm meant to turn harm away — and stood as the girl's equivalent of the boy's bulla. Romans wore amulets against evil forces, demons and sorcery, and above all against the evil eye. In Plautus's Epidicus, Epidicus asks the girl Telestis whether she remembers his bringing her a gold lunula on her birthday and a little gold ring for her finger; in Rudens, Palaestra says her father gave her a golden bulla on the day she was born. Lunulae were common across the whole Mediterranean, while the bulla stayed mostly Italian.

As a sign rather than an amulet the crescent is older and travels further. It stands for the moon and for the moon deity Nanna or Sin in Akkadian cylinder seals as early as 2300 BCE. Egypt's logograph for the moon is a crescent. Phoenicians carried it as far as Carthage and Numidia in the eighth century BCE. The star-and-crescent pair arises in the ancient Near East for the moon and Ishtar as the planet Venus, often with the solar disk as a third, and was inherited in Sassanian and Hellenistic iconography. It moved into Islamic iconography from Sassanian use after the Muslim conquest of Persia, and into Marian iconography in Christianity through the Woman of the Apocalypse, with the moon under her feet.

*Inference —* two different things share this outline and this atlas does not merge them. The Roman lunula is a birth-gift to a named child; the star-and-crescent is a dynastic and then a religious emblem. Nothing read here shows the second growing out of the first.
kin: lunula — the amulet itself — the gold crescent a Roman girl was given
kin: bulla — the boy's locket, given at birth where the girl got this; the pair is the clearest gendered split in Roman charms
kin: horn — the other two-pointed sign of the Mediterranean, and the one this is most often mistaken for
kin: cimaruta — the Neapolitan silver sprig that grows a crescent moon on one of its branches
kin: silver — the metal the crescent is tied to through Luna in the alchemical scheme
kin: eye — the harm Roman amulets were worn against, this one included
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition that fixed it as a child's charm

## The cross (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/cross/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/cross.json
id: cross
native: crux (Latin)
aliases: Latin cross · Greek cross · tau cross · saltire · crux ansata · Coptic cross · Agadez cross
when: 101 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IT GR EG ET IE NE ES MX PH FR GB
object: form=pendant materials=silver,gold,wood,thread,copper worn=neck,skin,roof,wall,door
against: house — said by Irish practice: a Brigid's cross hung from the rafters for the saint's blessing and protection through the year [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: bad-luck — said by Tuareg users of the tanaghilt, some of whom describe it as a grigri or a reserve of wealth [s:wp-agadez-cross]
against: travel — said by Dieterlen and Ligers, recording a father's words on giving the cross to a son leaving to live as a nomad [s:wp-agadez-cross]
what: Two lines crossing, usually at right angles. The variations are named and they matter: the †-shaped crux immissa, the T-shaped crux commissa or tau, the X-shaped crux decussata or saltire, the crux ansata with a loop on top. Worn as a pendant, tattooed at the wrist, woven from rushes, cast in Saharan silver, hung over a door.
story: Two intersecting lines are the cheapest mark a hand can make, so the shape has no single origin. Cross-shaped incisions appear from deep prehistory, as petroglyphs in European cult caves from the beginning of the Upper Palaeolithic and right through to the Iron Age. The cross mark also turns up as a number independently — Roman X for ten, Chinese rod numeral 十 for ten, the Brahmi numeral that becomes 4 — and in the Phoenician alphabet it is taw, whose name means mark.

The Christian cross is a later, dated adoption of an existing shape. It came into use as an emblem of Christianity from the second century CE, in the Latin letter T form, after Ichthys. Clement of Alexandria in the early third century calls it the Lord's sign. Tertullian, writing De Corona in 204, says it was already a tradition for Christians to trace the sign repeatedly on their foreheads — a cross made of a gesture before it is made of metal. Crosses with intersecting beams appear in Christian art towards the end of Late Antiquity; the patriarchal cross first appears in the tenth century; heraldry multiplies the forms from the Crusades onward.

What gets hung on a neck varies by church and by craft. The Coptic cross is two bold equal bars, each ending in three points for the Trinity, twelve points in all for the Apostles, often with a circle at the centre for God's love; the trefoil form developed locally from the short Greek cross. Many Copts have a cross tattooed on the inside of the right wrist as a sign of faith. In Ireland the cross is woven: the National Museum of Ireland sorts Brigid's crosses into seven categories by build rather than by outline, including a bent-armed type and a wheel type.

The Tuareg Agadez cross is the case that resists the word. Only a few tanaghilt actually resemble a cross; most are pendants with a varied silhouette, cast by blacksmiths in silver by lost-wax and never hammered. Asked what it means, users generally give vague answers; some call it a grigri or a reserve of wealth. The ethnologists Germaine Dieterlen and Ziedonis Ligers recorded a father giving the jewel to his son at the age of virility, marriage and nomadism with the words: my son, I give you the four directions of the world, because we do not know where you will go to die.

*Inference —* filing all of these under one sign is a convenience of shape, not a claim of common descent, and the Agadez piece is here mainly to show where the convenience breaks.
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the cross put in the skin rather than on a chain, at the inside of the right wrist
kin: brigids-cross — the cross woven from rushes on 1 February and hung in the rafters
kin: tuareg-cross — the Saharan pendant called a cross in French and something else in Tamashek
kin: rowan-cross — two twigs of rowan bound crosswise, which is a cross made of the material's power rather than the shape's
kin: ankh-amulet — the crux ansata — the same figure with a loop, and a meaning Egypt fixed long before Rome
kin: fish — the sign the cross succeeded as the emblem of Christianity in the second century
kin: swastika-sign — the bent-armed cross, filed separately here because its twentieth-century history is not the cross's
kin: st-christopher-medal — the mass-produced Catholic metal the cross now shares a neck with
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that governs what a blessed cross is and is not
kin: silver — the metal the Agadez smiths cast it in, by lost wax and never hammered
sources: s:wp-cross s:wp-coptic-cross s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-agadez-cross s:wp-ankh s:wp-copts

## The eye (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/eye/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/eye.json
id: eye
aliases: eye motif · apotropaic eye · eye-against-the-eye
when: 3000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG GR TR IT IL PS SY IR IQ IN PK MX BR GB AL GE AM MA TN
object: form=bead materials=glass,faience,carnelian,terracotta,silver worn=neck,wrist,cradle,door,vehicle,shop
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across the Mediterranean, West and South Asia, Africa and Latin America [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: envy — said by the usual explanation given by carriers, recorded across the same range [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: child-harm — said by parents; the eye is put on infants more than on anyone else [s:wp-evil-eye]
what: An eye, drawn or moulded, worn where another person will see it. It is the most widespread sign in this atlas and the only one whose logic is stated out loud by its carriers everywhere it appears: harm arrives by looking, so the answer looks back.
story: Amulets against a harmful look have been found dating to around five thousand years ago, and the belief runs through the Mediterranean, the Balkans, Eastern Europe, West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. Jewish rabbinic literature returns to it repeatedly.

The sign takes two different bodies. In Egypt it is a drawn eye with a falcon's cheek-line, cut in faience and carnelian from the Old Kingdom onward. Around the eastern Mediterranean it becomes a bead: after glass-bead production got going in the region around 1500 BCE, blue-and-white concentric eye beads spread among Phoenicians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs and Ottomans, and that bead is what a shop in Istanbul or Athens sells today.

What is striking is what stands in for the eye where the eye is not drawn. Illyrians used shapes of the phallus, the hand, the leg and animal teeth against the same harm. Romans used the fascinum, a winged phallus. Southern Italy still cuts a horn. *Inference —* the substitutions have one thing in common: each is a thing that catches a glance. The mechanism carriers describe is interception, and anything startling enough to take a look can do the job. That is why this atlas files the horn, the hand and the fist as kin of the eye rather than as unrelated signs.

*Tradition holds —* the harm is usually attributed to envy, and often to admiration that has not been qualified. That is why the eye is put on children, on livestock and on new houses more than on anything else.
kin: wedjat-eye — the oldest dated amulet in this family, and the one that fixes the sign's shape for three thousand years
kin: nazar — the sign as a glass bead, which is the form most of the world now buys it in
kin: hamsa — the hand that usually has this eye set in its palm — two signs stacked on one object
kin: horn — the substitute sign in southern Italy, doing the same interception with a different shape
kin: fist — another substitute: a gesture frozen in coral or jet, aimed at the same look
kin: phallic-sign — the Roman substitute — the fascinum caught the glance meant for the child
kin: nimbu-mirchi — South Asia's answer to the same harm, hung in a doorway instead of worn
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that follows this sign across four continents and asks what travelled and what was invented twice
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian who catalogued the sign across Europe in 1895 and is still the reason many of these objects are grouped together
kin: glass — the material that turned the sign into something a market could sell by the tray
sources: s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-hamsa s:wp-amulet s:wp-apotropaic-magic

## The fig fist (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/fist/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/fist.json
id: fist
aliases: fig sign · mano fica · manus fica · manus obscena · higa · figa · cigua · kukish · shish · dulya
said: in Italian, mano fica or far le fiche; in Spanish, higa; in Portuguese and Galician, figa
when: 200 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IT GR ES PT BR TR RU UA PL RS HR SI LT LV AM AZ MN ZA
object: form=pendant materials=jet,coral,silver,gold,bone,wood worn=neck,cradle
against: evil-eye — said by ancient Greeks, who wore amulets of the gesture at the neck [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: spirits — said by the Roman pater familias, who made the sign during the Lemuria against the spirits of the dead [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: child-harm — said by Asturian practice — jet higas are usually given to young children [s:wp-fig-sign]
against: bad-luck — said by Portuguese, Brazilian, Galician and Asturian use, where the gesture wishes good luck [s:wp-fig-sign]
what: A closed fist with the thumb pushed up between the index and middle fingers, carved or cast small and hung at the neck. In jet it is black and matte; in coral it is red; in silver it is the size of a thumb joint. The gesture it copies is obscene, and that is the working part.
story: Rome called it the manus fica. The pater familias made it during the Lemuria to turn away the spirits of the dead. Early Christians called the same shape the manus obscena, the obscene hand. Greeks wore amulets of the gesture at the neck against the evil eye and drew it in their art; what they took to be an overtly sexual gesture was expected to distract harm from its target.

The fist also fused with another sign. Roman soldiers carried the fist-and-phallus amulet — a phallic pendant with a clenched fist at the base of the shaft, facing away from the glans, several of them making the fig sign. The largest known collection of them comes from Camulodunum, Roman Colchester. Some examples carry vulvar imagery as well.

The insult and the amulet never separated. In Italy the gesture was rude enough that Dante uses it in Inferno XXV; it has long since fallen out of use there. In Russia, Belarus and Ukraine it is shish, kukish or dulya, a flat refusal. In Turkey it is the equivalent of the middle finger. In Poland it means no. In Croatia, Serbia and Slovenia a fig hidden in a pocket marks a false oath.

In Portugal, Brazil and parts of Spain — Galicia and Asturias — the same hand is a wish of good luck and a guard against the evil eye. Asturian ones are made of jet and it is usual to give them to young children; Spanish calls them higas, Galician and Portuguese figas, Asturleonese ciguas. *Inference —* the same shape reads as a curse in one country and a christening present in the next, which is the clearest case in this atlas of a sign whose meaning is entirely local. In Britain, Ireland, France, Germany and North America it survives mainly as the game where an adult pretends to have stolen a child's nose.
today: Jet figas are still made and sold in Asturias and at Santiago de Compostela, where the jet trade grew up around pilgrims at the end of the Middle Ages. Brazilian figas are sold in wood, horn and gold.
kin: figa — the amulet itself, cut in jet and put on a baby in Asturias and Brazil
kin: phallic-sign — the sign it is welded to on the Roman fist-and-phallus pendants soldiers carried
kin: hand — the wider family of hand signs; this is the closed one
kin: open-palm — the other hand, flat and public, aimed at the same harm from the opposite posture
kin: eye — the harm all of this is aimed at — the fist is one of the shapes that takes the look
kin: jet — the black stone Asturias cuts it from, and the reason so many survive
kin: azabache — the Spanish jet charm the figa is the commonest form of
kin: cornicello — Naples reaches for a horn where Asturias reaches for a fist
sources: s:wp-fig-sign s:wp-fascinus s:wp-jet-gemstone s:wp-evil-eye

## The fish (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/fish/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/fish.json
id: fish
native: ΙΧΘΥΣ (Greek)
aliases: ichthys · ichthus · Jesus fish · fish charm · yu
said: ikh-THOOS
when: 101 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TR IT GR SY IL CN NZ
object: form=pendant materials=copper,silver,stone worn=neck,grave,wall,vehicle
against: child-harm — said by Chinese practice, in which fish and lock charms were worn mainly by young children and infants [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: the-dead — said by early Christian funerary use — the sign is cut on stelae and in catacombs [s:wp-ichthys]
what: A fish in outline, usually two curved strokes crossing at the tail. In Christian use the Greek letters ΙΧΘΥΣ are sometimes written inside it. In China it is cast as a coin charm shaped like a fish and hung on a child. In Aotearoa the related shape is not a fish but the hook that catches one.
story: The Christian fish is an acrostic before it is an animal. ΙΧΘΥΣ spells out Ἰησοῦς Χρῑστός Θεοῦ Υἱός Σωτήρ — Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour. It appears in Christian art and literature from the second century CE and is widespread by the late second to fourth. It is found in the Catacombs of Saint Sebastian and the Catacomb of Priscilla, in the marble ruins of Ephesus, and on funerary stelae carrying inscriptions such as ΙΧΘΥϹ ΖΩΝΤΩΝ, fish of the living.

The story most people have heard about it is disputed. Robert Mowat proposed in 1900 that it was a secret sign among persecuted Christians, arguing from silence. Modern scholarship disputes that: Rasimus lists it among solutions that were once popular, and no early Christian source ties the fish to persecution. The connections the early sources do make are to baptism, to the Eucharist and to the feeding of the multitude.

The fish also turns up on a dated amulet with a word square on its back. The earliest Sator square with explicit Christian imagery is a sixth-century bronze amulet from Asia Minor: two fish turned towards one another on one side, the Sator square in Greek characters on the other, and ICHTHUS written above the square. It is in the Berlin State Museums.

China's fish is a coin. Among the shapes Chinese numismatic charms took as they separated from circulating coinage were spades, locks, fish, peaches and gourds, and fish and lock charms were worn mainly by young children and infants — daily wear rather than festival wear.

*Inference —* this atlas has not found a source connecting the Christian fish and the Chinese fish charm, and does not connect them. A fish is a common animal and an easy outline; two traditions reaching for it is not evidence of contact.
kin: cross — the sign that succeeded the fish as the emblem of Christianity from the second century
kin: palindrome-word — the sixth-century amulet carries both — two fish on one face, the Sator square on the other
kin: charm-coin — the Chinese fish-shaped charm, worn mainly by infants and young children
kin: hei-matau — the Māori fish hook, which is a different object with its own account and no line to either of these
kin: cimaruta — one of the shapes that sprouts from the Neapolitan silver sprig is a fish
kin: coin-square — the shape the Chinese fish charm departs from — the round coin with the square hole
kin: divine-name — the fish spells a name; it belongs with the written charms as much as with the animal ones
sources: s:wp-ichthys s:wp-sator-square s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-hei-matau

## The footprint (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/footprint/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/footprint.json
id: footprint
native: बुद्धपद (Devanagari)
aliases: Buddhapada · Buddha footprint · Phra Phutthabat · Sri Pada
said: buddhapada, 'the Buddha's foot'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IN LK TH KH MM JP CN
object: form=plaque materials=wood,shell,glass,terracotta worn=wall,shop
against: bad-luck — said by Buddhist practice, in which the marks on the sole are named auspicious signs [s:wp-buddha-footprint]
against: bad-luck — said by Theravada communities in Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia, who read the swastika as the Buddha's footprints [s:wp-swastika]
what: The print of a foot, or of two feet side by side, cut in stone or wood or painted. A dharmachakra is often set at the centre of the sole, or the 32, 108 or 132 auspicious signs of the Buddha are engraved or painted across it. There are two kinds and the tradition distinguishes them: prints found in stone or rock, and prints made by hand.
story: The footprint is a way of showing a person by showing where they stood. As a sculptural object it starts in India, in the pre-Greco-Buddhist phase, at sites like Sanchi and Bharhut — that is, in the period when the Buddha was represented by signs rather than by a body. Many of the prints found in rock are acknowledged within the tradition not to be prints of the Buddha's foot but replicas or representations, which can count as cetiya, relics.

The count is large. The Japanese scholar Motoji Niwa found more than 3,000 footprints, about 300 of them in Japan and more than 1,000 in Sri Lanka. The named sites include Sri Pada in Sri Lanka and Phra Phutthabat in Thailand, with more in Cambodia and Burma. In China, the discovery of a large footprint of the Buddha at Chengzhou during the Tang led the Empress Wu Zetian to declare a new era name in 701 CE — a footprint that reset the calendar.

One of the marks on the sole is a sign in its own right elsewhere in this atlas. In Buddhism the swastika is read as standing for the auspicious footprints of the Buddha, and a left-facing one is often imprinted on the chest, feet or palms of Buddha images. Theravada communities in Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia commonly associate the sign with the Buddha's footprints.

Portable versions exist. A Lanna buddhapada of the late fifteenth to early sixteenth century is teak decorated with mother of pearl and glass.

*Inference —* this is the only sign in this batch that is an absence rather than a thing: the shape of somebody who is no longer standing there. Whether it belongs among amulets at all depends on whether a thing you visit counts beside a thing you carry, and this atlas files it here because the small ones are carried.
kin: swastika-sign — in Buddhism that sign stands for these footprints — the two records are one object seen twice
kin: phra-khrueang — the small Thai tablet the footprint's country presses by the million; the same tradition, at hand size
kin: milagro — the other body part sold small and left at a shrine, for the opposite reason
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the practice the large footprints belong to — you travel to them rather than wear them
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition that keeps Phra Phutthabat and presses its amulets
kin: wood — what the portable Lanna versions are made of — teak, with mother of pearl and glass
kin: tibetan-protection — the neighbouring Buddhist tradition, which carries its marks in boxes rather than in stone
sources: s:wp-buddha-footprint s:wp-swastika s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## The hand (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/hand/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/hand.json
id: hand
aliases: hand motif · apotropaic hand · khamsa hand · afus
when: 800 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: MA DZ TN LY EG IL PS SY IQ TR ES IT GR
object: form=pendant materials=silver,gold,brass,jet,glass,terracotta worn=neck,door,wall,wrist,vehicle
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across North Africa and the Middle East, as reported of the hamsa [s:wp-hamsa]
against: demons — said by von Kemnitz, on hand-of-Ishtar amulets in Mesopotamia and Babylon, used to keep evil or disease out of a building [s:wp-hamsa]
against: infertility — said by the names Hand-of-Venus and Hand-of-Mary attach to hand amulets said to help women's fertility and lactation [s:wp-hamsa]
against: child-harm — said by Asturian practice, where jet hands are given to young children [s:wp-fig-sign]
what: A human hand, cast or cut flat and hung where it can be seen. It comes in three postures this atlas keeps apart: the palm open with five fingers spread, the fist with the thumb pushed between two fingers, and two fingers extended with the thumb folded over. Each is a gesture first and an object second — the metal copies something a living hand does.
story: Open-hand motifs run through the ancient Near East. Von Kemnitz records amulets of the hand of Ishtar used in Mesopotamia and Babylon to keep evil or disease from entering a building. At Khirbet el-Qom in Judah an Iron Age tomb carries an engraved hand beside an inscription; what it meant is argued over, and the usual reading is a protective sign in a funerary setting. One of the first appearances of the hand as the amulet now called the hamsa is in Israelite tombs of around 800 BCE.

The name it travels under is not one name. Khamsa is Arabic for five. Hand of Fatima is a label Europeans popularised in French colonial North Africa, not an Arabic term. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews call it the hand of Miriam; Levantine Christians call it kef Miryam, the hand of Mary; in Berber languages afus is simply hand. One shape, five communities, five names, and the argument over which name to print is live.

In al-Andalus the hand is well documented from the thirteenth century onward. Among Moriscos in Granada, khamsa pendants were described as large engraved medals with a hand inscribed with letters, likely Qur'anic. A reform council banned them in 1526 as Islamic symbols and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the ban in 1554. Christians wore them anyway — a Nasrid-period gold pendant is inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

*Inference —* filing the open palm, the fist and the horned hand as one family is this project's decision, not a claim any of their carriers make. What they share is a gesture arrested in metal and aimed outward. Each has its own record here.
kin: open-palm — the flat five-fingered posture, and the one most of the world now buys
kin: fist — the closed posture — a rude gesture cast in silver and hung on a baby
kin: hamsa — the amulet this sign is named for across North Africa and the Middle East
kin: eye — the sign usually set in this one's palm; two answers to the same harm stacked on one object
kin: figa — the Iberian and Brazilian hand, carved in jet and given to children
kin: cornicello — Naples pairs the horn with the mano cornuta, a hand held with two fingers out
kin: milagro — a tin hand nailed to a votive wall asks for a hand to be healed — the same shape doing the opposite job
kin: nazar — the glass bead this hand is sold beside, and is often set into
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read that puts hand, horn and eye in one family and asks whether they belong there
sources: s:wp-hamsa s:wp-fig-sign s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-cornicello s:wp-islam-and-magic

## The horn (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/horn/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/horn.json
id: horn
native: cornicello (Latin)
aliases: cornetto · corno · corno portafortuna · curniciello · Italian horn · mano cornuta
said: kor-nee-CHEL-lo, 'little horn'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IT US AR AU
object: form=horn materials=coral,gold,silver,plastic,bone,terracotta worn=neck,vehicle,wall
against: evil-eye — said by southern Italian wearers; the harm is named malocchio [s:wp-cornicello]
against: bad-luck — said by the amulet's own Italian name, corno portafortuna — the horn that brings luck [s:wp-cornicello]
against: infertility — said by historic use, for fertility and virility [s:wp-cornicello]
against: livestock — said by the malocchio is described as reaching milking animals and fruiting trees as well as people [s:wp-cornicello]
against: child-harm — said by the same account names nursing mothers and their babies first [s:wp-cornicello]
what: A single twisted horn, tapering to a point, hung at a neck or a rear-view mirror. Gold, silver, plastic, bone, terracotta, or the red coral that is the version Naples is known for. A few centimetres long. The hand version — the mano cornuta, two fingers extended and held pointing downward with a swivelling motion — is the same sign made of fingers.
story: The horn is worn against the malocchio, the evil eye, and against bad luck generally, and historically for fertility and virility. It is a regional amulet before it is an Italian one: most often worn by men in southern Italy, above all in Campania, then Lazio, Apulia and Basilicata, and less in Sicily and Calabria.

What the horn is a horn of is an open question. Cornicelli are thought to be modelled on an eland horn. The red ones look like a chili pepper, and dried chilies are hung in some southern Italian houses against the malocchio — but chilies reached Europe only after the Columbian exchange, so the resemblance is younger than the shape. The classical lines pull in several directions at once: the cornucopia broken from a goat by Zeus; coral sacred to Venus; silver sacred to Luna; the phallic outline and the red pointing to Priapus; the horn itself to Pan.

What the harm is said to reach is specific. The malocchio is described as harming nursing mothers and their babies, fruiting trees, milking animals and the sperm of men — the forces of generation, in that order.

The horn moved from the animal to the machine without changing shape. Cornicelli hang from rear-view mirrors now, which the sources trace to the older custom of hanging them on draft horses.

*Inference —* this atlas files the horn beside the eye rather than as an unrelated sign, because the logic its carriers describe is the same interception: a thing conspicuous enough to take the look meant for somebody else.
today: Made in gold and silver for jewellers, and in plastic by the tray for the tourist trade. San Gregorio Armeno in Naples sells both, on the same street, a few metres apart.
kin: cornicello — the amulet itself — the twisted coral horn in a Neapolitan window
kin: eye — the harm it is aimed at, and the sign it stands in for in southern Italy
kin: coral — the red material that gives the Neapolitan horn its colour and half its story
kin: crescent — the other two-pointed sign in the Mediterranean, and one it is regularly confused with
kin: hand — the mano cornuta makes the same horn out of two fingers
kin: phallic-sign — the Roman answer to the same harm; the horn's phallic outline is one reading of why it works
kin: san-gregorio-armeno — the Naples street where it is sold by the hundred, beside the crib figures
kin: cimaruta — the Neapolitan silver sprig that hangs a crescent and a snake and a key on one stalk

## The key (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/key/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/key.json
id: key
aliases: crossed keys · key of life · Legba's key
when: 3000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: HT PH IT EG
against: spirits — said by Vodouists, for whom Papa Legba is the key to the spirit world and is matched with the key-holding Saint Peter [s:wp-haitian-vodou]
against: evil-eye — said by southern Italian wearers of the cimaruta, one form of which carries a key among its sprigs [s:wp-cimaruta]
what: A key, drawn or hung. Nobody in this record carries one to open anything. The sign works on the idea that somewhere there is a door, that somebody holds the key to it, and that showing the key shows whose side you are on.
story: Haiti keeps the clearest statement of it. Most lwa are matched to Roman Catholic saints by an analogy between their functions, and Papa Legba, as the key to the spirit world, is typically associated with Saint Peter, who traditionally holds keys in Roman Catholic imagery. That is not a resemblance somebody noticed later; it is the documented mechanism by which Vodou and Catholicism were joined, and the key is the hinge of the pairing.

Manila carries the keys on a building. Quiapo Church, built in the Baroque style, had a quatrefoil window in the centre of its pediment sealed up in the late 1980s and replaced with a relief of the crossed keys and tiara of the pope, marking its status as a minor basilica. The keys sit above a plaza where amulets and remedies are sold from stalls.

Naples hangs one on a sprig. The cimaruta's branches sprout small charms in combinations that vary by region, and the cited account gives one example outright: a cimaruta might bear the collective imagery of a key, dagger, blossom and moon.

Egypt supplies a key that is not one. The ankh is known in English as the ankh or as the "key of life", the second name based on its meaning rather than its shape; the sign is a T topped by a droplet loop, it wrote the three consonants of the word for life, and it appears in Egyptian art as an object held by deities and handed to the pharaoh. *Inference —* the key reading came from outside. Nothing in the account of the sign's Egyptian use involves a lock, a door or an opening; the loop over a bar was named a key by people who already had a sign for a key and wanted one here. This atlas files it under this motif because that is the name the ankh now travels under, and marks where the name came from.

So: one documented loan, one badge of rank, one component on a compound charm, and one English gloss. The Neapolitan key sits inside the same Catholic world as the papal keys, and it would be easy to join them; no source read here does, and neither does this record.
notes: A short record, and short on purpose. Four appearances, two traditions, and one of the four is a translator's name rather than a carrier's. It is filed under the tool family, added to the vocabulary for it; house would fit it about as well, since half of what a key means here is the door it belongs to.
kin: ankh-amulet — the sign English calls the key of life, on the strength of its meaning and not its shape
kin: cimaruta — the compound charm that carries a key alongside a dagger, a blossom and a moon
kin: quiapo-church — where the crossed keys sit on the pediment, over a plaza full of charm sellers
kin: cross — the other Catholic sign that travelled into Vodou by the same route of matched functions
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice this sign points at, even where no key is actually hung
kin: patua — the other Atlantic charm made where Catholic imagery and an African pantheon meet
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read on borrowed names, which is what the key of life is
sources: s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-quiapo-church s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-ankh
tier: cited · confidence: low · updated: 2026-09-17

## The knot (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/knot/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/knot.json
id: knot
aliases: knot motif · tyet · knot of Isis · girdle of Isis · sacral knot · tied thread
when: 3100 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG GR IE BG MK RO MD IL JP
object: form=knot materials=thread,cloth,carnelian,faience,glass,wood worn=neck,wrist,waist,grave,roof,sewn-in
against: the-dead — said by Book of the Dead chapter 156, which calls for a red jasper tyet at the mummy's neck [s:wp-tyet]
against: illness — said by Bulgarian and Macedonian practice: the red and white threads are described as a wish for good health [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: war — said by Japanese women who stitched senninbari for departing soldiers; the commonest slogan sewn in is bu-un chō-kyū, eternal good luck in war [s:wp-senninbari]
against: house — said by Irish practice — a Brigid's cross hung from the rafters for the saint's blessing and protection over the year [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: witchcraft — said by hadith reporting a charm worked against Muhammad, in one version undone only when the knot was taken apart [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
what: A tie, either made in cloth and thread or copied in stone and metal. Two kinds sit under one heading: the knot that is actually tied — a red string on a wrist, a thousand stitches in a soldier's belt, rushes woven on a feast day — and the knot that is depicted, cut in jasper or drawn as a hieroglyph, with nothing to untie.
story: Egypt gives the depicted knot its clearest case. The tyet resembles a knot of cloth and may have started as a bandage to absorb menstrual blood. An early example comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, excavated by Zaki Saad in the 1940s — old enough to predate the first written references to Isis, whom it was later tied to. From the early New Kingdom, roughly 1550 BCE, tyet amulets went into the wrappings, usually on the upper torso, and from then to the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck and says the power of Isis will protect the body and drive away whoever would commit a crime against it. Green faience examples were made too, the colour standing for renewed life. The tyet can be compared with the Minoan sacral knot at Knossos — a knot with a projecting loop — and the comparison is offered as a resemblance, not a descent.

The tied knot is a different object with a different working part: somebody's hands did it, at a named time, and it can be undone. Bulgarian and Macedonian martenitsi are twisted red and white yarn, given never bought, worn from 1 March and taken off at the sight of a stork or a blossoming tree — sometimes tied then onto a fruit tree. Romanian mărțișor uses the same two threads and is described by observers as funia anului, the year's rope, winding summer into winter. Irish Brigid's crosses are woven from straw or rushes on 1 February and hung in the rafters. Japanese senninbari carry a thousand knots, each made by a different woman, for a soldier going to war.

Undoing is part of the grammar. Islamic hadith describe a charm worked against Muhammad; in one variant he is cured only after the charm — a knot — is taken and taken apart. *Inference —* a knot is the one amulet form that carries its own cancellation in its shape, which is why so many traditions put a date on when it comes off.
kin: tyet-knot — the Egyptian amulet this sign is cut as, in red jasper at the mummy's neck
kin: red-thread — the knot reduced to one strand and one wrist
kin: martenitsa — twisted red and white yarn with a date to put it on and a bird that says take it off
kin: brigids-cross — rushes woven on 1 February and pinned in the rafters for the year
kin: senninbari — a thousand knots, one woman each, sewn into a belt for a soldier
kin: knotting — the practice — the hands, the count, the moment it is tied
kin: thread — what most of these are made of, and the reason so few old ones survive
kin: corn-dolly — the other European straw-work, made from the last sheaf rather than for a saint's day
kin: swastika-sign — one of the seven shapes the National Museum of Ireland sorts Brigid's crosses into is the bent-armed cross
sources: s:wp-tyet s:wp-martenitsa s:wp-m-r-i-or s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-senninbari s:wp-red-string-kabbalah s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-corn-dolly
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

against: illness — said by the astral-medical text LBAT 1597, which ties lamashtu-disease to the moon in the region of Leo [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: demons — said by Lamashtu's own amulets, worn, attached to the body or garments, or placed near beds and doorways [s:wp-lamashtu]
against: bad-luck — said by the Sirr al-Asrar's kings' talisman, a crowned man riding a lion, said to keep harm away [s:wp-talisman]
what: A lion's head on a human body, a lioness's paws on a hippopotamus, or a lion reared up on its hind legs. The sign is a predator set between a person and whatever is coming, and it is nearly always attached to something else — this is a face and a set of paws borrowed onto another body rather than a whole animal drawn on its own.
story: Egypt put the lion in the birth room. The two gods most frequently invoked in Egyptian household apotropaic ritual were Taweret and Bes, and Bes is described in that account as the lion-deity, developed from the earlier dwarf god Aha, 'fighter'. James Romano, Egyptologist and former Curator of Egyptian Art at the Brooklyn Museum, holds that in its earliest inception Bes was a representation of a lion rearing up on its hind legs. Taweret takes the form of a female hippopotamus with the tail of a Nile crocodile and the paws of a lioness, features that parallel other ferocious protective deities, in her case Sekhmet the lioness goddess; her predatory form is what lets her ward evil away from the innocent.

Mesopotamia gave the face to the thing being warded off. Lamashtu has "the head of a lion, the teeth of a donkey, naked breasts, a hairy body, hands stained (with blood?), long fingers and fingernails, and the feet of Anzû", and her amulets vary: a canine or leonine face, talons, wings. An obsidian amulet in the Metropolitan Museum of Art gives her a lion-griffin-like head, raised clawed hands and the feet of a bird of prey. The lion is also overhead — the astral-medical text LBAT 1597 reads, "If (the moon is) in the region of Leo, lamaštu, labašu, and ahhazu-demons, the seized-by-lamaštu(-disease), seized by lamaštu day-and-night(-disease), the god is a lion related to a belligerent god, Ištar, and Hand of the Ghost-disease, (in the region of) Venus and Leo."

This is one of the few families in the atlas where transmission is argued from excavated objects rather than from resemblance. Some scholars hold that Bes is a counterpart of the Mesopotamian Pazuzu: both are protector demons of the home, both have lion parts, wings, a long phallus and similar facial features, both sit similarly on protective amulets, and both are associated with protecting pregnant women and mothers. The contact is physical. A possible Pazuzu figure has been found in Egypt and Bes amulets at sites in Iran, and in a seventh-century-BCE fort at Nimrud five Pazuzu heads were found near a Bes amulet. The derivation, though, stays open: one theory connects both names to the king name Bazi, and the cited account states that neither Pazuzu's name has been shown to come from Bazi nor Bes's name proved to be foreign.

Late antiquity mixed the head into a composite. E. A. Wallis Budge, describing the figure that carries the name Abraxas on magical gems, wrote that "as a Pantheus, i.e. All-God, he appears on the amulets with the head of a cock (Phœbus) or of a lion (Ra or Mithras), the body of a man, and his legs are serpents which terminate in scorpions, types of the Agathodaimon." On other gems Abraxas stands upon a lion borne by a crocodile, and departed spirits ride the back of a crocodile or a lion on the journey to judgment. Budge's gloss names the borrowing outright: the lion head is read as Ra or Mithras, which is a syncretism rather than a coincidence.

The last dated appearance here is an instruction rather than an object. The Pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-Asrar, in the Arabic Hermetica perhaps dating to the ninth century CE, gives a kings' talisman that keeps harm away: under certain astrological marks, a ruby-red stone is carved on a Thursday with a winged, crowned man riding a lion with a flag, six hairless men bowing beneath his hands, and the stone is then burned in an extended ritual.
notes: No source read here documents a living lion amulet, so this record closes in the ninth century CE rather than at the present day. That is a gap in the sources, not a statement that the sign died; it is marked so a later pass can fill it.
kin: bes-amulet — the household god Romano reads as a lion rearing on its hind legs in its earliest form
kin: taweret-amulet — a hippopotamus with a crocodile's tail and a lioness's paws — the sign borrowed onto another animal
kin: lamashtu-plaque — the lion head on the demon rather than on the guard, which is what makes this family two-sided
kin: pazuzu-head — the Mesopotamian half of the documented contact: five of these were found beside a Bes amulet at Nimrud
kin: magical-gem — where the lion head ends up in late antiquity, stacked with a cock's head and serpent legs on the same figure
kin: tooth-and-claw — the neighbouring sign: this one borrows the predator's face, that one carries the predator's parts
kin: serpent — what the lion-headed figure stands on and what its legs turn into on the gems
kin: wallis-budge — whose description of the Abraxas figure is the reason the lion head on these gems is read as Ra or Mithras
kin: mesopotamian-apotropaic — the tradition that fixed the lion-headed demon and the lion-parted guard against her
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the other tradition in the pair, and the one whose objects turned up in Iran
sources: s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-bes s:wp-taweret s:wp-lamashtu s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-abraxas s:wp-talisman

## The mirror (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/mirror-sign/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/mirror-sign.json
id: mirror-sign
native: 八卦鏡 (Han)
aliases: bagua mirror · pa kua mirror · toli · neker-toli · shaman's mirror
said: bāguà jìng, the eight-trigram mirror; in Mongolian, toli
when: undated (still carried)
countries: CN HK TW MN RU SG MY
object: form=mirror materials=copper,brass,glass,steel worn=door,wall,neck,chest
against: house — said by feng shui practitioners, on sha qi — poison arrows from a building's sharp corner or a road running at the door [s:wp-bagua]
against: spirits — said by Taoist masters, whose mirror techniques are described as revealing or destroying evil spirits [s:wp-bagua]
against: witchcraft — said by Mongolian and Buryat shamans, whose mirrored costume is called armour against hostile spirit attack [s:wp-toli-shamanism]
what: A disc of polished metal, worn or hung so it faces outward. Two well-documented kinds: the Chinese bagua mirror, octagonal or circular, with the eight trigrams ringed around a flat, convex or concave glass, fixed above a door or window; and the Mongolian and Buryat toli, a round brass, copper or bronze mirror ornamented on one face and polished on the other, worn at a shaman's neck or sewn in quantity onto the deel or apron.
story: The bagua mirror is a feng shui remedy rather than a feng shui instrument, and its users are clear about the difference: a luopan measures, this one acts. Modern ones descend from ancient bronze-cast versions used by Taoist masters to perform mirror techniques, 鏡術, said to reveal or destroy evil spirits and to overcome natural calamities. The three shapes do three jobs in the tradition's own account: flat reflects, convex disperses, concave converges or absorbs external sha qi — poison arrows — and so changes the feng shui of a house.

What counts as a poison arrow is concrete: the sharp corner of a neighbouring building, or an open road running at your front door. Hang a mirror above the door or window facing it and the arrow is turned away. The problem is where it goes. Anything reflected is understood to be sent in the direction the mirror faces, so pointing a bagua mirror at a neighbour's house is offensive and is a feng shui taboo. The mirrors are cheap and self-installed, which makes them easy to misuse; feuds over offensively aimed mirrors are well known in Hong Kong and other dense Chinese communities, and have been parodied in popular culture. *Inference —* this is the only charm in this atlas whose standard grievance is that somebody else used one correctly.

The toli is worn, not hung. Shamans in parts of Mongolia and in the Republic of Buryatia wear them at the neck or on the ritual costume, which is often called armour, because these pieces protect the shaman from hostile spirit attack. Among the Daur the front and back of the costume were covered with small toli laid like overlapping scales, with up to eight large mirrors on the front and a medium one over the heart — the neker-toli, sometimes plated in nickel. The mirrors are also said to collect and store the power called wind horse, to house helper spirits, and to purify water or vodka. Among the Daur the number a shaman owns says how powerful they are.

*Inference —* a polished disc worn outward does the same physical thing in both traditions: it sends back whatever arrives. The explanations attached to it are not the same, and this record keeps them apart rather than writing one logic across both.
kin: bagua-mirror — the Chinese object itself — trigrams round a disc, fixed above a door
kin: toli-mirror — the Mongolian and Buryat shaman's mirror, worn on the body rather than fixed to a building
kin: eye — the other sign whose stated mechanism is sending a look back where it came from
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the bagua mirror belongs to, and the one that makes it a neighbour's problem
kin: coin-square — sold from the same shelf, and appearing on Chinese lock charms as a design
kin: ongon — the Mongolian spirit-figure the same shamans keep; the mirror houses helper spirits too
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition the bagua mirror's mirror techniques belong to
kin: wearing-hidden — the contrast the toli sets up: this is armour worn on the outside, where it can be seen
sources: s:wp-bagua s:wp-toli-shamanism s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-ongon

## The name (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/divine-name/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/divine-name.json
id: divine-name
native: שדי (Hebrew)
aliases: divine name · Shaddai · the 99 names · Ayat al-Kursi · Abraxas · fulu · talismanic script
said: Shaddai, one of the biblical names of God
when: 700 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL PS EG SY IQ MA DZ TR IR SA PK CN JP KR
object: form=scroll materials=parchment,paper,silver,agate,cloth worn=door,lintel,upper-arm,head,neck,pocket,wall
against: demons — said by hadith on the Throne Verse, which say reciting it turns away devils and fiends [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: evil-eye — said by the tradition around Ayat al-Kursi, which extends its protection to the evil eye [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: travel — said by Muslims who recite the Throne Verse before setting out on a journey and before sleeping [s:wp-throne-verse]
against: witchcraft — said by Surah Al-Falaq, used as a prayer to God against black magic [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: house — said by the reading of Shaddai on a mezuzah as Shomer Daltot Yisrael, Guardian of Israel's doors [s:wp-mezuzah]
against: illness — said by the Gnostics of Basilides, who used the written formula to call beneficent spirits against disease and misfortune [s:wp-abracadabra]
RESTRICTED: Practical Kabbalah's techniques for writing divine and angelic names are restricted within the tradition itself: they were held to be reserved for an elite, to require conditions of holiness and purity, and most Kabbalists taught their use is forbidden. Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets. Most practical Kabbalistic writing stayed in manuscript rather than going into print. This atlas prints that position and does not reconstruct the formulae.
what: A name of God, or of an angel, or a string of characters that stands in for one, written on the object and doing the work. Sometimes it is legible and sometimes it is deliberately not. On a mezuzah it is three Hebrew letters on the outside of the parchment. On an Islamic amulet it is one of the ninety-nine names, or a Qur'anic verse. On a Taoist fu it is a character that resembles Chinese writing and is not meant to be read.
story: Each tradition here has its own account and this record keeps them separate.

In Jewish practice the name on the doorpost is Shaddai, written on the outside of the mezuzah parchment opposite the space between the two passages; it also reads as an acronym for Shomer Daltot Yisrael, Guardian of Israel's doors, and many cases carry just the letter shin for it. The same three letters are built into tefillin: the head-strap's knot forms a dalet, the arm-strap's a yud, and with the shin on the head-box they spell Shaddai. But the practice is contested from inside. Maimonides allows the name on the outside and then condemns what people do with it: those who write the names of angels, other sacred names, verses or forms inside a mezuzah, he writes, are among those who do not have a portion in the world to come — they nullify the commandment, and turn a great commandment about the unity of God's name into a talisman for their own benefit. A bathroom and a small closet get no mezuzah, because the name of God is forbidden there.

Practical Kabbalah, Kabbalah Ma'asit, is the branch that uses divine and angelic names for amulets and incantations. Gershom Scholem's account is that much of its content predates the speculative Kabbalah and does not depend on it, being an accumulation of magical practices from Talmudic times through the Middle Ages. The Talmud and Midrash call the theurgic technique using the Divine Name. In the Hekhalot literature the angels guarding each heavenly level are bound by formulae and seals. The tradition restricts itself: it was held to be permitted only to an elite, and only under conditions that were holy and pure, and most Kabbalists taught that its use is forbidden.

In Islamic practice the amulet usually contains one of God's ninety-nine names, or the names of angels or prophets, or a Qur'anic verse, a pious phrase or an invocation, and has been described as a supercharged prayer. Virtually all Muslim scholars permit a talisman that calls on God or on an intercessor; addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, al-Baqara 2:255, is the verse most often used: hadith say reciting it turns away devils and fiends, and it is recited before a journey, before sleep, and after every obligatory prayer. Because of that association it is also used against the evil eye. Letter-and-number work, ʿilm al-ḥurūf, combines the letters of one of the ninety-nine names with those of a desired object — the technique called jafr.

In Taoist practice the writing is meant to defeat reading. Fulu are talismanic script written on talismans by Taoist priests. Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, by the Eastern Jin, 317–420, that it was already unnecessary for the user to decipher the writing for it to work. Scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz argue the incomprehensibility is central to the talisman's perceived authority; Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls it a deliberate linguistic archaism. The method of writing the characters is passed in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples. Fulu were taken into forms of Chinese Buddhism and inspired the Japanese ofuda and the Korean bujeok.

Gnostic gems give the oldest surviving objects in this family that carry a name and nothing else. Abrasax, later spelled Abraxas, appears in nearly all the legends on the gems, in the Greek Magical Papyri and in Gnostic texts; the attempts to derive the name from Greek, Hebrew, Coptic or Egyptian have not succeeded. The seven letters may stand for the seven classical planets.

*Inference —* the four traditions agree on one thing only: the name is not decoration and the object is not the charm. What they disagree about is whether writing a name down is prayer, permitted craft, or an offence against the name itself.
kin: mezuzah — the doorpost case with Shaddai written on the outside of its parchment
kin: tefillin — the straps whose knots spell the same name with the box's shin
kin: kamea — the Jewish written amulet this tradition's restrictions are about
kin: taweez — the folded Islamic amulet the names and verses are written on
kin: quran-pendant — the verse worn as an object, most often Ayat al-Kursi
kin: fu-talisman — the Taoist sheet whose script is meant not to be legible
kin: ofuda — the Japanese descendant of that script, and bujeok is the Korean one
kin: magical-gem — Abraxas stones — the oldest surviving objects here that carry a name and little else
kin: magic-square — regularly paired with the names in Islamic practice, and a different kind of writing
kin: palindrome-word — the neighbouring practice: writing that works by its shape rather than by whose name it is
kin: washing-off-ink — the practice of drinking the writing, which follows from the name being the active part
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition that names this technique and then restricts it
sources: s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-tefillin s:wp-throne-verse s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-fulu s:wp-abraxas s:wp-abracadabra s:wp-ketef-hinnom s:wp-kabbalah

## The number square (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/magic-square/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/magic-square.json
id: magic-square
native: وفق الأعداد (Arabic)
aliases: magic square · wafq · kamea · Luo Shu · Nine Halls · Chautisa Yantra · planetary square · bhadraganita
said: wafq al-aʿdād, 'harmonious disposition of the numbers'; in Hebrew, kamea; in Chinese, Luoshu
when: 190 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN IN IQ IR DZ EG NG ES IT DE PL JP
object: form=plaque materials=paper,parchment,silver,copper,cloth worn=neck,upper-arm,pocket,sewn-in,wall
against: childbirth — said by Vrnda's Siddhayog, c. 966 CE, which prescribes the 3×3 square to women in labour for an easy delivery [s:wp-magic-square]
against: infertility — said by Jābir ibn Hayyān and al-Ghazālī, in whose works the order-three square is described as a child-bearing charm [s:wp-magic-square]
against: bad-luck — said by the Gargasamhita, which recommends the 3×3 to pacify the nine planets [s:wp-magic-square]
against: evil-eye — said by Islamic talismanic practice, in which squares are used against the evil eye, misfortune, jinn and demons [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: attraction — said by the same tradition, which also uses them to bring good fortune and to preserve attractiveness [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
what: A grid of numbers in which every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same total. The order is the number of cells along a side; the total is the magic constant. Written on paper, engraved on metal, sewn into a shirt, cut into a temple wall. The 3×3 and the 4×4 do most of the amulet work.
story: This one has to be told four times, because four traditions arrived at the same grid and gave four accounts of what it was for.

China has it first. The 3×3 square was known to Chinese mathematicians as early as 190 BCE, in a text called Shushu jiyi, and is given explicitly by the first century CE in the Da Dai Liji. That earliest use is for divination and astrology. Chinese mathematicians called it the Nine Halls; the identification with the legendary Luoshu chart — the pattern of dots on a turtle's shell that rose out of the river Lo while King Yu was channelling a flood — was only made in the twelfth century, after which it was called the Luoshu square.

India's first uses are medical and practical. The 3×3 square first appears in the Gargasamhita, recommended to pacify the nine planets, the navagraha; the oldest version of that text is from 100 CE, though the planetary passage cannot be earlier than 400 CE. The first dateable 3×3 in India is in a medical text, Vrnda's Siddhayog of about 966 CE, prescribed to women in labour for an easy delivery. The oldest dateable fourth-order square in the world is in Varahamihira's Brhat Samhita of about 550 CE, and it is not a charm at all: it is a recipe grid for making perfumes from sixteen substances, with no magical properties attributed. A 4×4 square was inscribed on the wall of the Parshvanath temple at Khajuraho around the twelfth century, and is called the Chautisa Yantra after its magic sum of 34. Narayana Pandit, writing in 1356, says the point of studying these squares is to construct yantra, to deflate bad mathematicians, and for the pleasure of good ones.

The Islamic world produced the mathematics and then the amulets. The first dateable 3×3 in Arabic appears in Jābir ibn Hayyān's Kitab al-mawazin al-Saghir, tied to alchemy; the Arabic name, wafq al-aʿdād, means the harmonious disposition of the numbers, and the earliest treatises are purely mathematical. Squares of orders 3 to 9 appear in the Baghdad encyclopedia Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa of about 983. From the thirteenth century the squares were increasingly put to occult purposes: the Algerian Ahmad al-Buni, around 1225, attributed mystical properties to them in Shams al-Ma'arif and described how to construct them. The 3×3 was described as a child-bearing charm from its first literary appearances in Jābir and in al-Ghazālī, and it kept that role in the tradition of the planetary tables. The pairing of seven squares with the seven heavenly bodies first appears in Ibn Zarkali's Kitāb tadbīrāt al-kawākib, in eleventh-century al-Andalus, and survives in Greek, Arabic and Latin versions. In Islamic talismanic practice the 3×3 with the constant 15 was often associated with the four archangels; 6×6 squares are attested by the late tenth century but did not enter the magical vocabulary until the thirteenth. Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Kishnawi wrote on their theory in eighteenth-century West Africa.

Europe got them last, as occult objects, and had to rediscover the mathematics. They came through Spain and Italy; Ibn Zarkali's work was translated as Libro de Astromagia in the 1280s under Alfonso X. The magic square of three was discussed numerologically by Abraham ibn Ezra of Toledo in the early twelfth century, which influenced later Kabbalists. Around 1315 Manuel Moschopoulos wrote a mathematical treatise that left the mysticism out. Agrippa gave the planetary squares in De occulta philosophia in 1531; Paracelsus reproduced them in garbled form in 1567; Dürer put a 4×4 into Melencolia I in 1514. By the eighteenth century the earlier mysticism had gone and the subject was recreational mathematics.

*Inference —* the same grid carries a Chinese divination, an Indian childbirth charm, an Islamic archangel invocation and a Renaissance planetary correspondence. Transmission is documented for some of those links and not for others; where it is not documented, this record says so rather than assuming.
kin: kamea — the Jewish amulet that is a square of letters and numbers, from the tradition Abraham ibn Ezra fed into
kin: taweez — the folded Islamic amulet a wafq is most often written on
kin: talismanic-shirt — the garment magic squares get painted onto, alongside Qur'anic text
kin: yantra-plate — Narayana Pandit gives constructing yantra as one reason to study these squares
kin: palindrome-word — the other square on a charm — letters instead of numbers, and its own separate history
kin: divine-name — in Islamic practice the square is regularly paired with the names of God and of the archangels
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition that turned the mathematics into amulets, from the 13th century onward
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition that took the 3×3 from Abraham ibn Ezra's numerology
kin: paper — what most of them are written on, which is why almost none survive from before the modern period
kin: inscribing — the practice — the square only works, in every one of these traditions, once somebody writes it out
sources: s:wp-magic-square s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-practical-kabbalah s:wp-kabbalah s:wp-yantra s:wp-talismanic-shirt
