id: open-palm
native: خمسة (Arabic)
aliases: khamsa · khmisa · hand of Fatima · hand of Miriam · hand of Mary · afus · Mano Pantea
said: KHAM-sa, Arabic for five
when: 800 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: MA DZ TN LY EG IL PS SY TR ES
object: form=pendant materials=silver,gold,brass,glass worn=neck,door,wall,vehicle
against: evil-eye — said by carriers across North Africa and the Middle East [s:wp-hamsa]
against: infertility — said by the Hand-of-Venus and Hand-of-Mary names, attached to hand amulets said to protect women, help lactation and strengthen a pregnancy [s:wp-hamsa]
against: child-harm — said by the Mano Pantea reading, in which the sign calls a child's parents to protect it [s:wp-hamsa]
what: A flat hand, palm forward, five fingers spread and usually symmetrical — the two outer fingers drawn as thumbs so the sign reads the same either way up. Cast in silver or brass, cut in gold, pressed in glass. An eye is often set in the middle of the palm. It hangs at a neck, over a door and off a mirror from Morocco to Iraq.
story: Five is the count and the name. The standard Arabic term is khamsa, five, with Maghrebi khmisa beside it. Hand of Fatima is a French colonial nickname, popularised by Europeans in North Africa rather than used in Arabic; in colonial-era French, fatma meant a Muslim or Arab woman. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews say hand of Miriam. Levantine Christians say kef Miryam, hand of Mary. Berber afus just means hand.

Inside the Islamic world the amulet's documented use sits in the west — the Maghreb and historic al-Andalus — and is sparse in the Mashriq, where a hand in ritual use more often belongs to Shi'i iconography and not to this tradition. Von Kemnitz traces the route: Berbers brought the khamsa to al-Andalus; the expelled Muslim and Jewish population carried it back to North Africa with new motifs and techniques. In al-Andalus its use as an amulet is well documented from the thirteenth century.

The sign has an Egyptian claimant too. One account connects the khamsa with the Mano Pantea, an amulet Egyptians knew as the Two Fingers, where the two fingers stand for Isis and Osiris and the thumb for their child Horus, invoking a parent's protection over a child. *Inference —* that is a theory of origin, offered as one among several, and this atlas prints it as a theory.

In Jewish use the hand doubles as the letter shin, first letter of Shaddai, a name of God — one sign carrying two readings at once. It decorates ketubot and Torah pointers. It largely dropped out of Ashkenazi use by the mid-twentieth century and stayed in Sephardi and Mizrahi practice throughout.
today: Sold everywhere on the Mediterranean rim and online, in silver, in enamel, on phone cases and on keyrings, worn by people with no tie to any of the five naming communities. Whether a mass-produced khamsa is the same object as a Moroccan silversmith's is an argument with named people on both sides; this atlas reports it and does not settle it.

kin: eye — the sign set in this palm more often than any other
kin: fist — the other hand, closed and obscene, aimed at the same harm
kin: divine-name — in Jewish use the palm reads as the letter shin, for Shaddai — a hand that is also a name
kin: nazar — the bead it is most often sold with, and often set with
kin: silver — the metal the Maghreb casts it in

against: house — said by Roman householders, who hung phallic wind chimes at doorways and thresholds [s:wp-tintinnabulum-rome]
against: witchcraft — said by Augustine, reporting Varro: the image was carried in procession at the festival of Liber to repel fascinatio from the fields [s:wp-fascinus]
what: An erect phallus, modelled in bronze, bone or wood and worn, hung or fixed. Roman versions are frequently winged, and turn up as pendants, finger rings, relief carvings, lamps and wind chimes. Thai palad khik are small carved rods worn at the waist. The sign is not decorative and was not treated as decorative.
story: In Roman religion the fascinus was the divine phallus. Pliny called it a medicus invidiae — a doctor, or remedy, for envy and for the look that carries it. The Vestal Virgins tended the cult of the fascinus populi Romani, and when a general celebrated a triumph they hung an effigy of it under his chariot to protect him from invidia. Augustine, drawing on Varro, records a phallic image carried in procession at the festival of Father Liber to keep enchantment off the fields.

Who wore one is a narrower question than it looks. There are very few Roman images of people wearing a phallic charm. Varro notes the custom of hanging one at a baby's neck, and phallus-bearing rings have been found too small for anyone but a child. A 2017 experimental archaeology project suggested some types were designed to stay pointing outwards, in the wearer's direction of travel, so as to face whatever was coming.

The explanation Roman writers give is not only fertility. The protective function is usually tied to the regenerative power of an erect phallus, but in most cases what diverts the look is the shame or the laughter that obscenity produces. The victory is sometimes drawn literally: a phallus ejaculating at a disembodied eye, a motif known from reliefs at Leptis Magna in present-day Libya and from several places on Hadrian's Wall, and from a first-century BCE terracotta of two small phallus-men sawing an eyeball in half.

Soldiers carried a compound version, the fist-and-phallus amulet, with a clenched fist at the base of the shaft — often making the fig sign. The largest known collection is from Camulodunum.

The sign is not only Roman. In Thailand the palad khik is carved, blessed and worn at the waist, and Thai practice has its own account of what it is for, which this atlas records in that amulet's own file rather than folding into Rome's.
kin: fascinum — the Roman amulet itself — the winged bronze in the tray
kin: palad-khik — Thailand's carved phallus, worn at the waist, with its own tradition behind it and no line of descent from Rome that this project can show
kin: fist — the hand fused to the shaft on the soldiers' fist-and-phallus pendants
kin: eye — the harm it is aimed at, and in Roman art the thing it is drawn attacking
kin: bell — the tintinnabulum hung a phallus and bells together at a Roman doorway
kin: horn — southern Italy's later substitute — a shape that catches a glance without the obscenity
kin: bulla — the locket a Roman boy wore, which is where a phallus was often put
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition this sign sits at the centre of
sources: s:wp-fascinus s:wp-tintinnabulum-rome s:wp-fig-sign s:wp-palad-khik s:wp-evil-eye
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## The red thread (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/red-thread/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/red-thread.json
id: red-thread
native: חוט השני (Hebrew)
aliases: red string · scarlet thread · kautuka · martenitsa thread · mărțișor
said: khutt hashani, the scarlet thread
when: 1490 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL BG MK RO MD AL GR IN CN US
object: form=cord materials=thread,cloth worn=wrist,finger,neck,chest
against: evil-eye — said by the Jewish folk custom, which names the harm as ayin hara [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: bad-luck — said by the same custom, described as a way to ward off misfortune [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: illness — said by Bulgarian and Macedonian practice: the red and white threads are a wish for good health [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: house — said by Romanian and Moldovan observers, who record the pendant as a talisman for the wearer's health and beauty [s:wp-m-r-i-or]
what: A length of red wool or silk tied round a wrist. In the Jewish folk custom it is thin scarlet wool worn as a bracelet or band. In Bulgaria and North Macedonia red is twisted with white into a martenitsa, usually as two small dolls, Pizho in white and Penda in red. In Romania and Moldova the same two threads make a mărțișor with a charm hung from them.
story: The thread's Jewish version is a folk custom, and the sources are careful about how thin its textual footing is. A scarlet thread tied about the wrist appears at Genesis 38, when Tamar gives birth to twins. As early as Rabbi Shmuel ben Hafni Gaon, commentators noted that a red string on the hand may be a good omen, and some say it could go round a finger; one early commentary, Aggadas Bereishis, says Joseph's coat was the same as his brothers' except that Jacob put a red string on the cuffs. But there is no written requirement in the Torah, in halacha or in Kabbalistic texts to tie a red string on a wrist, and it is not clear the mentions of red string as a good omen describe a widespread practice. The one public exhortation on record is from the 1490s: when Jews were barred from wearing tefillin, Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended wearing a red string on the hand instead, to remember the commandment.

The modern trade is documented. Elderly women sell scarlet thread to pilgrims and visitors in Israel, especially in the Old City of Jerusalem. Outside Israel it became popular in the late 1990s with celebrities, many of them not Jewish — Madonna and her children, Leonardo DiCaprio, Michael Jackson, Ariana Grande, Tucker Carlson, Jared Kushner — and the wider popularity is often linked to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. Whether that is the same object as the thread a Jerusalem woman sells is an argument with named parties on both sides; the Kabbalah Centre's critics include the Kabbalist Michael Laitman, who holds that practical Kabbalah has no use for red strings.

The Balkan thread runs on a calendar instead. Martenitsi are given, never bought for oneself, from Baba Marta Day on 1 March, and worn pinned to clothing or at the wrist or neck until the wearer sees a stork or a swallow back from migration, or a tree in blossom — then taken off, and in some places tied to the branch of a fruit tree to give the tree health and luck. Red and white are read as a wish for good health; white for the purity of melting snow, red for the setting sun and for life. Both martenitsa and mărțișor are inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

*Inference —* the red string is worn on wrists in Jewish, Hindu and Chinese practice, and the Jewish source itself says so without claiming a link between them. This atlas reports the three and does not draw a line between them, because nothing read here draws one.
kin: red-string — the amulet itself — the scarlet wool on a wrist
kin: martenitsa — the Balkan version, with a date to put it on and a bird that says take it off
kin: knot — the wider family: a charm whose working part is that somebody tied it
kin: thread — the material, and the reason almost none of these survive in a museum drawer
kin: tefillin — the commandment Rabbi Abraham Saba proposed the string as a reminder of, in the 1490s
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition the string is popularly attached to, and which several Kabbalists say has no use for it
kin: unesco-ich — the body whose Representative List carries the martenitsa and the mărțișor
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice the Balkan thread runs on: a start date, a sign, an end
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the other thing sold off a tray in Jerusalem and Istanbul for the same stated harm

## The serpent (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/serpent/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/serpent.json
id: serpent
aliases: snake motif · cobra · uraeus · nāga · entwined snakes · rainbow serpent
when: 3000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG IQ GR IT IN KH TH LA BJ MX GT HT CN JP KR AE
object: form=pendant materials=silver,gold,agate,copper,terracotta worn=neck,finger,door,lintel,head
against: snakebite — said by Egyptian texts: charms against snakes were inscribed or chanted, some invoking the snake deity Nehebkau, and some to protect the dead [s:wp-snake-worship]
against: spirits — said by Angkorean builders, who set hooded multi-headed nāgas as guardians of temples and other premises [s:wp-serpent-symbolism]
against: war — said by Egyptian tradition, which has Wadjet spit fire at the enemies of the pharaoh and of Ra [s:wp-snake-worship]
against: illness — said by the Asclepius staff and the Ningizzida rod, both healing emblems in their own traditions [s:wp-serpent-symbolism]
against: livestock — said by German popular belief, in which the house snake looks after the cows and the children [s:wp-snake-worship]
what: A snake, drawn coiled, reared, entwined in pairs, or hooded above a head. It is cut into rings and pendants, cast on the branches of Neapolitan silver charms, hooded in stone over Angkorean doorways, and worn as the cobra on an Egyptian crown. Nothing else in this atlas is so evenly split between a thing to be guarded against and a thing that does the guarding.
story: Snakes make good guardians for a reason their observers state plainly: a cornered cobra or rattlesnake holds its ground, displays, and fights rather than retreating. So it gets set where something cannot be moved out of harm's way. At Angkor, hooded multi-headed nāgas guard temples in stone, and from about the twelfth century CE a favourite subject was the Buddha meditating on the coils of a nāga whose flared hood shields him — the story of Mucalinda, who came up from the roots of a tree when the storm began.

Egypt puts the snake at the top. Wadjet, the Egyptian cobra, is from the earliest records the patron and protector of the country, of the other gods and of the pharaohs, worn entwined around the papyrus staff and set in the crown. Nehebkau, the two-headed serpent, guarded the entrance to the underworld, and charms against snakes were inscribed or chanted invoking him — which is the whole ambivalence in one deity: the snake keeps snakes off.

The entwined pair is older than the caduceus. The oldest known representation of two snakes coiled round a rod is the Sumerian god Ningizzida, later a god of healing and magic; a green steatite vase carved for King Gudea of Lagash, dated variously to 2200–2025 BCE, carries an inscription dedicated to him and is in the Louvre. The Greek physician Asclepius carries the single-snake staff that modern medicine still uses. Moses set a serpent on a pole, the Nehushtan, at Numbers 21:8.

Europe kept a domestic version. German popular belief records the house snake that looks after the cows and the children, whose appearance is an omen of death, and whose life is often held to be bound to the master's and the mistress's.

*Inference —* the snake turns up in this role on every inhabited continent, and the sources read here do not show one tradition teaching another. Where the same posture appears — reared, hooded, entwined — the likeliest account is that people in many places watched the same animal do the same thing.
kin: cimaruta — the Neapolitan silver sprig that grows a snake on one of its branches, beside a key and a crescent
kin: magical-gem — the engraved stones that carry snakes, snake-legged figures and serpent-haired heads
kin: eye — the other sign that is both the harm and the answer to it
kin: tree — the snake is almost always coiled around one — Eden, the Hesperides, Yggdrasil, the Bodhi tree
kin: tooth-and-claw — the animal reduced to its dangerous part; the serpent is kept whole instead
kin: lion — the other guardian animal set at doorways, and the one Egypt paired Wadjet with as Sekhmet
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the guardian snake belongs to, in stone rather than in metal
kin: west-african-charm-craft — one of the living traditions that names and serves serpent figures, and which speaks for itself rather than through this record
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition the German house snake and the Neapolitan silver snake both belong to
sources: s:wp-serpent-symbolism s:wp-snake-worship s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-haitian-vodou

## The spiral (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/spiral/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/spiral.json
id: spiral
aliases: triskelion · triple spiral · spiral inscription · the coil
when: 4400 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: MT IE IM IT GR IQ SY EG RU
object: form=bead materials=terracotta,ink,copper worn=foundation,wall,neck
against: demons — said by the householders of Nippur, in John Charles Arnold's reading of the bowls [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: evil-eye — said by the bowls' own inscriptions, which name the evil eye among the influences they act against [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: weapons — said by the hoplites who bore the triskeles on their shields from the late sixth century BCE [s:web-wp-triskelion]
what: A line that winds in on itself. It is cut into stone, painted on pottery, blazoned on a shield, and — once, and importantly — used as the direction in which to write, so that the words themselves coil inward.
story: Mesopotamia is the only place in this record where somebody says what the spiral is for. Incantation bowls were usually inscribed in a spiral, beginning at the rim and moving toward the centre, most of them in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, made in Upper Mesopotamia and Syria from the sixth to the eighth centuries. The scholar John Charles Arnold describes how they worked: "When placed upside down under each corner of a house, demons would follow the inscribed charms that spiraled from the outer rim inward, only to be caught in the center." The geometry is the mechanism. The spiral is a trap, and a text written that way is a corridor with no exit.

Europe cut it into tombs long before anyone wrote in it. The triple spiral, the triskelion, first appears in Malta between 4400 and 3600 BCE, and then in the astronomical calendar of the megalithic tomb at Newgrange in Ireland, built around 3200 BCE. It runs through European Neolithic and Bronze Age artefacts and into the Iron Age, especially in the La Tène culture. From the late sixth century BCE it appears on hoplite shields and Greek pottery, and it was adopted as an emblem by the rulers of Syracuse, possibly in connection with the island's Greek name Trinacria, 'having three headlands'. It survives in the arms and flags of the Isle of Man.

Egypt kept a spiral on the eye. The wedjat has a line extending below and toward the rear of the eye that ends in a curl or spiral; the Egyptologist Richard H. Wilkinson suggests the curling line derives from the facial markings of the cheetah, which Egyptians associated with the sky because its spots were likened to stars. In New Kingdom elaborations the rear spiral could become a bird's tail feathers.

The Caucasus keeps a spiralled version of another sign: according to Vakhushti of Kartli, the tribal banner of the Avar khans depicted a wolf with a standard bearing a double-spiral swastika.

Transmission or convergence: unknown, and the sources read here do not say. The triskelion page sets out the recurrences and declines to explain them. The distances are the argument against a single story — Malta and Newgrange are separated by twelve hundred years and a sea, and the Mesopotamian bowl spiral comes three and a half thousand years after either and is not an ornament at all but a way of arranging letters. *Inference —* the shield blazon and the bowl inscription are doing different jobs with the same curve: one is a face shown to an enemy, like a gorgoneion, and the other is a floor plan for a maze. This record files them together because they share a shape and says plainly that sharing a shape is all they are known to share.
notes: Filed under the geometric family, which this record's own objection got added to the vocabulary: the spiral is a line that turns back on itself and belongs with shape rather than with rope.
kin: incantation-bowl — the only object in this atlas where the spiral is load-bearing: the words follow it inward and the demon follows the words
kin: wedjat-eye — carries the sign as a tail — the curl below the eye that Wilkinson traces to a cheetah's markings
kin: swastika-sign — the neighbouring turning sign, and the one whose Avar banner version is recorded as a double spiral
kin: gorgoneion — the other thing a Greek put on a shield, which is how this record reads the triskeles blazon
kin: knot — the family this sign is filed under: a line that turns back on itself and does not let go
kin: ink — what the spiral is made of in the bowls — the shape exists only as writing there
kin: terracotta — the surface that kept the spiral legible for fourteen centuries
kin: foundation-deposit — the practice the bowls belong to: face down, under each corner of the house
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read on signs that recur without a route, which this one is a clean example of
sources: s:web-wp-triskelion s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-swastika

## The square hole (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/coin-square/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/coin-square.json
id: coin-square
native: 厭勝錢 (Han)
aliases: yansheng coin · huaqian · flower coin · cash coin hole · round coin with a square hole
said: yàn shèng qián, 'charm coin'; the hole itself is called an eye, 眼 yǎn
when: 206 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN JP KR VN ID TW SG
object: form=coin materials=copper,brass,jade,gold,silver worn=neck,waist,wall,roof,door
against: spirits — said by Han-era users: the coins were cast to speak to the dead, to pray for favourable outcomes and to terrify ghosts [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: demons — said by feng shui practice, in which coin-swords are hung to frighten away demons and evil spirits [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: child-harm — said by Buddhist and Taoist priests, who tied lock charms round children's necks; the hundred family lock was funded by a hundred families for one newborn [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: illness — said by a Han pendant charm inscription, bi bing mo dang — avoid hostilities and ward off sickness [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: attraction — said by collectors of the five-emperors string, said to bring wealth and good fortune [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: exams — said by lock charms, said to bring high results in the imperial exams as well as protection and long life [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
what: A round disc of copper alloy, brass or bronze with a square hole punched through the middle, the four sides of the hole framed by characters. It is the shape of Chinese money for two thousand years, and it is also the shape of a charm that was never money. Most numismatic charms imitate whatever circulating cash coin was current when they first appeared; some were cast instead as spades, locks, fish, peaches and gourds.
story: The charm coin — yansheng qian, now more often called huaqian, flower coin — first appears under the Western Han as a variant of the Ban Liang and Wu Zhu cash coins. It was used to speak to the dead, to pray for a good outcome, to frighten ghosts and as lucky money. Over centuries it became a separate commodity with its own shapes and sizes. Unlike a cash coin, which carries two or four characters on a side, a charm often carries more characters, and pictures on the same side.

These were mostly privately funded and cast by wealthy families for their own ceremonies, though governments and religious orders cast some. They circulated alongside official coinage and held value because they were made of copper alloy and Chinese coins were valued by weight in bronze or brass. In periods of copper scarcity they worked as alternative currency — temple coins were issued by Buddhist temples under the Yuan when copper was short or deliberately limited by the Mongol government.

The square hole is not only an opening. It is called an eye, yǎn, and Chinese charms are built on visual puns: a gourd charm made of two Wu Zhu replicas with a bat covering the character where they meet reads as happiness is before your eyes, because bat sounds like happiness and coin sounds like before. A charm's meaning is frequently a rebus you have to hear rather than see.

The forms multiply from there. Open-work charms have irregular openings between the design elements and usually a single large round hole, or a square one where the design is a building. Lock charms are flat, have no moving parts, resemble the character 凹, and were tied around children's necks by Buddhist or Taoist priests; the hundred family lock was funded by a poor family asking a hundred other families each to give a cash coin for a newborn. Pendant charms were worn at the neck or waist from the beginning of the Han, or fixed to rafters, pagodas, temples and lanterns; fish and lock charms were worn mainly by young children and infants. Han pendant charms carry inscriptions like chu xiong qu yang, do away with evil and dispel calamity, and bi bing mo dang, avoid hostilities and ward off sickness.

Qing-era cash coins of the five emperors Shunzhi, Kangxi, Yongzheng, Qianlong and Jiaqing are strung together as a set said to bring wealth and good fortune. Strung coins are also built into swords: in feng shui, coin-swords are hung to frighten demons and evil spirits away.

Chinese charms inspired the same tradition in Japan, Korea and Vietnam, and charms from those countries are regularly mistaken for Chinese ones because the symbolism and inscriptions are close. Chinese cash coins themselves are treated as lucky charms outside China.
today: A Chinese Numismatic Charms Museum opened on 1 February 2015 in Haikou, Hainan, in a building that replicates the Szechuan Kanting Civilian Commercial Bank in Movie Town Haikou, with about 530 square metres of exhibition space and more than 2,000 charms from the Han to the Republic.
kin: charm-coin — the object this sign is the shape of — the charm in the tray
kin: bagua-mirror — hung on the same walls and sold from the same shelf, and appearing on lock charms as a design
kin: ping-an-fu — the other Chinese thing tied round a child's neck for safety
kin: fu-talisman — the drawn Taoist talisman; some coin charms are cast as imperial decrees in the same voice
kin: divine-name — Taoist charms carry writing meant to command rather than to be read, which is a different use of script from this one
kin: eye — the square hole is called an eye in Chinese, which is a pun and not this atlas's eye family
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition that casts, inscribes and reads them
kin: copper — the alloy that gave the charm its weight and therefore its value
kin: challenge-coin — the modern coin carried for belonging rather than for luck, and the nearest living parallel outside Asia
sources: s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-numismatic-charm s:wp-fulu s:wp-bagua

## The swastika (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/swastika-sign/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/swastika-sign.json
id: swastika-sign
native: स्वस्तिक (Devanagari)
aliases: svastika · sauvastika · manji · 卍 · 卐 · wanzi · yungdrung · arevakhach · nkontim · whirling log · tsin náálwołí · Naa Ukuryaa · Hakenkreuz · hooked cross · fylfot · gammadion
said: SWOS-tih-kuh
when: 10000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IN NP LK BT TH MM KH ID CN JP KR VN MN ET GH PA US AM IR BG UA ES DE AT AU
root: Sanskrit svastika, from svasti — su 'good, well' + asti 'it is' — plus the suffix -ka; svasti occurs frequently in the Vedas meaning health, luck, success, prosperity, and was used as a greeting
object: form=door-piece materials=earth,paper,wood,cloth,copper,seed worn=door,lintel,wall,roof,skin,neck
against: bad-luck — said by Hindu, Buddhist and Jain practice, in which the sign is auspicious; the Sanskrit root svasti means health, luck, success, prosperity [s:wp-swastika]
against: attraction — said by Chinese use: declared the source of all good fortune in 693 under Wu Zetian, and read as longevity and infinity through the homophone for ten thousand [s:wp-swastika]
against: illness — said by Navajo practice, in which the whirling log, tsin náálwołí, is used in healing rituals [s:wp-swastika]
against: house — said by Hindu householders, who put it at entrances and on doorways of homes and temples [s:wp-swastika]
RESTRICTED: Public display of this sign is a criminal offence in several countries when it is the Nazi emblem, and the religious exemptions are written narrowly. This atlas prints the sign's name and history and does not reproduce the Nazi flag.
what: An equilateral cross with each arm bent at a right angle, so the figure has four-fold rotational symmetry and no mirror symmetry. It comes in two mirror forms: right-facing 卐 and left-facing 卍. Drawn in coloured sand on a doorstep, made in rice in front of a Jain altar, imprinted on the palms of a Buddha image, cast into Chinese lattice, worn as a Japanese family crest, woven into Navajo textiles — and, rotated 45 degrees onto a white disc on a red ground, flown as the flag of Nazi Germany from 1935.
story: Take the living practice first, because it is older, larger and still going.

In Hinduism the sign goes before entrances and on doorways of homes and temples, marks the starting page of financial statements, and is built into mandalas for weddings and for welcoming a newborn. It has a particular tie to Diwali, drawn in rangoli — coloured sand — or laid out in deepak lights on the floor outside a house. Both turns are used and they are read differently: the clockwise form is solar, for Surya; the counter-clockwise, sometimes called sauvastika, connotes night and in tantric traditions stands for Kali.

In Buddhism it stands for the auspicious footprints of the Buddha, and a left-facing swastika is often imprinted on the chest, feet or palms of Buddha images. It is homologous with the dharma wheel, and the shape is read as eternal cycling, the theme of samsara. In the Bon tradition of Tibet it is the left-facing yungdrung.

In Jainism it is the emblem of Suparśvanātha, the seventh tīrthaṅkara, and in the Śvētāmbara tradition one of the eight auspicious aṣṭamaṅgala. All Jain temples and holy books must contain it. Ceremonies begin and end by making the mark several times in rice around the altar, and an offering is set on it — a fruit, a sweet, a coin or a note. The four arms are read as the four places a soul may be reborn before it attains moksha.

East Asia took it with Buddhism from India. In 693, under the Tang, it was declared the source of all good fortune and named wan by Wu Zetian. The character is a homonym for ten thousand and for infinity, so it also reads as immortality and longevity, and adding it to another auspicious pattern multiplies the wish by ten thousand. It has been part of the Chinese writing system since at least the Liao dynasty, 907–1125, as a variant of 萬. In Japan it entered with the writing system in the eighth century as the manji, became the crest of families including the Tsugaru and the Hachisuka, flies as the official flag of Hirosaki, and is the map symbol for a Buddhist temple under Japan's Survey Act.

It is far from only Asian. Armenians call it arevakhach and it appears on Copper Age petroglyphs. Islamic use runs from the Umayyad palaces of Walid, 705–715, and Hisham, 724–743, through Abbasid Raqqa and Cordoba to the Persianate world from the Seljuk period onward; on the Gonbad-e-Sorkh of 1147 it seems to have stood for the soul and resurrection. In Ethiopia one is carved in a window of the twelfth-century Biete Maryam at Lalibela. In Ghana the Akan adinkra symbol nkontim takes this form and stands for loyalty. Hopi, Navajo and Tlingit peoples have used it; the Navajo symbol tsin náálwołí, whirling log, represents humanity and life and is used in healing rituals. The Guna people of Panama adopted a flag carrying the sign in 1925 and call it Naa Ukuryaa. The earliest known swastikas are older still: a meander pattern of joined-up swastikas on a late Palaeolithic mammoth-ivory bird figurine from Mezine in Ukraine, dated 10,000 to 17,000 BCE, and mirror-image swastikas on pottery in the Devetashka cave in Bulgaria dated to 6000 BCE. In South Asia the sign first appears in the archaeological record around 3000 BCE in the Indus Valley Civilisation.

Now the other history, which is specific, recent and European.

Heinrich Schliemann excavated more than 1,800 ancient swastikas and variants at Hisarlik from 1871 to 1875 and linked them to the Sanskrit word. In 1872 Émile-Louis Burnouf, director of the French School at Athens, wrote to him that the swastika should be regarded as a sign of the Aryan race, adding that the Jews had completely rejected it. Schliemann accepted that reading and tied his Trojan finds to objects found in Germany. Before the Nazis, the sign tilted 45 degrees was already in use by the German nationalist Völkisch movement. The Nazi Party formally adopted it in 1920: a black swastika rotated 45 degrees on a white circle on a red ground, used on the party flag, badge and armband. Hitler described designing it in Mein Kampf in 1925 and said the hooked cross carried the mission of the struggle for the victory of the Aryan man. Racial hygiene and scientific racism were central to Nazism, and the party co-opted the sign as an emblem of an Aryan master race. On 14 March 1933 the NSDAP flag was hoisted beside Germany's national colours; as part of the Nuremberg Laws, on 15 September 1935 it became the sole national flag of Germany. Since the 1930s, in the West, the sign has been read as a symbol of hate and, in many Western countries, of white supremacy. Neo-Nazi organisations still use it; the Anti-Defamation League records it among hate symbols used as graffiti in United States schools, and in 2010 said it had for some become a more generalised symbol of hate while remaining predominant among American white supremacists, particularly as a tattoo.

The two histories now collide in law and in shop aisles. German and Austrian criminal law forbids public display of the swastika, with the swastikas on Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples exempt, because religious symbols cannot be banned in Germany. Poland's ban likewise exempts religious use; a Latvian court held in 2007 that it may be used as an ethnographic symbol. In 2022 Victoria became the first Australian state to ban display of the Nazi swastika. Goods carrying the Jain, Buddhist or Hindu sign, exported to North America and Europe, have been read by buyers as Nazi emblems and withdrawn: Pokémon cards in 1999, Christmas crackers in Canada in 2002, a Shein necklace in 2020.

Hindu, Buddhist and Jain organisations have asked publicly that the two not be conflated, and they have names. When Berlin proposed an EU-wide ban in early 2007, Hindu groups across Europe campaigned against it, pointing out that the sign had been a symbol of peace for 5,000 years; the proposal was dropped on 29 January 2007. The Hindu American Foundation opposed New York bills A8545 and S6648 in July 2020, objecting that the bills defined the swastika as a symbol of Nazi Germany without explaining its origins and its continuing use in Hinduism, Sikhism, Jainism and Buddhism, and warning that teaching that definition could expose Hindu American students to prejudice. In May 2022 the Coalition of Hindus of North America, with the Heiwa Peace and Reconciliation Foundation of New York and the Buddhist Council of New York, objected to California's AB2282 for keeping the phrase Nazi Swastika; its president Nikunj Trivedi said the wording perpetuates the false idea that there is a good swastika and a bad one. Their proposal is a vocabulary one: reserve swastika for the sacred sign and use Hakenkreuz, or Nazi hooked cross, for Hitler's emblem. The Rev. T.K. Nakagaki, a Buddhist priest in New York and author of The Buddhist Swastika and Hitler's Cross, 2018, argues the same distinction.

The objection to that distinction also has names. Mark Pitcavage of the Anti-Defamation League's Center on Extremism has acknowledged the sign's sanctity in several faiths while holding that Hitler's association with it cannot be entirely removed. Shelley Rood Wernick, managing director of the Jewish Federations of North America's Center on Holocaust Survivor Care, has said the symbol stands for the annihilation of an entire people and can re-traumatise survivors. Hitler himself, speaking in Munich on 13 August 1920, said the Nazi sign was the same one found carved in temple pillars as far as India and Japan.

This atlas reports that argument and does not settle it. It records the two histories separately because they are separate: one runs from prehistory to this morning's rangoli, the other begins in 1920 and ends in a genocide.
how: Drawn rather than made, more often than not. Rangoli sand or deepak lights outside a Hindu house at Diwali; rice laid in the shape before a Jain altar and an offering set on it; painted or carved on a temple; woven into cloth; cast into lattice; imprinted on a Buddha image's palms.
today: Living and daily across South, Southeast and East Asia as of 2026, and prohibited or criminalised in its Nazi use in Germany, Austria, Poland, Latvia, Lithuania, Brazil, Geneva and the Australian state of Victoria, with religious exemptions written into several of those laws.
kin: the-swastika-problem — the long read this record hands off to: two histories, one shape, and what a catalogue owes each
kin: cross — the unbent figure, which this atlas files separately because the twentieth century is not shared
kin: footprint — in Buddhism this sign IS the footprint's mark — the two records are one object seen twice
kin: brigids-cross — the National Museum of Ireland sorts one whole class of these woven crosses as the bent-armed type
kin: charm-coin — Chinese charms that carry the wan character, multiplying the wish by ten thousand
kin: omamori — sold at Japanese temples whose map symbol is this sign
kin: lungta-flag — Tibetan and Bon material carries the left-facing yungdrung
kin: spiral — the other rotating figure, and the one it is often grouped with in prehistoric assemblages
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on who gets to say what a sign means, which this record is the hardest case for

## The tooth and the claw (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/tooth-and-claw/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/tooth-and-claw.json
id: tooth-and-claw
aliases: pierced tooth · animal tooth amulet · whale tooth · tabua · lei niho palaoa · wolf's tooth
when: 23 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR IT GB AL FJ TO US GL CA
object: form=pendant materials=tooth,bone,gold,hair,shell,coral,wood worn=neck,grave
against: child-harm — said by the Pitt Rivers Museum, on a wolf's tooth worn by a child as a remedy for convulsions and chewed during teething [s:web-prm-wolf-tooth]
against: illness — said by Pliny the Elder, cited by the museum: a wolf's tooth could also prevent a child from being startled [s:web-prm-wolf-tooth]
against: evil-eye — said by Illyrians, who used animal teeth against it alongside the phallus, the hand and the leg [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: the-dead — said by Fijian practice: the dead were buried with their tabua [s:wp-tabua]
against: spirits — said by Inuit accounts, in which an amulet's efficacy is attributed to its corresponding spirit [s:wp-inuit-religion]
RESTRICTED: Removing a tabua from Fiji is highly restricted — 225 exports a year — and needs a permit from the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs as well as CITES permits, because the tooth comes from an endangered species. Original CITES permits must be shown to the importing country's border officials. In 2007 New Zealand authorities returned 146 tabua to Fiji after seizing them as illegally exported.
what: A tooth, a tusk or a claw, pierced or mounted and hung. Sometimes the animal part is left as it came off the animal; sometimes it is carved past recognition. A wolf's canine set in gold, a sperm whale's tooth polished and strung on plaited coir, a whale tooth cut into a hook and hung from a rope of braided human hair.
story: The clearest documented European case is small and specific. The Pitt Rivers Museum holds a wolf's canine mounted in gold, from the Haute-Marne in north-eastern France, accession 1985.52.105, acquired before 1931 and transferred from the Wellcome Institute in 1985. The museum records it as worn by a child as a remedy for convulsions, and chewed or rubbed on the gums during teething. The practice is old: Pliny the Elder writes that a wolf's tooth could also stop a child being startled.

Illyrians used animal teeth against the evil eye, alongside shapes of the phallus, the hand and the leg — so the tooth sits in the same substitution set as the other signs in this atlas's eye family.

In the Pacific the tooth is a whale's and its meaning is social before it is protective. A Fijian tabua is a polished sperm whale tooth, given as sevusevu for atonement or esteem, and used in negotiations between rival chiefs. The dead were buried with their tabua. Originally the teeth were rare — from beached whales, or traded from Tonga, where the practice may have begun — but once the market was known in the early nineteenth century thousands of teeth, and fakes made from ivory and walrus tusk, entered it. That trade is where the European art of scrimshaw grew up. A Hawaiian lei niho palaoa is a neck ornament worn by aliʻi of both sexes, most nineteenth-century examples a whale tooth carved into a hook and suspended on plaited human hair. What it means is not known; it may represent a tongue that speaks the law, or a vessel for mana. Pre-contact ones were under two inches long and made of shell, bone, wood, stone and coral as well as whale ivory. The Bishop Museum holds one whose hair bundle has a circumference of 7.5 inches: a single eight-ply square braid cord 1,708 feet long, looped back and forth over a thousand times on each side.

Inuit use of amulets is documented but the sources read here describe the class rather than the material. The Netsilik used a great many, unlike the Iglulik; even dogs could have them; one boy was recorded with eighty, so many he could hardly play. The efficacy is attributed to the amulet's corresponding spirit, and amulets could be made by an angakoq or by a lay person.

*Inference —* a tooth is the part of an animal that did the animal's work, and it is the part that survives burial. Both of those are reasons it turns up; this atlas cannot separate them from the evidence read here.

This record does not name every people among whom teeth and claws are worn. Where a source names a people, that name is printed above. Where none does, the gap stays a gap.
kin: inuit-amulet — the Arctic class this sign belongs to, described by its holders rather than by its material
kin: tooth — the material file — tooth, tusk and claw, and what keeps them intact in the ground
kin: eye — Illyrians used animal teeth against the same harm the eye is aimed at, in the same substitution set
kin: horn — the other piece of an animal worn for what the animal could do
kin: rabbits-foot — the same logic reduced to a keyring, and the one everybody in the anglophone world has seen
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — the amulet collection the wolf tooth sits in, catalogued and published online
kin: wellcome-lovett — the collection the wolf tooth came from before 1985
kin: bone-ivory — the neighbouring material, and what a whale tooth is filed as once it is carved
sources: s:web-prm-wolf-tooth s:wp-tabua s:wp-lei-niho-palaoa s:wp-inuit-religion s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum

## The tree (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/tree/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/tree.json
id: tree
aliases: sacred tree · portal tree · tree pillar · the tied tree
when: 1550 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE JP EG IQ HT BJ TG IN NP
against: witchcraft — said by Victorian folklorists reporting English and Scottish practice: Edwin Lees in 1856, James Frazer in 1890, Charles Godfrey Leland in 1891 [s:wp-rowan]
against: spirits — said by Thomas Keightley's account of the fairy rades, watched safely from behind a rowan branch laid over the door [s:wp-rowan]
against: bad-luck — said by Japanese shrine-goers, who tie a bad omikuji to a pine so the luck waits by the tree rather than following them home [s:wp-o-mikuji]
against: travel — said by the rowan's English by-names, wayfarer's tree and traveller's tree, given because it was said to keep travellers from getting lost [s:wp-rowan]
what: A tree standing where it stands. This is the one sign in the atlas that is often not drawn at all: the mark is the tree, and what a reader would notice is not a carving but the things tied to it, planted beside it, or cut from it.
story: Scotland plants it at the gate. British folklorists of the Victorian era reported the rowan's warding of witches — Edwin Lees for the Wyre Forest in 1856, James Frazer in 1890 for Scotland, where the tree was often planted near a gate or front door, and Charles Godfrey Leland in 1891 citing the Denham Tracts collected between 1846 and 1859. A flying rowan, grown as an epiphyte in the fork of an oak or a maple from a bird-dropped seed, was held especially potent against witches and black magic. Thomas Keightley recorded that mortals could safely witness the fairy rades by placing a rowan branch over their doors. In Neo-Druidism the rowan is the portal tree, and Elen Sentier's description of it is a definition of the whole sign: "Threshold is a place of both ingress (the way in) and egress (the way out). Rowan is a portal, threshold tree offering you the chance of 'going somewhere ... and leaving somewhere."

Japan ties bad luck to it and walks away. When an omikuji fortune comes out badly, the custom is to fold the strip and attach it to a pine tree — or to a wall of metal wires — alongside other bad fortunes on the shrine grounds. The reason given is a pun: matsu is both pine and to wait, so the bad luck waits by the tree instead of attaching itself to the bearer. A good fortune can be tied there too, to make it work harder, or taken home.

Haiti treats particular trees as the altar. Certain trees are held to have resident spirits and are used as natural altars, with different species linked to different lwa — Oyu with mango trees, Danbala with bougainvillea — and some have metal affixed to them to form shrines to Ogou, who is associated with iron and the roads. In Benin and Togo, plant material is central to building a shrine, and offerings may be given to the tree from which the material is harvested.

Egypt, which had almost no trees, made a pillar out of one. Erich Neumann calls the djed a tree fetish, and points out that this matters because Egypt was primarily treeless; he suggests the myth may record the importation of trees from Syria. The Osiris story is the tree in question: a sacred tree took root and grew around the coffin at Byblos, enclosing it in its trunk, and the king had it cut down and installed as a pillar in his palace. Sidney Smith proposed in 1922 a parallel with the Assyrian sacred tree, noting the bands on both; Cohen and Kangas connect that tree to Enki and point out that the Assyrian king is shown beside the sacred tree much as the pharaoh is shown at the raising of the djed.

And a tree can be a category rather than a plant. The Babylonian Talmud lists coral among trees, and Rashi, writing in eleventh-century France, calls it "a type of tree that grows underwater" — an animal filed under this sign because of its shape.

*Inference —* on transmission, this atlas will say three different things in one record, because the evidence differs. Between the djed and the Assyrian sacred tree, transmission is argued by named scholars from shared features and a plausible route, and remains an argument. Between the Haitian altar tree and the West African shrine tree, the historical connection is the documented one that produced the religion itself. Between the Scottish rowan at the gate and the Japanese pine on the shrine ground, nothing at all is claimed: no source read here proposes a link, the two acts are different — one plants, the other ties — and the resemblance is the kind this project refuses to build on.
how: Planted at a threshold, tied to, cut from under rules, or carved into a pillar. Where the tree stays alive, the charm is maintained by returning to it; where it is cut, the taboo tends to follow the wood — in the Highlands no part of the rowan was to be used save the berries, except for ritual purposes.
today: The tied tree is the version most visible now. Shrine grounds in Japan carry racks of metal wire beside the pines precisely because the custom outgrew the trees, which is a small and exact record of what happens to a living sign under volume.
kin: rowan-cross — the charm cut from the tree at the gate, which is this sign reduced to two sticks and a thread
kin: omikuji — the paper fortune that ends its life knotted to a pine, on a pun between the tree and the verb to wait
kin: djed-pillar — the sign as a pillar: Neumann's tree fetish, in a country that had to import its timber
kin: wood — the same thing felled — where the tree becomes a material and the rules about which parts may be cut begin
kin: coral — the sea animal the Talmud files among trees, and Rashi calls a tree that grows underwater
kin: lungta-flag — cloth strung between high points, doing at a mountain pass what the tied fortune does at a pine
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the rowan belongs to: the sign is placed at the threshold, not worn
kin: seed — how a flying rowan gets into the fork of an oak — the potency came from a bird's droppings
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read on signs that recur across unrelated traditions, which this record answers with three different verdicts
sources: s:wp-rowan s:wp-o-mikuji s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-west-african-vod-n s:wp-djed s:wp-coral
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-17

## The word that reads both ways (motif)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/sign/palindrome-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/motif/palindrome-word.json
id: palindrome-word
aliases: ABRACADABRA · abracadabra triangle · Sator Square · Rotas-Sator Square · Templar Magic Square
when: 50 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IT SY EG GB FR DE PT HU SE IS US BR BA RS
object: form=scroll materials=parchment,paper,copper,wood,stone worn=neck,wall,door,swallowed
against: fever — said by Serenus Sammonicus, who prescribed the triangle amulet to malaria sufferers and claimed it makes lethal diseases go away [s:wp-abracadabra]
against: illness — said by the 16th-century Italian Jewish codex Ets ha-Da'at, which calls it a cure from heavens for all sorts of fevers, consumption and fire [s:wp-abracadabra]
against: fire — said by medieval German practice: disks bearing the square thrown into fires, required of every settlement by a 1743 edict of Duke Ernest Auguste of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach [s:wp-sator-square]
against: childbirth — said by the 12th-century Trotula, which has the words written on cheese and butter and eaten, and a 13th-century Aurillac parchment giving a chant for women in labour [s:wp-sator-square]
against: animal-attack — said by medieval European practice against dog bites and rabies, the cure eaten on inscribed bread; and 19th-century Brazil, against dog and snake bites [s:wp-sator-square]
against: witchcraft — said by medieval charms built on the square, used to ward off evil spells and to test whether somebody was a witch [s:wp-sator-square]
what: Writing arranged so its shape is part of the instruction. Two forms carry most of it. ABRACADABRA is written as a triangle, a letter dropped from each line, worn on parchment at the neck. The Sator square is a 5×5 grid of five five-letter Latin words — SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS — using eight letters, that reads the same across, down, backwards and upwards.
story: ABRACADABRA is first attested in the second century CE, in the Liber Medicinalis of Serenus Sammonicus, physician to the emperor Caracalla. In chapter 52 he prescribes that sufferers from malaria wear an amulet with the word written in the form of a triangle; he claimed the amulet makes lethal diseases go away. The origin of the word is unknown. Conjectures point to an Aramaic phrase meaning 'I create like the word', to abraxas, or to the first four letters of the Greek alphabet, and the Oxford English Dictionary says no documentation has been found to support any of them. The historian Don Skemer suggests the Hebrew ha brachah dabarah. The Aramaic linguist Steve Caruso argues it cannot be Aramaic at all, and traces the popular Aramaic etymology to a long thread on an early internet message board.

The Gnostics of the sect of Basilides used it as a formula to call beneficent spirits against disease and misfortune, and it is found on Abraxas stones worn as amulets. Its use spread past them. A sick person wore the triangle on parchment at the neck, and the explanation recorded is that written that way it worked like a funnel, driving the sickness out of the body. A sixteenth-century Jewish codex from Italy, Ets ha-Da'at, gives it as an amulet and describes it as a cure from heavens for all sorts of fevers, for consumption and for fire. Not everyone agreed: the Puritan minister Increase Mather dismissed the word as having no power in it, and Daniel Defoe wrote dismissively about Londoners who posted it on their doorways during the Great Plague. Today it is mostly a stage-magic word.

The Sator square has harder dates and no agreed meaning. The oldest known one was found in November 1936, in ROTAS form, etched on column LXI of the Palestra Grande near the amphitheatre at Pompeii; graffiti on those columns predates the earthquake of AD 62. A second at the house of Publius Paquius Proculus, found in October 1925, dates between AD 50 and AD 79. Four were found at Dura-Europos in Syria in 1931–32, on the walls of military buildings, dated about AD 200. One was scratched on plaster at Cirencester in Roman Britain, found 1868; one on a roof tile at Aquincum near Budapest, found 1954; one on Roman pottery at Manchester, about AD 185; one on an unfired brick at Conímbriga in Portugal, second century. The earliest square with explicit Christian imagery is a sixth-century bronze amulet from Asia Minor with two fish facing one another on one side and the square in Greek characters on the other, the word ICHTHUS written above it, now in the Berlin State Museums. After more than a century of research there is no consensus on where the square came from or what it means.

What it was used for is much better documented than what it says. In medieval Germany the square was inscribed on disks thrown into fires to put them out; an edict of 1743 by Duke Ernest Auguste of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach required every settlement to make them. By the fifteenth century it was a touchstone against fire at the Château de Chinon and the Château de Jarnac. It appears as a remedy during labour in the twelfth-century Trotula, where the instruction is to write the names on cheese and butter and give them to the woman to eat, and a thirteenth-century parchment from Aurillac gives a Sator chant for women in childbirth. It was widely cited against dog bites and rabies, the cure administered by eating bread inscribed with the words. Jean du Choul in 1555 describes a man from Lyon who recovered from insanity after eating three crusts of bread inscribed with the square, then reciting five paternosters for the five wounds of Christ. In Bosnia it was used against fear of water; in Iceland it was etched into the fingernails against jaundice. In nineteenth-century Brazil it was used against dog and snake bites; among German settlers in the Allegheny Mountains it was used to prevent fire, stop fits and prevent miscarriages. It appears in eighteenth-century Pennsylvania Dutch Pow-wow books such as The Long Lost Friend.

*Inference —* both forms share a property their users describe out loud: the writing is doing something by its shape, not by its sense. The triangle funnels; the square holds whichever way you read it. Neither needs to be understood by the person wearing it, and in the Sator's case nobody understands it yet.
kin: abracadabra — the word itself, with its own etymology file and its own arguments
kin: magic-square — the other square on a charm — numbers instead of letters, and a different history entirely
kin: magical-gem — Abraxas stones carry the word, and are the earliest objects it is found on
kin: fish — the sixth-century Sator amulet has two fish on its other face and ICHTHUS written above the square
kin: divine-name — the neighbouring practice: writing that works because of whose name it is, rather than because of its shape
kin: parchment — what the triangle was written on and worn at the neck
kin: inscribing — the practice — in several of these cures the writing is eaten, which is as far as inscribing goes
kin: washing-off-ink — the related practice of taking the writing into the body, here by eating bread and cheese instead of drinking ink
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition that carried the Sator square from a Pompeian gymnasium wall to a Pennsylvania farmhouse
sources: s:wp-sator-square s:wp-abracadabra s:wp-abraxas s:wp-amulet

## Amber (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/amber/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/amber.json
id: amber
aliases: succinite · Baltic amber · elektron · kahraba
said: AM-ber
when: 330 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: PL LT RU DE IT GR CN
root: Arabic 'anbar, from Middle Persian ambar, 'ambergris', via Middle Latin ambar and Middle French ambre; the sense shifted to fossil resin in the Romance languages from the late 13th century
against: illness — said by the European tradition of amber teething and colic necklaces, which argues from succinic acid [s:wp-amber]
against: child-harm — said by parents who put the necklaces on infants [s:wp-amber]
what: Fossilised tree resin. Baltic amber, succinite, is found as irregular nodules in a marine glauconitic sand called blue earth, in Upper Eocene strata of Sambia, and comes from conifers of the family Sciadopityaceae. It is soft — 2 to 2.5 on the Mohs scale — warm to hold, floats in strong brine, smells of pine when rubbed, and burns. Rub it and it picks up chaff, hair and scraps of cloth, which is the property its users noticed first and named it for.
story: The static charge is not a footnote to amber, it is the reason amber has a reputation. Pliny records that in Syria women made the whorls of their spindles from it and called it harpax, the snatcher, "from the circumstance that it attracts leaves towards it, chaff, and the light fringe of tissues". Persian speakers called it kah-ruba, straw-snatcher. Greek called it elektron. A material that visibly reaches out and takes hold of things is a material people will hang on a child.

It also travelled further than almost anything else in this atlas. There were well-established routes connecting the Baltic with the Mediterranean, known as the Amber Road; Pliny states that the Germans exported amber to Pannonia and the Veneti distributed it onward. The Romans traded for Baltic amber at least as far back as Nero. Italic peoples in the south of Italy worked it, and the National Archaeological Museum of Siritide at Policoro holds important surviving examples. China's first written record of amber is from 200 BCE.

Pliny also got the substance right, against competition. Nicias held that amber was a liquid produced by the rays of the setting sun, sweated out of the soil and thrown up on the shores of Germany. Pliny quotes it and then reports the older, correct Latin view: succinum, from sucus, juice — the resin of a pine.

*Tradition holds —* amber necklaces are a European remedy for colic and teething pain, on an argument about the analgesic properties of succinic acid. The claim is live and so is the argument against it: there is no evidence that this is an effective remedy or delivery method, and the American Academy of Pediatrics and the US Food and Drug Administration have warned strongly against the necklaces, which present both a choking and a strangulation hazard. Both positions belong on this page.
today: Sold everywhere, imitated everywhere. Copal and kauri gum, celluloid and glass have all been passed off as amber; Baltic amber is sometimes coloured artificially and still sold as true amber. What the trade calls black amber is not amber at all, but jet.
kin: jet — the other fossil that holds a charge when rubbed; what the trade sells as black amber is jet
kin: coral — the other organic charm traded the length of a continent and hung on children
kin: glass — one of the things amber has been imitated with, alongside copal, kauri gum and celluloid
kin: worry-stone — a charm that works by being rubbed — which is also the gesture that wakes amber's charge
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition the teething necklace belongs to, and still sells into
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read this material lands squarely in: the commonest amber charm goes on an infant
kin: crystal-pendant — its shelf-mate in the present-day stone trade, sold on a claim about the substance itself
sources: s:wp-amber
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Bone and ivory (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/bone-ivory/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/bone-ivory.json
id: bone-ivory
aliases: ivory · tusk · whale ivory · scrimshaw
when: 4400 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG TH US GL FJ CN GB ID
against: weapons — said by Thai amulet practice, where bone-bearing charms are among those blessed for invulnerability [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: attraction — said by makers of the palad khik, carved in wood, metal, bone, horn or ivory [s:wp-palad-khik]
against: spirits — said by Greenlandic accounts of the tupilaq, assembled from bone, skin, hair and sinew [s:wp-tupilaq]
what: Two related things a charm gets cut from: bone, from any animal including a human one, and ivory, meaning tusk — from African and Asian elephants above all, and also from hippopotamus, walrus, narwhal and mammoth. Both carve finely, take a polish, and yellow with handling. Both come out of a body, and every tradition that uses them says something about whose body it was.
story: Bone is on the first list of Egyptian amulet materials: faience above all, then stone, metal, bone, wood and gold. It is still on the list four thousand years later and half a world away. Thai amulets are made from plaster, metal, wood or bone, sometimes with ash, monk's hair or temple relics worked into them. The palad khik, the Thai phallic charm, is made from wood, metal, bone, horn or ivory by monks who specialise in them, and engraving its inscriptions can take days.

In the Pacific the material is a tooth as much as a tusk. The lei niho palaoa, worn at the neck by Hawaiian ali'i of both sexes, is in its nineteenth-century form a whale tooth carved into a hook and hung on plaited human hair; precontact examples were under two inches long and were also made from shell, bone, wood, stone and coral. In Greenland a tupilaq was made by an angakkuq from animal parts — bone, skin, hair, sinew — and, in the accounts that survive, from parts taken from the corpses of children.

*Inference —* bone and ivory sit on the opposite side of the survival line from cloth and herb. They last in the ground, so they are heavily represented in museum trays, and they last in a collection, so they are heavily represented in the ethics literature too. Those are the same fact seen twice.
today: Ivory is the material in this atlas with the hardest live constraint on it. Asian elephant ivory was barred from international trade by a CITES Appendix One listing in 1975; the African elephant was moved to Appendix One in October 1989, enacted in January 1990. Through the 1980s about 75,000 African elephants a year were killed for the trade, and the African elephant population fell from roughly 1.3 million to 600,000 between 1979 and 1989. China ended its domestic ivory trade and processing, with commercial activity halting on 31 March 2017. The UK Ivory Act 2018 received Royal Assent on 20 December 2018. A museum drawer of ivory charms is therefore a drawer of objects that in most cases cannot lawfully be traded now, whatever they were when they were carved.
kin: tooth — the same body, one step along: a tusk is a tooth, and the Pacific charms cut from whale ivory are both records at once
kin: palad-khik — carved from wood, metal, bone, horn or ivory by monks who specialise in it
kin: phra-khrueang — pressed with bone, ash, hair and relics worked into the body of the tablet
kin: tupilaq — made from bone, skin, hair and sinew, and in the accounts that survive from human remains too
kin: hei-matau — the hook cut from bone as readily as from pounamu
kin: inuit-amulet — the Arctic charm cut from what the hunt provided, which is the whole of the material argument here
kin: rabbits-foot — the same logic at the cheap end: a part of an animal, kept because it was part of an animal
kin: nagpra — the United States law that governs human remains and funerary objects in collections, and therefore some of this material
kin: hair — the other material taken from a body, and the one that does not survive as well
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read for objects whose trade is now illegal and whose display is argued about
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-ivory-trade s:wp-palad-khik s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-tupilaq s:wp-lei-niho-palaoa
