## Carnelian (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/carnelian/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/carnelian.json
id: carnelian
aliases: cornelian · sard · aqiq · 'aqiq
said: kar-NEE-lee-an
when: 4500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: BG PK IN IR IQ EG GR IT LK ID BR RU DE PE
root: Medieval Latin corneolus, from Latin cornum, the cornel cherry, whose translucent red fruit the stone resembles; English cornelian from the 14th century, carnelian a 16th-century corruption by analogy with caro, carnis, 'flesh'
against: evil-eye — said by writers on Islamic amulet practice, summarising why this stone is chosen [s:wp-amulet]
against: infertility — said by Islamic amulet practice, where carnelian set with jade is read as fertility and embryogenesis [s:wp-amulet]
what: A brownish-red to orange chalcedony — silica, coloured by impurities of iron oxide — hard enough to take a polish and to hold a cut line. Sard is the same family, generally harder and darker, and the boundary between the two names is blurry enough that dealers use them interchangeably. Hot wax does not stick to carnelian, which is why Rome cut its seal-rings from it.
story: Carnelian is one of the first stones anybody strung. Red chalcedony was worked into beads in the Early Neolithic in Bulgaria, and the Varna Chalcolithic necropolis, middle of the fifth millennium BCE, gives the first faceted carnelian beads — thirty-two facets, sixteen a side. At Mehrgarh in the fourth and fifth millennia BCE a bow drill was already going through it. The Indus Valley Civilisation made etched carnelian beads through the third millennium BCE, and the stone reached Bronze Age Knossos by about 1800 BCE.

What the stone was asked to carry changed with who cut it. Sard went into Assyrian cylinder seals, into Egyptian and Phoenician scarabs, into early Greek and Etruscan gems. Rome used carnelian for the engraved gems of signet rings, the seal a letter was closed with. The Hebrew odem, first stone of the High Priest's breastplate, was a red stone — probably sard, possibly red jasper.

In the Islamic world the stone's own biography is the argument. Carnelian, 'aqiq, is often favoured because it was taken as the stone of Muhammad, who was said to have worn a carnelian seal set in silver on the little finger of his right hand. Writers on Islamic amulets set out the reasoning plainly: the protective value claimed for a material rests on its natural rarity, its monetary value and its symbolic implications. Carnelian's reddish translucency is read as blood, and the reading is anchored to the clot of congealed blood of Qur'an 96:2. Set beside jade, the pair is read as fertility and embryogenesis.

*Inference —* carnelian is cut, never moulded, and that is the whole of its class position on a museum tray. The same wedjat eye that came out of a mould in faience by the thousand had to be ground from this stone one at a time. Where a drawer holds both, the stone ones cost more to make, and the tray is a price list as much as a typology.
today: Still cut for beads and seal rings, and still sold as 'aqiq across West and South Asia. The mineral literature names Yanacodo in Peru and Ratnapura in Sri Lanka among significant localities, with the stone also found in Indonesia, Brazil, India, Iran, Siberia and Germany.
kin: wedjat-eye — the eye ground out of this stone rather than pressed from paste — the costlier half of the same tray
kin: scarab — sard is named as a stone of Egyptian and Phoenician scarabs, engraved on the flat underside
kin: magical-gem — the Greek and Roman engraved gem, for which this stone's refusal to hold hot wax made it the seal-cutter's default
kin: taweez — the Islamic amulet whose makers argue from the stone itself — rarity, price, and a prophetic seal worn on the right little finger
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition that states its materials doctrine out loud, and puts carnelian near the top of it
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the workshops that cut this stone alongside the moulds that undercut it
kin: faience — the cheap answer to this stone: quartz paste, moulded and glazed to look like something mined
kin: turquoise — the other stone Egypt's kilns were asked to counterfeit in glaze
kin: glass — the later imitation, poured rather than ground, and sold by the tray
sources: s:wp-carnelian s:wp-amulet s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-eye-of-horus
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Cloth (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/cloth/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/cloth.json
id: cloth
native: tılsımlı gömlek ()
aliases: flannel · brocade · linen · the bag · the shirt
said: tilsimli gomlek, the talismanic shirt
when: 601 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TR IR IN SN ML US JP CN FR DE CH IL
object: form=bag materials=cloth,thread,paper worn=neck,chest,sewn-in,pocket,waist,roof
against: weapons — said by Hürrem Sultan, who told Suleiman the Magnificent the shirt's inscriptions would protect him from bullets [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: war — said by the women who stitched senninbari and the soldiers who carried them — the same source records soldiers who rejected the claim and kept the belt as a memento [s:wp-senninbari]
against: evil-eye — said by Jewish families in Alsace, southern Germany and Switzerland, who set a coin or coral on a boy's brit milah neckband [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: bad-luck — said by Hoodoo conjure workers, for whom red flannel carries protection and spiritual power [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: illness — said by the Muslim wearers of talismanic shirts, whose textual model is Joseph's shirt healing Jacob's blindness [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
what: Woven fibre doing three different jobs: a bag that holds a charm, a garment that is one, and a strip that records how many people worked on it. Cloth is the material where this atlas's survival problem is most visible, because the tradition is old and the objects are not.
story: The talismanic shirt is the grand version. Worn textile talismans are found throughout the Muslim world and group into four types — Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and West African — inscribed with verses from the Qur'an, the names of God and of prophets, or with numbers, and sometimes carrying images or symbols including astrological ones. Most seem intended as a shield in battle. Hürrem Sultan gave one to Suleiman the Magnificent and told him its inscriptions would protect him from bullets. The textual backing is Surah Yusuf, where Joseph's shirt heals his father's blindness: "Go with this my shirt, and cast it over the face of my father: he will come to see."

And here is the sentence this record exists for: the earliest surviving examples were made in or near the fifteenth century, though the tradition of talismanic shirts might be much older. That is what a survival gap looks like when somebody writes it down.

The commonest form is a bag. A gris-gris is a small cloth pouch, usually holding Qur'anic scripture written on paper together with herbs, worn round the neck; non-Muslims in the same region wore them under the name saffis. Across the Atlantic the Hoodoo mojo bag is a flannel bag, and most Southern-style conjure bags are red flannel — a choice traced to Bakongo minkisi, with red standing for protection and spiritual power, and research from the National Museum of African American History and Culture noting that red signifies sacrifice, transition and power in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of Congo and Gabon. When red cloth was not to hand, people used whatever cloth they had. Enslaved quilt makers sewed mojo hands into quilts, a technique traced from Mississippi and Alabama to Connecticut. Japan's omamori are small items kept inside a brocade bag; they were originally made of paper or wood, and the bag came later.

Cloth also counts. A senninbari is a strip of cloth carrying a thousand stitches, each normally sewn by a different woman and given to a soldier leaving for war, typically 15 cm wide and 90 to 120 cm long, most often white cloth with a thousand red stitches. The custom began in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. Tibetan lung ta prayer flags are squares or rectangles strung along their top edges on a long thread and hung from high to low; darchog are single rectangles fixed to poles and planted in ground, cairns and rooftops.

Europe wore its cloth on the shoulders. The monastic scapular appears perhaps as early as the seventh century in the Order of Saint Benedict, a length of cloth hanging front and back, and item 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict refers to it; the devotional scapular that grew out of it is two small rectangles of cloth, wood or laminated paper a few inches across, joined by two bands, one square on the chest and one down the back. In Alsace, southern Germany and Switzerland, Jewish boys wore textile neckbands at their brit milah with a coin or a piece of coloured coral set in the middle, to draw the evil eye away from the child during the circumcision; the practice continued into the early twentieth century.

Cloth is also a component taken from a person. Curse tablets included hair or pieces of clothing, to give the spell the ousia — the central essence — of the target.

*Inference —* textiles need to be dry, frozen or airless to last, and almost nowhere is. Set the fifteenth-century shirts against the ten thousand years of weaving behind them and the conclusion is not that cloth charms are recent; it is that cloth charms are invisible.
how: Cut and sewn, or woven and inscribed, or stitched by many hands in sequence. Most cloth charms have an end written into them: a senninbari goes to war, a prayer flag is left to weather, a mojo bag is made for one client and one purpose and cannot be reused for another.
today: The senninbari records its own dissent, which is rare in this field: the cited account says some soldiers rejected the idea that the belt could protect them and carried it instead as a keepsake of the women who made it. Both positions are in the same source, from the same object, and this record prints both.
kin: talismanic-shirt — the garment that is the charm, and the record that says in one sentence how much older the tradition may be than its oldest surviving example
kin: gris-gris — the West African cloth pouch of written verses and herbs, and the ancestor of the American bagged charm
kin: senninbari — a thousand stitches by a thousand women, 15 cm by 90 to 120 cm, and a soldier who may or may not have believed in it
kin: omamori — paper or wood first, brocade bag afterwards — the cloth here is the wrapper, not the charm
kin: lungta-flag — cloth hung to weather rather than worn, strung top-edge to a thread from high to low
kin: thread — what cloth is made of, and what does the work when the count matters more than the fabric
kin: hair — the other thing curse tablets took from a person: hair, or a piece of their clothing
kin: sewing-in — the practice that hides a charm inside a garment, where the cloth is both container and concealment
kin: wearing-hidden — why so few of these were ever seen, let alone collected
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on why this atlas's timeline is made of stone, metal and fired clay
sources: s:wp-talismanic-shirt s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-senninbari s:wp-omamori s:wp-prayer-flag s:wp-scapular s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-curse-tablet
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Copper and bronze (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/copper/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/copper.json
id: copper
native: 厭勝錢 (Han)
aliases: bronze · brass · copper alloy · lamella
said: yansheng qian, the Chinese charm cast in copper alloy
when: 400 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN NE TR IQ EG IT GB US
object: form=coin materials=copper,brass worn=neck,pocket,grave,door,vehicle
against: childbirth — said by ritual texts from Uruk, which prescribe a bronze Pazuzu necklace against miscarriage [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: poverty — said by the charms' own inscriptions, which ask for longevity, wealth and honour and for wealth and treasure to be attracted [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: the-dead — said by the families who put 'laid to rest' charms in the mouths of their dead [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: evil-eye — said by the account of the Turkish eye bead, which names copper among the shielding ingredients [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
against: spirits — said by Chinese householders, whose house charms include small bronze statues set to protect the house from evil spirits [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
what: Copper and its alloys: bronze with tin, brass with zinc. It casts, it takes an inscription, it corrodes to a green skin and then stops, and it was cheap enough to make a charm by the thousand in places where silver was not. Where iron rusts away and lead poisons, copper mostly just sits in the ground and waits.
story: China cast the most of it. Yansheng coins — Chinese numismatic charms — originated in the Western Han as variants of the Ban Liang and Wu Zhu cash coins, and were valuable in themselves because they were often made of copper alloys and Chinese coins were valued by their weight in bronze or brass. Supply drove the practice: temple coins were issued by Buddhist temples during the Yuan dynasty when the copper currency was scarce, or when copper production was intentionally limited by the Mongol government.

The measurements exist because these were struck to a standard. "Laid to rest" burial charms are bronze, 2.4 to 2.45 centimetres across and 1.3 to 1.4 millimetres thick, carrying the inscription rù tǔ wéi ān, "to be laid to rest", with a blank reverse. Most come from late Qing graves, and one turned up in a hoard of Northern Song coins. They are routinely left out of reference books on Chinese charms: they were placed in the mouths of the dead, and collectors find them unlucky and disturbing.

In the Sahara the metal marks a grade. The Agadez cross has two forms, and the cross-shaped tanaghilt is made of stone or copper, while talhakim are cut from platelets of copper, aluminium or other metal; the blacksmiths who make the silver ones cast by lost wax and never hammer the metal. Han China graded the same way in wire: an emperor's jade burial suit is sewn with gold, princes and marquises with silver, their children with copper, and lesser aristocrats with silk thread.

Mesopotamia used bronze where the stakes were highest. Pazuzu heads are chiefly terracotta but also bronze, and ritual texts from Uruk state that a woman could be given a bronze necklace or amulet of Pazuzu to protect her from miscarrying through the interference of Lamashtu. In Anatolia copper is named as an ingredient rather than a shape: the account of the eye bead gives it as "a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil".

Europe's luckiest object started in bronze and only later turned to iron. In 1897 four bronze horseshoes with what are apparently nail holes were found in an Etruscan tomb dated around 400 BCE, and around 1000 CE cast bronze horseshoes with nail holes became common in Europe, with a scalloped outer rim and six nail holes; the widespread manufacture of iron horseshoes belongs to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Copper's colour shows up in Egypt too, where copper pigments give faience its blue-green lustre, and copper, like lead, was imported in prosperous periods when local ores ran short.

*Inference —* copper's real advantage is archaeological rather than protective. Iron was valuable and worn-out items were generally reforged and reused, which makes early iron charms hard to find; bronze was cast, buried and left. What looks like a preference for bronze in the record may be a preference for bronze in the ground.
how: Cast in a mould, or beaten into a thin sheet — a lamella — and inscribed. Roy Kotansky's corpus of inscribed protective sheets is titled Greek Magical Amulets: the inscribed gold, silver, copper and bronze lamellae, which is the shortest statement of what this metal was used for in the Greco-Roman world.
today: Copper-alloy charms are still cast and still collected, and the collecting is where the arguments are. The Chinese burial charm is the clearest case in this atlas of an object excluded from the published record for reasons that have nothing to do with the object: it is complete, dated, measured, inscribed, and left out of the reference books because of where it sat in a corpse's mouth.
kin: charm-coin — the object this metal made possible in bulk: a cast coin that was never legal tender and circulated anyway
kin: tuareg-cross — the Saharan pendant whose plainer forms are cut from copper where the silver ones are cast by lost wax
kin: pazuzu-head — cast in bronze for the cases that mattered most, and prescribed by name in the Uruk texts
kin: horseshoe — bronze before it was iron: the Etruscan tomb of c. 400 BCE and the cast shoes of c. 1000 CE both predate the iron ones
kin: iron — the metal copper is always measured against, and the one that rusts and gets reforged out of the record
kin: silver — the grade above it — in a Han burial suit the wire says who you were
kin: lead — the other base metal beaten into inscribed sheets, used for the curses rather than the guards
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that put a measured bronze disc in a dead person's mouth
kin: faience — where copper is a colour instead of a shape: the pigment that makes Egyptian blue-green
sources: s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm s:wp-agadez-cross s:wp-jade-burial-suit s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-horseshoe s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-curse-tablet
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Cowrie (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/cowrie/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/cowrie.json
id: cowrie
native: कौड़ी (Devanagari)
aliases: cowry · kaudi · buzios · miigis · money cowrie
said: KOW-ree
when: 4000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: MV IN LK NG BJ GH CA US BR FJ EG CN KE SL
root: Hindi kaudi, from Sanskrit kaparda
against: infertility — said by users in parts of Africa, where cowries were prized charms associated with fecundity [s:wp-cowrie]
against: bad-luck — said by the same accounts, which name good luck alongside fertility [s:wp-cowrie]
against: the-dead — said by predynastic Egyptian and Neolithic Levantine burial practice, and the Bengali ferry-fare for the departed soul [s:wp-cowrie]
what: The shell of a sea snail of the family Cypraeidae: egg-shaped, glossy as glazed porcelain, with a long toothed slit down the flat underside. Species run from 5 mm to 19 cm. The shells used as money and as charms come mostly from the Indian Ocean — collected around the Maldives, Sri Lanka, the Malabar coast, Borneo, Maluku, Papua New Guinea, and along the African coast from Ras Hafun in Somalia to Mozambique.
story: No other amulet material in this atlas was also the currency. Cowries were the most widely used shell money in the world. The Chinese character for money, 貝, began as a stylised drawing of a Maldivian cowrie, and words for money, property and wealth take it as their radical; shells or copies of them circulated in China from more than three thousand years ago. After the 1500s the shell's monetary use widened sharply: European traders, chiefly through the slave trade, moved enormous numbers of Maldivian cowries into Africa. Between 1500 and 1875 at least 30 billion cowries were imported into the Bight of Benin, accounting for 44% of the total value of trade; the shell money literature puts profits on the traffic as high as 500%, and the resulting inflation damaged local economies. In parts of British West Africa cowries were accepted for tax until the early twentieth century, and Ghana named its currency, the cedi, after them in 1965.

The ritual record is just as wide. Cowries are used in divination among the Yoruba, and in Brazil, carried there by the Atlantic slave trade, buzios are thrown to consult the Orixas. The Kaniyar Panicker astrologers of Kerala used them for divination. In West Bengal a cowrie is given as the token fare for the departed soul's ferry across the Vaitarani, and shells are used at cremations and in the worship of Lakshmi. The Ojibwe use cowrie shells, miigis or whiteshells, in Midewiwin ceremonies, and Whiteshell Provincial Park in Manitoba is named for them; how shells from that far away came to be that far inland is an open question, with oral accounts and birch bark scrolls describing them as found in the ground or washed up on lakeshores. This atlas prints what the published accounts say about Midewiwin and stops there.

In parts of Africa cowries were prized charms and were said to be associated with fecundity, sexual pleasure and good luck; in Mende and Kikuyu usage the shell stands for womanhood, fertility, birth and wealth. One modern ethnographic writer reads the underside as a vulva or an eye. On Fiji a drilled golden cowrie was worn on a string at the neck by chiefs as a badge of rank.

The shell is also old in graves. In predynastic Egypt and the Neolithic southern Levant, cowries were placed in the burials of young girls, modified and arranged around the skull; by the Bronze Age they are commoner as funerary goods, with women and children. Egypt then made the cowroid — a seal amulet imitating the shell — and copies in stone and faience appear from the early second millennium BCE.
today: Still strung, still sold, still thrown for divination on three continents. The cowrie is also the material in this atlas with the heaviest history attached to its supply: the same shell that a West African household kept as a charm arrived, in the millions, on ships in the trade in people.
kin: cowrie-strand — the strung form of this shell, and the amulet most of the world means when it says cowrie
kin: scarab — the cowroid is the Egyptian seal amulet that copies this shell, cut the way a scarab is cut
kin: faience — the paste Egypt used to counterfeit the shell once the shell itself was scarce
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition where this shell is charm, currency and divining instrument at once
kin: akodessewa-market — a West African market where shells and animal parts are sold for exactly these uses
kin: grave-deposit — the practice that puts cowries around a girl's skull, and the reason we have any from 4000 BCE
kin: gris-gris — the West African charm packet whose contents and whose route out of Africa run alongside this shell's
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read for a material whose supply history is the Atlantic slave trade
sources: s:wp-cowrie s:wp-shell-money s:wp-ojibwe
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Faience (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/faience/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/faience.json
id: faience
native: tjehenet (Egyptian hieroglyphic)
aliases: Egyptian faience · glazed composition · sintered quartz · glazed frit
said: fay-ONSS
when: 4000 BCE to now
countries: EG IQ SY GR IT GB
root: French faience, from Faenza near Ravenna, a centre of tin-glazed pottery — a name borrowed for a material that has nothing to do with it
what: Crushed quartz or sand, a little lime and a mixture of alkalis, shaped and fired until a soda-lime-silica glaze forms on the surface, usually blue or green from copper. No clay, and so not pottery; closer to glass, but porous where glass is not. It was the most common material for scarabs, for amulets of every other form, and for the ushabti figures buried with the dead.
story: Faience is a counterfeit that outlived what it counterfeited. From its first appearance in the Egyptian record the glaze colours sit in a narrow band of blue-green, and Egyptologists read that as deliberate: the material stands in for turquoise out of Sinai and lapis lazuli out of Afghanistan. The archaeologist David Frederick Grose puts the same logic behind early glass — the quest to imitate precious stones "explains why most all early glasses are opaque and brilliantly colored", with the deep blue of lapis the most sought after. Quennou's funerary papyrus names his office as overseer of faience-making using the word that strictly means lapis lazuli; by the New Kingdom the word for the stone also meant the substitute.

It has been called the first high-technology ceramic, an artificial medium made to function as a precious stone. Three glazing methods are known — slurry applied by brush or dip, efflorescence where soluble salts mixed into the body migrate out and crystallise on the surface, and cementation, where the object is fired buried in a glazing powder. The last was recognised only after the same method was observed in use at Qom in Iran in the 1960s.

Scale is the point. Moulding came in during the Middle Kingdom: press a model into wet clay, fire the clay, and the mould will give you the object again and again. Several thousand small open-face earthenware moulds were excavated at Tell el-Amarna. That is what an amulet industry looks like from the floor of the workshop.

*Inference —* faience is the reason a museum tray of Egyptian amulets looks the way it does. It was cheap to mould, buried by the thousand, and made of something that does not rot, corrode or burn. The cloth, dough, reed and papyrus charms that stood beside it are simply gone. A drawer of faience is a record of what survives, not a census of what was worn.
how: Modelled by hand, or pressed into a fired clay mould, or ground to shape cold, then glazed and fired. The paste is thixotropic and short — it slumps when wet and cracks if worked too hard — so detail comes from the mould and from abrasion afterwards, not from the modelling. From the Middle Kingdom, different coloured pastes were worked together for striped bodies, and inlay and incising followed.
today: Not made in Egypt as tjehenet any more. The technology carried on eastward as Islamic stonepaste, or fritware, which adds clay to the same quartz body. Museums hold the ancient material in quantity: the Victoria and Albert Museum in London has a faience sceptre 215.9 cm long dated 1427-1400 BC, at the far edge of what the material will do.
kin: wedjat-eye — the amulet this material made cheap enough to bury by the thousand, and durable enough to still be here
kin: scarab — the form the sources name first when they say what faience was mostly used for
kin: ankh-amulet — moulded in the same workshops, off the same kind of clay mould
kin: bes-amulet — a moulded figure whose survival in quantity is a fact about the paste, not about how many Bes charms Egypt wore
kin: turquoise — the Sinai stone this glaze was coloured to stand in for
kin: glass — made in the same New Kingdom workshops, from close to the same recipe, at a higher temperature
kin: carnelian — the cut stone the moulded copy competed with, and undercut
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition this material industrialised
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator who sorted the moulded output into the classes museums still shelve it by
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on why a material that survives distorts every date in this atlas
sources: s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-faience s:wp-amulet s:wp-eye-of-horus
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Fired clay (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/terracotta/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/terracotta.json
id: terracotta
aliases: terracotta · earthenware · stoneware · glazed composition · baked clay
when: 2000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IQ IR SY EG GR IT TH GB JP
object: form=plaque materials=terracotta worn=neck,wall,foundation,grave,door
against: demons — said by the householders of Nippur, in the reading of the bowls given by John Charles Arnold [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: childbirth — said by ritual texts from Uruk, which prescribe a Pazuzu amulet against miscarriage caused by Lamashtu [s:wp-pazuzu]
against: evil-eye — said by the bowls' own inscriptions, which name the evil eye, Lilith and Bagdana among the influences they act against [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: curse — said by Egyptian officials, who wrote enemies' names on clay and smashed it under a foundation [s:wp-curse-tablet]
what: Clay pressed into a mould or worked by hand, then fired until it stops being clay. Fired clay is the cheapest way to make the same charm a thousand times, and the one that survives burial best: it does not rot, rust, corrode or dissolve. A great deal of what this atlas can date at all, it can date because somebody fired it.
story: Start with the bowls, because they are the clearest case of the material doing the work. Incantation bowls are clay bowls inscribed in a spiral from the rim inward, made in Upper Mesopotamia and Syria from the sixth to the eighth centuries, most of them in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic. The scholar John Charles Arnold sets out how they were used: "When placed upside down under each corner of a house, demons would follow the inscribed charms that spiraled from the outer rim inward, only to be caught in the center." Almost every house excavated in the Jewish settlement at Nippur had them buried in it.

Mesopotamia also gives the mass-produced amulet. Large numbers of Pazuzu heads have been found, chiefly of terracotta though also of bronze, iron, gold, glass and bone, with holes or loops at the top so they could hang at a neck; ritual texts from Uruk record a woman being given a Pazuzu amulet to protect her from miscarrying through the interference of Lamashtu. One larger stone example, from a house in the Neo-Assyrian town of Dur-Katlimmu, was found on the floor of the main reception room and is thought to have hung on the wall facing the entryway.

Greece fired the face. Two groups of seventh-century BCE terracotta gorgoneion masks survive: wearable helmet masks from Tiryns, and non-wearable votive masks from the Sanctuary of Orthia at Sparta, the Spartan ones with deep S-shaped furrows either side of a wide-mouthed grimace — features that resemble much earlier terracotta plaques of Humbaba. Rome fired the joke: a first-century BCE terracotta figurine shows "two little phallus-men sawing an eyeball in half".

Clay also gets fired in order to be destroyed. Egyptian execration texts, appearing around the Twelfth Dynasty, listed enemies' names on clay figurines or pottery, which were then smashed and buried beneath a building under construction or in a cemetery.

The trade is old and still running on one street. In classical times a temple to Ceres stood on what is now Via San Gregorio Armeno in Naples, and citizens offered small terracotta figurines made in the workshops nearby; the Neapolitan nativity trade dates from the end of the eighteenth century, and the same street's workshops now turn out figurines all year round. Elsewhere the fired tablet is a temple's income: Buddhist votive tablets are small clay or terracotta plaques bearing images and text, left at sacred sites by pilgrims, with rarer and more expensive ones made of metal — in Thailand they are the Thai Buddha amulets, produced to raise temple funds.

*Inference —* the survival argument runs both ways. Fired clay is over-represented in every museum tray in this atlas, and hair, herb, cloth and wood are under-represented, and neither fact says anything about what people actually carried.
how: Moulded or thrown, dried, fired. A mould is the point: Pazuzu heads, votive tablets and nativity figures are all made the same way, which is why they exist in numbers and why two examples can be compared.
today: Fired clay is also the atlas's clearest live ethical problem, and the bowls are where it sits. Only around 2,000 incantation bowls have been registered as archaeological finds, but they are widely dug up in the Middle East, and the cited account estimates there may be tens of thousands in the hands of private collectors and traders. A bowl without a findspot cannot be dated by its context, cannot be tied to the house it protected, and cannot be returned. Naples fires figures for a living and Nippur is dug for one, and only one of those trades keeps a record.
kin: incantation-bowl — the charm that is a clay bowl and nothing else — the material and the object are the same thing here
kin: pazuzu-head — chiefly terracotta, drilled to hang, and found in numbers because a mould made it cheap
kin: gorgoneion — fired as masks at Tiryns and Sparta in the seventh century BCE, which is the earliest physical form of that face
kin: phra-khrueang — the Thai clay votive tablet, pressed in its thousands and sold to fund the temple that pressed it
kin: glass — the other fired material, and the other reason half this atlas has dates
kin: san-gregorio-armeno — the Naples street that has been firing small figures since there was a temple to Ceres on it
kin: witch-bottle — begins as a salt-glazed stoneware Bartmann jug with a bearded face on it, before glass takes over
kin: foundation-deposit — the practice that puts fired clay under a building, whether to protect it or to curse somebody beneath it
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this record's last paragraph belongs to: bowls dug without a findspot, and who ends up holding them
sources: s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-gorgons s:wp-fascinus s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-via-san-gregorio-armeno s:wp-votive-offering s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-cornicello s:wp-maneki-neko
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Glass (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/glass/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/glass.json
id: glass
native: nazar boncuğu ()
aliases: eye bead · boncuk · glass paste
said: boncuk is Turkic for bead
when: 1600 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: TR GR EG IQ IR IT TN LB GB US
against: evil-eye — said by Turkish sellers and wearers, who name the blue and the ingredients [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
against: evil-eye — said by carriers of the concentric blue-and-white bead from the Phoenicians to the Ottomans [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: infertility — said by enslaved African Americans at the Hermitage plantation, Nashville, whose hexagonal glass beads archaeologists read as used for fertility and other spiritual purposes [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: witchcraft — said by English householders who buried glass witch bottles under thresholds and hearths [s:wp-witch-bottle]
what: Silica melted, coloured through and worked hot. Glass does two things no other material in this atlas does at once: it holds a colour all the way through a bead the size of a fingernail, and it comes out of the ground three thousand years later looking much as it went in. That is why the eye bead has a continuous record from the Bronze Age to a rack by a shop till, and why a reader can compare one to the other.
story: The eye bead is the oldest thing here. Written documentation and extant beads date from as early as the 16th century BCE, and the design spread with glassmaking itself — Mesopotamia to Egypt, Carthage to Greece, Phoenicia to Persia, and right through the Roman imperial period. The account of the evil eye puts the same turn slightly differently: after glass-bead production got going around the eastern Mediterranean about 1500 BCE, blue-and-white concentric eye beads spread among Phoenicians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs and Ottomans.

Egypt supplies the join. Beginning in the thirteenth century BCE, glass beads bearing eye-like spots were strung on necklaces together with wedjat amulets, and that pairing may be the origin of the modern nazar. Wedjat amulets themselves were cut in faience, glass, gold and semiprecious stones such as lapis lazuli, so the same drawer holds the drawn eye and the spotted bead side by side.

Glass and faience are cousins, not twins, and the British Museum's collection note is the clearest statement of the difference: glazed composition is related to glass, but glass is formed by completely fusing the ingredients in a liquid melted at high temperature, while Egyptian faience is a quartz body only partly fused and considerably more porous than glass proper.

Glass turns up where you would not look for it. Pazuzu heads were made chiefly of terracotta but also of bronze, iron, gold, glass and bone. At the Hermitage plantation in Nashville, Tennessee, archaeologists found hexagonal glass beads used by enslaved African Americans for fertility and other spiritual purposes, alongside blue beads, mojo hands and lucky roots in a slave cabin. English witch bottles start as salt-glazed stoneware and end as glass: the later ones are glass bottles and small glass vials, and the one dug from a threshold in Cornwall and shown on Antiques Roadshow in 2016 was glass.

*Inference —* glass is the reason this atlas can draw a timeline for the eye and cannot draw one for thread. Nothing about a bead is more durable than a stitch except the material. Where a tradition used both, the glass is what survived to be counted.
how: Melted, gathered on a rod, and dotted while soft: concentric circles or a teardrop in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes rimmed in yellow or gold. Turkish sellers give the ingredients as part of the claim, not as a manufacturing note: "The bead is made of a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil."
today: Traditional production of the nazar boncuğu is now carried on at Nazarköy in Kemalpaşa, in İzmir province, using a few simple hand tools and mostly blue and white glass, and the Cultural Research Foundation runs research, documentation and documentary film work on it. Everywhere else the bead is factory output, sold by the tray at the Grand Bazaar, at Monastiraki, in airport shops and on phone cases. Whether a moulded bead is the same object as a lampworked one is argued by sellers and buyers alike; this record describes both the same way.
kin: nazar — the bead this material was invented for, and the form most of the world now buys the eye in
kin: eye — the sign glass carries better than any other material, because a dot of colour set in a dot of colour is what glass does easily
kin: wedjat-eye — the Egyptian amulet that shared a string with the first spotted glass beads, from the thirteenth century BCE
kin: faience — the near relation: the same quartz and alkali, only partly fused, porous where glass is solid
kin: terracotta — the other fired material, and the other reason this atlas can date anything at all
kin: witch-bottle — the English charm that changed material under the practice: stoneware jug first, glass bottle later, same buried job
kin: pazuzu-head — made chiefly in terracotta, but glass is one of the six materials the heads turn up in
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the factory descendant, which this atlas describes in the same words as a lampworked bead
kin: grand-bazaar — the counter where the bead reaches most of its buyers now
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on what a mass-produced charm is, which the glass bead is the largest case of
sources: s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-eye-of-horus s:wp-egyptian-faience s:wp-pazuzu s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-mojo-bag s:web-kultur-evil-eye-izmir
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Gold (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/gold/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/gold.json
id: gold
aliases: aurum
when: 5000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: BG EG IQ IT GB CN MX
against: child-harm — said by Roman parents, who hung a bulla on a boy nine days after birth and a lunula on a girl [s:wp-bulla-amulet]
against: evil-eye — said by Roman use as summarised by Isidore of Seville and by writers on Roman dress [s:wp-lunula-amulet]
against: illness — said by the givers of milagros, votive charms made in gold where a family can afford gold [s:wp-milagro-votive]
what: A bright yellow metal, dense at 19.3 grams per cubic centimetre, soft, and so malleable that a single gram beats out into a sheet a metre square. It occurs native, usually in solid solution with silver. It does not corrode and it does not tarnish, which is the property every tradition that uses it eventually says something about.
story: Gold is the earliest metal on the human record. Small quantities appear in Spanish caves from around 40,000 BCE; the oldest gold artefacts in the world come from the Varna Necropolis in Bulgaria, fifth millennium BCE — the same cemetery that produced the first faceted carnelian beads. Egyptian and Mesopotamian gold objects follow in the fourth millennium BCE.

In amulets, gold's job is usually to say who is wearing it. A Roman boy wore a bulla, a locket-like pouch with a protective amulet inside, from nine days after birth until he put on the toga of manhood. Upper-class families could afford bullae of gold or covered in gold foil; everyone else used lead, leather and cloth. The girls' equivalent is defined by Isidore of Seville: "Lunulae are female ornaments in the likeness of the moon, little hanging gold bullae." Plautus has Epidicus ask a girl, "Don't you remember my bringing you a gold lunula on your birthday, and a little gold ring for your finger?" The same charm, on two children, in two price brackets.

Elsewhere gold is one option in a list. Egyptian amulets were made of faience above all, but also of stone, metal, bone, wood and gold. Late antique sheet amulets from Palestine and Syria were rolled from silver, gold, copper and lead. Milagros, the Latin American votive charms, are made from gold, silver, tin, lead, wood, bone or wax, depending on local custom and on what the person can spend. Part of the Thetford treasure in Norfolk is a gold box made to hang round the neck, found to contain sulphur for its evil-repelling qualities.

Gold is also the benchmark other materials are measured against, and sometimes beaten by. Jade reaching the Chinese court from Khotan is described as having status-value exceeding that of gold or silver. In the Han jade burial suits the gold is demoted to thread: emperors' suits were sewn with gold wire, princes and marquises with silver, their children with copper, lesser aristocrats with silk. *Inference —* a material hierarchy written into a burial regulation is the clearest statement in this atlas that what a charm is made of is a claim about the person in it.
today: Gold amulets are sold everywhere amulets are sold, and are the class of charm most likely to be melted rather than kept — which is a survival bias running the opposite way to faience. The Aztecs, the gold literature notes, called the metal literally "god excrement".
kin: bulla — gold for the families that could pay for gold, lead and leather for the rest — the same charm, sorted by price
kin: lunula — defined in the sources as a little hanging gold bulla in the likeness of the moon
kin: milagro — made in gold, silver, tin, lead, wood, bone or wax, according to local custom and what the giver has
kin: jade — the material that outranked gold at the Chinese court, and demoted it to the thread holding a burial suit together
kin: silver — the metal one step down, and the one most of the world's amulets are actually made of
kin: lead — the poor man's bulla, named as such in the same sentence
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition whose charms for children this metal grades
kin: magical-gem — the engraved stone that was set in gold when the owner could manage it
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on value, ownership and what happens to a charm worth melting
sources: s:wp-gold s:wp-bulla-amulet s:wp-lunula-amulet s:wp-amulet s:wp-milagro-votive s:wp-jade s:wp-jade-burial-suit

## Hair (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/hair/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/hair.json
id: hair
native: οὐσία (Greek)
aliases: nail clippings · ousia · conjure hair
said: ousia — the essence of a person, in the Greek of the binding spells
when: 500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GR IT GB BE US
against: attraction — said by the writers of Greek erotic binding spells, which call for hair from the head of the love target [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: witchcraft — said by English householders, whose bottles held their own hair and urine as countermagic against a spell already cast [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: curse — said by conjure workers in the American South, who put hair into bags meant to protect against conjure or to work it [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: bad-luck — said by the makers of goofer bags, built from goofer-root, cloth, strands of hair, needles and graveyard dirt [s:wp-mojo-bag]
what: Hair cut from a named person and put inside something else. It is almost never the charm on its own. It is the component that makes a general formula point at one particular body, and every tradition here says so out loud.
story: The Greek binding spells give the theory. Curse tablets included hair or pieces of clothing, and the cited account explains why: this was seen as a way to give them strength through the inclusion of the central essence — ousia — of the person. Love spells are the strongest case, calling for "hair from the head of the love target", and some have been found "folded around some hair", probably to bind the spell itself.

England put it in a bottle. A witch bottle historically contained the victim's urine, hair or nail clippings, or red thread from sprite traps; older accounts list rusty nails, urine, thorns, hair, menstrual blood, and pieces of glass, wood and bone. The bottle was buried at the farthest corner of a property, under the hearth, or hidden in a wall, and was held to work as long as it stayed hidden and unbroken.

One of those bottles has been opened in a laboratory, which is the only time in this record that hair gets analysed rather than described. A glass bottle found buried in the threshold of a house at Trelissick in Cornwall appeared on Antiques Roadshow in 2016; a 2019 episode reported that Loughborough University had analysed the contents and identified "urine, a tiny bit of alcohol, and one human hair", alongside brass pins dating from the late 1840s and an ostracod.

In the American South the same component travels under a different name. A former slave from Texas described how a conjure bag was assembled: they "would take hair and brass nails and thimbles and needles and mix them up in a conjure bag." A goofer bag is made with goofer-root, cloth, strands of hair, needles and graveyard dirt, and camel hair is added to increase a bundle's potency.

*Inference —* one hair, from one Cornish bottle, is the entire physical record this atlas can point to. Hair survives in the right conditions — dry, sealed, frozen — and rots everywhere else, and the bottles that preserved it did so by accident of being corked. Set that single strand against the thousands of surviving lead tablets that once had hair folded into them, and the shape of the gap is visible: the metal is in the museum and the person is gone.
how: Cut, or collected after cutting, and then enclosed — folded inside a lead sheet, corked into a bottle, sewn into a flannel bag. The enclosing is the point. Hair on its own is not treated as a charm in any account read here.
notes: This record describes a component taken from a named living person, sometimes without that person's knowledge. It names no living person and reproduces no procedure for obtaining it.
kin: curse-tablet — where the theory is written down: hair carries the ousia, the essence, and makes the sheet point at one person
kin: witch-bottle — the container that preserved the only analysed strand in this atlas, corked under a Cornish threshold
kin: gris-gris — the West African bagged charm whose American descendants take hair among their ingredients
kin: cloth — the other component curse tablets took from a person's body — a piece of clothing, doing the same pointing job
kin: thread — the other material that leaves no museum tray, and for the same reason
kin: lead — the sheet the hair was folded into, and the half of the pair that survived
kin: sewing-in — the practice of enclosing, which is the only thing done to this material
kin: burying — how a hair charm is delivered: the farthest corner of the property, or under the hearth
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on why the timeline in this atlas looks the way it does, which this record is the extreme case of
sources: s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-mojo-bag

## Herb and root (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/herb/

id: herb
native: cima di ruta ()
aliases: rue · roots · simples · hierbas · goofer-root
said: cimaruta, Neapolitan for 'sprig of rue'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IT GB MX SN US PH CD
object: form=bag materials=herb,seed,cloth,paper worn=neck,door,hearth,pocket,swallowed
against: evil-eye — said by stallholders at the Mercado de Sonora, who sell chains of garlic to ward off evil and a deer's-eye seed against the evil eye [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
against: evil-eye — said by southern Italian households, who hang dried chili peppers against the malocchio [s:wp-cornicello]
against: witchcraft — said by English folk healers, in whose bottles evil is impaled on the pins, drowned by the wine and sent away by the rosemary [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: illness — said by Mexico City herb sellers, whose ten-herb blend against the 2009 flu sold at 80 pesos per kilo [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
against: bad-luck — said by Hoodoo conjure workers, for whom the lucky hand root was a gambler's ingredient [s:wp-mojo-bag]
what: Leaves, roots, bark, bulbs and dried fruit, used either as the charm itself or as the filling of one. Herbs are the cheapest material in this atlas and the hardest to study, because almost none of it survives and most of what we know comes from a market stall or a court record rather than a dig.
story: Southern Italy named a silver charm after a plant. The cimaruta — Neapolitan cima di ruta, sprig of rue, after the flowering medicinal herb — is worn at the neck or hung over an infant's bed against the malocchio, and is usually made of silver. From a central stalk of rue, branches sprout into small charms: a rose, a hand holding a wand or a sword, a flaming heart, a fish, a crescent moon, a snake, an owl, a plumed helmet, a vervain blossom, a dolphin, a cock, an eagle. One might carry a key, a dagger, a blossom and a moon together. Most are double-sided and some are almost four inches across. The plant is the armature; the metal is the survival strategy.

The same region hangs the plant itself. Dried chili peppers are hung in some southern Italian homes against the malocchio, and the cited account is careful about the chronology: chili reached Europe only after the Columbian exchange, so a red cornicello's resemblance to a chili postdates the amulet, whose horn shape is far older.

England put herbs in the bottle. Later witch bottles were filled with rosemary, needles and pins, and red wine, and the account states what each component does: the bottle captures evil that is impaled on the pins and needles, drowned by the wine, and sent away by the rosemary. Other bottles held sand, stones, knotted threads, feathers, shells, herbs, flowers, salt, vinegar, oil, coins or ashes.

Mexico City sells the material by the kilo, and the supply routes are on the record: medicinal herbs at the Mercado de Sonora come from Puebla, Morelos and the State of Mexico. Avocado leaves are sold for inflammations, chiranthodendron for the heart, jacaranda flowers for the stomach. The magical aisles carry chains of garlic to ward off evil, crosses of ocote wood for good luck, and a seed called deer's eye against the evil eye. During the H1N1 scare in 2009, when business at the market fell about fifty per cent, a ten-herb blend designed to prevent and treat the flu — eucalyptus, bougainvillea and tejocote fruit among them — kept herb sellers solvent at 80 pesos per kilo.

West Africa bags them with scripture. Gris-gris were usually made as small sacks holding Qur'anic verses written on paper together with herbs, worn at the neck. In the American South the same bagging carried on: mojo ingredients include graveyard dirt, roots, herbs, animal parts, minerals, coins and crystals, with African religious preparation applied to North American plants and Native American herbal knowledge; the lucky hand root was favoured by gamblers, and a goofer bag takes goofer-root. Islamic practice approved by strict conservatives includes water to which have been added "salt, rose essence, oil of black caraway, or the leaves of the lote tree".

*Inference —* there is no herb in a museum tray. The record for this material is written, spoken and photographed, and the one time the contents of a herbal charm in this atlas were identified by a laboratory, it was because somebody had corked them in glass. Every date in this record is the date somebody wrote something down.
how: Dried, bundled, hung, strung, stuffed into a bag or a bottle, or brewed. The Highland taboo around the rowan shows how carefully the rules can be drawn: no part of the tree was to be used save the berries, except for ritual purposes — a threshing tool of rowan called a buaitean was used on grain meant for rituals and celebrations.
today: Herb sellers work at the edge of the law in two of the places this atlas names, and both cases involve women with no other option. Around Quiapo Church in Manila, peddlers sell unsafe abortifacients, gastric irritants and untested herbal remedies from stalls surrounding the basilica and Plaza Miranda; abortion is illegal in the Philippines, and people who cannot afford a surgical procedure go to these vendors. At the Mercado de Sonora, as late as the 1990s and before medical abortion was legalised in Mexico City, an herbal abortifacient was sought there; the sellers did not administer it but told the client what to use and how, leaving her to carry the medical and legal risk, and the treatment always led to haemorrhaging that required medical attention. Both accounts are printed here as they stand.
kin: cimaruta — a sprig of rue cast in silver: the plant kept as a shape once the plant itself had rotted
kin: nimbu-mirchi — South Asia's hung plant charm, doing at a doorway what the Italian chili string does
kin: gris-gris — the West African sack of written verse and herbs, and the parent of the American bagged charm
kin: witch-bottle — the only sealed container in this atlas whose herbal contents were ever named by a laboratory
kin: mercado-de-sonora — the market where this material is still weighed, priced and argued over
kin: quiapo-church — the other place where herb selling runs against the law, and the reason this record's last paragraph exists
kin: rowan-cross — the tree whose berries were permitted and whose wood was not, except for ritual
kin: seed — the hard part of the same plant, which does survive, and therefore does have a record
kin: wood — the other plant material, kept for its structure rather than its chemistry
kin: feeding-the-charm — the practice that keeps a plant charm renewed, since the material itself will not last
sources: s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-cornicello s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-mercado-de-sonora s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-rowan s:wp-quiapo-church

## Ink (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/ink/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/ink.json
id: ink
native: لوح (Arabic)
aliases: erasure water · talismanic script · fulu ink · tattoo ink
said: lawh, the wooden writing board; alwah in the plural
when: 501 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NG CM GH SN IQ IR SA CN JP TR IN TH
object: form=scroll materials=ink,paper,wood,parchment,cloth worn=swallowed,neck,sewn-in,wall
against: illness — said by users of the washed slate in Nigeria and Cameroon, where the collected water is consumed or used in healing rituals [s:web-wp-quran-boards]
against: illness — said by the Islamic healing literature Remke Kruk summarises, which prescribes drinking water over which Qur'anic passages have been recited [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: demons — said by the householders of Nippur, whose spiral-written bowls were buried face down under thresholds [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: evil-eye — said by the same bowls' inscriptions, which name the evil eye, Lilith and Bagdana [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: spirits — said by Taoist priests, whose coin talismans mostly request Lei Gong to protect the carrier from evil spirits and misfortune [s:wp-fulu]
what: Pigment suspended in a liquid: charcoal and water in West Africa, sometimes with saffron added, and driven under the skin elsewhere. Ink is the only material in this atlas with a whole branch of practice built on destroying it at the moment of use. A verse is written so it can be washed off and swallowed, and what was an object for a minute becomes a dose.
story: West Africa does it as part of learning to read. A Quran board is a wooden tablet — lawh, plural alwah — cut from locally available woods such as mahogany or baobab, on which students copy verses to memorise them. The inks are typically made from natural pigments mixed with charcoal and water, and may include ingredients said to be spiritually important, such as saffron. Once a verse or chapter has been mastered, the writing on the board is washed off and the water collected, and that water is then consumed or used in healing rituals. The practice is documented in Nigeria and Cameroon and among the Hausa and Fulani.

Islamic legal writing draws a fine line through the same act. Summarising how narrow the gap between approved and disapproved practice can be, Remke Kruk notes that dissolving Qur'anic texts written on paper in water is forbidden, while "writing in bowls with ink that is washed off by the water poured into the bowl" is recommended by the well-known Wahhabi-oriented cleric Wahid 'Abd al-Salam Bali. The bowl form persisted: in the Islamic medieval period, talismanic bowls, most often made of metal rather than clay, were covered in Arabic script, usually Qur'anic verses or a hadith, and were most often used for healing by drinking the water left in them overnight.

One famous neighbour is not part of this. The Ethiopian talismanic scroll, the other great written-charm tradition of the region, is made of parchment and pigment and is used by being read aloud to the afflicted by a third party literate in Ge'ez, or draped around the body — the account read here records no washing and no drinking. This atlas names the absence rather than assuming the practice crossed the Red Sea.

Mesopotamia wrote inward. Incantation bowls were usually inscribed in a spiral, beginning at the rim and moving toward the centre, most of them in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, from the sixth to the eighth centuries. An estimated ten per cent are not written in any real language but in pseudo-script, thought to be forgeries by illiterate scribes sold to illiterate clients — a fact that says something plain about how the writing was read.

China made illegibility the credential. Fulu are asemic Taoist talismanic scripts, painted on talismans by priests; Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, in the Eastern Jin, that so long as the inscription was correct, successful use did not depend on the user being able to decipher it. Yang Zhaohua records that early talismans were simple and legible and later ones deliberately cryptic in order to signal their divinity; James Robson, Gil Raz and Ge Zhaoguang all treat the incomprehensibility as central to the script's authority, Ge Zhaoguang calling it a linguistic archaism, "a veil of unfathomable otherwordliness". The method of writing the characters passes in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples, and the ofuda of Japan and the bujeok of Korea are downstream of it.

*Inference —* ink on a lead sheet lasts two thousand years, ink on a wooden slate lasts until the next bucket of water, and museums are built out of the first case. A survey of written charms assembled from collections will always undercount the second.
how: Ground, mixed and brushed — onto a board, a bowl's inside, a paper slip, a shirt, or a strip of linen. Egyptian ritual rubrics instruct the practitioner to draw the wedjat eye on linen or papyrus to serve as a temporary amulet, which is the same instruction as a Hausa slate: write it, use it, lose it.
today: The live argument about ink is chemical and is about the tattooing branch. The European Chemicals Agency has proposed restricting the intentional use or concentration of roughly 4,000 substances in tattoo inks; the EU Observatory for Nanomaterials reports that a number of modern inks contain nanomaterials and raises nanotoxicological concerns; and in October 2024 an analysis in the European Union found that nine out of ten blue and green inks sold were not compliant with the REACH legislation.
kin: washing-off-ink — the practice this material was made for: written, dissolved, drunk, gone
kin: incantation-bowl — ink written in a spiral on clay, which is the oldest dated use of the material in this atlas
kin: fu-talisman — the Taoist charm whose script is deliberately unreadable, and whose authority rests on that
kin: ofuda — the Japanese descendant of the Taoist talisman, printed from woodblocks and renewed each year
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the neighbouring written tradition that is read aloud and draped, not washed off — named here to mark the difference
kin: talismanic-shirt — ink on a garment: Qur'anic verses, the names of God and of prophets, or numbers, worn into battle
kin: skin — the ground ink is driven into when the charm is meant never to wash off
kin: paper — the surface ink usually sits on, and the one Islamic legal opinion treats differently from a bowl
kin: wood — the West African slate: chosen because the ink will lift off it cleanly
kin: inscribing — the practice of writing the charm, before anybody decides whether to keep it
kin: spiral — the shape the writing takes in the bowls, where the geometry is the mechanism

## Iron (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/iron/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/iron.json
id: iron
aliases: cold iron · meteoric iron · sky-iron · thogcha
when: 3500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE DK LT EE EG TR CN ID IN
against: spirits — said by English, Irish and Scottish folk tradition as recorded by folklorists [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
against: witchcraft — said by the same tradition: an iron knife buried under the entrance to a house [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
against: bad-luck — said by horseshoe customs in England, Denmark, Lithuania and Estonia [s:wp-iron-in-folklore]
against: evil-eye — said by the recipe given for a Turkish nazar bead, which puts iron in the batch [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
what: The commonest useful metal and the one that rusts. Because it corrodes so readily, ancient iron objects are far rarer in the ground than gold or silver ones — the survival order of the metals runs opposite to how common they were in life. In folk practice iron is not a support for a charm; the metal is the charm.
story: Iron arrived twice. The first iron anybody in Egypt held came out of the sky: beads made from meteoric iron at Gerzeh, 3500 BCE or earlier, identified by G. A. Wainwright, carrying 7.5% nickel, which is the signature of meteoric origin because crustal iron holds almost none. A dagger of meteoric iron was found in the tomb of Tutankhamun with iron, cobalt and nickel proportions matching a meteorite found in the same area. Smelting is the second arrival: samples from Asmar in Mesopotamia and Tall Chagar Bazaar in northern Syria date between 3000 and 2700 BCE, and the Hittites were smelting between 1500 and 1200 BCE.

The sky-iron did not stop being special once furnaces existed. Thogcha, 'sky-iron', is meteoric iron in Tibet, prized across the Himalayas and alloyed into ritual implements. Robert Beer writes that meteoric iron "is the supreme substance for forging the physical representation of the vajra or other iron weapons, since it has already been tempered by the celestial gods in its passage across the heavens", and records that a piece of the metal was often returned to the site the meteorite fell. In Java the same logic runs through the kris: the best pamor, the pattern in the blade, comes from meteorite iron, and the smiths of the Yogyakarta and Surakarta courts worked from an iron meteorite that fell near the Prambanan temple complex at the end of the eighteenth century.

In Britain and Ireland the metal works by being ordinary. Folklorists working across Britain, Ireland and northern Europe recorded cold iron as repelling, containing or harming ghosts, fairies and witches: a horseshoe nailed to a door, an iron fence round a cemetery to contain the souls inside it, an iron knife buried under the entrance to keep witches out. Irish and Scottish fishermen used "cold iron" as a substitute name for animals and incidents counted unlucky, so as not to say the real word. One account of the horseshoe's luck is the story of Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury from 959 and a blacksmith by trade, who nailed a shoe to the Devil's hoof and removed it only on a promise that the Devil would never enter a place with a horseshoe over the door.

The metal also goes into other charms as an ingredient. A Turkish nazar bead is described as "a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil".
today: Iron is the cheapest metal there is. Wikipedia's article, read on 16 September 2026, prices it at a few dollars a kilogram and gives no date for that figure, so it is reported here as a magnitude and not as a price. The charm did not get cheaper as the metal did: a horseshoe over a door in England is still required in many tellings to have been used, found rather than bought, and touchable.
kin: horseshoe — the commonest iron charm in Europe, and the one whose rules — used, found, touchable — are all about where the metal came from
kin: witch-bottle — filled with iron: rusty nails, pins and needles, sealed and buried
kin: keris-pusaka — the Javanese blade whose pamor pattern is worked from meteorite iron
kin: takrut — the rolled metal scroll — the sheet is the amulet's body, the inscription its voice
kin: nazar — iron goes into the glass batch itself, named in the recipe among the things said to shield the wearer
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition where cold iron is a rule rather than an object
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that names sky-iron as the supreme substance and returns a piece of it to where the meteorite fell
kin: silver — the other metal folklore arms against monsters, and the one that survives in the ground
kin: lead — the metal at the other end of the hardness scale, chosen for the opposite reason: too soft to resist a nail
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice iron is most often put to — over the lintel, under the threshold, around the graveyard

## Jade (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/jade/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/jade.json
id: jade
native: 玉 (Han)
aliases: nephrite · jadeite · fei cui · pounamu · greenstone
said: yù in Mandarin; pounamu in Maori
when: 6000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: CN MM GT MX NZ KR TW PH CA
root: Spanish piedra de ijada, 'flank stone', first recorded 1565, via French l'ejade and Latin ilia, the flanks and kidney area
against: illness — said by the Spanish name-givers, who called it flank stone for a reputed power over the loins and kidneys [s:wp-jade]
against: the-dead — said by Han burial practice, which encased the body in plaques sewn with wire graded by rank [s:wp-jade-burial-suit]
against: weapons — said by writers on Islamic amulets, who record a claim of victory in battle for jade and jasper [s:wp-amulet]
what: Two different rocks under one word. Nephrite is a felted mass of calcium-magnesium amphibole, slightly softer but very tough; jadeite is a sodium-aluminium pyroxene, harder, rarer, documented from fewer than a dozen places on earth. The French mineralogist Alexis Damour separated them in 1863; before that they were one stone in every language that had a word for it. Neither can be flaked. Jade is abraded to shape with quartz or garnet sand and polished with bamboo, which is why a jade object represents time more than skill.
story: China worked jade before it worked bronze. The Neolithic nephrite sources were Ningshao in the Yangtze delta, worked by the Liangzhu culture between 3400 and 2250 BCE, and Liaoning and Inner Mongolia, worked by the Hongshan between 4700 and 2200 BCE; Dushan jade was being mined as early as 6000 BCE. White jade came as tribute from the Kingdom of Khotan down the southern Silk Road, and its status-value is described as exceeding that of gold or silver. Han royalty were buried in jade burial suits, plaques drilled at the corners and sewn together with wire, and the Book of Later Han sets out who got which thread: gold for emperors, silver for princes, princesses, dukes and marquises, copper for their children, silk for lesser aristocrats, and nobody else at all.

In Mesoamerica the Olmec, the Maya and their neighbours had a single source, the Motagua River valley in Guatemala, and jade stayed an elite good — carved into figurines, inscribed with glyphs, hung on a goddess as water. Burmese jadeite reached China in quantity only after about 1800, as fei cui, kingfisher jade, and became the Qing aristocracy's stone while scholars kept to white nephrite.

In Aotearoa New Zealand nephrite is pounamu, and its record is about ownership rather than trade. Pounamu is a taonga, a treasure, found only in the South Island — Te Wai Pounamu, the land of greenstone water. Taonga gain mana as they pass down the generations; pounamu is held to absorb the mana of its past owners, and the most prized pieces have known histories going back many generations and were given to seal agreements. In 1997 the Crown returned ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu to Ngai Tahu under the Ngai Tahu Claims Settlement. The same source notes the market reality beside it: "much of the carved 'greenstone' sold in souvenir shops is jade sourced overseas".

Islamic amulet writing puts jade alongside jasper as a material credited with protective and medicinal properties — victory in battle, protection from lightning, treatment of diseases of the internal organs — and reads jade set with carnelian as fertility and embryogenesis.
today: Myanmar is estimated to produce upwards of 70% of the world's high-quality jadeite, most of it from the Jade Tract in Lonkin Township, Kachin State, and most of it cut elsewhere. Mining there was a state enterprise from 1964 to 1981, after which the gemstone laws were changed in 1981, 1985 and 1995 to admit private operators. New Zealand's pounamu is at the other pole: the resource belongs to an iwi by law, and the souvenir stone next to it on the shelf usually does not come from the country it is sold in.
kin: hei-tiki — the pendant this stone is best known as outside Asia, and a taonga whose mana is held to accumulate with each owner
kin: hei-matau — the hook, carved from pounamu or from bone, worn at the neck
kin: ping-an-fu — the Chinese safety charm cut from this stone and hung on a cord
kin: maori-taonga — the tradition in which this stone is not a material but an inheritance
kin: te-papa-taonga — where pounamu taonga are held and shown in the country they come from
kin: gold — the metal jade outranked at the Chinese court, and reduced to thread in a burial suit
kin: carnelian — its partner in Islamic amulet practice, where the pair is read as fertility
kin: inheriting — the practice that makes a jade object worth more than the stone in it
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this stone's 1997 settlement belongs to
sources: s:wp-jade s:wp-pounamu s:wp-jade-burial-suit s:wp-jade-use-in-mesoamerica s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Jet (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/jet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/jet.json
id: jet
aliases: azabache · gagate · oltu stone · Whitby jet · lignite
said: jet
when: 10000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GB ES FR TR US DE
root: French jaiet, modern jais, ultimately from the ancient town of Gagae
against: evil-eye — said by Roman users in Britain, for whom jet amulets and pendants were held to deflect the gaze [s:wp-jet-gemstone]
against: snakebite — said by Pliny the Elder [s:wp-jet-gemstone]
against: child-harm — said by Puerto Rican families, whose azabache bracelet is the usual protection put on a baby [s:wp-evil-eye]
what: Fossil wood. Jet is lignite, the lowest rank of coal, formed from wood under pressure — commonly from trees of the family Araucariaceae — and it is a mineraloid, not a mineral. It is soft, 2.5 to 4 on the Mohs scale, cuts easily but chips at fine detail, takes a high polish, and burns like coal with a coal smell. Rubbed, it can pick up a charge the way amber does. Held, it is not cold: black glass is, and that is the oldest test for telling them apart.
story: The earliest worked jet anybody has is a model of a botfly larva from about 10,000 BCE, found in Baden-Wurttemberg among the Venuses of Petersfels. Britain has used it since the Neolithic, through the Bronze Age for necklace beads, then not at all through the Iron Age, until it came back in Roman Britain in the early third century CE. Whitby jet was collected by beachcombing and worked at Eboracum, modern York, into rings, hair pins, beads, bracelets, bangles, necklaces and pendants. Jet pendants were cut cameo-style, and the Medusa head was a favourite subject — a gorgon face carved from fossil wood, aimed at whoever looked at the wearer.

The Roman period is where jet is named as a magical material outright, used in amulets and pendants for its supposed protective qualities and its ability to deflect the gaze of the evil eye. Pliny the Elder gives the claims: "the kindling of jet drives off snakes and relieves suffocation of the uterus. Its fumes detect attempts to simulate a disabling illness or a state of virginity." Solinus and Galen refer to it too.

Then it becomes a pilgrim's stone. At the end of the Middle Ages the trade in religious objects and jet amulets reached great development at Santiago de Compostela, sold to pilgrims walking the Camino; the workshops were at Santiago, the deposits up the coast in Asturias, where beads and rosary beads were also cut. Near Erzurum in Turkey the same material is oltu stone and is made into prayer beads. In New Mexico, Navajo and Pueblo people were using regionally mined jet for jewellery and to ornament weapons when Spanish explorers reached the area in the 1500s.

Victorian Britain turned it into mourning. Queen Victoria wore a jet necklace as part of mourning dress in the 1850s and again for Prince Albert, and the trade followed her. Use peaked in the early 1870s; Whitby went from more than a thousand workers in the trade to three hundred by 1884, as Art Nouveau turned away from black jewellery; by the end of the Second World War three jewellers were left, and the industry ended with them.
today: Jet jewellery came back into fashion in the 1980s and new jewellers took up production. The Puerto Rican azabache bracelet is the material's busiest survival as a charm: it carries a black or red coral amulet in the shape of a fist with the index-finger knuckle protruding, and it is the commonest protection put on an infant there. Imitations are old and numerous — glass sold as French jet or Vauxhall glass, ebonite that fades, anthracite, offcuts bound with glue and moulded, and museum reproductions in epoxy resin.
kin: azabache — the bracelet named after this material in Spanish, and the commonest thing put on an infant in Puerto Rico
kin: figa — the fist with the knuckle out, cut in jet where the bracelet is black rather than red
kin: gorgoneion — the Medusa head Roman Britain liked to cut into jet cameos, aimed at whoever looked
kin: hamsa — most commonly carved in jet or formed in silver, per the same sources
kin: amber — the other fossil that takes a charge when rubbed; what dealers call black amber is this
kin: coral — the red half of the azabache bracelet, where jet is the black half
kin: glass — sold as French jet in imitation of it, and told apart because glass is cold to the touch and jet is not
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on imitation, which this material has supported since the nineteenth century
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that bought jet by the shipload at Santiago de Compostela
sources: s:wp-jet-gemstone s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-hamsa s:wp-charm-bracelet
