## Lead (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/lead/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/lead.json
id: lead
native: tabella defixionis ()
aliases: lead sheet · lamella · defixio · katadesmos
said: defixio, from the Latin for pierce and bind
when: 500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GR IT GB EG KH US
object: form=plaque materials=lead worn=grave,wall,neck
against: theft — said by the writers of the Bath tablets: all but one of the 130 concern the restitution of stolen goods [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: lawsuit — said by Athenian litigants, whose tablets ask that the opposing speaker botch his performance, forget his words and become dizzy [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: attraction — said by the users of erotic binding spells, which Christopher Faraone divides into spells for inducing passion and spells for encouraging affection [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: the-dead — said by those who laid tablets at the graves of people who died young or violently, to help settle their souls [s:wp-curse-tablet]
what: A soft grey metal, cheap, heavy, and soft enough to scratch with a stylus and then fold in the hand. It is also poisonous, which is the whole of its modern story. Lead is the curse tablet's material, and this atlas files the curse tablet beside the amulet on purpose rather than in a separate room.
story: Curse tablets are typically very thin sheets of lead with the text scratched on in tiny letters. They were rolled, folded, or pierced with nails, and then put out of reach: buried in graves or tombs, thrown into wells or pools, sequestered in underground sanctuaries, or nailed to the walls of temples. Around 1,600 have been found, most of them inscribed in Greek, with 220 from Attica. The first group discovered came from Selinus in Sicily — twenty-two tablets, mostly from the early fifth century BCE, directed at someone the writer was suing.

Britain holds the largest single deposit. In 1979 and 1980 the Bath curse tablets were found at Aquae Sulis, and all but one of the 130 concern the restitution of stolen goods; over eighty more came from the temple to Mercury at West Hill, Uley nearby, which makes south-western Britain one of the major centres for finds of Latin defixiones. Roger Tomlin published the Bath group in 1988 under a title that names the metal twice over: Tabellae Sulis: Roman inscribed tablets of tin and lead from the sacred spring at Bath.

What is written on them is not always a curse. Texts are addressed to infernal or liminal gods — Pluto, Charon, Hecate, Persephone — sometimes through a dead person, usually the corpse in whose grave the tablet lay. Many list the target's crimes in detail and hand the punishment to the gods, and some scholars refuse the word curse for those, preferring judicial prayers. Tablets were also used to help the dead: those laid at the graves of people who had died young or violently were meant to settle their souls.

*Inference —* the tablet and the amulet are one technology used in two directions. Both name a person. Both write a formula on metal. Both are folded, pierced or rolled, and both are put where nobody will read them — sewn in, buried, nailed up. Kotansky's corpus of protective amulets is titled Greek Magical Amulets: the inscribed gold, silver, copper and bronze lamellae; the tablets are the same lamellae in a base metal, aimed the other way. Filing them apart would hide the fact that the same hands made both.

Lead also moved as a raw material rather than an object: Egyptian faience workshops imported lead and copper during periods of prosperity, when the ores were not available locally.
how: Hammered into a sheet, scratched with a stylus, then rolled, folded or nailed. Sometimes the tablet was made in advance with a blank left for a name: "Not all tablets included a personal name, but it is clear especially in the Roman period, that tablets were sometimes prepared in advance, with space left for inserting the names provided by paying customers." Hair or a piece of the target's clothing could be folded in with the sheet.
today: Lead is still worn and it still poisons children. In March 2009 a one-year-old boy in New York City had a blood lead level of 10 µg/dL, which reached 20 µg/dL three months later. The source was an amulet: a knotted string onto which grey metallic beads had been moulded, bought by the boy's mother in a rural Cambodian market, worn since he was three months old and observed being mouthed. The beads' total lead content was 450,000 mg/kg, or 45 per cent. Eight days after the amulet was removed his level was 14 µg/dL; at six weeks 10, and at five months 5. The report's recommendation is that health-care providers ask parents about their use of amulets, particularly in Southeast Asian families and where a child has an elevated blood lead level. New York City's health department names the class of object plainly — amulets, sheesha, tabiz, metal charms, necklaces and bracelets given to children can contain high levels of lead — and asks that they be kept out of a child's mouth, naming no country of origin.
kin: curse-tablet — the object this material exists for in the atlas, and the reason lead has a record at all
kin: magical-gem — the protective side of the same late-antique workshop, cut in stone instead of scratched in lead
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the same idea in silver: a thin sheet, a written formula, rolled and worn, aimed at protecting rather than binding
kin: hair — what gets folded into the sheet to make the writing point at one named person
kin: inscribing — the practice of scratching the words, which is the only step lead requires
kin: burying — how a lead tablet is delivered: into a grave, a well, or a temple wall
kin: christopher-faraone — the scholar who sorted the erotic tablets into passion spells and affection spells, and found men and women using different ones
kin: copper — the metal the protective lamellae were beaten from, where the tablets used the cheap one
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read the modern lead story belongs to: the charm that poisoned a child was put on him at three months old
sources: s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-egyptian-faience s:web-cdc-mmwr-cambodian-amulet s:web-nyc-hazardous-amulets

## Palm leaf (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/palm-leaf/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/palm-leaf.json
id: palm-leaf
aliases: tala patra · lontar · bai lan
when: 500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IN LK TH KH LA MM ID NP
against: weapons — said by Thai makers of takrut, which are blessed for kong grapan, invulnerability [s:wp-takrut]
against: attraction — said by the same makers, for maha sanaeh and metta mahaniyom — attraction and popularity [s:wp-takrut]
against: travel — said by Thai wearers, who take takrut on work journeys and to war [s:wp-takrut]
what: Leaves of the Palmyra or talipot palm, cooked, dried and smoke-treated until they take a line. The writing is not laid on the surface but cut into it with a stylus; colouring is then rubbed over the leaf so the pigment settles into the grooves and the letters appear. The result is flexible, light, and cheap wherever the palms grow.
story: Palm leaf carries scripture across half of Asia, and carries charms with it. It is in use in the Indian subcontinent as early as the fifth century BCE and spreads to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia — Cambodia from Angkorian times, Myanmar from twelfth-century Bagan, Indonesia in the Majapahit period of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

In Thailand the takrut, the tubular amulet worn on a cord, is made of metal or of palm leaf: a strip inscribed with yant, the sacred geometry and Pali phrases usually written in Khom script, or in Lan Na Tai Tham in the north, then rolled and cased. Whether a given takrut is metal or leaf is not a difference in the spell. It is a difference in what will survive.

*Inference —* this is the clearest survival-bias case in the atlas. A palm-leaf text lasts between a few decades and roughly six hundred years before moisture, insects, mould and sheer fragility take it, and the oldest survivals are all from colder, drier places — parts of Nepal, Tibet, Central Asia. In the monsoon belt where palm leaf is actually from, nothing lasts. Hindu temples and monasteries handled this by copying texts onto new leaves as the old ones wore out, which keeps the words and destroys the objects. So the amulet record of mainland Southeast Asia is weighted almost entirely to metal, clay and stone, and the leaf charms that stood beside them for two thousand years are simply absent.
how: Cut to a strip, inscribed with a stylus, inked or coloured so the grooves show, then rolled and tied, or bound between boards. A takrut of leaf is rolled tight, bound with cord, and often cased so the leaf is never touched.
today: Still written, still copied, and now digitised in large collections. As an amulet material it survives mainly in Thai and Khmer practice, alongside the metal sheet that has always been its more durable alternative.
kin: takrut — the amulet that is either metal or this leaf, rolled the same way, saying the same thing
kin: yantra-plate — the same yant, put on a surface that will outlast the leaf
kin: sak-yant — the same designs again, put where nothing can be stolen and nothing survives the wearer
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition whose written charms this leaf carried before metal was common
kin: paper — its successor: cheaper still, printable, and just as perishable
kin: parchment — the dry world's equivalent, and the reason the Mediterranean amulet record is fuller than the monsoon one
kin: inscribing — the practice this material demands — a stylus cutting, not a pen laying down ink
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on why the surviving objects are not a sample of what was worn
sources: s:wp-palm-leaf-manuscript s:wp-takrut s:wp-yantra-tattooing

## Paper (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/paper/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/paper.json
id: paper
aliases: kamifuda · fu · bujeok · tarsh
when: 901 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP CN KR EG ML GH US
against: demons — said by Taoist practitioners of fulu, whose calligraphy is made against evil spirits [s:wp-amulet]
against: bad-luck — said by Shinto shrines, which issue ofuda for calamity and misfortune and for safety in the home [s:wp-ofuda]
against: evil-eye — said by the makers of block-printed Islamic paper amulets, and the Qur'anic verses printed on them [s:wp-amulet]
what: The cheapest surface a charm can be written on, and the one that lets a charm be printed. Paper amulets are issued, folded, sealed into cases, pasted to doors, swallowed, and burnt at the end of a year. Writers on amulets draw the line here: an amulet proper is usually made of something durable, metal or hard stone, and the word talisman is more often used for these less robust, more individual forms.
story: Paper made the amulet a print run. In medieval Egypt, block-printed prayers were struck from a die called a tarsh and folded down small enough for a tiny wearable case. The Aga Khan Museum in Toronto holds an Egyptian block-printed amulet of the tenth or eleventh century: minuscule ink script on paper, 7.2 by 5.5 cm, whose final line is a verse of the Qur'an — "So God will safeguard you from them. He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing". Such text amulets were housed in lead cases stamped with surat al-Ikhlas, with lugs so the package could be sewn to clothing or hung from the body, and were most likely kept sealed shut — so the buyer never saw the text inside, which is one reason they were affordable.

East Asia industrialised it differently. Taoist specialists developed fulu, a calligraphy made to act; the Japanese equivalent is the ofuda, made of paper, wood, cloth or metal, with paper ones called kamifuda. The three shrines of Kumano stamped their paper talismans with stylised crows; those sheets were used in oath-taking and contract drafting, with the terms written on the blank side. The Ise talismans, the Jingu Taima, were handed out across the country by wandering shrine officials: a document of 1777 indicates that eighty-nine to ninety per cent of all households in Japan owned one. The distribution was nationalised — an imperial decree of 1871 abolished the oshi who carried them, a new department took over production in 1900, the National Association of Shinto Priests took distribution in 1927, and the Association of Shinto Shrines has it now. In Korea the paper bujeok is carried inside a small brocade bag.

West African gris-gris were fashioned as small sacks holding Qur'anic scripture written on pieces of paper, with herbs, worn at the neck; the practice moved with the Atlantic slave trade into Louisiana Voodoo and Haitian Vodou.

*Inference —* paper is the reason the amulet record after about 1700 looks so much fuller than the record before it, and it has nothing to do with more people wanting charms. Printing made the charm cheap, and the same fragility that lost every earlier paper charm is still running.
how: Written, stamped, or block-printed; then folded, rolled, cased, pasted up or carried. A paper charm usually has a term. Japanese ofuda and omamori are renewed at the year's turn and the old one returned to the shrine to be burnt.
today: Still the world's commonest amulet material by volume, and the one most likely to be bought at a counter. Paper also marks a boundary in Jewish practice: a mezuzah must be handwritten on parchment by a qualified scribe, and a text photocopied onto paper and sold with a case is not a valid mezuzah.
kin: ofuda — the Japanese paper talisman, issued by a shrine, placed on the household altar and renewed yearly
kin: omamori — the pocket version of the same sheet, sewn into brocade so the paper is never seen
kin: fu-talisman — the Taoist written charm this whole family descends from
kin: bujeok — the Korean paper talisman, carried inside a small brocade bag
kin: omikuji — the paper drawn at a shrine and tied up there — the same material, spent in one use
kin: taweez — the folded or printed Qur'anic text in its case, which is where paper met the printing die
kin: gris-gris — Qur'anic verses on scraps of paper, sewn in a sack with herbs and worn at the neck
kin: parchment — the material paper is not allowed to replace, in the one tradition that says so in writing
kin: ink — the other half of every charm on this page
kin: burning-retirement — the practice a paper charm usually ends in
kin: folding — how a printed sheet becomes something small enough to wear
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-ofuda s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-fulu

## Parchment (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/parchment/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/parchment.json
id: parchment
native: קלף (Hebrew)
aliases: klaf · vellum · hide
said: klaf
when: 300 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL EG CN
against: demons — said by early Egyptian Christians, whose parchment and papyrus amulets carried Gospel incipits and Psalm 91 against them [s:wp-amulet]
against: illness — said by the same writers, who made the amulets to cure bodily illnesses [s:wp-amulet]
against: house — said by Jewish households, who fix the inscribed klaf to the doorpost as the commandment directs [s:wp-mezuzah]
what: Animal skin, scraped, limed and dried until it will take ink and keep it. It is the durable end of the written charm: stronger than papyrus, far stronger than paper, and in one tradition the only surface a charm may legally be written on at all.
story: Jewish practice states the material rule in law. A mezuzah is a piece of parchment, klaf, inscribed with passages from Deuteronomy and fixed in a case to a doorpost. It must be written on parchment by a specially trained scribe, a sofer stam, in indelible black ink, with a quill made from a feather or — now quite rare — a reed. A photocopy of the text on paper, sold with a decorated case, is not a valid mezuzah. Observant households have the parchments checked by a scribe for tears and faded lettering at least twice every seven years.

Tefillin put the same material inside leather. The boxes are fashioned from a single piece of animal hide; inside are scrolls of parchment carrying four passages, the arm box holding all four on one strip and the head box holding one scroll in each of its four compartments. There are 3,188 letters to write, and a sofer can take as long as fifteen hours over a complete set. The letters must be written in sequence: a mistake found later cannot be corrected, because the replacement letter would have been written out of order. That is a material discipline as much as a legal one — parchment takes a correction visibly.

Early Egyptian Christians wrote textual amulets on strips of papyrus, parchment and other materials, using scriptural incipits — the opening words of the Gospels, the Lord's Prayer, Psalm 91 — in Greek and Coptic, to cure bodily illness and to keep demons off. Those survive from late antiquity, roughly 300 to 700 CE, and almost all of them come out of Egypt. Tibetan Buddhist practice encloses prayers on a parchment scroll inside a prayer wheel, where each rotation counts as one recitation of everything written inside.

*Inference —* parchment is a skin, and the tradition that guards it most closely is also the one that will not make images. A charm that refuses a picture still puts the words on an animal.
how: Written by hand with a quill, in ink the tradition specifies; rolled, then cased in wood, metal, leather or clay. Checked, repaired and replaced on a schedule where the tradition sets one.
today: Still written by scribes, still checked, still sold with the case as a separate purchase — and the distinction between the parchment and its case is where most of the market confusion sits.
kin: mezuzah — the parchment itself is the object; the case is decoration, and a paper copy in a case is not one
kin: tefillin — 4 passages, 3,188 letters, written in order on klaf and sealed into boxes of a single piece of hide
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the other great parchment charm, cut to the owner's height and rolled
kin: kamea — the written Jewish amulet, on parchment where it is not on metal
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition that legislates this material and rejects every substitute for it
kin: paper — the cheap replacement this tradition refuses by name
kin: skin — the same substance, on a living body instead of a scraped one
kin: ink — the other half: indelible, black, and specified by law
kin: inscribing — the practice that makes the object — in sequence, with no correction possible
sources: s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-tefillin s:wp-amulet s:wp-phylactery
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Red coral (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/coral/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/coral.json
id: coral
native: 珊瑚 (Han)
aliases: precious coral · corallo
said: shanhu in Chinese
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IT CN PR DE CH GB
against: evil-eye — said by southern Italian wearers of the cornicello, where the coral is part of the argument [s:wp-cornicello]
against: child-harm — said by Jewish families in Alsace, southern Germany and Switzerland, who set coral on a boy's brit milah neckband to pull the eye off him [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: bad-luck — said by Chinese court usage, which ties red coral to auspiciousness and longevity [s:wp-coral]
what: The hard red skeleton of a colonial marine animal, cut and polished like a stone. What it is has been argued about for as long as it has been worn: Theophrastus described red coral, korallion, in his book on stones, implying a mineral, and as a deep-sea plant in his work on plants. Pliny the Elder placed several sea creatures, coral among them, as "neither animals nor plants, but are possessed of a third nature". The Babylonian Talmud lists coral among trees, and Rashi, writing in eleventh-century France, calls it "a type of tree that grows underwater".
story: Coral's amulet career runs on two things: it is red, and it comes out of the sea already branched. In southern Italy the cornicello, the little twisted horn worn against the malocchio, is carved from red coral as often as it is cast in gold or silver, and the coral is read as sacred to Venus. In Puerto Rico the azabache bracelet — the commonest protection put on a child there — carries a black or red coral amulet in the shape of a fist with the index-finger knuckle protruding. In Alsace, southern Germany and Switzerland, Jewish boys wore textile neckbands for their brit milah with a coin or a piece of coloured coral set in the middle, to draw the evil eye away from the child during the circumcision; the practice continued into the early twentieth century.

At the other end of the network, coral is court material. Chinese writing has long associated red coral with auspiciousness and longevity, for its colour and its resemblance to deer antlers. It peaked under the Qing, when it was almost exclusively reserved for the emperor, worked into coral beads for court jewellery, often with pearls, or into decorative miniature trees. The Qianlong Emperor established a code in 1759 setting strict rules for its use. The route that supplied it is named: an early-modern coral network beginning in the Mediterranean and reaching Qing China through the English East India Company.

By the middle of the nineteenth century coral fisheries were working the Mediterranean, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. The gear is described plainly: two heavy wooden beams crossed at right angles, weighted with stones, netting slung beneath, lowered on a strong rope over an outcrop and dragged by the boat until the coral breaks off into the net.
today: Intensely red coral is still prized as a gemstone, and it is now scarce. Writers on coral say why in the same breath: red coral is very rare because of overharvesting, and giving coral as a gift is inadvisable while corals are in decline from climate change, pollution and unsustainable fishing. A charm cut from a reef animal is the clearest case in this atlas of a material whose supply is a live argument, and the argument is not about amulets.
kin: cornicello — the horn cut from this material, and the reason Naples has a coral trade at all
kin: azabache — the Puerto Rican child's bracelet, whose fist is black jet or red coral
kin: figa — the same closed fist with the thumb through, cut in coral where coral is to hand
kin: horn — the sign this material is most often cut into around the Mediterranean
kin: fist — the other sign it is cut into, for the same harm and the same wearer
kin: jet — coral's black opposite in the same bracelet: one red, one black, both on the same infant
kin: amber — the other organic material traded far from where it is found and hung on children
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read: nearly every coral charm named here goes on a baby
sources: s:wp-coral s:wp-cornicello s:wp-evil-eye
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Salt (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/salt/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/salt.json
id: salt
native: 塩 (Han)
aliases: blessed salt · shio · sodium chloride
said: shio in Japanese
when: undated (still carried)
countries: JP IT IL IN MX GB
against: witchcraft — said by English folk practice, which sealed salt among the fillings of a witch bottle [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: demons — said by Catholic teaching, which permits lay use of holy water and blessed salt for warding off evil [s:wp-amulet]
against: spirits — said by Mahayana Buddhist practice of throwing salt over the left shoulder on returning from a funeral [s:wp-salt]
against: evil-eye — said by the published recipe for a Turkish nazar bead, which names salt among the ingredients [s:wp-nazar-amulet]
what: Sodium chloride, got by evaporating seawater in ponds, by mining rock salt, or from mineral springs. It preserves, it purifies, and it dissolves. That last property is why the archaeology of salt charms is always the container and never the salt.
story: Salt is a ritual material in more traditions than almost anything else in this atlas, and it is rarely worn. It is thrown, sprinkled, blessed, offered and put at thresholds.

In Judaism it is customary to spread salt on the bread or dip it in salt when it is passed round the table after the Kiddush. In Catholic practice salt is used in the Tridentine Mass and permitted in the preparation of holy water, and blessed salt is a sacramental: lay Catholics are not permitted to perform solemn exorcisms, but they may use holy water, blessed salt and other sacramentals for warding off evil. In Shinto, shio is used for ritual purification of places and entrances, and salt is among the offerings — with rice, water and sake — set before the kamidana beside the household ofuda. Mahayana Buddhists throw salt over the left shoulder on returning from a funeral. Hindu practice uses salt at house-warmings and weddings; Jains offer it before deities and sprinkle it on cremated remains. Aztec religion had Huixtocihuatl, a goddess of salt and saltwater.

It also goes inside other charms. The earliest documented witch bottles are salt-glazed stoneware Bellarmine jugs, and later bottles are filled with sand, stones, knotted thread, feathers, shells, herbs, flowers, salt, vinegar, oil, coins or ashes. A Turkish nazar bead is described as "a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil" — the salt is in the batch, fired into the glass.

Salt was also a major traded good, moved along Mediterranean routes, along dedicated salt roads and by Saharan camel caravan. The English word salary comes from the Latin for salt, though the story that Roman legions were paid in it is unsubstantiated.

*Inference —* every other material in this batch can be excavated. Salt cannot: it goes into water, into food, into the ground, and leaves nothing. A practice this widespread with this little to show for it is the clearest warning in the atlas against reading a museum drawer as a census.
today: Still sold at shrine gates, still blessed in churches, still thrown at doorways. Almost none of it is ever an object.
kin: witch-bottle — the salt-glazed jug, and the salt inside it — the container survives and the contents rarely do
kin: nazar — salt is named in the batch the bead is made from, fired into the glass
kin: ofuda — the household altar where salt is offered with rice, water and sake
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that blesses salt and tells the laity exactly what they may do with it
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that puts salt at an entrance rather than on a person
kin: herb — the other material that goes into a charm and rots or dissolves out of the record
kin: hanging-at-door — where salt is most often put: a threshold, a gate, a shop entrance
kin: burying — the practice a filled bottle ends in, and the reason we have the bottles at all
sources: s:wp-salt s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-amulet s:wp-sacramental s:wp-ofuda s:wp-nazar-amulet

## Seed and nut (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/seed/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/seed.json
id: seed
native: रुद्राक्ष (Devanagari)
aliases: stone · pit · bead · ojo de venado · blueberry bead
said: rudraksha — rudra-aksha, 'eye of Rudra'
when: undated (still carried)
countries: IN NP ID MX CN
object: form=rosary materials=seed,thread worn=neck,wrist
against: evil-eye — said by stallholders at the Mercado de Sonora, who sell a seed called deer's eye against it [s:wp-mercado-de-sonora]
against: infertility — said by Chinese marriage charms, whose lotus seeds stand for continuous births and whose pomegranates stand for fertility [s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm]
against: bad-luck — said by the Upanishadic account attributed to Kalagni-Rudra, which promises the benefit of giving cows in charity for uttering, seeing and touching the bead [s:wp-rudraksha]
what: The hard inner stone of a fruit, dried, drilled and strung, or carried whole. Seeds are the part of a plant built to survive being eaten and buried, which makes them the one plant material in this atlas with any chance of lasting — and the reason a plant charm can be a bead rather than a bundle.
story: The best-documented one is the rudraksha, the dried stone of Elaeocarpus ganitrus. The tree grows 18 to 24 metres, is evergreen and fast-growing, and puts out buttress roots as it matures; it starts bearing fruit three to four years from germination and then yields between 1,000 and 2,000 fruits a year. The ripe stone sits inside a blue fleshy husk, and the blue is not a pigment but structural colour, which is why the beads are sometimes called blueberry beads. The stones carry ridges called faces — mukha — usually between one and twenty-one, rarely up to twenty-six or twenty-seven, and the count is the grading system: the single-faced ekamukha is the rarest, an eleven-faced bead is worn by renunciants, a married person wears a two-faced bead, and a five-faced bead stands for Hanuman. Nepali beads run 20 to 35 mm, Indonesian ones 5 to 25 mm.

The origin story is an eye. Sage Bhusunda asks Kalagni-Rudra where the beads come from, and the answer given in the late-medieval Upanishads is that Rudra closed his eyes for the destruction of the Tripurasura, drops of water fell from them to the earth, and those tears became rudrakshas. The name is the same claim: rudra, Shiva, and aksha, eye.

The stringing is specified. Beads are commonly strung on silk or on black or red cotton thread, less often on copper, silver or gold wire, and may be damaged if strung too tightly. There is a long tradition of 108 beads plus one — the extra, called the meru, bindu or guru bead, marks the beginning and end of a cycle — with garlands also made as 27+1 and 54+1.

The supply chain is named. Rudraksha are primarily sourced from India, Indonesia and Nepal for jewellery and malas and are valued similarly to semi-precious stones; the popular varieties come from around Kathmandu and the Arun valley in Nepal and from Kulu and Rameshwaram in India, with groves mostly in Uttarakhand and natural trees in the alpine forests of the Dhauladhar and lower Shivalik ranges. There is a dedicated 184-acre grove, the Ch. Devi Lal Rudraksha Vatika in Yamunanagar district, Haryana, which also holds over 400 endangered ayurvedic medicinal herbs. The fruit was studied enough for an alkaloid, rudrakine, to be identified in it in 1979.

Mexico sells a different eye. At the Mercado de Sonora, among the magical and religious plant items, is a seed called deer's eye, sold against the evil eye. China puts seeds on metal instead of stringing them: Chinese marriage charms depict dates and peanuts for reproduction, lotus seeds for continuous births, chestnuts for male offspring and pomegranates for fertility — the seed as a sign cast in bronze rather than as an object worn.

*Inference —* every date in this record is textual. The Upanishads and the Tirumurai describe the garlands; no excavation dates one, because the cord rots and the beads scatter. A seed charm is durable in the hand and invisible in the ground.
how: Picked, husked, dried, drilled and strung — on silk, on black or red cotton, or on wire. The Devi Bhagavata Purana sets out the preparation of rudraksha garlands, and one Upanishadic passage lists the permitted materials for the beads of a garland as coral, pearl, crystal, conch, silver, gold, sandal, Putra-Jivika, lotus or rudraksha, bound with golden thread, silver caps on the right and copper on the left, each bead's face meeting the next bead's face and tail meeting tail, in a circle.
today: Rudraksha are grown as a crop and valued like semi-precious stones, and the cultivation is documented down to named groves and districts. The seed is also the only material in this batch that carries its own quality grading in public — a count of faces, visible on the bead, which a buyer can check and a seller can argue about.
kin: rudraksha — the seed itself, graded by the count of faces on its surface
kin: ojo-de-venado — the Mexican deer's-eye seed, sold in the same market aisle as the herbs
kin: counting-beads — the practice the string is for: 108 and one, marked by the meru bead
kin: thread — the cord the tradition specifies — silk, or black or red cotton — and the part that rots first
kin: herb — the soft part of the same plant, which leaves no trace where the stone would
kin: eye — the sign in the name: rudra-aksha, the eye of Rudra, and in Mexico the eye of a deer
kin: cowrie — the other small hard object strung by the hundred, where the shell does what the stone does
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition that sets out which beads may be strung, in what order, and on what
sources: s:wp-rudraksha s:wp-mercado-de-sonora s:wp-chinese-numismatic-charm
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Silver (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/silver/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/silver.json
id: silver
aliases: argentum · sterling
when: 630 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL SY IT GB US EG DZ CN
root: Latin argentum, hence the chemical symbol Ag
against: evil-eye — said by Egyptian users of the hirz and the hamsa, where the silver itself is part of the claim [s:wp-hamsa]
against: witchcraft — said by European folklore, which holds a silver bullet the only weapon effective against a witch or werewolf [s:wp-silver]
against: demons — said by the incised sheet amulets of late antique Palestine and Syria, which name God against them [s:wp-amulet]
what: A soft, white, very reflective metal that occurs native and is mostly recovered as a by-product of lead-zinc, copper and gold mining. It takes a high polish, it beats out into sheet thin enough to write on with a needle, and it blackens: silver sulfide forms wherever sulfur reaches it, which is why old silver charms in a drawer go dark. Pure silver is soft, so working silver is alloyed, usually with copper, and quoted per mille.
story: The oldest surviving text of the Hebrew Bible is an amulet, and it is silver. In 1979 two tiny silver scrolls came out of a Judahite burial chamber at Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem's Old City, inscribed with portions of the Priestly Blessing from Numbers and apparently worn as amulets. They date to the late seventh or early sixth century BCE. Unrolling them without destroying them took three years, and they are now in the Israel Museum.

That is the metal's characteristic use: a sheet, incised with a needle, rolled up, and carried in a tube. Flat metal amulets of silver, gold, copper and lead were popular in late antiquity across Palestine, Syria, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Iran — rolled and placed in a metal container with loops for a cord, and covered with incantation formulae and the names of God, mostly in Aramaic and Hebrew. Jewish amulet practice, which will not make images, puts the divine name on parchment or on metal, and the metal is usually silver.

The metal also carries claims of its own. The hamsa was most commonly carved in jet or formed from silver, a metal held to represent purity and to hold power. The hirz, another Egyptian amulet against the evil eye, is a silver box holding verses of the Qur'an. The Neapolitan cimaruta is commonly silver, and the cornicello is cut from gold or silver as often as from coral; silver, in that reading, belongs to Luna. In Europe silver turns up as a weapon: folklore holds that a bullet cast from silver is the only thing effective against a werewolf or a witch, and the metal is also credited with detecting poison and easing passage into the realm of the fairies.

*Inference —* silver sits between gold and iron in every sense that matters to a charm. It survives in the ground where iron does not, and it costs less than gold, which is why so much of the world's amulet stock is silver — it is the most expensive metal an ordinary household will put on a child.
today: Still the default metal of the amulet trades from Morocco to Nepal. The silver jewellery now identified with the Navajo and other peoples of the American Southwest is dated by writers on turquoise to around 1880 and described as a modern development following European contact — a reminder that a material can be old and the craft made from it recent.
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — two rolled sheets of this metal, and the oldest surviving text of the Hebrew Bible
kin: kamea — the written Jewish amulet, put on parchment or on metal, and the metal is usually this one
kin: hamsa — carved in jet or formed in silver, which its makers tie to purity
kin: cimaruta — a sprig of rue cast in silver — the herb made permanent by changing what it is made of
kin: cornicello — cut from silver as readily as from coral, and in that reading silver belongs to Luna
kin: hirz-pouch — a silver box with Qur'anic verses inside it
kin: takrut — the same technique at the other end of Asia: metal sheet, incised, rolled, worn on a cord
kin: gold — the metal above it, and the one a household reaches for only when it can
kin: turquoise — the stone silver is set with from Tibet to Arizona
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition that made this metal a page
sources: s:wp-silver s:wp-ketef-hinnom s:wp-amulet s:wp-hamsa s:wp-cimaruta s:wp-cornicello s:wp-turquoise

## Skin (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/skin/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/skin.json
id: skin
native: สักยันต์ (Thai)
aliases: the tattooed charm · irezumi · sicanje · yantra tattoo
said: sak yant — sak is Khmer for 'to prick'
when: 3351 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: TH KH LA MM EG SD IT AT BA IN PH PK AF
object: form=tattoo materials=skin,ink worn=skin,upper-arm,wrist,chest,head
against: weapons — said by sak yant wearers in dangerous work — the cited account names military personnel, police and taxi drivers [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: spirits — said by Austronesian carriers, among whom tattoos were regarded as wards against evil spirits and illnesses, and tattooed people in Rajasthan [s:wp-tattoo]
against: illness — said by readings of Ötzi's 61 tattoos, which correspond to areas of degeneration in his bones and have been read as pain treatment [s:wp-tattoo]
against: childbirth — said by women in Egypt and Nubia tattooed with Bes, the god associated with fertility and childbirth [s:wp-tattoo]
against: witchcraft — said by Catholic Croats of Bosnia, who used sicanje against forced conversion under Ottoman rule [s:wp-tattoo]
RESTRICTED: This record does not print which yant a master gives to which person, the conditions attached to a given design, or the words said over it. The tradition itself makes that the point: the cited account states that a yantra tattoo confers its powers only so long as the bearer observes rules and taboos set for them, such as abstaining from a particular food. Those rules are given to a named person by a named master, and they are not ours to publish as a list.
what: The only amulet material a person cannot put down. Pigment is driven into the dermis — the layer of skin under the surface — where macrophages engulf it and hold it in a band just below the boundary between the two layers. The surface flakes away and takes the loose pigment with it; what stays, stays for life, migrating slowly deeper, which is why an old tattoo looks blurred.
story: The dates here are good, and they come from bodies rather than from objects. Ötzi, found in glacial ice in the Alps and dated to 3250 BCE, carried 61 tattoos; radiological examination showed age- or strain-induced degeneration of his bones — osteochondrosis and slight spondylosis in the lumbar spine, wear in the knee and especially the ankle — corresponding to many of the tattooed areas, which has been read as a form of pain treatment. In 2018 the oldest figurative tattoos in the world were identified on two Egyptian mummies dated between 3351 and 3017 BCE. One of them, the naturally mummified Gebelein man from a shallow grave in upper Egypt, has two overlapping tattoos on his right forearm: a bovine, and another horned animal. He was eighteen to twenty-one when he died, so he was marked young.

By 500 BCE men in Nubia were tattooed, typically on the hands or arms and rarely on the face. A female mummy from Aksha, dated to the fourth century BCE, carries a tattoo of Bes on her thigh — Bes, the dwarfed god associated with fertility and childbirth, was a popular image tattooed onto women in both Egypt and Nubia.

Southeast Asia runs the largest living version. Sak yant originates in the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, built on indigenous mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing practices dating back as far as 2,500 BCE, with designs influenced by Indian yantras. Sak is a native Khmer word from the Proto Mon-Khmer root *cɔkʔ, 'to prick'; yant is the sacred geometry. Carriers name three effects: something that benefits the wearer, such as eloquence; protection, which the account says is used by military personnel, police, taxi drivers and others in dangerous work; and an effect on people nearby, such as invoking fear.

Elsewhere the mark is a declaration. Many Copts have the cross tattooed on the inside of the right arm at the wrist as a sign of faith. Catholic Croats of Bosnia, especially children and women, used sicanje for protection against conversion to Islam during Ottoman rule. Among Austronesian societies tattoos were regarded as magical wards against dangers including evil spirits and illnesses, and in Rajasthan they were held to protect the wearer from evil spirits and bring good fortune.

*Inference —* every dated charm in this record comes from a body that did not rot. Ice, desert sand and deliberate mummification are the only three conditions under which this material reaches an excavator, and each of them is rare. Forensic pathologists note the other half of it: pigment lies encapsulated deep in the skin, so tattoos are not easily destroyed even when the skin is burned. The material survives; the person has to survive first.
how: Some traditions cut the design into the skin and rub the wound with ink, ashes or other agents, as an adjunct to scarification. Others hand-tap the ink in with sharpened sticks or animal bone needles fitted with clay discs, or, now, actual needles. The modern electric machine drives its needles in and out 80 to 150 times a second.
today: Two arguments are running. In 2011 Thailand's Culture Ministry sought to stop the tattooing of Buddha images on foreign visitors; the ministry's position and the tattooists' were both reported at the time, and this atlas prints the disagreement rather than settling it. The other argument is chemical: the European Chemicals Agency has proposed restricting the intentional use or concentration of about 4,000 substances in tattoo inks, the EU Observatory for Nanomaterials has raised nanotoxicological concerns about modern inks, and an analysis in the European Union in October 2024 found that nine out of ten blue and green inks sold were not compliant with the REACH legislation. A 2025 United States opinion poll found 37 per cent held favourable and 26 per cent unfavourable views of tattoos.
kin: sak-yant — the largest living tradition written in this material, and the one that sets rules the bearer has to keep for it to hold
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the same material used as a declaration rather than a shield — inside the right wrist, where it will be seen
kin: ink — what is actually driven in; skin is the ground, ink is the mark
kin: tattooing — the practice that makes it, from cut-and-rub to hand-tapping to a machine at 80 to 150 strokes a second
kin: bes-amulet — the same god, worn as a pendant in Egypt and cut into a woman's thigh at Aksha in the fourth century BCE
kin: yantra-plate — the same sacred geometry on cloth or metal, put in a house or a vehicle instead of into a person
kin: wearing-hidden — the opposite instruction: this material cannot be taken off, so hiding it means covering it
kin: yant-flash — the drawn designs, which is as far as this atlas goes in showing them
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read behind this record's restricted block
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the 2011 Thai argument belongs to
sources: s:wp-tattoo s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-coptic-cross s:wp-bes s:web-ap-buddha-tattoo-ban s:web-saiyasombut-religious-tattoos
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Thread and cord (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/thread/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/thread.json
id: thread
native: חוט השני (Hebrew)
aliases: red string · yarn · cord · stitches
said: khutt hashani, the scarlet thread
when: 202 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL BG MK RO MD AL GR JP CN IN
against: evil-eye — said by wearers of the Jewish red string, and the commentators who call it a good omen [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: illness — said by Bulgarian and Macedonian wearers of the martenitsa, whose red and white threads carry a wish for good health [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: weapons — said by the women who stitched senninbari, and the soldiers who carried them [s:wp-senninbari]
against: war — said by the stitched slogan itself, bu-un cho-kyu, 'eternal good luck in war' [s:wp-senninbari]
what: The cheapest amulet material there is, and the only one whose meaning is carried by an action rather than by a shape. A thread charm is made by tying, winding, knotting or stitching; the colour is nearly always red, or red and white, and the count usually matters.
story: The Jewish red string is thin scarlet or crimson wool, khutt hashani, worn as a band on the wrist against the evil eye. A scarlet thread tied about the wrist appears in Genesis 38, at the birth of Tamar's twins; commentators as early as Rabbi Shmuel ben Hafni Gaon noted that a red string placed on the hand may be a good omen. The custom is popularly tied to Kabbalah, and the same red string is worn in Hindu and Chinese practice, for luck, for love, and against harm.

In Bulgaria and North Macedonia the martenitsa is white and red yarn, usually made into two small wool dolls, Pizho the male in white and Penda the female in red. It goes on at Baba Marta, 1 March, and comes off when the wearer first sees a stork, a swallow or a tree in blossom. Ethnologists read the red and white as life and purity, sunset and melting snow, and the pair as a balance. Romania and Moldova keep the same custom as martisor, Albania as verore, worn on 14 March.

Japan counts. A senninbari, a thousand-person-stitch belt, is a strip of cloth carrying a thousand stitches, each normally sewn by a different woman, and given to a soldier leaving for war. They are typically 15 cm wide and 90 to 120 cm long, most often white cloth with a thousand red stitches, sometimes worked into tigers or into the slogan bu-un cho-kyu, "eternal good luck in war". The custom began in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. Not everyone who wore one accepted the claim: some soldiers rejected the idea that it could protect them and carried it instead as a keepsake of the women who made it.

Thread also holds other charms together, and the holding is graded. In a Han jade burial suit the plaques are sewn with gold wire for an emperor, silver for princes and marquises, copper for their children, and silk thread for lesser aristocrats.

*Inference —* thread is the material that leaves no museum tray. It rots, it is cut off at the end of its term by design, and its whole cost is a person's time. Every count in this record — a thousand stitches, two dolls, one wrist — is doing the work a carved stone does elsewhere.
how: Tied on, wound, knotted, or stitched, usually by somebody other than the wearer. Most thread charms have an end written into them: the martenitsa comes off at the first stork, the senninbari goes to war and does not come back.
kin: red-string — the simplest object in this atlas: scarlet wool, a wrist, a knot
kin: martenitsa — white and red yarn with an expiry date written into the custom — the first stork ends it
kin: senninbari — a thousand stitches by a thousand women, 15 cm by 90-120 cm, given to a man going to war
kin: red-thread — the sign this material is, wherever it is worn
kin: knot — what thread turns into when the tying itself is the charm
kin: knotting — the practice that makes it, and the reason the count is recorded
kin: sewing-in — the practice of stitching a charm into clothing, where the thread is both charm and fixing
kin: rudraksha — beads strung on silk or on black or red cotton — the cord is specified, not incidental
kin: gold — the thread of an emperor's burial suit, where rank is written in what the stitching is made of
sources: s:wp-red-string-kabbalah s:wp-martenitsa s:wp-senninbari s:wp-jade-burial-suit s:wp-rudraksha s:wp-witch-bottle

## Tooth, tusk and claw (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/tooth/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/tooth.json
id: tooth
aliases: tabua · whale tooth · wolf tooth · animal teeth
when: undated (still carried)
countries: FJ TO US IT NZ
against: evil-eye — said by wearers in Italy, who used a tooth or a tuft of fur of the Italian wolf against it [s:wp-evil-eye]
against: curse — said by Fijian practice, in which a tabua is presented in atonement [s:wp-tabua]
against: the-dead — said by Fijian burial custom, which put a man's tabua in the grave with him [s:wp-tabua]
what: A tooth worn as a charm is the one material that arrives already shaped, already pointed, and already the property of something that could bite. Teeth, tusks and claws are carved very little: drilled at the root, polished, hung. The class includes sperm whale teeth in Fiji and Hawaii, wolf teeth in Italy, and the animal teeth the Illyrians used against the harmful look.
story: Fiji's tabua is a polished sperm whale tooth and one of the most important objects in Fijian society. Tabua are presented as sevusevu, in atonement or esteem, and were central to negotiation between rival chiefs; men were once buried with their tabua alongside their war clubs. They were originally very rare, available only from beached whales and by trade from Tonga, where the practice may have begun. When the European market learned of the demand in the early nineteenth century, thousands of teeth — and fake teeth cut from ivory and walrus tusk — entered Fiji, and the trade that supplied them produced the European craft of scrimshaw. A tabua darkens as the oils in human hands work into it, so its age shows.

In Hawaii the lei niho palaoa hangs a carved whale tooth at the throat of an ali'i, on a cord of plaited human hair. Around the Mediterranean the tooth is smaller and the claim narrower: a tooth or a tuft of fur of the Italian wolf was worn as a talisman against the evil eye, and Illyrians used animal teeth against the same harm alongside the phallus, the hand and the leg.

*Inference —* every use listed here works the same way. The charm is a piece of a dangerous animal, kept whole enough to be recognised as one. That is a different argument from the one a cut stone makes, and it is why this atlas files tooth with claw rather than with ivory.
today: Tabua are not sold in Fiji; they are still given, at weddings, birthdays and funerals, and they appear on the twenty cent coin and in airline branding. Because the sperm whale is an endangered species, removing a tabua from Fiji is capped at 225 exports a year and requires permits from the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs as well as CITES permits, with the original CITES paperwork presented to the importing country's border officials. In 2007 New Zealand authorities returned 146 tabua to Fiji that had been seized for lacking valid permits.
kin: bone-ivory — the wider class this sits inside, and the one that gets carved rather than kept whole
kin: tooth-and-claw — the sign this material is: a piece of a dangerous animal, left recognisable
kin: hei-matau — the hook that reads as a tooth and is worn in the same place, at the throat
kin: cornicello — the Italian horn worn for the same harm the wolf tooth was worn for
kin: te-papa-taonga — where a tabua can be seen outside Fiji, in a museum that publishes what it holds
kin: inuit-amulet — the Arctic version of the same argument: the charm is a part of the animal it came from
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read for an object under export caps, permits and a 2007 repatriation
sources: s:wp-tabua s:wp-lei-niho-palaoa s:wp-evil-eye

## Turquoise (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/turquoise/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/turquoise.json
id: turquoise
native: فیروزه (Arabic)
aliases: firuzeh · pirozah · chalchihuitl · callais
said: firuzeh in Persian; chalchihuitl in Nahuatl
when: 1500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IR EG MX US CN MN GR
root: Old French turquois, 'Turkish', because the stone reached Europe through the Ottoman Empire from Khorasan in Iran
against: illness — said by the several ancient cultures whose common belief held that the stone changed colour with the wearer's health [s:wp-turquoise]
against: bad-luck — said by Navajo use, described in the sources as spiritual protection and blessing [s:wp-turquoise]
against: war — said by Apache tradition, which holds that the stone affords the archer dead aim [s:wp-turquoise]
what: A hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium, opaque, sky-blue where copper dominates and green where iron replaces it. It is soft for a gemstone — just under 6 on the Mohs scale, about the hardness of window glass — and porous, so it takes colour and oil from whatever touches it. It almost never forms crystals; it fills veins and fractures, or replaces a fossil.
story: The claim made for turquoise almost everywhere it is worn is the same one, and it is unusual: the stone reports. Writers on the ancient cultures that used it — Egypt, the Aztecs, Persia, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, Shang China — record a common belief that turquoise held prophylactic qualities, that it changed colour with the wearer's health, and that it protected the wearer from untoward forces. A porous stone that darkens with skin oil and sunlight will in fact change, which is a rare case of a claim and a material property lining up.

In Iran it was the national stone for millennia, worked into everything from turbans to bridles, and used on domes because its blue stood for heaven on earth. Persian turquoise was often engraved with devotional words in Arabic script and the letters inlaid with gold. The Persian style went to India with the Mughals.

In Mesoamerica the Aztecs took turquoise as an embodiment of fire and gave it properties of heat and smokiness, inlaying it with gold, quartz, malachite, jet, jade, coral and shell into mosaic masks, some built on a human skull, and into knives and shields, bedded in resin, bitumen and wax. In the North American Southwest the Pueblo, Navajo and Apache prized it for amuletic use; Apache tradition holds that the stone gives an archer dead aim, and in Navajo use it is described as "a spiritual protection and blessing". Writers on the stone credit the Ancestral Puebloans of Chaco Canyon and the surrounding region with prospering greatly on producing and trading it.

Egypt mined it in Sinai and then imitated it: the blue-green glaze on faience exists in order to look like this stone and like lapis lazuli.
today: Tibetan and Mongolian silver and gold work still sets imported turquoise beside coral, with a greener hue preferred. Writers on the stone report both halves of the present trade without settling it: most pieces made today are roughly polished cabochons set simply in silver, meant for inexpensive export to Western markets, and are probably not accurate representations of the original style. The stone has also been devalued in finer grades by treatments, imitations and synthetics. Mining boomed and broke: prices peaked in 1890 and had collapsed by 1912, ending large-scale operations.
kin: faience — the glaze invented to look like this stone, and the reason Egypt could sell the colour without the mine
kin: coral — its partner in Tibetan and Mongolian silverwork, red against blue on the same setting
kin: silver — the metal it is nearly always set in, from Nishapur to Arizona
kin: gau-box — the Himalayan amulet box this stone is set into, with coral, on silver
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition that imports the stone and prefers the greener grades of it
kin: jet — one of the materials inlaid beside it in Aztec mosaic masks
kin: crystal-pendant — the present-day trade in treated and synthetic stone, sold on a claim about the substance
kin: the-fake-market — the long read: this stone has been imitated for so long that grading it is its own profession
sources: s:wp-turquoise s:wp-egyptian-faience
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Wood (material)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/material/wood/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/material/wood.json
id: wood
native: 絵馬 (Han)
aliases: timber · board · slate · kifuda · carved figure
said: ema, 'picture-horse', the wooden plaque hung at a shrine
when: 710 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP GB NG CM GH CD MX US NO SE FI
object: form=plaque materials=wood,ink worn=wall,door,neck,cradle,burnt
against: exams — said by Japanese worshippers who buy ema for examination success — and the shrines criticised in 1979 for profiting from them [s:wp-ema-shinto]
against: witchcraft — said by British folklorists of the Victorian era, reporting the rowan's warding of witches; James Frazer recorded the tree planted at a Scottish gate or front door in 1890 [s:wp-rowan]
against: spirits — said by Thomas Keightley's account: a rowan branch over the door let mortals watch the fairy rades safely [s:wp-rowan]
against: child-harm — said by Ojibwe mothers and grandmothers, in the account Frances Densmore recorded in 1929, who wove willow hoops for children [s:wp-dreamcatcher]
against: infertility — said by young Fanti women seeking to conceive, who keep an akua'ba and have it washed and cared for in the homestead [s:wp-akuaba]
against: witchcraft — said by Kongo communities, whose publicly held nkondi were used to affirm oaths and to protect villages from witches or evildoers [s:wp-nkondi]
what: Cut, carved, split or planed. Wood is probably the commonest amulet material in the world and one of the rarest in a museum tray older than a few centuries, because it burns, rots, and in a great many traditions is meant to.
story: Japan writes on it and then burns it. Ema are small wooden plaques, typically 15 cm wide and 9 cm tall, on which Shinto and Buddhist worshippers write prayers or wishes and hang them at the shrine, where they stay until they are ritually burned at special events — the burning understood as releasing the wish. The substitution behind them is documented: horses were held to carry messages from the kami, live horses were expensive, and a wooden statue or painted plaque could stand in as a katashiro, a substitute effigy. The earliest text record of such a substitution is the Honcho Bunsui of 1013, recording an offering of three paper horses at the Kitano Tenjin shrine, and clay or wood horse figures survive from the Nara period.

Japan also keeps a sliver of it. Ofuda are made of paper, wood, cloth or metal, and the wooden ones are called kifuda; the best-known form of the Jingū Taima is a wooden tablet containing a sliver of cedar known as the gyoshin, the sacred core, wrapped in paper printed with the shrine's name and stamped with its seals. A document of 1777 indicates that between eighty-nine and ninety per cent of households in the country owned an Ise talisman at the time.

West Africa writes on it and then washes it. The Qur'an board is a wooden tablet of locally available woods such as mahogany or baobab, on which a student copies verses; when the passage is mastered the writing is washed off and the water is collected and drunk or used in healing.

Central and West Africa carve it. An nkondi is most often a carved human figure with open cavities in its body — most commonly in the belly, but also on the head or in pouches at the neck — for the bilongo, the medicines that make it the home of a spirit, usually hidden behind resin-fixed mirrors; people drive nails into the figure as a petition for help, healing or witness, and the nailing is described as waking and sometimes enraging it. Akua'ba are wooden fertility dolls with large disc-like heads, from western Ghana and particularly associated with the Fanti, used by young women seeking to conceive; when not in use they are ritually washed and cared for in the homestead.

Europe's protective wood has a species. The rowan, Sorbus aucuparia, is a small deciduous tree 4 to 12 metres tall; its wood is dense and used for carving, turning, tool handles and walking sticks. James Frazer reported in 1890 a Scottish tradition of planting it near a gate or front door, and Thomas Keightley recorded that mortals could safely watch the fairy rades by placing a rowan branch over their doors. In the Highlands there were strong taboos against using any part of the tree save the berries, except for ritual: a threshing tool of rowan called a buaitean was used on grain meant for rituals and celebrations. The Old English name cwic-bēam survives as quickbeam, and by the nineteenth century had been reinterpreted as connected to the word witch, producing wicken-tree, wich-tree, wicky and wiggan-tree.

North America bends it. A dreamcatcher is a handmade willow hoop with a net woven across it; Frances Densmore recorded in 1929 that mothers and grandmothers wove webs for children using willow hoops and sinew or plant cordage, and that in old times the netting was made of nettle fibre. Mexico sells crosses of ocote wood for good luck at the Mercado de Sonora.

*Inference —* look at what those examples have in common. The ema is burned, the ofuda is replaced yearly, the slate is washed, the dreamcatcher's hoop is green wood. This material is chosen for traditions with an expiry date built into them, and a museum collects the ones that failed to expire.
how: Carved, split, planed into a board, or bent green into a hoop. The Kongo case is the most explicit about who: an nkondi is built by an nganga, often isolated in a hidden camp away from the village, and the figure is composed at the edge of the village because the edge and the entrances are what need guarding.
today: Akua'ba are now more commonly seen as mass-produced works of art or souvenirs than as heirlooms in ritual use, though traditional use continues in some areas among the Fante and other Akan peoples, and the form has become a symbol of good luck more broadly. Europeans visiting Africa in the 1800s were keenly interested in Fante dolls, which is why so many are in European museums. Japan's ema have their own commercial argument: two shrines dedicated to education sold ema for examination success in 1979 and, after public outcry, turned the funds into a scholarship in 1980.
kin: ofuda — the Japanese talisman whose grandest form is a wooden tablet wrapped round a sliver of cedar called the sacred core
kin: omikuji — the paper fortune that ends up tied to a pine, which is the tree doing the holding
kin: akuaba-figure — carved wood with a disc for a head, washed and kept in the house between uses
kin: nkisi — the carved figure with a cavity cut in its belly for the medicines that make it inhabited
kin: dreamcatcher — a bent willow hoop with a net across it, hung over a cradle
kin: rowan-cross — the European protective wood with a species name, and a taboo about which parts may be used
kin: ink — what the West African slate is for: a surface chosen because the writing will lift off it
kin: burning-retirement — the practice most of this material is built for — a wish released by fire
kin: renewing-yearly — the other reason wooden charms are young: they are replaced on a schedule
kin: tree — the standing version of the same material, where the charm is the tree and not the plank
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read behind the Fante dolls that ended up in European museums after the 1800s
sources: s:wp-ema-shinto s:wp-ofuda s:web-wp-quran-boards s:wp-nkondi s:wp-akuaba s:wp-rowan s:wp-dreamcatcher s:wp-mercado-de-sonora
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Blessing at a shrine (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/blessing-at-a-shrine/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/blessing-at-a-shrine.json
id: blessing-at-a-shrine
aliases: the shrine counter · having it blessed · taking it to the saint
said: the step that happens at the power's own address rather than at home
when: 1336 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP TW TH PH MX BO IT FR CA ES
object: form=packet materials=paper,wood,cloth,silver,lead,ink worn=neck,pocket,wall,door,vehicle,shop
against: traffic — said by Japanese shrines, which issue kōtsū-anzen omamori consecrated before they reach the counter [s:wp-omamori]
against: bad-luck — said by visitors who draw an omikuji and tie a bad one to a pine tree on the grounds, on the pun that the bad luck will wait by the tree rather than follow them [s:wp-o-mikuji]
against: illness — said by petitioners who pin a milagro shaped like the afflicted part to a saint's image, and the pilgrims who left hundreds of crutches, canes and braces on the grilles of the Votive Chapel at Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal [s:wp-ex-voto]
against: house — said by Japanese households, whose kanai-anzen charm and household-altar ofuda are both issued from a shrine [s:wp-ofuda]
against: drowning — said by the model ships among the ex-votos at Notre-Dame de la Garde in Marseille, and the Lod mosaic, thought to be an ex-voto for rescue from a shipwreck [s:wp-ex-voto]
against: curse — said by the Catholic Church's own classification, which lists exorcisms among the three kinds of sacramental alongside blessings and consecrations [s:wp-sacramental]
RESTRICTED: The words said over an object at a shrine belong to the shrine, the priesthood or the lineage that says them, and this record prints none of them. It names the sequence where a source publishes the sequence — incense, a name, a birth date, divination blocks, three passes over the censer — and stops there. It does not reconstruct a rite from a neighbouring tradition's, and it does not supply the wording of a blessing whose text a tradition keeps.
what: Taking an object to where the power is, rather than bringing the power to the object. The move has two directions and this record keeps them apart. Outward: a shrine or temple charges a thing and issues it to you to carry away. Inward: you bring a thing and leave it there, pinned to a saint's robe, tied to a tree, hung on a wall. Same address, opposite traffic.
story: Japan runs the outward direction at national scale and describes the mechanism in its own words. The practice says of omamori that they are made sacred through ritual and contain busshin — spiritual offshoots — in a Shinto context, or kesshin, manifestations, in a Buddhist one. An ofuda is considered imbued with the power of the kami or Buddhist figure revered at the place that issued it, containing that essence, in the practice's own phrase, by virtue of its consecration. Both are available at shrines and temples to anybody, regardless of religious affiliation. Fushimi Inari Taisha, which the cited account credits with as many as 32,000 branch shrines across Japan, is one address at which that happens.

The drawing counter is a third thing again. An omikuji is a paper fortune drawn at a shrine or temple. If the prediction is bad, custom is to fold the strip and tie it to a pine tree or a rack of metal wires on the grounds, alongside the other bad fortunes — the reported reason being a pun between matsu, pine, and matsu, to wait: the bad luck waits by the tree rather than following the bearer. If the fortune is good, the bearer can tie it up anyway so that it takes greater effect, or keep it. A prayer written on a wooden ema and tied to a scaffold works the same way.

Taiwan states a sequence. Issuing a ping'an fu, a peace-and-safety slip, involves the petitioner's name and birth date, incense, divination blocks and passing the slip in circles over the censer before it is handed over. This record names those steps because the source publishes them, and prints no wording.

In Catholic practice the Church has legislated the whole category. The Catechism sorts sacramentals into three kinds — blessings, consecrations and dedications, and exorcisms — and defines them as sacred signs bearing a resemblance to the sacraments, whose effects are obtained through the Church's intercession. The inward traffic is where its charm objects live: an ex-voto is placed in a church or chapel where the worshipper seeks grace or gives thanks, and is meant as a testimony to later visitors as much as to the figure invoked. Notre-Dame de la Garde in Marseille holds paintings, plaques, model ships, war medals and football shirts given by players and supporters of Olympique de Marseille. The Votive Chapel at Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal has hundreds of crutches, canes and braces fixed to iron grilles, left by pilgrims who said they were healed after meeting Brother André. A milagro is pinned to a saint's image as a reminder of what is needed or in thanks for an answer.

The scale of the inward traffic can be very large. Quiapo Church in Manila holds a novena every Friday, attended by thousands, at which devotees climb a narrow flight of stairs to kiss the foot of the Nuestro Padre Jesús Nazareno or wipe it with the handkerchiefs they bring every visit. At the Feast of Jesús Nazareno on 9 January 2024, 6.5 million devotees took part in the Traslación.

And the two directions can meet on one day. At Alasitas in La Paz, people acting as shaman bless the miniatures at the fair, and at midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses the same gifts at the main cathedral.

*Inference —* the thing that separates this from consecration proper is who the recipient is. A consecration is usually performed for a person, by a specialist who knows them, on an object that is already theirs. A shrine blessing is performed for anybody, in advance, on stock, in exchange for a donation. That is not a lesser rite; it is a different social arrangement, and it is the one that makes a counter possible.
how: Outward: the object is prepared, the rite is performed by the shrine or temple, the object is placed on a counter or in a case, and a visitor receives it for a donation. The Japanese wording is deliberate — omamori and ofuda are not bought but received, sazukaru or ukeru. Inward: the object is brought, sometimes made for the occasion, and left in a designated place — pinned to an image, hung on a grille, tied to a tree or a rack, fixed to a wall — where it stays as a record for the next visitor. In both directions the place, not the person, is what does the work, which is why people travel to it.
today: Live at every address in this record. Japanese shrines have extended the outward direction into categories that did not exist a generation ago — Kanda Myojin in Tokyo issues charms for IT equipment and electronics — and in 2022 Sega released free digital omamori. Quiapo's Traslación drew 6.5 million people in 2024, and the Archdiocese of Manila has proposed to the Holy See that 9 January be declared the national feast of the Jesús Nazareno. The inward traffic is the one that leaves walls and grilles full of objects, and those walls are the best-documented evidence in this atlas of what people actually ask for.
kin: omamori — the outward direction in one object: a pouch made sacred by ritual before anyone sees it, then handed over for a donation
kin: ofuda — the tablet whose power the practice describes as held by virtue of its consecration
kin: omikuji — the third kind of counter — a draw rather than an issue, with the paper tied up on the grounds if the answer is bad
kin: ping-an-fu — the case where the sequence is published: a name, a birth date, incense, divination blocks, and passes over the censer
kin: milagro — the inward direction: the object exists to be left at the shrine, not carried away from it
kin: ekeko — where both directions land on one day — blessed at the fair, and blessed again at the cathedral at midday on 24 January
kin: consecration — the same transfer done privately, by somebody who knows the recipient, on an object already theirs
kin: votive-wall — what the inward direction builds: a wall of other people's petitions, left where the next petitioner will read them
kin: fushimi-inari — the practice at the scale of 32,000 branch shrines
kin: quiapo-church — the inward direction at its largest — 6.5 million people in the Traslación of 9 January 2024, and thousands every Friday
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that wrote this step into canon law, and set out what it does and does not do
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that turned the counter into a national distribution system with four changes of administrative owner
kin: renewing-yearly — what happens next: a charm issued at a counter comes back to it in a year
