## Burning at retirement (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/burning-retirement/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/burning-retirement.json
id: burning-retirement
native: どんど焼き (Hiragana)
aliases: Sagichō · daruma kuyō · ritual burning · o-takiage
said: dondoyaki
when: 1764 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP KR BT NP CN IE GB
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,wood,cloth worn=burnt,wall,lintel
against: bad-luck — said by Japanese carriers, for whom burning the year's omamori is a sign of respect to the deity that helped them through it [s:wp-omamori]
against: spirits — said by Korean mudang, who close a gut by burning name tags, ancestors' clothes, straw shoes and imitation money to send the spirits off [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
against: witchcraft — said by English folk practice, in which a witch bottle thrown on the fire broke the spell when it burst [s:wp-witch-bottle]
what: Ending a charm in fire, on purpose and in public. Old talismans go back to the place that issued them and are burnt together at a set ceremony; wish-plaques are burnt to release the wish; worn prayer flags are burnt rather than binned; a shaman's paraphernalia is burnt after the rite that used it. Burning is disposal and it is also thanks — several of these traditions say the fire is owed to the thing.
story: Japan burns by the ten thousand on a date. Old ofuda and omamori are burnt at a ceremony called Sagichō or Dondoyaki, held at the Little New Year on 14 or 15 January, at the end of the New Year season. The reason given in the omamori literature is not tidiness: old omamori should not be discarded but burnt, as a sign of respect to the deity that helped the person through the year.

Daruma dolls get their own fire. At the end of the year the dolls are brought back to the temple they came from for the daruma kuyō, held once a year and usually right after New Year's Day, most famously at Nishi-Arai Daishi in Tokyo and Dairyū-ji in Gifu. People express gratitude to the dolls, hand them over, buy new ones, and after the monks enter, read sutras and blow horns, tens of thousands of figures are set alight together.

Ema burn for a different reason. The small wooden plaques on which Shinto and Buddhist worshippers write a wish are hung at the shrine for the kami to receive and are then ritually burnt at special events, which the practice describes as symbolically liberating the wish into the world. Some are taken home and hung there instead, and still burnt at a ceremony later.

Tibetan practice puts it as a rule of respect: because the symbols and mantras on prayer flags are sacred, they should not be put on the ground or used on clothing, and old flags should be burnt. Korean practice burns at both ends of a rite. Before a gut, the altar is purified with fire and water, often by burning white paper for purity; at the close, the summoned spirits are sent off by burning name tags, the josang ot — clothes for ancestors — cloth, straw shoes and imitation money. Much modern ritual gear is made cheaply in South Korea precisely because it is going to be burnt. After a mudang's death, their musindo paintings were often de-animated and burnt through the twentieth century; some practitioners hold that the deity leaves the image when it is donated to a museum instead.

Europe's version is less organised and often a choice. In Ireland, discarded Brigid's crosses were burned or buried, with burial preferred because of Brigid's associations with agriculture. In English folk practice a witch bottle could be thrown into a fire, and when it burst the spell was held to be broken.

*Inference —* the museum problem lives here. A tradition that ends its objects in fire produces almost no old objects, so a drawer of surviving charms over-represents the traditions that bury, hide or inherit them. Japanese and Korean material in Western collections is largely material that escaped the fire.
how: Return the old object to the place that issued it, or gather it with others. Wait for the date. Burn them together, with clergy present in the Japanese and Korean cases. New objects are obtained at the same event.
today: Live and annual. Japanese shrines and temples run the January fires, accepting talismans from other shrines in practice, though Buddhist ofuda are often not accepted at Shinto shrines or the reverse. Korean gut still burn their paper and cloth at the close. Prayer-flag burning continues wherever the flags are flown.
kin: omamori — the charm this fire is mostly made of, returned in January by the sackful
kin: ofuda — burnt at Sagichō or Dondoyaki on 14 or 15 January, at the end of the New Year season
kin: daruma — the doll with its own fire — tens of thousands at a time, after sutras and horns
kin: ofuda — the wish-plaque burnt to release the wish rather than to dispose of the board
kin: lungta-flag — worn flags burnt because the mantras on them cannot be put on the ground
kin: senso-ji — a temple where the year's talismans are obtained and the old ones handed back
kin: renewing-yearly — the cycle this fire closes
kin: burying — the other way of ending a charm, preferred in Ireland for the same objects
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that runs the calendar this fire sits on
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read this practice skews: traditions that burn leave almost nothing to date
sources: s:wp-omamori s:wp-ofuda s:wp-daruma-doll s:wp-ema-shinto s:wp-prayer-flag s:wp-korean-shamanism s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-brigid-s-cross
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Burying (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/burying/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/burying.json
id: burying
aliases: putting it in the ground · hiding it in the fabric of a house · spiritual midden
said: out of sight and meant to stay there
when: 1501 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB US BE IE GR IT IQ IR KR BG
object: form=packet materials=glass,terracotta,lead,iron,leather worn=foundation,hearth,grave,field
against: witchcraft — said by English and American folk practice, which treats the buried bottle as drawing in and trapping harm aimed at its owner [s:wp-witch-bottle]
against: curse — said by the writers of Greek and Roman defixiones, who buried the lead to hand the target to the gods below [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: demons — said by the users of Mesopotamian incantation bowls, buried face down under thresholds and in the corners of houses [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: spirits — said by Korean mudang, whose gear is burned or buried at death to cut their deities off from the family [s:wp-korean-shamanism]
what: Putting a charm in the ground and leaving it. Under a hearth, at the far corner of a property, in the threshold, in a well, in a wall. Some of these objects are working while buried and stop if disturbed; others are being got rid of. Archaeologists call the hidden caches spiritual middens, and they are the reason a great deal of this material survives at all.
story: The English witch bottle is the clearest case of burial as the working position. Joseph Glanvill's Saducismus Triumphatus of 1681 records an old man's advice to a Suffolk household: put the wife's urine in a bottle with pins, needles and nails, cork it and set it by the fire — and when the cork blew out and that failed, bury it in the earth instead, which is what the account says worked. Folk practice holds the bottle to be active as long as it stays hidden and unbroken, and people went to trouble to hide them: bottles under fireplaces have turned up only after the rest of the building had gone.

The finds carry dates and names. Marshall Becker identified the first American witch bottle in an archaeological context, the Essington bottle, recovered on Great Tinicum Island in Delaware County, Pennsylvania. A mid-nineteenth to early twentieth-century enslaved or tenant site in Dorchester County, Maryland, produced a buried bottle whose cork bristled with straight pins. In 2016 a bottle full of nails came out of the hearth of a Civil War site in Virginia. A glass bottle found buried in a threshold in Trelissick, Cornwall, was analysed at Loughborough University and found to hold urine, a little alcohol and one human hair, with brass pins dating from the late 1840s and an ostracod. In 2020 a sixteenth-century jug turned up during the renovation of the De Zwarte Ruiter pub in Turnhout, Belgium.

The Greek and Roman world buried to deliver. Curse tablets were rolled, folded or pierced with nails and then put beneath the ground — buried in graves or tombs, thrown into wells or pools, put in underground sanctuaries or nailed to temple walls — and the ones in graves were often addressed through the dead person whose grave it was, usually somebody who had died young or violently. Mesopotamian incantation bowls were buried face down under the threshold, in courtyards, in the corners of the homes of the recently dead and in cemeteries. In Egypt, execration texts naming enemies were written on clay figurines or pottery, then smashed and buried beneath a building under construction, so that the names were symbolically smothered, or buried in a cemetery.

Burial is also how some traditions end a charm. In Ireland a discarded Brigid's cross was burned or buried, and burial was preferred because of Brigid's associations with agriculture. In Korea, a mudang who does not want a relative to inherit the vocation may have their ritual gear burned or buried at their death, which severs the connection between their personal deities and the surviving family. A Bulgarian martenitsa can be put under a stone rather than tied to a tree, and whichever creature is closest to it the next day reads the year.

*Inference —* burial is why the record is shaped the way it is. A charm hidden under a hearth was meant to be permanent and to be unseen, so it survives and it is undocumented; the finder is usually a builder, and the date usually comes from the bottle rather than from anyone's account of putting it there.
how: Dig at the place the tradition specifies — hearth, threshold, far corner, grave, well, under a wall going up — put the object in, close the ground, and say nothing. In the counter-magic cases the object stays there and stays whole; in the disposal cases it does not matter what happens to it afterwards.
today: Still done, and mostly found by accident. Witch bottles continue to be buried at the corner of a property or under a hearth in present folk practice, and fewer than a dozen probable examples have been identified in the United States to date. Objects turn up in renovations across England, Belgium and the American northeast, which is why the reporting is patchy and the dating comes from the glass.
kin: witch-bottle — the charm whose working position is underground — active while hidden and unbroken
kin: curse-tablet — lead folded and put in a grave or a well, so that the dead carry the message
kin: incantation-bowl — buried face down under the threshold, with the writing spiralling inward
kin: concealed-shoe — the other thing found in the fabric of a house, and the commonest of them all
kin: martenitsa — put under a stone at the end of its month, to be read by whatever creature is nearest it
kin: foundation-deposit — burial done deliberately at the start of a building rather than into an existing one
kin: grave-deposit — the same verb pointed at a person rather than a place
kin: burning-retirement — the other end for a charm, and the one Irish practice weighs against burial
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition that filled English hearths and thresholds with this material
kin: the-charm-in-the-wall — the long read that follows what builders find when they take a house apart
sources: s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-concealed-shoes s:wp-korean-shamanism s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-martenitsa s:wp-magic-supernatural
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Buying one in a market (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/buying-in-a-market/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/buying-in-a-market.json
id: buying-in-a-market
aliases: acquiring a charm · the counter · the stall
said: the commonest way anybody in this atlas gets a charm
when: 1382 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TR EG MA TH JP MX BO PE PH ET GB IT
object: form=plaque materials=terracotta,silver,glass,paper,seed,herb,cloth worn=shop,pocket,neck
against: theft — said by the Grand Bazaar's own arrangements: gates closed at night, guards paid by the merchants' guilds, and an imperial edict required to enter after hours — the concentration of the trade in one place was itself a security measure [s:wp-grand-bazaar-istanbul]
against: bad-luck — said by buyers at Alasitas in La Paz, where purchasing a miniature and giving it away is the claim on the full-sized thing within the year [s:wp-alasitas]
against: poverty — said by the Japanese shrine counter, which issues shōbai-hanjō charms for success in business and treats the money paid as a donation rather than a price [s:wp-omamori]
what: Money changes hands and an object becomes yours. It is the ordinary route to a charm almost everywhere — a tray in a lane, a counter inside a temple gate, an aisle at the back of a municipal market, a stall in a churchyard — and it is the step this atlas's records most often have a price, a date and an address for, because a transaction leaves paperwork that a rite does not.
story: Markets that sell charms are old institutions with rules, and the rules are usually about control rather than about faith. Under the Mamluks, Cairo's souq areas were progressively replaced by fixed stone structures with built-in shops, partly because the authorities wanted more control: fixed structures could be counted, taxed and regulated more easily than makeshift stalls that could come and go. Khan al-Khalili itself was built at the heart of the city during the first reign of Sultan Barquq (1382–1389) by his Master of the Stables, Jaharkas al-Khalili, and the name spread from the one building to the whole district.

Istanbul's Grand Bazaar shows the same logic taken further. By the early 17th century it had 67 streets each named for the sellers of a particular good, 18 gates opened each morning and closed in the evening, and 3,000 shops plus 300 in the surrounding hans. Gates were closed at night and the bazaar was patrolled by guards paid by the merchants' guilds; entering after hours required an imperial edict. A guild formed once there were enough traders of one good, at which point the number of traders and shops was frozen and entry came only by co-optation — as the son of a deceased member, or by paying a suitable sum to a member who wanted to retire. The guild chief, the Kethüda, was paid by the guild but appointed by the Kadı of Istanbul, and set prices and taxes. The guilds were abolished in 1913.

The regulating impulse is not only medieval. Mexico City's Mercado de Sonora was established by the city government on 23 September 1957, with other public markets, to help organise and regulate retail commerce; the aisles of medicinal herbs and of magical and occult goods sit at the back of a single metal nave, and the account notes the two categories are not kept separate. Sensō-ji in Tokyo granted the shops that became the Nakamise permission to trade on its main approach in 1685, in exchange for their paying local residents to sweep the grounds.

What the buyer is actually buying differs by tradition, and the differences are sharp. At Tha Phrachan in Bangkok the buyer arrives with a loupe, because a phra khrueang's value turns on appearance, scarcity, maker, age and reputation, and because forgeries are common enough that expert authentication is a standing part of the transaction. Nobody there is assessing beauty; they are assessing which temple pressed it and which monk chanted over it. At a Japanese shrine counter the transaction is framed the other way round: omamori and ofuda are technically not bought but received — sazukaru, ukeru — and the money is treated as a donation. At Alasitas in La Paz, buying is the rite itself: the fair's name is Aymara for 'buy from me', and you purchase a miniature to give to somebody else so that the full-size version follows within the year.

Prices and seasons are on the record where sources publish them. The Jatukham Rammathep amulet's market reached twenty billion baht in 2007 before the bubble burst late that year. The Mercado de las Brujas on Calle Linares in La Paz puts roughly 60 per cent of its year's sales in October, when Pachamama offerings cluster. Edward Tabor gives US$3 to US$10 for an azabache in a botánica and US$9 to US$55 online, at the time he wrote in 2023.

The practice also built this atlas's evidence base, and that deserves saying. Edward Lovett's method was buying and swapping on London streets rather than excavating; what he assembled is now spread across the Pitt Rivers Museum, the Cuming Museum, the Wellcome collection and two museums of childhood. Frederick Elworthy bought in Spain and Italy while writing. Siegfried Seligmann gathered more than 1,500 amulets for his survey. *Inference —* the shape of what museums hold follows the shape of what was for sale to a European collector with money, which is a fact about markets before it is a fact about charms.

And the argument: whether a charm sold to a stranger is the same object as one made for a neighbour. It has named participants in several traditions at once. Japanese priests have complained about the quality of factory omamori ordered when demand outruns a shrine's own production. Manufacturers in China mass-produce hei matau lookalikes in bone-and-resin paste for the New Zealand visitor market and have been criticised for appropriating Māori designs. Thai authentication culture exists because the trade's own participants do not trust the trade. This atlas reports every side of that and joins none of it, and describes a factory charm in the same terms it describes a hand-cut one.
how: Approach, look, ask, pay, and in several traditions have something done on the spot: a red cord tied on, a certificate handed over, a blessing said, a stamp applied. In Thailand the loupe and the authenticator's fee come between looking and paying. In Japan the wording of the exchange is deliberately not commercial. In La Paz the object is bought to be given away rather than kept. In Manila the stall is in a churchyard and the book of incantations is thrown in with the amulet.
today: Live everywhere, and increasingly not physical. The same objects are sold online, by the tray and by the individual piece, with the authentication problem moved rather than solved; in 2021 a Thai project issued monk-blessed amulets as NFTs on a blockchain, which is a purchase with the provenance problem written into the transaction. The old addresses are still trading: Tha Phrachan, the Grand Bazaar, Khan el-Khalili, the Mercado de Sonora, the Nakamise, Calle Linares.
kin: tha-phrachan — the practice at its most exacting — loupe, certificate, forgery, and a monk's name as the thing being priced
kin: grand-bazaar — the practice under a roof, with 18 gates locked at night and a guild deciding who may sell
kin: khan-el-khalili — where this record's earliest date comes from: a quarter of stone shops built partly so the trade could be counted and taxed
kin: mercado-de-sonora — the practice inside a building the city put up in 1957 to regulate it
kin: senso-ji — the approach road licensed by the temple in 1685, with sweeping the grounds as the rent
kin: mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz — the practice with a published season — roughly 60 per cent of the year's trade in October
kin: phra-khrueang — the object with the largest figure attached to this practice anywhere in the atlas: twenty billion baht in a single year
kin: ekeko — the case where buying is not the preliminary to the rite but the rite
kin: omamori — the counter that refuses the verb — received, not bought, and the money a donation
kin: inheriting — the practice this one is defined against, and the one whose rules a purchase keeps testing
kin: renewing-yearly — the other half of the cycle: an annual expiry is also an annual sale
kin: edward-lovett — the collector whose whole method was this — buying and swapping in the street while other men read about the past
kin: the-fake-market — the long read that starts at this counter, because this is where trust is priced
sources: s:wp-grand-bazaar-istanbul s:wp-khan-el-khalili s:wp-mercado-de-sonora s:wp-sens-ji s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-alasitas s:wp-the-witches-market s:wp-omamori s:wp-ofuda s:wp-edward-lovett s:wp-frederick-thomas-elworthy s:web-siegfried-seligmann-dewiki s:web-hektoen-azabache s:wp-hei-matau s:web-coconuts-crypto-amulets s:wp-quiapo-church s:wp-agimat

## Consecration (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/consecration/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/consecration.json
id: consecration
aliases: charging · empowerment · blessing an object · phutthaphisek · abhiseka · batèms
said: the step that turns an object into a charm
when: 1200 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TH JP IN LK CN CD BJ HT IT VA NG
object: form=plaque materials=terracotta,paper,copper,wood worn=neck,wall,shop
against: bad-luck — said by Thai amulet practice, as summarised in the cited account [s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet]
against: spirits — said by Kongo banganga, as described by scholars of minkisi [s:wp-nkisi]
against: illness — said by Taoist zhuyou practice, used in China alongside medicine, meditation, acupuncture and massage [s:wp-fulu]
RESTRICTED: The words said over an object are restricted in several of these traditions, and this atlas does not print them. Tibetan Buddhism gates the practices themselves: without having gone through initiation, one is generally not allowed to practise the higher tantras. Taoist talismanic craft is transmitted in secret from priest to disciple. Where a rite is closed, this record describes its structure and its purpose and stops there.
what: The step that makes a made thing a charm. A clay tablet pressed in a temple yard is clay until somebody chants over it; a printed slip is paper until a shrine stamps and empowers it. Traditions that agree on almost nothing agree on this: the object arrives inert and a qualified person, in a set rite, puts something into it. Who counts as qualified is the part each tradition guards.
story: Thailand states the labour plainly. Monks chant and bless amulets in a process that can take from a week to several years, and an amulet's later value turns on which temple pressed it and which monk consecrated it. Takrut — rolled metal or palm-leaf scrolls — were being made by monks in Thailand by 1200–1300 CE, on a practice the sources say predates Buddhism's arrival there.

Hinduism puts the requirement as a negative. Occult yantras are consecrated and energised by a priest using mantras tied to the specific deity, and practitioners hold that a yantra not energised with a mantra is lifeless. Japan says the same thing about paper: an ofuda carries the kami's essence, in the words of the practice, by virtue of its consecration, and omamori are made sacred through ritual and said to contain busshin — spiritual offshoots — in a Shinto frame, or kesshin, manifestations, in a Buddhist one.

In Kongo practice the substances go in and the figure is then woken. The nails driven into an nkisi nkondi are not ornament: each nail or metal piece stands for a vow or an agreement, and scholars of the tradition describe the driving as a requirement of awakening the spirit. In Haitian Vodou a batèm, a baptism, makes an object a vessel for the lwa, and an object consecrated for ritual use is held to contain nanm, a spiritual essence; the ason rattle cannot be used before it. The Catholic Church files the same move under law: the Catechism lists three kinds of sacramental — blessings, consecrations and dedications, and exorcisms.

*Inference —* set those side by side and the shared structure is a transfer with a gatekeeper. The rite differs, the gate does not. That is also why consecration is the point where this atlas stops writing.
how: Structure only, which is all that is public in several of these traditions: an object is made; a person the tradition recognises — monk, priest, nganga, oungan, sofer's client, shrine office — performs a set rite over it, often with words fixed by the lineage; the object is then handled differently from how it was handled an hour earlier. In Thailand mass consecrations are held in temple halls with many monks chanting over trays of amulets for hours or days. In Japan the object then bears a shrine's seal. In Tibetan Buddhism the equivalent transfer runs the other way, into a person: an initiation or empowerment (Sanskrit abhiseka, Tibetan wangkur) consecrates a practitioner into a particular tantric practice.
today: Live everywhere, and contested at the edges. Japanese priests have complained about the quality of factory-made omamori that shrines order when demand outruns their own production, and shops sell generic omamori carrying licensed characters that no shrine issued. Among Yoruba egúngún societies, some people make masks for sale on the international art market without consecrating or using them, and other members of the society disapprove of the practice. Both arguments are about the same thing: whether an unconsecrated copy is the object at all.
kin: phra-khrueang — the object this step is priced by — which temple pressed it and which monk chanted over it is most of its value
kin: takrut — the earliest dated thing in this record: monks in Thailand rolling and empowering metal scrolls by 1200–1300 CE
kin: ofuda — paper that carries a kami's essence, in the practice's own words, by virtue of this step
kin: omamori — the packet made sacred through ritual, then never opened by the person carrying it
kin: yantra-plate — the diagram a priest energises with a mantra; practitioners hold that one left un-energised is lifeless
kin: nkisi — the figure woken rather than blessed — each nail a vow driven into it
kin: agnus-dei — the Catholic wax disc whose whole standing comes from who blessed it
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that wrote this step into canon law: blessings, consecrations and dedications, exorcisms
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition where the consecrating monk's name is the object's provenance
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the same transfer done over the counter, to a stranger, for a donation
kin: inscribing — the step before this one — the writing that has to be right before anyone chants over it
kin: tattooing — consecration with no object at all: the words go over skin, and the rules stay on the person
sources: s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-takrut s:wp-yantra s:wp-ofuda s:wp-omamori s:wp-nkisi s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-sacramental s:wp-tibetan-buddhism s:wp-fulu s:wp-west-african-vod-n

## Counting beads (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/counting-beads/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/counting-beads.json
id: counting-beads
aliases: prayer beads · mala · misbaha · rosary · komboskini · japamala
said: four traditions, four counts, four reasons — the English phrase 'prayer beads' merges them and this record does not
when: 201 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IN NP CN TH SA TR EG IT GR RU RS ES IR
object: form=rosary materials=seed,wood,bone,glass,iron,thread,amber,coral,silver worn=wrist,neck,pocket,hair
against: illness — said by wearers of rudraksha, which the cited account says are worn by believers for protection and for chanting mantras such as Om Namah Shivaya [s:wp-rudraksha]
against: bad-luck — said by the Sikh simranee, 27 beads often of iron, worn on the wrist [s:web-prayer-beads]
what: A string of a fixed number of beads or knots, run through the fingers so that the hand keeps count while the mouth says something. The object is a counter before it is an ornament, and the number is not decoration: each tradition publishes its own count for its own reason, and a string with the wrong number is the wrong instrument.
story: Take them one at a time, because merging them is the mistake this record exists to avoid.

The Catholic rosary: 59 beads, in the form attributed to Saint Dominic — an attribution some scholars doubt. Materials published include glass, amethyst, rose quartz, crystal, onyx and pearl. The Church's own filing is split: it treats the rosary as a popular devotion rather than as a sacramental, and the beads themselves as a devotional article.

The Eastern Orthodox prayer rope: 33, 50 or 100 knots, not beads — knotted wool, though bead versions exist. It is called chotki in Russian, komboskini in Greek and brojanica in Serbian and Macedonian, and its origin is placed with the Desert Fathers in the third to fifth centuries. This is the only member of the family in which the counting unit is a knot the user can tie.

The Muslim misbaha: 99 beads with separators, or 33 cycled three times — the count follows the ninety-nine names of God. The names in Arabic are misbaha, subha and tasbih, and the practice is traced back in the tradition to Abu Hurayra.

The Hindu japamala: 108 beads, most commonly of rudraksha seeds or tulasi stems. The rudraksha account gives the arithmetic precisely: most garlands hold 108 plus one, because 108 is held sacred and a suitable number of repetitions for a short mantra, and the extra bead — the meru, bindu or guru bead — marks where a cycle begins and ends. Shorter strings run 27+1 or 54+1 on the same principle. Om Namah Shivaya is a mantra often counted on them, within Shaivism, because Shiva is described as wearing rudraksha garlands.

The Buddhist mala: also 108, adopted from the Hindu practice, with 27 in Pure Land Buddhism. Published materials include rudraksha, tulsi wood, bone, Bodhi seeds, lotus and sandalwood.

Two more that the English phrase also swallows. Sikh: 27 beads, often of iron, worn on the wrist, also called a simranee. Bahá'í: 95 beads, or 19 with five counters, for a prayer recited 95 times daily.

*Inference —* the counts are not interchangeable and neither are the reasons. 99 follows a list of divine names. 108 follows a number held sacred, with one extra bead added for a purely mechanical purpose — knowing where you are. 33, 50 and 100 are round numbers on a rope. 59 is the structure of a specific sequence of prayers. Only one of those is arithmetic about God; the rest are arithmetic about repetition, and the guru bead is the clearest evidence that at least part of this object is an engineering solution to losing your place.

Where the string meets the atlas's other records is in the object doubling as a charm. Rudraksha are worn for protection as well as counted — the same seeds, on the same cord, doing two jobs. A prayer rope is worn on the wrist. A misbaha sits in a pocket. The count is what makes it an instrument; being on the body is what makes it an amulet, and most carriers are not obliged to choose.
how: One bead or knot per repetition, moved by the thumb, going round until the marker comes back under the hand. On a Hindu or Buddhist mala the meru or guru bead marks the start and end of a cycle of 108. On a misbaha the separators divide 99 into three runs of 33. A prayer rope's knots are tied by the user's own tradition rather than strung. Walking versions exist: at the Barkhor in Lhasa the circuit is walked clockwise, one round of the ring to one round of the string.
today: Live in every tradition listed, and sold far outside them. The mala in particular has a large secular retail market attached to yoga and wellness, in which the count is often kept and the mantra is not — an argument this atlas reports rather than settles, and which runs among practitioners rather than between practitioners and outsiders. Rudraksha remain commercially sourced from India, Indonesia and Nepal for jewellery and malas, and are valued similarly to semi-precious stones.
kin: rudraksha — the string this record's arithmetic is clearest on — 108 plus one, the extra bead there to mark where a cycle begins and ends
kin: knotting — the same cord with knots instead of beads: an Orthodox prayer rope carries 33, 50 or 100 of them
kin: worry-stone — the single-bead version — repetition in the hand with the count taken out
kin: cowrie-strand — the other fixed-number string in this atlas, where handling a set number becomes a throw and a reading rather than a tally
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition that turns a string into an instrument: 108 and one
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that files the rosary as a popular devotion and the beads as a devotional article — two different categories for one object
kin: islamic-talismanic — the neighbouring tradition whose count follows a list rather than a number: 99 names, 99 beads, or 33 taken three times
kin: barkhor-lhasa — the circuit walked with one of these, one round of the ring to one round of the string
kin: divine-name — what the Muslim string is counting: the ninety-nine names, one bead each, or thirty-three taken three times
sources: s:web-prayer-beads s:wp-rudraksha s:wp-sacramental s:wp-devotional-medal s:wp-barkhor s:wp-tibetan-buddhism s:wp-kavacha
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-17

## Feeding the charm (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/feeding-the-charm/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/feeding-the-charm.json
id: feeding-the-charm
aliases: dressing a mojo · manje lwa · offerings to an object
said: giving the thing something, so it keeps working
when: 1501 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US CD AO HT BO PE JP ID MN
object: form=figurine materials=wood,iron,cloth,terracotta,herb,earth worn=shop,wall,hearth,pocket
against: witchcraft — said by Kongo banganga, whose nkondi are loaded with substances and gunpowder aimed at the ndoki [s:wp-nkisi]
against: poverty — said by Bolivian owners of Ekeko figures, who clip banknotes to them and light a cigarette once a year [s:wp-ekeko]
against: bad-luck — said by hoodoo practitioners, who feed a mojo to keep it working [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: house — said by Japanese households making daily offerings of rice, salt, water and sake at the kamidana [s:wp-ofuda]
what: Giving the object something to consume. Liquor poured on a cloth bag, a lit cigarette in a plaster figure's mouth, rice and salt and water set out in front of a paper talisman, a nail driven into a carved figure, banknotes clipped to a statue. The traditions that do this describe the charm as alive, and feeding as what keeps it working rather than as thanks for work done.
story: Hoodoo states it outright. A mojo bag is first fixed — filled and, in the cited account's words, awakened to life, by smoking it over incense and candles, or breathing on it, with prayers said over it. Once prepared it is dressed or fed with a liquid: alcohol, perfume, water or bodily fluids. The reason given for feeding is that the bag is alive with spirit, and feeding keeps it working.

In Kongo practice the substances go in at the start and the object is kept in service by use. The bilongo or milongo packed into an nkisi are usually translated as medicine, though they are not applied to or swallowed by the sick; scholars of the tradition suggest therapeutic substances is closer, and note the ingredients are often chosen for metaphor — bird claws to catch a wrongdoer. In the aggressive subclass, nkondi, each nail or metal piece driven in stands for a vow, a signed agreement or an effort to abolish an evil, so the object accumulates its history in iron.

Haitian Vodou feeds the spirits rather than the object, and does it constantly. Offering rites are termed manje lwa, feeding the lwa, and offering food and drink is the most common ritual in the religion, done communally and at home; Danbala takes white foods, especially eggs, Legba's offerings are grilled on a fire, the Ogu and Nago lwa prefer raw rum or clairin, and Ayizan avoids alcohol.

The Andes feeds on a timetable. Ekeko figures are loaded with miniature goods, and banknotes are clipped to them as offerings; modern statues have a hole in the mouth for a cigarette, and the recent custom is that Ekeko smokes one lit cigarette a year to secure a year of prosperity. Grain is offered for good harvests. Japan feeds the household altar: the Association of Shinto Shrines recommends daily worship before the shinsatsu, with offerings of rice, salt, water or sake, and more food on special occasions. In Java, warriors made offerings to their kris at a shrine, because specific rites had to be completed to avoid calling down bad fates.

*Inference —* feeding is the clearest test of whether a tradition treats a charm as an object or as a resident. Nobody feeds a lucky coin. The traditions here that feed also say, in their own words, that something lives in the thing — and those are the same traditions whose objects a museum has the hardest time labelling, because a fed figure that stops being fed is, by its own tradition's account, not the same object on the shelf.
how: Pour, light, set down, or drive in. A liquid is poured or rubbed on a cloth bag. A cigarette is lit in a figure's mouth. Food and drink are set in front of an altar or a figure and left. A nail is hammered into a carved body to seal an agreement. Each has its own schedule, from daily to once a year.
today: Live. Conjure workers still fix and dress mojo bags commercially. Ekeko figures are sold loaded at the Alasitas fair in La Paz every January and smoke through the year in Bolivian houses. Japanese households keep kamidana and make the daily offerings the Association of Shinto Shrines recommends. Minkisi in European and American museums are not fed, and Kongo commentators and curators disagree about what that makes them.
kin: nkisi — the object this practice is clearest in — loaded, woken, and nailed once per agreement
kin: gris-gris — fed with alcohol, perfume or water because, in the tradition's words, it is alive
kin: ekeko — the figure that smokes one cigarette a year and wears banknotes the rest of it
kin: ofuda — the paper on the household altar in front of which rice, salt, water and sake are set out daily
kin: keris-pusaka — the blade warriors made offerings to at a shrine, and still wash once a year
kin: bakongo-nkisi-craft — the tradition that keeps the ledger of vows in nails
kin: andean-illa-practice — the tradition where feeding and buying happen on the same January morning
kin: consecration — the step that wakes the thing; feeding is what keeps it awake
kin: renewing-yearly — the calendar version of the same upkeep, done to the object instead of with food
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this practice complicates: a figure that is no longer fed is, in its own tradition's account, not the object on the shelf
sources: s:wp-nkisi s:wp-nkondi s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-ekeko s:wp-ofuda s:wp-kris

## Folding (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/folding/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/folding.json
id: folding
aliases: rolling a charm · kenharai · sealing a packet
said: closing the writing so nobody reads it again
when: 600 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL PS JP TH IT GB GR IN PK SN
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,parchment,silver,copper,lead,palm-leaf,cloth worn=neck,waist,pocket,wall,grave
against: bad-luck — said by carriers of omamori, who keep the packet shut so the protection is not lost [s:wp-omamori]
against: curse — said by the Greek and Roman writers of defixiones, who folded the lead before burying it [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: house — said by Japanese households, who keep folded shrine talismans on a kamidana facing east, south or southeast [s:wp-ofuda]
RESTRICTED: What is inside a sealed packet is, in several of these traditions, not the carrier's information and not this project's. Omamori are customarily not opened; Taoist talismanic craft is transmitted in secret. This record describes the fold and what it is for, and does not describe the contents of packets a tradition keeps shut.
what: The step after the writing: the sheet is rolled into a tube, folded into a packet, or creased into a shape, and then cased, sewn or sealed. From that point the text is inside and nobody reads it. A takrut is a rolled scroll in a tube; a mezuzah's parchment is rolled and dropped into its case; a Japanese kenharai is a sliver of wood inside a fold of paper cut so the packet resembles a sword blade.
story: Two silver scrolls from a burial chamber at Ketef Hinnom, near Jerusalem, were found rolled in 1979 and took three years to unroll without disintegrating. They carry the Priestly Blessing and date to around 600 BCE. Whoever wore them never read them either: the text went in, the metal closed, and it stayed closed for twenty-six centuries.

Japan folded the same logic into a distribution system. Wandering preachers attached to the shrines of Ise, the oshi, handed out purification wands called Oharai Taima to households across the country as proof that prayers had been said on their behalf. The wands travelled either in folded paper packets — kenharai, named because the packet's shape resembles a sword blade, ken — or in boxes, oharaibako. Distribution began in the Muromachi period and peaked in the Edo: a document of 1777 records that between eighty-nine and ninety per cent of households in the country owned an Ise talisman. Kenharai are still given out at Ise.

The Greco-Roman world folded to bind. Lead curse tablets were rolled, folded or pierced with nails before they went into the ground, and some love spells have been found folded around a piece of the target's hair, which the tablets' own texts treat as carrying that person's ousia, their central essence.

The seal creates a rule of its own. Omamori are customarily not opened, so that the protection is not lost — the carrier holds a brocade bag whose contents are the shrine's business, not theirs. *Inference —* that single custom is the clearest statement in this atlas of what a fold is for. Once the packet is closed, the object stops being a text a person can check and becomes a thing a person has to trust. Scribal traditions and sealed-packet traditions split exactly here: a mezuzah is opened and inspected by a scribe twice in seven years, and an omamori is never opened at all.
how: Roll, or fold, then contain. Metal foil rolls around a former and slides into a tube or a case. Parchment rolls and goes into a mezuzah case or a tefillin box. Paper folds into a packet that is itself the shape of something — a blade, in the Ise case. Lead folds over on itself, sometimes around hair or a scrap of clothing, and can then be nailed through. Cloth versions are folded and sewn shut rather than cased, which crosses into sewing-in.
today: Live and industrial. Shrines and temples across Japan issue folded and cased talismans year-round, with the Association of Shinto Shrines distributing Jingū Taima to affiliated shrines nationally. Thai takrut are still rolled and cased and worn at the neck or the waist. Where a sealed charm is sold to somebody outside the tradition, the seal is also what makes it unverifiable, which is the trade's oldest complaint about itself.
kin: takrut — the rolled tube this practice is named for in Thailand — metal or palm leaf, cased, strung
kin: ofuda — the folded paper packet cut to the shape of a sword blade and handed out by the shrines of Ise
kin: omamori — the sealed brocade bag nobody opens, which is this practice's strictest rule
kin: mezuzah — parchment rolled into a case at the door — and unrolled again by a scribe twice in seven years
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest rolled charm this atlas dates, found still rolled in a Jerusalem burial chamber
kin: curse-tablet — lead folded over hair, then nailed — the same gesture used to bind rather than to guard
kin: taweez — the folded paper charm of Islamic practice, cased in metal and worn at the neck or the arm
kin: paper — the material that made folding cheap, repeatable and issuable by the ten thousand
kin: inscribing — the step this one closes over
kin: sewing-in — the cloth branch of the same move: fold, then stitch shut instead of casing
sources: s:wp-ofuda s:wp-omamori s:wp-ketef-hinnom s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-takrut s:wp-tefillin s:wp-fulu

## Foundation deposit (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/foundation-deposit/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/foundation-deposit.json
id: foundation-deposit
aliases: foundation peg · foundation figure · building deposit · spiritual midden
said: what goes under a building before it goes up
when: 3000 BCE – 1964 CE
countries: EG IQ LB IR GB US DE AU CA
object: form=figurine materials=copper,terracotta,leather,glass,faience,silver worn=foundation,hearth,roof,wall
against: house — said by Egyptian builders, whose deposits were meant to keep the building from falling into ruin [s:web-foundation-deposit]
against: demons — said by the users of incantation bowls buried under thresholds and in house corners [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: witchcraft — said by Brian Hoggard, reading the find spots of concealed shoes as protection against demons, ghosts and witches [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
against: infertility — said by one of the competing explanations for concealed shoes, alongside the protective one; Ralph Merrifield records Lancashire women trying on the shoes of a woman who had just given birth [s:wp-concealed-shoes]
what: Objects buried under a building, at the start of it, by people who did not expect anyone to see them again. Egyptian deposits are mudbrick-lined pits cut at set points beneath a temple or a tomb; Mesopotamian ones are cast copper-alloy pegs and figures driven into the ground at the corners of a temple; European ones are shoes, bottles and written charms pushed into hearths, thresholds and roof voids of houses already standing. This is the practice that fills museum drawers, because a deposit nobody was meant to find is a deposit nobody disturbed.
story: Egypt formalised it. Foundation deposits there took the form of ritual mudbrick-lined pits or holes dug at specific points under temples or tombs, filled with ceremonial objects — usually amulets, scarabs, food or ritual miniature tools — and intended to stop the building falling into ruin. Deposits are documented at Hatshepsut's tomb, KV20. A fenestrated silver axehead of the Middle Bronze Age from near Byblos belongs to the same family of buried building offerings.

Mesopotamia buried figures with names on them. Foundation figures were used in temple construction from the Early Dynastic period, marking the boundary of sacred ground, buried deliberately and never meant to be looked at. Early pegs and wall-mounted examples are limestone or clay; the buried figures are typically cast copper alloy, running from plain inscribed cones to fully modelled human forms. A peg of Ur-Namma, c. 2112–2094 BCE, carries his bust and an inscription to Inanna, lady of Eanna, recording that he built her temple. Figurines of Shulgi were found under the Temple of Nimintabba at Ur, inscribed for Nimintabba, his lady. Deposits have been recorded at Ur, Uruk and Nippur, and the Temple of Ningirsu at Girsu produced pegs dated to about 2130 BCE. The practice ran from around the third millennium BCE to at least the reign of Rim-Suen of Larsa, 1822–1763 BCE.

Curses went under buildings too. In Egypt, execration texts naming enemies were written on clay figurines or pottery, then smashed and buried beneath a building under construction so that the names were symbolically smothered. In Mesopotamia, incantation bowls were buried face down under thresholds and in the corners of houses, including the houses of the recently dead; in John Charles Arnold's account, demons would follow the inscribed charms spiralling inward from the rim and be caught in the centre.

Northern Europe put shoes in the walls. Concealed shoes have been found in buildings across European countries and in North America and Australia since at least the early modern period, in chimneys, under floors, above ceilings, around doors and windows and in roofs. Northampton Museum keeps a Concealed Shoe Index, which held more than 1,100 reports by 1998 and 1,900 by 2012, almost half of them from the nineteenth century. June Swann's 1996 analysis of the index found the commonest hiding place to be the chimney, fireplace or hearth, at 26.2 per cent, then under the floor or above the ceiling at 22.9 per cent, with almost as many in the roof. Only thirteen of the shoes in her analysis were in actual foundations — she raised, cautiously, a possible link to the Carthaginian practice of putting infants in foundations, and suggested the shoe stood in for a person. Almost 98 per cent of the shoes had been worn, many repaired, and about half belonged to children. The earliest reported is from behind the choir stalls of Winchester Cathedral, installed in 1308. Archaeologist Brian Hoggard reads the find spots as evidence that at least some were hidden as charms against demons, ghosts and witches; others may have been fertility charms or offerings to a household spirit, a reading M. Chris Manning connects to the household helper found from Ireland to western Russia.

*Inference —* the excavation record is skewed in this practice's favour twice over. A foundation deposit was buried in a place that had to stay undisturbed for the building to stand, and it was made of metal, stone, fired clay or leather, so it survives. The reed, dough and cloth charms that stood in the same houses did not.
how: Before the walls go up: dig pits at set points, line them, fill them, close them. Or, into a building already standing: push the object into a chimney flue, under floorboards, above a ceiling, into the void around a door frame, and plaster over. Nothing marks the spot in either case.
today: Largely finished, with late exceptions. The custom of concealing shoes in buildings had more or less died out by some time in the twentieth century, with only about fifty recorded instances after 1900 — among them the shoe manufacturer Norvic, which put a pair of its women's high-leg boots into the foundations of a new factory in 1964, and an estate worker's shoe at Knebworth House in 1991, replacing a court shoe found behind panelling. Almost everything else in this record reaches us through excavation.
kin: concealed-shoe — the commonest thing found in the fabric of a European house, and the reason Northampton keeps an index of them
kin: witch-bottle — buried under the hearth of a standing house rather than under a new one, and working while it stays there
kin: incantation-bowl — buried face down under the threshold, which is the deposit as trap
kin: scarab — among the objects Egyptian deposits were filled with, alongside amulets, food and miniature tools
kin: curse-tablet — the hostile version: execration texts smashed and buried under a building going up
kin: mesopotamian-apotropaic — the tradition whose kings signed their foundation pegs
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that filled lined pits under temples with the same amulets it buried with people
kin: burying — the same verb, without a building over it
kin: grave-deposit — the other great undisturbed context, and the other reason the drawers are full
kin: the-charm-in-the-wall — the long read about what comes out of houses during renovation
kin: british-museum-room-1 — where deposits meant never to be seen are now on shelves
sources: s:web-foundation-deposit s:web-foundation-figure s:wp-concealed-shoes s:wp-witch-bottle s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-british-museum
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Grave deposit (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/grave-deposit/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/grave-deposit.json
id: grave-deposit
aliases: burial goods · amulets in the wrappings · grave goods
said: what goes into the ground with the person
when: 2686 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG IL PS CN IT GR NZ FJ US SD
object: form=pendant materials=faience,carnelian,gold,jade,silver,tooth,lead worn=grave,chest,neck
against: the-dead — said by Egyptian funerary religion, in which the heart scarab binds the heart to silence at the weighing or speaks in its place [s:wp-heart-scarab]
against: illness — said by Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead, on the red jasper tyet placed at a mummy's neck [s:wp-tyet]
against: spirits — said by Fijian practice, in which men were buried with their tabua and war clubs to help them in the afterlife [s:wp-tabua]
against: curse — said by Greek and Roman clients whose tablets went into graves, addressed through the person buried there [s:wp-curse-tablet]
what: Amulets put into a burial — on the body, in the wrappings, in the chest cavity, in the hand, around the coffin. This is where most of the ancient charms in the world's museums come from, which means the drawers are a record of what people were buried in rather than of what they wore to work.
story: Egypt made the grave the standard destination. Amulets of gold, faience and carnelian appear in Old Kingdom burials in various shapes to protect different parts of the body, and the mummification sequence put them into the linen as it went on: the body was wrapped in strips with amulets while a priest recited prayers and burned incense. By the Late period a burial could carry heart scarabs, djed columns in gold and faience, Eye of Horus amulets, figures of deities and magical bricks set at the four compass points.

Particular amulets carry their own placement rules. A heart scarab went directly over the heart and was wrapped into the bandages; in a Third Intermediate Period variant, smaller and uninscribed, it went inside the chest cavity alongside the real heart. The amulet's job, in the Egyptian account, was to keep the heart silent at the weighing in the Duat, so that it did not testify against its owner, or to stand in for it. The first known depictions are Sixteenth or Seventeenth Dynasty, around 1690 BCE. Tyet amulets — the knot of Isis — began going into burials in the early New Kingdom, from Amenhotep III, and from then until the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one in the wrappings, usually on the upper torso; Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for one in red jasper at the neck.

Jerusalem produced the oldest surviving biblical text this way. In 1979, two tiny silver scrolls inscribed with portions of the Priestly Blessing and apparently once used as amulets were found in one of the Iron Age Judahite burial chambers at Ketef Hinnom, a site whose 1975 salvage excavation Gabriel Barkay reported. They date to around 600 BCE and took three years to unroll. They are in the Israel Museum.

Han China buried its dead in stone. Jade burial suits were made of plaques joined through drilled corners with gold, silver, copper or silk thread, with the wire assigned by rank in the Book of Later Han — gold for emperors, silver for princes and marquises, copper for their children, silk for lesser aristocrats, and everyone else forbidden. Two complete suits found in 1968 in the tombs of Liu Sheng and Dou Wan at Mancheng, Hebei, settled a long argument about whether such suits existed. A suit took several years to make; some were too small for the body and were laid on a wooden effigy instead. Emperor Wen of Wei banned their production in 223 CE to reduce tomb looting, which is a dated statement about how much of this material was already being dug up.

Elsewhere the grave takes the same objects the living used. Fijian men were buried with their tabua, the polished sperm-whale teeth, along with war clubs. Hei-tiki were often buried when their kaitiaki, their guardian, died, and retrieved later to be kept somewhere special and brought out at tangihanga. Greek and Roman curse tablets were put in graves so that the dead person could carry the message, chosen often from those who had died young or violently. In Rome, by contrast, a boy's bulla left him at manhood and went to the household Lares rather than to the ground.

*Inference —* the timeline and the map in this atlas are built on graves. A material that survives burial and a custom of burying it together decide which traditions look old and which look recent; Egypt looks enormous partly because it buried faience by the thousand in dry ground. That is a fact about preservation before it is a fact about devotion.
how: Put on the body, wrapped into the bandages at the position the texts specify, laid in the coffin, or set at the compass points of the chamber. In several traditions the placement is the whole instruction and the amulet is otherwise an ordinary one.
today: Now mostly a question of who holds the objects. Grave goods are the most contested class in museum collections: in the United States the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act sets out how human remains and funerary objects in federally funded collections are returned, and repatriation claims elsewhere turn on the same distinction between an object given to the dead and an object traded by the living. Egyptian funerary amulets remain on open display in many collections, and the asymmetry between those two situations is itself an argument.
kin: heart-scarab — the amulet with the strictest placement in this practice — over the heart, or later inside the chest
kin: wedjat-eye — the amulet Egypt buried in the greatest numbers, and the reason museum trays of it are so deep
kin: tyet-knot — in the wrappings on the upper torso from Amenhotep III to the end of dynastic Egypt
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — silver worn in life and found in a burial chamber, carrying the oldest surviving biblical text known
kin: hei-tiki — buried when its guardian died, then lifted again and brought out at tangihanga
kin: bulla — the counter-case: a Roman boy's charm went to the household gods at manhood, not into the ground
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition that made this the default destination for a small object
kin: nagpra — the law that governs what happens to funerary objects held in United States collections
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator whose cemetery work produced the amulet series museums still sort by
kin: foundation-deposit — the other undisturbed context that fills the drawers
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this practice leads straight into
