## Hanging at the door (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/hanging-at-door/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/hanging-at-door.json
id: hanging-at-door
aliases: fixing to the doorpost · over the lintel · on the barn
said: put where everyone entering passes it
when: 301 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL PS US JP IE GB IT DE TR IN PK CN
object: form=door-piece materials=parchment,iron,wood,paper,silver,terracotta worn=door,lintel,wall,roof
against: house — said by Jewish households; Chabad representatives ran a campaign for the systematic checking of mezuzot after attacks at Ma'alot in the 1970s, on the assumption that keeping the commandment would guarantee personal safety [s:wp-mezuzah]
against: livestock — said by Irish households, who hung Brigid's crosses in the outhouses and stables as well as the dwelling [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
against: spirits — said by European households nailing worn horseshoes above doorways, and the legend of Saint Dunstan attached to the custom [s:wp-horseshoe]
against: demons — said by Japanese households placing Tsuno Daishi gofu on doorways and entrances [s:wp-ofuda]
what: Putting the charm on the way in. A parchment case screwed to a doorpost, a horseshoe nailed above a door, a woven cross in the rafters, a painted star on a barn, a paper talisman pasted at an entrance. The position is the argument: harm is treated as something that arrives, and the door is where it arrives.
story: Jewish law makes the door a legal obligation with a measured position. A mezuzah's parchment goes in a case on the right side of the doorway, in the upper third of the post, at roughly shoulder height and within about three inches — eight centimetres — of the opening. Many Ashkenazi Jews tilt it so that the top slants into the room, a compromise proposed by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, c. 1269–1343, between Rashi's vertical and Rabbeinu Tam's horizontal; most Sephardi, Mizrahi and other non-Ashkenazi Jews fix it vertically. In the diaspora it goes up within thirty days of moving into a rented home; in a purchased home, or anywhere in Israel, immediately. The person holds it to the spot and recites a blessing, and one blessing covers all the doors done in a session. Samaritans set select verses above the house door or on a prominent wall, and stone plaques of the Ten Commandments from the Byzantine and Early Muslim periods, the fourth to the eleventh centuries, are now in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

The door is also where the practice gets litigated. A Chicago condominium association at Shoreline Towers banned objects outside unit doors and in 2004 read the ban as absolute, and management removed residents' mezuzot; complaints went to the Chicago Commission on Human Relations, the Illinois Attorney General and the federal housing department. Alderman Burton Natarus drafted an amendment making it illegal to prohibit a religious sign, symbol or relic on a door, doorpost or entrance, and it became Chicago law that December with a maximum $500 fine, the first such legislation in North America.

Japan assigns doors by deity. Protective gofu such as Tsuno Daishi, the Horned Great Master — the Tendai monk Ryōgen drawn as a yaksha or an oni — go on doorways and entrances; hearth deities go in the kitchen; a talisman of Ucchuṣma, the wrathful figure who purifies the unclean, may go in the toilet. Europe nails iron. Worn horseshoes were placed above or beside doorways to guard houses, barns and stables across Italy, Germany, Britain and Scandinavia, traditionally held with seven nails; whether the ends point up or down is a live disagreement, with much of Europe, the Middle East and Latin America hanging them downward so that blessing pours out, and parts of Ireland and Britain hanging them upward so that luck is caught and cannot run out. The two habits travelled to the United States with their carriers. A legend attached to the tenth-century blacksmith-saint Dunstan has the Devil promising never to enter a household with a horseshoe nailed to the door.

Ireland hangs a woven cross. Saint Brigid's crosses are typically woven on 1 February, and hanging one from the rafters, or over an entryway, was held to bring the saint's blessing and protection for the rest of the year; on the feast day crosses went up in the main dwelling, the outhouses and the stables. Pennsylvania painted the wall instead of the door: barn stars in circular borders appear on Pennsylvania Dutch barns in Berks, Lancaster and Lehigh counties, beginning in the early nineteenth century and spreading once ready-mixed paint became affordable. Two readings of the barn signs run side by side in the same communities — one holds them protective, the other decorative — and both sides agree that particular designs carry folk beliefs. The Amish do not use them.

*Inference —* the door is the most crowded position in this atlas. It is also the only one where the charm is aimed at people who are not its owner: a doorpost charm is read by every visitor, which makes it a statement of who lives here as much as a guard.
how: Fix, nail, paste or hang, at the position the tradition specifies, often with words said at the moment of fixing. Height, side and orientation carry rules; so does the date, in the Irish case.
today: Live and legally protected in at least one American city. Mezuzot are fixed in Israel and across the diaspora, with cases made in silver, wood, stone, ceramic, pewter and polymer clay; a case sold with a photocopied paper text is a case, since a valid mezuzah is handwritten on parchment by a qualified scribe. Japanese households renew door talismans at the New Year. Hex signs are sold as mountable boards for barns and houses, a trade Jacob Zook of Paradise, Pennsylvania claimed to have started in 1942 for shops along the Lincoln Highway.
kin: mezuzah — the door charm with a measured position, a blessing at fixing and a deadline for putting it up
kin: horseshoe — iron nailed over the opening, with an argument about which way up that crossed the Atlantic intact
kin: brigids-cross — rushes in the rafters from 1 February, and again the following February
kin: hex-sign — the same idea painted at barn scale, and argued over as protective or decorative in the same county
kin: ofuda — paper assigned by room — entrance, kitchen, toilet — with a different figure on each
kin: nimbu-mirchi — South Asia's hanging version, strung in a doorway rather than fixed to it
kin: bagua-mirror — the Chinese door fitting that answers the same question about what arrives at an entrance
kin: iron — the material doing the work in the European case, before any shape is given to it
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition that put iron over the doors of houses, barns and stables
kin: renewing-yearly — the clock several door charms run on, in Ireland and Japan alike
kin: foundation-deposit — the same threshold, treated from underneath
sources: s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-horseshoe s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-hex-sign s:wp-ofuda s:wp-incantation-bowl
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Inheriting (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/inheriting/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/inheriting.json
id: inheriting
aliases: handing on · pusaka · heirloom charm · taonga tuku iho
said: the charm outlives its owner
when: 1830 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ID MY NZ FJ TO CN NP IT AU
object: form=pendant materials=iron,jade,tooth,agate,gold worn=waist,neck,grave
against: bad-luck — said by Javanese owners, for whom a kris carries piyandel, the property of adding self-confidence to its holder [s:wp-kris]
against: infertility — said by Māori practice as recorded by Robley, in which a hei-tiki was often given to a woman by her husband's family when she had trouble conceiving [s:wp-hei-tiki]
against: evil-eye — said by the account of dzi beads, whose etched eyes are described as meeting the harm with its own image [s:wp-dzi-bead]
RESTRICTED: Among Arrernte groups, ownership of sacred tjurunga was determined by a person's conception site within a patrilineal totemic clan, and access was limited to a small number of people. Australian institutions restrict access to material of this kind to people with the permission of the relevant community. This atlas prints that rule and holds nothing further about those objects or their transmission.
what: A charm that passes from one person to the next and gathers weight as it goes. The object is the same object; what changes is that it now carries a line of people. Traditions that inherit charms tend to have rules about who may receive one, which is what separates an heirloom from a second-hand purchase.
story: Java files the inherited blade under a word of its own. A kris is revered as tosan aji, sacred heirloom weapon, and counted a pusaka. Heirloom blades were handed down through successive generations and worn at weddings and other ceremonies; a fighter might carry three — his own, one from his father-in-law and one that was the family's. A pusaka kris given by a Javanese king to a noble or a subject stood for the king's confidence in the receiver and counted as a great honour. When Prince Diponegoro was defeated and detained at the end of the Java War and had to hand his kris to the Dutch in 1830, the event marked the disarming of the kris among the Javanese populace; its ceremonial life as heirloom and personal amulet continued.

Fiji keeps its whale teeth out of the market on purpose. Tabua are not sold, but traded as gifts at weddings, birthdays and funerals, and were traditionally given for atonement or esteem in sevusevu and in negotiations between rival chiefs. Age shows on them: contact with the oils in human hands darkens the tooth. The law now constrains the handing on — removal from Fiji is capped at 225 exports a year, requires permits from the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs and CITES papers, and in 2007 New Zealand returned 146 tabua seized for lacking valid export permits.

Māori hei-tiki pass through the ground. Hei-tiki are taonga, treasures, usually of pounamu, and Horatio Gordon Robley recorded two main readings of them: memorials to ancestors, or representations of Hineteiwaiwa, goddess of childbirth. Under the first, they were often buried when their kaitiaki — their guardian — died, and retrieved later to be kept somewhere special and brought out at tangihanga. Under the second, a hei-tiki was often given to a woman by her husband's family when she was having trouble conceiving.

Rome is the counter-case. A freeborn Roman boy wore his bulla until he came of age, and before putting on the toga virilis he placed it in the care of the household gods, the Lares. It went sideways into the house's keeping, not down to a son.

*Inference —* inheritance and the market pull against each other in every one of these cases, and the pull is visible in prices. Ancient dzi beads reach hundreds of thousands of US dollars, with beads carrying more eyes and the iron-inclusion marks called bloodspots worth more; new dzi run from about ten to two thousand US dollars depending on quality and lustre. An object that can be inherited can be sold, and the rules that make inheriting possible — who may receive, from whom — are exactly the rules a sale breaks.
how: By the tradition's own rule: down a male line, from a father-in-law at a marriage, from a king to a subject, out of the ground after a guardian's death, or as a gift at a funeral. Several traditions attach maintenance to receipt — a kris inherited is a kris that has to be cleaned yearly.
today: Live, and regulated. Tabua move within Fiji as gifts and across borders only with permits. Kris are worn as part of Javanese ceremonial dress and kept as family pusaka. Dzi beads are traded at high prices alongside machine-made copies sold by the strand for less than two US dollars, which the trade distinguishes by whether the decoration penetrates the bead's core.
kin: keris-pusaka — the inherited object with its own legal word — tosan aji, pusaka, and a blade that comes with a yearly duty
kin: hei-tiki — the taonga that goes into the ground with its guardian and comes out again for mourning
kin: dzi-bead — the heirloom with the widest gap between what it means and what it fetches
kin: bulla — the counter-case: handed to the household gods at manhood rather than to an heir
kin: maori-taonga — the tradition whose word for treasure already contains the idea of handing on
kin: te-papa-taonga — where inherited taonga sit when a museum holds them instead of a family
kin: renewing-yearly — the upkeep an inherited blade carries — jamasan, the yearly cleaning
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice inheritance is defined against, and the one that keeps testing its rules
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read that starts where an heirloom leaves the family
sources: s:wp-kris s:wp-tabua s:wp-hei-tiki s:wp-dzi-bead s:wp-bulla-amulet s:wp-pounamu s:wp-tjurunga s:wp-australian-institute-of-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-studies
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Inscribing (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/inscribing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/inscribing.json
id: inscribing
aliases: writing a charm · ktav stam · yant · fulu · voces mysticae
said: putting the words on
when: 600 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IL PS IQ IR GR IT GB CN JP TH KH LA TR IN
object: form=scroll materials=lead,parchment,silver,paper,copper,palm-leaf worn=neck,upper-arm,door,grave,foundation
against: demons — said by the Aramaic and Syriac incantation bowls themselves, addressed to the demons they name [s:wp-incantation-bowl]
against: curse — said by Greek and Roman clients, whose tablets hand the target over to underworld gods [s:wp-curse-tablet]
against: weapons — said by Hürrem Sultan, who told Suleiman the Magnificent the inscriptions on the talismanic shirt she gave him would protect him from bullets [s:wp-talismanic-shirt]
against: illness — said by Taoist zhuyou healers, in use in China since at least the Eastern Han [s:wp-fulu]
RESTRICTED: Taoist talismanic script is transmitted in secret from priest to disciple, and its incantations and hand-forms differ from sect to sect. This atlas prints what the practice is for and who may write it, and does not reproduce a talisman's strokes or the words that accompany them.
what: Writing the words that do the work. Lead scratched with a stylus, parchment ruled and lettered with a quill, silver foil punched with a blessing, metal foil incised with Khom Pali, paper painted with strokes nobody is meant to read. In most of these traditions the writing is the charm and the material is packaging: get the letters wrong and there is no object, only a blank.
story: The oldest dated example in this atlas is two silver scrolls found in 1979 in a Judahite burial chamber at Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem's Old City, in a site first reported by Gabriel Barkay in 1975. They carry portions of the Priestly Blessing from Numbers, date from around 600 BCE, and took three years to unroll without destroying. They are the oldest surviving texts from the Hebrew Bible known, and they were worn.

Jewish practice still treats the letters as the object. A mezuzah's klaf is written by a qualified scribe, a sofer stam, trained in the law and in the calligraphy of Ktav Stam, in indelible black ink with a quill made from a feather or, rarely now, a reed; tearing or damaging the wording invalidates it. Tefillin are stricter still: 3,188 letters across the parchments, as long as fifteen hours of a scribe's work for a set, and the letters must be written in order — find a mistake later and it cannot be corrected, because the replacement letter would have been written out of sequence.

The Greek and Roman world wrote to bind rather than to bless. Curse tablets — tabella defixionis, katadesmos — are thin lead sheets scratched in tiny letters, then rolled, folded or pierced with nails. Writers added palindromes, boustrophedon lines and otherwise meaningless words such as Bazagra or Bescu, and professionals sometimes prepared tablets in advance with a space left for the customer's name. Mesopotamian incantation bowls run their text in a spiral from the outer rim inward, so that, in John Charles Arnold's description, demons following the charms would be caught in the centre.

China took the logic to its end and made the writing unreadable on purpose. Fulu are talismanic script — strokes that resemble Chinese characters without being them. Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, in the Eastern Jin (317–420), that a talisman worked whether or not its user could decipher it, and Fudan University's Ge Zhaoguang describes the illegibility as deliberate archaism, a veil that leaves only qualified clergy able to produce them. Thai yant are written in Khom Pali, a Thai variant of Khmer script, or in Lan Na Tai Tham in the north. Islamic talismanic shirts carry Quranic verses, names of God and of prophets, and numbers; the earliest surviving examples were made in or near the fifteenth century.

*Inference —* two opposite strategies run through all of this. One camp writes to be read by a power that reads: the blessing, the verse, the name. The other writes to be unreadable by anyone: the meaningless words on a lead sheet, the Taoist strokes, the letters that only a scribe's hand can form. Both are ways of putting the text beyond the ordinary user's reach.
how: Materials first, because they decide the tool: lead takes a stylus, parchment takes a quill and a ruled line, silver takes a punch, metal foil takes a stylus and then rolls, paper takes a brush. Then the text, in a script the tradition specifies. Then, in several traditions, a check: many observant Jews have a scribe examine mezuzah parchments for tears and faded letters at least twice every seven years.
today: Still a paid trade. Scribes write mezuzot and tefillin to order, and sellers who supply a photocopied text on paper with a decorated case are selling a case: a valid mezuzah has to be handwritten on parchment by a qualified scribe. Thai and Cambodian masters still write yant on metal, cloth and skin. Chinese folk healers still use zhuyou, the talismanic branch of healing, which traditional Chinese medicine rejects and which was reinterpreted in the twentieth century as a local counterpart to hypnosis.
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the oldest dated thing this practice made: a blessing punched into silver and worn to the grave around 600 BCE
kin: tefillin — the strictest version — 3,188 letters in order, and a mistake found afterwards cannot be fixed
kin: mezuzah — the parchment a scribe writes and another scribe checks twice in seven years
kin: takrut — the rolled scroll this writing goes onto in Thailand, in Khom Pali or Lan Na Tai Tham
kin: fu-talisman — writing built to be unreadable, which is the point its own scholars make about it
kin: curse-tablet — the same craft aimed at somebody: lead, tiny letters, then nails
kin: incantation-bowl — text spiralling inward on clay, buried face down to catch what follows it
kin: talismanic-shirt — a whole garment as the writing surface, Quranic verse over the body in battle
kin: ink — the material that carries this entire practice, and whose indelibility is a legal requirement in Jewish law
kin: divine-name — the single most common thing written, from the Priestly Blessing to the names of God on a shirt
kin: folding — what happens to the writing next — rolled, folded, sealed away from the eye that reads
kin: washing-off-ink — the branch where the writing is meant to be destroyed and drunk rather than kept
sources: s:wp-ketef-hinnom s:wp-tefillin s:wp-mezuzah s:wp-curse-tablet s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-fulu s:wp-takrut s:wp-talismanic-shirt s:wp-yantra s:wp-magic-supernatural
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Knotting (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/knotting/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/knotting.json
id: knotting
aliases: tying · binding a thread · kroke · khutt hashani
said: tying the thing shut, or tying it on
when: 1550 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: EG BG MK RO MD GR AL IL JP IE IN CN
object: form=knot materials=thread,cloth,carnelian,faience,leather,wood worn=wrist,neck,waist,grave,lintel
against: evil-eye — said by wearers of the scarlet wrist thread, a Jewish folk custom with no basis in Torah, halakha or kabbalistic law [s:wp-red-string-kabbalah]
against: illness — said by the Bulgarian and Macedonian custom, in which the red and white threads stand for a wish for good health [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: weapons — said by Japanese women who stitched senninbari for soldiers; some soldiers rejected the claim and wore the belt as a keepsake instead [s:wp-senninbari]
against: the-dead — said by Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead, which calls for a red jasper tyet at the mummy's neck [s:wp-tyet]
what: Tying, as the whole of the charm. A knot needs no words, no metal and no kiln — two colours of wool twisted together, a leather strap knotted into the shape of a letter, a thousand stitches pulled tight by a thousand different hands. Where a knot is the object, the tying is the making, the charging and often the giving all at once.
story: Egypt made the knot a sign. The tyet, the knot of Isis, resembles a knot of cloth and may have begun as a bandage; an early example comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, excavated by Zaki Saad in the 1940s. Tyet amulets started going into burials in the early New Kingdom, from the reign of Amenhotep III, and from then to the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one in the wrappings, usually on the upper torso. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck, saying the power of Isis will be the protection of the body and that the amulet will drive away whoever would commit a crime against it.

In the Balkans the knot is worn for a month and then untied by the calendar. A martenitsa is twisted from white and red yarn, usually as two small wool dolls, Pizho and Penda, and is put on at Baba Marta Day on 1 March. It comes off when the wearer first sees a stork, a swallow or a tree in blossom — then it is tied to the branch of a fruit tree, or put under a stone so that whichever creature is nearest it the next day reads the coming year: a worm or larva for health and success, an ant for success won by hard work, a spider for trouble. Photios' Lexicon records an older Greek version in which priests wrapped a red thread, kroke, around the right hand and foot; ethnographers who trace the custom back that far do so tentatively, and the tradition itself names Thracian, Hellenic or Roman origins without settling on one. The practice is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Jewish practice knots leather into letters. The head-tefillin strap's knot forms the letter dalet or a double dalet, the arm strap's knot forms a yud, and with the shin on the head box those three letters spell Shaddai, one of the names of God. A separate folk custom ties a thin scarlet wool thread round the wrist against the evil eye; there is no requirement for it in the Torah, in halakha or in kabbalistic texts, and the only public exhortation to wear one that the sources name is from the 1490s, when Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended it to Jews forbidden to wear tefillin, as a reminder of the commandment.

Japan counted knots. A senninbari, a thousand-person-stitch belt, was decorated with a thousand knots or stitches, each normally made by a different woman; the custom began in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95, when the earliest versions were handkerchief-sized squares knotted to strengthen the cloth, the implication being that the strength passed to the man carrying it.

*Inference —* knots are the cheapest charm in this atlas and the most evenly distributed. That is worth saying plainly rather than reading as a single ancient custom travelling: thread is everywhere, tying is learned by every child, and a knot is the one amulet a person with nothing can make.
how: Twist, tie, or stitch. Martenitsi are twisted from red and white wool and pinned to clothing or tied at the wrist or neck. Brigid's crosses are woven from rushes or straw gathered the evening before. Senninbari stitches were solicited one at a time from women passing a temple, a train station or a department store, with a woman born in a Tiger year entitled by custom to sew twelve stitches or as many as her years; some belts were lined with women's hair, a practice the sources trace to folk belief on Okinawa, and coins were sewn in as well.
today: Martenitsi are worn every March in Bulgaria and North Macedonia and given, never bought for oneself, with modern versions adding coloured beads. Red wrist threads are sold by elderly women to pilgrims and tourists in the Old City of Jerusalem and were taken up in the late 1990s by celebrities with no connection to the custom, a spread often traced to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. Tefillin knots are tied the same way every weekday morning.
kin: knot — the sign this practice makes — and the rare case where making the sign and making the object are the same act
kin: tyet-knot — the knot cut in stone: Egypt's version, tied by a carver rather than by hand
kin: martenitsa — the knot with an expiry date — 1 March to the first stork, then tied to a fruit tree
kin: red-string — the plainest form: scarlet wool at the wrist, and an argument about where it came from
kin: senninbari — a thousand knots from a thousand hands, solicited one at a time outside train stations
kin: tefillin — leather knotted into letters — dalet and yud, spelling a name of God with the shin on the box
kin: brigids-cross — the woven version: rushes gathered on 31 January, tied the same night, hung the next morning
kin: thread — the material that makes this the cheapest charm in the atlas
kin: red-thread — the colour that runs with the knot from the Mediterranean to Mongolia
kin: counting-beads — the same cord, knotted to count with instead of to bind — an Orthodox prayer rope carries 33, 50 or 100 knots
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice a martenitsa belongs to: worn for a season, then taken off on a sign from a bird
sources: s:wp-tyet s:wp-martenitsa s:wp-red-string-kabbalah s:wp-senninbari s:wp-tefillin s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:web-prayer-beads
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Renewing yearly (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/renewing-yearly/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/renewing-yearly.json
id: renewing-yearly
aliases: annual replacement · tokowaka · jamasan · the year's charm
said: swapping last year's for this year's
when: 1764 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP BG MK RO ID IE IL BT NP
object: form=folded-paper materials=paper,wood,thread,iron worn=wall,lintel,wrist,hearth
against: bad-luck — said by the omamori custom, in which amulets are replaced once a year to ward off the previous year's bad luck [s:wp-omamori]
against: illness — said by Bulgarian and Macedonian wearers, for whom the red and white threads carry a wish for health and are then given to a fruit tree [s:wp-martenitsa]
against: house — said by Irish households, who hung a new Brigid's cross in the rafters on 1 February for the saint's blessing over the year [s:wp-brigid-s-cross]
what: A charm with an expiry date. The old one is taken down, returned, burnt, buried or tied to a tree, and a new one takes its place on a fixed day. The date is usually a turn in the calendar — a new year, a saint's feast, the first day of spring — and the swap is the practice, not the object.
story: Japan does this at scale and gives a reason. Japanese practice places great weight on purity and newness — tokowaka, eternal youth — and it is on that ground that annual replacement of ofuda and omamori is encouraged. New ofuda are obtained before the end of the year or during the New Year season; the old ones are returned to the shrine or temple where they came from as a form of thanks, though most Shinto shrines in practice accept talismans from other shrines. Omamori are customarily replaced once a year and returned on or shortly after the New Year, so that the coming year starts with a fresh one. Old ones are not thrown away: they are burnt at a ceremony called Sagichō or Dondoyaki held at the Little New Year, on 14 or 15 January.

Daruma dolls date the system precisely. Charms drawn at Shorinzan Daruma Temple in Takasaki were given with an effectiveness of one year, so parishioners needed new ones every year; the ninth priest, Togaku, handled the demand by giving the people wooden block moulds and letting them make their own papier-mâché charms, near the beginning of the Meiwa period, 1764–72. Takasaki now produces eighty per cent of Japan's daruma, and the city's annual Daruma Doll Festival draws, by the city's own account, more than 400,000 people buying the year's dolls.

Bulgaria and North Macedonia run a spring version. Martenitsi go on at Baba Marta Day, 1 March, and come off when the wearer first sees a stork, a swallow or a blossoming tree — or at the end of March. The old one is tied to the branch of a fruit tree, giving the tree the health and luck the wearer had while wearing it, or put under a stone to be read the next day by whichever creature is nearest it. Ireland weaves a new Saint Brigid's cross on 1 February from rushes gathered the evening before; crosses were either taken down annually and replaced or left to accumulate between feasts, and discarded ones were burned or buried, with burial preferred because of Brigid's associations with agriculture.

Jewish practice keeps a different clock and it is worth naming as a contrast. A mezuzah is not replaced annually; many observant Jews have a qualified scribe check the parchments for tears and faded lettering at least twice every seven years. The object is meant to last, and the maintenance is inspection rather than replacement.

*Inference —* the parallel between a Japanese year-end burning, a martenitsa on a March branch and a yearly kris cleaning is real at the level of structure: each treats potency as something that runs down and has to be topped up on a date the calendar sets, not on a date the owner picks. What is this project's own reading, and not any tradition's claim, is the further step of grouping them — the reasons given differ completely, purity in one case, the return of spring in another, upkeep of a blade in a third, and no source read here connects them.
how: Take it off or take it down; return it, burn it, bury it or leave it on a branch; obtain the replacement; put it where the old one was. In Java the equivalent is not replacement but cleaning: jamasan, the yearly cleaning of a kris, is required by the tradition and has left ancient blades worn thin.
today: Live, and commercially organised. Japanese shrines and temples stock the year's talismans in quantity and hold the January fires; Takasaki's daruma market runs annually. Martenitsi are sold across Bulgaria and North Macedonia every February and hang on fruit trees through April. Mezuzah checking is a paid scribal service.
kin: omamori — the charm with the clearest expiry: replaced yearly, returned to its shrine, burnt in January
kin: ofuda — the household talisman whose replacement is argued for on the ground of purity, not of wear
kin: daruma — the doll sold with an effectiveness of one year — and the reason a temple started handing out moulds
kin: martenitsa — the spring version, whose end date is set by a bird rather than by a date
kin: brigids-cross — woven fresh each 1 February from rushes gathered the night before
kin: keris-pusaka — the blade that is cleaned annually rather than replaced, and worn thin by the cleaning
kin: mezuzah — the opposite clock: checked by a scribe twice in seven years, and meant to last
kin: burning-retirement — where last year's charm goes on 14 or 15 January
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition that runs this cycle at national scale
kin: buying-in-a-market — the other half of the cycle — an annual expiry is also an annual sale
sources: s:wp-ofuda s:wp-omamori s:wp-daruma-doll s:wp-martenitsa s:wp-brigid-s-cross s:wp-kris s:wp-mezuzah
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Sewing in (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/sewing-in/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/sewing-in.json
id: sewing-in
aliases: stitching a charm into cloth · quilting a hand in · lining a garment
said: putting it inside the clothes, not on them
when: 1773 CE to now (still carried)
countries: SN ML US JP TR IN PK HT
object: form=packet materials=cloth,leather,paper,hair,coin,herb worn=sewn-in,chest,waist,pocket
against: witchcraft — said by hoodoo practitioners, for whom the sewn bag houses a spirit that does protective and healing work [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: weapons — said by Japanese women who stitched senninbari for soldiers going to war [s:wp-senninbari]
against: bad-luck — said by wearers of gris-gris across West Africa and the Caribbean [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
against: infertility — said by women in Senegal, where a 1982 survey placed gris-gris among the three best-known traditional methods of contraception [s:wp-gris-gris-talisman]
RESTRICTED: What goes inside a sewn packet is the maker's knowledge in these traditions, and this record does not list contents as a recipe. Hoodoo practice holds that a mojo is made for one individual and concealed on that person; the cited accounts describe that rule rather than publishing the fillings, and this atlas does the same.
what: Putting the charm inside the cloth rather than on a cord. A pouch is stitched shut over what it holds; coins and hair are sewn into a belt; a charm is quilted into a bedcover; a shirt is itself the charm, worn under armour. Once stitched, the object cannot be checked without being destroyed, which is the point and the problem.
story: The gris-gris came out of the Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa: a small cloth pouch, inscribed with verses from an ancestor and holding a ritual number of small objects, worn on the person. The Atlantic slave trade carried it to the Americas, where it became a significant practice in Haitian Vodou and in the Louisiana tradition the cited account calls "Louisiana Voodoo", and where the earliest legal mentions of that Louisiana tradition are New Orleans court cases of 1773, in which enslaved people were convicted of using gris-gris against those who held them. A 1982 survey in Senegal found gris-gris among the three methods of contraception best known to women there, alongside abstinence and roots and herbs.

The Kongo-derived mojo bag took the same shape in the United States and then went into bedding. African American quilt makers sewed mojo hands into quilts for protection — a practice the sources trace to Central African peoples such as the Bakongo, who adapted nkisi practice into the 'Pineapple quilt', and which spread from Mississippi and Alabama to Connecticut.

Japan sewed the charm into a belt and then sewed things into the belt. A senninbari was stitched a thousand times, usually one stitch per woman; some were lined with a woman's hair, or several women's, a form of added protection the sources trace to folk belief on Okinawa, and coins were sewn in as well. Some senninbari were never worn at all: they were folded and placed inside helmet liners, pockets or packs.

The Islamic world put the writing on the garment itself. Talismanic shirts — tılsımlı gömlek in Turkish, pirâhan telesmat in Persian — are found across the Muslim world in Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and West African types, the earliest surviving examples made in or near the fifteenth century, inscribed with Quranic verses, names of God and of prophets, and numbers. Most seem intended as a shield in battle. Hürrem Sultan gave one to Suleiman the Magnificent and told him its inscriptions would protect him from bullets.

*Inference —* sewing solves a problem the cord cannot. A pendant announces itself and can be taken off you; a stitched charm passes a search, survives a change of owner's rules, and travels in a garment that has an innocent reason to exist. The practice is heaviest exactly where carrying a charm openly was dangerous.
how: A pouch is cut, filled and stitched shut; a belt is embroidered and its lining closed over coins or hair; a quilt takes the charm between its layers; a shirt is written on before it is made up. In hoodoo practice the filled bag is then fixed and fed — smoked over incense or candles, breathed on, prayed over, and dressed with a liquid — which is a separate step this atlas files under feeding the charm.
today: Gris-gris are worn across Senegalese society, by, in the words of the cited account, everyone from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives. Conjure shops sell made-up mojo bags and the materials to make them; Dr Jim Jordan, a conjure doctor in North Carolina, ran a Hoodoo store and a paid practice through the Jim Crow era and became a multi-millionaire doing it. Senninbari stopped being made at scale with the end of the Second World War and are now a collectors' category, catalogued and sold.
kin: gris-gris — the pouch this practice is named after, stitched shut in Mande communities and carried to Louisiana
kin: senninbari — the belt where the stitching is the charm and a thousand strangers did it
kin: talismanic-shirt — the garment version — the writing goes on the cloth and the cloth goes under the armour
kin: hirz-pouch — the sewn leather or cloth case of Islamic West and North Africa, holding written verses
kin: taweez — the same folded verse, cased in metal instead of stitched into cloth
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition the gris-gris comes out of, and which the Atlantic trade moved west
kin: thread — the material that does the work here — the stitch is the closure and, in the senninbari, the charm itself
kin: wearing-hidden — the rule sewing exists to serve
kin: feeding-the-charm — what happens after the bag is stitched — fixed, woken and dressed
kin: folding — the paper-and-metal branch of the same move: close the charm over its contents
sources: s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-senninbari s:wp-talismanic-shirt s:wp-nkisi
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Tattooing (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/tattooing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/tattooing.json
id: tattooing
native: สักยันต์ (Thai)
aliases: sak yant · yantra tattooing · សាក់យ័ន្ត · ສັກຢັນ
said: sàk yan
when: 2500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: TH KH LA MM PH ID EG BA ET PE NZ
object: form=tattoo materials=ink,skin worn=skin,chest,upper-arm,head
against: weapons — said by bearers in dangerous trades — military personnel, police, taxi drivers and others — as summarised in the cited account [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: bad-luck — said by the tradition's own account of the three effects: benefit to the bearer, protection, and effect on the people around them [s:wp-yantra-tattooing]
against: spirits — said by Austronesian societies, where tattoos were regarded as wards against evil spirits and illness [s:wp-tattoo]
against: illness — said by the Chimu of coastal Peru, who wore tattoos for magic and medical purposes [s:wp-tattoo]
RESTRICTED: The words a master says over a tattoo, and the rules governing which design goes to which person, are held within the lineage. The cited account records that the practice is defined by strict rules intended to maintain the tattoos' power and that the power holds only while the bearer keeps taboos the master sets. This atlas prints that structure and does not print the formulae, the assignment of designs, or anything that would work as instructions.
what: The charm put into the skin, where it cannot be dropped, stolen, sold or taken off. A long needle drives ink under the surface in a design that is often script — Pali phrases in Khom, Khmer, Lao Tham, Shan, northern Thai or Tai Lu letters, wrapped around animals and deities. The bearer carries the object and the obligations together, because in several of these traditions the tattoo works only while its rules are kept.
story: Sak yant names its own mechanics. Sak, from a Proto-Mon-Khmer root meaning to prick, is a native Khmer word — Chuon Nath's 1967 dictionary holds that it is not a loan from Sanskrit or Pali — and yant comes from Sanskrit yantra, from yam, to hold or sustain, plus tra, instrument. The practice originated in the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, on indigenous mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing that the cited account traces back as far as 2,500 BCE, with the designs drawn from Indian yantras. It runs today in Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and parts of Burma, and the script changes with the country: Khmer in Cambodia, Khom in central Thailand, Shan or northern Thai or Tai Lu in the north, Lao Tham in Laos.

What the tattoo is said to do splits three ways in the tradition's own account: effects that benefit the bearer, such as making them more eloquent; effects that ward off evil and hardship, taken up by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and people in other jobs they judge dangerous; and effects on other people, such as invoking fear. The same designs are applied to cloth and metal and put in a house, a temple or a vehicle instead of on skin.

Elsewhere the mark is the membership. Many Copts have the cross tattooed on the inside of the right arm at the wrist as a sign of faith. Catholic Croats in Bosnia used sicanje, tattooing, for protection against conversion to Islam under Ottoman rule. Ancient Egyptians tattooed dedication to a deity, and the marks were held to carry divine protection. Among Austronesian societies tattoos were regarded as magical wards against evil spirits and illness as well as records of raids and status, and the Chimu of coastal Peru wore them for magic and medical purposes; tattoos on Chancay bodies of around 1250 CE have been studied with lasers by researchers at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

*Inference —* the tattoo is the limit case of everything else in this atlas. Every other charm here can be lost, pawned, inherited or buried; this one is disposed of only with the person. That is also why it is the practice most tightly governed by rules attached to the bearer rather than to the object.
how: Public structure only. A master applies the design with a long needle, in a rite that the tradition holds transfers spirits into the design — in the words of the cited study, spiritual tattooing functions as the bridge between the wearer and gods or wild spirits. The practice is defined by strict rules meant to maintain the tattoos' power, and the tattoo confers its powers only so long as the bearer observes those rules and taboos, such as abstaining from a certain type of food. What the master says, and which design is given to whom, are the master's, and this record stops there.
today: Both a living practice and a trade selling to visitors. Hollywood attention has moved the market: Angelina Jolie was tattooed by Ajahn Noo Kanpai with Old Khmer script sak yant in Thailand, and took a Bengal tiger yantra in 2004 to mark acquiring Cambodian citizenship. Buddhist images and figures used as tattoos by visitors who do not follow local rules about the respectful display of such images have caused public controversy in Buddhist countries. Both of those are arguments the traditions are having about themselves, and this atlas reports them rather than settling them.
kin: sak-yant — the object this practice makes, and the one case in this atlas where object and owner cannot be separated
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the same needle used for membership rather than power — a cross at the right wrist
kin: yantra-plate — the identical design put on metal or cloth instead of skin, and hung in a house or a truck
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition that holds the lineages, the rules and the refusals
kin: skin — the material, which is also the wearer — the reason this practice has rules no object needs
kin: ink — what carries the writing here, as it does on paper and parchment elsewhere in this atlas
kin: consecration — the same transfer, with a person instead of an object on the receiving end
kin: inscribing — the writing step, done with a needle and at the bearer's expense
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the page that explains why the rite, the formulae and the design assignments are missing from this record
sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-tattoo s:wp-coptic-cross s:wp-yantra
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Washing off the ink (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/washing-off-ink/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/washing-off-ink.json
id: washing-off-ink
aliases: drinking the writing · erasure water · swallowed charm
said: the charm is taken, not worn
when: undated (still carried)
countries: SA EG SN NG ET PH IN PK
object: form=scroll materials=ink,paper,wood,earth worn=swallowed
against: illness — said by Islamic healing practice as summarised in the cited account, which records treating a stomach ache by drinking water over which Quranic passages have been recited [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: witchcraft — said by the same body of practice, which prescribes drinking and bathing in water over which an incantation has been recited for the condition it calls sihr al-nazif [s:wp-islam-and-magic]
against: bad-luck — said by Filipino agimat practice, in which an amulet may be consumable — enchanted mud, or a mutya that is ingested [s:wp-agimat]
RESTRICTED: Which texts are written, and who may write and administer them, is governed within these traditions and disputed between authorities inside Islam. This record describes the method and the dispute, and does not print texts, formulae or dosages.
what: The charm written and then destroyed on purpose, so that a person can take it. Words are written inside a bowl, water is poured in, the writing comes off into the water, and the water is drunk. What was an object for a minute becomes a dose. Nothing survives, which is why almost no museum drawer holds an example of the practice that may be the commonest use of written charms alive.
story: Islamic legal writing draws a fine line through this. Remke Kruk, summarising how close the approved and disapproved practices sit, notes that dissolving Quranic texts written on paper in water is forbidden, while the well-known Wahhabi-oriented cleric Wahid 'Abd al-Salam Bali recommends, in the cited account's words, writing in bowls with ink that is washed off by the water poured into the bowl. The same body of practice records treating a stomach ache by drinking water over which Quranic passages have been recited, and prescribes, for the condition called sihr al-nazif, drinking water over which an incantation has been recited and bathing in it for three days.

The Philippines has a swallowed branch of its own. An agimat can take the form of consumable enchanted mud, putik in Tagalog, and a mutya — described in one account as a drop of liquid taken from the heart of a banana tree at midnight — is ingested rather than worn.

*Inference —* this practice is the reason a survey of amulets built from museum collections will always undercount written charms. A takrut rolled into metal lasts a thousand years; the same verse written to be washed off lasts a minute and leaves a person, not an object. Where a tradition uses both, the collections show one and not the other.

It is worth marking what this record does not claim. Mesopotamian incantation bowls, which are the other famous case of writing inside a bowl, were buried face down under thresholds in the accounts read here, not washed and drunk, and nothing in those accounts connects the two customs.
how: Public structure only: a text is written on a surface chosen so the ink will lift — the inside of a bowl, a wooden slate — water is poured on, and the water is drunk or used for washing. Which text is written, and by whom, is the part the traditions govern, and this record does not set it out.
today: Live and contested inside Islam. The practices of healers who claim to speak with jinn to cure or prevent the evil eye are held by some conservative Muslims to be shirk, a serious sin; the cited account sets out how narrow the difference between approved and disapproved practice can be, with the washing-off method on the approved side of the line drawn by the cleric it names. This atlas reports that disagreement between Muslim authorities and takes no side in it.
kin: quran-pendant — the kept version of the same verses — worn instead of drunk
kin: taweez — the folded written charm of the same tradition, cased to last rather than washed to be taken
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition this practice sits inside, and where the argument about it is being had
kin: ink — the material that has to be chosen to lift rather than to last, which inverts every other use of it in this atlas
kin: anting-anting — the Filipino charm that can be eaten, described as consumable mud or an ingested mutya
kin: incantation-bowl — the other writing-inside-a-bowl practice, which in the accounts read here was buried rather than drunk — the parallel is a shape, not a link
kin: inscribing — the writing step, done here in the knowledge that the writing is about to be destroyed
kin: ethiopian-scroll-craft — the neighbouring tradition of written healing charms, whose relation to this practice this record does not assert
sources: s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-agimat s:wp-incantation-bowl s:wp-throne-verse
tier: cited · confidence: low · updated: 2026-09-16

## Wearing hidden (practice)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/practice/wearing-hidden/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/practice/wearing-hidden.json
id: wearing-hidden
aliases: carrying concealed · under the shirt · next to the skin
said: kept out of sight, on purpose
when: 1281 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US TH IT VA JP AU HT
object: form=packet materials=cloth,leather,copper,silver,paper worn=chest,sewn-in,pocket,waist,skin
against: witchcraft — said by hoodoo practitioners, who hold that a mojo made for one person has to stay concealed on that person [s:wp-mojo-bag]
against: bad-luck — said by Catholic wearers of the devotional scapular, worn under the clothes as a pledge and a reminder [s:wp-scapular]
against: weapons — said by Thai wearers of takrut, worn at the chest or the waist to protect specific parts of the body [s:wp-takrut]
RESTRICTED: Among Arrernte groups, tjurunga were kept apart from the camp in a sacred place closed to women and to uninitiated men, and in the period described only initiated men could see or touch them. Australian collecting institutions hold material of this kind under access restrictions set by the relevant communities. This atlas prints the restriction and holds no description of those objects or their keeping places.
what: The rule that a charm is not to be seen. Hoodoo mojo bags are made for one person and kept on that person, out of sight: men in a trouser pocket, women clipped to the bra, either pinned to clothing below the waist. Catholic devotional scapulars hang front and back under the outer clothes and are designed to be unobtrusive. A Thai takrut goes under the shirt at the chest or the waist. The charm that hides and the charm that stares out from a windscreen are doing opposite jobs.
story: Concealment has a legal history in hoodoo. Some conjurers hid their charms and others, who made a living from conjure, wore their mojo bags on the outside of their clothes — the cited account records both, and the trade sign and the private charm were different objects. Where the mojo holds a love working, practitioners sometimes specify that it be worn next to the skin; the hiding place is treated as part of whether it works.

Catholic practice built hiding into rule. The Carmelite constitution of 1281 required the scapular to be worn even in bed, under penalty of serious fault, and the constitution of 1369 attached automatic excommunication to a Carmelite saying Mass without one. Short devotional scapulars given to people outside the orders were designed to disappear under ordinary clothes at home and at work. John Paul II said he received his first Brown Scapular at ten and wore it into his papacy.

Thailand hides the object and also fixes its height. The rule reported in the amulet literature is not to wear Buddhist amulets below the waist: they go at the neck or above the waist, out of respect for the Buddha, while takrut, which carry no Buddha image, may go in trouser pockets. Japan hides the contents rather than the object: omamori are carried openly on a bag or a phone strap and customarily never opened, so that the packet is visible and its inside is not.

*Inference —* two opposite logics run through this atlas and they meet here. The eye, the horn and the hand work by being seen — they intercept a look. The sewn bag, the scapular and the takrut work by being unseen. A collection that files both as amulets is filing two different mechanisms under one word, and the clearest way to tell them apart in a museum tray is to ask where the object sat on the body.
how: Under the shirt on a cord; pinned inside clothing; in a pocket; sewn into a lining; clipped where another person will not look. Several traditions add a height rule, a side rule or a no-opening rule on top of the hiding.
today: Live everywhere the practice is. Scapulars are still worn under work clothes; mojo bags are still made to order and concealed; Thai amulets are worn under the shirt in cased frames and lifted out to be examined by dealers with loupes, which is the moment the private object becomes a traded one.
kin: gris-gris — the charm with the strictest hiding rule in this atlas — one owner, on the body, out of sight
kin: brown-scapular — cloth worn front and back under the shirt, and once required even in bed
kin: takrut — the cased scroll worn under the shirt, with a height rule attached to it
kin: omamori — the opposite arrangement: carried in plain view and never opened
kin: nazar — the charm built to be seen, which is what this practice is defined against
kin: sewing-in — how a charm gets hidden when a pocket is not enough
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the tradition that wrote concealed wearing into an order's constitution
kin: most-of-them-are-for-children — the long read on who charms are actually put on, which is also where hiding and showing part company
sources: s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-scapular s:wp-takrut s:wp-thai-buddha-amulet s:wp-omamori s:wp-tjurunga s:wp-australian-institute-of-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-studies

## Akodessawa fetish market (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/akodessewa-market/

native: Marché des Féticheurs (Latin)
aliases: Akodessewa market · Marché d'Akodessewa · Lomé fetish market
said: a-ko-des-SA-wa; the French name is mar-SHAY day fay-tee-SHUR

RESTRICTED: What is done with the materials sold here belongs to Vodun practitioners, and the sources read for this record do not publish it. This atlas prints the trade and stops. It does not reconstruct a rite from scattered accounts and does not fill the gap with a neighbouring tradition's practice.
what: A supply market in the Akodessawa district of Lomé, Togo, for the materials used in Vodun practice. The stock is animal: monkey heads, skulls, dried birds, crocodiles, skins. Sellers work from tables, buyers come with a need, and a practitioner puts the material together for them. The encyclopedia calls it "the world's largest voodoo market", using a spelling this atlas otherwise keeps out of its own sentences.
story: Vodun is long established in Togo, and the route it took is a loop rather than a line. Enslaved people carried Yoruba gods to the Caribbean and South America; there the gods were joined to Catholic saints and church symbols and changed meaning; when freed people and their families came back to West Africa, they built a Vodun practice in the country their families had left.

The word in the market's French name is the difficult one. A fetish here is comparable to an orisha: it may be a god, or a person, a plant, an animal or a material, depending on the rite and the situation, and in the rite it is activated and strengthened. Some are held to have been particular people.

This atlas does not print rite detail. What a practitioner does with a material bought at these tables is the practitioner's to publish, and the sources read for this record do not publish it. What is on the record is the trade: a district, a named market, sellers, stock, and customers who come for a specific thing.

*Inference —* the market is photographed more than it is documented. This project found no published price list, no seller interview and no survey it could cite; the record therefore stays with what the encyclopedia states and says plainly that the rest is missing rather than filling it from a travel column.
today: In trade, on the published account this project has read. No day is marked open or closed below, and no prices are recorded, because none were read.
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition this market supplies materials to
kin: gris-gris — the West African charm whose name travelled to New Orleans while the practice stayed here
kin: nkisi — the Kongo container-object built from assembled materials — the nearest kin in this atlas to what a practitioner makes from these tables

kin: vodou-not-voodoo — the spelling argument this record runs into in its first sentence, and the reason the two-o form appears here only in quotation marks
kin: tooth-and-claw — the sign family most of the stock belongs to, taken from the animal it came from
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this market sits inside: who gets to describe a practice, and in whose words

## El Mercado de las Brujas (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz.json
id: mercado-de-las-brujas-la-paz
native: El Mercado de las Brujas (Latin)
aliases: La Hechicería · The Witches' Market, La Paz
said: mer-KA-do de las BROO-has
when: undated (still carried)
countries: BO
what: A run of stalls on Calle Linares in the El Rosario neighbourhood of La Paz, spilling into Jiménez, Santa Cruz and Illampu. Stock: medicinal plants, retama, amulets, talismans, powders, dried frogs, armadillos, and the sullus — dried llama foetuses — that are buried under the foundations of Bolivian houses as an offering to Pachamama.
story: The market's Spanish name was chosen to be recognisable to foreigners, which is a fact about naming rather than about what is sold. Most of the stallholders are Aymara women, the chifreras. The yatiri who work here are identifiable by their black hats and coca pouches, and the pouches hold amulets, talismans and powders sold for luck, beauty and fertility; they also read fortunes and take commissions for love work and for curses.

The year has a shape. October is the busiest month, because Pachamama offerings cluster there — sellers put roughly 60 per cent of the year's sales in that one month — and February, at Carnival, is the other peak.

One street over in the calendar sits Alasitas. From 24 January, for a month, La Paz holds a fair for Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance, where people buy miniature versions of what they want — food, tools, a house, a car, a diploma — to give to somebody else, on the understanding that the full-sized version follows within the year. Men and, less often, women acting as shaman bless the miniatures; at midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses them too, at the cathedral. The name is Aymara for buy from me.

In 2019 the market was named Intangible Cultural Heritage of La Paz. *Tradition holds —* many of the rituals served here have been adapted to an urban setting, which the encyclopedia attributes to the long aftermath of colonisation rather than to tourism.
today: Trading, on published accounts. October and Carnival are the peaks. No day is marked open or closed below; stall hours are the sellers' own.
kin: ekeko — the god of abundance whose fair, Alasitas, runs from 24 January in the same streets

## Fushimi Inari-taisha (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/fushimi-inari/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/fushimi-inari.json
id: fushimi-inari
native: 伏見稲荷大社 (Han)
aliases: Fushimi Inari Shrine · Oinari-san
said: foo-shee-mee EE-na-ree TIGH-sha
when: 711 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
what: The head shrine of Inari, at the foot of a 233-metre mountain in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto. Paths climb four kilometres to smaller shrines, roofed most of the way by torii gates — roughly 10,000 of them, each one paid for by a Japanese business, about 800 set close enough together to make a tunnel. Tens of thousands of rock altars, otsuka, stand along the way, set up by private people and cut with their own names for Inari.
story: The shrine was formally founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, immigrants from the Korean peninsula who brought irrigation, sericulture and sake brewing into Yamashiro. The Yamashiro fudoki tells it as an arrow, a rice cake that turned into a white bird, and rice growing where the bird came down. Inari began as the kami of rice and agriculture and stays that; merchants took Inari up as the patron of business, which is why the gates are donated by companies.

Donating a torii to have a wish granted, or in thanks for one granted, spread from the Edo period onward and has not stopped. Unlike most Shinto shrines, this one leaves the main object of worship — a mirror — in open view. Foxes stand at the gates as Inari's messengers, often with a granary key in the mouth.

The shrine was in the first rank of state-supported shrines from 1871 to 1946. Police counted 2.69 million worshippers over three days of the new year in 2006, the largest count in western Japan. Around 32,000 branch shrines carry Inari elsewhere in the country.

On the approach, sweet shops sell tsujiura senbei, a folded fortune cracker documented at least to the 19th century and argued to be the ancestor of the American fortune cookie.

*Inference —* an omamori bought at a shrine gate is the shrine's own object, and a head shrine of this size is one of the places the practice runs at scale. This atlas has read no published stock list for this shrine's own counter, so the charm records below are linked as kin rather than as inventory.
today: Open, with no entrance fee. The approach and the main hall are lit all night.
kin: omamori — the brocade packet a shrine issues and renews each year; this is the head shrine of the kami most of Japan asks for business luck
kin: ofuda — the paper or wood tablet taken home to the house shelf from a shrine like this one
kin: omikuji — the drawn fortune, cousin of the folded senbei cracker sold on this approach since the 19th century
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition of luck-bringing objects this shrine's counter belongs to
kin: maneki-neko — the beckoning cat a shop keeps for the same reason a company pays for a torii here
kin: mirror-sign — the sign in the sanctuary — Inari shrines leave the mirror in open view
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the practice, at the scale of 32,000 branch shrines
kin: senso-ji — the other end of Japan's charm trade in this atlas: a temple approach lined with 72 shops rather than a mountain of gates
sources: s:wp-fushimi-inari-taisha s:wp-omamori s:wp-o-mikuji

## Insa-dong (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/insadong/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/insadong.json
id: insadong
native: 인사동 (Hangul)
aliases: Insadong · Mary's Alley
said: IN-sa-dong
when: 1910 CE to now (still carried)
countries: KR
what: A neighbourhood of Jongno District, Seoul, 12.7 hectares of galleries, antique shops, paper and brush shops and tea houses along Insadong-gil and the alleys off it. It holds 40 per cent of South Korea's antique shops and art galleries and 90 per cent of its traditional stationery shops — which means it is where the brush, the ink and the paper a talisman is written on are bought.
story: The antique trade here began as a forced sale. During the Japanese occupation wealthy Korean residents were made to move and to sell their belongings, and the district became the place that trade happened. After the Korean War it turned into a centre of artistic life and cafés; foreign visitors in the 1960s called it Mary's Alley; the 1988 Olympics brought the international trade. In 2000 the area was renovated, and after protest its rapid modernisation was halted for two years.

The temple in the neighbourhood is Jogyesa, a principal Korean Buddhist temple; the central temple of Cheondoism stands nearby, finished in 1921. Calligraphy is demonstrated on the street daily.

The Korean protective charm does not come from a shop here, and the distinction is the point of this record. A pujŏk — bujeok — is produced by a mudang, a shaman, usually built out of hanja characters, handed to clients at the end of a rite and stuck to the inside wall of a house. Mudang are concentrated in Seoul more thickly than anywhere else in the country except Jeju; a late 20th-century Korean Gallup survey found 38 per cent of South Korean adults had consulted one. *Inference —* what Insadong sells is the material and the antique, not the charm; the charm is commissioned, and this atlas has read no source that puts a bujeok counter on this street.
today: Trading, with the backstreets gentrified into cafés and guest houses. About 100,000 visitors on a Sunday were reported in 2000. No day is marked below: the shops keep their own hours and nobody publishes them as one timetable.
kin: bujeok — the Korean written charm — made by a mudang, not sold over a counter; this district supplies the paper and ink it is drawn with
kin: korean-bujeok-craft — the tradition behind that charm, concentrated in Seoul more than anywhere else in the country
kin: paper — the material 90 per cent of the country's traditional stationery shops sell from these alleys
kin: ink — the other half of a written charm, ground and demonstrated on this street daily
kin: inscribing — the practice a stationery district exists to equip
kin: dolhareubang — the Jeju stone grandfather, the Korean object a visitor is likeliest to carry out of a shop here as a miniature

## Khan el-Khalili (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/khan-el-khalili/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/khan-el-khalili.json
id: khan-el-khalili
native: خان الخليلي (Arabic)
aliases: Khan al-Khalili · the Cairo bazaar
said: khaan el-kha-LEE-lee
when: 1382 CE to now (still carried)
countries: EG
what: Cairo's bazaar quarter, in the medieval city between al-Muizz Street, al-Muski Street and the mosque and shrine of al-Hussein. Shops sit at ground level in the walls of old khans — multi-storey merchant inns built round a courtyard — with workshops above and behind them. Goldsmiths hold their own souq inside it, and it is the goldsmiths' lane that matters to this atlas: a charm in Cairo is usually something small, stamped or cast in metal, and bought where metal is sold.
story: The quarter is named after a stable-master. During Sultan Barquq's first reign, between 1382 and 1389, his amir akhur Jaharkas al-Khalili pulled down the Fatimid royal mausoleum that stood here — the Turbat az-Za'faraan, the Saffron Tomb — and put up a large khan in its place. He is reported to have thrown the bones of the Fatimid caliphs onto the rubbish hills east of the city. The khan took his name, then the whole district did.

Sultan al-Ghuri, the last effective Mamluk sultan, demolished al-Khalili's building and rebuilt it in 1511, laying out a souq with monumental stone gates. Two of those gates still stand on Sikkat al-Badistan. By the end of the Mamluk period there were 21 khans and wikalas here; by the end of the 18th century, some 39. El-Fishawy's coffeehouse, still in the lanes, was established in 1773.

The present trade is aimed at visitors and at Cairenes in different lanes. Shops sell souvenirs, antiques and jewellery; the goldsmiths' souq still serves locals; crafts workshops run in the courtyards and upper floors. The scholar Remke Kruk found books on magic and sorcery well represented in street stalls and bookshops across the Muslim world around 2005, from Marrakesh to Cairo to Yemen, alongside religious pamphlets condemning the practices those books describe — an argument conducted stall to stall, in print, in the same streets.

*Inference —* the pharaonic amulet shapes a visitor buys here — scarab, wedjat eye, ankh — are jewellery made now, not survivals. This atlas has read no source that surveys what the Khan's stalls actually stock, so the record stops at what the goldsmiths' souq and the workshops are documented to be.

The market has twice been attacked. A suicide bombing on 7 April 2005 killed 21 people; a second attack on 22 February 2009 killed a 17-year-old French visitor and injured 22 people.
today: Trading, and oriented to tourism in its best-known lanes, as of the most recent published account this project has read. No day is marked open or closed below: the district's hours are the individual shopkeepers' and nobody publishes them as a timetable.
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition whose shapes are cut in this city's gold four thousand years after the workshops that invented them closed
kin: scarab — sold here now as jewellery; the excavated ones are a mile away in the Egyptian Museum
kin: hamsa — the hand sold across this trade's whole range, from Morocco to the Gulf
kin: taweez — the written charm the bookstalls serve — Kruk found the handbooks and the pamphlets against them on the same streets
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition those handbooks belong to, argued over in print in this quarter
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice, in a quarter purpose-built for it since the Mamluks taxed stalls into stone shops
kin: grand-bazaar — the Ottoman answer to the same problem — how to roof a city's trade and lock it at night
kin: marrakesh-souk — the other end of Kruk's line, where the same books are sold
sources: s:wp-khan-el-khalili s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-amulet

## Mana Whenua, Te Papa (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/te-papa-taonga/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/te-papa-taonga.json
id: te-papa-taonga
native: Mana Whenua ()
aliases: Taonga Māori at Te Papa · Level 4, Te Papa
said: MA-na FE-nu-a
when: 1998 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NZ
RESTRICTED: Photography is not permitted in Mana Whenua, on the museum's own rule. Te Papa separately asks that images of taonga be used only for research, study, personal and educational purposes, because the material holds significant cultural importance to iwi. This atlas prints those limits, keeps to them, and does not reproduce Te Papa taonga images or print detail about restricted taonga beyond what the museum itself publishes.
what: Te Papa's permanent Māori exhibition, on Level 4 of the Wellington waterfront building. The museum's own description: taonga tuku iho — treasures handed down — "ranging from weaving, carving, and pounamu pendants, to waka and whare". A whare is a house; the whare here is Te Hau ki Tūranga, a carved meeting house standing inside the gallery. A waka is a canoe; Teremoe, a waka taua or war canoe from the Whanganui region used in the wars of the mid-1800s, is in the same room. Photography is not allowed. The lighting is deliberately low.
story: These are not curios, and the museum does not frame them as any. Its collections page states the principle it works under: "Mana Taonga is a recognition of the power of taonga to communicate deep truths about our people." It counts more than 30,000 taonga registered in the Taonga Māori collection, from ancestral carvings, personal ornaments, garments and weaponry through to flaked stone, bird bone and shell from excavations, and it says the Mana Taonga principle guides its approach to access and research, aiming at "the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga".

The hei-tiki make the point about how objects travel. Te Papa holds over 200 of them, the largest single group anywhere; the British Museum has about fifty. Some were exchanged or given to European travellers and sailors at the earliest point of contact, and, in the encyclopedia's flat phrasing, "the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes". The stone itself is now legally Māori: in 1997 the Crown handed ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu back to the South Island iwi Ngāi Tahu as part of their Claims Settlement. Pounamu is nephrite jade and bowenite, found only in the South Island, and Māori classify it by colour — kahurangi, īnanga, kawakawa, tangiwai.

The whare at the centre of the gallery is the clearest case in the building. Te Hau ki Tūranga is a nineteenth-century Rongowhakaata carved meeting house, confiscated by the Crown in 1867 and later held by Te Papa; ownership was returned to Rongowhakaata through the iwi's Treaty settlement, and the house stayed in the museum while the iwi-in-residence exhibition Ko Rongowhakaata: Ruku i te Pō, Ruku i te Ao ran from September 2017 to February 2022. The museum kept the object and gave back the title.

Te Papa also does the asking. Karanga Aotearoa is, in the museum's own words, "the government mandated authority that negotiates the repatriation of Māori and Moriori ancestral remains on behalf of Māori and Moriori"; Cabinet agreed in May 2003 that Te Papa should act for the government in returning kōiwi and kōimi tangata — ancestral skeletal remains — and toi moko, preserved tattooed heads held in institutions abroad. Between 1 July 2003 and 1 May 2024 it repatriated 850 Māori and Moriori ancestral remains from overseas institutions, from Australia, Austria, Canada, France, Germany, Sweden, the United Kingdom, the United States and elsewhere, and returned 76 to iwi within New Zealand. A Repatriation Advisory Panel oversees it, and iwi representatives set the place, the time and the details of each return.

From 29 August 2026 the carving argument is on show at scale. He Toi Whakairo: The Art of Māori Carving, running to August 2031 inside Mana Whenua on Level 4, puts more than 140 whakairo — carvings — from seven centuries in one place, many never exhibited before, under the whakataukī he toi whakairo, he mana tangata: the art of carving is the dignity of people.
today: Open every day, 10am to 6pm, except Christmas Day. Entry is free for New Zealanders and people living in New Zealand and NZ$35 for international visitors aged 16 and over, as published on 17 September 2026; some exhibitions and experiences are ticketed on top. Mana Whenua is free with museum entry, is listed as wheelchair accessible, has variable lighting, and carries a no-photography rule. This project has not stood on Level 4.
kin: te-papa — the museum this gallery is the heart of, and the one that asks other institutions worldwide for ancestral remains back
kin: hei-tiki — the pounamu neck pendant held here in the largest number anywhere, over 200 of them
kin: hei-matau — the hook pendant of the same stone and the same collection
kin: maori-taonga — the tradition whose own terms — taonga tuku iho, mana taonga, kaitiaki — this gallery is written in
kin: jade — the stone, called pounamu here, whose naturally occurring supply the Crown returned to Ngāi Tahu in 1997
kin: inheriting — the practice the word taonga tuku iho names: a treasure handed down, not a thing acquired
kin: quai-branly — the Paris museum this one asked for Māori remains and got them back from in January 2012
kin: british-museum-room-1 — the other side of the same argument: a London room that keeps what it holds, where this one gave a meeting house's title back
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the long read on restriction; the no-photography rule on Level 4 is one of its worked examples
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on ownership, argued from the claimant's side — 850 ancestors returned since 2003

What customers ask for is not what the market's name implies. Ramos reports that money, not love, is the most common request — prosperity formulas outsell love potions at the stalls she stood at.
