## Mercado de Sonora (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/mercado-de-sonora/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/mercado-de-sonora.json
id: mercado-de-sonora
native: Mercado de Sonora (Latin)
aliases: Sonora Market · the Sonora witchcraft market
said: mer-KA-do de so-NO-ra
when: 1957 CE to now (still carried)
countries: MX
what: A municipal covered market in Colonia Merced Balbuena, southeast of Mexico City's historic centre: one long metal nave, narrow aisles, traders grouped by what they sell. Pottery in one section, party supplies in another, live animals in a third. Two aisles at the back carry medicinal plants and the goods for ritual — candles, amulets, oils, soaps, powders — and those two aisles are why the market is known outside the city.
story: The city built it. Mercado de Sonora opened on 23 September 1957, one of a set of public markets set up to organise and regulate retail trade, descended from the pre-Hispanic tianguis, the street market. At the market's fiftieth anniversary in 2007 the party included mariachis and a limpia, a cleansing, to clear the building of bad energy.

Herbal medicine and ritual goods are not two trades here but one, because Mexican herbal medicine has been tied to religious and magical practice for centuries. Avocado leaves for inflammation, chiranthodendron for the heart, jacaranda flowers for the stomach. Dried rattlesnake against cancer. Crosses of ocote wood for luck; chains of garlic against harm; and a seed called deer's eye — ojo de venado — against the evil eye. Candles come in sizes, shapes and colours, each colour with its own function.

The traffic is countable. An estimated 2,000 people come each weekend specifically for that section, which is one of the city's centres for Santería and for the veneration of Santa Muerte. The most popular goods are for love: candles, oils, amulets, soaps, needles, lotions, herbs, and services — spell casting, cleansings — sold under names like ven a mi, come to me, and miel de amor, honey of love.

Prices carry their moment. During the H1N1 scare of 2009 trade fell by about half, but a ten-herb blend against flu — eucalyptus, bougainvillea, tejocote — kept herb sellers solvent at 80 pesos a kilo; Santa Muerte sellers reported moving white dresses for the images, white being the colour of health.

The market carries its costs in public. Street peddlers fill what is left of the car park and spill into the surrounding lanes on Saturdays; the building leaks, its floors and ramps are in poor condition, and market representatives put that down to borough corruption and to officials extorting traders. Police have raided the animal aisles over protected species.
today: Trading, with Saturday the busiest day and the widest stock. The Linares family, five generations of cartonería makers and the inventors of the alebrije, still work in workshops just behind the market. No day is marked open or closed below: stall hours are the traders' own.

kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the tradition the candles, saints and cleansings belong to
kin: milagro — the stamped metal votive of the same devotional economy, offered where these goods are bought
kin: horseshoe — sold here too — a European charm that crossed and stayed
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice, in a building the city put up in 1957 to regulate it
kin: mercado-de-las-brujas-lima — the Lima counterpart, the same trade under a different name

## Merkato (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/merkato-addis/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/merkato-addis.json
id: merkato-addis
native: መርካቶ (Ge'ez)
aliases: Addis Mercato · Addis Merkato
said: mer-KA-to, from the Italian for market
when: 1936 CE to now (still carried)
countries: ET
what: An open-air market covering several square miles of the Addis Ketema district of Addis Ababa, and the name of the neighbourhood it fills. An estimated 13,000 people work in about 7,100 business entities. Most of it is wholesale, sorted into sections the traders call terras: coffee, spices, scrap metal, furniture, electronics. Coffee is the main good passing through.
story: The market is a product of occupation policy. Addis Ababa's older market stood near St George's Church, where the City Hall is now; the Italian occupiers of the 1930s moved it west, to land around the premises of Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis Dinagde, and kept the old site — renamed Piazza, with European-style shop windows — for Europeans. The Arab traders of Piazza moved half a mile west after them; local shopkeepers displaced those traders in turn, and since the 1960s Merkato has been a mostly local market. It grew without a plan.

This record has to state a gap rather than fill it. The Ethiopian protective object in this atlas is the talismanic scroll — the ketab, written in Ge'ez on hide — and it is not a market good. A scroll is commissioned by the patient from a dabtara, an unordained figure in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, who cuts it to the patient's own measure: to the height of the body for head-to-toe protection, longer to hang on a wall. The making includes a sacrifice of the animal whose hide is used, standing for the person the scroll is for. Activation needs a third party literate in Ge'ez to read it aloud.

*Inference —* that is why a market this size is thin in this atlas. A commissioned object made to a body's measurements does not have a stall. This project searched for a published source placing the scroll trade inside Merkato and found none it could cite; the record says so instead of inventing an aisle.
today: Trading, as Africa's largest open-air market. It is not primarily a tourist market: most sections are wholesale. No day is marked open or closed below.
kin: ethiopian-magic-scroll — the Ethiopian protective object this atlas expects near a market this size and cannot source at this address — it is commissioned, not sold
kin: ethiopian-scroll-craft — the tradition behind that scroll: a dabtara, a hide, and a text in Ge'ez cut to one person's height
kin: coptic-cross-tattoo — the other Ethiopian and Coptic mark in this atlas, worn on the body rather than carried
kin: parchment — the material the scroll is written on, and the reason its making starts with an animal
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice this record is filed under, and the one the Ethiopian scroll does not use

## Monastiraki (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/monastiraki/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/monastiraki.json
id: monastiraki
native: Μοναστηράκι (Greek)
aliases: Monastiraki flea market · Monastiraki Square
said: mo-na-sti-RA-ki, 'little monastery'
countries: GR
what: A flea-market neighbourhood in the old town of Athens, built round Monastiraki Square and running along Pandrossou and Adrianou streets. Clothing, souvenirs and specialist shops; a metro station on the square; and, in the souvenir windows, trays of the blue glass eye.
story: The district takes its name from the square, and the square from the Church of the Pantanassa standing in it. It is one of Athens's main shopping districts and its best-known bargain quarter.

The object this atlas comes for has a Greek name. The bead a Turkish seller calls nazar boncuğu is máti in Greek, the eye, and it belongs to a tradition Greek authors were already describing in classical antiquity: Hesiod, Callimachus, Plato, Theocritus and Plutarch all mention the harmful look, and Peter Walcot's Envy and the Greeks listed more than a hundred ancient works that do. Greeks hung talismans in the house and wore amulets; Peisistratus hung a grasshopper figure before the Acropolis, a few hundred metres uphill from this square.

The trade is not a museum piece. A 2015 Pew survey of central and eastern Europe found a median of 48 per cent of adults reporting belief in the evil eye, with 66 per cent in Greece — the joint highest figure in the survey. The bead is also, in the encyclopedia's phrase, a popular choice of souvenir with tourists, and both those sentences describe the same stall.

*Inference —* the Monastiraki article itemises no charm, and this record does not claim a particular shop. What it claims is the pairing: the densest souvenir trade in Athens, in a country where two adults in three report the belief the object answers.
today: Trading, as a flea market and a tourist quarter. No day is marked open or closed below; the shops keep their own hours and no timetable is published for the district.

## Quiapo Church (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/quiapo-church/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/quiapo-church.json
id: quiapo-church
native: Basilika Menor at Pambansang Dambana ni Jesus Nazareno (Latin)
aliases: Minor Basilica and National Shrine of Jesus Nazareno · Simbahan ng Quiapo · Parish of Saint John the Baptist
said: kee-AH-po
when: 1588 CE to now (still carried)
countries: PH
what: A Catholic basilica in the Quiapo district of Manila, housing the Jesús Nazareno, a dark statue of Christ carrying the cross. Outside it, on Plaza Miranda and in the streets around the building, stalls sell herbs, oils, candles and amulets. Two systems trade at one address, and both have said so in public.
story: The church has burnt, fallen and been rebuilt since 1588: destroyed by Limahong's men in 1574, burnt in 1603, damaged by the British in 1762, burnt in 1791 with the image spared, thrown down by the earthquake of 1863, burnt again in 1929. The present reinforced-concrete building, by the architect Juan Nakpil, was finished in 1935 and expanded in 1984-86. Pope John Paul II raised it to a minor basilica in 1987; it was declared a national shrine in December 2023.

The devotion is enormous. The feast of the Traslación on 9 January re-enacts the image's transfer from Intramuros, and 6.5 million devotees took part in 2024. Every Friday is Quiapo Day, with a novena and thousands in attendance; devotees climb a narrow stair to kiss the statue's foot or wipe it with a handkerchief they bring each visit. Men who carry the image walk under a panata, a vow. In October 2024 the Archbishop of Manila decreed the church's name changed to the Minor Basilica and National Shrine of Jesus Nazareno, dropping the usual English name to shift attention from the image's colour to the name of Christ.

The plaza trade is the other half. Agimat — anting-anting in its folklorised form — is the Filipino word for an amulet, and the practice that goes with it: most bear Latin inscriptions, most come with a small book of incantations to be read on Good Friday. Agimat merchants set up near churches, in the courtyard or the marketplace alongside, and Quiapo is the district the encyclopedia names when it names one. Filipino fighters wore anting-anting against the Spanish and the Americans; Macario Sakay wore a vest of religious images and Latin phrases.

The church has not been quiet about what else the stalls sell. Published accounts record peddlers of unsafe abortifacients and untested herbal remedies working the vicinity, and the Archdiocese of Manila condemning practices connected with them; Cardinal Gaudencio Rosales issued canonical excommunications in relation to abortion near the shrine. Abortion is illegal in the Philippines, and the accounts tie the trade to people who cannot afford a surgical procedure.
today: In use as a basilica and a national shrine, with the plaza trade running alongside it. This project has not read the basilica's own published timetable, so no day is marked open or closed below — the Friday novena is a cited fact about the week, not a statement that other days are shut.
kin: anting-anting — the amulet sold at this address — the encyclopedia names Quiapo when it names where agimat merchants set up
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the church's own class of blessed object, sold and worn a few metres from the other trade
kin: latin-american-folk-catholic — the parallel from across the Pacific: the same galleon route, the same doubling of saint and charm
kin: divine-name — the sign most agimat carry, in Latin, cut or printed on metal
kin: blessing-at-a-shrine — the practice that draws millions here on 9 January and thousands every Friday
kin: herb — the other stock of the plaza stalls, and the part the Archdiocese has condemned
kin: milagro — the Catholic votive kin — metal offered for a body part, where the panata offers a walk
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this address argues in public: two systems, one plaza, both naming the other

## Room 1: Enlightenment, the British Museum (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/british-museum-room-1/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/british-museum-room-1.json
id: british-museum-room-1
aliases: The Enlightenment Gallery · The King's Library · BM Room 1
when: 1753 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: One long room off the Great Court, lined with tall wall presses and galleried in dark wood. The museum calls it the oldest room in the present building, put up for King George III's library and now holding a permanent display of eighteenth-century collecting. The objects are not grouped by country. They are grouped in seven disciplines an eighteenth-century collector would have recognised — the natural world, the birth of archaeology, art and civilisation, classifying the world, ancient scripts, ritual and religion, trade and discovery — so a Pacific shield, a Sumerian tablet and an astrolabe stand within a few steps of each other.
story: This is the room about how the rest of the museum filled up. Sir Hans Sloane's cabinets are here; the museum's own gallery text says his collection, with several additional libraries, became the foundation of the British Museum, established by Act of Parliament on 7 June 1753.

The museum does not hedge about what else the period was. Its own page for this room says the Enlightenment "witnessed the aggressive global expansion of European colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade" and that "This room's displays reflect the close connection between Enlightenment and empire." Under Ritual and religion it writes that "Christian mistrust of superstition and idols, rituals and magic led to ignorance about other religions", that scholars set out to dispel that by studying the religions they met, collecting religious artefacts and grouping gods into families — and that "Much of this activity took place within the context of colonialism." Under Trade and discovery it names the East India and Royal Africa Companies, "whose wealth was made possible through the use of enslaved labour".

One object in this room carries a live claim. The museum's catalogue places a bark-and-wood shield, registration number Oc1978,Q.839, on display in Room 1, Trade & Discovery, Wall Press 96; it was donated by the Lords of the Admiralty and first registered and given a Q number in 1978. Rodney Kelly, a Gweagal man from Bermagui, began campaigning for the shield's return after it appeared in the exhibition Encounters at the National Museum of Australia, 27 November 2015 to 28 March 2016, and travelled to Britain three times, once in 2016 and twice in 2017; the chair of the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council, Noeleen Timbery, has backed the return. The British Museum has refused, on the ground that British law does not permit it to hand the object over.

The identification is itself contested, and the museum says so on its own object page. Its curator's comments open: "Once thought to have been obtained on Captain Cook's first voyage to the Pacific, when he visited Botany Bay near present day Sydney, New South Wales, in 1770." The record now dates the shield "1771 (or earlier)" and finds the match with Sydney Parkinson's and John Frederick Miller's drawings only an apparent one. *Inference —* an object whose owner and whose date are both argued over is the right object to meet first in a museum, and this room is where a reader of this atlas should start before walking to the Egyptian cases.
today: Open with the rest of the museum, free, and unchanged in layout. The museum's own warning stands beside its hours: "Occasionally we may need to close galleries at short notice." This project has not stood in the room.

kin: met-egyptian-galleries — the comparison across the Atlantic: rooms that show what was dug, where this one shows who did the collecting

## Sensō-ji (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/senso-ji/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/senso-ji.json
id: senso-ji
native: 浅草寺 (Han)
aliases: Asakusa Kannon · Kinryū-zan Sensō-ji
said: SEN-soh-jee
when: 628 CE to now (still carried)
countries: JP
RESTRICTED: The temple's principal image of Kannon is a hibutsu — a hidden Buddha, never shown to the public. Accounts give it as gold and about 5.5 centimetres high, and say its true details are unknown. This atlas prints the restriction and stops there.
what: Tokyo's oldest-established Buddhist temple, in Asakusa, dedicated to Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion. You reach the main hall through two gates and a shopping street: the Kaminarimon with its 700-kilogram red lantern, then Nakamise-dōri, 250 metres and about 72 shops, then the Hōzōmon. Omikuji stalls stand inside the precinct and along the approach — shake a numbered stick from a metal canister, read the answer out of one of a hundred drawers.
story: The temple's origin story is a statue in a net: in 628 two brothers fishing the Sumida pulled up an image of Kannon, and the village headman turned his house into a temple for it. The first documented mention is later, in the Kamakura-period Azuma Kagami, which has Asakusa carpenters called to Kamakura in 1181. Tokugawa Ieyasu made it an official place of prayer for the shogunate in 1590.

The shops came with permission. In 1685 the temple licensed businesses on the main approach in exchange for their cleaning the grounds, and Nakamise has been a selling street ever since — cleared by government order in May 1885, rebuilt in brick that December, flattened by the 1923 earthquake, rebuilt in concrete in 1925, burnt out in the firebombing of 10 March 1945. The main hall went in that raid too and was rebuilt between 1951 and 1958, now under a titanium roof.

The temple is the 13th stop on the Bandō Sanjūsankasho pilgrimage route and the most visited religious site in the world, at over 30 million people a year. For a suggested donation of 100 yen a visitor may consult the omikuji oracle.

*Tradition holds —* the shops on a temple approach are not a later commercial layer but a continuous trade in selling to pilgrims who walked here, which is the encyclopedia's own framing of Nakamise.
today: Open, with the Nakamise shops on the approach and the omikuji stalls in use. This project has not read the temple's published timetable, so no day is marked open or closed below.
kin: omikuji — the drawn fortune, at 100 yen suggested and a hundred possible drawers, taken at stalls inside this precinct
kin: omamori — the packet a temple or shrine issues; Nakamise is the selling street that grew on this approach in 1685
kin: ofuda — the tablet carried home from a temple like this one to the household shelf
kin: daruma — the round vow-doll of Japan's market fairs, kin of what the approach's shops have always sold
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition of luck objects this approach trades in
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice, licensed by the temple in 1685 in exchange for sweeping the grounds
kin: fushimi-inari — the Kyoto shrine at the other scale — a mountain of donated gates instead of a street of shops
kin: market-stall-sign — the drawn signage of a selling street, which Nakamise has carried through four rebuildings

## Tha Phrachan amulet market (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/tha-phrachan/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/tha-phrachan.json
id: tha-phrachan
native: ตลาดพระเครื่องท่าพระจันทร์ (Thai)
aliases: Tha Phra Chan market · Amulet Market, Bangkok
said: tàa prá-jan
countries: TH
what: Bangkok's main amulet market, running in the lanes beside Thammasat University and the Chao Phraya river pier of the same name. Stalls are trays and glass-topped cases; buyers arrive with jeweller's loupes and go over a two-centimetre clay tablet the way a coin dealer goes over a coin.
story: Tha Phrachan is the market Thai writing on amulets names first when it names any. Wikipedia's account puts it plainly: famous markets for amulets include Tha Phrachan Market next to Thammasat University, and rare pieces often require expert authentication because forgeries are common.

What the loupes are for is the trade's central problem. A phra khrueang is valued by which temple pressed it, which monk consecrated it, and when — facts that live in the clay's texture, the mould's flaws and a certificate, not in the image on the front. *Tradition holds —* the specialist who reads those tells for a fee is as much a part of this market as the seller.

The scale is not small. When the Jatukham Rammathep amulet peaked in 2007, that single type's market reached twenty billion baht in a year before the bubble burst in late 2007, leaving stock that could be had cheap. *Inference —* a market that can move that much in twelve months is a financial market with devotional objects in it, and the argument over which of those two things it mainly is runs among Thai commentators, not between Thais and outsiders.
today: Still trading as of the most recent published accounts this project has read. Hours are not published as a timetable: stalls keep their own, the lanes are busiest in daylight, and weekends draw the collectors. This project has not stood there, so no day is marked either way below.
kin: phra-khrueang — the object this whole market exists to trade, authenticate and argue about
kin: takrut — sold from the same trays — the rolled metal scroll beside the clay tablet
kin: palad-khik — also sold here, and the one stall-holders are likeliest to keep behind the counter
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition whose economy this market is
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice in its densest form — price, loupe, certificate, and a monk's name
kin: the-fake-market — the long read about authentication, which starts here because this is where the loupes are

## Thamel (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/kathmandu-thamel/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/kathmandu-thamel.json
id: kathmandu-thamel
native: ठमेल (Devanagari)
aliases: Tha Bahi · Thamel, Kathmandu
said: TA-mel
when: 1970 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NP
what: A commercial neighbourhood of narrow alleys in Kathmandu, about 1.4 kilometres north of Durbar Square. Shops run wall to wall: trekking gear, handicrafts, woollens, music, groceries, guest houses. It is the district a visitor to Nepal buys things in, which makes it the counter across which most Himalayan protective objects leave the country.
story: The name comes from Tha Bahi, which places the district's root in the Newar community, the indigenous people of the Kathmandu Valley. Thamel has been the centre of Kathmandu's tourist trade for over four decades, since the years of the overland hippie route, and it is now the valley's densest concentration of shops aimed at outsiders.

What the shops stock is where this atlas has to be careful. The encyclopedia's account lists food, trekking gear, music, handicrafts, souvenirs and woollens, and itemises no charm. *Inference —* prayer flags, rudraksha strings, dzi beads and gau boxes are what a Himalayan souvenir lane carries, and this project has read no survey of Thamel's stalls, so the objects below are linked as kin of the district rather than asserted as stock.

What can be cited is where the materials come from. Rudraksha — the seed of Elaeocarpus ganitrus, strung and counted by Shaivites — is cultivated in the Himalayan foothills, and the most popular varieties are found around Kathmandu and the Arun Valley. Printed cloth prayer flags reached Nepal and Tibet through the Indian monk Atisha, who died in 1054. Dzi beads are found in Tibet and in neighbouring Nepal, Bhutan, Ladakh and Sikkim, and Tibetans treat them as hereditary gems rather than as purchases.
today: Trading, and the pre-base camp for mountaineering: gear shops, money changers, agents, guest houses. No day is marked below, because the alleys keep shop hours and nobody publishes them.
kin: rudraksha — the seed whose best-known varieties grow in this valley and the Arun, strung for counting before it is ever sold to a visitor
kin: lungta-flag — the printed cloth flag Atisha brought to Nepal and Tibet, hung on passes above this city
kin: dzi-bead — the Himalayan agate a shop here will offer and a Tibetan family would not sell; the difference is the whole argument
kin: gau-box — the amulet case the Himalaya wears at the throat, made in metal by the valley's own smiths
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition most of the objects in these alleys belong to
kin: barkhor-lhasa — the pilgrim circuit on the other side of the range, where the same objects are bought by the people who use them
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on copies, which a souvenir lane selling a hereditary object cannot dodge

## The amulet and charm cases, Pitt Rivers Museum (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/pitt-rivers-charms/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/pitt-rivers-charms.json
id: pitt-rivers-charms
aliases: Amulets and Charms, Pitt Rivers · Cases C26A–C31B
when: 1884 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: Eight glass-topped cases on the Court, the ground floor of the museum, with deep drawers under them. The museum's own guide names them: C26A, C27A and C28A hold Amulets and Charms; C29A, Amulets, Charms, and Divination; C30A, Charms against the Evil Eye; C30B, Amulets, Cures, and Charms; C31A, Magic and Trial by Ordeal; C31B, Amulets and Charms for Animals. A Neapolitan silver cimaruta, a blue glass eye bead from Hebron, a Japanese glass hy-o-tan, a string of blue beads that hung round a donkey's neck in Istanbul and an Algerian sheep's shoulder blade written on in Arabic all sit within arm's reach of one another, because they answer the same problem.
story: The museum publishes the total: almost 6,000 amulets and charms in the collections, though not all of them are on display. They come from everywhere, England included.

The largest single block arrived by sale and then by transfer. Adrien de Mortillet, 1853–1931, son of the archaeologist Gabriel de Mortillet and later a lecturer and chair at the School of Anthropology in Paris, built an amulet collection drawn from five continents and from antiquity to the early twentieth century. In 1931, a few months before he died, he sold it to Henry Wellcome's museum in London. It was transferred to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985. In 2012 the museum catalogued more than 2,500 of them under a project called Small Blessings, funded by Arts Council England's Designation Development Fund and running February to September that year, and put the records online.

The English cases owe a bank cashier. Edward Lovett swapped alpine plants grown in seashells for the charms Londoners had in their pockets and gave the results to Oxford; the museum's own England: The Other Within project counts 216 objects from him, 55 of them English, accessioned 1893 to 1911 — the encyclopedia gives the span as 1896 to 1911, and this record prints both rather than choosing. Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets, bought across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, came by the same 1985 route out of Wellcome.

The cases are grouped by what an object does, not by where it is from, because the founder's 1884 Deed of Gift requires it: a clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers". The museum states plainly that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm, and that it has kept the arrangement because the Deed does.

So it has gone at the labels instead. Labelling Matters, led by the director Laura Van Broekhoven with the research associate Marenka Thompson-Odlum and funded through the TORCH Heritage Seed Fund and Knowledge Exchange, reviews the language of the permanent displays; its stated aim is to "identify areas of improvement and to trial ways of changing our public texts where derogatory and other problematic language is used". In 2020 the museum took human remains off display, including the tsantsas shown since the 1940s. With the Museum of Natural History it returned the remains of 17 Aboriginal Australians to the Australian government in 2022, and in 2026 agreed to repatriate Naga skeletal remains, some of which had been shown in a case titled Treatment of Dead Enemies. That last one reaches these cases directly: the museum's own amulets guide describes an object made to be put in the spring of the Rengma Naga village of Tesophenyu, and lists what its wrappings hold.

The guide is careful about the claims and this atlas keeps its wording. It defines an amulet with the Oxford English Dictionary — "Anything worn about the person as a charm preventative against evil, mischief, disease, witchcraft, etc." — and explains sympathetic magic as meaning "that the appearance of an object resembles, in some way, the cure or protection it is believed to offer". Of the Maasai ivory amulet hung round a cow's neck it reports the Maasai term inkonyek, people with 'eyes', whose envious glance is held to be deadliest to young children and calves. Of a Yoruba ori box it records that the original owner assured the collector it was filled with 'juju' but could not say what was inside.

*Inference —* a case that puts a Naples cimaruta next to a Nagaland packet is making an argument, and the museum now argues with its own furniture.
today: On the Court floor, free, and still laid out on the founder's principle while the museum rewrites what is written on the cards. Displays are rotated, and the guide this record leans on was revised in March 2010 by Kate White, then Head of Access and Public Relations, so a case number is the museum's last published word and not a promise about today. This project has not stood in the Court.
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — the museum these cases sit in, and the Deed of Gift that keeps them laid out this way
kin: augustus-pitt-rivers — the founder whose sorting rule — by purpose, not by place — is the reason a cimaruta and a Naga packet share a case
kin: edward-lovett — the donor of the English charms, 216 objects accessioned between 1893 and 1911
kin: walter-hildburgh — the other collector whose amulets came here from Wellcome in the 1985 transfer
kin: cimaruta — the Neapolitan silver sprig the guide singles out, made against the malocchio and always of silver
kin: nazar — the blue glass eye in these cases, one of them donated as early as 1885
kin: hamsa — the Hand of Fatima in gold filigree from Tunis, and a silver Hebrew-inscribed hand beside it
kin: hagstone — the perforated pebble on a string that sits at the front of the sympathetic magic material
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — the shop-bought descendant of the glass eyes in case C30A, which the guide says are still being made
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition these cases document most densely, because Lovett walked London
kin: wellcome-lovett — the London end of the same story: what Wellcome kept, and what came here in 1985
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read; this museum answers it out loud, on its own labels, since 2020
sources: s:web-prm-amulets-guide s:web-prm-visit-us s:web-prm-small-blessings s:web-prm-small-blessings-intro s:web-prm-small-blessings-mortillet s:web-prm-labelling-matters s:web-prm-lovett s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum s:web-walter-hildburgh-wikipedia s:wp-edward-lovett

## The Barkhor (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/barkhor-lhasa/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/barkhor-lhasa.json
id: barkhor-lhasa
native: བར་སྐོར་ (Tibetan)
aliases: Barkhor Street · Bakuo · Pargor
said: bar-KOR; Wylie bar-skor
when: 600 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN
what: A ring of street about a kilometre round, circling the Jokhang temple in the old city of Lhasa. It is at once the city's commercial centre and a circuit walked as devotion. Traffic goes one way, clockwise, and some of the people on it are not walking but measuring the ring out in full-body prostrations.
story: The circuit came from the temple. Songtsen Gampo and Princess Wencheng led the move to Lhasa and built the Jokhang; people began to turn around the temple, and the path their feet wore became a road. That road is one of the three circumambulation routes of Lhasa — the others are the Lingkhor and the Woesor — and it is the oldest street in the city, dated in origin to the 7th century CE and still carrying the plan of the old town.

Tibetans call it the holy road. The direction is not decorative: you walk with the turning of the prayer cylinder, which is to say clockwise, right shoulder to the temple.

The street is also the busiest commercial one in the old city. *Inference —* the objects this atlas is about are made and worn across this region — the agate dzi bead, the amulet box at the throat, the printed cloth flag — but no source read for this record itemises a Barkhor stall, and this record does not furnish one. On the street's present policing and regulation this atlas has read nothing it can cite, and it does not speculate.
today: In use as both a market street and a kora, on the published accounts this project has read. No day is marked open or closed below.
kin: tibetan-protection — the tradition whose objects this circuit's walkers carry
kin: gau-box — the amulet case worn at the throat on this plateau, holding what a lama has given
kin: dzi-bead — the agate Tibetans hold as a hereditary gem, not a purchase; Lhasa is the city it is priced in
kin: sungkhor — the folded protection-wheel a monastery issues, which is what a pilgrim on this ring is likeliest to be carrying
kin: lungta-flag — the wind horse printed on cloth, replaced across Tibet at the new year
kin: counting-beads — the practice the circuit is walked with, one round of the ring to one round of the string

## The Egyptian galleries, the Metropolitan Museum of Art (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/met-egyptian-galleries/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/met-egyptian-galleries.json
id: met-egyptian-galleries
aliases: Met Egyptian Art · Department of Egyptian Art
when: 1870 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US
what: A chain of rooms along the museum's north side, running from the predynastic material through to Roman Egypt and ending at the Temple of Dendur in its glass hall. For this atlas it is the densest walkable run of amulets anywhere: wedjat eyes in faience, carnelian, obsidian and gold, scarabs, cippi, and trays of small figures, laid out in numbered galleries a visitor can name. Faience, which the labels use constantly, is crushed quartz fired with a glaze that comes out of the kiln blue or green.
story: The Met's Egyptian collection was not mostly bought. The department's own page says the museum's three decades of archaeological work in Egypt began in 1906, and the encyclopedia account puts almost half the present collection down to the excavation seasons of 1906 to 1941. That is why a Met amulet more often carries a find-spot than a dealer's name: a small gold amulet in Gallery 109, accession 22.1.58, is credited to MMA excavations, 1920–22, from the Memphite Region.

The size of the collection is published two ways and this record prints both. The Wikipedia account gives more than 26,000 pieces across forty galleries, almost all on display; the department's own page, read on 17 September 2026, says "approximately 30,000 objects". Neither is wrong on its own terms and this project has not read a reconciliation.

Walk it and the amulets sort themselves by gallery. Gallery 120 holds a run of faience wedjat eyes from about 1386–1347 BCE, entered in 1911 on the Rogers Fund. Gallery 127 holds one cut in gold, 332–30 BCE, and one in obsidian. Gallery 130 holds a long faience-and-aragonite wedjat, 6.5 centimetres, bought in 1926 on the Edward S. Harkness Gift. Gallery 128 holds the Metternich Stela, catalogued as Magical Stela with Horus the Child, 360–343 BCE, and Gallery 134 a shelf of smaller cippi in steatite, soapstone and faience — the same design shrunk from 83.5 centimetres to under 5.

How the objects got here is still being worked out in public, and not always by the museum first. In September 2022 New York law enforcement seized 27 objects on three warrants for return to Italy and Egypt. The museum has since published a statement on collecting practices and hired a provenance-research manager with a team of three. *Inference —* an excavation credit line is a stronger provenance than a purchase, and the 1906–1941 seasons are the reason this room reads differently from a room filled by a dealer; it is not the same thing as saying every object here arrived cleanly.

The licence is the other half of why this atlas keeps pointing here. Since 2017 every Met image of a public-domain work carries a Creative Commons Zero dedication, which is on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list. A photograph of a Met wedjat can be reproduced, cropped and altered with no permission asked. The dedication covers the museum's photographs. It says nothing about who the objects belong to.
today: Open six days a week; closed Wednesdays. General admission on 17 September 2026 is US$30 for adults, US$22 for seniors and for visitors with a disability, US$17 for students and free for children 12 and under, with pay-what-you-wish admission for New York State residents and for New York, New Jersey and Connecticut students. The museum lists the Ancient West Asia and Ancient Cyprus galleries as closed for renovation as of that date; the Egyptian galleries are not on that list. This project has not stood in them.
kin: metropolitan-museum — the institution these rooms sit in, and the licence that lets this atlas show its photographs
kin: wedjat-eye — the amulet this walk is really about — seven galleries of them, in faience, carnelian, obsidian and gold
kin: scarab — the other Egyptian class the 1906–1941 seasons supplied with find-spots attached
kin: heart-scarab — the large scarab laid on the chest of the dead, held in the same department
kin: cippus-of-horus — Gallery 128 has the big one — the Metternich Stela — and Gallery 134 the pocket-sized versions of the same design
kin: faience — the material the labels repeat: crushed quartz, fired, glazed blue or green
kin: carnelian — the red stone the same eye is cut from a few cases along
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition these rooms document more completely than any other single building in the Americas
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator whose method the museum's own Egyptian Expedition followed; he published plates, the Met kept galleries
kin: british-museum-room-1 — the comparison in London: a room about the collectors, where these are rooms about the dig
kin: free-to-use — the long read on licensing, where the CC0 dedication behind these object records is the case that works
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on dates; an excavation credit line is why these objects carry narrow ones

## The Grand Bazaar (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/grand-bazaar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/grand-bazaar.json
id: grand-bazaar
native: Kapalıçarşı (Latin)
aliases: Kapalicarsi · Büyük Çarşı · Covered Market, Istanbul
said: ka-pa-luh-CHAR-shuh, 'the covered market'
when: 1455 CE to now (still carried)
countries: TR
what: A roofed market of 61 streets and more than 4,000 shops on 30,700 square metres in the walled city of Istanbul, between the Beyazit and Nuruosmaniye mosques. Traders of one good still hold one street, the way the guilds arranged it. Two domed stone halls, the bedestens, sit at the centre; the eye beads a visitor carries out are sold in the jewellers' and souvenir lanes around them.
story: Mehmed II started it in the winter of 1455/56, months after taking Constantinople, with a building for textiles and jewels: the Cevahir Bedesten, the Bedesten of Gems, finished in the winter of 1460/61 and endowed to the waqf of Hagia Sophia. A second hall, the Sandal Bedesten, followed. Sellers filled the ground between them, and a quarter grew that did nothing but trade.

By the 17th century the shape was fixed: 67 named streets, 18 gates opened at dawn and shut at dusk, 3,000 shops plus 300 in the surrounding hans. Evliya Çelebi described it around 1638. Until the repairs that followed the 1894 earthquake there were no shops as western Europe knew them — a merchant sat on a wooden divan in a space six to eight feet wide and three to four feet deep, the precious stock kept in cabinets rather than displayed, and the day ended by drawing a drape across it.

The eye bead is the market's smallest export. In Turkey it is the nazar boncuğu; in Greece the same object is the máti. It is blue glass with white, black and yellow at the centre, a design whose written record and surviving examples run back to about 1500 BCE, and it is now, in the encyclopedia's flat phrase, a popular choice of souvenir with tourists.

*Inference —* a market that concentrated one trade per street for five centuries is the reason the bead has a fixed look at all. Mass production did not flatten this design; a guild had already fixed it.
today: Employs 26,000 people and takes between 250,000 and 400,000 visitors a day. Wikipedia's account, read on 16 September 2026, states the complex opens each day except Sundays and bank holidays, from 9:00 to 19:00. This project has not read that timetable on the bazaar's own page, so no day is marked open or closed below.
kin: nazar — the bead this market sells by the tray, and the reason most of the world pictures the eye as blue glass
kin: eye — the sign under the glass — the same interception the Nile cut in faience, four thousand years later
kin: glass — the material that made the sign cheap, and the trade that has worked it here since the bedesten was built for gems
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — what the bead becomes on a string, sold at the airport as well as here
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice under a roof, with the gates locked at night and a guild deciding who may sell
kin: monastiraki — the Athens lanes where the same bead is sold under its Greek name, máti
kin: khan-el-khalili — the Mamluk quarter al-Ghuri rebuilt in 1511, possibly in imitation of complexes like this one
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on copies and their price, which a market of 4,000 shops cannot avoid

## The Lovett charms at Wellcome Collection (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/wellcome-lovett/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/wellcome-lovett.json
id: wellcome-lovett
aliases: Lovett Collection, Wellcome · Charmed Life
when: 1916 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: An address rather than a room. Walk into 183 Euston Road today and there is no case of Edward Lovett's London charms to look at: the permanent show of Henry Wellcome's own collecting, Medicine Man, closed for good on 27 November 2022 after fifteen years, and the permanent exhibition now is Being Human. What Wellcome still holds under Lovett's name is paper — a collection dossier in the archive of the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum, catalogued as 'Lovett Collection', reference WA/HMM/CM/Col/64, a summary sheet dated to about the 1980s — and two exhibitions' worth of history.
story: Lovett collected by swap. He was chief cashier at a bank in the City, lived in Croydon and later Caterham, and spent his free time asking dockers, costermongers and sailors' families what they carried and why, trading them alpine plants grown in seashells for it. He wrote it up in "Magic in Modern London" in 1925 and he did not theorise: he recorded who gave him the thing and what they said about it, and left the explaining alone. That restraint is why his labels still work a century later.

He and Henry Wellcome corresponded for years. In 1916 Lovett curated an exhibition, 'Folklore of London', at the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum at 54a Wigmore Street. In 1930, three years before Lovett died, Wellcome's museum bought from his collection of British amulets and charms: a mole's foot from Downham Market in Norfolk, carried loose in a pocket in the 1890s or 1900s, is still catalogued with that purchase note and is now in the Science Museum Group collection as A79966.

Wellcome's own writing on those objects reports the claims and names the claimants. In "Moles' feet, dried frogs and other folk medicines", published on its website by Kate Wilkinson on 21 May 2019, it gives the reasoning as its owners gave it: "the digging-foot of a mole (with its cramped appearance) is thought to be a cure for cramp". A dried frog in a silk bag was carried against fits; snake vertebrae were strung against pain in the lower back; a coil of eel skin was wound round the fingers, in Scotland, against cramp; a potato was the one people were still carrying, in a pocket, against rheumatism. An old woman in Devonshire used quartzite on warts.

The charms themselves went to Oxford. When Wellcome Collection showed them again in 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, the museum's own page says the 1,400 amulets the artist Felicity Powell worked with were "borrowed from Oxford University's Pitt Rivers Museum" — the same building Lovett had been giving to since the 1890s. Powell was one of few people to have had access to them; the page describes her as caught by the silent witness they bore to personal stories now lost. Her films and medals hung beside them.

The institution has since said how the wider collecting worked. In 2021 Wellcome Collection acknowledged that Henry Wellcome's collecting was shaped by colonialism, that many objects bought at auction around the turn of the twentieth century carried no record of how they had been got, and that they may have been "unjustly taken"; in 2025 it returned a group of Jain manuscripts to India. *Inference —* Lovett sits oddly inside that account, because his method was a trade on a street with the owner present, and this project has not read a Wellcome statement that treats his material as contested. Saying so is not a defence of it; it is a note about what is and is not on the record.
today: The galleries, library, café and shop at 183 Euston Road are free, and the building's own line is that "All our permanent and temporary exhibitions, and most of our events, are free." Photography is allowed for personal use in most exhibitions except where signs say otherwise. To see a Lovett charm you go to Oxford or to the Science Museum Group catalogue; to read his file you book the library here.
kin: wellcome-collection — the institution this address is, and the one that showed Lovett's charms in 1916 and again in 2011
kin: edward-lovett — the man who swapped alpine plants for the charms in Londoners' pockets and wrote down what they said about them
kin: lovett-collection — the collection itself, which this address holds the paper trail of rather than the objects
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — where the charms actually are — the 1,400 amulets shown here in 2011 were borrowed back from Oxford
kin: caul — the birth membrane Lovett recorded in the hands of London sailors' families, bought against drowning
kin: hagstone — the naturally perforated stone that runs all through his English material
kin: rabbits-foot — the pocket animal part of the same English habit as the mole's foot Wellcome bought in 1930
kin: walter-hildburgh — the other amulet collector whose material passed through this building and out of it in 1985
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the living tradition he recorded on the street while other collectors read about its past
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read; a charm swapped face to face on a barrow is the awkward case in it
sources: s:web-wellcome-lovett-folk-medicines s:web-wellcome-lovett-dossier s:web-wellcome-charmed-life s:web-wellcome-visit s:web-wellcome-opening-times s:web-wellcome-whats-on s:web-wellcome-accessing-collections s:web-sciencemuseum-lovett-mole-foot s:wp-edward-lovett s:wp-wellcome-collection

## The Marrakesh souk (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/marrakesh-souk/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/marrakesh-souk.json
id: marrakesh-souk
native: أسواق مراكش (Arabic)
aliases: Souks of Marrakesh · Marrakech souks
said: SOOK
when: 1070 CE to now (still carried)
countries: MA
what: The market streets of the Marrakesh medina, running north from the square called Jemaa el-Fnaa into the old city. The lanes follow the road that once linked the Almoravid stone fortress to the city's first Friday mosque, and they still hold the main axis of the souks. Each lane is one trade.
story: Marrakesh was founded in 1070. Its two focal points were the Ksar el-Hajjar, the fortress of stone, and the first Friday mosque; the souk streets grew along the roads between them and have kept that line ever since. At the fortress end lay a large open space for temporary and weekly markets, called Rahbat al-Ksar, then as-Saha al-Kubra, the grand square. That space is today's Jemaa el-Fnaa, and the souk is edged along one side by it.

What the square sells changes by the hour. By day: orange juice, water sellers with leather bags and brass cups, snake charmers. Later the charmers leave and the square fills with storytellers, musicians, magicians and peddlers of traditional medicines; after dark, food stalls. UNESCO's programme for intangible heritage began with people worried about exactly this square, and the label followed.

The written trade is documented across the region rather than lane by lane. The scholar Remke Kruk found books on magic and sorcery well represented in street stalls and bookshops from Marrakesh to Cairo to Yemen around 2005; from about 1990 religious pamphlets condemning those practices sold beside them.

*Inference —* the herbalists' stalls are what most visitors come away describing, and this atlas has not yet read a source it can cite for them. The record therefore names the square's medicine peddlers, which is published, and stops there rather than furnishing the lanes from guidebooks it could not open.
today: Trading. The square went into a renovation programme from May 2025, budgeted at 160 million dirhams and scheduled to finish by the end of that year, to rework infrastructure and reorganise the public and commercial space. Hours are the stallholders' own; none are marked below.
kin: hamsa — the hand this region cuts in silver, and the sign a Moroccan market is likeliest to sell
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition whose handbooks Kruk found on stalls here, with the pamphlets against them alongside
kin: taweez — the written charm those handbooks instruct; the writing is a specialist's work, not a stall's
kin: khan-el-khalili — the other end of Kruk's line, Cairo to Marrakesh, selling the same books
kin: herb — the material the square's medicine peddlers trade in, named in UNESCO's file on the place
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice, in lanes laid out by trade since 1070
sources: s:wp-jemaa-el-fnaa s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-hamsa

## Via San Gregorio Armeno (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/place/san-gregorio-armeno/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/place/san-gregorio-armeno.json
id: san-gregorio-armeno
native: Via San Gregorio Armeno (Latin)
aliases: the crib-makers' street · Naples nativity street
said: VEE-a san gre-GO-ryo ar-MEH-no
when: 300 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IT
what: A narrow street in the old centre of Naples, lined with workshops that make figures for the presepe, the Neapolitan nativity scene. Terracotta heads, wired limbs, cloth, cork and plaster; shepherds beside this year's footballers and politicians. Coral and silver horns hang in the same windows, because the trade that models a figure by hand is the trade that cuts a charm by hand.
story: The street is a stenoporos, one of the narrow cross-lanes of the Greek grid Neapolis was laid out on, running between the two main streets of the ancient city — today's Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli — and crossing at the old agora.

The figures have a long root in the same ground. A temple of Ceres stood on this street in classical times, and citizens offered her small terracotta figurines made in the workshops nearby. The church of San Gregorio Armeno was founded around 930 on that temple's foundations. The Neapolitan nativity scene itself is much later, from the end of the 18th century. The workshops now run all year, with the main displays from early November to 6 January.

Naples is also a capital of the horn. The cornicello — curniciello in Neapolitan — is a twisted horn charm in gold, silver, bone, terracotta, plastic or red coral, worn against the malocchio and hung from rear-view mirrors, a custom the article traces back to protecting draught horses. Coral is the material that carries it, and coral is sacred to Venus.

Edward Lovett, the London folklorist, published a paper in 1909 called Amulets from Costers' Barrows in London, Rome, and Naples. He was reading three street trades as one subject, and this street is the one still working.

*Inference —* a lane whose craftsmen have modelled votive figures on the same ground for two thousand years is the clearest case in this atlas of a workshop outliving the religion it started in. Both halves of that sentence are cited; the joining of them is this project's.
today: Workshops produce figures year-round, traditional and topical. The heavy display season runs from early November to 6 January. No weekday is marked open or closed below: the shops set their own hours and no timetable is published for the street.
kin: cornicello — the horn this city cuts in coral and silver, hung in the same windows as the crib figures
kin: coral — the material the horn is cut from, and the one Naples has worked longest
kin: horn — the sign itself — southern Italy's substitute for the eye, aimed at the same look
kin: cimaruta — the other Neapolitan silver charm, a sprig of rue hung with signs
kin: ex-voto-wall — what the classical version of this street's output ended on: figurines offered to Ceres, made next door
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition these workshops supply
kin: edward-lovett — the folklorist who in 1909 read the barrow trade of London, Rome and Naples as one subject
kin: catholic-sacramentals — the blessed objects sold a few doors from the horn, by the same hands

## Alan Dundes (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/alan-dundes/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/alan-dundes.json
id: alan-dundes
when: 1934 CE – 2005 CE
countries: US
what: American folklorist, 1934–2005, who taught at the University of California, Berkeley for forty-two years. For this atlas he matters for one book: "The Evil Eye: A Casebook", University of Wisconsin Press, 1992, which he edited — a gathering of the arguments about the eye rather than a single account of it. He also gave the field the working definition of 'folk' that lets a charm carried by an office or a football team count as folklore at all.
story: Dundes studied English at Yale, spent two years maintaining artillery on a ship in the Mediterranean, then took a folklore doctorate at Indiana under Richard Dorson. Berkeley hired him into anthropology in 1963 and he stayed until he collapsed while teaching a graduate seminar on 30 March 2005.

His definition is the part that reaches into these records. Dundes wrote in 1969 that any group of people sharing a common linking factor, an urban group such as a labor union for instance, can and does have folklore, and that 'folk' is a flexible concept which can refer to a nation or to a single family. The critical issue, he said, is which groups in fact have traditions. *Inference —* that is the sentence that lets a challenge coin, a phone charm and an exam charm sit in the same atlas as a Middle Kingdom scarab without special pleading.

He insisted that collecting without theory is wasted work, and said so to his own field at the American Folklore Society in 2004. His students in the introductory course each had to collect, identify and analyse forty items; about 500,000 items are housed in the Berkeley Folklore Archives as a result.

He was also the most publicly argued-with folklorist of his generation. His 1980 presidential address on German culture, published as "Life is Like a Chicken Coop Ladder", drew a reaction strong enough that he stayed away from the society's annual conference for years, and the linguist Anatol Stefanowitsch in 2012 called it "unstructured, poorly argued and flimsily sourced" and "methodologically flawed because he only looked for evidence supporting his theory, and not — as even a folklorist should — for evidence against his theory". His psychoanalytic essay on American football earned him death threats. This atlas reports the quarrel and does not take a side in it.
today: The casebooks he edited are still the fastest way into a contested subject — the evil eye in 1992, the walled-up wife in 1996, the blood libel legend in 1991 — because each prints the opposing readings side by side instead of choosing. A donation from an anonymous former student endowed a Distinguished Professorship of Folkloristics at Berkeley, which is why the subject survived his retirement.
kin: eye — the sign his 1992 casebook assembled the arguments about, from a dozen scholars at once
kin: nazar — one subject of that casebook — the Mediterranean bead, argued over by the writers he collected
kin: challenge-coin — an object his definition of 'folk' makes legible: a group with a tradition, not a survival from anywhere
kin: luck-word — the word whose folk use he treated as data rather than as error
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read; his casebook is the single best map of who disagrees with whom about this sign
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian whose eye material his casebook inherited, read through a century of argument
sources: s:wp-alan-dundes s:wp-evil-eye

## Augustus Pitt Rivers (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/augustus-pitt-rivers/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/augustus-pitt-rivers.json
id: augustus-pitt-rivers
aliases: Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers · Augustus Henry Lane-Fox · Lieutenant-General Pitt Rivers
when: 1827 CE – 1900 CE
countries: GB
what: English soldier and archaeologist, 1827–1900, who arranged objects by what they are for rather than by where they came from. He gave more than 20,000 of them to the University of Oxford in 1884 on conditions that still bind the display. Every amulet case in this atlas that groups a Japanese charm beside a Neapolitan one is standing inside his idea.
story: He was commissioned into the Grenadier Guards on 16 May 1845 and served until 1882, ending as a Lieutenant-General. His combat was limited — the Battle of the Alma in 1854 — and most of his service went on musketry instruction; he founded the Hythe School of Musketry and published "On the improvement of the rifle as a weapon for general use" in 1858. Testing rifle after rifle is where the method comes from: he was already comparing small variations in a made object for a living.

Reading Darwin and Herbert Spencer, he arranged his collection typologically and, within types, chronologically, meaning to show progression in design and evolution in human culture from the simple to the complex. He treated archaeology as an extension of anthropology and built matching archaeological and ethnographic collections so the two could be read together.

In 1880 he inherited estates in Cranborne Chase carrying Roman and Saxon material and excavated them over seventeen seasons, from the mid-1880s until his death, insisting that everything be collected and catalogued rather than only what looked worth keeping. Under the Ancient Monuments Protection Act 1882 he became the first Inspector of Ancient Monuments, and put railings round sites including Kit's Coty House in Kent.

The 1884 gift to Oxford came with conditions: a permanent lecturer in anthropology, which made Edward Burnett Tylor the first lecturer in anthropology in the United Kingdom in 1885, and a building for the collection used for no other purpose. A further clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers".

That clause is why the argument about his method is still live rather than historical. The museum's own account states that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm for archaeological and anthropological objects, and that it has broadly retained the typological organisation because the Deed of Gift requires it.
today: The museum he founded holds more than 600,000 items, nearly all acquired by donation from colonial officials, travellers, scholars and missionaries. In September 2020 it removed human remains from display, including the shrunken heads shown since the 1940s; the director said exhibiting them "reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's core values". *Inference —* a bequest that fixes a nineteenth-century argument into the furniture is a different kind of object from the things inside the cases, and it is the one the museum cannot deaccession.
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — the museum his 1884 gift created, and whose layout his Deed of Gift still governs
kin: pitt-rivers-charms — the charm cases, which are his typological principle applied to amulets
kin: edward-lovett — one of the donors who fed the collection, giving between 1896 and 1911
kin: walter-hildburgh — the collector whose amulets reached the museum in 1985, long after the founder's scheme was set
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read; his museum is where the question of who a charm in a case belongs to is asked most directly
kin: flinders-petrie — his contemporary in method — both sorted by small differences, one in trenches, one in cases
kin: horseshoe — the kind of ordinary English object his scheme put in a case beside its equivalents from everywhere else
sources: s:web-augustus-pitt-rivers-wikipedia s:wp-pitt-rivers-museum
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Campbell Bonner (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/campbell-bonner/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/campbell-bonner.json
id: campbell-bonner
when: 1876 CE – 1954 CE
countries: US EG GR
what: American classicist, 1876–1954, of the University of Michigan, who wrote the book that made carved magical gems a subject with a method. "Studies in Magical Amulets, Chiefly Graeco-Egyptian", Ann Arbor, 1950, described and classified the engraved stones of the late Roman eastern Mediterranean — the ones cut with Abraxas, the reaper, the womb-symbol, strings of vowels — and set out how to read the images and the inscriptions together.
story: Bonner was born in Nashville, Tennessee, on 30 January 1876 and died in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on 11 July 1954. His published work runs from 1921 and covers magical papyri as well as gems; the amulets sat inside a wider study of popular religion in the late pagan and early Christian world.

The gems are small, hard and portable, cut in haematite, jasper, carnelian and chalcedony, and they carry a mixture nobody else had sorted: Egyptian gods, Greek vowels, Hebrew divine names, Roman medical language. Bonner's 1950 volume is where that mixture stopped being a curiosity list and became a corpus with types.

*Inference —* the tell of a corpus that worked is that it grew after its author died. The Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest runs the Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database, named for him, launched in 2010, and it estimates the entire corpus at around 5,600 pieces. That is a number nobody could have counted before the material had a shared vocabulary.
today: The database at the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest carries his name and, in its own words, has "the primary aim ... to bring the entire corpus of magical gems online". This project has not read a published academic criticism of Bonner's framing and does not assert that none exists.
kin: magical-gem — the object class his 1950 book defined, named and made countable
kin: divine-name — the sign his gems carry most consistently — names and vowel-strings cut beside the figure
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition his corpus belongs to, at its late and most mixed end
kin: carnelian — one of the stones the gems are cut from, alongside haematite and jasper
kin: christopher-faraone — the classicist working the same Greek material two generations on, and asking how the amulets changed under Rome
kin: inscribing — the practice his method reads — image and cut text taken together, never separately
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on dating; an uninscribed gem with no find-spot is the hard case his typology exists for
sources: s:web-campbell-bonner-wikipedia s:web-cbd-magical-gems
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Christopher A. Faraone (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/christopher-faraone/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/christopher-faraone.json
id: christopher-faraone
aliases: Christopher Faraone
when: 1955 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US GR IT
what: American classicist, born 1955, Edward Olson Distinguished Service Professor in Classics at the University of Chicago. He works on Greek poetry, religion and magic, and wrote "The transformation of Greek amulets in Roman imperial times" in 2018 — a study of how the Greek protective object changed shape, material and claim once Rome was running the Mediterranean.
story: Faraone's first book, "Talismans and Trojan horses: guardian statues in ancient Greek myth and ritual", 1992, took the largest protective objects the Greeks made: statues buried or set up to guard a city. "Ancient Greek Love Magic" followed in 2001, on the other end of the same practice — the spells and objects aimed at one person rather than a wall.

The 2018 book is the one an amulet record reaches for. *Inference —* its subject is change rather than origin, and that is the useful move: the Greek amulet did not simply persist into the Roman empire, it acquired new stones, new inscriptions and new customers, and a record that dates an object by its shape alone will get it wrong.

He founded and directed the University of Chicago's Center for the Study of Ancient Religions from 2008 to 2018, and co-edited "Masks of Dionysius" with Thomas H. Carpenter in 1993 and "Prostitutes and Courtesans in the Ancient World" with Laura K. McClure in 2006.
today: He holds the Edward Olson chair from the 2021–22 school year. His honours include a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1995, a National Endowment for the Humanities Fellowship in 2013, a fellowship at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 2021, and the Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit from the Society for Classical Studies in 2024.
kin: magical-gem — the Roman-period object his 2018 book tracks the Greek amulet turning into
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition he studies, and the one he argues was remade rather than simply continued under Rome
kin: curse-tablet — the other half of the Greek magical record — the tablet aimed at somebody, beside the amulet aimed at nobody
kin: gorgoneion — the guardian face; his first book took the guardian statue, of which this is the portable end
kin: campbell-bonner — the scholar who first made the late Greek amulets a corpus he is now reading for change over time
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read on the two words; his 1992 title puts the talisman question in the Greek material directly

## E. A. Wallis Budge (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/wallis-budge/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/wallis-budge.json
id: wallis-budge
aliases: Sir Ernest Alfred Thompson Wallis Budge · Ernest Alfred Wallis Budge · Wallis Budge
when: 1857 CE – 1934 CE
countries: EG IQ SD GB ET
what: English Egyptologist and Orientalist, 1857–1934, Keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities at the British Museum from 1894 to 1924. He bought for that museum across Egypt, Sudan and Iraq, wrote over a hundred books, and in 1930 published a 543-page compendium of amulets and talismans that is still the volume a second-hand shop is likeliest to have. Egyptologists who use it warn about it in the same breath.
story: Budge left school at twelve and clerked at W. H. Smith for eight years, studying Assyrian in his lunch hours at St Paul's until the cathedral organist raised money to send him to Cambridge. He entered the British Museum in 1883 and stayed forty-one years.

Between 1886 and 1892 he made three missions to Mesopotamia and then went to Egypt almost yearly and to Sudan five times. He came back with cuneiform tablets, Syriac, Coptic and Greek manuscripts and hieroglyphic papyri — the Papyrus of Ani among them, and the Amarna letters. On the 1888 Baghdad trip his baggage was searched under new Ottoman customs rules; he got the Tell Amarna tablets out by bribery, and said so himself in his 1920 memoir By Nile and Tigris. Museum officers of the period, Budge included, moved antiquities in diplomatic pouches and paid customs officials to look away. The archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called him "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities".

The amulet book is "Amulets and superstitions", Oxford University Press, 1930: xxxix plus 543 pages, twenty-two plates, and a subtitle that lists what it covers — Egyptian, Sumerian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Christian, Gnostic and Muslim amulets and talismans, the evil eye, the pentagon, the swastika, the cross, the properties of stones, rings, divination, numbers, the Kabbalah, ancient astrology. It is the widest single sweep anybody attempted, and it was assembled by one man who had handled most of the objects.

The warnings are on the record and they are specific. The Egyptologist James Peter Allen writes that Budge's books "were not too reliable when they first appeared and are now woefully outdated". Wikipedia's own summary says the writing style of his era — a lack of clear distinction between opinion and incontrovertible fact — is no longer acceptable in scholarly works. Adam H. Becker's article "Doctoring the Past in the Present: E. A. Wallis Budge, the Discourse on Magic, and the Colonization of Iraq", in History of Religions 44:3 (2005), puts the vocabulary Budge used for other people's religions next to the politics of the occupation he wrote it under.

On one point his colleagues were wrong and he was not: Budge argued that Egyptian religion had grown out of the religions of northeastern and central Africa. That was regarded as impossible at the time, when nearly everyone followed Flinders Petrie's invading "Dynastic Race".
today: Because Budge's books entered the public domain they have stayed continuously in print and are scanned in full online, so his translations and his framing reach far more readers than any corrected edition does. *Inference —* a search for almost any amulet term still lands on him first, which is why this atlas cites him for what he saw and not for what he concluded.
kin: british-museum — the collection he bought for and then kept, and the one his acquisition methods are now argued about inside
kin: budge-plates — the plates from his 1930 compendium, the widest single spread of amulet types anybody printed
kin: flinders-petrie — his opponent: Petrie put Egyptian civilisation's origin in an invading race, Budge put it in Africa
kin: incantation-bowl — the Mesopotamian object his Iraq missions brought to London in quantity
kin: magical-gem — the Gnostic and Graeco-Egyptian engraved stones his 1930 compendium gathered and illustrated alongside everything else
kin: amulet-word — the word whose history his first chapter set out for a general readership, and largely fixed there
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on acquisition; his own account of getting tablets out of Baghdad is one of its documents
sources: s:wp-e-a-wallis-budge s:web-budge-amulets-1930 s:wp-british-museum
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Edward Lovett (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/edward-lovett/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/edward-lovett.json
id: edward-lovett
when: 1852 CE – 1933 CE
countries: GB BE NL
what: English folklorist, July 1852 – 1933, who collected charms off London streets while working as a chief cashier at a bank in the City. He gathered the things people were actually carrying — a mole's foot, a dried frog, a blue bead, a caul — and wrote them up in "Magic in Modern London" in 1925. His material is now spread across the Pitt Rivers Museum, the Cuming Museum in Southwark, the Wellcome collection and two museums of childhood.
story: Lovett collected on his walks. He lived in Croydon and later Caterham, and worked the London streets, Sussex and Surrey in his spare time — costers' barrows, dock workers, sailors' families — asking what people had in their pockets and why. He grew alpine plants in seashells and traded the small specimens for amulets from the people he met. That is the whole method: a swap, on a street, recorded on the spot.

He donated to the Pitt Rivers Museum between 1896 and 1911. He joined the Folklore Society in 1900 and published in its journal: "The Modern Commercial Aspect of an Ancient Superstition" in 1902, "Superstitions and Survivals amongst Shepherds" and "Amulets from Costers' Barrows in London, Rome, and Naples" both in 1909. In a 1906 Museums Journal article he set out a plan for a folk museum of Britain and campaigned for it into the early 1920s. It was never built.

He corresponded with Henry Wellcome, and in 1916 curated an exhibition, 'Folklore of London', at the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum. In 1914 he showed over five hundred dolls at the National Museum of Wales, meaning to give adults what he called a "scientific history of the doll, from the standpoints of ethnography and folklore". His theory that the coffin dolls found on Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh in the 1830s were substitution burials for sailors lost at sea has not been supported by recent scholarship.

What separates him from most collectors of his generation is what he did not do. Lovett did not venture into theorising on folklore, confining his research to the collection of talismans and other objects with claims attached. *Inference —* that restraint is why his labels still work: he wrote down who gave him the thing and what they said about it, and left the explaining to other people.
today: The Wellcome Collection showed his amulets in 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, alongside new work by the artist and curator Felicity Powell. Wellcome also publishes an online piece on his collections, "Moles' feet, dried frogs and other folk medicines", by Kate Wilkinson, dated 21 May 2019.
kin: lovett-collection — the collection itself — the trays of London street charms he swapped alpine plants for
kin: wellcome-collection — the museum that exhibited his amulets in 1916 and again in 2011, and that publishes on them now
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — where his donations went between 1896 and 1911, and where a large part of the material still sits
kin: caul — one of the objects he recorded in the hands of London sailors' families rather than in a book
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the living tradition he recorded on the street while other collectors were reading about its past
kin: frederick-elworthy — his contemporary on the same subject, working Mediterranean markets where Lovett worked London barrows
kin: buying-in-a-market — the practice his method depended on — he bought and swapped rather than excavated
kin: charm-word — the word he used for what he collected, in the sense his informants used it
