## Flinders Petrie (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/flinders-petrie/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/flinders-petrie.json
id: flinders-petrie
aliases: William Matthew Flinders Petrie · Sir Flinders Petrie · W. M. F. Petrie
when: 1853 CE – 1942 CE
countries: EG GB IL PS
what: English Egyptologist, 1853–1942, who dug Egypt for half a century and sorted what came out of it. He held the first chair of Egyptology in the United Kingdom, at University College London, and in 1914 published a catalogue of amulets that arranged them into classes museums still shelve by. He also argued for eugenics in print, and the same books that fixed the amulet classes carry that argument.
story: Petrie taught himself to survey before he could vote. At nineteen he produced the most accurate survey of Stonehenge then made; in 1880 he went to Giza to measure the pyramids and found the place, in his words, "a house on fire, so rapid was the destruction". He called his own job that of a "salvage man".

From November 1884 he dug almost continuously — Tanis, Tell Nebesheh, the Fayum, Amarna from 1891, Tell el-Hesi in Palestine in 1890, the Merneptah stele at Luxor in 1896, the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in the winter of 1904–5. He cut the foreman out of his digs and paid the workmen direct, which he said stopped finds being pulled out fast and sloppily. In 1904 he set the method down in Methods and Aims in Archaeology. In 1913 he sold his Egyptian collection to University College London, where it is the Petrie Museum.

The amulet book is the one this atlas leans on. Amulets: illustrated by the Egyptian collection in University College, London, Constable, 1914, runs to 190 pages and sorts the material by what Petrie took the object to be doing — amulets of power, of property, protective amulets, the human-headed gods, the animal gods, the properties of stones. *Inference —* a museum drawer labelled by function rather than by find-spot is a drawer laid out on that scheme, and a visitor reading a case label in London, New York or Cairo is usually reading Petrie's categories at one remove.

The other half of the record is dated too. Petrie has been denounced for his pro-eugenics views; he was a dedicated believer in the superiority of the Northern peoples over the Latinate and Southern peoples, and he put the argument into his 1906 series Question of the day, blaming England's social problems on racial degeneration. It ran into his Egyptology: he held that Egyptian civilisation came from an invading "Dynastic Race" that conquered what he called in 1895 an "inferior, exhausted mulatto" population. E. A. Wallis Budge argued against him that Egyptian religion was of a piece with the religions of northeastern and central Africa; most of their colleagues at the time sided with Petrie.
today: The Petrie Museum at University College London holds the excavated amulet series he sold it in 1913. UCL marked the centenary of his 1923 knighthood by asking, in its own words, "Between investigations on eugenics, decolonial practice, and calls for repatriation, what has become of Flinderella?" *Inference —* both halves of him are still in the room: the typology is working equipment, and the racial theory it was written beside is now the subject of the museum's own labels.
kin: wedjat-eye — one of the classes his 1914 catalogue fixed, and the amulet his excavations turned up by the thousand
kin: scarab — the other Egyptian mass-produced amulet his sequence dating and his typology both had to handle
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition he catalogued; his class names are the ones the shelving still uses
kin: petrie-amulet-plates — the plates from his 1914 book, and the reason a museum drawer looks the way it does
kin: wallis-budge — his opponent on where Egyptian religion came from — Budge put it in Africa, Petrie in an invading race from outside
kin: british-museum — the museum whose Egyptology he fought with, and where he showed the Fayum portraits he forced Cairo to give back
kin: dating-a-charm — the long read on how a charm gets a date; his pottery seriation is where the method starts
kin: grave-deposit — the practice his cemeteries recorded — over seventeen cemeteries between Hu and Abadiya alone
sources: s:wp-flinders-petrie s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology s:web-petrie-amulets-1914 s:wp-e-a-wallis-budge

## Frederick Thomas Elworthy (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/frederick-elworthy/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/frederick-elworthy.json
id: frederick-elworthy
aliases: F. T. Elworthy
when: 1830 CE – 1907 CE
countries: GB IT ES
what: English philologist and antiquary, 1830–1907, of Wellington in Somerset. He wrote the two books that pulled the evil eye and its answering objects together as one subject in English — "The Evil Eye" in 1895 and "Horns of Honour" in 1900 — and he bought the objects while he was writing, in Spain, Italy and elsewhere. His collection went to the Somersetshire Archaeological Society's museum at Taunton after his widow's death.
story: Elworthy came to writing late. A woollen manufacturer's eldest son, schooled privately at Denmark Hill, he made his first name as a dialect scholar: "The Dialect of West Somerset", published for the English Dialect Society by Trübner between 1875 and 1886, in two volumes with a grammar and a word-book.

Then he turned to the eye. "The Evil Eye: an account of this ancient and widespread superstition", John Murray, 1895, gathered what he had seen on the road — the coral horn in Naples, the hand, the crescent, the amulets sold at street barrows — and set them beside Roman and Greek material. "Horns of Honour", the same publisher, 1900, took the horn on its own. He drew, and he drew well; the plates are his.

His obituarist in the Dictionary of National Biography wrote that in the course of those travels he made "perhaps the finest collection of charms, amulets, and such-like trinkets in existence". That sentence is the record of a whole period's vocabulary, and this atlas prints it as a quotation rather than borrowing it. Elworthy's own subtitle does the same work. The word he put on his title page is the verdict the book starts from, and everything inside is described by somebody who had already decided what the practice was.

*Inference —* what survived the framing is the evidence. Elworthy recorded which object was sold on which street, what a seller said it did, and what shape it took in one town against the next; those observations are still checkable and are still cited, including in this atlas, wherever a Mediterranean charm needs a dated nineteenth-century sighting.
today: His 1895 and 1900 books are out of copyright and circulate freely as scans, which keeps both the observations and the vocabulary in wide reach. The Pitt Rivers Museum's 'The Other Within' project, by Alison Petch, carries a biographical page on him as one of the collectors behind English ethnographic holdings.

kin: cornicello — the Neapolitan horn he bought, drew and gave a book of its own in 1900
kin: horn — the sign he argued was doing the eye's work by another shape
kin: cimaruta — one of the Italian charms his fieldwork put into English print
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition his two books first assembled as a single subject in English
kin: edward-lovett — his English contemporary, working the same decades on London streets rather than Mediterranean ones
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read his 1895 survey is the first English attempt at

## Joseph Naveh (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/joseph-naveh/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/joseph-naveh.json
id: joseph-naveh
when: 1928 CE – 2011 CE
countries: IL IQ IR
what: Israeli epigrapher and palaeographer, 1928–2011, who read the writing on the amulets. With Shaul Shaked he published the Aramaic texts of late antique metal amulet strips and of the clay incantation bowls — the objects buried upside down under house floors in Babylonia — in editions that print the text, the translation and the object together.
story: Naveh was born in Mukachevo, then Czechoslovakia, on 21 January 1928. He worked for the Israel Department of Antiquities from 1955 to 1971 and was a district archaeologist from 1958, then taught in the Department of Ancient Semitic Languages at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem from 1971 to 1991. His field was West Semitic epigraphy: the shapes of letters, and what the shapes date.

That is the skill the amulet material needs. A rolled silver or bronze lamella and a bowl written in a spiral both carry script and nothing else datable — no stratigraphy in a bowl bought on a market, no style in a thin strip of metal. "The Development of the Aramaic Script", his 1970 dissertation, and "Early History of the Alphabet", 1997, are the tools; the amulet volumes are what he used them on.

With Shaked he produced "Amulets and Magic Bowls: Aramaic Incantations of Late Antiquity" and then "Magic Spells and Formulae" in 1993. *Inference —* the dating in this atlas for any Aramaic amulet or bowl rests on that letter-by-letter work, whether or not the record says so.

He was elected to the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 1994. He died on 21 November 2011.
today: The bowls keep arriving on the antiquities market without find-spots, which is the reason his palaeography stays load-bearing and also the reason the objects are contested. This project has not read a published provenance study of the bowl corpus and does not assert what share of it was excavated.
kin: incantation-bowl — the object he and Shaked edited — text, translation and bowl printed together
kin: shaul-shaked — his co-author on the Aramaic amulet and bowl editions, over roughly three decades
kin: ketef-hinnom-scrolls — the rolled silver amulet strip from Jerusalem — the object class his palaeography dates
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the later tradition these late antique Aramaic texts sit behind
kin: divine-name — the sign his editions are mostly reading: the names written into the bowls and strips
kin: silver — the metal the rolled amulet strips are beaten from, and the reason their text survives at all
kin: inscribing — the practice his whole method addresses — what was written, in which hand, and when

## Shaul Shaked (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/shaul-shaked/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/shaul-shaked.json
id: shaul-shaked
native: שאול שקד (Hebrew)
when: 1933 CE – 2021 CE
countries: IL IQ IR
what: Israeli Iranist and philologist, 1933–2021, of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He read the Aramaic incantation bowls and metal amulets of late antique Babylonia alongside Zoroastrian and Middle Persian material, which is why his editions catch what the Jewish, Christian, Mandaean and Iranian texts borrowed from one another.
story: Shaked was born in Debrecen, Hungary, on 5 March 1933. He took his doctorate in Iranian languages at SOAS in 1964 and taught at the Hebrew University in Indian, Iranian and Armenian Studies and in Comparative Religion, holding the Schwarzman chair. He was elected to the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 1985 and chaired its humanities division from 1995 to 2001. He won the Israel Prize for Linguistics in 2000 and the Sándor Scheiber Prize in 2012.

His listed research interests are Zoroastrianism, Middle Persian lexicography, early Judaeo-Persian, Aramaic magical texts, and Aramaic and Arabic loan words in Iranian. The bowls sit at the join of all of those. A Babylonian bowl written in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and buried under a floor names demons with Iranian names and formulas with Jewish ones; a reader who knows only one side of that misses half the text.

With Joseph Naveh he published "Amulets and Magic Bowls: Aramaic Incantations of Late Antiquity" and "Magic Spells and Formulae" in 1993. He continued the corpus with others — "Aramaic Bowl Spells: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic Bowls", with James N. Ford and Siam Bhayro, volume one from Brill in 2013 and volume two in 2022. He died on 27 October 2021.
today: The bowl corpus is still being edited volume by volume, and the later volumes are appearing after his death. *Inference —* an amulet class whose standard edition is unfinished is a class whose dating and readings will move, so this atlas's Aramaic bowl records are marked as provisional wherever they lean on a text rather than on an object.

kin: islamic-talismanic — the neighbouring tradition in the same region, which inherited some of the same formulas

kin: taweez — the later pouched written charm of the same region, in Arabic rather than Aramaic

## Siegfried Seligmann (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/siegfried-seligmann/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/siegfried-seligmann.json
id: siegfried-seligmann
when: 1870 CE – 1926 CE
countries: DE
what: German ophthalmologist and independent scholar, 1870–1926, who wrote the largest survey of the evil eye anybody has attempted. "Der böse Blick und Verwandtes", two volumes, 1910, collects the belief and its objects across languages and centuries; German scholarship still calls it an indispensable standard work. He assembled a collection of more than 1,500 amulets while writing it.
story: Seligmann was born at Wandsbek on 12 June 1870 and practised in Hamburg. An eye doctor writing about the eye that harms is a coincidence he does not seem to have made much of; what he did was read everything. "Der böse Blick und Verwandtes" in 1910 was followed by "Die Zauberkraft des Auges und das Berufen" in 1922 and, after his death on 10 November 1926, by "Die magischen Heil- und Schutzmittel aus der unbelebten Natur" in 1927 — the protective and healing materials drawn from the mineral world.

He married Alice Bettina Warburg in 1904, and the family connection shows in where his papers went. His ethnological library was taken into the Warburg Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek in Hamburg; since 1987 his papers have been held by the Warburg Institute in London. The amulet collection itself was bought in 1927 for Hamburg's ethnological museum.

The German Wikipedia entry records that his Hamburg residence later became a Judenhaus — one of the buildings into which Jewish residents were forced under Nazi persecution. That happened after his death.

*Inference —* the reason this atlas cites Seligmann rather than paraphrasing him is that his footnotes name sources this project can chase; he was compiling, not theorising, and the compilation is what has lasted.
today: The books are in German and mostly untranslated, which is why English writing on the eye tends to reach for Elworthy's 1895 volume first even though Seligmann's is larger and later. His collection and his papers sit in two different cities and two different countries, which is the ordinary fate of a private amulet collection.

kin: nazar — the bead form of the sign, one of the many he catalogued rather than one he singled out
kin: frederick-elworthy — his English counterpart, fifteen years earlier and far shorter; Seligmann read him
kin: walter-hildburgh — another private amulet collector of the same decades whose collection also ended up in a public museum
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition his survey covers most densely, though he reached well past Europe
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read; his 1910 volumes are its largest single source in any language

## Walter Leo Hildburgh (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/person/walter-hildburgh/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/person/walter-hildburgh.json
id: walter-hildburgh
aliases: W. L. Hildburgh
when: 1876 CE – 1955 CE
countries: GB US ES
what: American collector and art historian, 1876–1955, who bought amulets in vast numbers across Europe, Asia and the Middle East and then wrote about them. His amulet collection was left to the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum and transferred to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985; his English medieval alabasters went to the Victoria and Albert Museum, 300 of them in 1946 for his seventieth birthday.
story: Hildburgh took a doctorate at Columbia on alternating current, then spent his life on objects. The University of London gave him a D.Litt. in the History of Art in 1937. He gave or bequeathed over 5,000 objects to the Victoria and Albert Museum alone, and further material reached the British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Cooper Hewitt and the UCL Institute of Archaeology.

The amulets are the part that concerns this atlas, and they are also the part that moved. They went first to Henry Wellcome's museum, and in 1985 the whole Wellcome amulet material was transferred to Oxford. *Inference —* that means a tray of Spanish hands or Japanese charms catalogued as Pitt Rivers material may have been bought by an American in a Madrid street in 1906, passed through a pharmaceutical fortune's private museum in London, and only reached Oxford eighty years later. The label says Pitt Rivers. The object's history says four other things first.

He published on what he bought rather than only accumulating it: articles on cowrie shells as amulets, on hand images as amulets in Spain, and on the psychology he thought underlay amulet use in Europe.
today: Hildburgh's amulets are the bulk of what a visitor to the Pitt Rivers charm cases is looking at, and the Wellcome connection is why the same names recur in both institutions' catalogues. This project has read no published account of how individual pieces were acquired, and does not assert that any particular object was bought fairly or unfairly.

## Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/aiatsis/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/aiatsis.json
id: aiatsis
aliases: AIATSIS · Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies · AIAS
when: 1964 CE to now (still carried)
countries: AU
RESTRICTED: AIATSIS holds material that is secret or sacred to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and restricts access to it: restricted visual media are stored apart from the rest of the collection, audio and moving-image items are not played until cultural requirements are checked, and depositors may set access and use conditions on what they deposit. This atlas prints those conditions and stops. It does not reconstruct restricted Australian designs, objects or rites from other sources, and does not fill the gap with a neighbouring tradition's practice.
what: Australian Government statutory authority in Canberra, founded in 1964 as the Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies and renamed under the AIATSIS Act 1989. It collects, publishes and researches, and it holds over a million cultural items — roughly 42,000 hours of audio, around 700,000 photographs and about six million feet of film. Part of that collection is secret or sacred, and AIATSIS publishes the rules for handling it. Those rules are why this atlas leaves Australia largely blank.
story: The founding purpose was salvage, in the vocabulary of its time: to record language, song, art, material culture, ceremonial life and social structure before those traditions perished in the face of European ways. No Aboriginal people attended the 1961 conference that planned the institute. Before 1970 there had never been an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander member on its council. The 1989 Act changed the arithmetic: a council of nine, of whom the Act requires that at least five be Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, with one of the Minister's appointees a Torres Strait Islander.

The collection was built by donation, gift, purchase and fieldwork, and also by deposit — an arrangement that permits the original owners to assign access and use conditions appropriate to the cultural information in the items. That clause is the hinge. It means an item can sit in a national collection and still be governed by the people it came from.

The handling rules follow from it. AIATSIS holds material that is sensitive and/or secret/sacred to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and under its founding Act adheres to strict protocols when processing it. Restricted visual media are stored separately from the rest of the collection. Audio and moving-image items are not played until cultural requirements have been checked. Restricted material is digitised in secured conditions such as enclosed booths, by staff who can meet the protocols of the item being digitised. The institute also supports the protocols of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Library, Information and Resource Network.

On the research side, AIATSIS published the Guidelines for Ethical Research in Australian Indigenous Studies in 1999, updated them in 2012, and replaced them in 2020 with the AIATSIS Code of Ethics for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Research. The Code rests on four principles: Indigenous self-determination, Indigenous leadership, impact and value, and sustainability and accountability.
today: A new precinct, Ngurra, is planned on the shore of Lake Burley Griffin at a stated A$316.5 million, to include a resting place for ancestral remains of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people that cannot be returned to Country. AIATSIS Central Australia opened in Alice Springs / Mparntwe on 2 February 2024. The institute's Australian Indigenous Language Collection is registered in UNESCO's Memory of the World programme — a different UNESCO instrument from the intangible-heritage lists.

## Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/te-papa/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/te-papa.json
id: te-papa
native: Te Papa Tongarewa ()
aliases: Te Papa
when: 1992 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NZ
RESTRICTED: Te Papa asks that images of taonga be used only for research, study, personal and educational purposes, on the ground that the material holds significant cultural importance to iwi. This atlas does not reproduce Te Papa taonga images outside that scope, and does not print detail about restricted taonga beyond what the museum itself publishes.
what: New Zealand's national museum, in Wellington, established by the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa Act 1992 and opened on 14 February 1998. Te Papa is Māori for 'the treasure box'. It runs on a bicultural philosophy built into the building's design process through the Treaty of Waitangi, and it is the institution that asks other museums, worldwide, for Māori ancestral remains back.
story: Te Papa came out of a merger — the National Museum of New Zealand and the National Art Gallery, whose own line runs back to the Colonial Museum of 1865. The design process was led by Cliff Whiting with Cheryll Sotheran and Ken Gorbey and followed bicultural principles; Pete Bossley of Jasmax was the architect. The cultural collections hold Māori taonga and Pacific material alongside photography.

Since 2003 the museum has run a programme requesting the return of Māori remains held in institutions around the world. The clearest case in this atlas's range is the Musée du quai Branly: initially reluctant, it was able to move after a change in French law in 2010, and the mokomokai — tattooed preserved heads — were formally returned to New Zealand on 23 January 2012. They are held at Te Papa and are not on display.

The museum also draws the line inside its own building, and the argument about that is public. In 2010 it advised pregnant and menstruating women to avoid a behind-the-scenes tour of some collections; a spokeswoman said the policy was in place because of Māori beliefs surrounding the taonga collection included in the tour, "for their own safety". The advice generated outrage and claims that the museum was overbearing. This atlas reports both the reason given and the objection, and adjudicates neither.
today: Entry is free for New Zealanders and NZ$35 for international visitors as of September 2024. Collections Online publishes images under two rights statements, named on the museum's own page: some images are openly available with no restrictions on reuse, and others carry a Creative Commons Attribution – Non-Commercial – No Derivatives licence. For taonga the museum asks something further — that images of taonga be used only for research, study, personal and educational purposes, because the material holds significant cultural importance to iwi. *Inference —* that request is not a licence term, and this atlas treats it as binding anyway.

## Musée du quai Branly — Jacques Chirac (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/quai-branly/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/quai-branly.json
id: quai-branly
native: Musée du quai Branly — Jacques Chirac ()
aliases: Quai Branly · MQB
when: 2006 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR
what: Paris museum of the arts and cultures of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, opened to the public on 23 June 2006 in a Jean Nouvel building beside the Seine. It holds more than a million objects and shows about 3,500 at a time. It is also where the French argument about returning colonial-era collections is loudest, because 70,000 of France's 90,000 sub-Saharan objects are here.
story: The museum was assembled out of two older ones with incompatible purposes: the 25,000 objects of the Musée national des Arts d'Afrique et d'Océanie, created for the Colonial Exposition of 1931, and the 250,000-object ethnology collection of the Musée de l'Homme, created for the Paris Exposition of 1937. One was run by art historians, the other by anthropologists. The new museum was put under two ministries to match, and ten thousand further objects were bought.

Critics went at it from both directions on opening. Michael Kimmelman in the New York Times, 2 July 2006, called it "a missed opportunity and an inexplicable exercise" and asked whether religious, ceremonial and practical objects, never intended as art in the modern Western sense, would be showcased "like baubles, with no context". James Clifford wrote that in this museum "'illusion' and the 'work of art' coexist uneasily with the realism of ethnography and history". Others praised the same building: the Financial Times called the layered galleries an "animated, occasionally jarring dreamscape", the Washington Post called it visually stunning.

The returns argument has a paper trail. In 2016 the French government refused objects requested by the president of Benin on the ground that the national collections are inalienable. In 2018 the report Emmanuel Macron commissioned from Bénédicte Savoy and Felwine Sarr argued that artefacts taken unlawfully in the colonial period should go back when asked for. Macron then promised Benin 26 pieces taken by force from Dahomey; no French law then existed to permit it. By late 2021 the objects were ready and the museum staged a final exhibition around them. Separately, after a change in French law in 2010, the museum returned mokomokai — Māori tattooed heads — to New Zealand on 23 January 2012.
today: In December 2025, 77 works from the museum's Louvre selection were installed in the Louvre's new Gallery of the Five Continents, shown alongside Western art. This project has not read the museum's own image-rights statement and makes no claim about whether its collection photographs are openly licensed; the safe assumption for this atlas's picture pipeline is that they are not.

## The British Museum (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/british-museum/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/british-museum.json
id: british-museum
aliases: BM
when: 1753 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: London museum of human history, founded by act of parliament in 1753 and open to the public since 15 January 1759. It was the world's first public national museum and charges no admission except for loan exhibitions. For this atlas it is the largest single holding of Egyptian and Mesopotamian amulets in one building, and the institution whose keeper wrote the most-reprinted book about them.
story: The museum began with Sir Hans Sloane's 71,000 objects, bought for the nation for £20,000 after his death in 1753 — far under the £50,000 or more his collection was then reckoned at. Among them were 160 Egyptian objects, which is where the Egyptian collection starts. In 1802 George III presented the Rosetta Stone. Henry Salt, British consul in Egypt, supplied much of the rest from 1818 onward.

E. A. Wallis Budge ran the Egyptian and Assyrian department as keeper from 1894 to 1924 and did the buying, in Egypt, Sudan and Iraq. His methods are on the record in his own memoir and in later assessment: the archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called him "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities".

The collection's size is stated two ways in the same account: eight million artefacts in the permanent collection, and over 13 million objects in total. This record gives both rather than picking one.

The museum's published position on returns rests on statute. It argues that the British Museum Act 1963 prevents any object from leaving the collection once it has entered it — "The Museum owns its collections, but its Trustees are not empowered to dispose of them" — and that the "restitutionist premise, that whatever was made in a country must return to an original geographical site, would empty both the British Museum and the other great museums of the world". It has nevertheless returned Tasmanian Aboriginal burial remains where legislation allowed, and it has a published policy on human remains. The Parthenon sculptures claimed by Greece, the Benin Bronzes claimed by Nigeria and the Ethiopian tabots are the standing claims; preliminary talks with the Greek government began in late 2022.
today: On 28 April 2020 the museum put over 1.9 million images of its collection online. Most images that are © The Trustees of the British Museum carry a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International licence: free to share and adapt for non-commercial use with a credit to the museum, and a separate licence from British Museum Images for anything the museum deems commercial. *Inference —* that licence is not on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list, because Commons requires that commercial use be allowed. So this atlas can link to a British Museum image and cannot host one, and that is a fact about the licence, not a judgement about the museum.

## The Metropolitan Museum of Art (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/metropolitan-museum/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/metropolitan-museum.json
id: metropolitan-museum
aliases: the Met · Metropolitan Museum
when: 1870 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US
what: New York museum founded in 1870, holding about 1.5 million works across seventeen curatorial departments. Its Egyptian department runs to more than 26,000 pieces, almost all of them on display across forty galleries, and almost half of those came out of the museum's own excavations between 1906 and 1941. Since 2017 every image of a public-domain work in the collection has carried a CC0 dedication.
story: The New York State Legislature incorporated the museum on 13 April 1870; an 1893 act required that the collections be kept open and accessible free of charge throughout the year. The Egyptian holdings began as private collections and were then built by digging: the excavation seasons from 1906 to 1941 supply almost half the current collection, which is why a Met amulet more often has a find-spot than a bought one does.

The Michael C. Rockefeller Wing, opened in 1982 around Nelson Rockefeller's gift of more than 3,000 pieces, holds over 11,000 works from sub-Saharan Africa, the Pacific and the Americas. The museum's own account notes what changed with that wing: the material was now shown as art, in a Western art museum, where before objects from those regions had been treated as ethnographic work.

The acquisition record is contested and documented. The Euphronios Krater, bought with deaccession proceeds under Thomas Hoving, proved to be looted and went back to Italy in 2006. In September 2022 New York law enforcement seized 27 objects on three warrants for return to Italy and Egypt; in March 2023 fifteen more tied to Subhash Kapoor; in December 2023 the museum announced the return of fourteen Khmer sculptures to Cambodia and two to Thailand. In April 2023 ProPublica reported on the museum's Indigenous American holdings and on a loan-versus-own distinction that kept objects outside the reach of NAGPRA, since objects on loan do not trigger the repatriation process. The museum has since issued a statement on collecting practices and hired a provenance-research manager with a team of three.
today: The Open Access initiative began at the start of 2017. In the museum's own words six months in: "It's been six months since the Met launched its Open Access initiative, which made available all 375,000+ images of public-domain works in the Met collection under Creative Commons Zero (CC0)." Open access images and data have since been viewed over 1.2 billion times with over 7 million downloads. CC0 is on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list, so a Met amulet photograph can be hosted, reused and altered here with no permission sought. The dedication covers the museum's images of public-domain works; it says nothing about who the objects belong to.

## The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/nagpra/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/nagpra.json
id: nagpra
aliases: NAGPRA · Pub. L. 101–601
when: 1990 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US
what: United States federal law, Pub. L. 101–601, enacted on 16 November 1990. It requires federal agencies and any institution receiving federal funding to return Native American cultural items — human remains, funerary objects, sacred objects and objects of cultural patrimony — to lineal descendants and to culturally affiliated tribes, Alaska Native villages and Native Hawaiian organizations. It also makes trafficking in those items a criminal offence.
story: The Act has three sets of provisions, and the difference between them decides most arguments about it. The repatriation provisions reach backwards: they apply to remains or objects discovered at any time, before or after 1990, wherever found, so long as the holder receives federal funding. The disposition provisions govern discovery or excavation on federal or tribal land after 16 November 1990, and they do not apply to private or state land outside a reservation boundary. The criminal provisions make trafficking an offence.

Maria Pearson is generally credited as the first catalyst. In the early 1970s her husband, an Iowa Department of Transportation engineer, told her that road construction at Glenwood had turned up both white and Native American remains: twenty-six white burials were reburied quickly, while the remains of a Native American mother and child went to a lab. She sat outside Governor Robert D. Ray's office in traditional dress until he saw her. "You can give me back my people's bones and you can quit digging them up." The Iowa Burials Protection Act of 1976 followed, then a decade of lobbying, then the looting of the Slack Farm mound in Kentucky in 1987 and the protests at Dickson Mounds in Illinois, and then the federal Act.

It has moved a great deal of material: the remains of about 32,000 individuals, nearly 670,000 funerary objects, 120,000 unassociated funerary objects and 3,500 sacred objects. It is also slow, and the burden of proving cultural affiliation falls on tribes, which is hardest in California, where many small bands were extinguished before they could be federally recognised. Some archaeologists object that remains untraceable to a historic tribe are being put beyond study. The Act itself says Congress meant to strike a balance between scientific examination and the fact that Native Americans, like people from every culture, hold their ancestors' remains in religious and spiritual reverence.

Penalties were raised in 2022. A first conviction for trafficking Native American human remains went from twelve months to one year and one day, which makes it a felony, and a subsequent conviction from five years to ten. A first conviction for trafficking cultural items remains a misdemeanour of up to one year; a subsequent one went from five years to ten.
today: Revised Interior Department regulations took effect on 12 January 2024 and state that museums and federal agencies "must defer to the Native American traditional knowledge of lineal descendants, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations". The gaps are still real. ProPublica reported in April 2023 that the Metropolitan Museum of Art had held Indigenous American objects on long-term loan rather than owning them, and objects on loan do not trigger the repatriation process. *Inference —* the law is a US statute with a funding hook; it does nothing about a private collector, a foreign museum or an object sold abroad before 1990, and a reader should not treat it as a general rule about who owns a charm.

kin: grave-deposit — the practice the Act exists to answer: what was buried with somebody, and who it still belongs to
kin: aiatsis — the Australian counterpart, working by protocol and deposit conditions where this works by statute and funding
kin: te-papa — the national museum running the same argument from the claimant's side, across borders rather than inside one

## The Pitt Rivers Museum (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/pitt-rivers-museum/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/pitt-rivers-museum.json
id: pitt-rivers-museum
aliases: PRM
when: 1884 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: Oxford museum of archaeology and anthropology, founded in 1884 on Augustus Pitt Rivers' gift of about 22,000 objects and now holding more than 600,000. It is arranged by what things are for rather than by where they are from, so charms from a dozen continents share a case. Nearly the whole collection came in by donation from colonial officials, travellers, scholars and missionaries.
story: The Deed of Gift set the terms. Oxford had to appoint a permanent lecturer in anthropology — Edward Burnett Tylor, in 1885, the first in the United Kingdom — and had to put up a building used for nothing else. Construction ran 1885 to 1886. A further clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers".

That is why the typological layout survived its own justification. The museum's account states that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm for archaeological and anthropological objects, and that the original organisation has broadly been kept because the Deed requires it.

The amulet material arrived by two routes and they matter. Edward Lovett donated London street charms between 1896 and 1911. Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets, bought across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, were bequeathed to the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum and transferred here in 1985.

Since 2020 the museum has changed what it shows. During the COVID closure it removed human remains from display, including the tsantsas shown since the 1940s; the director said that exhibiting them "reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's core values". It is meeting originating communities to correct its records and discuss returns — the Living Cultures work with the Maasai group Oltoilo Le Maa and InsightShare among them. With the Museum of Natural History it returned the remains of 17 Aboriginal Australians to the Australian government in 2022, and in 2026 agreed to repatriate Naga skeletal remains, some of which had been displayed in a case titled Treatment of Dead Enemies.
today: Collections Online is browsable and its images are not openly licensed. The museum's terms allow images to be used for non-commercial educational and community purposes and state that they "cannot be used freely or without permission for commercial purposes"; publication needs a licence application to photographic services, and credit must read "© Pitt Rivers Museum, University of Oxford" with the object's accession number. No Creative Commons licence is named. *Inference —* this atlas can therefore cite a Pitt Rivers accession and link to it, and cannot host the picture.

## UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/unesco-ich/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/unesco-ich.json
id: unesco-ich
aliases: the 2003 Convention · Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage · ICH
when: 2003 CE to now (still carried)
what: The UNESCO programme run under the 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. It lists practices, not objects. A charm cannot be inscribed; the craft of making it, the festival it is sold at or the rite it belongs to can be. States Parties nominate, and an intergovernmental committee meets annually and decides.
story: Article 2 of the Convention defines intangible cultural heritage as traditions or living expressions inherited from our ancestors and passed on to our descendants — oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals, festive events, knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe, and the knowledge and skills to produce traditional crafts. Those are the five domains.

Two statements in the Convention's own summary matter more than the lists. The first is that intangible cultural heritage is "traditional, contemporary and living at the same time" — it is not a survival, and an element does not have to be old. The second is that it is "community-based: intangible cultural heritage can only be heritage when it is recognized as such by the communities, groups or individuals that create, maintain and transmit it". A state cannot inscribe a practice over the heads of the people doing it.

There are three registers: the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding, and the Register of Good Safeguarding Practices. The committee meets annually to evaluate nominations proposed by States Parties and decide whether or not to inscribe them.
today: What inscription is not: a ranking, a mark of quality, a property title, a trademark, or a bar on anyone making or selling anything. UNESCO's own wording is that intangible cultural heritage "is not merely valued as a cultural good, on a comparative basis, for its exclusivity or its exceptional value". *Inference —* this atlas therefore counts an inscription as attention paid and never as a verdict, and it never reads an absence from the lists as evidence that a practice is less real. Most of the practices in these records have never been nominated by anybody.
kin: thai-wicha — the kind of living craft tradition the Convention's traditional-craftsmanship domain is written for
kin: japanese-engimono — a shrine-linked making and selling practice of the sort the lists take in
kin: maori-taonga — a tradition where the community-recognition clause does the work, not the list
kin: aiatsis — the Australian institute often confused with this programme; its language collection sits on UNESCO's Memory of the World register instead
kin: nagpra — the contrast in kind: a binding national statute about objects, against an international list about practices
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on ownership, where inscription is the thing most often mistaken for a property claim
kin: the-fake-market — the long read on authentication; an inscription settles nothing about whether a given object is what a seller says it is
sources: s:web-unesco-ich-what-is s:web-unesco-ich-lists
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Wellcome Collection (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/wellcome-collection/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/wellcome-collection.json
id: wellcome-collection
when: 2007 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB
what: London museum and library at 183 Euston Road, opened to the public in June 2007 and part of the Wellcome Trust. It rests on what Sir Henry Wellcome, 1853–1936, bought: books, paintings and objects on the history of medicine worldwide, gathered on a scale no individual has matched since. Its holdings are described as including 17,500 magic-medical amulets, talismans and charms that Wellcome picked up in Islamic North Africa and elsewhere.
story: Wellcome's museum came first — the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum at 54a Wigmore Street. Edward Lovett curated an exhibition there in 1916, 'Folklore of London'; the two men corresponded for years. Wellcome bought at auction on an industrial scale, and Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets were bequeathed into the same collection.

The institution has published its own account of how that buying worked. In 2021 the Collection acknowledged that Wellcome's collecting was shaped by colonialism: many objects bought at auction in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century carried no documentation of how they had been acquired, and may have been "unjustly taken" from communities across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Middle East. It has committed to working with communities on provenance, and in 2025 returned a group of Jain manuscripts to India after researchers found they had been acquired without the consent of the communities they belonged to.

The display has moved too. Medicine Man, the permanent show of part of Wellcome's own collection, closed permanently on 27 November 2022 after fifteen years; the closure was perceived to follow concerns over racist, sexist and ableist theories and language.

The amulets themselves have been on the move for longer. Hildburgh's amulet material was transferred out of Wellcome to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985. The figure of 17,500 magic-medical amulets is published as a description of the Wellcome holdings; this record prints the two statements side by side and does not reconcile them, because it has not read a catalogue that says what stayed and what left.
today: Wellcome is digitising and openly licensing its collection: as of January 2020 over 40 million images from 325,000 items were available on wellcomecollection.org and through third-party services. The licensing is mixed, per item — in the Collection's own words, digitised materials "can be accessed and downloaded for use under a variety of Creative Commons non-commercial, attribution and Public Domain licences, depending on the material". *Inference —* attribution and public-domain items clear Wikimedia Commons; non-commercial ones do not, so the licence has to be read on the item and never assumed from the institution. Its exhibition 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, showed Lovett's amulets beside new work by Felicity Powell.
kin: wellcome-lovett — the Lovett material inside it, which is the part of this collection this atlas sends a reader to
kin: edward-lovett — the folklorist who curated here in 1916 and whose charms it showed again in 2011
kin: walter-hildburgh — the collector who bequeathed his amulets here before they went on to Oxford
kin: pitt-rivers-museum — where the Hildburgh amulet material was transferred in 1985
kin: hirz-pouch — the North African written charm class Henry Wellcome bought in bulk
kin: wikimedia-commons — where its attribution and public-domain items can be hosted; its non-commercial ones cannot
kin: free-to-use — the long read on licensing, where a per-item licence like this one is the awkward middle case

## Wikimedia Commons (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/org/wikimedia-commons/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/org/wikimedia-commons.json
id: wikimedia-commons
aliases: Commons
when: 2004 CE to now (still carried)
what: Media repository run by the Wikimedia Foundation, launched on 7 September 2004, holding over 147 million free-to-use files as of September 2026. Every picture in this atlas comes from here or from a source under the same terms. That is a constraint on what this atlas can show, and it shapes which museums are visible in it.
story: Commons takes only files that are out of copyright or published under a free licence, and its definition of free is strict: a licence must specifically and irrevocably allow anyone to use the material for any purpose. Republication and distribution must be allowed. Commercial use must be allowed. The licence must be perpetual and non-revocable. A file must also be free of copyright restrictions in both the United States and the source country of the work.

What that admits: CC0, public domain, Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (CC BY-SA), the Free Art License, and free software licences. What it refuses: CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-NC-ND, and fair use — in Commons' own words, it "does not accept fair use justifications", and material licensed exclusively under non-commercial-only licences is not accepted either.

*Inference —* run that rule across the museums in this atlas and the map goes uneven. The Metropolitan Museum of Art put its public-domain images under CC0 in 2017, so a Met amulet can be shown here. The British Museum released 1.9 million images in 2020 under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which bars commercial use, so a British Museum amulet cannot. The Pitt Rivers Museum names no Creative Commons licence at all. Wellcome Collection licenses per item, so each picture has to be checked on its own page.

The consequence is worth stating plainly rather than hiding in a caption: a reader looking at this atlas is looking at the collections that chose an open licence, not at the collections that hold the most material.
today: This atlas accepts CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and the Free Art License, and nothing else. Every image record carries its file name, its licence, its licence URL and its author, and a picture whose licence cannot be read is not published. Candidate files are listed on each record before they are fetched, so the licence is checked at the point of collection rather than at the point of publication.
kin: free-to-use — the long read this record is the machinery behind — what this atlas may show, and why the gaps are where they are
kin: metropolitan-museum — the collection whose CC0 release clears this bar, which is why Met photographs run through these records
kin: british-museum — the collection whose non-commercial licence does not clear it, however large the collection is
kin: wellcome-collection — the mixed case: some of its items clear the bar and some do not, so each file is checked singly
kin: te-papa — a collection with openly available images and, separately, a request about taonga this atlas honours regardless of licence
kin: aiatsis — the opposite premise: a collection where access conditions travel with the item and open reuse is not the default
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on ownership; a free licence on a photograph settles nothing about the object in it
sources: s:web-wikimedia-commons-wikipedia s:web-commons-licensing s:wp-metropolitan-museum-of-art s:web-bm-images-ianvisits s:web-prm-collections-terms s:web-wellcome-accessing-collections

## abracadabra (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/abracadabra/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/abracadabra.json
id: abracadabra
aliases: Abrahadabra
said: ab-ra-ka-DAB-ra
when: 100 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IT GB US
root: Origin unknown. Wikipedia's article reports the Oxford English Dictionary's position: 'no documentation has been found to support any of the various conjectures'.
what: A word that was an object. Written out as a shrinking triangle on a piece of parchment and hung at the neck, it was a prescription — the earliest surviving instruction for it is a doctor's, for fever. It is now what a stage magician says at the end of a trick, which is a demotion with a date.
story: Serenus Sammonicus, physician to the Roman emperor Caracalla, wrote in chapter 52 of the Liber Medicinalis that a sufferer from malaria should wear an amulet with Abracadabra written on it in the form of a triangle. He claimed the amulet makes lethal diseases go away. Other emperors who followed his medical teaching — Geta and Severus Alexander — may have used the formula too.

The form was understood to do the work. Written in the shrinking triangle, the word was taken to act like a funnel, driving the sickness out of the body. That is a claim about a shape, not about a language, which fits a word nobody could translate then either.

It was picked up by the Gnostics of the sect of Basilides, who used it invoking beneficent spirits against disease and misfortune, and it is found on Abraxas stones worn as amulets. From there its use spread past the Gnostics.

It kept turning up on parchment. A sixteenth-century Jewish codex from Italy, Ets ha-Da'at (The Tree of Knowledge), a collection of magical spells, carries it as an amulet described as a 'cure from heavens' for 'all sorts of fever[s]', consumption and fire.

It was also argued with, in print, for centuries. The Puritan minister Increase Mather dismissed the word as bereft of power. Daniel Defoe wrote dismissively about Londoners who posted it on their doorways to keep sickness out during the Great Plague of London.

By the early 1800s it had become an example of what magicians say, and that is where it stayed; today it is the tag line at the end of a trick. Aleister Crowley took it back the other way, adapting it into Abrahadabra in The Book of the Law, the central text of Thelema.

*Inference —* the arc is from a prescription written by a named imperial physician to a punchline, with the shape doing the work at one end and the sound doing it at the other. Very few objects in this atlas can be dated to a chapter number.
kin: palindrome-word — the family this belongs to: a written formula whose arrangement is the claim
kin: magic-square — the other arrangement-as-claim — letters or numbers laid out so the grid does the work
kin: magical-gem — where the word turns up cut in stone, on Abraxas stones worn as amulets
kin: curse-tablet — the opposite-facing object from the same Roman world: writing folded to do harm rather than to lift it
kin: inscribing — the practice the whole thing consists of — no material, no shape, just the writing of it
kin: charm-word — the English word that began exactly here, at the spell said rather than the object worn
kin: the-drawn-signs — the picture piece where the triangle is set beside the other written figures
sources: s:wp-abracadabra s:wp-abraxas s:wp-sator-square s:wp-magic-square
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## amulet (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/amulet-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/amulet-word.json
id: amulet-word
aliases: amuletum · amulette · amalettys
said: AM-yoo-let
when: 1450 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB US IT
root: Latin amuletum > Middle French amulette > English amulet
what: The English cover-word for a protective object, and the word this atlas is written in. English-language museums, catalogues and scholarship use it as the wide category and file everything else inside it — Wikipedia's article calls amulet the proper, inclusive term and puts good luck charm and devotional article underneath it as subsets. Other writers split the pair: an amulet turns harm away, a talisman brings fortune in. The same encyclopedia carries both positions, one article apart. Which sense a reader meets depends on who wrote the label in front of them.
story: Pliny's Natural History pins the Latin word to a thing: an amuletum is an object that protects a person from trouble. Beyond that the Latin is dark. The Online Etymology Dictionary calls its origin uncertain, floats a link to amoliri, 'to avert, to carry away', and turns down the Arabic derivation that gets repeated in popular writing.

English took the word late, and then dropped it. The Online Etymology Dictionary records amalettys in the middle of the fifteenth century, probably through French, and then nothing again until about 1600. A hundred and fifty years of silence, and then it came back to stay.

The split with talisman is the argument the word carries. Wikipedia's amulet article states flatly that talismans and amulets have interchangeable meanings, and in the next breath that an amulet is generally worn for protection and made from a durable material. Its talisman article keeps the functions apart: protection against evil on one side, good fortune on the other. Museum labels follow one convention or the other without announcing which.

*Inference —* the category is European and it was laid over the world from outside. An Egyptian wore a wedjat; a Bangkok collector buys a phra khrueang by temple and by monk; a visitor to a Kyoto shrine takes home an omamori. None of them reaches for a word meaning amulet-in-general. The wide word belongs to the cataloguer, and it is the word on the spine of this project. Saying so is the least the reader is owed.
kin: talisman-word — the word it is paired with and sometimes distinguished from — protection on this side, fortune on that, when a writer bothers to split them
kin: charm-word — the older English word, which started as the spoken spell and only later meant the object
kin: phylactery-word — used as a general synonym for any amulet, and at the same time the fixed English word for tefillin
kin: periapt — the near-dead English synonym, kept alive by antiquarians and by translators out of Greek
kin: apotropaic-word — the scholar's adjective for the same objects, describing the function and claiming nothing for it
kin: fetish-word — the other European cover-word for other people's objects — and the one this atlas uses for its own history only
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read that takes this disagreement apart instead of settling it
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-talisman s:web-etymonline-amulet s:web-wiktionary-amulet

## apotropaic (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/apotropaic-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/apotropaic-word.json
id: apotropaic-word
native: ἀποτρόπαιος (Greek)
aliases: apotropaion · apotropaia
said: ap-oh-troh-PAY-ik
when: 500 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: GR GB US
root: Greek apo 'away' + tropos 'turn' > apotrepō (ἀποτρέπω) 'to turn away, to ward off' > apotropaios (ἀποτρόπαιος) 'averting' > English apotropaic
what: The scholar's adjective, and nobody's own. No wearer calls a bead apotropaic. It is the word a museum label, an excavation report and a doctoral thesis use for anything meant to turn harm aside — and its one virtue is that it names a purpose without taking a view on whether the purpose is met. This atlas uses it for that reason and no other.
story: Greek did not need one word, because it had a crowd of them. The ancient sources carry apotropaia, probaskania, periammata, periapta, profylaktika, phylaktiria, antipharmaca, alexicaca, alexipharmaca and alexima pharmaca, all for protective objects, with no one of them dominant.

The gods came in matching sets. Offerings went to the apotropaioi theoi, the averting gods, and to the Apopompaioi theoi, who send evil away, and the Apōsikakoi theoi, the evil-averting gods. Zeus, Apollo, Heracles and Leucothea all carried the epithet Alexicacus, averter of evil; Heracles was also Keramyntes, another averter.

English boiled the crowd down to one adjective and handed it to the academy. *Inference —* that reduction is why an Egyptian birth tusk, a Roman fascinum, an Irish Brigid's cross and a Japanese ofuda can hang on one wall under one heading. The category is a translation choice, made once, in Greek, and then carried by people writing in English about everybody else.

*Tradition holds —* the practices the word covers rarely describe themselves as a category at all. A household rite in Egypt, spitting into the folds of a garment in Greece, a grasshopper hung before the Acropolis by Peisistratus: these were separate acts to the people doing them, and the adjective that gathers them is ours.
kin: ward-word — the Old English verb that translates this Greek one — the same act, arriving in English from the other direction
kin: periapt — one of the Greek protective words this adjective outlived, and the only other to reach English
kin: greco-roman-apotropaic — the tradition the word was quarried out of, and the one it now labels
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the practices that never used the word and get filed under it anyway
kin: fascinum — the Roman object this adjective is applied to more often than any other
kin: amulet-word — the noun beside this adjective; one names the thing, the other names what it is for

## charm (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/charm-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/charm-word.json
id: charm-word
aliases: charme · carmen
said: charm
when: 1300 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB US FR
root: Latin carmen 'song, verse, enchantment, religious formula' (from canere 'to sing') > Old French charme 'magic charm, magic spell, incantation; song, lamentation' > Middle English charme > English charm
what: A word that has been three things in sequence and is still all three. A charm is a said or sung formula; a charm is a small object worn against harm or for luck; charm is what a person has who is pleasant to be near. English keeps no marker between them, so charm bracelet, charm offensive and charm against toothache are the same word doing different work.
story: It started as the words themselves. Latin carmen is a song, a verse, a formula — from canere, to sing — and Old French charme is the spell spoken aloud. English has it by about 1300 in that sense only: an incantation. There is no object in the word yet.

The object arrives around 1590, when charm starts to mean any item worn to avert evil. The pleasing-person sense follows in the seventeenth century, and the weaker sense of being highly pleasing in the early eighteenth. The bracelet sense is the newest of the four and can be dated: 1865, for a small object fastened to a watch-chain.

*Inference —* the drift is from what is said, to what is worn, to what is admired, and the hinge is the same idea each time — a thing with the power to move somebody who is not choosing to be moved. That is also why this atlas files a spoken formula and a hung pendant under one heading without apology: English already did.

*Tradition holds —* the older English charm was as often spoken over an injury as hung round a neck, and the practical difference between a verse and an object narrows to nothing once the verse is written down and folded into a case.
kin: abracadabra — the charm that never stopped being only words, and the one with a dated first appearance
kin: amulet-word — the Latinate cover-word that took over the object sense in catalogues, leaving charm to the bracelet and the compliment
kin: luck-word — the word it is welded to — good luck charm is the compound most English speakers actually use
kin: four-leaf-clover — the object a British or American reader is likeliest to name when the word is said
kin: exam-charm — the sense alive on a student's desk this year: an object carried for one occasion
kin: mascot-word — the nineteenth-century French import that took over the luck-bringing sense in sport and in advertising

## fetish (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/fetish-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/fetish-word.json
id: fetish-word
aliases: feitiço · Fetisso · fétiche · fatisso · fetishism
said: FET-ish
when: 1610 CE to now (still carried)
countries: PT FR GB TG BJ
root: Latin facticius 'made by art, artificial' (William Pietz points instead to facere, 'to make') > late medieval Portuguese feitiço 'spell' > sixteenth-century pidgin Fetisso on the West African coast > French fétiche > English fetish
what: A European word, applied from outside, to objects Europeans met on the West African coast and could not file. This atlas carries the word for its own history and for nothing else: no object anywhere in this project is described as a fetish. What the word describes is an act of labelling, and the labelling had consequences — it supplied the bottom rung of a ladder of religions that European writers then climbed, with themselves at the top.
story: William Pietz, whose 1994 ethno-historical study is the standard account, argues the term originated on the coast of West Africa in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, in the encounter itself. He keeps two things apart: actual African objects that Europeans called fetishes, together with the local theories of those objects, and 'fetish' as an idea about a kind of object. The second is European property.

He traces the chain in one sentence: from the late medieval Portuguese feitiço, to the sixteenth-century pidgin Fetisso on the African coast, to various northern European versions of the word by way of the 1602 text of the Dutchman Pieter de Marees. The Portuguese developed the concept for objects used in West African religious practice. What went into the category was then decided by exclusion: objects were classed as fetishes indiscriminately because, from a European standpoint, they did not fit anywhere else.

The travel literature spread it. Ramusio's Viaggio e Navigazioni of 1550, de Bry's India Orientalis of 1597, Purchas's Hakluytus Posthumus of 1625, Churchill's Collection of Voyages and Travels of 1732, Astley's A New General Collection of Voyages and Travels of 1746, Prevost's Histoire générale des voyages of 1748: these are the books the eighteenth-century theorists read.

Then it became a theory. Charles de Brosses popularised the term around 1760, in Du culte des dieux fétiches, comparing West African religion with the magical side of ancient Egyptian religion. Auguste Comte put fetishism first in his sequence of religious development, ahead of polytheism and monotheism. G. W. F. Hegel, in Lectures on the Philosophy of History, held that Africans were incapable of abstract thought and that a fetish object could therefore be anything arbitrarily given 'imaginary powers'. Modern scholarship reads the whole sequence as colonial: the Portuguese, Dutch and British deployed the category to criticise how colonised people dealt with material objects, and built European rationality by contrast.

The word then kept moving away from the coast. Around 1837 it meant an object of blind devotion among the New England Transcendentalists. In 1897 Havelock Ellis fixed the psycho-sexual sense, which is the sense most English speakers now hear first.

And it did not stay only in European mouths. The market at Akodessawa, a district of Lomé in Togo, carries the word in its own French name: Marché des Féticheurs. Wikipedia's account of it says the market sells fetishes used in vodún religious practice. *Inference —* a word coined about people can be taken up by them, for trade, for tourism, or because it is the word the customer knows. That does not undo the coinage, and this atlas still does not use it to describe an object.

*Tradition holds —* the objects themselves have their own names in their own languages — nkisi among Kikongo speakers is the clearest case — and those names are what this project files them under.
kin: nkisi — the Kikongo word for objects Europeans filed under this one — the name the makers use, and the one this atlas uses
kin: bakongo-nkisi-craft — the tradition most damaged by the labelling, and the one whose vocabulary replaces it here
kin: akodessewa-market — the market in Lomé that carries the word in its own French name, which is the complication this record cannot tidy away
kin: juju-word — the other outsiders' word for West African practice, contested in the same way and still current
kin: vodou-not-voodoo — the neighbouring case: a religion renamed by the people describing it, with a spelling to match
kin: amulet-word — the cover-word Europeans used for their own protective objects while this one was used for other people's
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read this record feeds: who gets to name a thing, and what the naming does
sources: s:wp-fetishism s:web-etymonline-fetish s:wp-akodessawa-fetish-market s:wp-nkisi s:wp-cultural-appropriation
