## fu (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/fu-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/fu-word.json
id: fu-word
native: 福 (Han)
aliases: 福 · 符 · fulu · fú · fú zì
said: fú
when: 960 CE to now (still carried)
countries: CN TW MY
root: Chinese 福 (fú) 'fortune, good luck'. A different character, 符 (fú), means a tally or talismanic graph and gives fulu (符籙), 'talismanic script'; 籙 (lù) is a registry of priests' memberships and of the skills they are trained in.
what: One character, printed on a square of red paper and pasted at the entrance, usually turned upside down. Fú means fortune or good luck; it is also the name of a god, one of the trio of star gods Fú, Lù and Shòu, who is often shown as a figure carrying the character. Mounted fu appear at the doors of Chinese homes worldwide at New Year, and the practice runs across every level of income.
story: The custom is old enough to date: mounting the character goes back at least to the Song dynasty, 960 to 1279 CE.

The upside-down part is a pun, and the pun is the mechanism. In nearly all varieties of Chinese the word for upside-down and the word for to arrive are homophones — dào, written 倒 and 到. 'Upside-down fu' therefore sounds all but identical to 'good luck arrives', so pasting the character inverted on a door or doorpost states a wish that prosperity descends on the house.

A second story explains the same thing differently. It puts the origin with the family of a nineteenth-century Qing prince: on a New Year's Eve the prince's servants pasted fu characters through the house as a joke, one illiterate servant put his on upside down, and when the prince was furious another servant saved him by pointing out that the mistake announced prosperity arriving. Two accounts, one practice; the encyclopedia carries both without choosing.

The sound does further work. Bats — 蝠 — are among the most common of Chinese symbols and carry the same sound as fu, which is why textiles and ceramics show bats in flight, sometimes more than a hundred at once. Bran, 麩子, fūzi, is a rarer match.

The other fu is a different trade. In Taoist practice, 符 are instructions to deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions and cures, written by priests of the fulu pai. Their illegibility is not a failure: Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, by the Eastern Jin dynasty of 317 to 420, that successful use did not depend on the user's being able to read the script, and scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz argue the incomprehensibility is central to the talisman's authority.

The fortune character now has a code point: Unicode 10, in 2017, added a rounded version at U+1F260 🉠 ROUNDED SYMBOL FOR FU.
kin: fu-talisman — the object the second character names: the drawn Taoist talisman, written by a priest
kin: ping-an-fu — the peace-and-safety charm that carries the word in its name
kin: chinese-fu-craft — the tradition both characters belong to
kin: ofuda — the Japanese descendant of fulu — the same word, crossed over and re-cut
kin: bujeok — the Korean descendant of the same script, kept in a small brocade bag
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the fortune character exists for: paper, paste, doorpost, once a year
kin: luck-word — the English word that translates 福 and carries none of the pun
sources: s:wp-fu-character s:wp-fulu s:wp-ofuda s:wp-korean-shamanism
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## gris-gris (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/gris-gris-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/gris-gris-word.json
id: gris-gris-word
aliases: grigri · gri-gri · gregory · gerregery · saffi
said: GREE-gree
countries: SN ML GH HT US
root: From the Mande languages spoken by Mandinka and Bambara people in West Africa; Wikipedia's article reports the sense 'magic'. Carried to the Americas with enslaved Muslims and into Louisiana and Haitian French.
what: A word that names a small cloth sack worn on the person, holding Qur'anic verses written on paper and a set number of small objects. It began in Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa and crossed the Atlantic with enslaved people. On the western side of the ocean the same word carries two opposite charges, and which one a speaker means depends on where they are standing.
story: The trade route came first. Travellers through the Volta Basin, in what is now Ghana, reported Mande speakers such as the Dyula as central to making and distributing Islamic charms, which they called gris-gris. From them the practice spread to other Muslim groups — the Dagomba, who wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts 'with magic formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets'. The sacks held Qur'an verses on paper with herbs, worn at the neck. Sometimes the written charm alone counted, carried by priests. Non-Muslims in the region wore them too, under the name saffis.

The makers are named. Among Mande Muslims, scholars of the mystical division called siri, 'path', are marabouts, and they are the ones who produce gris-gris; scholars of seli, 'prayer', are karamokos, who study Qur'anic law. Some cross over. The whole practice is Karamokobara.

In the United States the word turned. Enslaved people used gris-gris against their owners, and the word came to name harm done to a target; some were found in burials; there are period reports of people cutting, drowning or otherwise handling somebody else's gris-gris to injure them. New Orleans court cases in 1773 convicted enslaved people of using gris-gris to kill enslavers — among the earliest legal mentions of Louisiana's tradition. Enslaved conjure women made gris-gris to start rebellions, and the bags were held to guide people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. By the 1800s the word was used in Louisiana to mean both bewitch and the object itself. In October 1849 authorities arrested an enslaved man carrying a human finger wrapped in flannel that he held brought good luck; people in New Orleans sought human remains from tombs for conjure and gris-gris, and gravesites were disturbed for it. In Cajun communities the word reads as harm and ill-fortune. In the Louisiana Creole community, Gris-Gris doctors have worked for centuries and are looked on favourably by the Black community at large.

In Haiti, on the same account, the word kept its West African sense: an amulet with good intentions. In Hoodoo a gris-gris is taken to represent the self.

It is also current and ordinary. A 1982 survey put gris-gris among the top three methods of contraception known to women in Senegal, alongside abstinence and roots and herbs; over sixty per cent of women reported knowing such traditional methods, against a little over forty per cent for the pill. They are worn, in the article's own words, 'from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives, and can feature anything from monkey to snake to mouse.'
kin: gris-gris — the object this word names: the sack itself, its contents and its maker
kin: taweez-word — the Arabic word for the same idea — Qur'anic text folded and worn — which is what a Mande marabout is writing
kin: mojo-word — the other African-derived word for a worn sack in Louisiana, out of the Kongo rather than the Muslim west
kin: juju-word — the outsiders' cover-word that often swallowed this one in English writing
kin: vodou-not-voodoo — the tradition this word was carried into, and the spelling argument that comes with naming it
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition behind the paper inside the sack: written Qur'anic text, worn
kin: hirz-pouch — the same object under another name further east — a pouch holding written scripture
sources: s:wp-gris-gris-talisman s:wp-mojo-bag s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-islam-and-magic
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## hamsa (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/hamsa-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/hamsa-word.json
id: hamsa-word
native: خمسة (Arabic)
aliases: khamsa · khmisa · hamesh · afus · Hand of Fatima · Hand of Miriam · kef Miryam
said: KHAM-sa
countries: MA DZ TN EG IL LB TR ES
root: Arabic khamsa (خمسة) 'five' > English hamsa; Maghrebi variants khmisa; Hebrew hamesh (five) in Jewish usage; Berber afus, 'hand', names a similar motif
what: A word that is a number. Five — for the fingers — is what the object is called in Arabic, and hamesh, also five, in Hebrew usage. The names a shopper meets in Europe and America are all attachments: 'Hand of Fatima' (French Main de Fatma) was popularised by Europeans in French colonial North Africa and is a colonial nickname rather than an indigenous Arabic term. In Sephardi and Mizrahi Jewish contexts it is the Hand of Miriam. Levantine Christians call it kef Miryam, the hand of Mary.
story: The number is in the curses too, which is the strongest sign that the counting came first. Khamsa fi ainek — 'five [fingers] in your eye' — is said with the right hand raised, palm out, fingers slightly apart, to blind the aggressor. Khamsa wa-khamis, 'five and Thursday', is said without any gesture; Thursday, the fifth day, is held favourable for rites and for pilgrimages to saints' tombs against the evil eye. And there is the spitting formula: 'Khamsa, Khamsa, Khamsa, tfu, tfu, tfu', which Wikipedia's article compares to knocking on wood.

The name has been legislated against. Among the Morisco population of Granada and nearby regions, khamsa pendants were popular and described as 'large engraved medals ... with a hand inscribed with letters'. A reform council banned khamsas as Islamic symbols in 1526 and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the prohibition in 1554; an episcopal committee convened by Emperor Charles V decreed a ban on the Hand of Fatima and all open right-hand amulets in 1526. They went on being worn, including by Christians — a Nasrid-period gold pendant survives inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

It is argued over now from inside as well. Eva-Maria von Kemnitz, citing Bruno Barbatti, calls it the most important averting sign in the Islamic world; Salafi authorities reject it, and a fatwa states it is impermissible to hang the 'Khamsa', with hands of Fatima listed among prohibited amulets. The hamsa is also a national symbol of Algeria and appears in its emblem.

*Inference —* a name that is a number is very hard to suppress: you cannot ban five. What actually displaced the Arabic word in most of the world's shops was not a prohibition but a French colonial nickname, and that is the name on the label a buyer in London or Los Angeles reads today.
kin: hamsa — the object the word counts: the open hand, usually with an eye set in the palm
kin: hand — the sign the number is counting, and the reason the word means what it does
kin: open-palm — the gesture inside the word — the raised palm of khamsa fi ainek
kin: nazar-word — the other word for the same harm, naming the look where this one names the answer
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — where both words end up: the same two signs on one bought object
kin: marrakesh-souk — a market where the Arabic word and the French nickname are both on the same stall
sources: s:wp-hamsa s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-amulet
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## juju (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/juju-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/juju-word.json
id: juju-word
aliases: ju-ju · juju man
said: JOO-joo
when: 1860 CE to now (still carried)
countries: NG BJ TG CM GH
root: Contested. Two proposals are in print and neither has won. Wikipedia's article reports an origin in Hausa, where the term means 'evil spirit'. The same article, and the Online Etymology Dictionary, report a derivation from French joujou, 'toy, plaything' — the dictionary calls it supposed.
what: In central West Africa — Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Cameroon, Ghana — juju names a body of practice and the objects and spells inside it. In looser English it means magical properties dealing with luck, good or bad. Across the West African diaspora the word covers charms made in African traditional and African diaspora religions generally. Wikipedia's article records the practitioner's title plainly: a juju man is any man vetted by local traditions and well versed in traditional spiritual medicines.
story: The word reached English print through colonial officials. James George Frazer published it in Folk-Lore volume XXVI under the title 'A Priest-King in Nigeria', from a communication he received from P. A. Talbot, District Commissioner in southern Nigeria. Talbot described the dominant Ju-Ju of Elele, a town in the north-west of the Degema district, as a Priest-King elected for a term of seven years, and wrote: 'The whole prosperity of the town, especially the fruitfulness of farm, byre, and marriage-bed, was linked with his life. Should he fall sick, therefore, it entailed famine and grave disaster upon the inhabitants ...'

Others were already writing it down. Le Comte C. N. de Cardi documented the practice among Igbo, Ibibio and Yoruba people of the Niger Delta in an article of 1899; Alan Maxwell Boisragon in a book of 1897.

On what the word covers, Wikipedia's article is careful and worth quoting rather than paraphrasing: according to some authors, 'It is neither good nor bad, but it may be used for constructive purposes as well as for nefarious deeds.' Its commonest reported use is the treatment of physical and spiritual complaints — insect and animal bites, and the countering of curses. It is also used to bind a contract or secure compliance, with the practitioner paid for the service. Used against somebody, it is reported as a means of revenge and of causing misfortune.

*Inference —* the etymological fight matters because of what each answer implies. Hausa 'evil spirit' makes the word a local name for a serious thing. French joujou makes it a European joke about somebody else's religion. Which root a nineteenth-century writer preferred has usually said more about the writer than about the word, and the sources have not settled it.
kin: mojo-word — the American cousin: another word with contested African roots that popular music carried out of its home
kin: gris-gris-word — the Mande word for the object, where this one is an outsiders' word for the whole practice
kin: fetish-word — the earlier European coinage for the same coast, and the one that hardened into a theory of religion
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the tradition the word is pointed at, which has its own names for everything in it
kin: nkisi — a Central African object often swept under this word by writers who did not ask what its makers called it
kin: vodou-not-voodoo — the same argument one country over, where the spelling itself became the fight
sources: s:wp-juju s:web-etymonline-juju s:wp-west-african-vod-n

## luck (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/luck-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/luck-word.json
id: luck-word
aliases: luk · gelucke · gelücke · good luck charm
said: luck
when: 1480 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB US NL DE
root: Middle Low German, Dutch or Frisian luk, a short form of gelucke (Middle High German gelücke) > English luck
what: The word the whole 'good luck charm' category hangs on in English, and a late arrival that came in through a card game. Wikipedia's article sets out three conditions for it: luck is good or bad, luck is the result of chance, and luck applies to a sentient being. Nothing in that definition involves a god, which is exactly what changed when the word arrived.
story: English managed without it until the 1480s. What it had instead was speed — Old English spēd — which meant good fortune and also prosperity, profit and abundance, and which named help rather than chance. A bestower of success could be called a speed. Then luck came in from Low German, Dutch or Frisian, probably at a gaming table, and it named something else: a personal chance event, with nobody behind it.

The idea it needed had arrived a couple of centuries earlier. Chance, from Old French cheance and Late Latin cadentia, literally describes an outcome as a falling — as of dice — and English took it from the late thirteenth century. Fortuna, the Roman goddess, was a popular medieval allegory, and learned writers of the High Middle Ages made her a servant of God distributing success and failure in a fickle way, which is how chance was fitted into a Christian frame without being given a will of its own.

The symbols the word gathers are local and contradictory. Seven is a lucky number in Christian-influenced cultures, eight in Chinese-influenced ones. In Chinese and Japanese, four is unlucky because it sounds like the word for death. Greek practice counts entering and leaving a house by different doors, and breaking a mirror, as unlucky; Navajo practice counts throwing rocks into a whirlwind. In Western practice, opening an umbrella indoors may be counted unlucky partly because it can poke somebody in the eye, and shaking hands with a chimney sweep counted lucky partly because it is a kind but unpleasant thing to do.

The gods stayed on for a while beside it: Fortuna and Felicitas in Roman religion, Dedun in Nubian religion, the Seven Lucky Gods in Japan, Lakshmi and her inauspicious counterpart Alakshmi in Hinduism.

*Inference —* the arrival of luck is the arrival of the idea that the outcome is nobody's decision. An object bought against that is a different object from one bought to petition somebody, even when it is the same object on the same string. Half the arguments in this atlas about whether a charm is devotional or commercial are really arguments about which of those two words the buyer is using.
kin: charm-word — the word it is welded to — good luck charm is the compound, and neither half means what it used to
kin: mascot-word — the French import that took the luck-bringing job in sport and commerce four centuries later
kin: four-leaf-clover — the object an English speaker names first when the word is said
kin: rabbits-foot — the other one, and the one that shows how little the word cares where an object came from
kin: maneki-neko — what the word is used to translate in a Japanese shop window, flattening a beckoning cat into a luck object
kin: fu-word — the Chinese character English renders as luck, losing the pun the whole practice runs on
kin: game-day-charm — the sense at its most modern and most literal: an object carried against one specific uncertain outcome
sources: s:wp-luck s:wp-lucky-charm s:wp-list-of-lucky-symbols s:wp-four-leaf-clover
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## mascot (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/mascot-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/mascot-word.json
id: mascot-word
native: mascotte (Latin)
aliases: mascotte · masco
said: MASS-kot
when: 1867 CE to now (still carried)
countries: FR GB US
root: Provençal masco 'sorceress, witch' > French mascotte 'lucky charm' > English mascot
what: The only word in this batch whose modern sense is a job. A mascot is a human, an animal or an object thought to bring luck, or anything that stands for a group with a common public identity — a school, a team, a society, a military unit, a brand. The luck sense is still the first one the word carries; the costume is a twentieth-century addition.
story: The route is short and well-marked: masco, a Provençal word for a sorceress, into French mascotte meaning a lucky charm, used for anything that brought luck to a household. Wikipedia's article dates the first record to 1867 and the arrival in English to 1881, in the sense of a specific living creature attached to a human organisation as a symbol or live logo. What moved it from French gamblers' slang into general use was a stage piece: Edmond Audran's La mascotte, performed in December 1880.

Before all that the word sat on objects of a kind this atlas is full of — a lock of hair, a figurehead on a sailing ship.

The costume came later, and it came from puppetry. Animals were used first, by sports organisations, to entertain spectators and to unsettle opponents. Stylistic changes in American puppetry in the middle of the twentieth century, including the work of Jim Henson and of Sid and Marty Krofft, were adapted to sports mascots, and the three-dimensional costumed character followed — the Phillie Phanatic, the Flyers' Gritty, the Seattle Kraken's Buoy, the Washington Commanders' Major Tuddy. Marketers took the form from there.

The live argument attached to the word is over mascots based on human likenesses. Mascots using Native American tribes are contested, and many argue they are offensive exploitations of an oppressed culture. Several tribes have taken the other position: the Utah Utes and the Central Michigan Chippewas are sanctioned by local tribes, and Florida State's use of Osceola and Renegade is supported by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, though the university declines to call them mascots. Both sides are named here and neither is joined.
kin: luck-word — the word it imports into English commerce — mascotte glossed as lucky charm, nothing more complicated
kin: charm-word — the older English word it took the luck-bringing job from, in sport and in advertising
kin: game-day-charm — what a supporter carries, where the mascot is what the club owns
kin: challenge-coin — the military parallel: an object that stands for a unit and is carried by its members
kin: exam-charm — the private version of the same idea, with no costume and no crowd
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read the Native American mascot argument belongs to
sources: s:wp-mascot s:wp-luck s:wp-cultural-appropriation
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## mojo (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/mojo-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/mojo-word.json
id: mojo-word
aliases: mojo bag · toby · lucky hand · nation sack · conjure bag
said: MOH-joh
when: 1920 CE to now (still carried)
countries: US
root: Contested, and African on both proposals. Wikipedia's mojo bag article derives it from Kikongo mooyo, glossed as referring to the spirits that dwell within magical charms, and names the cavity of an nkisi where the charm's materials are kept. The Online Etymology Dictionary says 'probably of Creole origin' and points to Gullah moco, 'witchcraft', and Fula moco'o, 'medicine man'.
what: In Hoodoo, the African American spiritual tradition, mojo is both the conjure work and the bag that holds it — Wikipedia's article calls a mojo bag a prayer in a bag, a spell that can be carried on the body. Outside that, in general American English, mojo means sexual potency, then drive, then momentum in a meeting. The same word, one century, two rooms.
story: Both proposed roots point at the same shelf. On Wikipedia's account the Kikongo mooyo names the spirits inside a charm and the cavity of an nkisi where the charm's materials sit — so the word starts as the inside of a container. On the Online Etymology Dictionary's account it is Creole, beside Gullah moco and Fula moco'o. Neither source claims the other is wrong.

The object has an ancestry that is not contested. Bakongo people of the Congo River region made medicine bags of leather or cloth holding feathers, animal parts, roots and herbs; when Bakongo people were enslaved in the United States the practice continued and became a custom of Hoodoo. Nkisi bags looked like mojo bags and are named as their ancestor. The philosophy came with them: in Bakongo religion, simbi spirits can inhabit an nkisi bag, and the nganga makes the bag for a person with ingredients specific to a particular simbi.

The bag has other American names — toby, lucky hand, nation sack, conjure bag, package — and the word hand in that list has its own contested origin: from finger and hand bones of the dead used in the bags, or from lucky hand root, favoured by gamblers, or from the hand of cards the mixed ingredients resemble.

Then the word left. Wikipedia's account is blunt about it: mojo underwent a semantic change in American popular culture at the beginning of the twentieth century and came to refer to sexuality and virility, as musicians began to use the word outside its original context within African American culture. From there it became motivation in general.

*Inference —* this is the sharpest case in this batch of a word walking away from the people who made it. A term for the spirit inside a container now means the thing a commentator says a footballer has lost and an investor says a start-up has found. The bag is still made; the word on top of it now belongs to everybody.
kin: nkisi — the Central African object Wikipedia's account names as the mojo bag's ancestor, and whose cavity the word may be named after
kin: bakongo-nkisi-craft — the tradition the bag and the word both come out of
kin: gris-gris-word — the other African-derived word for a worn cloth sack in Louisiana, from the Muslim west rather than the Kongo
kin: juju-word — the parallel argument over an African etymology, fought with different candidates
kin: fetish-word — what European writers called the objects this word names, before anyone asked the makers
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on words and objects that leave the community that built them
sources: s:wp-mojo-bag s:web-etymonline-mojo s:wp-nkisi s:wp-gris-gris-talisman

## nazar (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/nazar-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/nazar-word.json
id: nazar-word
native: نَظَر (Arabic)
aliases: naẓar · nazar boncuğu · máti · cheshm nazar · nazar qurbāni
said: na-ZAR
countries: TR IR AZ AL GR IN PK BD
root: Arabic naẓar (نَظَر) 'sight, surveillance, attention' > borrowed into Albanian, Azerbaijani, Bengali, Hebrew, Hindi-Urdu, Kurdish, Pashto, Persian, Punjabi, Sindhi and Turkish
what: A word for a glance that has ended up as the name of a glass disc. Naẓar in Arabic is sight, surveillance, attention. Across a dozen languages it names the harmful look — in India and Pakistan nazar lag gai says somebody has been struck by it — and by extension the bead sold against it. Persian and Afghan usage says cheshm nazar or nazar qurbāni; Turkish says nazar boncuğu, the nazar bead; Greek, which did not borrow the word, says máti.
story: The phrase that keeps it away is its own small piece of evidence. In India and Pakistan the Hindi-Urdu chashm-e-baddoor — 'may the evil eye keep away' — is said aloud, without any object involved at all. The bead is the same sentence in glass.

What the bead is is described the same way by everyone selling it: handmade glass, concentric circles or teardrops in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes edged yellow or gold. Wikipedia's article quotes the recipe as “a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil”, and reports the colour logic in a wearer's terms: 'According to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity.' It also carries the argument from rarity — in the Middle East and the Mediterranean, blue eyes are uncommon, and light-eyed people were held able to curse with a look.

The bead is old and the word is not the oldest thing about it. The Turkish boncuk, the blue glass eye bead, is a design of great antiquity; written documentation and surviving beads date from as early as the sixteenth century BCE, and glass beads were made and used from Mesopotamia to Egypt, from Carthage to Greece, from Phoenicia to Persia and through the Roman imperial period.

And it now has a code point. Unicode added U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET in 2018. *Inference —* that is the moment the word finished its journey: a name for a look, then a bead, then a character available on every phone on earth, sent by people who have never heard the Arabic.

*Tradition holds —* wearers say a bead that breaks has taken a strong nazar and stored it, and broken in order to protect the person wearing it.
kin: nazar — the object the word rides on: the blue glass disc itself
kin: eye — the sign the word is about, and the one thing every language in its range agrees on
kin: evil-eye-bracelet — what the word now sells by the million, in airports and online
kin: hamsa-word — the other word for the same harm, which names a number instead of a look
kin: grand-bazaar — the market where the word and the bead are both on every stall
kin: the-eye-everywhere — the long read this word is the modern end of
sources: s:wp-nazar-amulet s:wp-evil-eye s:wp-nazar-battu

## omamori (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/omamori-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/omamori-word.json
id: omamori-word
native: 御守 / お守り (kanji and hiragana)
aliases: mamori · gofu · mamorifuda
said: oh-MAH-mo-ree
countries: JP
root: Japanese mamoru 'to protect' > noun mamori (守り) 'protection' > honorific prefix o- (御) + mamori = omamori (御守/お守り)
what: The Japanese word for a shrine or temple charm, and a rare case of a name that says who is doing the protecting rather than what the thing is made of. Omamori are sold at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples alike, with few exceptions, to anybody, regardless of religious affiliation — and are mainly understood as a donation to the shrine or temple the buyer is visiting, with the object as the receipt.
story: The word takes a compound for every need, which is how a reader can tell what a given charm is for without opening it: kōtsū-anzen for traffic safety, yaku-yoke for avoiding evil, kaiun for opening fortune, gakugyō-jōju for study and passing examinations, shōbai-hanjō for business, en-musubi for finding a partner and marrying, anzan for a safe pregnancy and delivery, kanai-anzen for the household's safety and peace.

The object is a brocade bag over paper or wood carrying a written prayer. Custom says not to open it — opening it loses the benefit — so the inscription is a thing the owner owns and does not read. Charms are customarily replaced once a year, returned to the shrine or temple they came from, and burnt rather than thrown away, as respect to the deity that helped through the year. Most returns come on or just after the Japanese New Year.

Yanagita Kunio, writing in 1969, put the dating carefully: 'Japanese have probably always believed in amulets of one kind or another, but the modern printed charms now given out by shrines and temples first became popular in the Tokugawa period or later, and the practice of a person wearing miniature charms is also new. The latter custom is particularly common in cities.'

The word is now on objects a shrine never touched. Materials have widened from paper and wood to bumper decals, bicycle reflectors and credit cards. Where popular shrines cannot meet demand they turn to factories, and priests have complained about the “quality and authenticity” of factory products. Shops sell generic omamori with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, not issued by any shrine or temple and not presented as religious. Both of those are called omamori, by their sellers and their buyers. This atlas reports that and leaves the argument where it is.
kin: omamori — the object the word names, bag and prayer and all
kin: ofuda — the paper tablet the same shrines issue for the household rather than the person
kin: japanese-engimono — the tradition this word sits inside, alongside the lucky objects that are not shrine issue
kin: renewing-yearly — the practice the word implies — an omamori has a term, and the term is a year
kin: burning-retirement — how it ends: returned to the shrine it came from and burnt
kin: fushimi-inari — one of the shrines the word is bought at, at the scale that makes factories an issue
kin: fu-word — the mainland word behind the paper charm this one wraps — fulu into ofuda into the bag
sources: s:wp-omamori s:wp-ofuda s:wp-fulu
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## periapt (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/periapt/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/periapt.json
id: periapt
native: περίαπτον (Greek)
aliases: periapta · periapte · períapton
said: PERR-ee-apt
when: 1500 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB GR
root: Greek peri- 'around' + haptos (ἅπτος) 'fastened' > períaptos 'hung round' > períapton (περίαπτον) 'amulet' > Middle French periapte > English periapt
what: An English word for an amulet worn hung round the neck, defined by the hanging rather than by the shape or the material. It is close to dead. It survives in antiquarian writing, in medical history, and in translations out of Greek, where the plural periapta sits in the ancient list of protective objects.
story: The Greek says what it is: períaptos, hung round. Not carved, not blessed, not written — fastened on. Ancient Greek sources list periapta among apotropaia, probaskania, periammata, phylaktiria and the rest, none of them the single dominant term.

The English quotations Wiktionary carries are all of a type. Walter Scott, in The Talisman in 1825, writes that the Persians were perhaps most remarkable for their unshaken credulity in amulets, spells, periapts and similar charms. Thomas Oswald Cockayne, in Leechdoms, Wortcunning, and Starcraft in 1864, records that the occipital bone of an ass's head in a skin is also a good periapt. Charles William King's The Natural History of Precious Stones of 1867 distinguishes a decoration from a periapt, for it was suspended round his neck by golden chains. Fielding H. Garrison's An Introduction to the History of Medicine of 1921 has a formula that became a charm for intractable haemorrhage, written on the part affected or worn as a periapt.

*Inference —* the word survived exactly where the Greek did — in the Victorian antiquarian's English, and in the vocabulary of men writing about other people's practices at a distance. It never made it onto a shop sign.

*Tradition holds —* the distinction the word preserves is worth keeping even if the word is not: an object that hangs is a different object from one sewn in, buried under a threshold or nailed to a door, and every one of those is in this atlas.
kin: amulet-word — the word that beat it — both mean a worn protective object, and only one is still sold in bookshops
kin: apotropaic-word — the other Greek survivor in English, and the one the academy kept instead of this
kin: phylactery-word — its neighbour in the ancient Greek list, phylaktiria beside periapta, and the one the New Testament made permanent
kin: magical-gem — the class of object Victorian writers were usually describing when they reached for this word
kin: frederick-elworthy — the Victorian cataloguer whose generation kept the word in print
kin: wearing-hidden — the practice this word rules out — a periapt hangs where it can be seen
sources: s:web-wiktionary-periapt s:wp-apotropaic-magic s:wp-amulet

## phylactery (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/phylactery-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/phylactery-word.json
id: phylactery-word
native: φυλακτήριον (Greek)
aliases: phylacteries · phylaktērion · phylaktēria
said: fih-LAK-ter-ee
when: 50 CE to now (still carried)
countries: IL GB US GR
root: Greek phylaktērion (φυλακτήριον) 'guarded post, safeguard, security', in later Greek 'amulet' or 'charm' > the Greek New Testament, where it occurs once > Latin and the languages of Europe > English phylactery
what: Three words wearing one spelling, and a reader has to know which is meant. In Bible translation and in older Jewish scholarship, phylactery is the English word for tefillin — the leather boxes of Torah text bound to arm and head. In general English it is a loose synonym for any amulet. In tabletop gaming it names the object a lich hides its life force in, which is where most English speakers under forty meet the word first.
story: The Greek starts as architecture and police work. Phylaktērion is a guarded post, a safeguard, a security; only in later Greek does it mean an amulet. The New Testament uses it once, at Matthew 23, for the boxes worn by Jews — a Greek word for a Jewish object, chosen by a Greek-writing author — and from that single occurrence it entered the European languages. Tefillin itself is a different word with a different history: the Targumim and the Peshitta are the first texts to use it, and Jastrow connects it to a Syriac word for attachments or hangings.

The archaeology and the word meet: finds at Qumran and the reference in Matthew 23 together show that by the first century CE many Jews were wearing some physical form of the object.

The third stage is datable and recent. The term appears in the first-edition Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Monster Manual in 1977, where a lich holds its status by conjurations, enchantments and a phylactery, and the nature and function of that phylactery is not explained. By the second edition in 1989 the object explicitly stores the lich's life force. The third-edition Monster Manual, in 2000, describes it as resembling a Jewish tefillin, and notes it can also be a ring or an amulet.

That borrowing has been argued with. Eric Silver has criticised the gaming term for its Jewish religious origin and proposed talisman as the neutral word instead. Wizards of the Coast has not retired the term; Paizo Publishing stopped using it in 2021, and its liches now keep their souls in a soul cage.

*Inference —* the arc is one word carried three times by people who were not its owners: a Greek writer naming a Jewish practice, European translators keeping his choice, and a game designer reaching past both for a container that sounded old.
kin: tefillin — the object the Greek word was put on, and still the standard English rendering in Bible translation
kin: amulet-word — the cover-word phylactery is sometimes swapped for, wrongly and often
kin: jewish-practical-kabbalah — the tradition whose written amulets English also reaches for this word to describe
kin: kamea — the written Jewish amulet a careless writer will call a phylactery, though the tradition keeps them apart
kin: divine-name — what is actually inside the boxes: text, not a sign
kin: the-charm-goes-digital — where the third sense belongs — a charm that exists only inside a game's rules
sources: s:wp-tefillin s:wp-phylactery s:wp-amulet s:wp-lich-dungeons-and-dragons
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## talisman (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/talisman-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/talisman-word.json
id: talisman-word
native: طِلَسْم (Arabic)
aliases: ṭilsam · ṭalāsim · telesma
said: TAL-iz-man; Arabic ṭilsam
when: 1630 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB US FR EG TR IR
root: Greek teleō 'I complete, perform a rite' (from telos 'end, fulfilment') > Byzantine Greek telesma 'completion, religious rite, payment' > Arabic ṭilsam (طِلَسْم, plural ṭalāsim) > French talisman > English talisman
what: The word for a made object whose power the maker claims to have put in it. Where amulet turns harm away, talisman brings fortune in — that is the split most English writers use, and Wikipedia's talisman article states it as the key difference. Its amulet article, one click away, says the two have interchangeable meanings. Both are in print. The Arabic ṭilsam behind the English word carries something the English lost: a sense of manufacture under conditions, made at a particular hour for a particular end.
story: The root is a verb about finishing a rite. Greek teleō, 'I complete, perform a rite'; telesma, the completion or the payment. Arabic took it as ṭilsam, French took it from Arabic, English took it from French in the 1630s.

What the Arabic word names is a craft with a timetable. The tenth-century Abbasid mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra was held to be the expert; in one of his texts on talismans he wrote, 'The noblest part of astronomy is the science of talismans.' In John of Seville and Limia's twelfth-century version of ibn Qurra's De imaginibus, talismans and astronomy matter more to wisdom than geometry or philosophy do. Adelard of Bath's translation of the same text insists on knowledge of both astronomy and astrology, because a talisman has to be made at the moment of an auspicious celestial event — and because, in that text, a maker who is distracted or in doubt produces a powerless one.

The instructions are specific about material. Adelard's translation specifies lead, iron, bronze, gold or silver for a talisman meant to earn love from a king, a family member or a peer; pitch and tar, bitumen and aloes for one meant to set people against each other, take money, defend or destroy a place, or win a legal case.

*Inference —* the English word kept the object and dropped the clock. A modern English speaker who calls a lucky coin a talisman is using a word that once meant a thing timed to a sky.
kin: amulet-word — the word it is set against — fortune in, harm away — by writers who split them at all
kin: taweez-word — the Arabic word for the worn object, where this one is the Arabic word for the made figure
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition whose own vocabulary this word was lifted out of
kin: magical-gem — exactly the thing the 1630s English sense named: a figure cut in stone under stated observances
kin: talismanic-shirt — the largest object the word covers — a garment written all over and worn under armour
kin: yantra-word — the Sanskrit parallel: another word meaning an instrument built to do work, later meaning a drawn figure
kin: amulet-or-talisman — the long read on this pair of words and the museum labels that pick between them
sources: s:wp-talisman s:wp-amulet s:web-etymonline-talisman s:wp-islam-and-magic
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## taweez (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/taweez-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/taweez-word.json
id: taweez-word
native: تعويذ (Arabic)
aliases: ta'wiz · taʿwīdh · tawiz · तावीज़ · تعویز
said: ta-WEEZ; Arabic taʿwīdh
countries: PK IN BD TR EG SA
root: Arabic verb ʿawwadha 'to fortify someone with an amulet or incantation' > noun taʿwīdh (تعويذ) 'amulet, charm' > Urdu and Hindi ta'wiz (تعویز, तावीज़)
what: The word across the Muslim world for a worn written charm and, by extension, for the object it is folded into: a pendant, letters carved on metal, a framed prayer. What goes inside is text — Qur'anic verses, hadith, the ninety-nine names of God, the names of prophets and their companions, or a religious narrative. The word and the permission arrive together, which is the whole argument: Wikipedia's article reports that Sunni Muslims are permitted to wear ta'wiz as long as it consciously strengthens their bond with Allah and does not come from a belief the ta'wiz itself cures or protects.
story: The verb underneath the noun is the point. ʿawwadha is to fortify somebody with an amulet or an incantation — the grammar makes the wearer the object of the action and the text the instrument.

What gets written is specific and named. The word Allah is especially common; touching it or seeing it is held to turn evil away. The names of prophets and religious figures connect the wearer to the person named, and the favoured figures are Solomon, Ali ibn Abi Talib and his sons Hasan and Husain, and the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus. Written accounts of those lives are also used, sometimes illustrated.

The clearest dated use is military. Scrolls carrying Qur'anic quotations, prophetic references and sacred symbols were common in war in the Ottoman Empire, with verses such as 'victory is from God and conquest is near' (Qur. 61:13) found on ta'wiz worn in combat. Texts packaged in tawiz were most often pre-made when used by the public; a literate wearer could change the verse at their own discretion.

*Inference —* that last detail is the useful one. A charm whose text a literate wearer can swap is a charm whose owner is also its author, and it puts the taweez in a different class from an object a specialist alone may make. This atlas files it as written, not as consecrated.

*Tradition holds —* objects of this kind are also criticised from inside the religion, and the criticism is about where the power is located rather than about the paper. The permission Wikipedia records carries its own limit in the same sentence.
kin: taweez — the object the word names: the case and the folded text inside it
kin: quran-pendant — the same idea in metal and glass — scripture carried where it can be seen
kin: hirz-pouch — the pouch form of the same practice, sewn rather than cased
kin: islamic-talismanic — the tradition this word belongs to, and the one that argues about it
kin: gris-gris-word — the West African word for the same object, where the Mande marabout writes what the Arabic word names
kin: talisman-word — the other Arabic word English took — that one for the made figure, this one for the worn text
kin: divine-name — what is written inside more often than anything else
sources: s:wp-amulet s:wp-islam-and-magic s:wp-throne-verse
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## Vodou and Vodún — and the spelling this atlas does not use (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/vodou-not-voodoo/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/vodou-not-voodoo.json
id: vodou-not-voodoo
native: vodún (Latin)
aliases: Vodou · Vodún · Vodu · Vodoun · Voudoun · vaudou · vaudoux · Ginen
said: vo-DOO
when: 1658 CE to now (still carried)
countries: HT BJ TG GH NG US
root: Fon vodún, from the Gbe languages of the Niger-Congo family, translating as 'spirit', 'God', 'divinity' or 'presence' > Haitian Creole Vodou
RESTRICTED: Vodou's initiations are not written out here. There are four grades, and the details of the ceremonies are kept secret by the tradition; this record names the structure and stops there.
what: Two religions and one misspelling. Vodún is the religion of Aja, Ewe and Fon people in Benin, Togo, Ghana and Nigeria, with priesthoods, initiatory societies and the divination system Fá. Vodou is Haiti's: formed in the mid-eighteenth century out of Fon, Kongo and Yoruba traditions under colonial Saint-Domingue, with Roman Catholic and Masonic material absorbed into it, and carrying temples (ounfò), priests and priestesses (oungan and manbo), four grades of initiation, a liturgy of drum, song and dance, and a diaspora in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, France, Canada and the United States. Vodou is the spelling used by scholars, by official Haitian Creole orthography and by the United States Library of Congress. Some scholars prefer Vodoun, Voudoun or Vodun; French also carries vaudou and vaudoux. The two-o spelling, on Wikipedia's account, “is now generally avoided by practitioners and scholars when referring to the Haitian religion”.
story: The word is older than any of the arguments about it. The Fon Vôdoun is first recorded in 1658, in the Doctrina Christiana, and in the kingdom of Dahomey it meant a spirit or a deity. Ouidah was a major slave embarkation point from the 1670s to the 1860s, and Vodún practitioners were among those shipped; with Kongo religion, theirs became one of the two main influences on what formed in Haiti. Many Haitian terms, the word Vodou included, come out of Fon.

What happened to the spelling in English has a date and an address. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the occupation produced tourist shows and a literature — Faustin Wirkus and William Seabrook wrote the books that reached American readers. Seabrook's The Magic Island was published on 3 January 1929 by Harcourt, Brace & Company; it is described as the first popular English-language work to describe the concept of a zombie, which Seabrook defined as “a soulless human corpse, still dead, but taken from the grave and endowed by sorcery with a mechanical semblance of life”. Time said it “introduced 'zombi' into U.S. speech”. The book inspired the 1932 stage play Zombie and fed Victor Halperin's 1932 film White Zombie, with Bela Lugosi — the first feature-length zombie film, and the one that “originated several fictional tropes”, chiefly the zombie as a mindless henchman under an evil magician's spell. Jacques Tourneur's I Walked with a Zombie followed in 1943. The film “London Voodoo” of 2004 is named on the same list of works that sensationalise the religion.

The doll most people picture belongs to that literature and not to either religion. Wikipedia's article states it plainly: “The voodoo doll is not prominent in either” Haitian Vodou or “Louisiana Voodoo”.

Who objects is on record. Scholars describe Vodou as one of the world's most maligned and misunderstood religions; Christians in Haiti have presented it as Satanic, and in Anglophone and Francophone writing generally it has been tied to sorcery and black magic, attitudes “sometimes linked with anti-black racism”. In U.S. popular culture Haitian Vodou is usually portrayed as destructive and malevolent, and the absence of any central Vodou authority has made those representations hard to answer. Practitioners answered anyway: after attacks on Vodouists following the overthrow of Jean-Claude Duvalier in 1986, they formed the civil rights groups Zantray and Bode Nasyonal. Haiti's 1987 constitution guaranteed freedom of religion, and President Jean-Bertrand Aristide granted Vodou official recognition in 2003. Hostility did not stop: Protestants blamed Vodou in part for the 2010 earthquake, and mobs attacked Vodouists afterwards.

So this atlas's word list bans the two-o spelling outside quotations and proper nouns, and the validator fails any record that uses it loose. The reason is not squeamishness about an old spelling. That spelling reached English through an occupation and an entertainment industry, and what it names in English is a thing those industries built — a zombie, a pin-stuck doll, a film villain. Calling a religion with clergy, liturgy, a constitution's protection and six million estimated practitioners by the name of its own caricature is the error the rule exists to stop. The exceptions are real and stay: “Louisiana Voodoo” is the proper name of a distinct tradition, and a quotation keeps its speaker's words.
kin: gris-gris — the object carried into Haiti and Louisiana under a Mande name, and kept in Haitian practice with its West African sense intact
kin: gris-gris-word — the word whose charge changed on the American shore, in the same crossing that changed this one
kin: juju-word — the neighbouring outsiders' word for West African practice, contested on its etymology rather than its spelling
kin: fetish-word — the older European coinage aimed at the same coast, and the one that hardened into a theory of religion
kin: nkisi — the Kongo side of what formed in Haiti, and another object renamed by the people describing it
kin: west-african-charm-craft — the practice the Fon word comes out of, before any of this reached print in English
kin: what-this-atlas-does-not-print — the statement of what is withheld here, including the initiations this record names and does not describe
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read on naming: who gets to spell somebody else's religion, and what the spelling then carries
sources: s:wp-haitian-vodou s:wp-west-african-vod-n s:wp-voodoo s:wp-the-magic-island s:wp-voodoo-in-popular-culture s:wp-gris-gris-talisman
tier: cited · confidence: high · updated: 2026-09-16

## ward (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/ward-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/ward-word.json
id: ward-word
aliases: ward off · weard · weardian
said: ward
when: 700 CE to now (still carried)
countries: GB IE US CA AU NZ FR
root: Proto-Germanic *wardōną 'to guard' > Old English weardian 'to watch, guard, keep, protect' (noun weard 'watching, ward, protection, guardianship') > Middle English warden > English ward; English guard is the same word returned through Old French
what: The English verb for what the carriers of every object in this atlas say it does. Ward off: fend off, repel, turn aside. It is the plainest word available for the job, it is older in English than amulet or talisman, and it has no scholarly air at all — which is why the adjective apotropaic, whose Greek verb means exactly this, is the one that ended up on museum labels.
story: Old English weardian is to watch, to guard, to keep, to protect; the noun weard is the watching itself. The Norman conquest sent the same Germanic root back across the Channel and returned it as guard, so English carries the word twice, once early and Germanic and once late and French, and uses the two for different registers.

The noun went somewhere the verb did not. In law a ward is not the thing that protects but the person protected: a minor or an incapacitated adult placed under a guardian or a court. That sense runs out of feudal wardship, where custody of a minor heir's lands, of the heir, and of the heir's choice of marriage partner were rights that got sold to the highest bidder or granted as a favour. Henry VIII sponsored the Statute of Uses in 1535 to protect his income from wardship and established the Court of Wards and Liveries in 1540. The court lost its function in 1646 with the abolition of feudal tenure in England and Wales, and was abolished in 1660.

The word then travelled with the common law. In Australia, New Zealand and the United States a child is a ward of the court; in Ireland and the United Kingdom, a ward of court with no article; in Canada, a permanent ward, except in Ontario, which says Crown ward. In France a pupille de l'État is a minor under the responsibility of the state.

*Inference —* one root, two ends that face each other. The horseshoe over a door wards. The child inside the house is a ward. English has kept both without ever needing to notice.
kin: apotropaic-word — the Greek adjective whose verb means precisely this, and the one the academy uses instead
kin: horseshoe — the object an English speaker is likeliest to use the verb about — nailed up, it wards
kin: hanging-at-door — the practice the verb is nearly always attached to in English writing
kin: european-folk-apotropaic — the tradition that thinks in this word rather than in the Greek one
kin: amulet-word — the noun for the thing that does the warding, arriving in English a thousand years later
kin: concealed-shoe — a warding practice found in walls and under floors, named in English long before anyone called it apotropaic
sources: s:web-wiktionary-ward s:wp-ward-law s:wp-apotropaic-magic
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## yantra (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/word/yantra-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/term/yantra-word.json
id: yantra-word
native: यन्त्र (Devanagari)
aliases: yantrá · yant · ยันต์ · y័ន្ត
said: YAN-tra; Thai yant
when: 1000 BCE to now (still carried)
countries: IN NP LK TH KH LA
root: Sanskrit root yam 'to sustain, support' + the instrumental suffix -tra > yantra (यन्त्र), 'instrument, machine, contraption'
what: A machine. That is the word's plain sense and it has never gone away: yantra is an instrument, a thing built to hold and to do work. The diagram sense — concentric triangles, circles, hexagons, lotus petals and an outer square with doors at the four directions, radiating from a central point called the bindu — is a later specialisation of the same idea. A yantra that has not been energised with its mantra is held by practitioners to be lifeless, which is consistent with the root: an instrument that is not driving anything is not doing its job.
story: The word travelled east and kept its shape. Sak yant, the tattooing practice of Cambodia, Thailand and Laos, splits into sak — a native Khmer word meaning to tattoo, from a Proto-Mon-Khmer root meaning to prick, which Chuon Nath's 1967 dictionary establishes is not a Sanskrit or Pali loan — and yant, the Sanskrit yantra arriving with Indian designs. One indigenous word, one borrowed one, welded into the name of a practice.

Gudrun Bühnemann sorts the diagrams into three kinds by use: those that a ritual implement such as a lamp or a vessel stands on; those used in regular worship, like the Sri Yantra of the goddess Tripura Sundari; and those made for a specific desire-driven rite, often on birch bark or paper, sometimes with flowers, rice paste or ashes worked in.

The dating of the form is where this record has to go carefully. Wikipedia's article says representations of the yantra in India 'have been considered to date back to 11,000–10,000 BCE', and in the next sentence reports that the Baghor stone, found in an Upper Palaeolithic context in the Son River Valley, was dated by G. R. Sharma, who excavated it, to 25,000–20,000 BCE, and that Kenoyer, also on the excavation, associated it with Shakti. Those two ranges do not agree with each other, and neither is a date for the word. *Inference —* what can be said is that a triangular engraved stone was excavated and read by its excavators as related to goddess worship; reading it as a yantra is an interpretation laid over an object by people who already had the word.

*Tradition holds —* the diagrams are consecrated and energised by a priest, using mantras tied to the particular deity, and in Sri Lankan Buddhism a practitioner is required to hold the yantra of the deity once that deity has shown acceptance of their prayer.
kin: yantra-plate — the object the word names in South Asia: the diagram drawn or engraved and then energised
kin: sak-yant — the word carried into Khmer, Thai and Lao as yant, welded to a native word for tattooing
kin: hindu-kavacha — the tradition the diagram belongs to at home
kin: thai-wicha — the tradition it belongs to at the other end of the journey
kin: magic-square — the numbered cousin — another figure whose power is claimed to sit in its arrangement
kin: inscribing — the practice the word requires: a yantra is drawn before it is anything
kin: talisman-word — the Arabic-derived English word for the same idea, an object made under conditions to do work
sources: s:wp-yantra s:wp-yantra-tattooing s:wp-kavacha
tier: cited · confidence: medium · updated: 2026-09-16

## Budge's amulet plates (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/art/budge-plates/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/art/budge-plates.json
id: budge-plates
aliases: Amulets and Superstitions (1930), plates · Budge 1930 plates
countries: EG IQ GB
what: Twenty-two plates and three hundred in-text illustrations bound into a 543-page book: E. A. Wallis Budge's "Amulets and superstitions", published in London and New York by Oxford University Press and H. Milford in 1930. The Wellcome Collection's catalogue record gives the collation as xxxix, 543 pages with illustrations, plates and facsimiles, 25 cm tall. A single plate will set an Egyptian scarab beside a Babylonian cylinder, a Hebrew amulet and a Gnostic gem, drawn or photographed to no common scale.
story: The subtitle is the argument. Budge's runs to a paragraph — Egyptian, Sumerian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Christian, Gnostic and Muslim amulets and talismans and magical figures, with chapters on the evil eye, the origin of the amulet, the pentagon, the swastika, the cross, the properties of stones, rings, divination, numbers, the Kabbâlâh and ancient astrology. Nobody had put that list on one shelf before, and the plates are the list made visible: this atlas's own habit of setting a Cairo object beside a Naples one descends directly from pages laid out like these.

The books have a reputation and it is not a good one. The Egyptologist James Peter Allen writes that Budge's books "were not too reliable when they first appeared and are now woefully outdated". The archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called Budge "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities": as the British Museum's buyer he smuggled cuneiform tablets out of Iraq by bribery, and gave his own account of one such trip in By Nile and Tigris.

*Inference —* the plates and the text fail differently, and the difference matters to a reader. A plate records what an object looked like in 1930, which is checkable. The caption records what Budge thought it meant, which is often not. So this atlas cites these pictures for shape and cites almost nothing here for meaning.
today: The Wellcome Collection's record for the 1930 edition carries the rights statement "In copyright. It is possible this item is protected by copyright and/or related rights." So the plates are not reproduced here, and no candidate image file is listed below. Later reprints of Budge circulate widely and have kept his readings in print long after Egyptology dropped them.
kin: wallis-budge — the keeper who assembled these plates, and the buyer whose acquisition methods are part of the record
kin: petrie-amulet-plates — the other amulet picture-book of the period — dug up and sorted, where Budge's was bought and compared
kin: british-museum — the collection Budge built and photographed from, and the one most of these objects still sit in
kin: incantation-bowl — one of the Mesopotamian classes these plates put in front of a European reader for the first time
kin: magical-gem — the Gnostic and Graeco-Egyptian stones that fill several of the plates
kin: who-owns-a-charm — the long read that starts from how objects like these reached London
kin: free-to-use — why these plates are named here and not shown here: the catalogue record says in copyright
sources: s:web-budge-amulets-1930 s:wp-e-a-wallis-budge s:wp-british-museum s:wp-amulet

## Petrie's amulet plates (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/art/petrie-amulet-plates/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/art/petrie-amulet-plates.json
id: petrie-amulet-plates
aliases: Amulets (1914), plates · Petrie 1914 plates · the UCL amulet plates
countries: EG GB
what: Plates of small Egyptian amulets, photographed in rows against a plain ground, printed at the back of a slim book: W. M. Flinders Petrie's "Amulets: illustrated by the Egyptian collection in University College, London", published by Constable in London in 1914. Objects sit side by side at a common scale with a class number under each, so a reader can lay a tray beside the page and match shape to shape. The Internet Archive's copy carries the rights note "no visible notice of copyright; stated date is 1914" and the status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
story: The plates are a sorting machine. Petrie arranged the amulets by what they are — head, limb, animal, sign, tool — rather than by reign or by site, and gave each class a number that ran across the whole collection. That arrangement is why a museum drawer in 2026 still holds wedjat eyes together and scarabs together instead of holding Eleventh Dynasty together.

Petrie had already written the reason down. "I believe the true line of research lies in the noting and comparison of the smallest details," he wrote of his method, and an amulet is nothing but smallest details — a mould flaw, a drill angle, a glaze that fired green instead of blue.

The pictures also carry the man. Petrie held the first chair of Egyptology in the United Kingdom and has been called the father of Egyptian archaeology; he has also been denounced for his pro-eugenics views, and believed in the superiority of northern over southern peoples. Alice Stevenson's UCL Press volume on the museum, and the 2014 book Archaeology of Race, put that record beside the excavations rather than after them. *Inference —* this atlas takes the plates as a finding aid and not as an authority on who made what, for the plain reason that the typology outlived the racial theory bolted to it.
today: Public domain, free to reproduce, and scanned at a resolution good enough to zoom. The collection they picture went to University College in 1913 and is now the Petrie Museum of Egyptian and Sudanese Archaeology at Malet Place in London — over 80,000 objects, entirely digitised, catalogue online, admission free.
kin: flinders-petrie — the excavator who made these plates, and whose sorting is still the shape of a museum amulet drawer
kin: budge-plates — the other great amulet picture-book of the period, made from purchases rather than from digs
kin: wedjat-eye — the class that fills the most rows on these plates, because Egypt made more of it than of anything else
kin: scarab — the other class that runs to page after page here
kin: egyptian-amulet-craft — the tradition these plates put in order
kin: faience — the material most of the objects in these rows are made of
kin: the-drawn-signs — the atlas's own answer to the same problem — one picture for a class, not a portrait of one object
kin: free-to-use — why these plates can appear here at all: no visible copyright notice, 1914
sources: s:web-petrie-amulets-1914 s:wp-flinders-petrie s:wp-petrie-museum-of-egyptian-archaeology s:wp-amulet

## The drawn signs (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/art/the-drawn-signs/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/amulet-atlas/api/art/the-drawn-signs.json
id: the-drawn-signs
aliases: the glyphs · the atlas glyphs · viz.py glyphs
what: Twenty-six line drawings, one per sign in this atlas: an eye, a hand, an open palm, a horn, a knot, a serpent, a scarab, a fish, a tooth and claw, a crescent, a cross, a coin with a square hole, a mirror, a red thread, a swastika, a magic square, a palindrome block, a divine name, a footprint, a key, a bell, a spiral, a tree, a lion, a phallic sign and a fist. Each is drawn inside a 48-by-48 box, in a single stroke weight of 2.1 with round caps and joins, in whatever colour the surrounding text is. They are SVG written into the page rather than images fetched into it.
story: They are drawn for this project. The file that holds them says so in its own header: the glyphs are drawn from published descriptions of the signs, not traced from any one object, and they go out under the project's own licence, which is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.

*Inference —* that sentence carries the whole argument. A photograph of a wedjat eye is a photograph of one wedjat eye, from one dynasty, in one material, in one museum's lighting. The sign is the class. When the atlas needs to say "this amulet carries the eye", a drawing of the class says it and a photograph of a specimen quietly says something narrower and slightly wrong. So the photographs go on the amulet records, where a specific object is the point, and the drawings go on the sign records, where it is not.

There is a second reason and it is not aesthetic. An SVG that is text in the page is an SVG a reader can select, a screen reader can walk and a slow connection still gets — the same file states that too. A drawn sign costs a few hundred bytes. A photograph costs a hundred times that and still needs a licence, an author, a page URL and a hash beside it.

One of the twenty-six is the swastika, and the atlas draws it for the same reason it draws the others: it is one of the oldest and most widespread signs in this material, and a global index of signs that skipped it would be lying by omission. The record that explains what the drawing does and does not mean is /story/the-swastika-problem, and the glyph links to it.
today: Reusable. Under CC BY 4.0 anyone may copy, modify and republish them, commercially included, with credit to this project. The same file also draws the world maps — Equal Earth, from Natural Earth outlines — and the timeline axis, so the signs and the maps share one visual grammar and one colour set, built around the blue-green of faience.
kin: eye — the first glyph in the set, and the one the whole drawing style was settled on
kin: hand — drawn twice here — as a hamsa-style hand and as an open palm, because the two are used differently
kin: horn — drawn as the twisted cornicello and not as a curled sheep's horn, on the published description
kin: swastika-sign — the glyph that needs a page of explanation beside it, and has one
kin: the-swastika-problem — the long read that sits behind one of these twenty-six drawings
kin: free-to-use — the licence record: what you may do with these drawings, in full
kin: petrie-amulet-plates — the 1914 ancestor of the same idea — a picture made to show a class rather than a specimen
